events.what: Movable-type press; Gutenberg Bible c.1455.
events.why: Paper had been cheap since the 1300s. Towns held a paying market of merchants, lawyers, clergy and students. Goldsmiths knew how to cast metal to fine tolerances. Gutenberg assembled parts that already existed.
events.sig: Identical copies let readers compare and correct one another's texts. Pamphlets reached readers faster than any bishop could answer them, which is how Martin Luther's case spread in 1517. Rulers and the Church replied with licensing and the Index of Forbidden Books of 1559.
events.hook: Movable metal type made books cheap and turned ideas into something no one could contain.
events.story: Europe in 1440 copied books by hand at a few pages a day. Mainz goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg combined cast metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press adapted from the wine trade. His Bible came off the press around 1455. By 1500 presses ran in more than 250 towns and had printed some twenty million books.
events.then: Identical copies let readers compare and correct one another's texts. Pamphlets reached readers faster than any bishop could answer them, which is how Martin Luther's case spread in 1517. Rulers and the Church replied with licensing and the Index of Forbidden Books of 1559.
events.now: Print broke the clergy's monopoly on knowledge and gave rulers a new problem, a public that read. Every state answer since, from the licensing of presses to the regulation of social media, descends from the censorship laws of the 1520s.
events.fact: About 180 Gutenberg Bibles were printed; around 49 survive.

q.problem: Books were copied by hand, so they were rare and expensive.
q.how: Movable metal type cast in a hand mould, oil-based ink, and a screw press.
q.replaced: Hand-copied manuscripts and woodblock printing.
q.spread: By 1500 presses were running in over 250 European towns.
q.next: The Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and mass literacy.

events.bluf: Mainz goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg set out to make a profit copying texts by machine. He got a working press and lost it to his creditor; the method spread to 250 towns within fifty years. Cheap, identical copies took control of information away from Church and crown, and the Reformation, the scientific journal and the standard national language all ran on it.
events.lens: Ask who controls the means of spreading information. When it becomes cheap or changes hands, established authorities usually lose control of the story first and reassert it later.

kv: pages a day from one press; a copyist managed a few
European towns with a press by 1500

events.who: Portuguese captains under Prince Henry the Navigator
events.what: First Africans captured and shipped to Portugal.
events.why: Portugal was a small, poor kingdom seeking gold and a sea route round Muslim-controlled trade. Slavery already existed in Africa, the Mediterranean and the Islamic world, so Portuguese captains could tap existing markets. Within a few years they were buying captives from African rulers instead of raiding.
events.sig: Portugal shipped enslaved Africans to the sugar islands of Madeira and São Tomé, where the plantation model of one export crop worked by enslaved labour took shape; Brazil and the Caribbean copied it. Demand for captives fed wars between African states, which sold prisoners for guns, cloth and metal.
events.hook: Portuguese sailors seized Africans off the Saharan coast, beginning a trade that would move 12.5 million people.
events.story: Portugal's ships had been working down the West African coast for a decade in search of gold. In 1441 an expedition sent by Portuguese Prince Henry the Navigator seized Africans on the coast of today's Mauritania and sold them in Portugal. A public sale of captives followed at Lagos in Portugal in 1444. Within decades Portugal was buying captives from African states along the coast.
events.then: Portugal shipped enslaved Africans to the sugar islands of Madeira and São Tomé, where the plantation model of one export crop worked by enslaved labour took shape; Brazil and the Caribbean copied it. Demand for captives fed wars between African states, which sold prisoners for guns, cloth and metal.
events.now: The trade shaped the population of the Americas (Brazil has the largest population of African descent outside Africa), created the racial hierarchies slavery required, and underlies today's debates over reparations and Africa's long-run development.

q.what: Enslaved Africans, along with gold and ivory.
q.who: Portuguese traders and the crown profited; captives and their communities paid.
q.scale: Small at first; over four centuries about 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic.
q.daily: Raids and trade made capture a constant danger along the coast.
q.system: The Atlantic slave trade that fed the plantations of the Americas.

events.bluf: Portuguese Prince Henry the Navigator sent captains down the West African coast for gold and a sea route round Muslim-held trade. In 1441 they seized captives on the coast of today's Mauritania, and within a few years Portugal was buying them from African rulers. The Atlantic slave trade that began there moved about 12.5 million Africans over four centuries, built the plantation economies of the Americas, enriched European merchants and states and drained much of Atlantic Africa.
events.trig: An expedition sent by Prince Henry seized Africans on the coast of today's Mauritania in 1441.
events.lens: Forced-labor systems grow around a profitable commodity. Follow the crop or the mineral and you will find who was coerced to produce it, and who profited.
events.fact: Royal chronicler Gomes Eanes de Zurara recorded the Lagos sale of 1444, 235 captives divided on the quayside, and wrote that the parting of families moved the crowd to tears.

kv: carried by Portuguese and Brazilian ships
figs.n: Estimates from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (SlaveVoyages).

events.what: A simple phonetic alphabet was created (published 1446).
events.why: Korean King Sejong wrote that ordinary people could not express their thoughts in writing because Chinese characters were too hard to learn. A script that fitted Korean speech could spread literacy beyond the aristocracy.
events.sig: Confucian officials, whose status rested on mastering Chinese, opposed the script, and it survived among women and commoners and in popular fiction and verse. It became the official script in 1894. Japanese colonial rule from 1910 to 1945 suppressed Korean, which turned Hangul into a symbol of national resistance.
events.hook: A Korean king invented an alphabet so simple that ordinary people could learn it in days.
events.story: Korea's written language was classical Chinese, which took years to master and matched spoken Korean poorly. Korean King Sejong and a group of court officials designed Hangul, completed in 1443 and proclaimed in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum, 'the correct sounds for instructing the people'. Its letter shapes follow the position of the mouth and tongue in forming each sound.
events.then: Confucian officials, whose status rested on mastering Chinese, opposed the script, and it survived among women and commoners and in popular fiction and verse. It became the official script in 1894. Japanese colonial rule from 1910 to 1945 suppressed Korean, which turned Hangul into a symbol of national resistance.
events.now: A script learnable in days broke the official class's monopoly on writing and gave Korea a literate public and a national identity separate from China; both Koreas write in it today.
events.fact: Both Koreas keep a national holiday for the alphabet, the only script in the world with one.

q.what: An alphabet for writing Korean, now 24 letters.
q.new: Letter shapes based on the mouth and tongue positions that make each sound.
q.audience: Commoners and women at first; scholars kept writing in Chinese.
q.reveals: A ruler's belief that reading should not belong only to the elite.
q.today: South Korea celebrates Hangul Day every October 9.

events.bluf: Korean King Sejong wanted a script that ordinary Koreans could learn, since classical Chinese took years to master and fitted spoken Korean badly. His commission produced Hangul, completed in 1443 and proclaimed in 1446, with letters shaped on the positions of the mouth and tongue. The Confucian official class, whose standing rested on Chinese, kept it out of government for 450 years; it became the script of Korean national identity and near-universal literacy.
events.lens: Scripts and languages are political: who can read, and in which language, decides who can take part in power.

kv: letters as created; 24 are used today
year it was published to the people

events.what: Mongols destroyed a Ming army and captured the emperor.
events.why: Steppe peoples wanted regular access to Chinese markets, and raids followed when the Ming restricted the tribute trade. At court, eunuch Wang Zhen pushed the inexperienced emperor to lead the army himself.
events.sig: The court enthroned the emperor's brother as the Jingtai Emperor, and Ming minister Yu Qian organised the defence of Beijing. The Oirats released their prisoner in 1450, and he retook the throne in a palace coup in 1457. The Ming gave up campaigns into Mongolia and in the 1500s rebuilt the Great Wall in brick and stone.
events.hook: Mongols captured the Ming emperor, and China turned inward behind the Great Wall.
events.story: The Ming had restricted the Oirat tribute trade, and Oirat leader Esen raided the frontier in 1449. The young Ming Zhengtong Emperor, urged on by court eunuch Wang Zhen, led a large and poorly supplied army north in person. At Tumu, north-west of Beijing, the Mongols surrounded the exhausted army, killed much of it and captured the emperor.
events.then: The court enthroned the emperor's brother as the Jingtai Emperor, and Ming minister Yu Qian organised the defence of Beijing. The Oirats released their prisoner in 1450, and he retook the throne in a palace coup in 1457. The Ming gave up campaigns into Mongolia and in the 1500s rebuilt the Great Wall in brick and stone.
events.now: The defeat turned the Ming from steppe campaigns to walls: most of the Great Wall standing today was built in brick and stone after Tumu, and the defensive posture it marks held until the dynasty fell in 1644.

q.why: The Oirats raided the frontier after trade disputes, and the court set out to punish them.
q.stakes: The security of Beijing and the dynasty's prestige.
q.decided: Poor leadership, supply failures and a Mongol ambush at a waterless camp.
q.cost: Much of the army and many senior officials killed, and the emperor taken prisoner.
q.changed: The Ming turned defensive and rebuilt the Great Wall.

events.bluf: The Ming Zhengtong Emperor marched in person against the Oirat Mongols in 1449 to punish a raid and show the dynasty's strength on the steppe. The Oirats destroyed his army at Tumu and took him prisoner. Ming confidence in offensive war on the steppe ended; China turned to a defensive strategy of walls and fortified garrisons that fixed its northern frontier for two centuries.
events.trig: An Oirat invasion in 1449, after a quarrel over the size of their tribute-trade missions.
events.lens: Major defeats often change a state's strategy more than victories do. Look for the trauma behind a country's defensive habits.
events.fact: Most of the Great Wall seen today is Ming work, built in the century after Tumu.

kv: Ming soldiers, by the traditional count
figs.n: Modern historians think the Ming army was smaller than the traditional figure, but still several times the Oirat force.

events.who: Sultan Mehmed II; last Byzantine emperor Constantine XI
events.what: Ottomans broke the walls with giant cannons.
events.why: The Fourth Crusade's sack of 1204 had left Byzantium a shell. A century of Ottoman conquest in Anatolia and the Balkans had surrounded it. The city sat astride the straits between the empire's two halves.
events.sig: The sultans claimed the Roman inheritance and pushed into the Balkans, the Arab lands and the Mediterranean. The Orthodox patriarchate survived under Ottoman protection. Moscow later called itself the Third Rome.
events.hook: After 1,100 years, the last piece of the Roman Empire fell to Ottoman cannons.
events.story: By 1453 the Byzantine Empire was the city and little else. Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II, aged 21, besieged it in April with about 80,000 men and bombards that broke the land walls. Byzantine Emperor Constantine XI died in the final assault on 29 May. The city became the Ottoman capital.
events.then: The sultans claimed the Roman inheritance and pushed into the Balkans, the Arab lands and the Mediterranean. The Orthodox patriarchate survived under Ottoman protection. Moscow later called itself the Third Rome.
events.now: The Ottomans ruled the Balkans and the Arab lands from the city for four centuries. Turkey still holds the straits between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, the lever in every Russian crisis from 1853 to 2022.
events.fact: Mehmed had his galleys dragged overland on greased logs into the Golden Horn to get past the harbour chain.

sites.d: 1,000-year-old land walls, breached by Orban's cannon near the St. Romanus Gate.
Harbor sealed with a chain; Mehmed dragged ~70 ships overland around it.
Greatest church in Christendom; turned into a mosque the day the city fell.

q.why: Mehmed II wanted the ancient capital to complete Ottoman control of the region.
q.stakes: The last remnant of the Roman Empire, and the straits between Europe and Asia.
q.decided: Huge cannon, ships hauled overland into the Golden Horn, and overwhelming numbers.
q.cost: Thousands of defenders killed; the city was sacked and many inhabitants enslaved.
q.changed: The Byzantine Empire ended, and Istanbul became the Ottoman capital.

events.bluf: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II wanted the city that split his European and Asian lands and the straits it commanded. He took it in 53 days with the largest guns yet cast, ending the Roman state after eleven centuries. The Ottomans gained the capital of a three-continent empire, and every fortress in Europe became obsolete.
events.trig: Mehmed built the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the Bosporus in 1452 to cut the city off by sea.
events.lens: Watch the chokepoints: whoever holds a strait or a crossing between regions gains leverage far beyond their size.
events.myth: The fall closed the spice routes and forced Europeans to sail round Africa. Portugal was already working down the African coast, and the Ottomans taxed the eastern trade rather than stopping it.

kv: since the land walls were built

toll.n: From contemporary accounts. Ottoman losses during the siege are not reliably known.

events.who: Kings of England and France; Joan of Arc (1429-31)
events.what: England lost all French lands but Calais.
events.why: Disputed lordship over Gascony came first. The claim to the crown through Edward III's mother gave it a dynastic form. The Flemish wool trade and France's alliance with Scotland kept both sides in.
events.sig: The French crown kept the taille, a tax raised without an assembly, and the ordinance companies, a standing army. England lost all but Calais, fell into the Wars of the Roses within two years and later turned to naval power.
events.hook: England's long fight for the French throne ended with England losing nearly everything in France.
events.story: English kings had held French lands as vassals since 1066. English King Edward III claimed the French crown in 1337, and the war ran on and off for 116 years. Joan of Arc broke the siege of Orléans in 1429. French cannon won the last battle at Castillon in 1453.
events.then: The French crown kept the taille, a tax raised without an assembly, and the ordinance companies, a standing army. England lost all but Calais, fell into the Wars of the Roses within two years and later turned to naval power.
events.now: The war gave France a permanent army and a permanent tax, and England a parliament that had learned to bargain over war money. Both kingdoms came out with a national identity defined against the other.
events.fact: Castillon was among the first battles decided mainly by field artillery.

sites.d: Joan of Arc lifted the siege, turning the war.
Final battle; French artillery crushed the English.
England's last foothold in France, until 1558.

q.why: English kings claimed the French throne and large French lands.
q.decided: Joan of Arc's revival of French morale, then French artillery.
q.cost: Generations of war and a devastated French countryside.
q.changed: England lost nearly all its French lands, and both kingdoms grew more national.

events.bluf: English kings fought for 116 years to hold or take the French crown. French King Charles VII drove them out with a standing army and field artillery, leaving England only Calais. France gained a king who could tax and raise troops without consent, the base of absolutism; England turned inward to civil war and later to the sea.
events.trig: French victories at Formigny in 1450 and Castillon in 1453 drove the English out of Normandy and Gascony.
events.lens: Long wars build states: armies and taxes created to fight them rarely disappear when the fighting stops.

kv: England's last foothold in France, lost in 1558

toll.n: Castillon ended the war. French cannon tore apart the English attack.

events.who: House of Lancaster vs. House of York
events.what: 30 years of civil war for the throne.
events.why: Defeat in France discredited the king's government and brought home nobles with armed retinues. A king who could not govern left rival magnates to fight for control of the court.
events.sig: Many noble lines died out or lost their lands. After 1485 Henry VII banned private armies, rebuilt the royal finances and ruled through councils of professional officials.
events.hook: Two branches of England's royal family fought for 30 years over the crown.
events.story: English King Henry VI lost his mind in 1453 and his grip on the nobility with it. Richard, Duke of York, claimed the right to govern. The first battle at St Albans in May 1455 opened thirty years of intermittent civil war between the houses of Lancaster and York.
events.then: Many noble lines died out or lost their lands. After 1485 Henry VII banned private armies, rebuilt the royal finances and ruled through councils of professional officials.
events.now: The wars destroyed the private armies of the magnates. The Tudor state that replaced them governed through royal officials and Parliament, the structure that carried England through the Reformation.

causes.why: Defeat in France discredited Henry VI's government, and rival noble factions, with soldiers home from France, turned on each other.

q.why: Rival claims to the throne and power struggles under a weak king.
q.decided: Battles and betrayals; Henry Tudor finally won at Bosworth in 1485.
q.cost: Many noble families were wiped out, and three kings died violently.
q.changed: The Tudor dynasty took power and strengthened the monarchy.

events.bluf: Two branches of the English royal family fought for the crown for thirty years. The fighting killed off much of the old nobility and ended with a Tudor on the throne. The winner, English King Henry VII, built a monarchy strong enough to break with Rome fifty years later.
events.trig: Richard, Duke of York, took up arms against the king's favourites at St Albans in May 1455.
events.lens: Losing a foreign war often brings a reckoning at home: discredited rulers and returning armed men are a recipe for civil conflict.
events.fact: The red and white roses were adopted as symbols long after; Shakespeare's history plays fixed the wars in popular memory.

kv: kings who died by violence: Henry VI, Edward V, Richard III

events.who: Johannes Gutenberg; his backer Johann Fust and assistant Peter Schöffer
events.hook: The first major book printed in Europe with movable metal type came off Gutenberg's presses in Mainz.
events.what: The first major book printed in Europe with movable metal type came off Gutenberg's presses in Mainz.
events.story: About 180 copies of the Latin Bible were finished in Mainz by 1455, a few on vellum, most on paper. Each page carried 42 lines in two columns, with initials added by hand. A future pope who saw sample pages in 1454 wrote that they could be read without spectacles.
events.why: Gutenberg had borrowed heavily from the Mainz financier Johann Fust. A Bible was the one book every religious house wanted and would pay for.
events.then: Fust sued in 1455 and took over much of the press with Gutenberg's assistant Peter Schöffer. Trained printers carried the method to other cities; by 1500 presses ran in more than 250 towns.
events.sig: Fust sued in 1455 and took over much of the press with Gutenberg's assistant Peter Schöffer. Trained printers carried the method to other cities; by 1500 presses ran in more than 250 towns.
events.now: The Bible showed that print could serve the Church as well as undermine it. Within seventy years the same technology carried Luther's attack on the Church that had bought the first copies.

causes.why: The Bible was the first big job for Gutenberg's new press, financed by loans he could not repay.

q.what: A two-volume Latin Bible of about 1,280 pages.
q.new: Hundreds of identical pages from reusable metal type, instead of one copy at a time by hand.
q.audience: Churches, monasteries and universities that could afford an expensive book.
q.reveals: Printing began as a business that imitated manuscripts, not a break with them.
q.today: Copies are held by the Library of Congress, the British Library and others.

events.bluf: Johannes Gutenberg needed a prestige product to repay his loans, and a Latin Bible had a guaranteed market in churches and monasteries. The book matched the finest manuscripts and proved printing could pay. Investors across Europe backed presses on that proof, and printing spread within a generation.
events.lens: New technologies spread once they first match the old standard in quality and then beat it on cost.
events.fact: Around 49 copies survive, the most valuable printed books in the world.

kv: lines per page, which gave it the name B42

events.who: Sultan Mehmed II; Emperor David of Trebizond
events.where: Trabzon, on Turkey's Black Sea coast
events.hook: The last Byzantine Greek state fell to Mehmed II, eight years after Constantinople.
events.what: The last Byzantine Greek state fell to Mehmed II, eight years after Constantinople.
events.story: The Empire of Trebizond, a Greek state on the Black Sea ruled by the Komnenos family since 1204, had sought an alliance against the Ottomans with Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan. Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II besieged the city by land and sea. Trebizond Emperor David Komnenos surrendered in August 1461. He was taken to Constantinople and executed with his sons in 1463.
events.why: Mehmed wanted every rival claimant to the Roman inheritance gone and the Black Sea trade in Ottoman hands. Trebizond's approach to Uzun Hasan made it a threat as well as a prize.
events.then: The Crimean Khanate became an Ottoman vassal in 1475 and the Black Sea an Ottoman lake. Greek Orthodox communities remained on the Pontic coast until the expulsions and the population exchange of the 1920s.
events.sig: The Crimean Khanate became an Ottoman vassal in 1475 and the Black Sea an Ottoman lake. Greek Orthodox communities remained on the Pontic coast until the expulsions and the population exchange of the 1920s.
events.now: Trebizond's fall gave the Ottomans the whole southern shore of the Black Sea and ended the last Greek claim to the Roman inheritance. The Pontic Greek communities that stayed under Ottoman rule were uprooted in the exchanges of the 1920s.

causes.why: Having taken Constantinople, Mehmed II went after the last Greek state that could claim the Byzantine throne.

q.before: The Grand Komnenos dynasty, which had ruled Trebizond since 1204.
q.how: Siege and negotiated surrender to the Ottoman sultan.
q.claim: Mehmed claimed the Roman (Byzantine) inheritance as conqueror of Constantinople.
q.winners: The Ottomans; the Komnenos family was wiped out two years later.
q.lasted: Yes: the city stayed under Ottoman and then Turkish rule.

events.bluf: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II set out to remove the last Greek state that could claim the Roman inheritance and to close the southern Black Sea to rivals. Trebizond surrendered after a siege in August 1461, and its emperor was executed two years later. The Byzantine world was fully absorbed, and the Black Sea became an Ottoman sea within two decades.
events.lens: Empires consolidate by eliminating rival claimants to legitimacy, not just rival armies.
events.fact: Trebizond outlived Constantinople by eight years, the last Byzantine successor state to fall.

events.h: Sonni Ali builds the Songhai Empire
events.what: Conquered Timbuktu and Djenné.
events.why: Mali was weakened by succession disputes and by attacks from the Tuareg and the Mossi. Whoever held the Niger bend controlled the exchange of Saharan salt for gold from the forest zone to the south.
events.sig: Songhai dominated the region for a century. A Moroccan army with firearms defeated it at Tondibi in 1591, and the region broke into smaller states.
events.hook: A warrior king built the largest empire in West African history.
events.story: The Mali Empire was losing its hold on the Niger bend to succession disputes and to Tuareg and Mossi raids. Songhai King Sonni Ali, on the throne from 1464, led cavalry and a war fleet on the river. He seized Timbuktu in 1468 and, after a long siege, Djenné, the trading and learning cities of Mali. By his death in 1492 Songhai controlled the great bend of the Niger.
events.then: Songhai dominated the region for a century. A Moroccan army with firearms defeated it at Tondibi in 1591, and the region broke into smaller states.
events.now: Songhai set the template for state power in the Sahel: control of the river, the salt and gold routes, and the cities that taxed them. The same corridors are now contested by jihadist groups, smugglers and three juntas.

q.before: The Mali Empire had controlled the Niger trading cities.
q.how: Conquest with cavalry and a river fleet.
q.claim: Military power, backed by traditional religious authority.
q.winners: Songhai; Timbuktu's Muslim scholars suffered under his harsh rule.
q.lasted: Songhai lasted until Morocco's invasion in 1591.

events.bluf: Songhai King Sonni Ali set out to take the Niger River cities from a fading Mali Empire and with them the trade in salt and gold. He took Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenné after a long siege, and by his death in 1492 he held the great bend of the Niger. Songhai became West Africa's largest empire, built on control of the river, the trans-Saharan routes and the cities that taxed them.
events.lens: In the Sahel, power has long followed control of trade corridors. The same routes matter for today's smuggling networks and insurgencies.
events.fact: Tradition holds that Sonni Ali drowned crossing a flooded river in 1492. Mali and Niger both claim Songhai as national heritage.

kv: Songhai at its height in the 1500s (est.)

events.what: Civil war wrecked Kyoto and central rule.
events.why: The Ashikaga shoguns depended on provincial governors they could not control. When the shogunal succession fell into dispute, the Hosokawa and Yamana factions backed rival candidates.
events.sig: Central authority collapsed. Lords built domains with their own laws and castles, adopted firearms after 1543 and fought one another until Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu reunified the country between 1568 and 1603.
events.hook: A succession fight burned Kyoto and plunged Japan into a century of civil war.
events.story: Japanese shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa named his brother heir in 1464; a son was born the next year and Yoshimasa's wife backed the child. In 1467 the dispute drew in Japan's great lords, led by Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sōzen. Fighting raged in the capital for ten years and burned much of Kyoto. When it ended in 1477 the Ashikaga shoguns had lost real control of the country.
events.then: Central authority collapsed. Lords built domains with their own laws and castles, adopted firearms after 1543 and fought one another until Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu reunified the country between 1568 and 1603.
events.now: The war began Japan's century of 'warring states', in which regional lords built the domains and warrior culture the Tokugawa later locked in place; the rigid central control imposed after 1603 was designed to prevent another collapse of this kind.

q.why: A succession dispute in the shogun's family, and rivalry between the great clans.
q.decided: Nothing: both sides exhausted themselves.
q.cost: Much of Kyoto destroyed.
q.changed: Power passed to local warlords, beginning the Warring States era.

events.bluf: Rival factions at the court of Japanese shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa fought to place their own candidate in the succession. Ten years of fighting burned much of Kyoto and settled nothing; the shogunate came out with no real authority over the provinces. Power passed to regional lords, the daimyo, whose century of competition ended in unification under the Tokugawa in 1603.
events.trig: Fighting broke out in Kyoto in 1467 over the shogunal succession and a feud within the Hatakeyama family.
events.lens: When a central government depends on regional strongmen it cannot discipline, one succession crisis can trigger generations of fragmentation.
events.fact: Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa left the war to his generals and retired to build the Silver Pavilion and refine the tea ceremony; the war takes its name from the Ōnin era in which it began.

kv: of fighting in and around Kyoto, 1467–1477
of the warring-states era that followed

events.who: Ferdinand of Aragon, Isabella of Castile
events.what: Union of Spain's two biggest kingdoms.
events.why: Isabella needed Aragonese support to beat a rival claimant. Aragon, a Mediterranean power, needed Castile's population and revenue against France.
events.sig: The two crowns kept separate laws and parliaments but acted together in war, foreign policy and religion. Their children married into the Habsburgs; their grandson became Holy Roman Emperor Charles V in 1519.
events.hook: One wedding joined two kingdoms and created Spain.
events.story: Castile faced a contested succession in 1469. Princess Isabella of Castile married Prince Ferdinand of Aragon in secret at Valladolid, against the wishes of her half-brother, Castilian King Henry IV. From 1479 the couple ruled both kingdoms as partners.
events.then: The two crowns kept separate laws and parliaments but acted together in war, foreign policy and religion. Their children married into the Habsburgs; their grandson became Holy Roman Emperor Charles V in 1519.
events.now: Spain was built as a union of kingdoms that kept their own laws. The tension between Madrid and regions with their own identity, Catalonia above all, descends from that founding bargain.

q.before: Castile and Aragon were separate kingdoms with their own rulers.
q.how: A marriage, then Isabella's succession in 1474 and Ferdinand's in 1479.
q.winners: The Catholic Monarchs; their rivals in Castile lost a civil war.
q.lasted: Yes: their union became the basis of modern Spain.

events.bluf: Isabella of Castile needed an ally to win a disputed succession; Ferdinand of Aragon wanted Castile's manpower against France. Their marriage joined the two largest Iberian kingdoms under one couple. The joint monarchy conquered Granada, founded the Inquisition, expelled the Jews and financed Columbus, and its grandson inherited a world empire.
events.lens: Many European states were assembled by dynastic marriage. The seams between the joined parts often still show in regional politics.
events.fact: Isabella's marriage contract gave her the governing power in Castile; Ferdinand signed as her consort.

kv: both crowns united under the couple

events.what: Church court targeting converted Jews and Muslims.
events.why: Resentment of successful converts gave the court a constituency. The monarchs wanted an institution answerable to the crown rather than Rome. Religious unity was their chosen basis for governing two separate kingdoms.
events.sig: The court pressed for the expulsion of the Jews in 1492 and of the Moriscos in 1609. Purity-of-blood statutes barred people of Jewish or Muslim descent from many offices. The Inquisition was abolished in 1834.
events.hook: Spain's monarchs set up a church court to police the faith of new Christians.
events.story: Spain held a large class of converted Jews, the New Christians, who had risen in trade and office since the forced conversions of 1391. Spanish King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella obtained papal permission for a royal tribunal in 1478. Under Grand Inquisitor Tomás de Torquemada it investigated, tortured and burned those it judged secret Jews.
events.then: The court pressed for the expulsion of the Jews in 1492 and of the Moriscos in 1609. Purity-of-blood statutes barred people of Jewish or Muslim descent from many offices. The Inquisition was abolished in 1834.
events.now: The Inquisition set the principle that a subject's ancestry could make his loyalty suspect, a doctrine later racial states adopted. It kept Spain closed to the Reformation and much of the printed learning of the north.

causes.why: The joint monarchs set up an Inquisition under royal, not papal, control to police the faith of Jewish converts to Christianity.

q.belief: Whether converts from Judaism and Islam were true Christians.
q.authority: The crown, not the pope, controlled the Spanish Inquisition.
q.believers: Converts and their descendants lived in fear of being denounced.
q.fallout: It strengthened royal power and helped drive the expulsions.
q.today: Spain abolished the Inquisition for good in 1834.

events.bluf: Spanish King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella wanted a royal court that could enforce one faith across two kingdoms. The Inquisition tried tens of thousands and burned a few thousand, most in its first decades, and tied Spanish identity to Catholic orthodoxy and purity of blood. It made religious conformity a function of the state for three centuries and drove the expulsions of 1492 and 1609.
events.lens: States consolidating power often define the nation by excluding an internal 'other'. Watch for laws that make loyalty a matter of descent.
events.fact: Its most active years were its first two decades; in the 1700s it tried a few dozen cases a year.

events.h: Ottomans land in Italy at Otranto
events.who: Gedik Ahmed Pasha; the people of Otranto
events.hook: An Ottoman army seized an Italian port, and Italy feared Rome would be next.
events.what: An Ottoman army seized an Italian port, and Italy feared Rome would be next.
events.story: Italy's states were at war with each other in 1480. Ottoman commander Gedik Ahmed Pasha landed in Apulia in July and took Otranto on 11 August after a two-week siege. About 800 townsmen who refused to convert were executed. Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II died in May 1481; the garrison surrendered in September.
events.why: Mehmed saw himself as heir to Rome and had conquered the Balkans. Italy's feuding states offered no united defence.
events.then: Neapolitan forces retook the town in 1481. The Ottomans pursued the Mediterranean through their fleet and the corsairs of North Africa rather than through Italy.
events.sig: Neapolitan forces retook the town in 1481. The Ottomans pursued the Mediterranean through their fleet and the corsairs of North Africa rather than through Italy.
events.now: Otranto showed that the Ottomans could land in Italy and that Italy's divided states could barely answer. Later sultans chose naval power and North African bases over invasion, which set the Mediterranean contest of the 1500s.

causes.why: Master of the old Roman capital, Mehmed II reached for Italy itself.

q.why: Mehmed wanted a foothold in Italy, perhaps as a step toward Rome.
q.stakes: Southern Italy, and the safety of the papacy.
q.decided: The sultan's death in 1481, not a battle.
q.cost: Much of the town killed or enslaved, including about 800 men executed.
q.changed: Italian states briefly united against the threat, then returned to their own wars.

events.bluf: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II sent a force to Italy to open a road to Rome. His commander took Otranto and held it a year; Mehmed's death in 1481 ended the campaign. The scare united the Italian states briefly and fixed the fear of Ottoman invasion in papal politics for a century.
events.lens: In personalized regimes, a ruler's death can reverse a strategy overnight. Ask how much a policy depends on one person.
events.fact: The 800 executed townsmen were canonised as the Martyrs of Otranto in 2013.

kv: townsmen executed for refusing to convert, the 'Martyrs of Otranto'

events.who: King João II of Portugal; commander Diogo de Azambuja; Akan rulers
events.what: First European fort in sub-Saharan Africa.
events.why: Portugal wanted the gold diverted from the desert routes to the sea. It wanted rivals, Castile above all, kept away.
events.sig: Gold flowed to Lisbon and financed Portugal's expansion. The Dutch captured Elmina in 1637 and expanded its role in the slave trade; dozens of European forts followed along the coast.
events.hook: Portugal built the first European fort in sub-Saharan Africa on the Gold Coast.
events.story: Gold from the Akan forest had gone north across the Sahara for centuries. In 1482 Portuguese King João II sent commander Diogo de Azambuja with pre-cut stone to build São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast, after negotiating with a reluctant local Akan ruler. The fort gave Portugal a secure base to buy gold at the coast. Later it held enslaved Africans awaiting ships to the Americas.
events.then: Gold flowed to Lisbon and financed Portugal's expansion. The Dutch captured Elmina in 1637 and expanded its role in the slave trade; dozens of European forts followed along the coast.
events.now: Elmina set the pattern of the European presence in West Africa for three centuries: forts on the shore, trade with African states behind them and no rule inland. That pattern held until the conquests of the 1870s to 1900s.
events.fact: Elmina is the oldest European building south of the Sahara. Captives passed through its 'Door of No Return', and it and Cape Coast Castle are central sites of memory for the African diaspora.

causes.why: Portugal fortified the Gold Coast to control its trade in gold and captives.

q.what: Gold at first; later enslaved people.
q.who: The Portuguese crown and Akan traders profited; captives paid.
q.scale: Elmina became the main European base on the Gold Coast for centuries.
q.daily: Akan traders brought gold to the castle in exchange for cloth, brass and other goods.
q.system: A model for fortified European trading posts along the African coast.

events.bluf: Portuguese King João II wanted the Akan forest's gold bought at the coast rather than carried north across the Sahara, and Castile kept away from it. His commander Diogo de Azambuja built São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast in 1482 with stone cut in Portugal. Elmina was the first permanent European fort south of the Sahara, and the chain of coastal forts that copied it became the channel through which Europeans bought gold and later shipped captives from West Africa.
events.lens: Coastal forts mark the shift from Europeans as traders on African terms to Europeans as armed competitors on African soil.

kv: oldest European building south of the Sahara
in European hands: Portuguese, then Dutch, then British

events.what: Ended the Wars of the Roses.
events.why: Richard's seizure of the throne and the disappearance of the princes turned nobles against him. Henry was the leading surviving Lancastrian claimant and had French money.
events.sig: Henry VII rebuilt the royal finances, banned private armies and governed through councils of lawyers and clerks. His son Henry VIII and granddaughter Elizabeth I used that state to break with Rome and fight Spain.
events.hook: Henry Tudor killed Richard III in battle and started England's most famous dynasty.
events.story: English King Richard III had taken the throne in 1483; his two young nephews had disappeared in the Tower. Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, landed in Wales with French-financed troops. At Bosworth Field in August 1485 the Stanley family changed sides, and Richard died fighting. Henry VII married Elizabeth of York, joining the two houses.
events.then: Henry VII rebuilt the royal finances, banned private armies and governed through councils of lawyers and clerks. His son Henry VIII and granddaughter Elizabeth I used that state to break with Rome and fight Spain.
events.now: The Tudors gave England a national church, a navy and a royal administration that outlived the dynasty. The national story Shakespeare told was written to justify their victory.

causes.why: Henry Tudor defeated and killed Richard III at Bosworth in 1485, ending three decades of on-and-off civil war.

q.before: Richard III, the last king of the House of York.
q.how: Victory in battle at Bosworth.
q.claim: Henry's distant Lancastrian descent, strengthened by marrying Elizabeth of York.
q.lasted: Yes: the Tudors ruled until 1603.

events.bluf: Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, invaded with French backing to take a crown held by a usurper. He killed English King Richard III at Bosworth and married the Yorkist heiress to end the civil wars. The Tudor monarchy he founded centralised the state, broke with Rome and built the navy that made England a sea power.
events.lens: New dynasties that win power by force usually spend their first years making sure no one can overthrow them the same way.
events.fact: Richard III's bones were found under a Leicester car park in 2012.

toll.n: Chroniclers' estimates. Richard III was the last English king to die in battle.

events.h: Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
events.what: First European to sail around Africa's tip.
events.why: Portugal had spent decades working down the African coast, funded by gold and slaves, looking for a way into the spice trade.
events.sig: Vasco da Gama used the route to reach India in 1498. Portugal was an Indian Ocean power within twenty years. The Cape later became a supply station for Dutch and British shipping and the base of white settlement in South Africa.
events.hook: A Portuguese captain proved you could sail around Africa.
events.story: Portugal had spent decades working down the African coast. In 1488 navigator Bartolomeu Dias, sent by Portuguese King João II, was driven south by storms and found he had rounded the southern tip of Africa. He reached the coast near today's Mossel Bay. His exhausted crew forced him to turn back.
events.then: Vasco da Gama used the route to reach India in 1498. Portugal was an Indian Ocean power within twenty years. The Cape later became a supply station for Dutch and British shipping and the base of white settlement in South Africa.
events.now: The Cape route moved the spice trade from Venice and Cairo to Lisbon within two decades and made the Indian Ocean a theatre of European naval power until the Suez Canal opened in 1869. When Suez or the Red Sea is blocked, as during the Houthi attacks on shipping from 2023, ships return to it.

q.what: A sea route around Africa to the Indian Ocean spice trade.
q.who: The Portuguese crown, which hoped to cut out Venetian and Arab middlemen.
q.scale: A voyage of about 16 months.
q.daily: Little at first; ten years later spices began arriving by sea.
q.system: The Cape route that carried trade between Europe and Asia for four centuries.

events.bluf: Portuguese King João II sent navigator Bartolomeu Dias to find the southern end of Africa and a sea route to the spices of Asia. Storms carried Dias past the Cape in 1488, and his exhausted crew forced him back near today's Mossel Bay. The Atlantic and Indian Oceans were proven to connect, and the route that bypassed Mediterranean and Middle Eastern middlemen made Portugal an Indian Ocean power within twenty years.
events.lens: Geography rules until technology changes it: new routes reshuffle which places are central and which are bypassed.
events.fact: Dias named it the Cape of Storms and King João renamed it the Cape of Good Hope. Dias drowned in a storm off the Cape in 1500.

kv: before da Gama used the route to reach India

events.who: Ferdinand and Isabella; Emir Muhammad XII (Boabdil)
events.hook: The last Muslim kingdom in Spain surrendered, ending nearly 800 years of Muslim rule in Iberia.
events.what: The last Muslim kingdom in Spain surrendered, ending nearly 800 years of Muslim rule in Iberia.
events.story: The Nasrid emirate of Granada had survived two centuries as a tributary of Castile. Spanish King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella began the conquest in 1482. Emir Muhammad XII, whom Spaniards called Boabdil, surrendered the city on 2 January 1492 on terms that promised Muslims freedom of worship.
events.why: Feuds inside the Nasrid family split the emirate. The union of Castile and Aragon gave the Christians the men and money for a ten-year war of sieges.
events.then: Forced conversions began in 1499 and the surrender terms were dead by 1502. Three months after the surrender the monarchs agreed to fund Columbus. The converted Moriscos were expelled in 1609-14.
events.sig: Forced conversions began in 1499 and the surrender terms were dead by 1502. Three months after the surrender the monarchs agreed to fund Columbus. The converted Moriscos were expelled in 1609-14.
events.now: The fall of Granada completed a Christian monarchy that then expelled its Jews, converted its Muslims by force and financed Columbus the same year; the Spanish state was built on religious uniformity and overseas conquest from its first months.

causes.why: The combined resources of Castile and Aragon let the monarchs finish a ten-year war against Granada.

events.fact: The Alhambra and the Arabic place names of Andalusia are what remain of eight centuries of Islamic rule.

q.before: The Nasrid emirs of Granada, the last Muslim rulers in Spain.
q.how: A ten-year war ended by a negotiated surrender.
q.claim: Christian 'reconquest' of lands once ruled by Visigothic kings.
q.winners: Ferdinand and Isabella; Granada's Muslims lost their promised rights within a decade.
q.lasted: Yes: Granada has been Spanish ever since.

events.bluf: Spanish King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella set out to finish the Christian conquest of Iberia. After a ten-year war the last emir surrendered Granada and the Alhambra on 2 January 1492. The monarchs then turned the crown's resources to religious uniformity and overseas ventures; Columbus sailed within the year.
events.lens: Promises of tolerance in surrender treaties tend to last only as long as the defeated keep some leverage.

kv: after the Muslim conquest of Iberia in 711

events.who: Ferdinand and Isabella; Spain's Jewish communities
events.hook: Spain ordered its Jews to convert or leave, ending one of the largest Jewish communities in the world.
events.what: Spain ordered its Jews to convert or leave, ending one of the largest Jewish communities in the world.
events.story: The Alhambra Decree of 31 March 1492 gave Spain's Jews until the end of July to convert or leave. Estimates of those who left run from 40,000 to over 100,000; many others converted and lived under the Inquisition's suspicion.
events.why: The Inquisition argued that practising Jews were drawing converts back to Judaism. With Granada taken, the monarchs made religious uniformity the basis of their rule.
events.then: Portugal forced its Jews to convert in 1497. Ottoman Sultan Bayezid II welcomed the refugees to Salonica and Istanbul. Sephardic merchants later built trading houses in Amsterdam, London and the Americas.
events.sig: Portugal forced its Jews to convert in 1497. Ottoman Sultan Bayezid II welcomed the refugees to Salonica and Istanbul. Sephardic merchants later built trading houses in Amsterdam, London and the Americas.
events.now: The expulsion set the principle of one realm, one faith, which the Peace of Augsburg made the European rule in 1555. The Sephardic communities it created built the trade networks of Amsterdam, Livorno and Salonica.

causes.why: Inquisitors argued that Jews were drawing converts back to Judaism. The monarchs' answer was the Alhambra Decree: convert or leave.

q.belief: Whether Jews could live in Spain without 'corrupting' converts.
q.authority: The Catholic Monarchs, pushed by the Inquisition.
q.believers: Jews faced exile or conversion; converts faced the Inquisition.
q.fallout: Spain lost merchants, doctors and scholars; the Ottomans and others gained them.
q.today: Ladino, the Judeo-Spanish language, survives among Sephardic communities.

events.bluf: Spanish King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella ordered the Jews of Spain to convert or leave within four months, to make one faith the basis of their joint rule. Tens of thousands left for Portugal, North Africa, Italy and the Ottoman Empire. Spain lost its physicians, financiers and artisans, and the Sephardic diaspora carried Spanish trade networks across the Mediterranean.
events.lens: Expelling a minority often hands its skills and networks to rival states.
events.fact: Spain and Portugal passed citizenship laws for Sephardic descendants in 2015.

kv: Spain offered citizenship to their descendants

events.who: Christopher Columbus, for Spain; Taíno people
events.what: First lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.
events.why: The Iberian kingdoms were competing for a sea route to Asian trade. Columbus underestimated the size of the earth and so believed Asia lay within reach. Castile, freed by the conquest of Granada, gambled on his plan.
events.sig: Spanish settlement, forced labour and epidemics destroyed the Taíno within decades. Maize and potatoes went east to Europe, Africa and Asia and fed population growth; horses, cattle, wheat and smallpox went west. American silver later financed Spain and flowed on to China.
events.hook: Columbus sailed west looking for Asia and connected two worlds that had been apart for 15,000 years.
events.story: Castile completed the conquest of Granada in January 1492. Genoese navigator Christopher Columbus sailed from Palos in August with three small ships funded by Spanish monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella, landed in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492 and went on to Hispaniola. The Taíno people received him. Within decades disease, forced labour and violence had reduced them to a remnant.
events.then: Spanish settlement, forced labour and epidemics destroyed the Taíno within decades. Maize and potatoes went east to Europe, Africa and Asia and fed population growth; horses, cattle, wheat and smallpox went west. American silver later financed Spain and flowed on to China.
events.now: The contact opened in 1492 set in motion the movement of people, crops, animals and disease that fixed the populations, languages, religions and racial hierarchies of the Americas over the following three centuries.
events.fact: Columbus died still believing he had reached Asia, which is why the Caribbean islands are the 'West Indies'. Tomatoes, potatoes, chocolate and chilli peppers all came from the Americas: Italy had no tomato sauce and India no chilli before this.

sites.d: Departure port, August 3, 1492.
First landfall, October 12, 1492.
First Spanish settlement, built from the wrecked Santa María.

causes.why: With the conquest of Granada complete, Isabella and Ferdinand finally agreed to fund Columbus.

q.before: Taíno chiefdoms governed Hispaniola and the Bahamas.
q.how: A claim by 'discovery', followed by settlement and conquest.
q.claim: Royal and papal grants to Spain.
q.winners: Spain; the Taíno were nearly wiped out.
q.lasted: Yes: Spain ruled its Caribbean islands for centuries.

events.bluf: Genoese navigator Christopher Columbus, funded by Castile, sailed west to reach Asia's trade by a shorter route. He reached the Bahamas and Hispaniola instead and returned convinced he had touched the outskirts of Asia. The landing opened permanent contact between the Americas and the rest of the world: the largest exchange of people, crops, animals and diseases on record, the depopulation of Indigenous societies and the European empires that grew on their ruins.
events.trig: Spanish monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella agreed in April 1492 to fund the voyage; Columbus landed in the Bahamas on 12 October.
events.lens: Biology can decide history: disease did more than guns to determine who would hold the Americas.

kv: from the Canary Islands to the Bahamas
figs.n: Within about fifty years the Taíno people of Hispaniola, perhaps several hundred thousand in 1492, had been reduced to a few thousand by disease, forced labour and violence.

events.what: Expanded empire and Islamic scholarship.
events.why: Muslim merchants and clerics had been uneasy under Sonni Ali, who held to traditional religion alongside Islam, and backed a ruler of their own faith. A standing army and governors let Songhai tax trade across a wider empire than cavalry raids could hold.
events.sig: Askia made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496-97 and returned with recognition as caliph of the western Sudan. He expanded the empire. His sons deposed him in 1528, and succession struggles weakened Songhai, which fell to Morocco in 1591.
events.hook: Under Askia Muhammad, Songhai reached its height and Timbuktu became a world center of learning.
events.story: Songhai King Sonni Ali died in 1492 and his son succeeded him. General Muhammad Ture, with support from Muslim merchants and clerics who had been uneasy under Sonni Ali, defeated the son in 1493 and took the title Askia. Askia Muhammad I organised a professional army and a provincial administration and promoted Islamic learning. Timbuktu's mosques and libraries drew learned men from across the Muslim world.
events.then: Askia made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496-97 and returned with recognition as caliph of the western Sudan. He expanded the empire. His sons deposed him in 1528, and succession struggles weakened Songhai, which fell to Morocco in 1591.
events.now: Askia's state fixed the alliance of Muslim rulers, merchants and jurists that governed the Sahel's cities until the Moroccan conquest of 1591. The Timbuktu manuscripts, on law, astronomy and medicine, are the record of it and refute the idea of a pre-colonial Africa without written history.
events.fact: Timbuktu produced hundreds of thousands of manuscripts. In 2012 librarians smuggled many out in rice sacks to save them from jihadists, who burned some of the rest in 2013.

causes.why: Askia Muhammad, one of Sonni Ali's generals, seized power from his son in 1493 and ruled the empire at its height.

q.before: Sonni Ali's son, Sonni Baru, briefly ruled.
q.how: A coup by the general Muhammad Touré, who took the title Askia.
q.claim: Islamic legitimacy, reinforced by a pilgrimage to Mecca.
q.winners: Muslim scholars and merchants of Timbuktu.
q.lasted: His dynasty ruled until Morocco's invasion in 1591.

events.bluf: Songhai general Muhammad Ture overthrew Sonni Ali's son in 1493 with the backing of Muslim merchants and clerics and took the title Askia. He built a professional army, provincial governors and a centralised Islamic state, and Timbuktu under his rule drew learned men from across the Muslim world. Songhai reached its peak as a state, and West Africa its fullest integration into the wider Muslim world.
events.trig: Askia defeated Sonni Ali's son, Sonni Baru, in 1493.
events.lens: Rulers who take power by force often seek religious legitimacy. Watch whom a new ruler courts.

events.who: France (Charles VIII), Spain, Holy Roman Empire, Italian states
events.what: 60 years of wars over Italy.
events.why: France and Spain, newly consolidated, held rival claims to Naples and Milan. Italy's wealth invited intervention and its divisions made it possible.
events.sig: Spain held Naples and Milan by the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559. Italian states invented the resident ambassador to manage alliances. The bastioned fortress spread from Italy across Europe.
events.hook: France invaded Italy and dragged all of Europe's big powers into a 60-year fight.
events.story: Italy in 1494 was five major states at war with each other. French King Charles VIII crossed the Alps with a siege train of modern bronze cannon and took Naples in February 1495. Venice, Milan, the Pope, Spain and the Emperor formed a league to drive him out. The peninsula was Europe's battlefield until 1559.
events.then: Spain held Naples and Milan by the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559. Italian states invented the resident ambassador to manage alliances. The bastioned fortress spread from Italy across Europe.
events.now: Italy stayed divided and under foreign influence until the 1860s. The balance-of-power system that Europe practised until 1914 was learned in these wars.

causes.why: Ferdinand of Aragon also claimed Naples, so France's invasion in 1494 drew Spain in; Italy became the battlefield of their rivalry for 65 years.

q.why: French claims to Naples and Milan, and the rivalry of France with Spain and the Habsburgs.
q.stakes: Control of Italy, Europe's richest region.
q.decided: Spanish infantry and Habsburg resources; the wars ended in 1559.
q.cost: Cities sacked, including Rome itself in 1527.
q.changed: Spain dominated Italy, and modern diplomacy and warfare took shape.

events.bluf: French King Charles VIII marched into Italy to claim the kingdom of Naples. He took it in five months, and every other power came in to stop him. Sixty-five years of war ended Italian independence under Spanish control and produced the balance of power, the resident ambassador and the modern fortress.
events.trig: Milanese ruler Ludovico Sforza invited Charles VIII to press his claim to Naples in 1494.
events.lens: Rich but divided regions attract intervention by larger neighbours, and internal rivals often invite the outsider in.
events.fact: Charles VIII's cannon reduced in hours castles that had held for months against medieval engines.

kv: troops Charles VIII led into Italy
Sack of Rome by imperial troops

events.h: Aldus Manutius opens his press in Venice
events.hook: A Venetian printer made the Greek and Latin classics accurate, cheap and portable.
events.what: A Venetian printer made the Greek and Latin classics accurate, cheap and portable.
events.story: Venice was the printing capital of Europe. Venetian printer Aldus Manutius founded his press around 1494 to issue edited texts of Aristotle and other Greek authors. From 1501 he printed small octavo classics in a new slanted type, italic, which packed more words on the page.
events.why: Venice had capital, trade routes and Greek refugees from the Ottomans who had brought their manuscripts. Demand for reliable texts was rising among the humanists.
events.then: Aldine editions of Aristotle, Plato and the Latin poets spread humanist scholarship across Europe. The small format let people read anywhere.
events.sig: Aldine editions of Aristotle, Plato and the Latin poets spread humanist scholarship across Europe. The small format let people read anywhere.
events.now: Aldus made the book a personal object. The reading public that the Reformation and the Enlightenment relied on grew from his portable, affordable editions.

causes.why: Within 40 years printing had spread from Mainz to Venice, which became Europe's busiest printing city.

q.what: Printed editions of Greek and Latin classics, many in a small format.
q.new: Italic type and books small enough to carry in a pocket.
q.audience: Scholars, students and wealthy readers across Europe.
q.reveals: Print turned the Renaissance revival of ancient learning into a Europe-wide movement.
q.today: Every italic font on a computer descends from Aldus's type.

events.bluf: Venetian printer Aldus Manutius set out to print accurate Greek and Latin texts in formats a reader could carry. He succeeded, with italic type and the small octavo. Classical learning became a shared European possession, and private reading away from the library became ordinary.
events.lens: Format matters: making knowledge portable and affordable changes who uses it.
events.fact: Italic type and the semicolon in its modern use both come from his press.

kv: first italic type and pocket-size classics

events.what: Divided the non-European world along a line.
events.why: Columbus's return set off a dispute over who owned newly found lands. Pope Alexander VI's decrees of 1493 favoured Spain, and Portugal negotiated directly to move the line west.
events.sig: Brazil's eastern coast fell on Portugal's side, and Portuguese commander Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed it in 1500. France, England and the Dutch rejected the treaty and held that land belonged to whoever occupied it.
events.hook: The Pope helped Spain and Portugal draw a line splitting the non-European world between them.
events.story: Columbus's return in 1493 raised the question of who owned the newly found lands. Pope Alexander VI issued bulls that year favouring Spain. Portuguese King John II negotiated directly with Spanish monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella, and on 7 June 1494 at Tordesillas they agreed a line about 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands: lands west of it for Spain, east for Portugal. No one asked the people who lived there.
events.then: Brazil's eastern coast fell on Portugal's side, and Portuguese commander Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed it in 1500. France, England and the Dutch rejected the treaty and held that land belonged to whoever occupied it.
events.now: The treaty established the practice of distant powers drawing colonial borders without the people inside them, which returned at the Berlin Conference of 1884-85; Brazil's Portuguese language is its direct legacy.
events.fact: The line ran 370 leagues west of Cape Verde. Brazil's eastern bulge sticks out past it, which is why Brazil alone in South America speaks Portuguese.

causes.why: Columbus's return set off a race between Spain and Portugal; the Pope and then the treaty drew a line between their claims.

q.before: Spain and Portugal disputed who owned newly found lands.
q.how: A treaty that moved the Pope's earlier dividing line further west.
q.winners: Portugal gained Brazil; Spain most of the Americas.
q.lasted: It shaped claims until the 1700s; its legacy is language.

events.bluf: Spain and Portugal wanted to settle who owned the lands their navigators were finding before the dispute turned to war. By treaty at Tordesillas in 1494 they divided the world outside Europe along a line 370 leagues west of Cape Verde, with no one who lived there consulted. The line gave Portugal the coast that became Brazil and set the precedent of European powers partitioning other continents on a map.
events.lens: Borders drawn by outsiders on maps tend to outlast the empires that drew them.

kv: west of Cape Verde: the dividing line, about 46°W
powers dividing the lands beyond Europe

events.who: John Cabot, Venetian sailing for England's Henry VII
events.what: First European landing in North America since the Vikings.
events.why: Columbus's voyage of 1492 had given Spain a western route, and Henry VII wanted England's share. Bristol merchants already fished far out into the Atlantic and could fund a voyage.
events.sig: England let the claim lie for most of a century, then revived it to justify Newfoundland in 1583 and Jamestown in 1607. Basque, Portuguese, French and English fleets worked the cod banks, and salt cod became a staple of European trade.
events.hook: England's first foothold claim on North America came from a Venetian sailor and a sea full of cod.
events.story: Venetian navigator John Cabot sailed from Bristol in 1497 under letters patent from English King Henry VII, hoping to reach Asia. He landed on the coast of Newfoundland and found no spices. His crew reported waters so thick with cod that the fish could be scooped up in baskets.
events.then: England let the claim lie for most of a century, then revived it to justify Newfoundland in 1583 and Jamestown in 1607. Basque, Portuguese, French and English fleets worked the cod banks, and salt cod became a staple of European trade.
events.now: England's title to North America rested on Cabot's landfall and was revived to justify Newfoundland in 1583 and Jamestown in 1607. The cod fishery built Canada's Atlantic provinces and ran until overfishing forced the moratorium of 1992.

q.before: The Beothuk people lived in Newfoundland.
q.how: Exploration and a claim of possession for the English crown.
q.lasted: Newfoundland became England's first overseas claim made good, in 1583.

events.bluf: Venetian navigator John Cabot sailed west for English King Henry VII to find a short route to Asia, and the king wanted a share of what Columbus had opened for Spain. Cabot found Newfoundland and seas full of cod rather than spices. His landfall gave England its legal claim to North America, the basis of every later English colony, and the fishery pulled the North Atlantic into the European economy.
events.lens: Legal claims are often made long before a state has the power to use them, then revived when it does.
events.fact: Henry VII rewarded Cabot with £10 for finding the 'new isle'.

events.what: First sea voyage from Europe to India, around Africa.
events.why: Portugal wanted direct access to Asian spices, which reached Europe through Muslim and Venetian middlemen at high markups. Decades of Portuguese voyages down the African coast had built the ships and the navigational knowledge.
events.sig: Portugal sent armed fleets from 1500, bombarded Calicut and imposed licensed trade, taking Goa in 1510, Malacca in 1511 and Hormuz in 1515. Indian Ocean commerce had been open to many merchant communities with no power controlling the sea; Portugal taxed and policed it by force, a model the Dutch and English companies expanded after 1600.
events.hook: Portugal sailed around Africa to India, opening the first sea link between Europe and Asia.
events.story: Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon in July 1497 with four ships, rounded the Cape of Good Hope and, with a pilot hired at Malindi on the East African coast, crossed the Indian Ocean to Calicut in May 1498. The Zamorin of Calicut received him; the gifts, hats, washbasins and honey, fell below what his court expected from a king's envoy. The pepper and spices the fleet brought home in 1499 were worth many times the cost of the voyage.
events.then: Portugal sent armed fleets from 1500, bombarded Calicut and imposed licensed trade, taking Goa in 1510, Malacca in 1511 and Hormuz in 1515. Indian Ocean commerce had been open to many merchant communities with no power controlling the sea; Portugal taxed and policed it by force, a model the Dutch and English companies expanded after 1600.
events.now: The sea route made the Indian Ocean a field for European naval power for 450 years and began the pattern of armed trading companies that ended in the conquest of India. The ocean is again a zone of naval competition among India, China and the United States.
events.fact: The Zamorin of Calicut was unimpressed by da Gama's gifts: hats, washbasins and honey.

causes.why: Dias proved a sea route around Africa existed; da Gama followed it to India.

q.what: Pepper, cinnamon, cloves and other spices.
q.who: Portugal's crown gained; Arab and Venetian middlemen lost their monopoly.
q.scale: Da Gama's cargo reportedly paid for the voyage many times over.
q.daily: Over time spices became cheaper in Europe.
q.system: European-controlled sea trade with Asia.

events.bluf: Portuguese King Manuel I sent navigator Vasco da Gama to find a sea route to India and reach the spice trade direct, cutting out the Muslim and Venetian middlemen. Da Gama reached Calicut in May 1498 and returned with pepper worth many times the cost of the voyage, having lost about half his crew. A direct sea link between Europe and Asia now existed, and Portugal used it to impose armed trade on an ocean no single power had policed.
events.lens: Control of sea lanes turns naval power into economic power. Watch who patrols the trade routes.

kv: crew who survived the round trip

events.what: Landed on the coast and claimed it.
events.why: The route round Africa took ships deep into the South Atlantic, and the coast lay inside the zone the Treaty of Tordesillas had given Portugal.
events.sig: Portugal first cut brazilwood for dye, then from the 1530s built sugar plantations in the northeast worked by enslaved Africans; gold strikes in the 1690s drew settlers inland. Brazil received about 40 per cent of all Africans shipped across the Atlantic.
events.hook: Portugal stumbled onto Brazil on the way to India.
events.story: Portugal's second fleet to India left Lisbon in March 1500 under Portuguese commander Pedro Álvares Cabral with 13 ships. Swinging far west into the Atlantic to catch the winds that carried ships round Africa, the fleet sighted the coast of Brazil in April 1500. Cabral claimed the land for Portuguese King Manuel I, stayed about ten days and sent a ship home with the news.
events.then: Portugal first cut brazilwood for dye, then from the 1530s built sugar plantations in the northeast worked by enslaved Africans; gold strikes in the 1690s drew settlers inland. Brazil received about 40 per cent of all Africans shipped across the Atlantic.
events.now: Brazil's plantation economy, built from the 1530s on enslaved African labour, produced the largest population of African descent outside Africa and the racial inequalities that run through Brazilian politics today.

causes.why: Brazil's eastern bulge lay on Portugal's side of the Tordesillas line.

q.before: Tupi-speaking peoples lived along the coast.
q.how: A claim of possession by a passing fleet.
q.claim: The Treaty of Tordesillas placed the land on Portugal's side.
q.lasted: Brazil was Portuguese until 1822.

events.bluf: Portuguese commander Pedro Álvares Cabral set out for India by the route Vasco da Gama had opened and claimed the Brazilian coast when his fleet swung west into the Atlantic. Portugal got a colony it held by treaty and showed little interest in for decades. Brazil grew on sugar, gold and enslaved African labour into the largest and richest part of the Portuguese empire and the largest slave society in the Americas.
events.lens: Whether a place becomes a colony often begins with accident; what happens next depends on what can be extracted there.
events.fact: Bartolomeu Dias, the first European to round the Cape of Good Hope, sailed with Cabral's fleet and drowned in a storm off that Cape weeks after the Brazilian landfall.

events.what: New dynasty made Shi'a Islam the state religion.
events.why: The fall of the earlier Turkmen states left a vacuum. Ismail combined charismatic religious authority over the Qizilbash with their tribal military strength. Shi'ism set the new state apart from the Sunni Ottomans and Uzbeks.
events.sig: Iran became the heartland of Shi'a Islam, with a clerical class that later gained power independent of the throne. The Ottoman-Safavid wars fixed a frontier through Mesopotamia and the Caucasus.
events.hook: A teenage shah made Shi'a Islam the faith of Iran.
events.story: The collapse of the Turkmen states of western Iran left no settled power there. Persian Shah Ismail I, hereditary head of the Safavid Sufi order and about 14 years old, took Tabriz in 1501 at the head of Turkmen warriors called the Qizilbash and crowned himself shah. He declared Twelver Shi'a Islam the state religion and enforced it, at times violently. He brought Shi'a jurists from Lebanon and Bahrain to build a clerical establishment.
events.then: Iran became the heartland of Shi'a Islam, with a clerical class that later gained power independent of the throne. The Ottoman-Safavid wars fixed a frontier through Mesopotamia and the Caucasus.
events.now: Iran remains the leading Shi'a state and backs Shi'a and allied movements across the region; the Saudi-Iranian rivalry is often framed in the Sunni-Shi'a terms fixed in 1501.

q.belief: Twelver Shi'ism as the true form of Islam.
q.authority: The shah, who claimed spiritual as well as royal authority.
q.believers: Iran's mostly Sunni population was converted over generations.
q.fallout: Two centuries of war with the Sunni Ottomans.
q.today: Around 90% of Iranians are Shi'a Muslims.

events.bluf: Persian Shah Ismail I set out to turn his Sufi following into a state and to bind it to him by a faith that set it apart from every neighbour. He took Tabriz in 1501, crowned himself shah and made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion of a mostly Sunni country, by force where needed. Iran gained a religious identity distinct from the Ottomans and the Uzbeks, and the Sunni-Shi'a line he drew still organises Middle Eastern politics.
events.lens: Religion can be a tool of state-building: a distinct faith gives a new state borders of identity, not just of territory.
events.fact: The Qizilbash, 'red heads', took their name from a red cap with twelve folds for the twelve Shi'a imams.

events.what: Most famous portrait in the world.
events.why: Leonardo's study of anatomy and optics let him paint lifelike transitions of light. The merchant market for portraits paid for the experiment.
events.sig: The half-length figure turned three-quarters against a landscape became the model for European portraiture. The painting passed to French King Francis I and, after the Revolution, to the Louvre as public property.
events.hook: Leonardo began the portrait that became the world's most famous painting.
events.story: Florentine merchant families commissioned portraits to display status. Florentine painter Leonardo da Vinci painted Lisa Gherardini, wife of the silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo, using sfumato, a soft blending of tones. He worked on it for years and never delivered it.
events.then: The half-length figure turned three-quarters against a landscape became the model for European portraiture. The painting passed to French King Francis I and, after the Revolution, to the Louvre as public property.
events.now: The painting marks the moment European art became an instrument of courts and states: Leonardo took it to the French king, and it has been a possession of the French state since, used in diplomacy and as a draw for Paris.
events.fact: Its global celebrity dates from its theft in 1911.

causes.why: When French troops took Milan in 1499, Leonardo lost his patron, Duke Ludovico Sforza, and moved to Florence, where he began the Mona Lisa around 1503.

q.what: A small portrait in oil on a poplar panel.
q.new: Sfumato blending, a relaxed three-quarter pose and an imaginary landscape behind the sitter.
q.audience: Leonardo kept it; it passed into the French royal collection.
q.reveals: The Renaissance interest in individual character and in how we see.
q.today: Behind glass in the Louvre, the most visited painting in the world.

events.bluf: Florentine painter Leonardo da Vinci took a merchant's commission for a portrait of his wife and kept the painting for the rest of his life. He carried it to the French court, and it has belonged to the French state since. The painting shows the Renaissance shift toward secular subjects, the individual face and techniques grounded in the study of nature.
events.lens: Art follows money: when merchants become patrons, art turns to portraits of merchants.

kv: stolen from the Louvre; recovered in 1913
visitors a year to the Louvre

events.what: Portuguese looted the Swahili city-state.
events.why: Portugal wanted the gold of Sofala and bases on the route to India. It tried to force the Muslim merchant cities to pay tribute and buy trade licences.
events.sig: Kilwa declined. Portugal held Fort Jesus at Mombasa until Omani Arabs drove it out in 1698; Oman, and later Zanzibar, then dominated the coast.
events.hook: Portuguese ships looted Kilwa, the jewel of the Swahili coast.
events.story: Kilwa Kisiwani, an island city in today's Tanzania, had grown rich on gold from the Zimbabwe plateau shipped through Sofala and had minted its own coins. In 1505 the fleet of Portuguese viceroy Francisco de Almeida stormed and plundered it. Almeida installed a ruler loyal to Portugal. Mombasa was sacked the same year.
events.then: Kilwa declined. Portugal held Fort Jesus at Mombasa until Omani Arabs drove it out in 1698; Oman, and later Zanzibar, then dominated the coast.
events.now: The sack of Kilwa began three centuries of European naval control of the Indian Ocean trade; the Swahili cities lost their independence and the ocean's commerce was redirected to Lisbon, then Amsterdam, then London.
events.fact: Kilwa's ruins are a World Heritage site; Swahili, with its Arabic and Persian loanwords, records the trade the city lived on.

causes.why: Da Gama's route ran up the Swahili coast; Portuguese fleets returned to seize its ports and tax its trade.

q.why: Portugal wanted to control the gold trade and the Swahili ports.
q.stakes: Command of the East African coast.
q.decided: Portuguese cannon and armoured troops.
q.cost: The city was looted and burned, and many inhabitants fled.
q.changed: Kilwa never recovered its wealth.

events.bluf: Portuguese viceroy Francisco de Almeida was sent to seize the gold of Sofala and bases on the route to India, and to force the Swahili cities to pay tribute. His fleet stormed and plundered Kilwa in 1505 and installed a ruler loyal to Portugal; Mombasa was sacked the same year. The city-states that had linked Africa to the Indian Ocean for centuries lost their independence, and the ocean's trade was redirected by force to Lisbon.
events.lens: Trading cities that live by openness are vulnerable to any power that brings guns to the market.

kv: ships in Francisco de Almeida's fleet

events.what: Four-year fresco of Genesis.
events.why: Julius aimed to restore papal authority in Italy and make Rome the capital of Christendom in stone and paint.
events.sig: The ceiling raised the artist's standing from craftsman to genius. Rebuilding St Peter's, begun under Julius in 1506, was financed through indulgence sales that Luther attacked in 1517.
events.hook: Michelangelo spent four years painting the story of Genesis on a chapel ceiling.
events.story: Pope Julius II, who led armies in person, hired Florentine sculptor Michelangelo in 1508 to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. Michelangelo, who regarded himself as a sculptor, covered it with scenes from Genesis, including the Creation of Adam, and finished in 1512.
events.then: The ceiling raised the artist's standing from craftsman to genius. Rebuilding St Peter's, begun under Julius in 1506, was financed through indulgence sales that Luther attacked in 1517.
events.now: The Renaissance papacy acted as an Italian prince, building and warring on borrowed money. That conduct, and the indulgences sold to cover it, supplied the Reformation's first grievance.
events.fact: Michelangelo painted standing on scaffolding, head tilted back; the legend that he lay on his back is false.

q.what: A ceiling fresco covering about 500 square metres.
q.new: Muscular, sculptural figures painted on an enormous scale.
q.audience: Popes, cardinals and visitors to the Vatican.
q.reveals: The papacy's wealth and its use of art for prestige.
q.today: Millions see it every year, and conclaves still meet beneath it.
