q.believers: Subjects had to follow their ruler's faith or move.
q.fallout: Calvinists were excluded, storing up trouble for the Thirty Years' War.
q.today: Germany's map of Catholic and Protestant regions still reflects it.

events.bluf: Holy Roman Emperor Charles V had failed to crush the Lutheran princes, and his brother Ferdinand settled for a deal: each ruler would choose his territory's faith. The peace held for sixty years. It replaced the idea of one Christian truth with a political bargain and, by leaving Calvinists out, set up the Thirty Years' War.
events.lens: Compromises that leave out a rising group store up the next conflict.
events.fact: Charles V refused to sign the peace himself and abdicated the following year.

kv: states, each choosing its ruler's religion
of uneasy peace until the Thirty Years' War

events.who: Emperor Akbar; his regent Bairam Khan
events.what: Expanded the empire and promoted religious tolerance.
events.why: The Mughals were a small Muslim ruling group over a mostly Hindu population. Lasting rule required local allies and a reliable tax base.
events.sig: Rajput rulers became his generals and in-laws. A ranked imperial nobility, the mansabdars, and a land survey under finance minister Todar Mal fixed revenue. Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679 and alienated Rajput and Maratha allies; revolts followed.
events.hook: Akbar built a vast, tolerant empire across most of India.
events.story: Mughal Emperor Akbar came to the throne in 1556 aged 13 under his regent Bairam Khan and took personal control in 1560. He expanded the empire across North India, Gujarat and Bengal, married a Rajput princess of Amber in 1562, abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1564 and hosted debates between Muslim, Hindu, Christian, Jain and Zoroastrian theologians at Fatehpur Sikri.
events.then: Rajput rulers became his generals and in-laws. A ranked imperial nobility, the mansabdars, and a land survey under finance minister Todar Mal fixed revenue. Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679 and alienated Rajput and Maratha allies; revolts followed.
events.now: Akbar's settlement with the Rajputs and his revenue system set the pattern of Mughal rule to 1707, and his pluralism is the precedent Indian secularists cite against Hindu nationalists in the debates of today.
events.fact: Akbar is thought to have been unable to read, yet built one of the greatest libraries of his age and had books read aloud to him.

causes.why: Babur's grandson Akbar turned a conquest into a lasting state, winning over Hindu Rajput princes through marriage alliances and tolerance.

q.before: His father Humayun, who had just regained the throne.
q.how: Inheritance at 13, then conquest and administrative reform.
q.claim: Mughal dynastic right, and later his own wider claim to rule all faiths justly.
q.winners: The Mughals, and Hindu Rajput nobles brought into imperial service.
q.lasted: The empire he built lasted until the 18th century.

events.bluf: Mughal Emperor Akbar set out to turn a conquest by a small Muslim ruling group into a durable empire over a mostly Hindu population. He brought Rajput rulers into the army and the imperial family, abolished the tax on non-Muslims and built a centralised land-revenue system. The accommodation kept the Mughals dominant in South Asia for 150 years, and its partial reversal under Aurangzeb after 1679 coincided with the revolts that weakened the empire.
events.lens: Conquerors who co-opt local elites rule longer than those who rely on force or religious exclusion.

kv: Akbar's age when he became emperor

events.who: Elizabeth I; her chief minister William Cecil
events.what: 45-year reign begins.
events.why: Mary's Catholic restoration had died with her. Elizabeth's claim rested on the break with Rome, so her survival required a Protestant England.
events.sig: She backed Dutch rebels and privateers against Spain, beat the Armada in 1588 and chartered the East India Company in 1600. The crown passed to Scottish King James VI in 1603.
events.hook: A Protestant queen began a 45-year reign that made England a power.
events.story: English Queen Mary I died childless in November 1558. Her half-sister Elizabeth I took the throne under Henry VIII's will, with William Cecil as chief minister. The religious settlement of 1559 created a Protestant church with Catholic forms.
events.then: She backed Dutch rebels and privateers against Spain, beat the Armada in 1588 and chartered the East India Company in 1600. The crown passed to Scottish King James VI in 1603.
events.now: The Anglican settlement, the beginnings of English sea power and the East India Company date from the reign. Her refusal to marry passed the crown to the Scottish Stuarts and so to the union of 1603.

causes.why: Henry's break made Elizabeth, daughter of the marriage Rome refused to recognise, a Protestant queen.

q.before: Mary I, who had restored Catholicism.
q.how: Peaceful succession.
q.claim: Inheritance under her father's will and Act of Succession.
q.lasted: She reigned for 45 years.

events.bluf: Elizabeth I inherited a divided, nearly bankrupt kingdom and set out to hold it together under a Protestant settlement broad enough to keep the peace. She reigned 45 years, kept England independent of Spain and never married. England came out a Protestant state turning toward the sea.
events.lens: Leaders who avoid forcing religious or ideological purity often hold divided countries together.
events.fact: She used the question of her marriage as a diplomatic tool for twenty years.

events.what: 36 years of civil war.
events.why: A minority on the throne left no arbiter. Calvinism gave noble factions an army of believers. Spain and England fed money to the sides.
events.sig: Henry of Navarre, the Protestant heir, became French King Henry IV, converted in 1593 and issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598. The 'politiques' argued that the state's survival outranked religious uniformity.
events.hook: France tore itself apart for 36 years over Catholic and Protestant faith.
events.story: French King Henry II died in a tournament in 1559, leaving young sons. Calvinism had spread among nobles and townsmen. The Guise, Bourbon and Montmorency families fought for control of the court and used religion to raise followers. Massacres were common on both sides.
events.then: Henry of Navarre, the Protestant heir, became French King Henry IV, converted in 1593 and issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598. The 'politiques' argued that the state's survival outranked religious uniformity.
events.now: France's tradition of a strong central state and its suspicion of religion in public life descend from the memory of these wars. The settlement of 1598 was the first in Europe to tolerate two faiths by law.

causes.why: A newly confident Catholic Church and fast-growing Calvinism (the Huguenots) collided in France, where great noble families took opposite sides.

q.why: Religious division, and noble families competing for control of weak kings.
q.stakes: The religion and the crown of France.
q.decided: Henry of Navarre's victories and his conversion to Catholicism.
q.cost: Perhaps two to four million deaths from fighting, famine and disease.
q.changed: France accepted limited toleration in 1598.

events.bluf: French noble factions took up religion to fight for control of a crown held by boys. Eight civil wars over 36 years killed hundreds of thousands and ended only when a Protestant heir converted to take Paris. The wars taught France that a strong crown mattered more than religious unity, the lesson behind the absolutist state.
events.trig: Men of the Duke of Guise killed Protestant worshippers at Vassy in March 1562.
events.lens: Religious wars are often elite power struggles in religious dress: ask who leads each side and what they stand to gain.
events.fact: The wars killed an estimated two to four million people, most by famine and disease.

kv: deaths from fighting, famine and disease (est.)

events.who: The Deccan sultanates vs. the Vijayanagara Empire
events.hook: An alliance of Muslim sultanates destroyed the Vijayanagara Empire, South India's great Hindu power.
events.what: An alliance of Muslim sultanates destroyed the Vijayanagara Empire, South India's great Hindu power.
events.story: Vijayanagara's regent Rama Raya, ruling in the name of King Sadashiva Raya, had intervened in the sultanates' wars for two decades. The sultans of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar united against him and met his army near Talikota on 23 January 1565. Rama Raya was captured and beheaded. The victors sacked Hampi, then one of the largest cities in the world, for months.
events.why: The sultanates and Vijayanagara competed for the Raichur Doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers. Rama Raya's habit of playing the sultanates off against one another united them against him.
events.then: A smaller Vijayanagara state survived at Penukonda and later Chandragiri while its governors, the nayakas of Madurai, Tanjore and Gingee, became independent. The sultanates fought each other and were conquered by Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, Bijapur in 1686 and Golconda in 1687.
events.sig: A smaller Vijayanagara state survived at Penukonda and later Chandragiri while its governors, the nayakas of Madurai, Tanjore and Gingee, became independent. The sultanates fought each other and were conquered by Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, Bijapur in 1686 and Golconda in 1687.
events.now: The destruction of Vijayanagara removed the last large Hindu state in the south and opened the Deccan to the Mughals a century later; the sultanates that won fell to Aurangzeb in turn.

q.why: The sultanates feared Vijayanagara's power and Rama Raya's meddling.
q.decided: The death of Rama Raya in battle, and the sultanates' combined artillery.
q.cost: The great city of Vijayanagara (Hampi) was sacked and abandoned.
q.changed: South Indian power fragmented.

events.bluf: Four Deccan sultanates allied to destroy Vijayanagara, the Hindu empire of South India whose regent had played them against one another for 20 years. At Talikota in January 1565 they beat its army, killed regent Rama Raya and sacked the capital at Hampi for months. The largest state in the south was gone, the Deccan fragmented, and the sultanates that won fell to the Mughals a century later.
events.lens: Playing rivals against each other works until it convinces them to unite.
events.fact: Hampi's ruins are a World Heritage site. Vijayanagara's armies included Muslim cavalry and the city had mosques, which its modern use as a symbol of Hindu resistance leaves out.

events.who: Spanish navigator Andrés de Urdaneta; Spanish, Chinese and Mexican merchants
events.what: Annual ships linking Mexico and Asia.
events.why: China's economy had shifted to silver for taxes and trade, so silver was worth far more there than in Europe. Spain needed a way to reach Asian markets from its American colonies.
events.sig: Silver flowed to China for 250 years. American crops such as maize, sweet potatoes and chillies spread to Asia and helped China's population grow. Chinese merchants settled in Manila.
events.hook: Spanish galleons linked Mexico and Asia, creating the first truly global trade route.
events.story: Spain had reached the Philippines but could not sail back east against the trade winds. In 1565 Spanish navigator Andrés de Urdaneta found the eastward route across the Pacific, using the westerly winds of the north Pacific. For 250 years galleons carried Mexican and Peruvian silver from Acapulco to Manila to buy Chinese silk and porcelain, and sailed back once or twice a year.
events.then: Silver flowed to China for 250 years. American crops such as maize, sweet potatoes and chillies spread to Asia and helped China's population grow. Chinese merchants settled in Manila.
events.now: The galleon trade linked American silver to Chinese demand from 1565 to 1815, the first exchange to run around the globe; the cultural ties between Mexico and the Philippines and the Chinese merchant communities of Southeast Asia date from it.
events.fact: For 250 years one or two ships a year, among the largest afloat, crossed the Pacific. Chinese porcelain shards still turn up in Mexican digs.

causes.why: Silver was worth far more in China, which needed it for taxes and coins; the galleons carried it across the Pacific to trade for silk and porcelain.

q.what: American silver for Chinese silk, porcelain and spices.
q.who: Merchants in Manila, Mexico and China; crews died in large numbers on the long voyages.
q.scale: One or two ships a year, each carrying a fortune.
q.daily: Chinese goods became common among Mexico's wealthy; chillies and maize reached Asia.
q.system: The first trade link connecting every inhabited continent.

events.bluf: Spain wanted a way to reach Asian markets from its American colonies, and in 1565 Spanish navigator Andrés de Urdaneta found the return route across the Pacific that made a regular trade possible. For 250 years galleons carried American silver from Acapulco to Manila and brought back Chinese silk and porcelain. The route completed the first global trade network and tied Ming China's economy to Spanish American mines.
events.lens: Trade follows price gaps: when a good is worth much more in one place than another, merchants will find a way to connect them.

events.who: William of Orange vs. Philip II of Spain
events.what: Eighty Years' War for independence.
events.why: Taxation came first, then the overriding of provincial privileges, then religion. The towns had money and the sea; Spain's armies had to march from Italy.
events.sig: Spain recognised the republic in 1648. The south stayed Spanish and became Belgium. Amsterdam founded its exchange bank in 1609 and the VOC in 1602.
events.hook: The Netherlands rebelled against Spain and created a new kind of country.
events.story: The Low Countries were the richest lands in Spanish King Philip II's empire. His taxes, his centralising officials and his persecution of Protestants alienated nobles and towns alike. The Duke of Alba executed leading nobles in 1568. Prince William of Orange led the armed revolt. The seven northern provinces declared independence in 1581.
events.then: Spain recognised the republic in 1648. The south stayed Spanish and became Belgium. Amsterdam founded its exchange bank in 1609 and the VOC in 1602.
events.now: The revolt split the Low Countries into the Netherlands and Belgium and created the Dutch Republic, whose stock exchange, public bank and chartered company are the tools of modern capitalism.

q.why: Spanish taxes, centralisation and persecution of Protestants.
q.stakes: Self-government and religious freedom for the Netherlands.
q.decided: Dutch sea power, water defences and Spanish exhaustion.
q.cost: Sieges and massacres, such as the sack of Antwerp in 1576.
q.changed: An independent Dutch Republic emerged as a trading superpower.

events.bluf: Spanish King Philip II set out to tax the Low Countries hard and stamp out Protestantism there. The provinces rose under William of Orange, and after eighty years of war the seven northern ones won independence. The Dutch Republic became the world's leading trading power and the model of a commercial, tolerant, decentralised state.
events.trig: Alba's Council of Troubles executed the Counts of Egmont and Hoorn in June 1568.
events.lens: Rulers who override local privileges to raise taxes meet the fiercest resistance in their richest, best-organized regions.
events.fact: Spain's army walked to the Netherlands along the Spanish Road through Savoy, Franche-Comté and Lorraine.

kv: people in the Dutch Republic, c. 1600

events.who: Holy League (Spain, Venice, Pope) vs. Ottomans
events.what: Largest galley battle; Ottoman fleet destroyed.
events.why: Venice wanted Cyprus back. Spain wanted its Italian coasts safe. The Pope wanted a crusade.
events.sig: Venice signed a separate peace in 1573 and gave up Cyprus. Spain turned to the Netherlands, the Ottomans to Persia.
events.hook: The largest galley battle in history stopped the Ottoman navy in the West.
events.story: The Ottomans had taken Venetian Cyprus in 1570. Pope Pius V formed a Holy League with Spanish King Philip II and Venice under Don John of Austria. About 200 galleys met on each side in the Gulf of Patras on 7 October 1571; the Ottomans lost most of theirs.
events.then: Venice signed a separate peace in 1573 and gave up Cyprus. Spain turned to the Netherlands, the Ottomans to Persia.
events.now: Lepanto fixed the Mediterranean as a stalemate between two exhausted empires. Spain and the Ottomans turned to other fronts, and Europe's growth moved to the Atlantic.
events.fact: Miguel de Cervantes, later author of Don Quixote, lost the use of his left hand in the battle.

sites.d: Holy League fleet gathered here.
~200 galleys a side; Ottoman fleet destroyed.

causes.why: Ottoman sea power, built up under Suleiman, dominated the Mediterranean until a Spanish-led Holy League fleet destroyed it at Lepanto. It was rebuilt within a year.

q.why: The Ottoman conquest of Cyprus.
q.decided: Venetian galleasses' firepower and Spanish infantry.
q.cost: Perhaps 30,000 Ottoman and 8,000 Christian dead; thousands of galley slaves were freed.
q.changed: Christian morale soared, though the Ottomans soon rebuilt their fleet.

events.bluf: Pope Pius V assembled a Holy League of Spain and Venice to recover Cyprus from the Ottomans. The league destroyed the Ottoman fleet off Greece and gained nothing: the Ottomans rebuilt in a year, kept Cyprus, and Venice made peace in 1573. The battle ended Ottoman naval expansion in the western Mediterranean and little else.
events.lens: Separate symbolic victories from strategic ones: ask what the loser could rebuild and what the winner actually gained.

toll.n: The largest galley battle in history. The Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within a year.

events.what: Spanish colonial capital founded.
events.why: Spain wanted a base near China and the Spice Islands. Manila had an excellent harbour.
events.sig: Manila became the hub of the galleon trade between Acapulco and Asia. Chinese merchants settled there in large numbers and were periodically expelled or massacred. Spain ruled the islands for 327 years, until 1898.
events.hook: Spain founded Manila, linking Asia and the Americas for the first time.
events.story: Spanish commander Miguel López de Legazpi captured the Muslim port of Maynila on Luzon from its ruler, Rajah Sulayman, in 1571. He made it the capital of the Spanish Philippines. Its harbour linked China's traders with the silver arriving from Mexico.
events.then: Manila became the hub of the galleon trade between Acapulco and Asia. Chinese merchants settled there in large numbers and were periodically expelled or massacred. Spain ruled the islands for 327 years, until 1898.
events.now: About 80 per cent of Filipinos are Catholic. Spanish names and loanwords, and the separate identity of the Muslim south, show where Spanish rule reached and where it stopped.

causes.why: Once a return route across the Pacific was found in 1565, Spain needed an Asian base. Manila, founded in 1571, became the port where Chinese merchants met the silver galleons from Acapulco.

q.before: Local rajahs and datus ruled the island ports.
q.how: Conquest by a small Spanish force.
q.claim: Possession for Philip II, after whom the islands were named.
q.lasted: Spain ruled until 1898.

events.bluf: Spanish commander Miguel López de Legazpi set out to give Spain a base near China and the Spice Islands. In 1571 he took the Muslim port of Maynila on Luzon from its ruler, Rajah Sulayman, and made it the capital of the Spanish Philippines, where Chinese traders met the silver arriving from Mexico. Spain ruled the islands for 327 years and made the Philippines Asia's leading Catholic nation.
events.lens: The places colonial power never fully controlled often mark a country's internal divides today: compare the Catholic north and Muslim Mindanao.
events.fact: The Manila galleon sailed between Manila and Acapulco for 250 years, from 1565 to 1815.

events.what: Thousands of Huguenots killed.
events.why: Catholic leaders feared Coligny's influence over the king and his push for war with Spain. The wedding had put the Huguenot leadership in one place.
events.sig: Huguenot writers developed theories of resistance and limited monarchy. The wars continued until 1598.
events.hook: A royal wedding turned into a slaughter of Protestants.
events.story: Huguenot nobles came to Paris in August 1572 for the wedding of Protestant Henry of Navarre to the king's sister. French Queen Mother Catherine de' Medici and the Guise faction, with French King Charles IX's assent, ordered the Huguenot leaders killed on 24 August. Admiral Gaspard de Coligny died first; Catholic mobs killed thousands in Paris and the provinces.
events.then: Huguenot writers developed theories of resistance and limited monarchy. The wars continued until 1598.
events.now: The resistance theories written after the massacre fed later ideas of limited and constitutional government. The religious wars ran 26 more years.

causes.why: The massacre of thousands of Huguenots in Paris and other cities was the bloodiest moment of France's civil wars.

q.why: Fear that Huguenot leaders would dominate the king.
q.stakes: Who would control the French crown.
q.decided: A royal order to kill the leaders, which mobs widened into a massacre.
q.cost: Thousands killed in Paris and many more across France.
q.changed: The wars of religion grew more bitter; Protestant writers began to justify resisting kings.

events.bluf: French Queen Mother Catherine de' Medici and the Guise faction ordered the killing of Huguenot leaders gathered in Paris for a royal wedding, to end their influence over the young king. Mobs then killed thousands across France. The massacre destroyed any chance of compromise and taught Protestants to argue that subjects may resist a tyrant.
events.lens: Atrocities meant to end a conflict often radicalize the other side instead.
events.fact: Pope Gregory XIII had a medal struck and a Te Deum sung to celebrate the news.

events.who: Túpac Amaru I; Spanish viceroy Toledo
events.what: Last Inca ruler executed.
events.why: Toledo wanted the last independent Inca state gone and Spanish control over Andean labour tightened.
events.sig: Toledo forced Indigenous people into new planned towns (reducciones), formalised the mita labour draft for Potosí and cracked down on the Inca nobility. Resistance went underground and resurfaced in later rebellions.
events.hook: Spain captured the last Inca ruler and executed him in Cusco.
events.story: For 35 years after the conquest, Inca rulers held out in the remote forest state of Vilcabamba. In 1572 Peruvian Viceroy Francisco de Toledo sent an army, which captured the last Inca ruler, Túpac Amaru. Toledo had him beheaded in Cusco's main square in September 1572.
events.then: Toledo forced Indigenous people into new planned towns (reducciones), formalised the mita labour draft for Potosí and cracked down on the Inca nobility. Resistance went underground and resurfaced in later rebellions.
events.now: Toledo's reorganisation after 1572, the planned towns and the formalised mita, set the terms of Andean labour until independence, and Túpac Amaru's name became the banner of resistance from the rebellion of 1780 onward.

causes.why: Inca resistance held out in the jungle state of Vilcabamba for four decades.

q.why: Spain wanted to end the last independent Inca state.
q.decided: A Spanish army penetrated the jungle refuge.
q.cost: Túpac Amaru was executed before a grieving crowd.
q.changed: Indigenous resistance went underground.

events.bluf: Peruvian Viceroy Francisco de Toledo set out to end the last independent Inca state and tighten Spain's hold on Andean labour. His army took Vilcabamba in 1572 and captured Inca ruler Túpac Amaru, whom he had beheaded in Cusco. The conquest of the Andes was complete, and Toledo reorganised Andean society to extract silver and tribute.
events.lens: Conquests are completed less by battles than by reorganizing how people live, work and pay.
events.fact: Túpac Amaru's name was taken up by the rebellion of 1780, by guerrilla movements in Peru and Uruguay and by the rapper Tupac Shakur.

kv: of Inca resistance after Cusco fell, 1536–1572
last Inca ruler, Túpac Amaru, executed

events.h: Tycho Brahe sees a new star
events.hook: A brilliant new star showed the heavens could change, against 2,000 years of teaching.
events.what: A brilliant new star showed the heavens could change, against 2,000 years of teaching.
events.story: On 11 November 1572 Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe saw a new star in Cassiopeia, at first brighter than Venus. His measurements showed it fixed among the background stars, far beyond the Moon. It was a supernova.
events.why: A rare exploding star appeared while an astronomer obsessed with precision was watching.
events.then: Danish King Frederick II funded Tycho's observatory on Hven. German astronomer Johannes Kepler inherited the data in 1601 and derived the laws of planetary motion.
events.sig: Danish King Frederick II funded Tycho's observatory on Hven. German astronomer Johannes Kepler inherited the data in 1601 and derived the laws of planetary motion.
events.now: Tycho set the standard that theory must answer to precise measurement. The Danish crown's funding of his observatory was the first state investment in research.

q.problem: Was the sky beyond the Moon really unchanging, as Aristotle taught?
q.how: Tycho measured the star's position with large instruments and found no parallax.
q.replaced: The belief in perfect, unchanging heavens.
q.spread: His short book On the New Star (1573) was read across Europe.
q.next: Kepler used Tycho's data to find the laws of planetary motion.

events.bluf: Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe measured a new star in 1572 to see whether it lay below or beyond the Moon. It showed no parallax, so it lay among the fixed stars, where ancient doctrine said nothing could change. The result broke Aristotle's unchanging heavens, and Tycho's later measurements gave Kepler the data for the laws of planetary motion.
events.lens: Better measurement often comes before better theory: those who collect reliable data make breakthroughs possible.
events.fact: Tycho wore a metal nose after losing part of his own in a duel over a mathematical dispute.

events.h: Akbar opens his House of Worship to all faiths
events.who: Emperor Akbar; Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian scholars
events.hook: The Mughal emperor hosted debates between scholars of every religion.
events.what: The Mughal emperor hosted debates between scholars of every religion.
events.story: In 1575 Mughal Emperor Akbar built the Ibadat Khana at his new capital, Fatehpur Sikri. Debates began among Muslim theologians, whose quarrels disappointed him; within a few years Hindu pandits, Jain monks, Zoroastrian priests and Jesuit priests from Goa took part. Akbar presided in person.
events.why: Akbar ruled a mostly non-Muslim empire, wanted to curb the influence of orthodox clerics over the throne and was curious about faith.
events.then: In 1579 a declaration drafted by his courtiers gave him the authority to decide disputed religious questions, and sulh-i kul, 'peace with all', guided appointments and law. Orthodox clerics resented it. Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1679.
events.sig: In 1579 a declaration drafted by his courtiers gave him the authority to decide disputed religious questions, and sulh-i kul, 'peace with all', guided appointments and law. Orthodox clerics resented it. Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1679.
events.now: The policy of sulh-i kul set Mughal religious practice from 1579 until Aurangzeb's reign, and Akbar's court is the precedent cited in South Asia's debates over secularism.

causes.why: Secure on his throne, Akbar opened a hall for debate among faiths.

q.belief: Whether any one faith held all the truth.
q.authority: The emperor, who claimed the final word on religious disputes.
q.believers: Most Indians kept their own faiths under a tolerant ruler.
q.fallout: Orthodox Muslim scholars resented Akbar's openness.
q.today: Fatehpur Sikri is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.bluf: Mughal Emperor Akbar built a House of Worship to hear the faiths of his empire argued in front of him and to set the throne above the clerics. Debates among Muslim jurists widened within a few years to Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuits. Religious policy became the emperor's to decide, and his 'peace with all' underpinned Mughal rule over a Hindu-majority population until his successors moved back toward orthodoxy.
events.lens: Rulers of diverse empires often place themselves above all faiths to limit the power of any one religious establishment.
events.fact: Akbar later devised the Din-i Ilahi, a court cult of his own, which drew only a handful of followers.

kv: faiths debated: Sunni, Shi'a, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian

events.who: Mary, Queen of Scots; Elizabeth I
events.hook: Elizabeth I executed her Catholic cousin, ending Spain's hope of a Catholic queen in England.
events.what: Elizabeth I executed her Catholic cousin, ending Spain's hope of a Catholic queen in England.
events.story: Mary, Queen of Scots, had been held in England for nineteen years. Her letters approving the Babington Plot to assassinate Elizabeth were intercepted by Secretary Francis Walsingham. She was convicted and beheaded at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587.
events.why: Catholic plotters, backed by Spain, treated Mary as Elizabeth's rightful heir. The intercepted letters gave the ministers their proof.
events.then: Philip II launched the Armada the next year claiming England for himself. Scottish King James VI became English King James I in 1603.
events.sig: Philip II launched the Armada the next year claiming England for himself. Scottish King James VI became English King James I in 1603.
events.now: The union of crowns in 1603 led to the union of parliaments in 1707. The question of Scotland's place in the United Kingdom has run since.

q.before: Elizabeth ruled England; Catholics saw Mary as heir.
q.how: A treason trial and the execution of an anointed queen.
q.claim: That Mary had plotted to kill Elizabeth.
q.winners: Elizabeth's Protestant government; Mary's son later inherited both crowns.
q.lasted: Yes: no Catholic heir threatened Elizabeth again.

events.bluf: English Queen Elizabeth I's ministers wanted the Catholic claimant removed before another plot succeeded. Mary, Queen of Scots, was tried for the Babington Plot and beheaded in 1587. Her death freed Spanish King Philip II to claim England for himself and cleared the way for her Protestant son to unite the crowns in 1603.
events.lens: A rival claimant in custody is a permanent focus for conspiracy, and regimes eventually choose between that risk and execution.
events.fact: Elizabeth signed the death warrant and then claimed it had been sent without her order.

events.hook: Drake 'singed the King of Spain's beard', burning Spanish ships and delaying the Armada by a year.
events.what: Drake 'singed the King of Spain's beard', burning Spanish ships and delaying the Armada by a year.
events.story: Spain was assembling an invasion fleet in 1587. English privateer Sir Francis Drake sailed into Cádiz harbour in April, destroyed some thirty ships and stores, and then burned thousands of seasoned barrel staves along the Portuguese coast.
events.why: Elizabeth I's government wanted Philip's invasion stopped before it was ready.
events.then: The Armada sailed in 1588 with casks of green wood that leaked and spoiled its food and water.
events.sig: The Armada sailed in 1588 with casks of green wood that leaked and spoiled its food and water.
events.now: The raid delayed the Armada by a year and showed that a fleet could be destroyed in harbour before it sailed; pre-emptive naval strikes from Copenhagen in 1807 to Pearl Harbor follow its logic.
events.wk: Singeing the King of Spain's Beard

q.why: To wreck Spanish invasion preparations.
q.decided: Speed and surprise against an unprepared harbour.
q.cost: Two dozen or more Spanish ships destroyed.
q.changed: The Armada was delayed until 1588.

events.bluf: English privateer Sir Francis Drake sailed to wreck Spanish King Philip II's invasion fleet before it could leave port. He burned dozens of ships and the seasoned barrel staves meant for the fleet's stores. The Armada sailed a year late with leaking casks, and the raid set the precedent for striking a fleet in harbour.
events.lens: Logistics is a target: destroying supplies can matter as much as sinking warships.
events.fact: Drake called the raid 'singeing the King of Spain's beard'.

events.who: ~115 English settlers led by John White
events.what: England's first attempt at a permanent settlement; found abandoned in 1590.
events.why: Raleigh wanted a base for raiding Spanish shipping and a claim to North American land. England's war with Spain, including the Armada year of 1588, kept every ship at home.
events.sig: War with Spain delayed resupply until 1590, by which time the colony was gone. England's next attempt, Jamestown in 1607, was organised by a joint-stock company with far more capital.
events.hook: England's first try at an American colony disappeared, leaving one carved word behind.
events.story: English courtier Sir Walter Raleigh held a royal patent to settle North America. About 115 settlers under Governor John White landed on Roanoke Island in 1587. White sailed to England for supplies and was kept there by the war with Spain. When supply ships returned in 1590 the colony was gone, and the only clue was 'CROATOAN' carved into a post.
events.then: War with Spain delayed resupply until 1590, by which time the colony was gone. England's next attempt, Jamestown in 1607, was organised by a joint-stock company with far more capital.
events.now: Roanoke showed that a colony run as one courtier's venture would starve without steady supply and capital. England's next attempt, Jamestown in 1607, was financed by a joint-stock company with far more money behind it.

q.before: Algonquian peoples, including the Croatoan and Secotan, lived on the Outer Banks.
q.how: A settlement founded under Sir Walter Raleigh's royal charter.
q.lasted: No: it was gone by 1590.

events.bluf: English courtier Sir Walter Raleigh, holding a royal patent, planted a colony on Roanoke Island as a base for raiding Spanish shipping and a claim to North American land. About 115 settlers under Governor John White landed in 1587; war with Spain delayed resupply, and when ships returned in 1590 the colony was gone. The failure taught England that a colony needed steady supply, capital and workable relations with Native peoples, the lessons behind the joint-stock company that founded Jamestown.
events.lens: Distant outposts live on their supply lines; when the home country is distracted by war, they wither.
events.myth: The colonists vanished without a trace. The carved word named Croatoan Island and its people, who had been friendly to the English, and the likeliest reading is that survivors joined them.
events.fact: Virginia Dare, the first English child born in America, was born at Roanoke in August 1587 and vanished with the colony.

kv: before a supply ship returned in 1590

events.what: Spain's invasion fleet broken by English ships and storms.
events.why: Philip wanted Catholicism restored in England, English support for the Dutch ended and English raids on his treasure fleets stopped.
events.sig: The war ran until 1604 and Spain rebuilt its navy. England and the Dutch expanded into the Atlantic and Asia. Protestantism became the core of English identity.
events.hook: England survived Spain's great invasion fleet, and its rise at sea began.
events.story: In 1588 Spanish King Philip II sent about 130 ships up the Channel to carry the Duke of Parma's army across from Flanders. English ships harried the fleet, fire ships broke its formation off Calais and the battle of Gravelines scattered it. Storms wrecked dozens of ships on the voyage home round Scotland and Ireland.
events.then: The war ran until 1604 and Spain rebuilt its navy. England and the Dutch expanded into the Atlantic and Asia. Protestantism became the core of English identity.
events.now: The defeat kept Protestant England and the Dutch Republic in being, which decided the religious map of northern Europe. The Armada became the founding story of British sea power.
events.fact: More Spanish ships were lost to storms off Scotland and Ireland than to English guns.

sites.d: Armada sailed from here, May 1588.
English fire ships scattered the fleet.
Storms wrecked dozens of ships on the way home.

causes.why: England's support for the Dutch rebels was one of the main reasons Philip II sent the Armada against England.
Philip II aimed to remove the Protestant Elizabeth, especially after she executed the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots, in 1587.
American silver funded Philip II's armies and fleets, including the Armada, though never enough to keep the crown solvent.
Mary's execution removed the Catholic heir, and Philip II pressed his own claim by force.
Drake's raid delayed the Armada a year and ruined its water casks.

q.why: Philip II wanted to restore Catholicism in England and stop English support for the Dutch.
q.decided: English fire ships at Calais, the fight at Gravelines, and storms on the way home.
q.cost: Perhaps a third or more of the Armada's ships and thousands of men lost.
q.changed: England survived and grew bolder at sea.

events.bluf: Spanish King Philip II sent 130 ships to escort an army from the Netherlands to England, to restore Catholicism there and end English aid to the Dutch rebels. English fire ships and gunnery broke the fleet off Calais and storms wrecked much of it on the voyage home. England and the Dutch kept their independence, Spain's bid to control northern Europe failed, and English sea power began.
events.trig: The execution of Mary, Queen of Scots in 1587 ended Philip's hope of a Catholic successor and freed him to claim England himself.
events.lens: Invading an island requires controlling the sea first. That logic shaped British strategy from 1588 to 1940.

toll.n: Most Spanish deaths came from shipwreck, disease and hunger on the voyage home around Scotland and Ireland. Thousands of English sailors died of disease afterwards.

events.what: Ended the warring-states era.
events.why: Toyotomi Hideyoshi took over Oda Nobunaga's armies and alliances after Nobunaga's assassination in 1582. He combined force with deals that let defeated lords keep their domains in return for loyalty.
events.sig: The 'sword hunt' of 1588 disarmed the peasantry, edicts fixed social status and a national land survey standardised taxes. He invaded Korea in 1592 and 1597 and failed both times. After his death in 1598 Tokugawa Ieyasu won the struggle for power.
events.hook: A peasant-born general reunited Japan after a century of war.
events.story: Warlord Oda Nobunaga was assassinated in 1582 with Japan half unified. Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who had begun as a foot soldier in Nobunaga's army, took over his armies and alliances. By 1590, with the fall of the Hōjō at Odawara, he had defeated or won over every rival lord. He then disarmed the peasantry and froze the social classes.
events.then: The 'sword hunt' of 1588 disarmed the peasantry, edicts fixed social status and a national land survey standardised taxes. He invaded Korea in 1592 and 1597 and failed both times. After his death in 1598 Tokugawa Ieyasu won the struggle for power.
events.now: Hideyoshi's sword hunt, land survey and separation of samurai from peasants fixed Japan's social order for 270 years; his invasions of Korea poisoned relations with it for four centuries and ended Japanese expansion until 1894.

causes.why: A century of warring domains ended only when Nobunaga and then Hideyoshi conquered or co-opted their rivals.
Firearms, soon mass-produced in Japan, helped the warlords who ended Japan's century of civil war.

q.before: Japan was divided among warring lords.
q.how: Military campaigns and alliances.
q.claim: Imperial titles granted by the court.
q.lasted: His family lost power after his death in 1598.

events.bluf: Japanese regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi set out to finish the unification Oda Nobunaga had begun and to make it permanent. By 1590 he had defeated or won over every rival lord, and he then disarmed the peasants and froze the social classes. The order he fixed held for 270 years under the Tokugawa; his two invasions of Korea failed, devastated the peninsula and left lasting bitterness there.
events.lens: Unifiers often turn their armies abroad once the wars at home end, to keep soldiers and lords occupied.
events.fact: Korean Admiral Yi Sun-sin, who destroyed Hideyoshi's fleets, is Korea's national hero.

events.who: Moroccan army with firearms; Sultan al-Mansur
events.what: Moroccan guns defeated Songhai.
events.why: Al-Mansur wanted the gold of the Sahel to fund his state and compete with the Ottomans. A disputed succession had weakened Songhai.
events.sig: The Moroccan commanders in Timbuktu soon became independent of Marrakesh, and the region fragmented. Gold reached Morocco in a fraction of the amounts al-Mansur hoped. Leading Timbuktu men of learning, among them the jurist Ahmad Baba, were deported to Morocco.
events.hook: Moroccan musketeers crossed the Sahara and destroyed Songhai.
events.story: A disputed succession had weakened Songhai. In 1590 Moroccan Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur sent about 4,000 soldiers, many armed with muskets, across the Sahara under the commander Judar Pasha. At Tondibi in March 1591 they routed Songhai's much larger army of cavalry and archers and took Gao and Timbuktu.
events.then: The Moroccan commanders in Timbuktu soon became independent of Marrakesh, and the region fragmented. Gold reached Morocco in a fraction of the amounts al-Mansur hoped. Leading Timbuktu men of learning, among them the jurist Ahmad Baba, were deported to Morocco.
events.now: No single state has controlled the Niger bend since 1591. The region's trade and power shifted from the desert routes to the Atlantic coast over the following two centuries, and Timbuktu's decline became the symbol of the end of West Africa's imperial age.

causes.why: Songhai's gold trade attracted Morocco's sultan, who sent musketeers across the Sahara; they won at Tondibi in 1591.

q.why: Morocco wanted Songhai's gold mines and trade.
q.decided: Moroccan firearms against cavalry and archers.
q.cost: Songhai's army destroyed; Timbuktu's scholars were later deported.
q.changed: Songhai broke apart into smaller states.

events.bluf: Moroccan Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur sent about 4,000 soldiers, many with muskets, across the Sahara to take the gold of the Sahel and fund a state that could stand up to the Ottomans. At Tondibi in March 1591 they routed Songhai's far larger army of cavalry and archers and took Gao and Timbuktu. Songhai, the last of the great Sahel empires, was destroyed; the Niger bend broke into smaller states, and West Africa's trade turned toward the Atlantic coast where Europeans bought.
events.lens: Firearms let small, disciplined forces beat large traditional armies, but conquering is easier than governing from across a desert.
events.fact: Tradition holds that Songhai drove a herd of cattle at the Moroccan line and the gunfire turned the animals back into Songhai's own ranks.

kv: Moroccan troops, ~2,500 of them with firearms

events.who: Hideyoshi; Korean Admiral Yi Sun-sin; Ming China
events.what: Imjin War: Korea and Ming China drove Japan out by 1598.
events.why: Having unified Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi needed new conquests to reward his lords and armies, and he aimed to replace China at the centre of the East Asian order.
events.sig: Korea was ravaged: cities burned, many thousands died, and potters and artisans were carried off to Japan. The cost of intervention helped empty the Ming treasury, one factor in the dynasty's collapse in 1644. Japan withdrew after Hideyoshi's death in 1598, and the Tokugawa later restored relations.
events.hook: Japan invaded Korea to reach China, and Korea's admiral sank its fleet.
events.story: Japanese regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi landed armies in Korea in 1592 after Korea refused passage for an attack on China. The armies took Seoul quickly and pushed north. Korean Admiral Yi Sun-sin's armoured 'turtle ships' cut Japanese supply lines along the coast, and Ming China sent an army. A second invasion in 1597 also failed.
events.then: Korea was ravaged: cities burned, many thousands died, and potters and artisans were carried off to Japan. The cost of intervention helped empty the Ming treasury, one factor in the dynasty's collapse in 1644. Japan withdrew after Hideyoshi's death in 1598, and the Tokugawa later restored relations.
events.now: Korea's memory of the invasions and of Admiral Yi still colours its relations with Japan; the war's cost weakened the Ming before their collapse in 1644, and Japan's withdrawal left the Chinese-centred order in place for another 250 years.
events.fact: Admiral Yi's armoured 'turtle ships' won battles against heavy odds; at Myeongnyang in 1597 he beat a fleet of more than 100 ships with 13. He lost no naval battle in his career.

causes.why: With Japan united and its samurai needing employment, Hideyoshi turned outward, aiming at Ming China through Korea.

q.why: Hideyoshi wanted to conquer Ming China, using Korea as a road.
q.stakes: Korea's survival and the balance of power in East Asia.
q.decided: Admiral Yi's navy, Korean guerrillas and Ming armies.
q.cost: Korea was devastated; many Koreans were killed or taken to Japan.
q.changed: Japan withdrew after Hideyoshi's death, and Ming finances were badly strained.

events.bluf: Japanese regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded Korea in 1592 to reach China and replace the Ming at the centre of the East Asian order. His armies took Seoul within weeks; Korean Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet cut their supply lines, a Ming army drove them back, and the invasions ended in withdrawal in 1598. Korea was laid waste, the Ming treasury was drained at a critical moment, and Korea kept a lasting memory of Japanese aggression.
events.trig: Korea refused to let Japanese armies pass through on their way to attack China.
events.lens: Korea's geography makes it the bridge, and the battlefield, between continental and maritime powers.

kv: Japanese troops in the first invasion

events.what: Granted Huguenots religious rights.
events.why: Neither side could win. Henry needed both communities to govern.
events.sig: Cardinal Richelieu took the Huguenot fortresses in 1628 as a state within the state. French King Louis XIV revoked the edict in 1685; about 200,000 Huguenots left for the Netherlands, England, Prussia and the Cape.
events.hook: France's king granted Protestants the right to worship.
events.story: French King Henry IV, a Protestant who had converted to take Paris, issued the edict at Nantes in April 1598. Catholicism remained the state religion. Huguenots received freedom of conscience, worship in named places, and control of about 150 fortified towns.
events.then: Cardinal Richelieu took the Huguenot fortresses in 1628 as a state within the state. French King Louis XIV revoked the edict in 1685; about 200,000 Huguenots left for the Netherlands, England, Prussia and the Cape.
events.now: Nantes was the first European settlement to tolerate two faiths by law. Its revocation in 1685 drove 200,000 skilled Huguenots to France's rivals, the first modern case of persecution exporting an economy.

causes.why: Decades of killing left France exhausted. Henry IV, a Protestant who converted to win Paris, granted the Huguenots toleration.

q.belief: Whether two faiths could live under one king.
q.authority: The king imposed toleration by decree.
q.believers: Huguenots gained safety, but only in certain places.
q.fallout: Peace returned, though many Catholics resented it.
q.today: It is remembered as an early landmark of religious toleration.

events.bluf: French King Henry IV needed Huguenot loyalty and Catholic acceptance to rebuild royal authority after 36 years of war. His edict kept Catholicism as the state religion and gave Protestants freedom of conscience, places of worship and 150 fortified towns. France got peace and a stronger crown; the edict held until a king who no longer needed it revoked it in 1685.
events.lens: Toleration granted by one ruler can be revoked by the next; durable rights need institutions that outlast the ruler.
events.fact: Henry IV was assassinated by a Catholic fanatic in 1610.

events.h: Shah Abbas makes Isfahan his capital
events.hook: Safavid Iran's greatest shah rebuilt his empire and made Isfahan one of the world's great cities.
events.what: Safavid Iran's greatest shah rebuilt his empire and made Isfahan one of the world's great cities.
events.story: Persian Shah Abbas I inherited in 1587 an empire losing land to the Ottomans and the Uzbeks and run by Qizilbash tribal chiefs. He reformed the army with musketeers and artillery and took back territory from both neighbours. In 1598 he moved his capital to Isfahan and built the Naqsh-e Jahan square and its mosques.
events.why: The Qizilbash chiefs had made and unmade shahs. Abbas needed forces loyal to him alone and a capital away from their power.
events.then: He built musketeer and artillery corps from converted Caucasian slave-soldiers, retook Tabriz and Baghdad, expelled the Portuguese from Hormuz with English help in 1622 and promoted the silk trade. His habit of confining royal princes in the palace produced weak successors.
events.sig: He built musketeer and artillery corps from converted Caucasian slave-soldiers, retook Tabriz and Baghdad, expelled the Portuguese from Hormuz with English help in 1622 and promoted the silk trade. His habit of confining royal princes in the palace produced weak successors.
events.now: Abbas rebuilt Persia as a centralised state with a slave army, a capital and a silk export monopoly, which let a Shi'a Persia survive between Sunni empires; the state he made is the ancestor of modern Iran.

causes.why: After defeat at Chaldiran, Abbas rebuilt Safavid power with firearms of his own and moved his capital away from the vulnerable frontier.

q.before: The Safavid state had been weakened by civil war and Ottoman and Uzbek attacks.
q.how: Military reform with musketeers and artillery, and loyal slave-soldiers from the Caucasus.
q.claim: Safavid dynastic right and Shi'a leadership.
q.lasted: Safavid power declined after his death in 1629.

events.bluf: Persian Shah Abbas I set out to free the throne from the Qizilbash chiefs who had put it there and to recover the land lost to the Ottomans and Uzbeks. He built an army of slave-soldiers and gunners loyal to him alone, took back Tabriz and Baghdad and moved his capital to Isfahan in 1598. Safavid Iran became a centralised state able to hold its own between the Ottomans and the Mughals for another century.
events.lens: Rulers who build armies loyal only to themselves can break the power of hereditary elites, but such systems depend on capable rulers.
events.fact: Abbas moved the Armenian merchants of Julfa to a new suburb of Isfahan, New Julfa, to run his silk trade with Europe.

kv: Naqsh-e Jahan square, among the largest in the world
people in Isfahan at its height (est.)

events.what: Decisive battle for control of Japan.
events.why: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's death in 1598 left a child heir, and the regents he appointed fought for power.
events.sig: Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun in 1603, confiscated or cut the lands of the losers and placed trusted allies in strategic domains. Defeated 'outside' lords, notably Chōshū and Satsuma, nursed the grievance for two and a half centuries and led the overthrow of the shogunate in 1868.
events.hook: One battle decided who would rule Japan for 250 years.
events.story: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's death in 1598 left a child heir and a council of regents who fought for power. On 21 October 1600 about 160,000 samurai met in a foggy valley at Sekigahara. Tokugawa Ieyasu's eastern army faced a western coalition led by Ishida Mitsunari in the heir's name. Western lord Kobayakawa Hideaki and others switched sides during the battle, and the coalition collapsed.
events.then: Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun in 1603, confiscated or cut the lands of the losers and placed trusted allies in strategic domains. Defeated 'outside' lords, notably Chōshū and Satsuma, nursed the grievance for two and a half centuries and led the overthrow of the shogunate in 1868.
events.now: The long Tokugawa peace built on this victory created a unified market, high literacy and a trained bureaucracy, which made Japan's rapid modernisation after 1868 possible.
events.fact: Western lord Kobayakawa Hideaki's 15,000 men decided the battle by attacking their own side; Ieyasu is said to have fired on his position to force his hand.

causes.why: Hideyoshi died in 1598 leaving a five-year-old heir. His regents split, and Tokugawa Ieyasu won the showdown.

q.why: Who would rule Japan after Hideyoshi.
q.decided: Defections by western lords during the battle.
q.cost: Thousands killed; defeated lords lost their lands.
q.changed: Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun three years later.

events.bluf: Tokugawa Ieyasu, the strongest of the regents left by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, fought a coalition loyal to Hideyoshi's child heir for control of unified Japan. He won in a day when key western lords changed sides. The victory gave his house 250 years of rule, and the line between his allies and his defeated enemies shaped Japanese politics until the losers' heirs overthrew the shogunate in 1868.
events.lens: The losers of a decisive civil war can shape politics for centuries: the defeated of 1600 became the revolutionaries of 1868.

events.what: Royal charter for Asian trade.
events.why: English merchants wanted Asian goods without Portuguese or Dutch middlemen. A joint stock spread the risk of voyages that took years.
events.sig: As Mughal power broke up after 1707, the Company's army fought French rivals and Indian states and won Bengal's revenues after Plassey in 1757. Parliament regulated it from 1773 and took India over after the rebellion of 1857.
events.hook: A group of London merchants got a charter to trade with Asia, and ended up ruling India.
events.story: English Queen Elizabeth I granted a group of London merchants a monopoly on English trade east of the Cape in 1600. Outcompeted by the Dutch in the spice islands, the Company traded cotton, indigo and saltpetre from fortified posts at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, and later Chinese tea.
events.then: As Mughal power broke up after 1707, the Company's army fought French rivals and Indian states and won Bengal's revenues after Plassey in 1757. Parliament regulated it from 1773 and took India over after the rebellion of 1857.
events.now: The Company is the clearest case of a corporation becoming a state. India's administrative system and its English-speaking elite descend from Company rule.
events.fact: At its peak the Company's private army was about twice the size of the British Army.

q.what: Spices at first, then Indian cotton cloth, indigo, saltpetre and Chinese tea.
q.who: Shareholders and Company servants grew rich; Indian weavers and peasants later paid.
q.scale: It grew to rule most of India with an army of about 200,000 men.
q.daily: Tea, cotton and pepper became everyday goods in Britain.
q.system: A chartered company that became a colonial state.

events.bluf: London merchants sought a share of the Asian trade held by Portugal and the Dutch, and Elizabeth I gave them a monopoly. Beaten in the spice islands, the Company turned to India and over two centuries became its ruler, with an army, tax powers and a foreign policy. Britain's Asian empire was built by a corporation, and the British state took it over in 1858.
events.lens: When a corporation can raise armies and taxes, the line between business and government disappears. Watch firms that control critical infrastructure.

kv: soldiers in its private army by 1803

events.what: First company to issue public shares.
events.why: Merchants wanted pooled capital for long voyages. The republic, at war with Spain, wanted a company that could fight the Iberians in Asia.
events.sig: The VOC drove the Portuguese from much of Asia, founded Batavia in 1619, conquered the Banda Islands and monopolised nutmeg, cloves and cinnamon. Corrupt and indebted, it was dissolved in 1799 and the Dutch state took its territories.
events.hook: The Dutch invented the modern corporation and the stock market.
events.story: The Dutch Republic merged its rival Asian ventures into the Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie in 1602. The company held a monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia and could build forts, sign treaties and wage war. Its capital was permanent, and investors sold their shares on the Amsterdam exchange.
events.then: The VOC drove the Portuguese from much of Asia, founded Batavia in 1619, conquered the Banda Islands and monopolised nutmeg, cloves and cinnamon. Corrupt and indebted, it was dissolved in 1799 and the Dutch state took its territories.
events.now: Tradable shares, the stock exchange and the chartered company descend from the VOC. Indonesia's borders follow the colonial state it began.
events.fact: The VOC paid dividends averaging about 18 per cent a year for nearly two centuries.

q.what: Spices, especially pepper, cloves and nutmeg.
q.who: Shareholders earned large dividends; Asian producers and the enslaved paid.
q.scale: It sent nearly 5,000 ships to Asia over two centuries.
q.daily: Spices and later coffee and tea became affordable in Europe.
q.system: Permanent shares traded on a stock exchange: the model for modern companies.

events.bluf: Dutch merchants and the Dutch state wanted one company strong enough to beat Portugal in Asia and fund voyages that took years. The VOC got a monopoly, permanent capital, and the power to make war and treaties. It built the Dutch empire in Indonesia and, with shares anyone could trade, the modern stock market.
events.lens: Financial innovation often comes from war and empire: the need to fund risky, armed ventures created modern capital markets.

kv: Europeans who sailed east on its ships

events.what: Military government established.
events.why: Victory at Sekigahara left Tokugawa Ieyasu the strongest lord in Japan, and a century of civil war made peace and order the overriding goal.
events.sig: Edo became one of the largest cities in the world and literacy spread. When Western warships arrived in 1853 the system could not respond, and the shogunate fell in 1868.
events.hook: The Tokugawa family began 250 years of peace and isolation in Japan.
events.story: In 1603 Emperor Go-Yōzei named Tokugawa Ieyasu shogun, and Ieyasu ruled from his castle town of Edo, now Tokyo. His heirs required the great lords to spend alternate years at Edo and to leave their families behind as hostages, which kept the lords loyal and drained their wealth. Japan's population, cities and commerce grew through the 1600s.
events.then: Edo became one of the largest cities in the world and literacy spread. When Western warships arrived in 1853 the system could not respond, and the shogunate fell in 1868.
events.now: Two and a half centuries of enforced peace gave Japan a unified market, a capital of a million people and high literacy by 1850, the base on which the Meiji state industrialised; the same controls left the shogunate unable to respond when Western warships arrived in 1853.
events.fact: By 1700 Edo was probably the largest city in the world, with about a million people.

causes.why: Victory let Ieyasu take the title of shogun in 1603. His family ruled Japan for 265 years.

q.before: Hideyoshi's family and a council of regents.
q.how: Victory in war, then appointment as shogun by the emperor.
q.claim: The emperor's appointment, backed by overwhelming military power.
q.winners: The Tokugawa family and its allies.
q.lasted: Yes: the shogunate lasted 265 years, until 1868.

events.bluf: Tokugawa Ieyasu, shogun from 1603, set out to make his victory at Sekigahara permanent after a century of civil war. His house ruled for 250 years by freezing the political and social order: hereditary classes, restricted foreign contact and forced attendance of the lords at Edo. The peace produced an urban, literate, commercial society that modernised fast after 1868, and a regime that could not answer Western warships when they came in 1853.
events.lens: Stability by freezing a system works until the outside world changes faster than the system can.

kv: people in Edo by 1720, then the world's largest city

events.who: Willem Janszoon and the Dutch ship Duyfken
events.hook: A Dutch ship made the first recorded European landing in Australia.
events.what: A Dutch ship made the first recorded European landing in Australia.
events.story: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) ran its Asian trade from Batavia and sent ships to probe for new markets. In early 1606 Dutch navigator Willem Janszoon took the Duyfken south from New Guinea and charted about 300 km of the west coast of Cape York Peninsula. Clashes with Aboriginal people left several of his crew dead. He reported swamps, hostile inhabitants and nothing to trade.
events.why: The VOC was searching for new trade and the rumoured Great South Land. A coast with nothing to sell gave it no reason to return.
events.then: Dutch ships charted much of Australia's west and north coasts over the next 40 years and named the land New Holland. The VOC found no profit in it and made no settlement. Britain's claim to the east coast in 1770 met no Dutch objection.
events.sig: Dutch ships charted much of Australia's west and north coasts over the next 40 years and named the land New Holland. The VOC found no profit in it and made no settlement. Britain's claim to the east coast in 1770 met no Dutch objection.
events.now: Dutch indifference left Australia to its Aboriginal peoples until Britain, with a different purpose, planted a penal colony in 1788. The 1606 contact is where the continent's two records, at least 50,000 years of Aboriginal occupation and four centuries of European writing, first touch, and how Australia tells that story is part of its politics.

q.what: A search for spices and gold beyond New Guinea.
q.who: The VOC, which found nothing it wanted.
q.scale: One small ship and about 300 km of coastline.
q.daily: No lasting effect on Aboriginal life yet.
q.system: The start of Dutch charting of 'New Holland'.

events.bluf: The Dutch East India Company sent navigator Willem Janszoon in the Duyfken to find trade south of New Guinea. He charted about 300 km of Cape York's west coast in 1606, lost several crew in clashes with Aboriginal people and reported nothing worth a return voyage. The company left the continent alone, and the first recorded European contact with Australia led to no settlement for another 180 years.
events.lens: Explorers see a land through their sponsors' interests: the Dutch saw no trade, so they saw no value.
events.fact: Janszoon took Cape York for part of New Guinea; Spanish navigator Luis Váez de Torres sailed through the strait that separates them the same year, and neither knew of the other.
events.btt: Exploration of Australia and the Pacific Islands

kv: before Cook reached Australia's east coast

events.who: Virginia Company of London; John Smith; Powhatan Confederacy
events.what: First permanent English settlement in America.
events.why: England wanted its share of the Americas after Spain's success, and investors hoped for gold and a passage to Asia. The joint-stock company let merchants spread the risk.
events.sig: Tobacco exports grew and settlers spread onto Powhatan land; the Powhatan struck back in 1622 and 1644. In 1619 Virginia created the House of Burgesses, the first elected assembly in English America. Labour came first from English indentured servants and increasingly from enslaved Africans.
events.hook: A failing company town in a Virginia swamp became the seed of English-speaking America.
events.story: In 1607 the Virginia Company of London, a joint-stock venture, sent about 100 men to found Jamestown in the territory of the Powhatan Confederacy. They hoped for gold and found disease, hunger and a powerful Native state. Most of the early settlers died, above all in the 'starving time' of 1609-10. Captain John Smith's discipline held the colony together in 1608-09, and tobacco, planted by colonist John Rolfe from 1612, made it pay.
events.then: Tobacco exports grew and settlers spread onto Powhatan land; the Powhatan struck back in 1622 and 1644. In 1619 Virginia created the House of Burgesses, the first elected assembly in English America. Labour came first from English indentured servants and increasingly from enslaved Africans.
events.now: Representative government, Native dispossession and slavery, central threads of American history, all appear together in Virginia's first decades.
events.fact: In the 'starving time' winter of 1609-10, about 80 per cent of the colonists died.

causes.why: Roanoke's failure taught English backers that a colony needed far more money and people. A joint-stock company provided both.
Cabot's voyage was the basis of England's claim to North America, which it finally acted on at Jamestown 110 years later.

q.before: The Powhatan Confederacy under Wahunsenacah ruled the Chesapeake region.
q.how: A company-funded colony with a royal charter.
q.claim: King James I's charter to the Virginia Company.
q.winners: Eventually the colonists; the Powhatan were pushed off their land.
q.lasted: Yes: Virginia became a royal colony in 1624.

events.bluf: The Virginia Company of London sent about 100 men to found a colony that would pay its investors in gold and a passage to Asia. They found disease, hunger and the Powhatan Confederacy; most early settlers died, and tobacco made the colony pay from 1612. Jamestown's survival on an export crop, land taken from Native peoples and bound labour that turned to African slavery set the model of the plantation South, and in 1619 it produced English America's first representative assembly.
events.lens: Colonies take the shape of their most profitable export: a cash crop needs land and labor, and colonists will take both.

kv: settlers landed, all men and boys

events.what: Permanent French base on the St. Lawrence.
events.why: France wanted control of the fur trade with Indigenous partners, and the narrows at Quebec commanded the St Lawrence.
events.sig: French traders and missionaries followed the rivers to the Great Lakes and the Mississippi, allied with the Wendat (Huron) and Algonquin against the Iroquois. With only about 70,000 settlers by 1760, New France fell to Britain in 1759-63.
events.hook: France planted a city on a cliff that would anchor a French empire in America.
events.story: French explorer Samuel de Champlain built a trading post in 1608 at a narrow point on the St Lawrence, where the river could be commanded. He allied with the Huron and Algonquin and traded guns and goods for beaver pelts, which Europe wanted for hats.
events.then: French traders and missionaries followed the rivers to the Great Lakes and the Mississippi, allied with the Wendat (Huron) and Algonquin against the Iroquois. With only about 70,000 settlers by 1760, New France fell to Britain in 1759-63.
events.now: Quebec's distinct identity, its language laws and its two independence referendums (1980 and 1995) trace back to this colony.

causes.why: Cartier's voyages gave France its claim to the St. Lawrence; Champlain built on them with a permanent post.

q.before: Indigenous nations such as the Huron (Wendat), Innu and Algonquin controlled the region.
q.how: A trading post and alliances with Indigenous partners.
q.claim: A royal monopoly on the fur trade.
q.winners: French traders and their Indigenous allies.
q.lasted: French rule lasted until 1763.

events.bluf: French explorer Samuel de Champlain built a post at the narrows of the St Lawrence to control the fur trade for France and its merchant backers. The post held, and New France grew as an empire of trade and Indigenous alliance rather than mass settlement, with about 70,000 settlers by 1760. Britain conquered it in 1759-63, and the French-speaking society it left has survived inside an English-speaking continent.
events.lens: Empires built on trade alliances cover huge territory lightly; empires built on settlement hold it densely. In a contest, density usually wins.
events.fact: The name Quebec comes from an Algonquin word for the place where the river narrows.

events.h: Kepler shows planets move in ellipses
events.hook: Using Tycho's data, Kepler found that planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, not circles.
events.what: Using Tycho's data, Kepler found that planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, not circles.
events.story: Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe died in 1601 and left his Mars observations to his assistant, German mathematician Johannes Kepler, who succeeded him as imperial mathematician in Prague. Kepler spent six years on the orbit. In 'Astronomia nova' of 1609 he published his first two laws: planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus, and sweep equal areas in equal times.
events.why: Copernicus's circles missed Tycho's Mars positions by eight minutes of arc, and Tycho's data were good to two. Kepler trusted the data over the circles.
events.then: The third law, relating orbital period to distance, followed in 1619. English mathematician Isaac Newton derived all three from gravity in 1687.
events.sig: The third law, relating orbital period to distance, followed in 1619. English mathematician Isaac Newton derived all three from gravity in 1687.
events.now: Kepler replaced the circles of ancient astronomy with laws derived from measurement, which made Newton's physics possible sixty years later and set the method modern science uses: fit the theory to the data.

causes.why: Kepler was a convinced Copernican who set out to make the Sun-centred system fit the data.
Kepler inherited Tycho's decades of precise observations of Mars.

q.problem: Copernicus's Sun-centred system with circular orbits still predicted planets' positions poorly.
q.how: Kepler tested shape after shape against Tycho's Mars data until an ellipse fitted.
q.replaced: The ancient assumption that heavenly motion must be perfectly circular.
q.spread: Slowly: even Galileo ignored the ellipses.
q.next: Newton's law of gravitation, which explained why orbits are ellipses.

events.bluf: Imperial mathematician Johannes Kepler set out to fit Tycho Brahe's measurements of Mars to the circles every astronomer assumed. The circles failed by eight minutes of arc, and he replaced them with ellipses. The first laws of planetary motion that matched observation made astronomy a physics and gave Newton the orbits his gravity had to explain.
events.lens: When the data refuse to fit, sometimes it is a hidden assumption, such as 'orbits must be circles', that has to go.
events.fact: Kepler's laws are still used to compute the orbits of planets, moons and spacecraft.

kv: error in Mars's position that broke the circle model

events.what: Saw Jupiter's moons, supported Copernicus.
events.why: Europe was already arguing over Copernicus. Galileo believed in testing ideas by experiment and saw at once what the instrument could decide.
events.sig: The Church banned Copernican books in 1616. Galileo's 'Dialogue' of 1632 appeared to mock Pope Urban VIII; he was tried in 1633 and confined to house arrest. His last book, on motion, was printed in Leiden in 1638.
events.hook: Galileo pointed a telescope at the sky and saw that Copernicus was right.
events.story: News of a Dutch spyglass reached Padua in 1609. Paduan mathematician Galileo Galilei built better ones and turned them on the sky: Jupiter's four moons, the phases of Venus, sunspots and mountains on the Moon. 'The Starry Messenger' of 1610 reported the findings in a style any educated reader could follow.
events.then: The Church banned Copernican books in 1616. Galileo's 'Dialogue' of 1632 appeared to mock Pope Urban VIII; he was tried in 1633 and confined to house arrest. His last book, on motion, was printed in Leiden in 1638.
events.now: Galileo's findings and his trial fixed the pattern of every later clash between evidence and authority. The Catholic Church acknowledged its error in 1992.
events.fact: Galileo named Jupiter's moons the Medicean Stars to win patronage from the Grand Duke of Tuscany; it worked.

causes.why: Galileo's observations of Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus were the first strong evidence for Copernicus.

q.problem: Was the Earth really the centre of everything?
q.how: A telescope magnifying about 20 times revealed moons around Jupiter and the phases of Venus.
q.replaced: Naked-eye astronomy.
q.spread: His book The Starry Messenger (1610) sold out quickly.
q.next: Strong evidence for Copernicus, and Galileo's clash with the Church.

events.bluf: Paduan mathematician Galileo Galilei built a telescope to see what the Dutch spyglass could show of the sky, and to make his name. He found Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus and mountains on the Moon, the first physical evidence for the Sun-centred model. His method of experiment and mathematics became the method of physics, and his clash with the Church became the defining story of evidence against authority.
events.lens: New instruments create new knowledge: ask what can now be measured that could not be before.

events.h: English beat the Portuguese at Swally
events.who: Captain Thomas Best (East India Company); a Portuguese fleet
events.hook: A small English fleet beat a Portuguese squadron off Surat and won a foothold in Mughal India.
events.what: A small English fleet beat a Portuguese squadron off Surat and won a foothold in Mughal India.
events.story: In November 1612 two East India Company ships, the Red Dragon and the Hosiander, under Captain Thomas Best fought a Portuguese squadron of four galleons off Swally Hole near Surat over several days. Mughal officials watching from shore let the English open a trading post, a 'factory', at Surat. In 1615 Sir Thomas Roe arrived as English King James I's ambassador to Mughal Emperor Jahangir.
events.why: Portugal had controlled India's sea trade with Europe for a century and tried to keep rivals out. Mughal officials wanted a counterweight to Portuguese naval power, which preyed on their pilgrim ships.
events.then: Surat became the Company's main base in India until Bombay replaced it in 1687. Roe's embassy of 1615-19 secured trading privileges from the emperor.
events.sig: Surat became the Company's main base in India until Bombay replaced it in 1687. Roe's embassy of 1615-19 secured trading privileges from the emperor.
events.now: The Company's presence in India began as a licensed guest of the Mughal emperor, and it traded under Indian rulers' permission for 140 years before it took territory at Plassey in 1757.

causes.why: The Company's ships had to fight Portugal for a foothold in India.

q.why: Portugal wanted to keep the English out of the Gujarat trade.
q.stakes: Access to the busiest port of Mughal India.
q.decided: English gunnery and seamanship against a larger fleet.
q.cost: Light casualties; the battle mattered for trade, not blood.
q.changed: The Mughals granted the English trading rights at Surat.

events.bluf: The English East India Company wanted a trading post at Surat, the Mughal Empire's main western port, and Portugal wanted to keep it out. Captain Thomas Best's two ships fought off a larger Portuguese squadron off Swally in November 1612. The Mughals licensed an English factory at Surat, and the Company's 335 years in India began with a trading permit rather than a conquest.
events.lens: Local rulers often welcome a new foreign power to balance an old one.
events.fact: Best's flagship, the Red Dragon, is reported to have staged the first performance of 'Hamlet' outside Europe, off Sierra Leone in 1607.

kv: the Mughals let the English open a trading post at Surat

events.what: Defenestration of Prague started war.
events.why: The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 had left Calvinists out and church lands in dispute. The Habsburgs wanted a Catholic, centralised empire; the princes, Sweden and France wanted it weak.
events.sig: Parts of Germany lost a third or more of their people. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 gave the princes the right to conduct their own foreign policy, made France and Sweden great powers and removed religion as a cause of war between European states.
events.hook: Central Europe fought its most destructive war before the 20th century.
events.story: Protestant nobles in Bohemia threw two imperial officials from a window of Prague Castle in May 1618 in protest at Habsburg curbs on their rights. Habsburg Emperor Ferdinand II crushed the revolt in 1620. The war drew in the Catholic League, the Protestant princes, Denmark, Sweden and in 1635 Catholic France, which fought on the Protestant side against the Habsburgs. Armies living off the land spread famine and plague across Germany.
events.then: Parts of Germany lost a third or more of their people. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 gave the princes the right to conduct their own foreign policy, made France and Sweden great powers and removed religion as a cause of war between European states.
events.now: The war fixed Germany's fragmentation until 1871 and made France the leading power in Europe. It is the model for every war in which outside powers fight their own contest on another country's ground.
events.fact: The two officials thrown from the window survived the fall; Catholics credited angels, Protestants a dung heap.

sites.d: Defenestration of 1618 started the war.
Catholic victory crushed Bohemian Protestants.
Sack killed ~20,000, worst atrocity of the war.
Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus killed in victory.

causes.why: Augsburg recognised only Lutherans and Catholics, leaving out the growing Calvinist states. The tensions it froze exploded in Bohemia in 1618.

q.why: Protestant-Catholic conflict, and a struggle over Habsburg power in Europe.
q.stakes: The religion of Germany and the balance of power in Europe.
q.decided: Exhaustion, and France and Sweden's intervention against the Habsburgs.
q.cost: Perhaps 4 to 8 million dead; some regions lost half their people.
q.changed: The Peace of Westphalia created a new European order of sovereign states.

events.bluf: Habsburg Emperor Ferdinand II set out to restore Catholic and imperial authority over the Protestant princes; the princes and then Denmark, Sweden and France fought to stop him. Thirty years of war on German soil killed a third of the population in places and ended in a settlement that made the sovereign state, rather than religious unity, the basis of the European order. Germany stayed fragmented for two centuries.
events.trig: The Defenestration of Prague in May 1618.
events.lens: Religious wars turn into power struggles: when Catholic France backs Protestants, interest has overtaken faith.

kv: of the German population died, far more in some regions

events.who: Jan Pieterszoon Coen; the Dutch East India Company
events.hook: The Dutch East India Company seized a Javanese port and made it the capital of its Asian empire.
