events.what: The Dutch East India Company seized a Javanese port and made it the capital of its Asian empire.
events.story: VOC Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen captured the town of Jayakarta in May 1619, razed it and built Batavia as the company's headquarters. He enforced the spice monopoly by force. In 1621 his troops killed, enslaved or drove out most of the people of the Banda Islands.
events.why: The VOC needed a secure base to control the spice trade and keep the English out.
events.then: From Batavia the VOC enforced its spice monopolies and took control of Java through wars and alliances with local rulers. The city's segregated colonial society included a large Chinese community, which Dutch troops and townsmen massacred in 1740.
events.sig: From Batavia the VOC enforced its spice monopolies and took control of Java through wars and alliances with local rulers. The city's segregated colonial society included a large Chinese community, which Dutch troops and townsmen massacred in 1740.
events.now: Jakarta grew from Batavia, and Indonesia's borders follow those of the Dutch East Indies that were ruled from here, a common pattern in which colonial administrative units became nation-states.

causes.why: The VOC needed a permanent headquarters in Asia; Coen chose Jayakarta.

q.what: Spices, later coffee and sugar.
q.who: The VOC profited; Javanese and Bandanese people and enslaved workers paid.
q.scale: Batavia became the hub of a trading network from Japan to the Cape.
q.daily: A mixed town of Dutch, Chinese, Javanese and enslaved people from across Asia.
q.system: A colonial capital that later ruled all of Indonesia.

events.bluf: VOC Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen wanted a secure headquarters from which the Dutch East India Company could control the spice trade and keep the English out. He captured Jayakarta in May 1619, razed it and built Batavia. From there the company enforced its monopolies by force and took Java piece by piece, and the territorial state it built became the Dutch East Indies and then Indonesia.
events.lens: Colonial capitals were built for extraction and control; their layouts often still show who was meant to live where.
events.fact: Coen's reported maxim was that there could be no trade without war and no war without trade.

events.h: First enslaved Africans arrive in Virginia
events.who: ~20 Angolans taken from a Portuguese slave ship; Virginia colonists
events.what: Africans sold to colonists, the start of slavery in English America.
events.why: Tobacco planters needed labour. English privateers had captives to sell after seizing them from a Portuguese slave ship bound for Mexico.
events.sig: The status of Africans varied at first and some gained freedom. From the 1660s Virginia laws made slavery lifelong and hereditary through the mother (1662) and tied it to race. After Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 planters shifted from indentured servants to enslaved Africans.
events.hook: Twenty Africans sold off a ship in 1619 marked the start of slavery in English America.
events.story: English privateers seized Angolans from a Portuguese slave ship bound for Mexico. In August 1619 they traded about 20 of them to Virginia colonists at Point Comfort for food. Virginia law said nothing yet about the status of Africans, and within decades the colony wrote race-based, lifelong slavery into its codes.
events.then: The status of Africans varied at first and some gained freedom. From the 1660s Virginia laws made slavery lifelong and hereditary through the mother (1662) and tied it to race. After Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 planters shifted from indentured servants to enslaved Africans.
events.now: Virginia's laws of the 1660s made slavery lifelong, hereditary and racial, the template every Southern colony copied; the inequality they built still shapes wealth and politics in the United States.

q.before: Virginia relied mainly on English indentured servants.
q.how: Privateers sold captives taken from a Portuguese slave ship.
q.claim: Property rights over people, later written into Virginia law.
q.winners: Planters; the enslaved and their descendants paid for generations.
q.lasted: Slavery lasted until 1865.

events.bluf: English privateers who had seized Angolans from a Portuguese slave ship traded about 20 of them to Virginia colonists for food at Point Comfort in 1619, the earliest recorded arrival of Africans in English North America. Their legal status was unfixed, and some gained freedom. Over the following decades Virginia wrote lifelong, hereditary, race-based slavery into law, a system that shaped the economy, Constitution and society of the future United States.
events.lens: Hierarchies are built by law: watch how statutes turn an economic arrangement into a fixed ranking of people.
events.fact: The ship that brought them, the White Lion, was an English privateer sailing under Dutch letters of marque.

kv: enslaved people in the US by 1860

events.what: First representative legislature in English America.
events.why: The Virginia Company offered a measure of self-government to attract settlers after a decade of deaths and losses.
events.sig: Every English colony acquired an elected assembly. Colonists grew used to governing themselves, and taxes imposed by Parliament without their consent in the 1760s looked illegitimate.
events.hook: In the same year slavery arrived, Virginia also got America's first elected assembly.
events.story: The Virginia Company of London reformed the colony's government in 1618-19 to attract settlers. In 1619 colonists elected burgesses who met at Jamestown with the governor and his council to make local laws. It was the first legislature of its kind in English America. The vote went to free men only, and later law narrowed it to property owners.
events.then: Every English colony acquired an elected assembly. Colonists grew used to governing themselves, and taxes imposed by Parliament without their consent in the 1760s looked illegitimate.
events.now: A century and a half of self-government through elected assemblies made Parliament's taxes of the 1760s look illegitimate; the Revolution was fought to defend what Virginia began in 1619.

causes.why: To attract settlers, the Virginia Company offered them a say in making local laws.

q.before: The Virginia Company's governor ruled by martial law.
q.how: Elected burgesses met with the governor and council.
q.claim: The Company's charter, to attract settlers.
q.lasted: Yes: it is the ancestor of today's Virginia General Assembly.

events.bluf: The Virginia Company let its colonists elect representatives to make local laws, to attract settlers to a colony that had nearly died. The assembly met at Jamestown in 1619, the first elected legislature in English America. Colonists grew used to governing themselves through their own assemblies, and taxes imposed by Parliament without their consent in the 1760s looked like tyranny; the same year's arrival of enslaved Africans meant freedom and slavery grew up together.
events.lens: Representative institutions often start as concessions to attract or keep people, and once granted they are hard to take back.
events.fact: The first assembly met in the church at Jamestown on 30 July 1619 and sat for six days in heat so severe that one burgess died.

events.what: Founded Plymouth Colony; signed the Mayflower Compact.
events.why: The Pilgrims had separated from the Church of England and faced persecution at home. They had lived in the Dutch city of Leiden and feared losing their children to Dutch ways.
events.sig: The alliance with the Wampanoag held for decades. Puritan migration to Massachusetts Bay followed from 1630. King Philip's War in 1675-76 destroyed Native power in southern New England.
events.hook: A ship of religious dissenters signed a pact to govern themselves before stepping ashore.
events.story: The Pilgrims, English Separatists, sailed on the Mayflower in 1620 to worship their own way. Blown off course, they landed at Cape Cod and signed the Mayflower Compact before going ashore, agreeing to make and obey their own laws. They settled at Plymouth. Half died in the first winter, and help from the Wampanoag under sachem Massasoit and the interpreter Squanto kept the rest alive.
events.then: The alliance with the Wampanoag held for decades. Puritan migration to Massachusetts Bay followed from 1630. King Philip's War in 1675-76 destroyed Native power in southern New England.
events.now: The Compact is the earliest American statement of government by consent, and Plymouth opened New England to the Puritan migration of the 1630s that shaped the region's religious and civic culture.
events.fact: Squanto (Tisquantum) spoke English because he had been kidnapped and taken to Europe years earlier.

q.before: The Wampanoag under Massasoit controlled the region, recently devastated by epidemics.
q.how: Settlers agreed in the Mayflower Compact to govern themselves.
q.claim: A patent from the Virginia Company, then self-government by consent.
q.winners: The Pilgrims, helped by the Wampanoag.
q.lasted: Plymouth merged into Massachusetts in 1691.

events.bluf: English Separatists who had left the Church of England sailed to America to worship their own way. Blown off course to Cape Cod, they signed the Mayflower Compact to make and obey their own laws, and half of them died in the first winter. The small colony survived on Wampanoag help, the Compact became a founding text of government by consent in America, and Plymouth opened New England to the Puritan migration that shaped American religious and civic culture.
events.lens: Founding myths simplify: the Thanksgiving story leaves out what happened to the Wampanoag fifty years later.

events.who: Imperial and Catholic League armies; the army of Frederick V, the 'Winter King'
events.hook: In about an hour of fighting, the Catholic Habsburgs crushed the Protestant rebels of Bohemia.
events.what: In about an hour of fighting, the Catholic Habsburgs crushed the Protestant rebels of Bohemia.
events.story: Bohemia's Protestant estates had rejected Habsburg Emperor Ferdinand II as king and elected Frederick V of the Palatinate in 1619. On 8 November 1620 imperial and Catholic League troops under Count Tilly routed Frederick's army on the White Mountain outside Prague. Frederick fled after one winter on the throne.
events.why: The estates had bet on Protestant Europe coming to their aid. Only a few thousand mercenaries came.
events.then: Twenty-seven rebel leaders were executed in Prague's Old Town Square in 1621. Their estates went to Catholic loyalists, many German-speaking, and Protestant worship was suppressed. Protestant princes across Germany armed for what came next.
events.sig: Twenty-seven rebel leaders were executed in Prague's Old Town Square in 1621. Their estates went to Catholic loyalists, many German-speaking, and Protestant worship was suppressed. Protestant princes across Germany armed for what came next.
events.now: The defeat ended Bohemia's Protestant nobility and its elective crown; the Habsburgs re-Catholicised the kingdom and ruled it as a hereditary possession until 1918, which is why Czech nationalism defined itself against Vienna.

causes.why: The Bohemian revolt that began the war was crushed at White Mountain.

q.why: Bohemian Protestants rebelled against Habsburg rule and Catholic restoration.
q.stakes: Religious freedom in Bohemia, and the Habsburg hold on the imperial crown.
q.decided: A larger, better-led Catholic army against an unpaid, divided rebel force.
q.cost: The Protestant Czech nobility was executed, exiled or stripped of its land.
q.changed: Bohemia was made Catholic again and the war widened into Germany.

events.bluf: Habsburg Emperor Ferdinand II sent an army to recover Bohemia from the Protestant nobles who had elected a rival king. His troops routed them outside Prague in an hour. Bohemia lost its elective crown and its Protestant nobility, and the Habsburgs ruled it as a hereditary Catholic possession until 1918.
events.lens: Crushing a revolt can widen a war if it convinces neutral parties they are next.
events.fact: Frederick V reigned one winter and is remembered as the Winter King.

kv: of Habsburg rule over Bohemia that followed

events.who: Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen; the Bandanese
events.hook: To control the world's only source of nutmeg, the Dutch company conquered the Banda Islands and destroyed their people.
events.what: To control the world's only source of nutmeg, the Dutch company conquered the Banda Islands and destroyed their people.
events.story: Nutmeg and mace grew only on the Banda Islands, whose people sold them to the English despite Dutch demands for exclusive rights. In 1621 VOC Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen invaded. Of perhaps 15,000 Bandanese, most were killed, starved or enslaved, and a few fled. The islands were divided into nutmeg plantations worked by enslaved labourers.
events.why: Nutmeg and mace grew only on Banda. The Bandanese kept selling them to the English despite Dutch demands for exclusive rights.
events.then: The VOC held the nutmeg monopoly for over a century, until the French and British smuggled seedlings to their own colonies. Its model of company rule by force spread across the archipelago.
events.sig: The VOC held the nutmeg monopoly for over a century, until the French and British smuggled seedlings to their own colonies. Its model of company rule by force spread across the archipelago.
events.now: Banda set the pattern of a trading company governing by force, the model the VOC and later the British East India Company applied for two centuries; it is now at the centre of Dutch debates about the colonial past.
events.wk: Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands

causes.why: The VOC used its charter to make war and seize a nutmeg monopoly.

q.what: Nutmeg and mace, among the most valuable spices in Europe.
q.who: VOC shareholders profited; the Bandanese paid with their lives and land.
q.scale: Most of the islands' people were killed, enslaved or driven out.
q.daily: Enslaved workers tended nutmeg groves for Dutch planters.
q.system: A monopoly plantation colony, a model for later colonial rule.

events.bluf: VOC Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen set out to give the Dutch East India Company a monopoly of nutmeg and mace, which grew only on the Banda Islands. In 1621 his troops killed, starved, enslaved or drove out most of the islands' perhaps 15,000 people and divided the land into plantations worked by slaves. The company held the nutmeg monopoly for over a century, and company rule by force became its model across the archipelago.
events.lens: Monopolies over a scarce commodity invite extreme violence to protect them.
events.fact: In 1667 the Dutch kept Run, the one Banda island the English had held, and England kept the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam, today's Manhattan.

events.what: Large, organized Puritan migration; Boston founded.
events.why: Puritans under pressure from English King Charles I and Archbishop William Laud wanted a community run on their own faith. The royal charter of 1629 let the company's government sit in America rather than London.
events.sig: About 20,000 English migrated in the 'Great Migration' of the 1630s. Town meetings, schools and Harvard (1636) took root, and minister Roger Williams founded Rhode Island on religious freedom. Expansion brought the Pequot War of 1637 and King Philip's War of 1675-76.
events.hook: A thousand Puritans set out to build a model 'city upon a hill.'
events.story: Puritan lawyer John Winthrop led about 1,000 settlers to Massachusetts Bay in 1630 and founded Boston. The colony's charter let its company govern itself in America. The settlers founded Harvard in 1636 and enforced strict religious conformity, banishing the dissenters Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson.
events.then: About 20,000 English migrated in the 'Great Migration' of the 1630s. Town meetings, schools and Harvard (1636) took root, and minister Roger Williams founded Rhode Island on religious freedom. Expansion brought the Pequot War of 1637 and King Philip's War of 1675-76.
events.now: New England's town meetings, public schools and Harvard descend from the colony, and the 'city upon a hill' remains the language of American national mission.

causes.why: Plymouth's survival encouraged a much larger Puritan migration, about 20,000 people in the 1630s.

q.before: Massachusett and other Algonquian peoples lived around the bay.
q.how: A self-governing chartered company that moved its charter to America.
q.winners: Puritan settlers; dissenters and Native peoples lost out.
q.lasted: Its charter was revoked in 1684, but the colony thrived.

events.bluf: Puritan lawyer John Winthrop led about 1,000 settlers to build a godly community beyond the reach of English King Charles I, under a charter that let their company govern itself in America. The migration was funded, organised and family-based, and it built a literate, town-governed and intensely religious society. Its ideals, from the 'city upon a hill' to the town meeting, and its intolerance, which banished dissenters, both shaped American civic culture.
events.lens: Societies founded on a mission tend to export it; the idea that America has a special role in the world starts here.
events.fact: Winthrop's 'city upon a hill' comes from a sermon written for the crossing of 1630; Presidents Kennedy and Reagan both quoted it.

events.who: Imperial army under Count Tilly and Pappenheim; the citizens of Magdeburg
events.hook: Imperial troops stormed a Protestant city, and about 20,000 people died in the fire and killing.
events.what: Imperial troops stormed a Protestant city, and about 20,000 people died in the fire and killing.
events.story: Magdeburg, a leading Lutheran city, had allied with Swedish King Gustavus Adolphus and waited for relief that came too late. Imperial troops under Count Tilly and Gottfried von Pappenheim stormed the walls on 20 May 1631. Fire swept the city while the soldiers plundered and killed. About 20,000 died.
events.why: The city had defied the emperor and bet on Swedish rescue. Tilly's unpaid troops expected a sack.
events.then: Saxony and Brandenburg joined Sweden. Gustavus Adolphus routed Tilly at Breitenfeld in September 1631.
events.sig: Saxony and Brandenburg joined Sweden. Gustavus Adolphus routed Tilly at Breitenfeld in September 1631.
events.now: Magdeburg made the Protestant cause a coalition. The emperor's armies lost the field within four months and the chance to win the war outright.

causes.why: After crushing Bohemia, imperial armies pushed deep into Protestant northern Germany.

q.why: The Catholic emperor set out to crush a defiant Protestant city allied to Sweden.
q.stakes: Control of the Elbe and Protestant resistance in northern Germany.
q.decided: Tilly's assault came before the Swedish army could arrive.
q.cost: About 20,000 defenders and civilians killed.
q.changed: Protestant princes joined Sweden, and the war grew even more brutal.

events.bluf: Imperial commander Count Tilly besieged Magdeburg to punish a Lutheran city that had allied with Sweden. His troops broke in, and fire and plunder killed about 20,000 of its 25,000 people. The atrocity drove Saxony and Brandenburg into alliance with Sweden and turned the war against the emperor.
events.lens: Atrocities can cost more politically than they gain militarily, by driving neutral parties to the other side.
events.fact: The German verb 'magdeburgisieren' came to mean to destroy a place completely.

events.who: Emperor Shah Jahan; thousands of craftsmen; chief architect Ustad Ahmad Lahauri
events.what: Mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
events.why: Shah Jahan's grief for his wife came first. The Mughal court used building to display wealth and piety.
events.sig: Shah Jahan's building and wars strained the treasury. His son Aurangzeb seized power in 1658 after a war of succession and confined him in Agra Fort, where he died in 1666.
events.hook: An emperor's grief produced the world's most famous tomb.
events.story: Mumtaz Mahal died in childbirth at Burhanpur in June 1631. Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan began a white marble tomb for her at Agra on the Yamuna in 1632, with Ustad Ahmad Lahauri as chief architect. About 20,000 workers built it over some 20 years, inlaying the marble with semi-precious stones.
events.then: Shah Jahan's building and wars strained the treasury. His son Aurangzeb seized power in 1658 after a war of succession and confined him in Agra Fort, where he died in 1666.
events.now: The Taj records the Mughal state at its richest, when it could spend a province's revenue on a tomb; the treasury strain of such building and of Aurangzeb's wars is part of why the empire broke within a century.
events.fact: Shah Jahan spent his last eight years a prisoner in Agra Fort, from which the tomb is visible across the river.

causes.why: Akbar's rich and stable empire reached its artistic peak under his grandson Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

q.what: A white marble mausoleum with gardens, a mosque and a guesthouse.
q.new: Perfect symmetry, inlaid stone flowers and a huge onion dome.
q.audience: The court, and later travellers from around the world.
q.reveals: The wealth and artistic confidence of the Mughal Empire at its peak.
q.today: It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site visited by millions every year.

events.bluf: Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan set out to build a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal that would display his grief and the empire's wealth. About 20,000 workers finished the white marble complex over some 20 years. The Taj Mahal shows the Mughal state at its richest, and the taxation that paid for building on this scale and for Aurangzeb's wars strained the treasury the empire depended on.
events.lens: Monuments reveal a state's surplus and priorities: ask who paid for them.

kv: to the top of the dome's finial

events.who: King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden; imperial general Albrecht von Wallenstein
events.hook: Sweden's warrior king won his last battle and died in it.
events.what: Sweden's warrior king won his last battle and died in it.
events.story: On 16 November 1632 Swedish King Gustavus Adolphus attacked imperial general Albrecht von Wallenstein's army in thick fog at Lützen in Saxony. The king rode into the mist at the head of his cavalry and was shot dead. His army took the field.
events.why: Sweden had entered the war in 1630 to save the German Protestants and to control the Baltic. Wallenstein's advance into Saxony threatened Sweden's main ally.
events.then: Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna kept Sweden in the war. France declared war on Spain in 1635 and took over the campaign in Germany.
events.sig: Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna kept Sweden in the war. France declared war on Spain in 1635 and took over the campaign in Germany.
events.now: Gustavus Adolphus's army of mobile guns, combined arms and drilled professionals became the model for every European army. Sweden stayed a great power in the Baltic until Poltava in 1709.

causes.why: Magdeburg's destruction drove German Protestants into Sweden's arms.

q.why: Sweden backed the Protestant cause and its own Baltic ambitions.
q.stakes: Whether the Catholic emperor would dominate Germany.
q.decided: Swedish infantry held its ground despite the king's death.
q.cost: Thousands dead on each side, and Sweden's king.
q.changed: The war became a power struggle among Sweden, France and the Habsburgs.

events.bluf: Swedish King Gustavus Adolphus attacked the imperial army under Albrecht von Wallenstein in fog near Leipzig to keep Saxony in the war. Sweden held the field and lost its king. Without him the Protestant cause lost its direction, the war dragged on for sixteen years, and France entered directly to hold the Habsburgs down.
events.lens: Military innovation can make a small state a great power, but often depends on one leader.
events.fact: Wallenstein was assassinated on the emperor's orders fifteen months later, suspected of negotiating his own peace.

kv: Gustavus Adolphus's age when he was killed

events.who: Galileo Galilei; Pope Urban VIII; the Roman Inquisition
events.hook: The Church forced Galileo to renounce the idea that the Earth moves.
events.what: The Church forced Galileo to renounce the idea that the Earth moves.
events.story: Paduan mathematician Galileo Galilei published the 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' in 1632 with the Pope's own argument in the mouth of a character named Simplicio. Pope Urban VIII, an old friend, took it as mockery. The Roman Inquisition found Galileo vehemently suspected of heresy in June 1633. He abjured and was confined to his villa near Florence.
events.why: A decree of 1616 had banned the Copernican doctrine. The Pope felt betrayed.
events.then: Galileo's last book, on motion, was smuggled out and printed in Leiden in 1638. French philosopher René Descartes shelved his own book on the Copernican universe.
events.sig: Galileo's last book, on motion, was smuggled out and printed in Leiden in 1638. French philosopher René Descartes shelved his own book on the Copernican universe.
events.now: The trial moved the centre of science from Italy to the Netherlands and England. It remains the standard case of religious authority suppressing evidence, which the Church conceded in 1992.

causes.why: Galileo's telescope discoveries made him the most prominent defender of Copernicus, and a target.

events.myth: Galileo muttered 'and yet it moves' as he rose from his knees. The story first appears more than a century after the trial.

q.belief: Whether the Bible's descriptions of a fixed Earth had to be read literally.
q.authority: The pope and the Roman Inquisition.
q.believers: Most Catholics were untouched; Catholic astronomers learned to keep quiet about Copernicus.
q.fallout: Catholic Italy lost its scientific lead to northern Europe.
q.today: The Church now accepts that Galileo was right and the trial was a mistake.

events.bluf: Pope Urban VIII put Galileo Galilei on trial for defending the Copernican system after the 'Dialogue' of 1632 appeared to mock the Pope's own argument. Galileo abjured on his knees and spent his last nine years under house arrest. The Church had used its authority against a scientific claim, and scientific publishing moved north to Protestant Europe.
events.lens: When authorities punish scientists, research moves to places where it can be published freely.

kv: under house arrest, until his death
the Pope acknowledged the Church had erred

events.hook: A French philosopher in the Dutch Republic set out to rebuild knowledge from doubt.
events.what: A French philosopher in the Dutch Republic set out to rebuild knowledge from doubt.
events.story: French philosopher René Descartes, living in the Dutch Republic, published the 'Discourse on the Method' at Leiden in 1637, in French so that ordinary readers could follow. Doubting everything he could, he found one certainty: 'I think, therefore I am.' He had shelved an earlier book on the Copernican universe after hearing of Galileo's condemnation.
events.why: The new science needed a method. Decades of religious war had made certainty precious and Dutch presses safe.
events.then: Cartesian philosophy and analytic geometry shaped science and mathematics for a century.
events.sig: Cartesian philosophy and analytic geometry shaped science and mathematics for a century.
events.now: Descartes's method gave the new science a philosophy and the Dutch Republic the role of Europe's press. The mind-body problem he posed still frames philosophy and neuroscience.

causes.why: News of Galileo's condemnation made Descartes shelve his own book on the Copernican universe.

q.idea: Start from doubt, and accept only what is clear and certain.
q.against: Reliance on ancient authorities such as Aristotle.
q.spread: Through the Dutch Republic's free presses and the letters of Europe's scholars.
q.enabled: A mechanical view of nature that Newton later built on and changed.
q.critics: Empiricists such as Locke argued that knowledge comes from experience, not pure reason.

events.bluf: French philosopher René Descartes set out to rebuild knowledge on reason alone, after religious war and the Galileo trial had discredited inherited authority. He found one certainty, his own thinking, and built a method of systematic doubt and a new geometry on it. Modern philosophy and the mathematics of science both descend from the book, and his choice to publish in the Dutch Republic shows where thought was free.
events.lens: Start from what you can verify, and build up from there.
events.fact: Every x-y graph uses Cartesian coordinates, named after him.

kv: essays it introduced: optics, weather and geometry

events.what: Sakoku: only the Dutch could trade, at Nagasaki.
events.why: The shogunate saw Christianity, with perhaps 300,000 converts, as a threat to its authority, and wanted to control foreign trade itself.
events.sig: Trade continued with China, Korea, the Ryukyu kingdom and the Dutch, so Japan stayed partly open, and Dutch books fed a body of 'Dutch learning'. Japan developed on its own terms until US warships forced it open in 1853.
events.hook: Japan shut its doors to the outside world for over 200 years.
events.story: Christian missions had won perhaps 300,000 converts in Japan by the early 1600s. Japanese shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu's government banned Christianity, forbade Japanese from leaving the country in 1635 and expelled the Portuguese traders in 1639. Only the Dutch could trade, confined to a small island in Nagasaki harbour.
events.then: Trade continued with China, Korea, the Ryukyu kingdom and the Dutch, so Japan stayed partly open, and Dutch books fed a body of 'Dutch learning'. Japan developed on its own terms until US warships forced it open in 1853.
events.now: The restrictions explain why Japan's encounter with Western power in 1853 was so sudden and why its modernisation after 1868 was so rapid and state-driven: the state that had controlled contact could redirect it.
events.fact: Dutch traders were confined to Dejima, a small artificial fan-shaped island in Nagasaki harbour.

causes.why: Japan expelled the Catholic Portuguese but kept trading with the Protestant Dutch, who did not try to convert anyone.

q.before: Portuguese and Spanish traders and missionaries were active in Japan.
q.how: A series of edicts expelling foreigners and banning Christianity.
q.claim: Protecting the country from Christianity and foreign interference.
q.winners: The shogunate, which controlled foreign trade.
q.lasted: Until US warships forced Japan open in 1853-54.

events.bluf: Japanese shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu wanted Christianity and foreign influence out of Japan and foreign trade under the shogunate's own control. In 1639 he expelled the Portuguese, completing a decade of edicts that banned the faith and forbade Japanese to leave; only the Dutch kept a post at Nagasaki. The regime was secured against foreign-backed revolt for two centuries, and Japan met the industrial West in 1853 with no navy and no modern army.
events.trig: The Shimabara Rebellion of 1637-38, a peasant revolt with many Christian participants, convinced the shogunate that Portuguese missionaries were dangerous.
events.lens: 'Closed' countries are rarely fully closed: ask which channels stay open and who controls them.

kv: European trading post allowed: the Dutch on Dejima

events.who: Francis Day and Andrew Cogan of the East India Company; a local Nayak ruler
events.hook: The Company leased a strip of coast and built Fort St George, the seed of the city of Chennai.
events.what: The Company leased a strip of coast and built Fort St George, the seed of the city of Chennai.
events.story: In 1639 Company agent Francis Day obtained a grant of coastal land from a local Nayak ruler. The Company, with Andrew Cogan as its agent, built Fort St George, finished in 1644. Weavers, dyers and merchants settled around it, and the town of Madras grew up.
events.why: The Company wanted cheap Coromandel cotton cloth for the Asian and European markets and a fortified base it controlled.
events.then: Madras became the first of the Company's three presidencies, joined by Bombay in 1668 and Calcutta in 1690.
events.sig: Madras became the first of the Company's three presidencies, joined by Bombay in 1668 and Calcutta in 1690.
events.now: Fort St George was the model for the Company's fortified presidencies at Bombay and Calcutta, the bases from which it took territory in the 1700s.

causes.why: With a base at Surat in the west, the Company looked for one on the cotton-rich east coast.

q.what: Painted and woven cotton cloth, bought for sale in Asia and Europe.
q.who: Company shareholders and their Indian merchant partners profited.
q.scale: A small fort grew into one of India's largest cities.
q.daily: Thousands of weavers worked to Company orders.
q.system: Fortified trading posts that later became bases for conquest.

events.bluf: The East India Company wanted a fortified base of its own on the Coromandel coast for the cotton cloth trade, held on terms it set rather than as a guest. Company agent Francis Day obtained a land grant from a local Nayak ruler in 1639 and the Company built Fort St George. Madras became the first of the Company's three presidencies, and the shift from trading under Indian rulers to holding territory began there.
events.lens: Fortified trading posts are the first step from commerce to colony.
events.fact: Fort St George still houses the Tamil Nadu state legislature; Chennai, as Madras is now called, is one of India's largest cities.

events.who: The VOC and the Sultanate of Johor; the Portuguese garrison
events.hook: After a five-month siege, the Dutch captured Portugal's great fortress on the Strait of Malacca.
events.what: After a five-month siege, the Dutch captured Portugal's great fortress on the Strait of Malacca.
events.story: The VOC, allied with the Sultanate of Johor, besieged Portuguese Malacca from August 1640. Famine and disease killed much of the population. Dutch troops stormed the city on 14 January 1641.
events.why: Control of the strait meant control of trade between the Indian Ocean and China. Johor's sultans descended from the rulers Portugal had driven out in 1511 and wanted the Portuguese gone.
events.then: The VOC centred its trade on Batavia, and Malacca became a secondary port. Britain took it in 1824.
events.sig: The VOC centred its trade on Batavia, and Malacca became a secondary port. Britain took it in 1824.
events.now: The Strait of Malacca is still one of the world's busiest shipping chokepoints, carrying much of the trade and oil between the Indian Ocean and East Asia, and who controls it remains a strategic question.

causes.why: From Batavia the VOC moved against Portugal's bases in Asia.
Portugal held Malacca for 130 years before the Dutch took it.

q.why: The Dutch wanted Portugal's last major base in Southeast Asia.
q.stakes: Control of the Strait of Malacca.
q.decided: A long blockade that starved the city.
q.cost: Thousands dead, mostly civilians, from famine and disease.
q.changed: The Dutch, not the Portuguese, dominated the spice trade.

events.bluf: The Dutch East India Company and its ally the Sultanate of Johor set out to take Malacca from Portugal and with it the strait between the Indian Ocean and China. They besieged the city from August 1640 and stormed it on 14 January 1641 after famine and disease had killed much of the population. Portuguese power in Southeast Asia ended, the VOC became the region's dominant European force, and Malacca declined as the Dutch routed trade through Batavia.
events.lens: New dominant powers move trade to their own hubs and let rivals' cities decline.
events.fact: The Dutch held Malacca for 183 years and built the Stadthuys of 1650, among the oldest Dutch buildings in Asia.

events.what: War between king and Parliament.
events.why: Taxation without consent came first. Religion, fear of Catholicism against Puritan radicalism, gave each side its believers. The king's claim to rule by divine right left no room for compromise.
events.sig: Charles I was executed in 1649. England became a republic under Cromwell, who conquered Ireland. The monarchy returned in 1660; Parliament's supremacy was fixed in 1688.
events.hook: King and Parliament went to war over who really ruled England.
events.story: English King Charles I ruled without Parliament from 1629 to 1640, raising money by contested means and pushing church reforms that Puritans read as Catholic. His attempt to impose a prayer book on Scotland started a war he could pay for only by recalling Parliament. In 1642 both sides raised armies. Parliament's New Model Army under Oliver Cromwell won by 1646 and again in 1648.
events.then: Charles I was executed in 1649. England became a republic under Cromwell, who conquered Ireland. The monarchy returned in 1660; Parliament's supremacy was fixed in 1688.
events.now: Parliamentary sovereignty and the rule that representatives must approve taxes descend from the wars. The American revolutionaries read their own cause in it.

q.why: King and Parliament clashed over taxes, religion and royal power.
q.stakes: Whether the king could rule without Parliament.
q.decided: Parliament's New Model Army.
q.cost: Perhaps 200,000 dead in England, and far more in Ireland and Scotland.
q.changed: The king was executed and England briefly became a republic.

events.bluf: English King Charles I tried to govern and tax without Parliament and to impose his church on three kingdoms; Parliament raised an army to stop him. Parliament's New Model Army won, and the king was executed. The wars settled, after one more crisis in 1688, that English monarchs rule under law and with Parliament's consent.
events.trig: Charles entered the Commons with soldiers to arrest five members in January 1642 and found them gone.
events.lens: Fights over who controls taxation are fights over who controls the state.
events.fact: About 4 per cent of England's population died in the wars, a higher share than in the First World War.

kv: deaths in England, about 3.7% of the population
figs.n: Including Scotland and Ireland, where war and famine were deadlier, the total was several times higher.

events.h: Abel Tasman reaches Tasmania and New Zealand
events.who: Abel Tasman (Dutch East India Company); Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri
events.hook: A Dutch explorer became the first European to see Tasmania and New Zealand, and lost four men in a clash with Māori.
events.what: A Dutch explorer became the first European to see Tasmania and New Zealand, and lost four men in a clash with Māori.
events.story: Dutch navigator Abel Tasman sailed from Batavia in August 1642 with two ships. He sighted Tasmania in November 1642 and named it Van Diemen's Land, then New Zealand's South Island in December. At Golden Bay on 19 December Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri warriors in canoes attacked a ship's boat and killed four sailors. Tasman named the place Murderers' Bay and sailed up the North Island's west coast without landing.
events.why: The VOC wanted the Great South Land and a route to South America. Tasman's instructions put trade before exploration, and nothing he saw promised trade.
events.then: The VOC filed the voyage and sent no follow-up. No European returned to New Zealand until British navigator James Cook in 1769. Dutch cartographers gave the islands the name Nova Zeelandia.
events.sig: The VOC filed the voyage and sent no follow-up. No European returned to New Zealand until British navigator James Cook in 1769. Dutch cartographers gave the islands the name Nova Zeelandia.
events.now: Empires followed profit rather than discovery: the Dutch saw nothing to trade and stayed away, which is why Britain rather than the Netherlands colonised New Zealand in 1840.

causes.why: Dutch East India Company voyages kept probing for the 'Great South Land' after the Duyfken's first landing.

q.what: A search for new lands and trade for the VOC.
q.who: The VOC, which found nothing profitable.
q.scale: A ten-month voyage with two ships.
q.daily: Little effect at the time on Māori or Aboriginal life.
q.system: European maps began to show the outline of Australasia.

events.bluf: The Dutch East India Company sent navigator Abel Tasman to find the Great South Land and a route to South America. He found Tasmania and New Zealand in 1642, lost four sailors to a Māori attack at Golden Bay and landed on neither. The company judged both worthless, and New Zealand stayed Māori for another 127 years until British navigator James Cook arrived in 1769.
events.lens: First encounters set the tone: a violent clash discouraged contact for over a century.
events.fact: Tasman called the land Staten Landt, believing it joined South America; no one from his ships set foot on New Zealand.

kv: before Cook landed in New Zealand

events.fact: The last Ming emperor hanged himself on Coal Hill, Jingshan, behind the Forbidden City as the rebels took Beijing.
events.who: Rebel leader Li Zicheng; the Chongzhen Emperor
events.hook: Rebels captured Beijing, and the last Ming emperor hanged himself.
events.what: Rebels captured Beijing, and the last Ming emperor hanged himself.
events.story: Decades of famine, epidemic, unpaid soldiers and an empty treasury fed peasant rebellions across north China. Rebel leader Li Zicheng's army entered Beijing in April 1644. The Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself on a hill behind the Forbidden City. The Ming had ruled since 1368.
events.why: The 'Little Ice Age' brought decades of cold, drought and famine. Disruption to the silver supply the tax system depended on and military costs on the northern frontier emptied the treasury. Factional paralysis at court left the government unable to respond, and unpaid soldiers and starving peasants joined the rebel armies.
events.then: Li Zicheng held Beijing for six weeks. Ming general Wu Sangui let the Manchus through the Great Wall at Shanhai Pass, and they took the capital in June 1644 and proclaimed the Qing.
events.sig: Li Zicheng held Beijing for six weeks. Ming general Wu Sangui let the Manchus through the Great Wall at Shanhai Pass, and they took the capital in June 1644 and proclaimed the Qing.
events.now: The Ming collapse is the standard case of fiscal crisis, climate shock and rebellion toppling a state together; it gave China a Manchu dynasty whose expanded borders the People's Republic still claims.

causes.why: Defending Korea cost the Ming vast sums and troops, one of several strains, along with fiscal crisis and famine, that weakened it before 1644.

q.before: The Ming dynasty, ruling since 1368.
q.how: Peasant rebellion captured the capital.
q.claim: Li Zicheng proclaimed his own Shun dynasty.
q.winners: Briefly the rebels; then the Manchus.
q.lasted: The Ming were finished; loyalists held out in the south for years.

events.bluf: Rebel leader Li Zicheng marched on Beijing in 1644 to replace a Ming dynasty that could no longer pay its soldiers or feed its people. His army entered the capital in April and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself. A dynasty that had ruled since 1368 ended, and the Manchus took the capital from Li within six weeks and founded the Qing, China's last imperial dynasty.
events.lens: States rarely fall to one cause: look for climate, money, army pay and elite paralysis arriving together.

events.who: Manchu regent Dorgon; Ming general Wu Sangui
events.hook: A Ming general opened the Great Wall to the Manchus, who founded China's last dynasty.
events.what: A Ming general opened the Great Wall to the Manchus, who founded China's last dynasty.
events.story: Rebel leader Li Zicheng took Beijing in April 1644. Ming general Wu Sangui, holding Shanhai Pass where the Great Wall meets the sea, let the Manchu army under regent Dorgon through. Together they routed the rebels, and the Manchus occupied Beijing in June 1644 and proclaimed the Qing dynasty rulers of all China. Conquering the south took nearly forty more years.
events.why: The Manchus, a state built north of the Wall, saw the Ming collapse as their chance. Ming general Wu Sangui wanted revenge on the rebels.
events.then: Qing emperors ruled through Chinese institutions while keeping a separate Manchu identity, and in 1645 ordered Chinese men to shave the front of the head and wear the Manchu queue on pain of death. The long reigns of the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors in the 1700s brought prosperity and expansion. The dynasty struggled to respond to Western powers after 1839.
events.sig: Qing emperors ruled through Chinese institutions while keeping a separate Manchu identity, and in 1645 ordered Chinese men to shave the front of the head and wear the Manchu queue on pain of death. The long reigns of the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors in the 1700s brought prosperity and expansion. The dynasty struggled to respond to Western powers after 1839.
events.now: The People's Republic grounds its claims to Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan in the Qing borders, while Taiwan's government and Tibetan and Uyghur exile bodies contest what those borders meant; the Qing decline after 1839 begins the 'century of humiliation' central to the Communist Party's story of itself.

causes.why: After Tumu the Ming relied on walls rather than campaigns against the steppe. In 1644 the Manchus came through the Great Wall at Shanhai Pass, when the Ming general Wu Sangui opened the gate to them.
With Li Zicheng's rebels in Beijing, the Ming general Wu Sangui let the Manchus through the Great Wall to defeat them.

q.why: The Manchus saw the Ming collapse as their chance to conquer China.
q.decided: Wu Sangui opening the pass, and Manchu cavalry.
q.cost: Millions died in decades of conquest, including massacres in the south.
q.changed: The Qing dynasty ruled China until 1912.

events.bluf: Manchu regent Dorgon wanted the Ming throne for his child emperor, and Ming general Wu Sangui wanted the rebels who held Beijing destroyed. Wu opened Shanhai Pass, the two armies routed Li Zicheng's rebels and the Manchus took Beijing in June 1644. The Qing ruled China until 1912 and roughly doubled its territory, adding Tibet, Xinjiang, Mongolia and Taiwan; the borders of today's People's Republic largely follow that expansion.
events.lens: Modern borders often reflect the maximum reach of a country's last empire.
events.fact: The Qing Shunzhi Emperor was six when he was enthroned in Beijing; his uncle Dorgon held the real power until his death in 1650.

events.hook: After 80 years of war, Spain accepted the Dutch Republic as an independent state.
events.what: After 80 years of war, Spain accepted the Dutch Republic as an independent state.
events.story: The Dutch and Spain had fought since 1568. The Peace of Münster, signed on 30 January 1648 during the Westphalia negotiations, ended the war. Spain recognised the republic's independence and its colonial conquests and closed the Scheldt to Antwerp's trade, which left Amsterdam the port of northern Europe.
events.why: Spain was exhausted and at war with France. The republic had won its war at sea and in the colonies.
events.then: The Dutch golden age ran for another quarter century as Europe's leading trading nation.
events.sig: The Dutch golden age ran for another quarter century as Europe's leading trading nation.
events.now: The Dutch Republic's recognition, part of the Peace of Westphalia, helped establish the idea that sovereign states, not dynasties or the Church, are the basic units of international order.

causes.why: Eighty years after the revolt began, Spain finally recognised the Dutch Republic.

q.before: Spain's Habsburg kings, who still claimed the northern Netherlands.
q.how: A peace treaty ending a long revolt.
q.claim: The Dutch provinces' right to govern themselves, won by arms.
q.winners: The Dutch Republic; Spain kept the southern Netherlands.
q.lasted: Yes: the Netherlands has been independent ever since.

events.bluf: Spain wanted to end an eighty-year war and turn its forces on France; the Dutch wanted recognition. At Münster in 1648 Spanish King Philip IV recognised the seven United Provinces as sovereign and let them keep their conquests in Asia and the Americas. A trading republic became a sovereign power, and Spain accepted the loss of northern Europe.
events.lens: Great powers make peace with rebels when a bigger rival demands their attention.
events.fact: The closing of the Scheldt kept Antwerp a dead port until 1863.

kv: of war between Spain and the Dutch ended

events.what: Ended the Thirty Years' War.
events.why: Thirty years of war had exhausted every treasury. France and Sweden had won enough to dictate terms and too little to rule Germany.
events.sig: The Holy Roman Empire became a loose association of some 300 territories. France became the leading power in Europe. Religion ceased to be a cause of war between European states.
events.hook: The treaties that ended the Thirty Years' War invented the modern state system.
events.story: Negotiators met at Münster and Osnabrück from 1644; Catholics and Protestants sat in separate towns. The treaties signed in October 1648 confirmed the princes' right to conduct their own foreign policy, extended the settlement of 1555 to Calvinists, recognised Dutch and Swiss independence and gave Alsace to France and Pomerania to Sweden.
events.then: The Holy Roman Empire became a loose association of some 300 territories. France became the leading power in Europe. Religion ceased to be a cause of war between European states.
events.now: Every argument over sovereignty and intervention since, from Kosovo to Syria, is conducted in Westphalian terms. China and Russia cite the principle of non-interference in the treaties' name.
events.fact: The negotiations ran for five years and the question of who should enter a room first took months.

causes.why: Thirty years of devastation, with no side able to win outright, forced a negotiated settlement.
After eighty years of war, Spain recognised the independent Dutch Republic in the Peace of Münster, part of the Westphalian settlement.
Sweden fought on after the king's death, and France's entry turned the war into a contest of exhaustion.

q.before: The Habsburg emperor claimed leadership over Germany's many states.
q.how: A set of negotiated treaties.
q.claim: Each ruler's sovereignty over his own territory and religion.
q.winners: France, Sweden and the German princes; the emperor lost power.
q.lasted: Its principle of sovereignty still underpins international law.

events.bluf: Every power in the Thirty Years' War wanted out, and none could win. Five years of negotiation in two towns produced treaties that let each German prince run his own foreign policy, extended toleration to Calvinists, recognised the Dutch and Swiss, and paid France and Sweden in territory. The sovereign state replaced religious unity as the basis of European order, and the Holy Roman Empire became a shell.
events.lens: International orders are born from exhaustion: big settlements come when no side can win.
events.myth: Westphalia invented the sovereign state. The treaties confirmed powers the princes already used; the doctrine was read back into them in the 1800s.

kv: towns hosting the talks, Münster and Osnabrück

events.who: Charles I; Oliver Cromwell; the 'Rump' Parliament's High Court of Justice
events.what: King beheaded; England becomes a republic.
events.why: Charles had negotiated with Parliament while plotting with the Scots, and the army decided no settlement with him would hold.
events.sig: England, Scotland and Ireland became a republic, and Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector from 1653. The monarchy returned in 1660 and the surviving regicides were executed.
events.hook: England put its king on trial and cut off his head.
events.story: After losing two civil wars, English King Charles I was tried by a High Court of Justice set up by the Rump Parliament, the remnant left after the army's purge. He refused to recognise the court. He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649.
events.then: England, Scotland and Ireland became a republic, and Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector from 1653. The monarchy returned in 1660 and the surviving regicides were executed.
events.now: The execution set the precedent that a ruler can be tried by his subjects. The French Revolution followed it, and it remains the clearest case of a monarch held to account by law.

causes.why: Parliament's victory led to the unprecedented trial of a king for treason against his own people.

q.before: King Charles I, defeated but still claiming divine right.
q.how: A public trial and execution.
q.claim: That a king could be guilty of treason against his own people.
q.winners: The army and the radical Parliamentarians.
q.lasted: No: the monarchy returned in 1660.

events.bluf: The army's leaders decided that a king who had restarted the war in 1648 could never be trusted with a settlement. A purged Parliament tried English King Charles I for treason against his people and beheaded him. A reigning king had been killed by law in the people's name, and the precedent ran to Louis XVI in 1793.
events.lens: Once a ruler has been tried by law, the idea that rulers stand above the law never fully recovers.
events.fact: Charles wore two shirts to the scaffold so that the January cold would not make him shiver and seem afraid.

kv: judges who signed the death warrant

events.what: Argued for strong sovereign to avoid chaos.
events.why: The English Civil War and a century of religious war had convinced Hobbes that the breakdown of order was the worst political evil.
events.sig: English philosopher John Locke and Genevan philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau answered with contracts that limited the sovereign or placed power in the people. The clergy attacked Hobbes's materialism for a century.
events.hook: Written after civil war, Hobbes argued that people need a strong ruler to avoid chaos.
events.story: English philosopher Thomas Hobbes, in exile in Paris, published 'Leviathan' in 1651. Life without government, he wrote, would be 'nasty, brutish, and short'. People escape it by agreeing to obey a sovereign who keeps the peace.
events.then: English philosopher John Locke and Genevan philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau answered with contracts that limited the sovereign or placed power in the people. The clergy attacked Hobbes's materialism for a century.
events.now: Every trade of liberty for security, from emergency powers to surveillance, is argued in Hobbes's terms. A 'Hobbesian' world is the realist's description of international politics.

causes.why: Hobbes wrote in the shadow of civil war, arguing that only a strong sovereign could prevent a 'war of all against all'.

q.idea: Without strong government, life would be 'nasty, brutish, and short', so people accept a sovereign for safety.
q.against: Civil war, and the claim that subjects may resist their ruler.
q.spread: Widely read and attacked across Europe.
q.critics: Locke argued people keep rights and may overthrow a tyrant.

events.bluf: English philosopher Thomas Hobbes wrote during the civil war to show why any government is better than none. He argued that authority rests on an agreement among individuals who surrender their freedom to a sovereign for security, with no divine right in it. The book founded the social contract and the secular justification of the state.
events.lens: Societies that have lived through chaos will accept strong authority; ask what kind of disorder a people fears most.
events.fact: Hobbes tutored the future Charles II in mathematics in Paris and returned to England the year the book appeared.

events.who: Jan van Riebeeck; Dutch East India Co.
events.what: Supply station for Asia-bound ships.
events.why: The Dutch East India Company needed fresh food and water for ships on the long voyage to Asia. Free farmers produced it more cheaply than Company gardens.
events.sig: Wars and a smallpox epidemic in 1713 destroyed Khoikhoi society. Dutch-speaking farmers spread inland and became the Afrikaners. Britain took the Cape in 1795 and for good in 1806, and the Boers trekked inland from the 1830s.
events.hook: The Dutch East India Company built a supply station at the Cape.
events.story: In 1652 Dutch East India Company commander Jan van Riebeeck landed at Table Bay to build a fort and gardens to supply Dutch ships sailing to Asia. From 1657 the Company released some employees as free farmers, who pushed into Khoikhoi grazing lands. It imported enslaved people from Madagascar, Mozambique, India and the East Indies.
events.then: Wars and a smallpox epidemic in 1713 destroyed Khoikhoi society. Dutch-speaking farmers spread inland and became the Afrikaners. Britain took the Cape in 1795 and for good in 1806, and the Boers trekked inland from the 1830s.
events.now: The colony's land seizures and slave labour set the pattern of South African society: Dutch-speaking farmers became the Afrikaners, the Khoikhoi lost their land, and the politics of race and land ownership ran from 1652 through apartheid to the present.

causes.why: The VOC needed a halfway station on the long voyage to Asia, where its ships could take on fresh water and food.

q.before: Khoikhoi herders grazed their cattle at the Cape.
q.how: A company supply station that grew into a colony.
q.winners: Dutch settlers; the Khoikhoi lost their land and cattle.
q.lasted: The Dutch ruled until Britain took the Cape in 1795.

events.bluf: The Dutch East India Company wanted a station where its ships to Asia could take on fresh food and water. Commander Jan van Riebeeck built a fort and gardens at Table Bay in 1652; from 1657 the Company released employees as free farmers who pushed into Khoikhoi grazing land, and it imported enslaved people from Asia and Africa. A supply post became a settler colony, the seed of white settlement in South Africa and of the racial order that ended in apartheid.
events.lens: A supply station can become a settler colony, and once settlers need land, conflict with the original inhabitants follows.
events.fact: Van Riebeeck planted a hedge of bitter almond to mark the colony's boundary against the Khoikhoi; parts of it survive in Kirstenbosch botanical garden.

events.what: Lord Protector, effectively a military dictator.
events.why: Parliament had failed to agree on a constitution or on reforms. The army was the real power and Cromwell commanded it.
events.sig: Jews were readmitted to England in 1656. The conquest of Ireland in 1649-53, with massacres at Drogheda and Wexford, transferred most Irish land to Protestants. The regime fell after Cromwell's death in 1658.
events.hook: England's republic became a military dictatorship.
events.story: Lord General Oliver Cromwell dissolved the Rump Parliament by force in April 1653 and took the title Lord Protector in December. He governed with a council and, for a time, through major-generals in the regions. Theatres closed and Christmas was suppressed.
events.then: Jews were readmitted to England in 1656. The conquest of Ireland in 1649-53, with massacres at Drogheda and Wexford, transferred most Irish land to Protestants. The regime fell after Cromwell's death in 1658.
events.now: The Protectorate showed that a revolution against royal tyranny could end in rule by a general. Its memory brought the monarchy back on Parliament's terms and kept the army under Parliament's control.

causes.why: The new republic soon fell under the control of its army and Oliver Cromwell.

q.before: The 'Rump' Parliament ruled the republic.
q.how: Cromwell dissolved Parliament with soldiers and became Lord Protector.
q.claim: A written constitution, the Instrument of Government, backed by the army.
q.lasted: No: the Protectorate collapsed within two years of his death.

events.bluf: Oliver Cromwell dissolved a Parliament that could agree on no constitution and ruled as Lord Protector with the army behind him. He gave Protestant sects toleration, readmitted the Jews and conquered Ireland by massacre. The regime collapsed within two years of his death, and Britain kept a lasting suspicion of standing armies.
events.lens: Revolutions often end with the strongest army in charge.
events.fact: Cromwell's body was dug up after the Restoration and hanged at Tyburn; his head stayed on a spike for twenty years.

events.who: Cardinal Mazarin for France; Luis de Haro for Spain
events.where: Pheasant Island, on the French-Spanish border
events.hook: France and Spain ended 24 years of war; France took Roussillon and Louis XIV married a Spanish princess.
events.what: France and Spain ended 24 years of war; France took Roussillon and Louis XIV married a Spanish princess.
events.story: France and Spain had fought on after Westphalia until France, with English help, beat Spain at the Dunes in 1658. On Pheasant Island in the Bidasoa, French chief minister Cardinal Mazarin and Spanish chief minister Luis de Haro signed peace on 7 November 1659. Spain ceded Roussillon and Artois. Louis XIV was to marry Maria Theresa, daughter of Spanish King Philip IV.
events.why: Both treasuries were empty. France held the military advantage.
events.then: Maria Theresa renounced her Spanish rights in return for a dowry Spain never paid, which the Bourbons used as grounds to claim the throne in 1700.
events.sig: Maria Theresa renounced her Spanish rights in return for a dowry Spain never paid, which the Bourbons used as grounds to claim the throne in 1700.
events.now: The Franco-Spanish border still follows the 1659 line, which cut Catalonia in two. The marriage clause produced the War of the Spanish Succession forty years later.

causes.why: France and Spain kept fighting after Westphalia until 1659.

q.before: Spain was Europe's leading Catholic power.
q.how: A peace treaty sealed by a royal marriage.
q.claim: Conquest, confirmed by treaty and marriage.
q.winners: France gained land and prestige; Spain lost both.
q.lasted: Yes, and the marriage led to the War of the Spanish Succession.

events.bluf: French chief minister Cardinal Mazarin wanted to close a war with Spain that had run on after Westphalia and to bind the Spanish succession to France. He got Roussillon and Artois and a Spanish princess for French King Louis XIV. France replaced Spain as Europe's leading power, and the marriage set up the succession war of 1701.
events.lens: Dynastic marriages made as peace terms can become the cause of the next war.
events.fact: Pheasant Island is still administered by France and Spain in alternate six-month turns.

events.what: Monarchy returned.
events.why: Without Cromwell the army and Parliament could not agree on anything. The monarchy was the only settlement most of the political nation would accept.
events.sig: The regicides were hunted and the Church of England re-established with penalties on dissenters. Charles II's Catholic sympathies and his brother James's open Catholicism revived fears of absolutism.
events.hook: England brought back its king, but on Parliament's terms.
events.story: Oliver Cromwell died in September 1658 and his son Richard resigned within nine months. General George Monck marched his army from Scotland to London in early 1660 and forced new elections. The Convention Parliament invited Charles II home. He entered London on 29 May 1660, his thirtieth birthday.
events.then: The regicides were hunted and the Church of England re-established with penalties on dissenters. Charles II's Catholic sympathies and his brother James's open Catholicism revived fears of absolutism.
events.now: The Restoration settled that England would be governed by king and Parliament together rather than by either alone; the crown returned on Parliament's terms, and lost power steadily after 1689 while keeping the throne.

causes.why: Cromwell's death left a power vacuum that only the monarchy could fill.

q.before: A collapsing republic.
q.how: Parliament invited the king back.
q.claim: Charles II's hereditary right, with an agreed amnesty.
q.winners: Royalists; some who had signed Charles I's death warrant were executed.
q.lasted: Yes, though monarchs had to work with Parliament.

events.bluf: After Cromwell's death the republic fell apart, and General George Monck marched on London to arrange elections. The new Parliament invited Charles II back from exile on its own terms. The monarchy returned without absolute power, and the unresolved questions of Catholicism and prerogative produced the revolution of 1688.
events.lens: Restorations rarely restore the old order fully: returning rulers come back on new terms.
events.fact: Samuel Pepys's diary, begun in January 1660, records the Restoration from the inside.

events.who: Christopher Wren, Robert Boyle and other experimenters; King Charles II
events.hook: London scientists formed a society to test ideas by experiment, under the motto 'Take nobody's word for it'.
events.what: London scientists formed a society to test ideas by experiment, under the motto 'Take nobody's word for it'.
events.story: On 28 November 1660, after a lecture by architect Christopher Wren at Gresham College, twelve men agreed to found a society for experimental learning. Chemist Robert Boyle and diarist John Evelyn were among them. King Charles II granted a royal charter in 1662. The Philosophical Transactions began in 1665.
events.why: Peace after the civil wars freed men of means for experiment. Francis Bacon's call to build knowledge from observation had a following among them.
events.then: The Society's licence appeared on Isaac Newton's 'Principia' in 1687. Every national academy of science copied the model.
events.sig: The Society's licence appeared on Isaac Newton's 'Principia' in 1687. Every national academy of science copied the model.
events.now: Scientific journals and peer review descend from the Philosophical Transactions. The Society's motto, 'take nobody's word for it', is still the stance of science toward authority.

q.problem: How to tell real knowledge of nature from speculation and tradition.
q.how: Members performed experiments in front of witnesses and published the results.
q.replaced: Learning based on authority and on secrets kept by individuals.
q.spread: Paris founded its Academy of Sciences in 1666, and other capitals followed.
q.next: Scientific journals and the public testing of results.

events.bluf: Twelve experimenters in London wanted a standing body to test claims about nature by demonstration rather than by authority. Charles II chartered it in 1662. The Society made the experimental method an institution, and its journal created the system of scientific publication that science still runs on.
events.lens: Knowledge advances fastest where institutions exist to test and share claims in public.
events.fact: The Philosophical Transactions is the oldest scientific journal still published.

kv: Philosophical Transactions began, the oldest scientific journal still published

events.who: The Kangxi Emperor; regent Oboi; Jesuit advisers such as Ferdinand Verbiest
events.what: Began a 61-year reign.
events.why: The Shunzhi Emperor died of smallpox, and Kangxi was chosen partly because he had already survived the disease. A Manchu minority ruling China needed Chinese officials invested in the dynasty.
events.sig: The Kangxi Emperor patronised Confucian learning, which kept Chinese elites invested in the dynasty, and tolerated the Jesuits until a dispute with Rome over Chinese rites. Under his grandson the Qianlong Emperor the empire reached its greatest extent.
events.hook: China's longest-reigning emperor brought peace and expansion.
events.story: The Qing Shunzhi Emperor died of smallpox in 1661 and his seven-year-old son became the Kangxi Emperor under a regency. At 15 Kangxi took personal power by arresting his overbearing regent, Oboi. Over a 61-year reign he crushed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, took Taiwan in 1683 and fixed the border with Russia in 1689. He studied mathematics and astronomy with Jesuit advisers such as Ferdinand Verbiest.
events.then: The Kangxi Emperor patronised Confucian learning, which kept Chinese elites invested in the dynasty, and tolerated the Jesuits until a dispute with Rome over Chinese rites. Under his grandson the Qianlong Emperor the empire reached its greatest extent.
events.now: Kangxi's sixty-one years fixed Qing rule over China, Taiwan, Mongolia and the Russian frontier, and set the pattern of a Manchu dynasty governing through Confucian institutions that held until 1911.

causes.why: The young Kangxi Emperor completed the Manchu conquest, crushing the Three Feudatories revolt (1673-81).

q.before: Regents ruled for the boy emperor.
q.how: Inheritance, then a palace move against his regent.
q.winners: The Qing dynasty, which secured all of China.
q.lasted: His 61-year reign was one of the longest in Chinese history.

events.bluf: The Qing Kangxi Emperor, enthroned at seven in 1661, set out to make Manchu rule over China secure and accepted. Over 61 years he crushed the last internal rebellion, took Taiwan, fixed the Russian border and won over much of the Chinese official class through Confucian patronage. The Qing became a stable, expanding empire, and the pattern of a Manchu dynasty governing through Chinese institutions held until 1911.
events.lens: Conquest dynasties last when they win over the conquered elite through its own institutions.
events.fact: His grandson the Qianlong Emperor abdicated in 1796 after 60 years on the throne so as not to reign longer than Kangxi.

kv: reign, 1661–1722, the longest in Chinese history
Kangxi's age when he became emperor

events.who: English fleet under Duke of York; Dutch governor Peter Stuyvesant
events.what: Dutch colony surrendered without a fight.
events.why: England and the Dutch Republic were rivals for trade, and the Dutch colony on the Hudson split England's colonies in two.
events.sig: England held an unbroken coast from Maine to the Carolinas. The Dutch retook the city in 1673 and gave it up for good at the Treaty of Westminster in 1674.
events.hook: The Dutch gave up Manhattan without a fight, and New Amsterdam became New York.
events.story: England and the Dutch Republic were rivals for trade. In August 1664 an English fleet sent by the Duke of York sailed into the harbour of New Amsterdam. Dutch Director-General Peter Stuyvesant had few defenders and little support from the townspeople and surrendered. The city was renamed New York for the king's brother.
events.then: England held an unbroken coast from Maine to the Carolinas. The Dutch retook the city in 1673 and gave it up for good at the Treaty of Westminster in 1674.
events.now: The seizure gave England the Hudson and a continuous coast from Maine to Carolina, and New York kept the Dutch habit of trade before creed, which made it the commercial capital of the continent.
events.fact: The surrender terms let the Dutch keep their property, religion and language, and Dutch was still spoken in the Hudson valley in the 1800s.

causes.why: The Dutch West India Company, modelled on the VOC, founded New Amsterdam in 1624; England seized it during its trade wars with the Dutch.

q.before: The Dutch West India Company governed New Netherland.
q.how: An English fleet forced a surrender without a fight.
q.claim: Charles II granted the land to his brother James, Duke of York.
q.winners: England; Dutch settlers kept their property and religion.
q.lasted: Yes, apart from a brief Dutch return in 1673-74.

events.bluf: English King Charles II wanted the Dutch colony that split his American colonies in two, and granted it to his brother, the Duke of York, before it was taken. An English fleet entered the harbour in 1664 and Dutch Director-General Peter Stuyvesant surrendered without a fight. England gained the Hudson, a superb harbour and an unbroken coast from Maine to the Carolinas, and New York kept the Dutch habit of trade before creed that made it the commercial capital of the continent.
events.lens: Trade rivalries become wars over the best ports.

events.what: Burned most of the city.
events.why: Tightly packed timber houses, a dry summer and a strong wind. The Lord Mayor refused to pull down houses to make firebreaks on the first night.
events.sig: Architect Christopher Wren rebuilt St Paul's and 51 churches. The Rebuilding Act of 1667 required brick or stone and wider streets. The Fire Office of 1680 sold the first fire insurance.
events.hook: A bakery fire burned most of the City of London.
events.story: The fire began in baker Thomas Farriner's shop in Pudding Lane early on 2 September 1666 and burned until 5 September, driven by an east wind. It destroyed about 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches and St Paul's Cathedral. Most of the City's 80,000 people lost their homes. A handful of deaths were recorded.
events.then: Architect Christopher Wren rebuilt St Paul's and 51 churches. The Rebuilding Act of 1667 required brick or stone and wider streets. The Fire Office of 1680 sold the first fire insurance.
events.now: The Rebuilding Act of 1667 was the first modern building code and the fire produced the first fire insurance companies. Both are now standard furniture of every city.
events.fact: A French watchmaker confessed to starting the fire and was hanged, though he had been at sea when it began.

q.what: A rebuilt City of London in brick and stone.
q.new: Building rules against timber houses, and the first fire-insurance companies.
q.audience: Londoners, who saw a medieval city rebuilt.
q.reveals: How crowded, flammable early modern cities were.
q.today: The Monument near Pudding Lane and Wren's St Paul's Cathedral.

events.bluf: A bakery fire in Pudding Lane spread through wooden houses after a dry summer and burned for four days. It destroyed 13,000 houses, 87 churches and St Paul's, and left most of the City homeless. London was rebuilt in brick and stone under a building act, and fire insurance was invented to cover the next one.
events.lens: Disasters are often what finally forces cities to adopt safety rules.

kv: of the City's ~80,000 people left homeless

events.hook: A Maratha warrior founded a kingdom that fought the Mughals for decades.
events.what: A Maratha warrior founded a kingdom that fought the Mughals for decades.
events.story: Maratha leader Shivaji Bhonsle, son of a general in Bijapur's service, took his first fort in 1646 and built a state in the Western Ghats through hill forts and fast-moving cavalry. He killed Bijapur general Afzal Khan at a parley in 1659, raided the Mughal port of Surat in 1664 and escaped Mughal custody at Agra in 1666. On 6 June 1674 he was crowned Chhatrapati, sovereign king, at Raigad.
events.why: Maratha warrior families wanted an independent state in place of service to the Deccan sultanates and the Mughals. The hills favoured guerrilla war over the sultanates' heavy armies.
events.then: Shivaji died in 1680. Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb spent his last 25 years fighting the Marathas in the Deccan. After his death the Marathas expanded across much of India, until the Afghans beat them at Panipat in 1761 and the British in 1818.
events.sig: Shivaji died in 1680. Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb spent his last 25 years fighting the Marathas in the Deccan. After his death the Marathas expanded across much of India, until the Afghans beat them at Panipat in 1761 and the British in 1818.
events.now: The Maratha state Shivaji founded fought the Mughals for the next 40 years and dominated India in the 1700s, and Shivaji is the founding hero of Marathi regional and Hindu nationalist politics today.

causes.why: The fall of Vijayanagara left the Deccan to sultanates and then the Mughals, against whom the Marathas rose.

q.before: The Bijapur Sultanate and the Mughals ruled the region.
q.how: Guerrilla warfare, hill forts and a formal coronation.
q.claim: Kingship as Chhatrapati, crowned with Hindu rites.
q.lasted: The Maratha state outlived him and became India's leading power in the 1700s.

events.bluf: Maratha leader Shivaji Bhonsle set out to build an independent kingdom in the Western Ghats out of lands the Deccan sultanates and the Mughals claimed. He took hill forts, beat sultanate armies, escaped Mughal captivity and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in June 1674. The Maratha state outlived him, tied down Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb for 25 years and became India's strongest power in the 1700s.
events.lens: Guerrilla war from mountain strongholds can bleed a great empire for decades.
events.fact: Mumbai's main airport and its main railway station bear Shivaji's name.

events.who: Wampanoag sachem Metacom ('King Philip') vs. New England colonists
events.what: Bloodiest war per capita in American history.
events.why: Colonists kept taking land and imposing their law. Native leaders saw their autonomy shrink with each treaty.
events.sig: Dozens of towns burned on both sides. Metacom was killed and many captives were sold into slavery in the Caribbean. The Native nations of southern New England never recovered their independence.
events.hook: The deadliest war per person in American history broke Native power in New England.
events.story: Colonists in New England had taken land and imposed their law on Native peoples for decades. Wampanoag sachem Metacom, whom the English called King Philip, led a coalition that included the Nipmuc and Narragansett against the colonies from June 1675. Dozens of towns burned. Metacom was killed in August 1676, and many Native captives, his wife and son among them, were sold into slavery in the Caribbean.
events.then: Dozens of towns burned on both sides. Metacom was killed and many captives were sold into slavery in the Caribbean. The Native nations of southern New England never recovered their independence.
events.now: The war ended Native independence in southern New England and set the pattern of land pressure, war and removal that ran across the continent to 1890.

causes.why: Puritan expansion onto Wampanoag and Narragansett land led to war in 1675.

q.why: Colonists kept taking Native land and imposing their courts.
q.stakes: The independence of New England's Native nations.
q.decided: Colonial numbers, and Native allies such as the Mohegan fighting on the English side.
q.cost: Thousands of Native people and hundreds of colonists killed; many captives sold into slavery.
q.changed: Native independence in southern New England ended.

events.bluf: Wampanoag sachem Metacom, called King Philip by the English, led a coalition of Native nations to stop colonists taking their land and imposing English law. The war of 1675-76 burned dozens of towns on both sides and killed, relative to population, a larger share than any later American war; Metacom was killed and many captives were sold into Caribbean slavery. Native independence in southern New England ended, and the pattern of land pressure, war, enslavement and removal repeated across the continent.
events.trig: Plymouth's execution in June 1675 of three Wampanoag men for killing John Sassamon, a Christian Native informer.
events.lens: Growing settler populations turn coexistence into conflict over land.
events.fact: Metacom's head was displayed on a pike at Plymouth for some twenty years.

toll.n: Thousands more Native people died of hunger and disease or were sold into slavery. Relative to population, it was the deadliest war in American history.

events.who: Nathaniel Bacon, poor white and Black servants vs. Gov. Berkeley
events.what: Armed uprising burned Jamestown.
