events.why: Frontier settlers wanted land and war on Native peoples. They resented a governor and elite who controlled land and the Native trade, at a time of low tobacco prices.
events.sig: Berkeley hanged 23 rebels. Planters shifted from indentured servants to enslaved Africans and passed laws giving poor whites privileges over Black people, dividing workers by race.
events.hook: Poor white and Black Virginians rose up together, and the colony's elite never forgot it.
events.story: Tobacco prices were low and Virginia Governor William Berkeley controlled land grants and the Native trade. In 1676 planter Nathaniel Bacon led frontier settlers, servants and enslaved people in attacks on Native peoples and then against the governor. They burned Jamestown in September 1676. Bacon died of dysentery in October and the revolt collapsed.
events.then: Berkeley hanged 23 rebels. Planters shifted from indentured servants to enslaved Africans and passed laws giving poor whites privileges over Black people, dividing workers by race.
events.now: The laws passed after the revolt gave poor whites privileges over Black people and tied slavery to race, the legal foundation of the racial hierarchy that governed the South until 1865 and shaped it after.

causes.why: By the 1670s, poor white servants and enslaved Africans worked side by side; both joined Bacon's revolt. Planters afterward turned to slavery and race laws to divide them.

q.before: Governor William Berkeley and a small planter elite ran Virginia.
q.how: An armed uprising that burned Jamestown.
q.claim: Defending the frontier and the rights of ordinary settlers.
q.winners: In the end the planter elite, who turned to enslaved Africans.
q.lasted: No: it collapsed after Bacon died of disease.

events.bluf: Planter Nathaniel Bacon led frontier settlers, indentured servants and enslaved people against Virginia Governor William Berkeley, demanding war on Native peoples and land for themselves. They burned Jamestown in 1676, and the revolt collapsed when Bacon died of dysentery. Frightened planters shifted from indentured servants to enslaved Africans and passed laws that gave poor whites privileges over Black people, the legal beginning of a racial order that divided workers by colour.
events.lens: Elites facing a revolt that crosses group lines often split the rebels along racial or ethnic lines.
events.fact: English King Charles II is reported to have said that Berkeley had hanged more men in that naked country than he had for the murder of his father.

events.what: Founded a colony with religious tolerance; Philadelphia planned.
events.why: Charles II repaid a debt to Penn's father with land. Penn wanted a refuge for Quakers and a 'holy experiment' in tolerance.
events.sig: Pennsylvania drew Germans, Scots-Irish and many others and became the most diverse colony. Penn's sons undermined his fair dealing with the Lenape, notably in the fraudulent Walking Purchase of 1737.
events.hook: A Quaker turned a royal debt into a colony built on religious freedom.
events.story: English King Charles II owed Admiral William Penn money and paid his son, Quaker William Penn, with a grant of land in 1681. Penn designed Pennsylvania as a 'holy experiment' with religious tolerance and fair dealing with the Lenape, and arrived in 1682. Philadelphia was laid out on a grid.
events.then: Pennsylvania drew Germans, Scots-Irish and many others and became the most diverse colony. Penn's sons undermined his fair dealing with the Lenape, notably in the fraudulent Walking Purchase of 1737.
events.now: Religious freedom and pluralism became core American ideals, and Philadelphia hosted both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitutional Convention.

q.belief: Freedom of conscience for all who believed in God.
q.authority: Penn as proprietor, under a royal charter.
q.believers: Quakers, Mennonites, German Lutherans and others found refuge.
q.fallout: A diverse, prosperous colony that later led the call for independence.
q.today: Pennsylvania is still officially a 'commonwealth', and Philadelphia means 'brotherly love'.

events.bluf: Quaker William Penn wanted a refuge for persecuted Quakers and a 'holy experiment' in religious tolerance; English King Charles II paid a debt owed to Penn's father with the land in 1681. The colony drew Germans, Scots-Irish and others and became the most diverse in English America. Religious freedom and pluralism became American ideals, and Philadelphia, Penn's planned capital, hosted the Declaration of Independence and the Constitutional Convention.
events.lens: Tolerance can be an economic strategy: open colonies attract settlers and capital.
events.fact: French writer Voltaire called Penn's treaty with the Lenape the only treaty never sworn to and never broken.

kv: debt to Penn's father the grant settled

events.what: Taiwan absorbed into China.
events.why: The Zheng family used Taiwan as a base for Ming loyalist resistance and maritime trade, and the Qing needed to eliminate it to secure the coast.
events.sig: The Qing at first ruled Taiwan reluctantly as part of Fujian province and restricted migration; Han Chinese settlers came anyway and displaced Indigenous peoples. Taiwan became a province in 1885 and was ceded to Japan in 1895.
events.hook: The Qing conquered Taiwan, the root of Beijing's claim today.
events.story: After the Ming fell, Ming loyalist general Koxinga drove the Dutch out of Taiwan in 1662, and his family ruled the island as a base against the Qing. In 1683 a Qing fleet under Admiral Shi Lang won the Battle of Penghu. Koxinga's grandson Zheng Keshuang surrendered.
events.then: The Qing at first ruled Taiwan reluctantly as part of Fujian province and restricted migration; Han Chinese settlers came anyway and displaced Indigenous peoples. Taiwan became a province in 1885 and was ceded to Japan in 1895.
events.now: Whether Taiwan is part of China is among the most dangerous disputes in world politics, and both sides draw on this history: Beijing cites two centuries of Qing rule as proof the island is Chinese; Taipei notes that the Qing ceded it in 1895 and that no government in Beijing has ruled it since.

causes.why: Kangxi took Taiwan from the last Ming loyalist regime in 1683, bringing it under Beijing's rule for the first time.

q.before: Koxinga's family, ruling as Ming loyalists.
q.how: A naval campaign and surrender.
q.claim: The Qing claim to all former Ming lands.
q.lasted: Taiwan stayed Qing until Japan took it in 1895.

events.bluf: The Qing Kangxi Emperor sent a fleet to destroy the Zheng family's Ming-loyalist base on Taiwan and secure the China coast. Admiral Shi Lang won at Penghu in 1683 and Koxinga's grandson surrendered. The island came under Chinese imperial rule for the first time, for two centuries, and that period is the historical basis on which Beijing claims Taiwan today and which Taipei reads differently.
events.lens: Territorial claims rest on history, but which history counts is itself contested: 1683, 1895 and 1949 tell different stories.
events.fact: The Qing court debated abandoning the island after conquering it; Admiral Shi Lang argued it would become a pirate base and won.

events.what: Polish cavalry broke the siege.
events.why: Kara Mustafa wanted the capital and the glory. French King Louis XIV, who wanted the Habsburgs weak, stayed out.
events.sig: A Holy League of Austria, Poland, Venice and Russia drove the Ottomans back. At Karlowitz in 1699 the Ottomans gave up Hungary. Kara Mustafa was strangled on the sultan's orders that December.
events.hook: The Ottomans' second siege of Vienna failed, and their long retreat from Europe began.
events.story: Ottoman Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa besieged Vienna in July 1683 with an army of perhaps 150,000, encouraged by a Hungarian revolt against the Habsburgs. Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I fled the city. On 12 September a relief army of Habsburg, German and Polish troops under Polish King Jan Sobieski broke the siege with a charge down the Kahlenberg.
events.then: A Holy League of Austria, Poland, Venice and Russia drove the Ottomans back. At Karlowitz in 1699 the Ottomans gave up Hungary. Kara Mustafa was strangled on the sultan's orders that December.
events.now: 1683 turned the Ottoman Empire from an expanding to a retreating power in Europe. The Habsburg conquest of Hungary that followed made Austria a Danubian empire and opened the Eastern Question.
events.fact: The charge of Sobieski's winged hussars is often called the largest cavalry charge in history.

causes.why: The Ottomans returned to Vienna 154 years later and suffered their most important defeat.

q.why: The Ottomans wanted to take the Habsburg capital.
q.decided: Jan Sobieski's cavalry charge with a combined Christian relief army.
q.cost: Thousands killed; the grand vizier was executed for his failure.
q.changed: The Habsburgs went on the offensive and won Hungary.

events.bluf: Ottoman Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa marched on Vienna to take the Habsburg capital and the prestige that went with it. A relief army under Polish King Jan Sobieski broke the siege after two months. Ottoman expansion in Europe ended there; within sixteen years the Habsburgs held Hungary, and the question of who would inherit the Ottoman Balkans entered European politics.
events.lens: Imperial decline shows first at the frontier: watch where expansion stops.

toll.n: Polish hussars led one of the largest cavalry charges in history. About 5,000 Ottomans were also captured.

events.what: Laws of motion and gravity.
events.why: Kepler and Galileo had described how planets and falling bodies move. Newton supplied the why in one law.
events.sig: Newtonian physics ruled science for two centuries. Thinkers looked for similar laws of society, the foundation of Enlightenment thought.
events.hook: Newton explained the motion of everything, from apples to planets, with a few laws.
events.story: Astronomer Edmond Halley visited Cambridge in 1684 to ask what orbit an inverse-square force would produce; English mathematician Isaac Newton answered that he had worked it out, an ellipse. Halley paid for the printing. The 'Principia' of 1687 set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation.
events.then: Newtonian physics ruled science for two centuries. Thinkers looked for similar laws of society, the foundation of Enlightenment thought.
events.now: Newton gave the Enlightenment its model: if the heavens obey laws, so might society, economics and politics. His laws still launch rockets.
events.fact: Halley paid for the printing because the Royal Society had spent its budget on a history of fishes.

causes.why: Newton combined Galileo's laws of motion with Kepler's laws of planetary orbits into one theory of gravity.
The Royal Society licensed the Principia and Halley paid for its printing.

q.problem: Why do planets move as they do, and objects fall as they do?
q.how: Three laws of motion and one law of gravity, worked out with new mathematics.
q.replaced: Separate explanations for heaven and Earth.
q.spread: Slowly on the Continent; by the 1750s it was standard.
q.next: Predictable mechanics, the Enlightenment's faith in reason, and modern engineering.

events.bluf: English mathematician Isaac Newton set out to derive the planets' orbits from one law of force, at the urging of astronomer Edmond Halley. He succeeded: three laws of motion and universal gravitation explained Kepler's orbits, the tides and the comets. The universe appeared predictable, and the Enlightenment took the book as its model of reason finding law in nature.
events.lens: The most powerful theories unify: when one explanation covers things once thought separate, a revolution follows.

events.who: William of Orange, Mary II; James II
events.what: Catholic James II deposed bloodlessly.
events.why: James's Catholicism and his use of prerogative united Whigs and Tories against him. William needed England against Louis XIV.
events.sig: The Bill of Rights of 1689 put taxes and the army under Parliament, which met every year from then on. The Bank of England of 1694 and a permanent national debt financed the wars against France. Ireland and Scotland were held by force.
events.hook: England replaced its king almost without bloodshed and made Parliament supreme.
events.story: English King James II was promoting Catholics, suspending laws by prerogative and building a standing army. In June 1688 his son's birth promised a Catholic dynasty. Seven leading politicians invited Dutch ruler William of Orange, husband of James's Protestant daughter Mary, to invade. William landed at Torbay in November with about 15,000 men. James fled to France.
events.then: The Bill of Rights of 1689 put taxes and the army under Parliament, which met every year from then on. The Bank of England of 1694 and a permanent national debt financed the wars against France. Ireland and Scotland were held by force.
events.now: Britain's constitutional monarchy and the American founders' idea of limited government rest on the settlement of 1689. The fiscal state it produced outfought richer France for a century.
events.fact: William's landing was the last successful invasion of England.

causes.why: James II's Catholicism, his use of royal power to override laws, and the birth of a Catholic heir united his opponents.

q.before: James II, a Catholic king who ruled without Parliament when he could.
q.how: A foreign invasion invited by English leaders, with little bloodshed in England.
q.lasted: Yes: it founded Britain's constitutional monarchy.

events.bluf: Seven English politicians invited Dutch ruler William of Orange to invade and remove the Catholic James II, and William wanted England's resources for his war on Louis XIV. James's army melted away and he fled; Parliament gave the crown to William and Mary on its own terms. Parliamentary supremacy, constitutional monarchy and a state that could borrow cheaply followed, the base of British power for a century and a model for the American constitution.
events.trig: The birth of James's son in June 1688 and the acquittal of seven bishops who had refused to read his declaration of toleration.
events.lens: Revolutions succeed when a foreign power's strategic interest lines up with domestic grievances.

events.hook: Locke argued that governments exist to protect people's rights, and may be overthrown if they don't.
events.what: Locke argued that governments exist to protect people's rights, and may be overthrown if they don't.
events.story: English philosopher John Locke published the 'Two Treatises of Government' anonymously in 1689, after returning from Dutch exile with William's fleet. People hold natural rights to life, liberty and property, he argued, and create governments by consent to protect them. A ruler who breaks the trust may be removed.
events.why: The revolution of 1688 needed a justification beyond Protestantism, and Locke had drafted one in exile.
events.then: Locke's argument became the standard defence of the 1688 settlement and, through the Enlightenment, of the American and French revolutions.
events.sig: Locke's argument became the standard defence of the 1688 settlement and, through the Enlightenment, of the American and French revolutions.
events.now: The Declaration of Independence restates Locke. Every argument over consent, property and the right to rebel is still conducted in his terms.

causes.why: Locke answered Hobbes: people create government to protect their rights, and may replace one that violates them.

q.idea: People have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and government exists by their consent to protect them.
q.spread: Through Europe and especially the American colonies.
q.enabled: Arguments for revolution and constitutional government.
q.critics: Conservatives feared it invited endless rebellion.

events.bluf: English philosopher John Locke wrote to justify resistance to James II and the settlement that replaced him. He argued that government exists by consent to protect natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that a ruler who violates them may be resisted. The book became the theory of liberal government and of the American Revolution.
events.lens: Legitimacy comes from protecting people's rights: ask what a government offers in return for obedience.
events.fact: Locke denied authorship of the book until his will.
events.btt: John Locke: Two Treatises of Government

kv: natural rights: life, liberty and property

events.who: The Kangxi Emperor's envoys; Russian envoy Fyodor Golovin; Jesuit interpreters
events.hook: China and Russia signed their first treaty, negotiated in Latin by Jesuit priests.
events.what: China and Russia signed their first treaty, negotiated in Latin by Jesuit priests.
events.story: Russian forts on the Amur River had clashed with Qing forces through the 1680s. Qing envoy Songgotu and Russian envoy Fyodor Golovin met at Nerchinsk in Siberia in 1689. They agreed a border along the Argun River and the Stanovoy mountains, and Russia gave up the Amur valley. Jesuits in Qing service, Jean-François Gerbillon and Thomas Pereira, translated, so the official text was in Latin.
events.why: The Qing wanted to secure Manchuria and keep Russia away from the Mongols. Russia wanted trade.
events.then: The border held until Russia, taking advantage of Qing weakness, annexed the Amur region in 1858 and the Pacific coast in 1860.
events.sig: The border held until Russia, taking advantage of Qing weakness, annexed the Amur region in 1858 and the Pacific coast in 1860.
events.now: The contrast between Nerchinsk, made on equal terms, and the 'unequal treaties' after 1842 remains part of Chinese historical memory, and the Amur line it drew is the one Russia tore up in 1858-60.

causes.why: Kangxi drove the Russians from the Amur and then negotiated a border.

q.before: Russian Cossacks had pushed into the Amur valley.
q.how: A negotiated treaty after Qing military pressure.
q.claim: Each side's claim to the frontier lands.
q.winners: The Qing kept the Amur; Russia gained trade rights.
q.lasted: Until 1858-60, when Russia took the region.

events.bluf: The Qing Kangxi Emperor wanted Russia out of the Amur valley and away from the Mongols; Russia wanted trade with China more than forts on the Amur. At Nerchinsk in 1689 the two agreed a border on the Argun River and the Stanovoy mountains, with Russia giving up the Amur. China's first treaty with a European state was made on equal terms, and the border held for 170 years.
events.lens: Treaties reflect the balance of power when signed; when the balance shifts, borders follow.
events.fact: The treaty's official text was in Latin, the only language the two sides' interpreters shared.

kv: treaty between China and a European power

events.who: Parliament; William III and Mary II
events.hook: Parliament wrote limits on the crown into law.
events.what: Parliament wrote limits on the crown into law.
events.story: The Convention Parliament presented the Declaration of Rights to William and Mary in February 1689 as the condition of their crown, and enacted it as the Bill of Rights in December. It barred the suspension of laws, taxation and a peacetime army without Parliament's consent and protected free elections and free speech in Parliament.
events.why: James II had ruled without Parliament and promoted Catholics. The new monarchs needed Parliament's money for war.
events.then: Parliament met every year from 1689. The Act of Settlement of 1701 fixed a Protestant succession.
events.sig: Parliament met every year from 1689. The Act of Settlement of 1701 fixed a Protestant succession.
events.now: Because Parliament had to approve money and the army every year, the crown had to govern through ministers with a majority, which is how cabinet government and the prime minister arose.

causes.why: The new monarchs, William and Mary, accepted limits on royal power as the price of the crown.

q.before: Kings claimed powers to suspend laws and raise taxes on their own.
q.how: An act of Parliament the new monarchs accepted.
q.claim: The 'ancient rights and liberties' of the English.
q.lasted: Yes: it is still part of the UK constitution.

events.bluf: Parliament wanted James II's successors bound by law before it handed them the crown. The Bill of Rights barred the monarch from suspending laws, taxing or keeping a peacetime army without Parliament's consent. Parliament became the centre of British government, and monarchs had to govern through ministers who could command it.
events.lens: Writing limits on power into law makes them harder to reverse than promises.
events.fact: The American Bill of Rights copied its ban on cruel and unusual punishments almost word for word.

kv: before the US Bill of Rights, 1791

events.who: William III; the deposed James II
events.hook: William III beat the deposed James II in Ireland, securing the Protestant succession.
events.what: William III beat the deposed James II in Ireland, securing the Protestant succession.
events.story: James II landed in Ireland in 1689 with French troops. English King William III brought his own army over in 1690. On 1 July 1690, 11 July by the modern calendar, William's army crossed the Boyne and defeated James's Irish and French force. James left for France within days. The war ended at Limerick in 1691.
events.why: Ireland was the one kingdom where James still had an army and a Catholic majority.
events.then: The penal laws barred Catholics from Parliament, the professions and most land ownership for more than a century.
events.sig: The penal laws barred Catholics from Parliament, the professions and most land ownership for more than a century.
events.now: The penal laws that followed the Boyne made religion the line of property and power in Ireland. The division runs through the Northern Ireland conflict and the Orange parades every 12 July.

causes.why: James II, driven out in 1688, tried to win back his thrones through Ireland.

q.why: James II tried to regain his crown from Ireland with French help.
q.stakes: Whether England would have a Protestant or a Catholic monarch.
q.decided: William's larger, more experienced army.
q.cost: About 2,000 killed; far more died in the wider war.
q.changed: Protestant rule in Ireland was secured, with lasting sectarian bitterness.

events.bluf: The deposed James II used Catholic Ireland, with French support, as a base to win back his thrones; William III crossed to Ireland to finish him. William won at the Boyne and James fled to France. The Protestant succession was secure, and Ireland entered a century of Protestant Ascendancy that shut Catholics out of land and power.
events.lens: When a community still marches to celebrate a 300-year-old victory, the conflict behind it is still alive.
events.fact: The Pope backed William, because France was his enemy and William's ally was the Habsburg emperor.

toll.n: Estimates. The defeat sent James II back to France for good.

events.who: Job Charnock of the East India Company
events.hook: A Company agent set up a trading post on the Hooghly River that became the capital of British India.
events.what: A Company agent set up a trading post on the Hooghly River that became the capital of British India.
events.story: The Company had fought a short war with the Mughal governor of Bengal from 1686 and lost. Company agent Job Charnock returned under a Mughal pardon and settled at Sutanuti on the Hooghly on 24 August 1690. In 1698 the Company bought the rights to the villages of Sutanuti, Kalikata and Gobindapur, and Fort William, begun in 1696, was built beside them.
events.why: Bengal produced silk, cotton cloth and saltpetre for gunpowder, and the Company needed a port it could fortify.
events.then: Calcutta became the base from which Company commander Robert Clive won Bengal at Plassey in 1757. It was the capital of British India until 1911 and grew into the second city of the empire.
events.sig: Calcutta became the base from which Company commander Robert Clive won Bengal at Plassey in 1757. It was the capital of British India until 1911 and grew into the second city of the empire.
events.now: Calcutta was the Company's base for the conquest of Bengal in 1757 and the seat of British rule in India until 1911; Bengal's revenue paid for the conquest of the rest.

causes.why: The Company expanded from Madras to Bengal, the richest province of Mughal India.

q.what: Bengal silk, cotton textiles and saltpetre.
q.who: The Company and its employees, who also traded on their own account.
q.scale: From three villages to the second city of the British Empire.
q.daily: Merchants, boatmen and weavers moved to the new town for work.
q.system: A Company port city that became a colonial capital.

events.bluf: The East India Company wanted a secure port in Bengal, the richest province of Mughal India, after losing a short war with the Mughal governor. Company agent Job Charnock settled at Sutanuti on the Hooghly in August 1690, and the Company bought three villages and built Fort William. Calcutta became the base from which the Company took Bengal in 1757 and the capital of British India until 1911.
events.lens: Ports chosen for trade become capitals of empire when the traders turn to conquest.
events.fact: The Calcutta High Court ruled in 2003 that the city had no founder, since the site was settled before Charnock arrived.

events.what: 20 people executed for witchcraft.
events.why: Local feuds in Salem Village came first. Frontier war with Native peoples and France had filled the region with refugees and fear, and Puritan doctrine made the Devil a daily presence.
events.sig: Massachusetts courts stopped accepting spectral evidence. The colony later apologised and in 1711 paid compensation to the victims' families.
events.hook: Village feuds and fear led a Puritan town to hang 19 people as witches.
events.story: Girls in Salem Village had strange fits early in 1692 and accusations of witchcraft spread through the surrounding towns. A special court under Massachusetts magistrates accepted 'spectral evidence' of dreams and visions. Nineteen people were hanged and one man was pressed to death before Governor William Phips halted the court in October 1692.
events.then: Massachusetts courts stopped accepting spectral evidence. The colony later apologised and in 1711 paid compensation to the victims' families.
events.now: The trials' collapse discredited spectral evidence and pushed colonial courts toward stricter proof; 'witch hunt' became the term for a panic that convicts on accusation, from the McCarthy hearings of the 1950s to today.
events.fact: Nobody was burned. Nineteen were hanged and one man, Giles Corey, was pressed to death under stones.

causes.why: Puritan Massachusetts, shaken by frontier war and the loss of its original charter, turned on its own people in 1692.

q.belief: Fear that the Devil was attacking the community through witches.
q.authority: A special court set up by the governor.
q.believers: Neighbours accused neighbours; more than 150 people were jailed.
q.fallout: Twenty executed; the court was dissolved and later apologies followed.
q.today: Salem draws tourists, and 'witch hunt' is a common phrase.

events.bluf: Puritan magistrates in Massachusetts set out to purge Salem Village of witchcraft after girls there had fits in 1692. A special court accepted 'spectral evidence' of dreams and visions, and 20 people were executed before Governor William Phips stopped the trials. The collapse discredited spectral evidence and pushed colonial courts toward stricter standards of proof, and 'witch hunt' became the name for every panic that convicts on fear.
events.lens: Panics feed on accusations that cannot be disproved: watch for charges that need no evidence.

kv: man pressed to death with stones

events.what: Gold discovered.
events.why: Bandeirantes searching the interior for captives and precious metals struck gold in Minas Gerais. Portugal, short of revenue, taxed the output at a fifth and policed the roads.
events.sig: Minas Gerais became Brazil's richest region, and the capital moved from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro in 1763, the port for the mines. Under the Methuen Treaty of 1703 Portugal bought British cloth and paid the difference in Brazilian gold. Diamonds were found in the same region in the 1720s.
events.hook: Gold in Brazil pulled in hundreds of thousands of migrants and enslaved Africans.
events.story: In the 1690s bandeirantes, slave-raiding explorers from São Paulo, found gold in the hills of Minas Gerais. Tens of thousands of Portuguese settlers and enslaved Africans poured in. Towns such as Ouro Preto grew rich on the output.
events.then: Minas Gerais became Brazil's richest region, and the capital moved from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro in 1763, the port for the mines. Under the Methuen Treaty of 1703 Portugal bought British cloth and paid the difference in Brazilian gold. Diamonds were found in the same region in the 1720s.
events.now: The gold moved Brazil's capital to Rio de Janeiro in 1763 and, through the Methuen Treaty of 1703, made Portugal a market for British cloth paid in bullion; Minas Gerais remains a mining state, and the dam collapses at Mariana (2015) and Brumadinho (2019) show the industry's continuing costs.

q.what: Gold, and later diamonds.
q.who: Portugal's crown and merchants; enslaved Africans did the dangerous work.
q.scale: Brazil became the world's largest gold producer in the 1700s.
q.daily: Enslaved miners worked in rivers and shafts in brutal conditions.
q.system: Brazilian gold flowed through Lisbon to Britain to pay for imports.

events.bluf: Bandeirantes from São Paulo searched the interior for captives and precious metals and found gold in Minas Gerais in the 1690s. The rush drew tens of thousands of Portuguese settlers and enslaved Africans inland and made Minas Gerais the colony's richest region. Brazil's centre of gravity moved south and inland, demand for enslaved Africans rose, and much of the gold flowed through Portugal to Britain, where it helped finance commercial expansion.
events.lens: Resource booms move people and capital quickly; follow where the profits end up, which may be far away.
events.fact: Ouro Preto's baroque churches were carved by Aleijadinho, the son of a Portuguese architect and an enslaved African woman.

kv: Portuguese emigrants to Brazil in the 1700s

events.what: Founded to lend to government.
events.why: Parliament's control of taxes after 1689 made government debt trustworthy for the first time.
events.sig: A permanent national debt serviced by parliamentary taxes became the backbone of the British war state. The Bank became the lender of last resort to the banking system in the 1800s.
events.hook: A bank set up to fund a war became the model for central banks.
events.story: English King William III needed money for the war against French King Louis XIV. In 1694 a group of investors led by Scottish merchant William Paterson lent the government £1.2 million at 8 per cent interest. In return they were chartered as the Bank of England, with the right to take deposits and issue notes.
events.then: A permanent national debt serviced by parliamentary taxes became the backbone of the British war state. The Bank became the lender of last resort to the banking system in the 1800s.
events.now: The Bank let Britain borrow at low rates against future taxes, which financed a century of war against France and is the model nearly every state's central bank follows.
events.fact: The loan was fully subscribed in twelve days.

causes.why: William III's wars against France needed new ways to borrow, backed by Parliament's taxes.

q.what: Loans to the government, and banknotes.
q.who: Investors earned steady interest; taxpayers paid it.
q.scale: Britain's national debt grew enormously, but it could keep borrowing cheaply.
q.daily: Banknotes slowly became everyday money.
q.system: A national debt managed by a central bank.

events.bluf: William III needed money to fight Louis XIV, and London investors wanted a safe return backed by Parliament. The investors lent £1.2 million at 8 per cent and were chartered as the Bank of England. The state could now borrow cheaply against future taxes, and that fiscal strength let Britain outspend richer France for a century.
events.lens: In long wars, credit can matter more than wealth: the side that can borrow cheaply can fight longer.

events.who: Prince Eugene of Savoy; Sultan Mustafa II
events.where: Senta, on the Tisza River, Serbia
events.hook: Prince Eugene caught the Ottoman army crossing a river and destroyed it.
events.what: Prince Eugene caught the Ottoman army crossing a river and destroyed it.
events.story: On 11 September 1697 Habsburg commander Prince Eugene of Savoy attacked the Ottoman army while it was crossing the Tisza at Zenta. Sultan Mustafa II watched from the far bank. The grand vizier and some 20,000 soldiers died; Habsburg losses were a few hundred.
events.why: The Habsburgs had been driving the Ottomans back since 1683, and Eugene moved faster than an army with its baggage half across a river.
events.then: The Ottomans made peace at Karlowitz in 1699.
events.sig: The Ottomans made peace at Karlowitz in 1699.
events.now: Zenta ended Ottoman power in Hungary and made Austria a Danubian great power, which it remained until 1918; the lands it won are the Hungarian and Balkan provinces that later pulled it into the Balkan wars.

causes.why: After Vienna the Habsburgs went on the offensive down the Danube.

q.why: To drive the Ottomans out of Hungary after the failed siege of Vienna.
q.stakes: Control of Hungary and the Balkans.
q.decided: A surprise attack while the Ottoman army was split by the river.
q.cost: Perhaps 25,000 to 30,000 Ottoman dead.
q.changed: The Ottomans accepted the loss of Hungary.

events.bluf: Habsburg commander Prince Eugene of Savoy caught Sultan Mustafa II's army crossing the Tisza and destroyed it. Tens of thousands of Ottomans died against a few hundred Habsburgs. The Ottomans accepted the loss of Hungary at Karlowitz two years later, and Austria became the dominant power on the Danube.
events.lens: Armies are most vulnerable while moving, above all when crossing rivers.
events.fact: Eugene had been rejected by Louis XIV for French service as too small and sickly; he beat French armies for the next forty years.

toll.n: The grand vizier was among the Ottoman dead. Many drowned trying to cross the Tisza.

events.what: Ended Portuguese control of the Swahili coast.
events.why: Oman wanted the trade of the coast and the Portuguese gone from it. Portuguese relief from Goa arrived too small and too late.
events.sig: Oman controlled the coast and its trade for 150 years. Its sultan moved his capital to Zanzibar in 1840.
events.hook: Omani Arabs captured Fort Jesus, ending Portuguese power on the Swahili coast.
events.story: Oman had expelled the Portuguese from Muscat in 1650 and was building its own Indian Ocean empire. In March 1696 a fleet sent by Omani Imam Saif bin Sultan laid siege to Fort Jesus, Portugal's main fortress at Mombasa. Disease and hunger killed most of the defenders. In December 1698 the Omanis stormed the fort after a siege of 33 months.
events.then: Oman controlled the coast and its trade for 150 years. Its sultan moved his capital to Zanzibar in 1840.
events.now: Oman's victory replaced Portuguese with Arab control of the Swahili coast and tied East Africa to the Gulf for two centuries, through Zanzibar's clove plantations and the slave caravans into the interior.
events.fact: Fort Jesus is a World Heritage site; Omani architecture and vocabulary shaped Swahili culture.

causes.why: Swahili resentment of Portuguese rule helped Oman, which had expelled the Portuguese from Muscat in 1650, drive them from Mombasa.

q.why: Oman was driving the Portuguese from the Swahili coast.
q.stakes: Control of the East African coast north of Mozambique.
q.decided: A long siege that starved the garrison.
q.cost: Nearly all the defenders died.
q.changed: Oman, not Portugal, dominated the coast for 150 years.

events.bluf: Omani Imam Saif bin Sultan set out to drive Portugal from the Swahili coast, as Oman had driven it from Muscat in 1650, and to build an Indian Ocean empire of his own. His fleet besieged Fort Jesus at Mombasa from March 1696 and stormed it in December 1698 after 33 months, when disease and hunger had killed most of the defenders. Portuguese power north of Mozambique ended, the coast was tied to Arabia for two centuries, and Zanzibar's rise as the centre of the clove and slave trades followed.
events.lens: Regional powers often replace a declining European empire before the next European empire arrives.

events.who: The Ottoman Empire; the Holy League of Austria, Poland, Venice and Russia
events.hook: For the first time, the Ottomans signed away large territories to Christian powers.
events.what: For the first time, the Ottomans signed away large territories to Christian powers.
events.story: Mediated by England and the Dutch Republic, the treaty was signed on 26 January 1699 at Sremski Karlovci. Austria received Hungary and Transylvania, Poland Podolia and Venice the Morea and Dalmatia. Russia's separate truce gave it Azov in 1700.
events.why: Defeats from Vienna in 1683 to Zenta in 1697 had left the Ottomans without an army in the field.
events.then: The Ottomans fortified the Danube and recovered the Morea in 1718. Austria governed Hungary as a conquered province, which produced the revolts of 1703 and 1848.
events.sig: The Ottomans fortified the Danube and recovered the Morea in 1718. Austria governed Hungary as a conquered province, which produced the revolts of 1703 and 1848.
events.now: Karlowitz began the Ottoman retreat from Europe that ran to 1913. English and Dutch mediation set the precedent of European powers managing Ottoman affairs, the Eastern Question in its first form.

causes.why: The disaster at Zenta forced the Ottomans to negotiate.

q.before: The Ottomans ruled most of Hungary.
q.how: A peace treaty after military defeat.
q.winners: Austria above all; the Ottomans lost Hungary.
q.lasted: Mostly: the Ottomans won back the Morea in 1718 but never Hungary.

events.bluf: The Ottomans wanted an end to sixteen years of defeat; Austria, Poland, Venice and Russia wanted their conquests confirmed. At Karlowitz the Ottomans gave Hungary and Transylvania to Austria, Podolia to Poland and the Morea to Venice. The empire turned from expansion to defence, and Austria rose as the power on the Danube.
events.lens: The first treaty in which an empire permanently gives up land often marks the start of its long retreat.
events.fact: The negotiating pavilion had four doors so that no delegation entered after another.

kv: powers gaining Ottoman land: Austria, Venice, Poland, Russia

events.what: Asante confederacy united under the Golden Stool.
events.why: The Akan states wanted Denkyira's rule and tribute gone. The Golden Stool gave the union a sacred bond above local allegiances.
events.sig: Asante expanded and sold gold and captives to Europeans on the coast for guns and goods. After Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 the two fought a series of wars. Britain annexed Asante in 1901 after the War of the Golden Stool.
events.hook: The Asante united around the Golden Stool and became West Africa's great power.
events.story: Denkyira ruled the Akan states of the forest and took tribute from them. Kumasi ruler Osei Tutu and his priest Okomfo Anokye bound a group of Akan chiefdoms into a confederation. By tradition Anokye summoned the Golden Stool from the sky; it held the soul of the nation, and every chief swore loyalty to it, a sacred bond above local allegiances. In 1701 the alliance crushed Denkyira at the battle of Feyiase.
events.then: Asante expanded and sold gold and captives to Europeans on the coast for guns and goods. After Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 the two fought a series of wars. Britain annexed Asante in 1901 after the War of the Golden Stool.
events.now: Asante's union of chiefdoms under one stool held through a series of wars with Britain from 1824 to 1900 and survived annexation. The Asantehene remains the strongest traditional authority in Ghana.
events.fact: The Golden Stool, said to have descended from the sky, holds the soul of the Asante nation. No one sits on it, even the king.

causes.why: European forts on the Gold Coast pulled trade, in gold, guns and captives, toward the coast, enriching forest states like Asante.

q.before: The Akan states paid tribute to Denkyira.
q.how: Union of states, victory over Denkyira in 1701, and a new national symbol.
q.claim: The Golden Stool, said to hold the soul of the nation.
q.lasted: Asante stayed independent until British conquest in 1900-01.

events.bluf: Kumasi ruler Osei Tutu and his priest Okomfo Anokye bound a group of Akan chiefdoms into a confederation to throw off the rule of Denkyira. The alliance crushed Denkyira at Feyiase in 1701, and the Golden Stool, which held the soul of the new nation, gave it a loyalty above local allegiance. Asante became the main power of the Gold Coast, sold gold and captives to Europeans at the coast for guns, and was Britain's hardest opponent there until 1901.
events.lens: Shared sacred symbols can bind separate communities into a state more durably than conquest.

events.who: France & Spain vs. Britain, Austria, Dutch
events.what: War over who inherits Spain.
events.why: A single Bourbon family ruling France, Spain and the Americas would have dominated Europe and its trade.
events.sig: Philip V kept Spain and renounced France. Britain took Gibraltar, Minorca and the asiento, the contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America. Catalonia, which had backed the Habsburg, lost its institutions in 1714.
events.hook: Europe fought to stop France and Spain from merging under one family.
events.story: Spanish King Charles II died childless in November 1700 and left his empire to Philip of Anjou, grandson of French King Louis XIV. Louis accepted. Britain, the Dutch Republic and Austria backed a Habsburg claimant and declared war in 1702. The Duke of Marlborough's victories from Blenheim in 1704 broke France's reputation. Peace came at Utrecht in 1713 and Rastatt in 1714.
events.then: Philip V kept Spain and renounced France. Britain took Gibraltar, Minorca and the asiento, the contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America. Catalonia, which had backed the Habsburg, lost its institutions in 1714.
events.now: The balance of power became the stated principle of European politics at Utrecht, and Britain its manager for two centuries. Spain's Bourbon dynasty still reigns.

causes.why: Louis XIV's marriage to a Spanish princess gave the Bourbons the claim that sparked the war.

q.why: Who would inherit the Spanish empire after Charles II died childless.
q.stakes: A union of France and Spain that would dominate Europe.
q.decided: Marlborough's and Eugene's victories, and the exhaustion of France.
q.cost: Hundreds of thousands of soldiers dead.
q.changed: A Bourbon kept Spain, but the two crowns stayed separate.

events.bluf: French King Louis XIV accepted the whole Spanish empire for his grandson and refused to rule out the union of the two crowns; Britain, the Dutch and Austria went to war to prevent it. Twelve years of war kept the crowns apart and left Philip V in Madrid. Britain came out with Gibraltar, Minorca, the slave-trade contract and the position of leading naval and commercial power.
events.trig: Charles II's will of 1700 and Louis XIV's acceptance of it.
events.lens: Coalitions form against any power that threatens to dominate the whole system.
events.fact: Catalonia's national day, 11 September, marks the fall of Barcelona in 1714.

toll.n: Blenheim saved Vienna and broke France's reputation for invincibility.

events.hook: Peter founded a new capital on marshland captured from Sweden, as Russia's 'window to Europe'.
events.what: Peter founded a new capital on marshland captured from Sweden, as Russia's 'window to Europe'.
events.story: On 27 May 1703 Russian Tsar Peter I laid the foundations of the Peter and Paul Fortress on the Neva, on marshland taken from Sweden weeks before. Tens of thousands of conscripted labourers built the city; many died of disease. It became the capital in 1712.
events.why: Russia had no port on the Baltic. Peter wanted the navy, the trade and the distance from Moscow.
events.then: St Petersburg remained the capital until 1918. The nobility was ordered to build houses there and did.
events.sig: St Petersburg remained the capital until 1918. The nobility was ordered to build houses there and did.
events.now: A capital on the Baltic turned Russia toward Europe by decree: the court, the navy and the civil service were built there, and the city's westernised elite governed an eastern empire for two centuries, a divide Russian politics still carries.

q.before: Moscow was the seat of the tsars.
q.how: A new capital built by decree.
q.claim: Russia's place among the European powers.
q.winners: Peter's modernisers; the old Moscow nobility lost out.
q.lasted: It was the capital until 1918.

events.bluf: Russian Tsar Peter I wanted a Baltic port and a capital free of Moscow's traditions. He founded a city on land just taken from Sweden and moved the court, the navy and the civil service there. Russia faced Europe by decree for two centuries, and the gap between a westernised elite and the peasant interior became the standing fact of Russian politics.
events.lens: Moving a capital is a statement of strategy: watch where a state puts its centre of power.
events.fact: Peter banned stone building elsewhere in Russia for a time so that every mason would come to the new city.

kv: forced labourers died building it (estimates vary)

events.what: Acts of Union joined the two kingdoms.
events.why: Scotland needed England's trade and empire. England needed Scotland bound to the Protestant succession.
events.sig: Scots served the empire out of proportion to their numbers as soldiers, administrators, doctors and merchants. The Scottish Enlightenment followed within a generation.
events.hook: England and Scotland joined into one kingdom.
events.story: Scotland's Darien scheme, a colony on the isthmus of Panama, had failed by 1700 and taken a quarter of the country's liquid capital with it. The English Parliament's Act of Settlement of 1701 fixed a Hanoverian succession that Scotland had not agreed to. The Acts of Union of 1707 merged the two parliaments at Westminster.
events.then: Scots served the empire out of proportion to their numbers as soldiers, administrators, doctors and merchants. The Scottish Enlightenment followed within a generation.
events.now: The union gave Scots the empire as a career and Britain a secure island. Scotland voted to stay in 2014; the question remains open and Brexit sharpened it.
events.fact: England paid Scotland the Equivalent, nearly £400,000, partly to compensate Darien's investors.

causes.why: England's financial strength contrasted with Scotland's ruin after its failed Darien colony; union offered Scots access to English markets.

q.before: England and Scotland shared a king but had separate parliaments.
q.how: Acts of Union passed by both parliaments.
q.claim: A single Parliament of Great Britain, with Scotland keeping its law and church.
q.winners: The union's supporters; many Scots opposed it bitterly.
q.lasted: Yes, though Scotland regained its own parliament in 1999.

events.bluf: Scotland was near bankruptcy after the Darien colony failed, and England wanted to stop Scotland choosing a different king and allying with France. The Acts of Union made one state, one parliament and one market. Scotland gained the empire's trade and England its northern border, and Great Britain became the base of imperial power.
events.lens: Unions are often driven by economic crisis on one side and security fears on the other, and they last only while both sides still benefit.

kv: Scots, against ~5.5 million in England and Wales

events.what: Last powerful Mughal emperor died.
events.why: Decades of war in the Deccan had drained the treasury and the nobility's patience. His religious policy had cost him Rajput and other Hindu allies.
events.sig: Six emperors followed in twelve years. The governors of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad made their posts hereditary in the 1720s, and the Marathas expanded north. The East India Company exploited the divisions from 1757.
events.hook: The last great Mughal died, and his empire broke apart.
events.story: Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb pushed the empire to its greatest size, taking Bijapur in 1686 and Golconda in 1687, and spent his last 25 years campaigning against the Marathas in the Deccan. He reimposed the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1679 and executed the Sikh Guru Tegh Bahadur in 1675. He died in the Deccan on 3 March 1707 aged 88. Three of his sons fought over the throne; Bahadur Shah I won.
events.then: Six emperors followed in twelve years. The governors of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad made their posts hereditary in the 1720s, and the Marathas expanded north. The East India Company exploited the divisions from 1757.
events.now: The succession wars after 1707 turned Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad into hereditary states by the 1720s, the fragmentation the East India Company picked apart from 1757. Aurangzeb's religious policy is a live quarrel in Indian politics today.

causes.why: Shah Jahan's son Aurangzeb imprisoned his father and spent decades on costly wars in the Deccan. His death in 1707 left an exhausted empire to quarrelling heirs.
Aurangzeb spent his last quarter-century fighting the Marathas in the Deccan, draining his treasury.

q.before: Aurangzeb ruled the largest empire India had yet seen.
q.how: Death followed by a war of succession.
q.claim: Mughal dynastic right, contested among his sons.
q.winners: Regional powers: Marathas, Sikhs and provincial governors.
q.lasted: The empire survived in name until 1857, but its power drained away.

events.bluf: Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb spent his reign extending the empire to its greatest size and holding it by force against Marathas, Rajputs and Sikhs. He died in 1707 aged 88 with the Deccan unconquered and the treasury strained by 25 years of war. His sons fought for the throne, and within 30 years the provinces were states in all but name, which the East India Company exploited from 1757.
events.lens: Empires at their territorial peak are often already overstretched: watch the cost of the last conquests.
events.fact: Aurangzeb asked to be buried in a plain open grave at Khuldabad, paid for with money he had earned sewing caps.

kv: India's share of world output, c. 1700 (Maddison est.)

events.who: Peter the Great vs. Charles XII of Sweden
events.what: Russia crushed Sweden.
events.why: Sweden held the Baltic coast and Peter wanted it. Charles gambled on a march to Moscow and lost his supply train.
events.sig: Russia won the Baltic coast at Nystad in 1721 and Peter took the title of emperor. Moscow cut back Cossack autonomy in Ukraine.
events.hook: Russia crushed Sweden and became a European great power.
events.story: Swedish King Charles XII invaded Russia in 1708 and turned south into Ukraine, where Cossack Hetman Ivan Mazepa had joined him. The winter of 1708-09 killed thousands of his men. On 8 July 1709 Russian Tsar Peter I's larger army crushed the Swedes at Poltava. The survivors surrendered at Perevolochna three days later.
events.then: Russia won the Baltic coast at Nystad in 1721 and Peter took the title of emperor. Moscow cut back Cossack autonomy in Ukraine.
events.now: Poltava ended Sweden as a great power and made Russia the dominant state in the Baltic and eastern Europe, the position it held until 1917 and sought again after 1945.
events.fact: In Ukraine the battle is remembered as a lost chance for independence, and Mazepa remains contested.

causes.why: Charles XII marched into Russia to undo Peter's gains on the Baltic, and lost everything at Poltava.

q.why: The Great Northern War over who would dominate the Baltic.
q.stakes: Russia's access to the Baltic and Sweden's empire.
q.decided: Russian numbers and fortifications against a worn-out Swedish army.
q.cost: Sweden lost almost its entire field army.
q.changed: Russia replaced Sweden as northern Europe's great power.

events.bluf: Swedish King Charles XII invaded Russia to knock Tsar Peter I out of the Great Northern War. His army was drawn south into Ukraine, starved through a winter and destroyed at Poltava. Sweden ceased to be a great power, Russia took the Baltic coast and became the dominant state in eastern Europe, and the Cossack hetman who had joined Sweden lost Ukraine's autonomy.
events.lens: Small powers that bet on an outside protector against a large neighbour risk everything if the protector loses.

toll.n: Three days later about 16,000 more Swedes surrendered at Perevolochna.

events.what: Ended Spanish Succession war; Britain got Gibraltar.
events.why: Twelve years of war had exhausted every power. Britain's new Tory ministry made peace without its allies.
events.sig: Savoy and Prussia rose in rank as kingdoms. France was contained and stayed strong. The asiento made Britain the largest carrier in the Atlantic slave trade.
events.hook: A peace that rebalanced Europe also handed Britain the slave trade to Spanish America.
events.story: The treaties signed at Utrecht in April 1713 ended the War of the Spanish Succession. Spanish King Philip V kept Spain and renounced the French succession. Britain gained Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and the asiento. Austria took the Spanish Netherlands and Spanish Italy.
events.then: Savoy and Prussia rose in rank as kingdoms. France was contained and stayed strong. The asiento made Britain the largest carrier in the Atlantic slave trade.
events.now: Utrecht made the balance of power an explicit principle of diplomacy and Britain the leading maritime power. Gibraltar is still a British territory and a Spanish grievance.

causes.why: The treaties that ended the war let the Bourbon Philip V keep Spain, on condition that France and Spain never unite.

q.before: Rival claims to the Spanish empire.
q.how: Negotiated treaties.
q.claim: A balance of power in which no state could dominate Europe.
q.lasted: Its main settlement held for decades; Gibraltar is still British.

events.bluf: Britain's Tory government wanted out of a war it had already won at sea and in trade. The Utrecht treaties kept France and Spain under separate crowns and gave Britain Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland and the slave-trade contract. The balance of power was written into a treaty for the first time, and Britain became its manager.
events.lens: Peace settlements that balance rival powers last longer than ones that crush the loser.
events.fact: The treaty's preamble names the balance of power as its purpose, the first treaty to do so.

kv: enslaved Africans a year Britain could sell to Spanish America under the asiento

events.what: A practical shogun lifted the ban on Western books, and 'Dutch learning' was born.
events.why: The shogunate needed practical knowledge, especially for astronomy and the calendar.
events.sig: Students of Dutch learning translated anatomy, chemistry and gunnery books over the next century, beginning with an anatomy text in 1774.
events.hook: A practical shogun lifted the ban on Western books, and 'Dutch learning' was born.
events.story: The shogunate had banned Western books along with Christianity. Japanese shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune wanted better calendars and farming, and in 1720 he allowed in Western books that contained no Christian teaching. Japanese students began on medicine, astronomy and geography through Dutch texts brought to Nagasaki.
events.then: Students of Dutch learning translated anatomy, chemistry and gunnery books over the next century, beginning with an anatomy text in 1774.
events.now: It explains why Japan could modernise so fast after 1868: a century of translators, doctors and gunnery students trained on Dutch texts was already in place.

causes.why: The only window to the West left open was the Dutch trading post at Nagasaki.

q.idea: Western science could be studied separately from Western religion.
q.against: The total ban on foreign books since the 1630s.
q.spread: Through translators at Nagasaki and private schools of 'rangaku' (Dutch learning).
q.enabled: A class of scholars who understood Western science long before Perry arrived.
q.critics: Conservative officials; in 1839 the scholars Watanabe Kazan and Takano Chōei were punished for criticising the expulsion policy.

events.bluf: Japanese shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune wanted better calendars, astronomy and farming, and in 1720 he lifted the ban on Western books other than Christian ones. Japanese doctors and astronomers began studying European science through Dutch texts landed at Nagasaki. Over the next century 'Dutch learning' built a body of scientific knowledge and trained translators, the base that made modernisation after 1853 fast.
events.lens: Even closed societies can import knowledge selectively; the channels left open matter.
events.fact: The field was called 'rangaku', from 'Oranda', the Japanese name for Holland, and 'gaku', learning.

kv: the Dutch were the only Westerners allowed to trade, 1641–1853

events.what: Stock bubble collapsed.
events.why: Government debt converted into shares, insiders talking up the price and a public that had seen the Mississippi bubble in Paris make fortunes that spring.
events.sig: Parliament passed the Bubble Act restricting new companies. Robert Walpole protected the court and the ministry and emerged as the dominant minister for twenty years.
events.hook: Britain's first great stock market crash ruined thousands, including Isaac Newton.
events.story: The South Sea Company proposed in January 1720 to convert much of the national debt into its own shares, with ministers and MPs holding stock they had paid nothing for. Shares rose from about £128 in January to about £1,000 in August and fell below £200 by December. Thousands were ruined.
events.then: Parliament passed the Bubble Act restricting new companies. Robert Walpole protected the court and the ministry and emerged as the dominant minister for twenty years.
events.now: The Bubble Act of 1720 kept the joint-stock company rare in Britain until 1825. Walpole's management of the crash made him the first prime minister.
events.fact: Isaac Newton lost a fortune and is reported to have said he could calculate the motions of the stars but not the madness of men.

causes.why: The South Sea Company was set up partly to rival the Bank in managing Britain's national debt.
The company's main trading asset was the slave-trading contract (asiento) Britain won at Utrecht; speculation in its shares became the bubble.

q.what: Shares in a company swapping government debt for trade rights.
q.who: Insiders who sold early profited; ordinary investors were ruined.
q.scale: Shares rose about eightfold in months, then crashed.
q.daily: Many families lost their savings.
q.system: Laws restricting new joint-stock companies for a century.

events.bluf: The South Sea Company offered to take over Britain's national debt in exchange for shares and trading rights, and bribed ministers and MPs to get the deal. Its shares rose from £128 to £1,000 in eight months and collapsed by autumn. Parliament restricted new companies for a century, and Robert Walpole rose to power by cleaning up.
events.lens: When politicians, insiders and the public all profit from rising prices, no one has an incentive to stop a bubble.

events.who: Peter I (Peter the Great); the Russian Senate
events.what: Westernized Russia; new capital.
events.why: Russia had lost to Sweden at Narva in 1700 and Peter concluded that survival required Western arms, ships and administration.
events.sig: The Table of Ranks of 1722 made state service the basis of noble rank. Serfdom deepened to pay for it. The elite westernised and the peasants did not, a divide that held until 1917.
events.hook: Peter dragged Russia toward Europe and declared it an empire.
events.story: Russian Tsar Peter I toured Western Europe in 1697-98, partly incognito, working in Dutch and English shipyards. At home he ordered nobles to shave and dress in European style, built a navy and a new army, replaced the patriarch with a Holy Synod and founded St Petersburg. After the Treaty of Nystad with Sweden in 1721 the Senate proclaimed him Emperor of All Russia.
events.then: The Table of Ranks of 1722 made state service the basis of noble rank. Serfdom deepened to pay for it. The elite westernised and the peasants did not, a divide that held until 1917.
events.now: Peter made Russia a European great power by force from above and left a westernised elite ruling a peasant country. Russia still argues over whether it is European, Eurasian or its own civilisation, and Vladimir Putin has compared himself to Peter.
events.fact: Peter taxed beards and issued tokens to prove the tax was paid.

causes.why: Victory over Sweden at Poltava made Russia the leading power on the Baltic; after peace in 1721 Peter took the title of emperor.
The new capital symbolised Russia's new status as an empire.

q.before: Russia's rulers had been tsars of Muscovy.
q.how: The Senate proclaimed Peter emperor after victory.
q.claim: Imperial status like that of European emperors.
q.lasted: Russia remained an empire until 1917.

events.bluf: Russian Tsar Peter I set out to make Russia a European military power by copying Western methods and forcing them on his nobles. He built a navy, reorganised the army and the state, put the Church under a government department and beat Sweden. Russia became a great power, and its model of coercive modernisation from the top, which later rulers repeated, began with him.
events.trig: The Treaty of Nystad in September 1721 confirmed Russia's conquest of the Baltic coast.
events.lens: Top-down modernization can work fast, but it widens the gap between a Westernized elite and the rest of society.

kv: soldiers in the regular army by 1725

events.what: Largest slave revolt in the British mainland colonies.
events.why: Brutal conditions on the rice plantations came first. Spanish Florida's offer of freedom to runaways, a deliberate tactic against Britain, gave the rebels a destination.
events.sig: South Carolina's Negro Act of 1740 barred enslaved people from gathering, growing their own food, earning money or learning to read.
events.hook: The largest slave revolt in Britain's mainland colonies marched under drums toward freedom in Florida.
events.story: Spanish Florida had offered freedom to enslaved people who fled the British colonies. On 9 September 1739 about 60 enslaved people, many from Kongo with military experience, seized weapons from a store near the Stono River and headed south for Florida. South Carolina militia caught and killed most of them.
events.then: South Carolina's Negro Act of 1740 barred enslaved people from gathering, growing their own food, earning money or learning to read.
events.now: Stono shows that enslaved Africans resisted from the start, and that the slave codes which defined Southern law were written in response to that resistance.

causes.why: Utrecht gave Britain the right to sell slaves to Spanish America, part of a trade boom that gave South Carolina a Black majority by 1739. Stono's rebels marched toward Spanish Florida, which promised them freedom.

q.why: Enslaved Africans sought freedom in Spanish Florida.
q.decided: Colonial militia caught the marchers.
q.cost: About 20 colonists and over 40 rebels were killed, and more were executed.
q.changed: South Carolina passed the harsh Negro Act of 1740.

events.bluf: About 60 enslaved people, many from Kongo with military experience, seized weapons near Charleston in September 1739 and marched for Spanish Florida, which promised freedom to runaways from the British colonies. Militia caught and killed most of them within days. It was the largest slave revolt in Britain's mainland colonies, and South Carolina answered it with the Negro Act of 1740, the pattern by which slave societies met resistance with tighter control.
events.lens: Rival powers exploit each other's internal weaknesses: Spain offered freedom to Britain's enslaved people to destabilize its colonies.
events.fact: Kongo had been a Catholic kingdom since 1491, which is one reason Catholic Spanish Florida drew the rebels.

toll.n: Most surviving rebels were captured and executed or sold to the Caribbean.

events.what: Looted the city and the Peacock Throne.
events.why: Nader Shah was drawn by Mughal wealth and a weak emperor. Mughal border defences in Kabul and the Punjab had collapsed.
events.sig: Mughal weakness was laid bare. Regional rulers, the Marathas and the British and French companies drew their own conclusions. Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani, once Nader Shah's officer, raided India repeatedly from 1748.
events.hook: A Persian warlord looted Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne.
events.story: Persian ruler Nader Shah crossed the Indus and crushed the army of Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah at Karnal on 24 February 1739. He entered Delhi; after a rumour of his death set off attacks that killed some of his soldiers, he ordered a massacre on 22 March in which perhaps 20,000 or more people died. He left in May with the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond.
events.then: Mughal weakness was laid bare. Regional rulers, the Marathas and the British and French companies drew their own conclusions. Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani, once Nader Shah's officer, raided India repeatedly from 1748.
events.now: The sack confirmed that the Mughal emperor could no longer defend his capital; regional rulers, the Marathas and the European companies acted on that from the 1740s.

causes.why: The weakened Mughal court could not stop the Persian ruler Nader Shah, who sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne.

events.wk: Nader Shah's invasion of the Mughal Empire

q.why: Nader Shah was drawn by Mughal wealth.
q.decided: Nader Shah's veteran army at Karnal.
q.cost: Tens of thousands killed in Delhi.
q.changed: Mughal weakness was exposed to rivals, including the British.

events.bluf: Persian ruler Nader Shah marched on Delhi to seize the wealth of a Mughal empire whose border defences had collapsed. He beat the Mughal army at Karnal in February 1739, occupied Delhi and left with the Peacock Throne, the Koh-i-Noor and treasure worth years of Mughal revenue. The emperor's weakness was now plain to every regional ruler and European company in India.
events.lens: One devastating raid can reveal a power's weakness to everyone watching, and invite more predators.
events.fact: The haul was so large that Nader Shah suspended taxes in Persia for three years. The Koh-i-Noor is now in the British Crown Jewels, and India still asks for it back.

kv: Delhi residents massacred in a single day
treasures carried off: the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor

events.who: Frederick II of Prussia; Maria Theresa
events.what: Prussia seized Silesia from Austria.
events.why: Silesia was rich, populous and Protestant. Frederick had a trained army, a full treasury and a rival whose title was contested.
events.sig: The War of the Austrian Succession to 1748 and the Seven Years' War to 1763 confirmed Prussia's hold. Maria Theresa reformed Austria's army, taxes and administration in response.
events.hook: Prussia's new king seized Austria's richest province.
events.story: Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI died in October 1740 after years spent winning promises, the Pragmatic Sanction, that his daughter Maria Theresa could inherit. Prussian King Frederick II, on the throne five months, invaded Silesia in December with 27,000 men. France, Bavaria and Spain joined the attack. Maria Theresa rallied Hungary and survived; Silesia stayed Prussian.
events.then: The War of the Austrian Succession to 1748 and the Seven Years' War to 1763 confirmed Prussia's hold. Maria Theresa reformed Austria's army, taxes and administration in response.
events.now: The Austro-Prussian rivalry over Germany ran from Silesia to Königgrätz in 1866. Frederick showed that a small state with a good army could seize territory and keep it, the lesson every later aggressor cited.

q.why: Frederick wanted Silesia's rich land and people.
q.decided: Prussian discipline and Frederick's generalship.
q.cost: Three wars and hundreds of thousands of dead.
q.changed: Prussia became Austria's rival for leadership of Germany.

events.bluf: Prussian King Frederick II saw a rich province to be had while Maria Theresa's right to inherit the Habsburg lands was in dispute, and took Silesia by surprise. He kept it through two wars. Prussia became a great power, Austria reformed itself to compete, and the two fought for Germany until 1866.
events.trig: The death of Charles VI on 20 October 1740.
events.lens: Successions are moments of maximum vulnerability: opportunists strike when a new ruler's legitimacy is in doubt.
events.fact: Silesia became Polish in 1945, and its German population was expelled.

events.who: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab; Muhammad bin Saud
events.hook: A preacher and a local ruler made a pact that still shapes Saudi Arabia.
events.what: A preacher and a local ruler made a pact that still shapes Saudi Arabia.
events.story: Central Arabia in the 1740s was a patchwork of oasis towns under local rulers. Preacher Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, expelled from his home town for calling for a return to a strict reading of Islam, found shelter in Diriyah. In 1744 he and Diriyah's ruler Muhammad bin Saud agreed that the Saud family would rule and the preacher's family would guide religion.
events.why: Each side needed the other. The ruler gained religious legitimacy and a cause to expand; the preacher gained protection and power.
events.then: The first Saudi state conquered much of Arabia, including Mecca and Medina, before Ottoman-Egyptian forces destroyed it in 1818. The alliance was revived twice, finally under Abdulaziz ibn Saud in the 20th century.
events.sig: The first Saudi state conquered much of Arabia, including Mecca and Medina, before Ottoman-Egyptian forces destroyed it in 1818. The alliance was revived twice, finally under Abdulaziz ibn Saud in the 20th century.
events.now: The partnership remains the foundation of the Saudi state. Oil wealth later funded the spread of Wahhabi-influenced teaching worldwide; since 2017 Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has curbed the clergy's power.

q.belief: A return to a strict, purified Islam.
q.authority: The Saud family ruled; Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's family led religion.
q.believers: Arabian tribes were brought under the new doctrine, often by force.
q.fallout: Ottoman-Egyptian armies destroyed the first Saudi state in 1818.
q.today: The partnership remains the basis of the Saudi state.

events.bluf: Preacher Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab wanted a ruler to enforce his strict reading of Islam; Diriyah's ruler Muhammad bin Saud wanted a cause and a legitimacy to expand beyond one oasis town. Their pact of 1744 gave the Al Saud the sword and the preacher's family the pulpit. It is the founding bargain of the Saudi state, which has been destroyed and refounded twice on the same terms.
events.lens: Rulers who depend on a religious establishment for legitimacy must share power with it, until they find another source of legitimacy, such as prosperity.
events.fact: Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's descendants, the Al ash-Sheikh, still hold senior religious posts in the kingdom.

events.who: Britain and colonists (incl. young George Washington) vs. France and Native allies
events.what: North American front of the Seven Years' War.
events.why: Both Britain and France claimed the Ohio Valley. The French built forts there to link Canada with Louisiana, and Virginia land speculators wanted the same ground.
events.sig: Britain won and took Canada at the Treaty of Paris in 1763. Its war debt led Parliament to tax the colonies. Native nations lost their ability to play the two empires against each other.
events.hook: A skirmish led by a 22-year-old George Washington lit the fuse of a world war.
events.story: Britain and France both claimed the Ohio River Valley, and the French built forts there in 1753-54. In May 1754 Virginia militia under Lieutenant Colonel George Washington attacked a French party at Jumonville Glen. The fighting spread to Europe, India and the oceans as the Seven Years' War, which Britain declared in 1756.
events.then: Britain won and took Canada at the Treaty of Paris in 1763. Its war debt led Parliament to tax the colonies. Native nations lost their ability to play the two empires against each other.
events.now: Britain's war debt produced the Stamp Act of 1765 and the taxes that drove the colonies to revolt, and the removal of France removed the colonists' need for British protection.

causes.why: French and British colonies collided over the Ohio Valley, where a young George Washington fired the first shots.

q.why: Rival claims to the Ohio Valley.
q.decided: Britain's larger colonial population and naval power.
q.cost: Thousands of soldiers, colonists and Native people killed.
q.changed: France lost Canada, and Britain was left with heavy debts.

events.bluf: Britain and France both claimed the Ohio valley, and France built forts there to link Canada with Louisiana. A Virginia militia party under Lieutenant Colonel George Washington attacked a French detachment in May 1754, and the clash spread into the Seven Years' War across Europe, India and the oceans. Britain won and removed France from North America, and the debt it ran up produced the colonial taxes that led to the American Revolution.
events.trig: Washington's attack on a French party at Jumonville Glen in May 1754.
events.lens: Skirmishes between great powers' local forces can escalate into world wars.
events.fact: Washington surrendered Fort Necessity to the French on 4 July 1754, the only surrender of his career.

events.who: The people of Lisbon; the Marquis of Pombal
events.what: Quake, tsunami and fire killed tens of thousands.
events.why: A great earthquake on the sea floor off Portugal.
events.sig: Pombal rebuilt central Lisbon on a grid with earthquake-resistant timber frames and sent a questionnaire to every parish, an early seismological survey. French writer Voltaire mocked the doctrine that all is for the best in 'Candide'.
events.hook: A giant earthquake on a holy day shook Europe's faith.
events.story: On the morning of 1 November 1755 an earthquake struck Lisbon while the churches were full for All Saints' Day. A tsunami and fires followed. The royal palace, the opera house and most of the lower city were destroyed. Portuguese chief minister the Marquis of Pombal took charge of relief and rebuilding.
events.then: Pombal rebuilt central Lisbon on a grid with earthquake-resistant timber frames and sent a questionnaire to every parish, an early seismological survey. French writer Voltaire mocked the doctrine that all is for the best in 'Candide'.
events.now: The earthquake destroyed a capital and the certainty that providence governed events: the state rebuilt Lisbon on a plan and the Enlightenment argued over whether a good God could permit it, which made disaster a matter for governments and science.
events.fact: Pombal's reported order was 'bury the dead and feed the living'.

q.idea: If God is good, why do disasters kill the innocent?
q.against: The optimistic view that 'all is for the best'.
q.spread: Voltaire's poem on the disaster and his novel Candide.
q.enabled: Scientific study of earthquakes and earthquake-resistant building.
q.critics: Rousseau answered that people, not nature, built crowded cities.

events.bluf: An earthquake off the Portuguese coast, a tsunami and fires destroyed Lisbon on All Saints' Day 1755 and killed perhaps 30,000 to 50,000 people. Chief minister the Marquis of Pombal rebuilt the city on a plan and surveyed every parish about the shock. Disaster became a matter for the state and for science, and the Enlightenment lost its confidence in a benevolent order.
events.lens: Disasters test a society's beliefs and its state: watch who takes charge and which ideas lose credibility.

events.who: Britain & Prussia vs. France, Austria, Russia
events.what: Global war.
events.why: Colonial rivalry between Britain and France came first. Austria wanted Silesia back and had built an alliance with France and Russia to get it.
events.sig: At Paris in 1763 France gave Canada and the land east of the Mississippi to Britain and Louisiana to Spain. Prussia kept Silesia. Britain's national debt nearly doubled, and Parliament turned to the colonies to pay.
events.hook: Britain and France fought a world war across five continents.
events.story: Britain and France were already fighting in the Ohio valley when Prussian King Frederick II invaded Saxony in August 1756. Austria, France and Russia fought Prussia in Germany; Britain fought France in North America, India, West Africa, the Caribbean and at sea. British forces took Quebec in 1759 and broke French power in India.
events.then: At Paris in 1763 France gave Canada and the land east of the Mississippi to Britain and Louisiana to Spain. Prussia kept Silesia. Britain's national debt nearly doubled, and Parliament turned to the colonies to pay.
events.now: The war began a century and a half of British primacy and set up both the American and the French revolutions through the debts it left.
events.fact: Fighting ran on four continents and three oceans, which is why it is often called the first world war.

sites.d: Frederick the Great routs France.
Britain takes Bengal.
Plains of Abraham; Britain takes Canada.
Became Fort Pitt, today's Pittsburgh.

causes.why: Fighting in the Ohio Valley merged into a global war between Britain and France in 1756.
Austria wanted back Silesia, which Frederick had seized in 1740. It allied with France and Russia, and Frederick struck first in 1756.

q.why: Colonial rivalry, and Austria's wish to recover Silesia.
q.stakes: Empire in America and India, and the balance of power in Europe.
q.decided: British sea power, and Prussia surviving against the odds.
q.cost: Perhaps a million dead.
q.changed: Britain became the leading colonial power.

events.bluf: Britain and France fought for North America and India; Austria fought to recover Silesia from Prussia. Britain won Canada, India and command of the seas, and Prussia kept Silesia. The debts Britain ran up produced the taxes that lost it the American colonies, and France's defeat and debts pushed it toward revolution.
events.lens: Winning a war for dominance can sow the next crisis: debt and overstretch follow victory.

events.who: Robert Clive (East India Co.) vs. Nawab of Bengal
events.what: Company won by bribing the Nawab's general.
events.why: The Nawab resented the Company's fortifications and its abuse of trade privileges. Clive plotted with discontented Bengali nobles and the Jagat Seth bankers.
events.sig: The Company installed Mir Jafar as Nawab and extracted payments running to millions of pounds. After Buxar in 1764 it won the right to collect Bengal's land revenue in 1765. Bengal's taxes paid for further conquest, and Company misrule contributed to the Bengal famine of 1770, which killed millions.
events.hook: A British company won Bengal, beginning British rule in India.
