events.story: Bengal Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah captured Calcutta in June 1756. Company commander Robert Clive retook it in January 1757 and marched north. Before the battle Clive secretly promised the throne to the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar, who held his troops back. On 23 June 1757 Clive's army of about 3,000 beat the Nawab's of about 50,000 at Plassey.
events.then: The Company installed Mir Jafar as Nawab and extracted payments running to millions of pounds. After Buxar in 1764 it won the right to collect Bengal's land revenue in 1765. Bengal's taxes paid for further conquest, and Company misrule contributed to the Bengal famine of 1770, which killed millions.
events.now: Plassey gave the Company Bengal's land revenue from 1765, which funded its armies and the conquest of India over the next 60 years. Indian nationalists date the 'drain' of India's wealth to Britain from it.
events.fact: Clive's about 3,000 troops beat about 50,000 because Mir Jafar stood aside; the Company counted around 20 dead.

sites.d: June 1757.
Company base; 'Black Hole of Calcutta' incident 1756.

causes.why: Mughal collapse left regional rulers, like the Nawab of Bengal, who could be defeated or bought by the East India Company.
A trading company with its own private army won Bengal, India's richest province, 157 years after its founding.
The Anglo-French war spread to India. At Plassey the East India Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal, who had French support.
Calcutta was the base the Nawab of Bengal attacked in 1756, provoking Clive's campaign.

q.why: The Company and the Nawab clashed over Calcutta and trade privileges.
q.stakes: Control of Bengal, India's richest province.
q.decided: Mir Jafar's betrayal more than the fighting.
q.cost: Light casualties; the cost came later in Bengal's plunder.
q.changed: The Company became a ruling power in India.

events.bluf: East India Company commander Robert Clive marched against Bengal Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah to recover Calcutta and secure the Company's trade. He won at Plassey on 23 June 1757 after bribing the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar to hold his troops back. A trading company became the power behind the throne in India's richest province, and Bengal's revenue paid for the conquest of the rest.
events.trig: The Nawab's capture of Calcutta in June 1756 and the deaths of British prisoners in the 'Black Hole', which the Company used to justify war.
events.lens: Empires are often built by exploiting local divisions: the decisive move at Plassey was a bribe, not a charge.

toll.n: Most of the Nawab's army never fought: its commander Mir Jafar had made a secret deal with Clive.

events.who: Edmond Halley (died 1742); amateur astronomer Johann Palitzsch
events.hook: A comet came back exactly when Newton's physics said it would, 16 years after the man who predicted it died.
events.what: A comet came back exactly when Newton's physics said it would, 16 years after the man who predicted it died.
events.story: English astronomer Edmond Halley argued in 1705 that three recorded comets were one body on a 76-year orbit and would return in 1758. Halley died in 1742. On Christmas night 1758 Saxon farmer and amateur astronomer Johann Palitzsch spotted it near Dresden. It passed closest to the Sun in March 1759.
events.why: Newton's gravity made it possible to compute a comet's orbit and the planets' pull on it.
events.then: The comet took Halley's name. It returned in 1835, 1910 and 1986 and is due in 2061.
events.sig: The comet took Halley's name. It returned in 1835, 1910 and 1986 and is due in 2061.
events.now: The comet's return made Newtonian science the accepted framework of educated Europe and prediction the test of a theory.

causes.why: Halley used Newton's laws to calculate the comet's orbit and its return.

q.problem: Comets seemed random omens that no one could predict.
q.how: Halley calculated orbits from old sightings using Newton's laws.
q.replaced: The idea of comets as unpredictable signs from heaven.
q.spread: The successful prediction was celebrated by academies across Europe.
q.next: Confidence that natural laws could predict the heavens, and perhaps much else.

events.bluf: Astronomer Edmond Halley used Newton's laws to argue that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object that would return in 1758. It returned on Christmas night, sixteen years after his death. A theory had forecast an event in the heavens decades ahead, and Newton's physics had no serious doubters left in Europe.
events.lens: Theories earn trust by making specific predictions that could fail, and then don't.
events.fact: Three French mathematicians had refined the prediction to within a month using Jupiter's and Saturn's pull.

events.who: Ahmad Shah Durrani of Afghanistan vs. the Maratha Empire
events.hook: An Afghan army crushed the Marathas in one of the 18th century's bloodiest battles.
events.what: An Afghan army crushed the Marathas in one of the 18th century's bloodiest battles.
events.story: The Marathas had taken Lahore in 1758, challenging Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani, founder of the Afghan state. The Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau camped at Panipat north of Delhi through late 1760, cut off from supplies. On 14 January 1761 Durrani's army, with allies from Awadh and the Rohilla Afghans, destroyed it; tens of thousands of soldiers and camp followers were killed or massacred.
events.why: Rivalry for control of the decaying Mughal Empire's northern lands came first. The Marathas had alienated the Rajputs, Jats and Sikhs, who gave them no help.
events.then: Maratha power in the north was broken for a decade, and Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao died within months. The Afghans withdrew, and Sikh chiefs filled the Punjab. The East India Company won Buxar in 1764 and Bengal's revenue in 1765.
events.sig: Maratha power in the north was broken for a decade, and Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao died within months. The Afghans withdrew, and Sikh chiefs filled the Punjab. The East India Company won Buxar in 1764 and Bengal's revenue in 1765.
events.now: Panipat removed the one Indian power able to unite the north just as the Company took Bengal; for the next 40 years the Company faced divided opponents and beat them one at a time.

causes.why: Ahmad Shah Durrani, the Afghan victor at Panipat, had been one of Nader Shah's commanders.

q.why: Who would control northern India as the Mughals collapsed.
q.decided: Afghan cavalry and artillery, and Maratha supply failures.
q.cost: Tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians killed.
q.changed: Maratha power in the north was broken for a decade.

events.bluf: Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani marched into India to end the Maratha advance into the Punjab; the Marathas fought to hold the north of the decaying Mughal empire. On 14 January 1761 his army destroyed the Maratha force, killing tens of thousands of soldiers and camp followers. Maratha power in the north was broken for a decade and the Afghans went home, leaving a vacuum the East India Company, which had taken Bengal in 1757, moved into.
events.lens: When two regional powers bleed each other, a third often reaps the benefit.
events.fact: A Maratha letter reported the loss in a jeweller's terms: two pearls dissolved, 27 gold coins lost, and the silver and copper beyond counting.

toll.n: Thousands of Maratha prisoners and followers were massacred after the battle. Afghan losses are not reliably known.

events.hook: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'
events.what: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'
events.story: Genevan philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau published 'The Social Contract' in 1762. Legitimate government, he argued, rests on a contract in which citizens together form a sovereign general will. The book was banned in Paris and burned in Geneva.
events.why: Enlightenment writers were asking what made authority legitimate, and Rousseau rejected both divine right and Hobbes's surrender to a sovereign.
events.then: The Jacobins governed in the name of the general will in 1793. The book was carried in Robespierre's pocket, by his own account.
events.sig: The Jacobins governed in the name of the general will in 1793. The book was carried in Robespierre's pocket, by his own account.
events.now: The French Revolution took its doctrine of popular sovereignty from the book. Every argument over majority rule against individual rights returns to the general will.

causes.why: The quake set off a famous debate: Voltaire asked how a good God could allow such suffering, and Rousseau replied that people had made it worse by crowding into cities.
Rousseau took Locke's social contract further, toward popular sovereignty and the 'general will'.

q.idea: Legitimate government expresses the 'general will' of the citizens.
q.against: Rule by kings and privileged orders.
q.spread: Despite bans, it was read across Europe.
q.enabled: Ideas of popular sovereignty in the French Revolution.
q.critics: Liberals warned the 'general will' could crush individual freedom.

events.bluf: Genevan philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau set out to show what could make political power legitimate once kings and tradition were ruled out. His answer was the general will of the people, formed by a social contract. Popular sovereignty became the French Revolution's doctrine, and the general will, which may override the individual, has served democrats and dictators alike.
events.lens: Popular sovereignty can justify both democracy and tyranny in the people's name: ask who gets to define 'the will of the people'.
events.fact: Rousseau opened with the line that man is born free and is everywhere in chains.
Catherine was born Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst, a minor German princess, and took the Russian throne by overthrowing her husband.
events.h: Catherine the Great seizes the throne
events.who: Catherine II; her husband, Tsar Peter III
events.hook: A German princess overthrew her husband and became Russia's longest-ruling empress.
events.what: A German princess overthrew her husband and became Russia's longest-ruling empress.
events.story: Russian Tsar Peter III had alienated the army and the Church within months of his accession. On 9 July 1762 guards regiments loyal to his wife, Catherine, proclaimed her empress; Peter abdicated and died in custody days later. Empress Catherine II corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot and pushed Russia's borders south and west.
events.why: Peter had ended a winning war against Prussia and mocked the Orthodox Church. Catherine had the guards and the court.
events.then: She annexed Crimea in 1783, founded Odessa, took the largest share of Poland in three partitions and crushed the Pugachev revolt of 1773-75. Serfdom spread into the conquered south.
events.sig: She annexed Crimea in 1783, founded Odessa, took the largest share of Poland in three partitions and crushed the Pugachev revolt of 1773-75. Serfdom spread into the conquered south.
events.now: Catherine's conquest of Crimea and southern Ukraine is the history Russian nationalists cite to claim them. Her reign fixed the pattern of an enlightened autocracy that reformed everything except its own power.

causes.why: Peter's Westernised state and army were the base for Catherine's expansion to the Black Sea and into Poland.

q.before: Tsar Peter III, Catherine's husband.
q.how: A palace coup by guards regiments.
q.claim: Saving Russia from an unpopular tsar.
q.winners: Catherine and the nobles who backed her.
q.lasted: She ruled for 34 years.

events.bluf: Catherine, a German princess married to Russian Tsar Peter III, built alliances among the guards regiments and overthrew her husband six months into his reign. She ruled 34 years, took Crimea and the Black Sea coast and the largest share of partitioned Poland, and deepened serfdom to pay for it. Russia became a dominant European power under an Enlightenment vocabulary and an autocratic state.
events.lens: Enlightened rhetoric and autocratic practice often coexist: judge rulers by the institutions they build, not the philosophers they write to.

events.h: Treaty of Paris: Britain wins Canada
events.what: France gave up Canada and land east of the Mississippi.
events.why: Britain had won the war in North America, India and at sea. France gave up its North American empire to make peace and kept the sugar islands that earned more.
events.sig: Free of the French threat, colonists needed British protection much less. Britain's Proclamation of 1763, meant to calm Native nations after Pontiac's War, barred settlement west of the Appalachians and angered colonists.
events.hook: France gave up almost all of North America in a single treaty.
events.story: Defeated in the Seven Years' War, France signed the Treaty of Paris on 10 February 1763. France ceded Canada and the land east of the Mississippi to Britain and had already given Louisiana to Spain. Spain ceded Florida to Britain. France kept Guadeloupe and Martinique. Britain dominated the continent's east.
events.then: Free of the French threat, colonists needed British protection much less. Britain's Proclamation of 1763, meant to calm Native nations after Pontiac's War, barred settlement west of the Appalachians and angered colonists.
events.now: Britain's victory produced both Canada's British identity and the American Revolution: the colonies needed Britain less, and Britain taxed them more to pay for the empire it had won.

causes.why: Britain's global victory was settled in this treaty, which gave it Canada and Florida.

q.before: France held Canada and the Mississippi valley.
q.how: A peace treaty.
q.winners: Britain; Native nations lost a French counterweight.
q.lasted: Canada stayed British; the Thirteen Colonies soon left.

events.bluf: Britain wanted its victory in the Seven Years' War turned into territory; France wanted peace and kept its sugar islands. France handed Canada and the land east of the Mississippi to Britain and Louisiana to Spain, and Britain dominated North America from Hudson Bay to Florida. The removal of the French threat removed the colonists' main reason to depend on Britain, and the cost of the new empire produced the taxes that drove them to revolt.
events.lens: Removing a common enemy can loosen the ties within an alliance.
events.fact: French writer Voltaire dismissed Canada as 'a few acres of snow'.

kv: British national debt, before and after the war

events.what: Tax on printed paper; met with boycotts and riots.
events.why: Britain needed to pay its war debt and the cost of keeping troops in America.
events.sig: Parliament repealed the act a year later and passed the Declaratory Act, asserting its right to legislate for the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever'. Colonists learned that united protest worked, and Britain kept trying new taxes.
events.hook: A tax on paper sparked the cry of 'no taxation without representation.'
events.story: To pay war debts and the cost of troops in America, Parliament under Prime Minister George Grenville passed the Stamp Act in March 1765, taxing newspapers, legal documents and playing cards in the colonies. Colonists boycotted British goods, crowds attacked stamp distributors, and nine colonies sent delegates to a Stamp Act Congress in New York in October 1765. Parliament repealed the act in March 1766.
events.then: Parliament repealed the act a year later and passed the Declaratory Act, asserting its right to legislate for the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever'. Colonists learned that united protest worked, and Britain kept trying new taxes.
events.now: The Stamp Act produced the first united colonial resistance and the principle that taxation requires the consent of the taxed; its repeal taught the colonies that resistance worked.

causes.why: Britain's national debt had nearly doubled during the war, and it decided the colonies should help pay for their own defence.

q.before: Colonial assemblies set most taxes.
q.how: Parliament taxed the colonies directly.
q.claim: Parliament's authority over the whole empire.
q.winners: The colonists, when the act was repealed.
q.lasted: No: it was repealed in 1766.

events.bluf: Parliament under Prime Minister George Grenville taxed newspapers, legal documents and playing cards in the colonies in 1765 to pay for the troops kept in America after the war. Colonists boycotted British goods, rioted and met in a Stamp Act Congress, and Parliament repealed the act in 1766 while asserting its right to legislate 'in all cases whatsoever'. The first direct tax produced the first united colonial resistance and the principle that taxation requires consent.
events.lens: Revenue measures provoke constitutional crises when they raise the question of who has the right to decide.
events.fact: The Sons of Liberty took their name from a speech in Parliament by Colonel Isaac Barré defending the colonists.

kv: a year the tax was expected to raise
colonies at the Stamp Act Congress

events.who: Burmese Konbaung dynasty; Kingdom of Ayutthaya (Siam)
events.hook: A Burmese army destroyed Ayutthaya, Siam's capital for 400 years.
events.what: A Burmese army destroyed Ayutthaya, Siam's capital for 400 years.
events.story: Ayutthaya had been Siam's capital for 400 years and one of Asia's great trading cities. The armies of Burmese King Hsinbyushin besieged it for 14 months. In April 1767 they stormed the city, burned it and carried off tens of thousands of captives.
events.why: The Konbaung kings wanted to crush their old rival. Ayutthaya's wealth made it a prize.
events.then: General Taksin drove the Burmese out within a year and founded a new capital at Thonburi. In 1782 General Chakri took the throne as Rama I and moved the capital across the river to Bangkok.
events.sig: General Taksin drove the Burmese out within a year and founded a new capital at Thonburi. In 1782 General Chakri took the throne as Rama I and moved the capital across the river to Bangkok.
events.now: The fall of Ayutthaya destroyed the Siamese state and forced its refounding at Bangkok under a new dynasty that still reigns; the memory fixed Burma as Siam's enemy for two centuries.

q.why: Burma's kings wanted to crush their old rival.
q.stakes: The survival of the Siamese kingdom.
q.decided: A long siege that broke the city.
q.cost: The city burned and tens of thousands were taken captive.
q.changed: Siam rebuilt under Taksin and then the Chakri kings.

events.bluf: Burma's Konbaung kings set out to crush Siam, their old rival. After a 14-month siege their armies stormed Ayutthaya in April 1767, burned the 400-year-old capital and carried off tens of thousands of captives. The Siamese state was refounded within a year at Thonburi and then at Bangkok under a new dynasty, and Burma was fixed as Siam's enemy for two centuries.
events.lens: The sack of a capital can end one dynasty and make room for a more vigorous one.
events.fact: Ayutthaya's ruins are a World Heritage site.

events.who: James Watt; his business partner Matthew Boulton
events.what: Efficient steam engine patented.
events.why: Britain had cheap coal and high wages, which rewarded a machine that saved labour. Its mines needed better pumps. Patent law and skilled instrument makers let an inventor profit from an improvement.
events.sig: Rotary steam engines powered textile mills and ironworks and later railways and steamships, which freed factories from rivers. British output and productivity grew. Industrialisation spread to Europe and North America in the 1800s.
events.hook: James Watt's improved steam engine powered the Industrial Revolution.
events.story: English ironmonger Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine had pumped water from mines since 1712 and wasted most of its fuel reheating the cylinder each stroke. In 1765, repairing a model of it for Glasgow University, Glasgow instrument maker James Watt saw the waste and designed a separate condenser, patented in 1769, which cut coal use by about three-quarters. Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton went into partnership with him and the firm sold engines from 1775. Later engines turned wheels and drove mills and factories.
events.then: Rotary steam engines powered textile mills and ironworks and later railways and steamships, which freed factories from rivers. British output and productivity grew. Industrialisation spread to Europe and North America in the 1800s.
events.now: Fossil-fuel-powered growth created modern prosperity and began the carbon emissions behind climate change; today's energy transition is an attempt to replace what Watt's engine started.
events.fact: Watt coined the term 'horsepower' to sell engines; the unit 'watt' is named after him.

causes.why: Newtonian science taught a culture of measurement; Watt, an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow, improved the engine by measuring its wasted heat.

q.problem: Steam engines wasted most of their fuel.
q.how: A separate condenser kept the cylinder hot, cutting coal use dramatically.
q.replaced: Water wheels, horses and inefficient Newcomen engines.
q.spread: Hundreds of Boulton and Watt engines worked in mines and mills by 1800.
q.next: Steam factories, railways and ships.

events.bluf: Glasgow instrument maker James Watt set out to stop the Newcomen engine wasting most of its coal reheating the cylinder on every stroke. His separate condenser, patented in 1769, cut fuel use by about three-quarters, and with Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton he built engines that could work far from the pits and later turn wheels. Steam freed factories from rivers and muscle, and the large-scale burning of fossil fuels began.
events.lens: Energy transitions reshape economies and power: the countries that master a new energy source first tend to lead.

kv: less coal than the older Newcomen engine

events.who: Lieutenant James Cook; botanist Joseph Banks; the Gweagal people
events.hook: James Cook charted Australia's east coast and claimed it for Britain.
events.what: James Cook charted Australia's east coast and claimed it for Britain.
events.story: British navigator Lieutenant James Cook sailed the Endeavour from Plymouth in 1768 with naturalist Joseph Banks aboard. He charted New Zealand's coasts in 1769-70, then reached Australia's east coast and anchored in Botany Bay in late April 1770, where Gweagal men confronted his landing party and were fired on. In August, at Possession Island off Cape York, he claimed the whole east coast for Britain.
events.why: The Royal Society wanted the transit of Venus observed from Tahiti to measure the solar system. Secret Admiralty orders told Cook to look for the southern continent and take possession of convenient sites.
events.then: Naturalist Joseph Banks told a parliamentary committee in 1779 that Botany Bay would suit a penal colony. The First Fleet arrived in 1788.
events.sig: Naturalist Joseph Banks told a parliamentary committee in 1779 that Botany Bay would suit a penal colony. The First Fleet arrived in 1788.
events.now: Cook's claim treated the east coast as land open to the Crown; the convict colony of 1788 and the dispossession of the Aboriginal nations followed from it, and the High Court overturned the legal fiction behind it only in 1992.

causes.why: Cook carried Tasman's charts; on this voyage he proved New Zealand was two islands and mapped its whole coast.

q.what: Scientific observation, charts and specimens, and a claim of land.
q.who: Britain gained; Aboriginal people would later lose their land.
q.scale: Thousands of kilometres of coastline charted.
q.daily: Little at first; the colony came 18 years later.
q.system: A British claim that became the basis for colonisation.

events.bluf: The Admiralty sent Lieutenant James Cook to observe the transit of Venus from Tahiti and then, under sealed orders, to search for the southern continent. He charted New Zealand's coasts in 1769-70 and Australia's east coast in 1770 and claimed the latter for Britain. The charts gave Britain the claim it used to found a penal colony in 1788, which began the dispossession of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
events.lens: Scientific expeditions often served imperial goals: knowing a coastline was the first step to claiming it.
events.fact: Cook's secret instructions told him to take possession 'with the consent of the natives'; he claimed the east coast without asking.

events.who: British soldiers; Boston crowd; Crispus Attucks among the 5 killed
events.what: Soldiers fired on a hostile crowd.
events.why: Tension over British troops stationed in Boston to enforce unpopular customs duties.
events.sig: Lawyer John Adams defended the soldiers in court; most were acquitted and two were convicted of manslaughter. Patriots marked the anniversary each year with speeches that kept anger alive until the war.
events.hook: Five dead in a snowy Boston street became the Revolution's most powerful propaganda.
events.story: British troops had been in Boston since 1768 to enforce customs duties. On 5 March 1770 a crowd pelted a sentry and the soldiers who came to his aid with snowballs and rocks; the soldiers fired, killing five, including Crispus Attucks, a man of African and Native descent. Silversmith Paul Revere's engraving of the scene spread the story through the colonies.
events.then: Lawyer John Adams defended the soldiers in court; most were acquitted and two were convicted of manslaughter. Patriots marked the anniversary each year with speeches that kept anger alive until the war.
events.now: Revere's engraving showed how one image can fix a political cause, and the annual massacre orations kept Boston's anger alive until the war in 1775.

causes.why: Troops sent to enforce new taxes and laws clashed with Bostonians.

q.before: British troops had been stationed in Boston since 1768.
q.how: A street confrontation in which soldiers fired into a crowd.
q.winners: Patriot propagandists, who used it to rally opinion.
q.lasted: Troops left the town for a time, but tensions remained.

events.bluf: British troops had been stationed in Boston since 1768 to enforce customs duties the town resisted. On 5 March 1770 soldiers facing a crowd throwing snowballs and rocks fired and killed five men, among them Crispus Attucks, a man of African and Native descent. Patriots turned the killings into their most powerful propaganda through silversmith Paul Revere's engraving, and the acquittal of most of the soldiers, defended by lawyer John Adams, showed the colonists' claim to the rule of law.
events.lens: Images and narratives can matter more than facts in political mobilization.
events.fact: Revere's engraving was copied from a drawing by artist Henry Pelham, who complained of the theft.

kv: soldiers tried: 6 acquitted, 2 convicted of manslaughter

events.hook: Arkwright built a water-powered cotton-spinning mill that became the model for the factory system.
events.what: Arkwright built a water-powered cotton-spinning mill that became the model for the factory system.
events.story: Demand for cotton cloth was rising and hand spinners could supply neither the quantity nor the strength of yarn the weavers wanted. Lancashire inventor Richard Arkwright, who had patented the water frame in 1769, opened a mill on the River Derwent at Cromford in 1771 that ran day and night in shifts. He built houses for his workers, many of them children.
events.why: Demand for cotton cloth was rising faster than hand spinners could meet it. The water frame could spin strong yarn and needed a river and a building rather than a cottage.
events.then: Hundreds of similar mills spread across Britain. Derbyshire-trained mechanic Samuel Slater, a former Arkwright apprentice, carried the design to the United States in 1790.
events.sig: Hundreds of similar mills spread across Britain. Derbyshire-trained mechanic Samuel Slater, a former Arkwright apprentice, carried the design to the United States in 1790.
events.now: Cromford was the first factory in the modern sense, a water-powered mill with hundreds of workers on shifts; the factory system of discipline, wage labour and mass production spread from it across Britain and the world.

causes.why: Water, then steam, powered the new spinning mills.

q.what: Cotton yarn.
q.who: Arkwright became one of the richest men in England; children worked 12-hour shifts.
q.scale: Hundreds of workers in a single building.
q.daily: Work set by the clock and the machine.
q.system: The factory system.

events.bluf: Lancashire inventor Richard Arkwright wanted to run his water frame, which spun strong cotton yarn, at a scale no cottage could match. The mill he opened at Cromford in 1771 put machines in one building and hundreds of workers on fixed shifts and wages, day and night. The factory system, with its discipline, wage labour and continuous production, spread from Cromford across Britain and then the world.
events.lens: The biggest economic changes are often in how work is organized, not just in the machines.
events.fact: Cromford is part of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage site.

kv: workers at first, many of them children
the mill ran, in two shifts

events.what: Neighbors seized Polish land.
events.why: Elected kings and a parliament that any one member could veto left Poland unable to reform or to resist. Prussia wanted the land joining Brandenburg to East Prussia. Russia and Austria preferred to compensate each other in Poland rather than fight over the Ottoman lands Russia was conquering.
events.sig: Poland's reforming constitution of 3 May 1791 provoked Russian intervention and the second partition in 1793. A rising under Tadeusz Kościuszko in 1794 was crushed, and the third partition of 1795 ended the state. Poland had no state of its own for 123 years.
events.hook: Three neighbors carved up Poland like a cake.
events.story: Poland-Lithuania had elected kings and a parliament in which any one member could veto legislation, and Russian troops had been fighting a noble revolt against Russian influence, the Bar Confederation, since 1768. In 1772 Russian Empress Catherine II, Prussian King Frederick II and Habsburg Empress Maria Theresa agreed to annex about a third of Poland-Lithuania's territory. Prussia took most of Royal Prussia, Austria took Galicia and Russia the eastern provinces. The Polish parliament ratified the loss in 1773 under duress. Further partitions in 1793 and 1795 divided the rest, and Poland vanished from the map until 1918.
events.then: Poland's reforming constitution of 3 May 1791 provoked Russian intervention and the second partition in 1793. A rising under Tadeusz Kościuszko in 1794 was crushed, and the third partition of 1795 ended the state. Poland had no state of its own for 123 years.
events.now: The partitions fixed the Polish reading of its geography: a state between Russia and Germany survives only inside an alliance, which underlies Poland's commitment to NATO since 1999 and its support for Ukraine since 2022.

causes.why: Russia dominated Poland. To avoid war with Austria and Prussia over Russian gains, the three powers each took a share, about a third of Poland's territory in all.

q.before: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, one of Europe's largest states.
q.how: Annexation agreed among three neighbouring powers.
q.claim: Keeping a balance of power among the partitioners.
q.lasted: Poland disappeared until 1918.

events.bluf: Prussian King Frederick II, Russian Empress Catherine II and Habsburg Empress Maria Theresa each wanted territory and a settled balance among themselves, and found it easier to take Poland's land than to fight each other for it. In 1772 they annexed about a third of Poland-Lithuania's territory without a war. Two more partitions in 1793 and 1795 erased the state for 123 years, and the rule that a weak state between strong neighbours can be removed by agreement among them entered European politics.
events.lens: A weak state between great powers is in greatest danger when those powers agree to divide it rather than compete for it.
events.fact: Maria Theresa wept over the partition and signed anyway; Frederick II remarked that 'she wept, but she took'.

events.what: Colonists dumped 342 chests of East India Co. tea.
events.why: Protest against the Tea Act, which gave the East India Company a monopoly in the colonies and reasserted Parliament's right to tax them.
events.sig: Britain closed Boston's port and took over Massachusetts' government, pushing the colonies to unite in the First Continental Congress (1774).
events.hook: Colonists dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor, and Britain cracked down hard.
events.story: The Tea Act of 1773 gave the East India Company a monopoly on tea in the colonies and kept Parliament's tax on it. Three tea ships lay in Boston harbour and the governor refused to let them leave unloaded. On the night of 16 December 1773 the Sons of Liberty, disguised as Mohawks, boarded the ships and dumped 342 chests of tea into the harbour.
events.then: Britain closed Boston's port and took over Massachusetts' government, pushing the colonies to unite in the First Continental Congress (1774).
events.now: Britain's response, the Coercive Acts of 1774, turned a Massachusetts dispute into a continental one; the First Continental Congress met within months.
events.fact: The East India Company tea they dumped would be worth over $1 million today.

causes.why: Protests against taxation without representation kept escalating.

q.before: Colonists bought smuggled Dutch tea to avoid British duties.
q.how: Protesters destroyed 342 chests of tea.
q.winners: Radical patriots, though Britain responded harshly.
q.lasted: The 'Intolerable Acts' followed, uniting the colonies.

events.bluf: The Sons of Liberty set out to stop East India Company tea landing in Boston under the Tea Act, which gave the company a monopoly and carried Parliament's tax. On 16 December 1773 men disguised as Mohawks boarded three ships and destroyed 342 chests of tea. Britain answered with the Coercive Acts, closing the port and taking over Massachusetts' government, which united the colonies in the First Continental Congress in 1774 and led within eighteen months to war.
events.lens: Harsh punishment of one protest can unite many others: Britain's crackdown turned a Boston quarrel into a continental cause.

events.h: Japan translates a Western anatomy book
events.what: Watching a dissection, Japanese doctors realized the Dutch anatomy book was right and Chinese medicine was wrong.
events.why: Japanese doctors trained in Chinese medicine wanted to test it against Western anatomy, and the shogunate's partial lifting of the book ban in 1720 had made Dutch texts available.
events.sig: Dutch learning spread from medicine to astronomy, chemistry and gunnery, giving Japan a body of Western-trained students before Perry arrived in 1853.
events.hook: Watching a dissection, Japanese doctors realized the Dutch anatomy book was right and Chinese medicine was wrong.
events.story: In 1771 physician Sugita Genpaku watched the dissection of an executed criminal at Edo with a Dutch anatomy book in hand and found the book's plates accurate. He, physician Maeno Ryōtaku and colleagues spent three years translating it with almost no dictionary. 'Kaitai Shinsho', the New Book of Anatomy, appeared in 1774.
events.then: Dutch learning spread from medicine to astronomy, chemistry and gunnery, giving Japan a body of Western-trained students before Perry arrived in 1853.
events.now: It shows Japan's habit of selective borrowing: learning foreign knowledge to strengthen itself while deciding for itself what to adopt.

causes.why: Relaxing the book ban made Dutch medical texts available.

q.problem: Traditional Chinese medical texts were wrong about human anatomy.
q.how: Careful comparison of illustrations with real dissections.
q.replaced: Classical Chinese anatomy.
q.spread: It became the founding text of Western medicine in Japan.
q.next: More translations in chemistry, physics and military science.

events.bluf: Physicians Sugita Genpaku and Maeno Ryōtaku set out to test a Dutch anatomy book against a dissected body, then to translate it. The book proved accurate where Chinese models failed, and after three years with almost no dictionary they published 'Kaitai Shinsho' in 1774. 'Dutch learning' became a scientific movement rather than a curiosity, and Japan had Western-trained doctors and translators eighty years before Perry arrived.
events.lens: Seeing evidence first-hand changes minds faster than argument.
events.fact: Physician Sugita Genpaku recalled that the team began knowing scarcely more Dutch than the alphabet, and spent whole days on single words.

kv: to translate, mostly without a dictionary

events.what: First shots of the American Revolution.
events.why: British troops tried to seize colonial weapons and powder stored at Concord.
events.sig: Within weeks colonial forces had Boston under siege. The Continental Congress formed the Continental Army under General George Washington in June 1775.
events.hook: 'The shot heard round the world' turned years of protest into a war.
events.story: British General Thomas Gage ordered about 700 regulars to march from Boston to seize colonial weapons and powder stored at Concord. Riders including silversmith Paul Revere warned the countryside. Militia met the column on Lexington green at dawn on 19 April 1775, where eight militiamen were killed, and at Concord's North Bridge, then harried the British all the way back to Boston.
events.then: Within weeks colonial forces had Boston under siege. The Continental Congress formed the Continental Army under General George Washington in June 1775.
events.now: The shots turned a political dispute into armed rebellion; Boston was under siege within weeks and the Continental Army existed within two months.

causes.why: Britain's crackdown, the 'Intolerable Acts', and the colonists' armed resistance led to the first battles.

q.why: British troops tried to seize colonial weapons.
q.stakes: Whether colonists would resist British authority by force.
q.decided: Militia harassing the British column on its long march back.
q.cost: 73 British and 49 colonists killed.
q.changed: Open war began.

events.bluf: British General Thomas Gage sent about 700 regulars to seize militia weapons and powder stored at Concord. Riders including silversmith Paul Revere gave warning, militia met the column at Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775 and harried it back to Boston. The first shots turned a political dispute into armed rebellion: within weeks New England militia had Boston under siege and Congress had created an army.
events.lens: Attempts to disarm a population can trigger the uprising they aim to prevent.
events.fact: 19 April is still Patriots' Day in Massachusetts, the day of the Boston Marathon.

events.who: Colonial militia under William Prescott; British troops under William Howe
events.hook: The British took the hill but lost over 1,000 men, showing colonial militia could fight.
events.what: The British took the hill but lost over 1,000 men, showing colonial militia could fight.
events.story: Militia under Colonel William Prescott fortified Breed's Hill overlooking Boston on the night of 16 June 1775. On 17 June British troops under Major General William Howe made three frontal assaults. They took the position when the defenders ran out of powder, at a cost of over 1,000 British casualties to about 450 American.
events.why: Both sides wanted the heights around besieged Boston, from which guns could command the town and the harbour.
events.then: The British left Boston in March 1776 after General George Washington placed cannon on Dorchester Heights.
events.sig: The British left Boston in March 1776 after General George Washington placed cannon on Dorchester Heights.
events.now: Bunker Hill showed that the Revolution would be a war rather than a riot, and that Britain faced a long and costly fight.

causes.why: After Lexington and Concord, militia besieged the British in Boston.

events.myth: 'Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes' was coined at Bunker Hill. The order was a commonplace of 18th-century war, and the evidence that anyone gave it there is thin.

q.why: Colonists besieging Boston fortified the heights, and Britain had to drive them off.
q.decided: British numbers, and the defenders running out of powder.
q.cost: About 1,050 British and 450 colonial casualties.
q.changed: Britain learned the war would be long and bloody.

events.bluf: Massachusetts militia under Colonel William Prescott fortified Breed's Hill to threaten the British in besieged Boston; British Major General William Howe attacked to clear it. On 17 June 1775 three frontal assaults took the position when the defenders ran out of powder, at over 1,000 British casualties to about 450 American. The cost made British commanders cautious for the rest of the war and gave the Americans confidence that militia could stand against regulars.
events.lens: A costly victory can hurt the winner more than defeat hurts the loser.
events.fact: Most of the fighting was on Breed's Hill; the battle took its name from the hill the militia had been ordered to fortify.

toll.n: Nearly half the British attackers were hit, one of the bloodiest days for the British army in the war.

events.hook: A plain-spoken pamphlet convinced many colonists to seek full independence.
events.what: A plain-spoken pamphlet convinced many colonists to seek full independence.
events.story: Fighting had begun in April 1775 and many colonists still hoped for peace with the king. English-born writer Thomas Paine published 'Common Sense' anonymously in Philadelphia in January 1776. It attacked monarchy itself and argued that an island was unfit to rule a continent. It sold perhaps 100,000 copies or more in its first year, in colonies of about 2.5 million people.
events.why: Fighting had begun, and many colonists still hoped to make peace with the king. Paine had arrived from England in late 1774 with an introduction from Benjamin Franklin and no loyalty to the crown.
events.then: Six months later Congress declared independence, using many of Paine's arguments.
events.sig: Six months later Congress declared independence, using many of Paine's arguments.
events.now: It is a model of political persuasion aimed at a mass audience, the ancestor of the modern pamphlet and opinion column.

causes.why: With blood spilled, Paine argued there was no going back to the king.

q.idea: Monarchy is unnatural, and America should be independent.
q.against: Loyalty to the king and hopes of reconciliation.
q.spread: Cheap reprints, read aloud in taverns and army camps.
q.enabled: Popular support for the Declaration of Independence.
q.critics: Loyalists called it dangerous nonsense; Paine's later attacks on religion cost him friends.

events.bluf: English-born writer Thomas Paine wrote to persuade colonists who still hoped for reconciliation with King George III that independence and a republic were the only sense. 'Common Sense' sold perhaps 100,000 copies or more in its first year, in colonies of about 2.5 million people, in language ordinary readers could follow. Six months after it appeared Congress declared independence, and the pamphlet showed what mass print persuasion could do.
events.lens: Ideas spread fastest when written in plain language for ordinary readers.
events.fact: Paine had failed as a corset-maker, exciseman and shopkeeper before he arrived in America in 1774.

events.what: Case for free markets.
events.why: Smith wanted to explain why some nations were growing richer than others. Mercantilist doctrine held that wealth meant gold earned by trade surpluses, and he set out to refute it.
events.sig: Britain moved toward free trade in the 1800s and repealed the Corn Laws in 1846. London stockbroker David Ricardo and English clergyman Thomas Malthus built on Smith; German philosopher Karl Marx built against him.
events.hook: A Scottish professor explained how markets make nations rich.
events.story: Scottish philosopher Adam Smith published 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' in 1776. He argued that dividing labour into specialised tasks multiplies output, and that individuals pursuing their own interest in competitive markets are led as by an 'invisible hand' to benefit society. He attacked mercantilism, monopolies such as the East India Company and trade barriers. Governments, he wrote, must provide defence, justice and public works.
events.then: Britain moved toward free trade in the 1800s and repealed the Corn Laws in 1846. London stockbroker David Ricardo and English clergyman Thomas Malthus built on Smith; German philosopher Karl Marx built against him.
events.now: Modern economics starts here. Today's renewed fights over tariffs, industrial policy and free trade are still argued in Smith's terms.
events.fact: The book appeared in 1776, the year of the American Declaration of Independence; its opening example is a pin factory where ten men make 48,000 pins a day.

q.what: Ideas: specialisation, free markets and free trade.
q.who: Merchants and manufacturers gained an argument against monopolies.
q.scale: It became the founding text of economics.
q.daily: His pin factory example showed how dividing work raises output.
q.system: Free-market capitalism.

events.bluf: Scottish philosopher Adam Smith set out to explain how nations grow rich and to refute the mercantilist doctrine that wealth means hoarding gold through trade surpluses. He argued that wealth comes from productive labour, the division of labour and free exchange, and that self-interest in competitive markets tends to serve the public. The book founded modern economics and supplied the case for free trade that Britain adopted in the 1800s.
events.lens: Ask whether a policy creates wealth or merely moves it around; Smith's question still cuts through economic arguments.

kv: pins a day per worker, with and without division of labour

events.who: Continental Congress; Thomas Jefferson as main author
events.what: Thirteen colonies declared independence from Britain.
events.why: War had begun, and independence was needed to win foreign allies, especially France, which would back a new nation rather than rebels seeking better terms.
events.sig: France saw a cause worth backing and joined the war in 1778, and the Declaration's language of universal rights was echoed in France's Declaration of the Rights of Man in 1789.
events.hook: Thirteen colonies declared that 'all men are created equal' and broke from the world's greatest empire.
events.story: Fifteen months into the war, on 4 July 1776, the Continental Congress adopted Virginian Thomas Jefferson's draft announcing independence. It argued that governments get their power from the consent of the governed and that people may overthrow tyrants, then listed grievances against King George III. Congress cut a passage condemning the slave trade from the draft; Jefferson himself enslaved hundreds of people over his life.
events.then: France saw a cause worth backing and joined the war in 1778, and the Declaration's language of universal rights was echoed in France's Declaration of the Rights of Man in 1789.
events.now: Its words inspired revolutions worldwide and were used by abolitionists, suffragists and civil rights leaders to demand that America live up to them.
events.fact: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson, rivals and friends, both died on 4 July 1826, the 50th anniversary.

causes.why: After a year of fighting, Congress declared independence.
Jefferson drew on Locke's ideas of natural rights and government by consent.
Generations of self-government made taxes imposed by a distant Parliament feel illegitimate.
Penn's Philadelphia, a planned city of religious toleration, grew into the largest city in the colonies and hosted the Continental Congress.
Paine's pamphlet won public opinion over to independence months before Congress declared it.

q.before: The colonies were ruled by the British crown and Parliament.
q.how: A formal declaration by the Continental Congress.
q.claim: Natural rights and the consent of the governed.
q.winners: The new United States, after winning the war.
q.lasted: Yes: July 4 is the national holiday.

events.bluf: The Continental Congress declared independence to turn a war already fifteen months old into a cause foreign powers could back, since France would arm a sovereign nation rather than rebels seeking better terms. The Declaration, drafted by Virginian Thomas Jefferson and adopted on 4 July 1776, justified the break by universal rights and government by consent. France allied with the United States in 1778, and the claim that 'all men are created equal' clashed from the start with slavery, a contradiction that has driven American politics since.
events.lens: Revolutionary principles often outrun the interests of those who wrote them, and later groups claim them.

kv: people in the colonies, ~1 in 5 enslaved

events.who: General Horatio Gates and Benedict Arnold; British general John Burgoyne
events.hook: A whole British army surrendered in upstate New York, convincing France to join the war.
events.what: A whole British army surrendered in upstate New York, convincing France to join the war.
events.story: British General John Burgoyne marched south from Canada in June 1777 with about 8,000 men to cut New England off along the Hudson. American General Horatio Gates's army, with Benedict Arnold leading in the field, fought him at Freeman's Farm on 19 September and Bemis Heights on 7 October. Burgoyne's army was surrounded and surrendered on 17 October 1777.
events.why: Britain planned to cut New England off along the Hudson, and poor coordination between British commanders left Burgoyne without support; General William Howe took his army to Philadelphia instead.
events.then: France signed an alliance with the United States in February 1778, and Spain and the Dutch Republic later joined the war, stretching British forces around the world.
events.sig: France signed an alliance with the United States in February 1778, and Spain and the Dutch Republic later joined the war, stretching British forces around the world.
events.now: Saratoga brought France into the war in February 1778, and with it the money, navy and troops that won Yorktown; it is the strategic turning point of the Revolution.

causes.why: The new nation had to win its independence on the battlefield.

q.why: Britain tried to cut off New England.
q.stakes: Whether the rebellion could win foreign allies.
q.decided: American numbers, militia reinforcements and Burgoyne's slow advance.
q.cost: About 6,000 British and German troops surrendered.
q.changed: France entered the war, followed by Spain.

events.bluf: British General John Burgoyne marched south from Canada to cut New England off from the other colonies along the Hudson, and American General Horatio Gates, with Benedict Arnold leading in the field, set out to stop him. Burgoyne's army was surrounded and surrendered on 17 October 1777. The loss of a whole British army persuaded France to enter the war in 1778, which turned a colonial rebellion into a global war Britain could not win.
events.lens: Battles matter most for how they change others' calculations: Saratoga's real result came in Paris.
events.fact: Arnold, wounded in the leg at Bemis Heights, was the hero of the battle; after his treason in 1780 the monument there shows a boot and no name.

kv: British and German troops surrendered on 17 October

events.h: France allies with the United States
events.who: Benjamin Franklin; Louis XVI's foreign minister Vergennes
events.hook: France signed an alliance with the American rebels and went to war with Britain.
events.what: France signed an alliance with the American rebels and went to war with Britain.
events.story: The American colonies had been at war with Britain since 1775 and needed a European ally. American envoy Benjamin Franklin negotiated in Paris from late 1776. News of the British surrender at Saratoga in October 1777 reached Paris in December. On 6 February 1778 France and the United States signed treaties of commerce and alliance, and French money, soldiers and above all the navy followed.
events.why: France wanted revenge for the loss of Canada in the Seven Years' War and to weaken Britain. Saratoga showed that the Americans could win and were worth backing.
events.then: Britain and France were at war by the summer of 1778 and Spain joined France in 1779. A French fleet under Admiral de Grasse closed Chesapeake Bay, and the Franco-American army took British general Lord Cornwallis's surrender at Yorktown in October 1781. France's war debts fed the crisis of 1788-89.
events.sig: Britain and France were at war by the summer of 1778 and Spain joined France in 1779. A French fleet under Admiral de Grasse closed Chesapeake Bay, and the Franco-American army took British general Lord Cornwallis's surrender at Yorktown in October 1781. France's war debts fed the crisis of 1788-89.
events.now: The cost of the war deepened the French crown's debts and produced the fiscal crisis that forced Louis XVI to summon the Estates-General in 1789.

causes.why: Saratoga convinced France the Americans could win.

q.before: The colonies were fighting Britain alone.
q.how: A treaty of alliance between a monarchy and a new republic.
q.winners: The United States; France won revenge but sank deeper into debt.
q.lasted: It won the war; the alliance formally ended in 1800.

events.bluf: French King Louis XVI and his foreign minister the Comte de Vergennes wanted revenge for the loss of Canada in 1763 and a weaker Britain; American envoy Benjamin Franklin wanted money, troops and a navy. The treaties of February 1778 delivered all three, and a French fleet trapped British general Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown in 1781. The United States won its independence, and the debt France took on to pay for it helped bring on its own revolution in 1789.
events.lens: Great powers back rebels to weaken their rivals, and the cost can come home in unexpected ways.
events.trig: The American victory at Saratoga in October 1777.
events.fact: Franklin went about the French court in a fur cap and without a wig, and Paris made a fashion of it.

kv: livres: France's cost of the war
of the troops at Yorktown were French

events.what: Largest Indigenous revolt in colonial Spanish America.
events.why: Crushing taxes came first. Forced purchases of goods from officials and the mita labour draft added to them.
events.sig: He was captured and executed in Cusco in May 1781, and Spain banned Inca dress, symbols and titles. The rebellion continued in Upper Peru (Bolivia) under Aymara leader Túpac Katari, who besieged La Paz in 1781.
events.hook: The largest Indigenous revolt in colonial Spanish America shook the Andes.
events.story: In November 1780 José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a wealthy mule-train owner and kuraka of Inca descent, seized and executed the Spanish corregidor Antonio de Arriaga. Calling himself Túpac Amaru II, he led tens of thousands of Indigenous and mestizo rebels against abusive officials and forced labour.
events.then: He was captured and executed in Cusco in May 1781, and Spain banned Inca dress, symbols and titles. The rebellion continued in Upper Peru (Bolivia) under Aymara leader Túpac Katari, who besieged La Paz in 1781.
events.now: The fear the rebellion left among Peru's Creoles kept them loyal to Spain longer than any other mainland elite, so independence came to Peru from outside in 1821-24 and left the Indigenous majority outside politics.

q.why: Abuse by Spanish officials and forced labour.
q.stakes: Spanish rule in the southern Andes.
q.decided: Spanish armies with Indigenous allies captured the leaders.
q.cost: Perhaps 100,000 dead; Túpac Amaru II was executed in Cusco in 1781.
q.changed: Spain cracked down on Inca symbols and culture.

events.bluf: José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a kuraka of Inca descent who took the name Túpac Amaru II, rose in November 1780 to end abusive officials, forced purchases and the mita. His rebellion, the largest Indigenous uprising in colonial Spanish America, was crushed within months and he was executed in 1781. The suppression left Creole elites afraid of Indigenous mobilisation, which shaped Peru's cautious, elite-led road to independence.
events.lens: Fear of mass revolt from below makes elites cautious revolutionaries.
events.fact: Túpac Amaru II was executed in the same Cusco square where Túpac Amaru I had been beheaded in 1572; the order was to tear him apart with four horses, and when that failed he was beheaded.

events.who: Washington, French under Rochambeau and de Grasse; British under Cornwallis
events.what: British army surrendered.
events.why: A French fleet under Admiral de Grasse blocked the Chesapeake, trapping Cornwallis's army against the sea.
events.sig: Lord North's government fell in March 1782, and peace talks led to the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
events.hook: A French fleet trapped the British army in Virginia, and the war was effectively over.
events.story: British General Charles Cornwallis fortified Yorktown on the Virginia coast in 1781. General George Washington and French General Rochambeau marched their armies south from New York while French Admiral de Grasse's fleet beat off the British navy at the Chesapeake Capes in September and blocked escape by sea. Cornwallis surrendered over 7,000 troops on 19 October after a three-week siege.
events.then: Lord North's government fell in March 1782, and peace talks led to the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
events.now: American independence was won with French troops, French money and a French fleet; the alliance of 1778 decided the war.

sites.d: First shots, April 1775.
American victory that convinced France to join the war.
Brutal winter camp, 1777–78.
Cornwallis surrenders; the war is effectively over.

causes.why: After the American victory at Saratoga in 1777, France entered the war; its fleet and troops were decisive at Yorktown.
A French fleet and army trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown.

q.why: Washington and the French saw a chance to trap Cornwallis.
q.decided: The French fleet's victory at sea and the land siege.
q.cost: Relatively light casualties; over 7,000 British troops surrendered.
q.changed: Britain gave up the fight.

events.bluf: General George Washington and French General Rochambeau marched south to trap British General Charles Cornwallis's army at Yorktown while French Admiral de Grasse's fleet closed the Chesapeake. Cornwallis surrendered over 7,000 troops on 19 October 1781 after a three-week siege. Sea power decided it: Britain could neither supply nor rescue an army it could not protect at sea, and the defeat brought down Lord North's government and ended the war in all but name.
events.lens: Control of the sea decides wars fought along coastlines: an army that cannot be supplied or evacuated by sea is a hostage.
events.fact: Cornwallis pleaded illness and sent a deputy to surrender his sword; Washington had a deputy of his own receive it.
events.btt: American Revolution: the surrender of Cornwallis

events.hook: A new dynasty moved Siam's capital to Bangkok; it still reigns.
events.what: A new dynasty moved Siam's capital to Bangkok; it still reigns.
events.story: King Taksin, who had ruled Siam from Thonburi since the fall of Ayutthaya, was deposed and executed in 1782. His leading commander, General Chakri, took the throne as King Rama I. He built a new capital on the east bank of the Chao Phraya river at Bangkok, modelled on Ayutthaya.
events.why: The kingdom needed rebuilding at a more defensible site. The east bank put the river between the capital and Burma.
events.then: Siam became the strongest power in mainland Southeast Asia, extending control over parts of Laos, Cambodia and Malaya.
events.sig: Siam became the strongest power in mainland Southeast Asia, extending control over parts of Laos, Cambodia and Malaya.
events.now: Thailand's king is still a Chakri, and the monarchy remains politically central, protected by strict lèse-majesté laws.

causes.why: After Ayutthaya's destruction, Siam's new rulers built a new capital at Bangkok.

q.before: King Taksin of Thonburi, deposed in 1782.
q.how: A coup, and a new capital across the river.
q.claim: Restoring the kingdom's stability and Buddhism.
q.lasted: Yes: the dynasty still reigns in Thailand.

events.bluf: General Chakri took the Siamese throne as King Rama I to rebuild the kingdom after Ayutthaya's fall on a more defensible site. He built a new capital at Bangkok on the east bank of the Chao Phraya, modelled on Ayutthaya, and extended Siam's control over parts of Laos, Cambodia and Malaya. Siam became the strongest power of mainland Southeast Asia, and the dynasty he founded still reigns.
events.lens: Small states survive between empires by modernizing and playing rivals off each other.
events.fact: Bangkok's full ceremonial name, which begins Krung Thep Maha Nakhon, is one of the longest place names in the world.

events.who: American envoys Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay; British negotiators
events.what: Treaty of Paris recognized US independence, border at the Mississippi.
events.why: Britain wanted to end a costly war, and to pull the United States away from France with generous terms.
events.sig: The new nation was free but weak, deeply in debt and loosely governed under the Articles of Confederation, problems that led to the Constitution four years later.
events.hook: Britain officially accepted that the United States was a free country.
events.story: Signed in Paris on 3 September 1783 by American envoys Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay and British negotiator David Hartley, the treaty recognised the independence of the United States and set its western border at the Mississippi River. Britain kept Canada and returned Florida to Spain in a separate treaty.
events.then: The new nation was free but weak, deeply in debt and loosely governed under the Articles of Confederation, problems that led to the Constitution four years later.
events.now: The treaty roughly doubled the area of the former colonies and opened the way west, onto the land of Native nations the treaty ignored.

causes.why: Defeat at Yorktown brought down Britain's war government and led to peace talks.

q.before: The Thirteen Colonies had been part of the British Empire.
q.how: A peace treaty after military defeat.
q.winners: The United States; Native nations, left out of the talks, lost.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: American envoys Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay wanted recognition and the widest possible borders; Britain wanted out of a costly war and the United States pulled away from France. The treaty signed on 3 September 1783 recognised American independence and set the western border at the Mississippi, roughly doubling the area of the former colonies. The first modern state born from a colonial revolt had room to expand west, at the expense of Native nations who were never consulted.
events.lens: A winner may offer a rival generous terms to pull it away from a bigger enemy.
events.fact: The Americans negotiated separately from France, against Congress's instructions, and got better terms for it.
events.btt: American Revolution: the Peace of Paris

kv: area of the new United States

events.who: Daniel Shays and farmers of western Massachusetts
events.hook: Indebted farmers closed courts in Massachusetts, and alarmed leaders called for a stronger national government.
events.what: Indebted farmers closed courts in Massachusetts, and alarmed leaders called for a stronger national government.
events.story: Squeezed by state taxes and debts payable in scarce hard money, farmers in western Massachusetts led by war veteran Daniel Shays shut down county courts in 1786 to stop foreclosures. In January 1787 a state militia funded by Boston merchants scattered them at the Springfield arsenal.
events.why: A post-war depression and heavy state taxes to pay off war debts drove the farmers. The Confederation Congress had neither money nor an army to send.
events.then: The revolt helped persuade the states to send delegates to the Philadelphia Convention in May 1787.
events.sig: The revolt helped persuade the states to send delegates to the Philadelphia Convention in May 1787.
events.now: The rebellion convinced the propertied leadership that the Confederation could not keep order, and it produced the Philadelphia convention within a year; the Constitution's strong federal government is its direct result.

q.before: A weak Confederation Congress with no power to tax or raise an army.
q.how: Armed farmers shut the courts; a militia crushed them.
q.claim: That the government was seizing farms to pay rich creditors.
q.winners: Creditors and supporters of a strong central government.
q.lasted: The rebels were pardoned, and a new Constitution followed.

events.bluf: Farmers of western Massachusetts led by war veteran Daniel Shays shut down county courts in 1786 to stop foreclosures, squeezed by state taxes and debts payable in scarce hard money. A privately funded state militia scattered them at the Springfield arsenal in January 1787. The revolt convinced the propertied leadership that the Articles of Confederation could neither keep order nor pay debts, and the Philadelphia convention met within the year.
events.lens: Domestic unrest often triggers state-building: elites centralize power when they fear disorder.
events.fact: Thomas Jefferson, then American minister in Paris, wrote that 'a little rebellion now and then is a good thing'.

events.who: Thomas Clarkson, Granville Sharp and Quaker campaigners; later William Wilberforce
events.hook: Twelve men founded the society that built the first mass campaign against the slave trade.
events.what: Twelve men founded the society that built the first mass campaign against the slave trade.
events.story: The Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade was founded on 22 May 1787 by nine Quakers and three Anglicans, among them campaigner Thomas Clarkson and lawyer Granville Sharp. Clarkson rode the country collecting testimony from sailors and ships' surgeons. The society printed the diagram of the slave ship Brookes and organised petitions and a sugar boycott. MP William Wilberforce led the cause in the Commons.
events.why: Quakers had opposed slavery for decades. Evangelical and Enlightenment criticism of the trade was growing among the wider public.
events.then: Wilberforce's first abolition bill failed in 1791 and the war with France stalled the campaign through the 1790s. Parliament banned the trade in 1807 after 20 years of campaigning.
events.sig: Wilberforce's first abolition bill failed in 1791 and the war with France stalled the campaign through the 1790s. Parliament banned the trade in 1807 after 20 years of campaigning.
events.now: The society's method, evidence plus petitions plus boycott plus emblem, is the template every pressure campaign since has followed, from Chartism to the climate movement.
events.wk: Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade
events.fact: Potter Josiah Wedgwood made the campaign's emblem, a kneeling man in chains asking 'Am I Not a Man and a Brother?'

q.idea: The slave trade is a crime that ordinary citizens can help to end.
q.against: Powerful West Indian planters and merchants.
q.spread: Pamphlets, lectures and petitions signed by hundreds of thousands.
q.enabled: The 1807 ban on the British slave trade.
q.critics: Planters argued the trade was vital to Britain's economy.

events.bluf: Campaigner Thomas Clarkson, lawyer Granville Sharp and nine Quakers founded a society in London to turn British opinion against the slave trade and to get Parliament to ban it. They invented the pressure campaign: evidence gathered from sailors and surgeons, mass petitions, a sugar boycott and a printed image of a packed slave ship. Parliament abolished the British trade in 1807, and the society's methods became the model for every later movement.
events.lens: Movements win by making a distant injustice visible and personal to ordinary people.

events.who: Madison, Washington, Hamilton and 52 other delegates
events.what: Replaced the weak Articles of Confederation with a federal system.
events.why: Under the Articles of Confederation the national government could neither tax, pay its war debts, regulate trade between states nor put down revolts such as Shays' Rebellion.
events.sig: After a fierce ratification fight that produced the Federalist Papers, it took effect in 1789, and the Bill of Rights followed in 1791.
events.hook: Fifty-five men in a hot Philadelphia room designed a government that still runs the US today.
events.story: The Articles of Confederation left Congress unable to tax, regulate trade or enforce laws. From May to September 1787, 55 delegates in Philadelphia, among them Virginian James Madison, New Yorker Alexander Hamilton and General George Washington presiding, wrote a new framework: a two-chamber Congress (the 'Great Compromise' between large and small states), an elected president, an independent judiciary and federal supremacy over the states. To keep the South in, they counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for representation and protected the slave trade until 1808.
events.then: After a fierce ratification fight that produced the Federalist Papers, it took effect in 1789, and the Bill of Rights followed in 1791.
events.now: It is the oldest written national constitution still in use. Debates over the Electoral College, the Senate's small-state advantage and federal versus state power are rooted in its compromises.
events.fact: Rhode Island refused to send anyone to the convention.

causes.why: The weak government under the Articles of Confederation, unable to tax or keep order, led to calls for a new constitution.
The revolt convinced many leaders that the Confederation was too weak.

q.before: The weak Articles of Confederation.
q.how: A convention wrote a constitution; state conventions ratified it.
q.claim: 'We the People', the sovereignty of the people.
q.winners: Federalists who wanted a stronger national government.
q.lasted: Yes: it is the oldest written national constitution still in force.

events.bluf: Delegates led by Virginian James Madison, General George Washington and New Yorker Alexander Hamilton met in Philadelphia in 1787 to replace a Confederation that could neither tax, regulate trade nor put down revolt. They produced a federal republic with separated powers, checks and balances and a national government able to tax, and kept the South in by counting enslaved people as three-fifths of a person and protecting the slave trade until 1808. It is the oldest written national constitution still in force, and its compromises set the terms of American politics for two centuries.
events.lens: Institutions built by compromise carry those compromises for generations: read a constitution for what it was trying to balance.
events.btt: Constitution of the United States of America

events.who: Captain Arthur Phillip; about 750 convicts; the Eora people
events.hook: Eleven British ships brought about 1,400 people, half of them convicts, to found a penal colony at Sydney.
events.what: Eleven British ships brought about 1,400 people, half of them convicts, to found a penal colony at Sydney.
events.story: Eleven ships left Portsmouth in May 1787 with about 750 convicts and their marine guard. New South Wales Governor Arthur Phillip found Botany Bay unsuitable and raised the British flag at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788. The colony came close to starvation in its first years while it waited for supply ships. Smallpox broke out among the local Eora people in April 1789 and killed a large share of them.
events.why: After 1783 Britain could no longer ship convicts to America and its prison hulks were full. A settlement at Sydney also gave Britain a base in the Pacific and a source of flax and timber.
events.then: Settlement spread along the rivers and, after 1813, across the Blue Mountains. Frontier violence and disease reduced Aboriginal populations across the continent; about 162,000 convicts were transported by 1868. One reading holds the 1789 smallpox came from the colony's medical stocks or its ships; the other holds it arrived from the north with Macassan fishermen; the records settle neither.
events.sig: Settlement spread along the rivers and, after 1813, across the Blue Mountains. Frontier violence and disease reduced Aboriginal populations across the continent; about 162,000 convicts were transported by 1868. One reading holds the 1789 smallpox came from the colony's medical stocks or its ships; the other holds it arrived from the north with Macassan fishermen; the records settle neither.
events.now: The colony fixed the terms of Australian settlement: Crown land granted to settlers, Aboriginal peoples without legal title, a convict labour force. The doctrine that the land belonged to no one stood until the High Court overturned it in 1992.

causes.why: Joseph Banks, Cook's botanist, recommended Botany Bay to Parliament as a site for a penal colony.
With America independent, Britain could no longer ship convicts there, and needed a new destination.

q.before: The Eora and other Aboriginal nations had lived there for tens of thousands of years.
q.how: A penal colony founded by naval officers.
q.claim: Cook's 1770 claim, treating the land as unowned.
q.winners: British settlers; Aboriginal peoples were dispossessed.
q.lasted: Yes: it grew into modern Australia.

events.bluf: Britain needed somewhere to send convicts after American independence closed the colonies to them, and wanted a foothold in the Pacific. New South Wales Governor Arthur Phillip landed about 750 convicts at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788, and the colony survived its first years of near-starvation. It founded settler Australia on Aboriginal land that British law treated as belonging to no one, and that premise governed Australian land law until 1992.
events.lens: Legal fictions about 'empty land' justify settler colonization, and reversing them reshapes politics centuries later.
events.fact: 26 January, the day Phillip raised the flag, is Australia Day and to many Aboriginal Australians Invasion Day. Phillip was speared through the shoulder at Manly in 1790 and ordered no reprisal.

events.hook: The general who won the war took the oath as the first president under the new Constitution.
events.what: The general who won the war took the oath as the first president under the new Constitution.
events.story: On 30 April 1789 General George Washington swore the oath on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York, then the capital. He set lasting precedents, from the simple title 'Mr President' to forming a cabinet of department heads.
events.why: Washington was the one figure trusted by every faction, and his record of giving up power made it safe to create a strong presidency.
events.then: He stepped down after two terms in 1797, setting a two-term tradition that held until 1940.
events.sig: He stepped down after two terms in 1797, setting a two-term tradition that held until 1940.
events.now: Washington's departure after two terms made rotation of power the norm; the rule held until Franklin Roosevelt broke it in 1940, and the 22nd Amendment of 1951 wrote it into the Constitution.

causes.why: The new Constitution created the office of president.

q.before: The Confederation Congress, with no executive at all.
q.how: Unanimous election by the new Electoral College.
q.claim: The Constitution, ratified by the states.
q.winners: Federalists who wanted a strong national government.
q.lasted: Yes: every president since has taken the same oath.

events.bluf: The states had ratified a Constitution that sketched a presidency without defining it, and the one man trusted by every faction, General George Washington, took the office to make it work. He set precedents the text did not require: a cabinet of department heads, the plain title 'Mr President' and a voluntary departure after two terms. The republic learned that power would rotate, and the two-term rule held until 1940 and became law in 1951.
events.lens: The first holder of an office defines it: founders set norms as much as rules.
events.fact: The electoral college chose Washington unanimously in 1789 and again in 1792, the only president so elected.

events.who: Third Estate; Paris crowds; Louis XVI
events.what: Bastille stormed; Declaration of the Rights of Man.
events.why: The state could not tax its privileged nobles and clergy and was bankrupt after its wars, including its aid to the Americans. An educated middle class was shut out of power. Failed harvests in 1788 put bread beyond the poor, and Enlightenment ideas supplied the vocabulary.
events.sig: France abolished feudalism, seized church lands, became a republic in September 1792 and executed Louis XVI in January 1793. War with Europe's monarchies and revolt in the Vendée brought the Terror of 1793-94. General Napoleon Bonaparte took power in 1799 and carried revolutionary legal reforms across Europe.
events.hook: France overthrew its king and declared the rights of man.
events.story: The state was bankrupt after the American war and bread prices had risen after the failed harvest of 1788. French King Louis XVI called the Estates-General, which met in May 1789 for the first time since 1614. The Third Estate declared itself a National Assembly on 17 June, Parisians stormed the Bastille on 14 July, and the Assembly abolished feudal privileges on 4 August and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man on 26 August. Over the next decade France became a republic, executed the king, fought most of Europe and lived through the Terror.
events.then: France abolished feudalism, seized church lands, became a republic in September 1792 and executed Louis XVI in January 1793. War with Europe's monarchies and revolt in the Vendée brought the Terror of 1793-94. General Napoleon Bonaparte took power in 1799 and carried revolutionary legal reforms across Europe.
events.now: Liberty, equality and nationalism, the language of 'left' and 'right', declarations of human rights, the secular state, and the argument over whether revolutions must turn violent all trace back here.
events.fact: When the Bastille was stormed it held only seven prisoners.

causes.why: Rousseau's ideas of popular sovereignty and the general will became watchwords of the revolutionaries.
France's spending on the American war deepened the debt crisis that forced Louis XVI to call the Estates-General.
The cost of the American war pushed France toward bankruptcy.

q.before: Louis XVI, an absolute monarch, with privileged clergy and nobles.
q.how: The Third Estate declared itself the nation's assembly, backed by popular uprisings.
q.claim: The sovereignty of the nation and the rights of man.
q.winners: At first the middle classes and peasants freed from feudal dues.
q.lasted: The monarchy fell in 1792, though it later returned for a time.

events.bluf: French King Louis XVI summoned the Estates-General to approve new taxes for a bankrupt state; the Third Estate used it to claim sovereignty for the nation. Within three months the Bastille had fallen, feudal privilege was abolished and the Rights of Man proclaimed; within four years France was a republic at war with Europe and the king was dead. Popular sovereignty, the nation and the language of left and right entered politics, and the Terror set the question of whether revolutions must turn violent.
events.trig: Louis XVI summoned the Estates-General to approve new taxes, during the bread crisis of 1788-89.
