events.lens: Revolutions often start with a fiscal crisis: when a state cannot pay its bills and the privileged will not pay taxes, the old order is at risk.

kv: people in France, Europe's most populous state
clergy and nobles, the first two estates

events.h: Declaration of the Rights of Man
events.who: The National Assembly; the Marquis de Lafayette
events.hook: France's revolutionaries declared that men are born and remain free and equal in rights.
events.what: France's revolutionaries declared that men are born and remain free and equal in rights.
events.story: The National Assembly had abolished feudal privileges on the night of 4 August 1789. On 26 August it adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Its 17 articles listed natural rights to liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression, with free expression, religious tolerance and equality before the law. French deputy and general the Marquis de Lafayette had drafted an early version with advice from American minister Thomas Jefferson.
events.why: The Assembly wanted principles agreed before it wrote a constitution. Deputies had read the American declarations and the Enlightenment case for natural rights.
events.then: The Constitution of 1791 placed the Declaration at its head. Playwright Olympe de Gouges answered in 1791 with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman; she was guillotined in 1793.
events.sig: The Constitution of 1791 placed the Declaration at its head. Playwright Olympe de Gouges answered in 1791 with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman; she was guillotined in 1793.
events.now: It is part of France's constitution today and inspired the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
events.wk: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

causes.why: The new National Assembly set out its principles in August 1789.

q.idea: Rights belong to every person by nature, not by royal grant.
q.against: A society of privileged orders under an absolute king.
q.spread: Revolutionary armies carried it across Europe.
q.critics: Edmund Burke attacked 'abstract' rights; women and enslaved people were left out at first.

events.bluf: The National Assembly wanted to set out the principles of the new order before it wrote France's constitution. On 26 August 1789 it adopted a declaration of natural, universal rights and the sovereignty of the nation, which replaced privilege and divine right as the basis of French law. The text became the model for rights declarations worldwide, and its silence on women and the enslaved marked the limits of 'universal' as the Assembly used it.
events.lens: Universal declarations invite excluded groups to claim them.
events.fact: The Declaration was adopted as the preamble to a constitution that took another two years to write.
events.btt: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

events.who: Parisian market women; Louis XVI; Marie Antoinette
events.hook: Thousands of Parisian women marched to Versailles over the price of bread and brought the king back to Paris.
events.what: Thousands of Parisian women marched to Versailles over the price of bread and brought the king back to Paris.
events.story: Bread was short and dear in Paris in the autumn of 1789, and reports said the king's bodyguards had insulted the tricolour at a banquet in Versailles. On 5 October 1789 a crowd of thousands of women marched 20 km to Versailles; the Marquis de Lafayette followed with the National Guard. Early on 6 October part of the crowd broke into the palace and killed guards. French King Louis XVI, Queen Marie Antoinette and their children were taken to the Tuileries Palace in Paris that day.
events.why: Bread prices came first. Rumours that the court was plotting against the Revolution came second.
events.then: The king lived in the Tuileries as a prisoner in effect. The National Assembly moved to Paris within days, where the clubs and crowds could press it.
events.sig: The king lived in the Tuileries as a prisoner in effect. The National Assembly moved to Paris within days, where the clubs and crowds could press it.
events.now: The march moved the king from Versailles to Paris and put him under the crowd's control, the step from which the Revolution's radical phase followed; it showed that women's collective action could change politics, which the Revolution's leaders then suppressed.

causes.why: The king's delay in approving the Declaration added to the anger that sent women marching.

q.before: The king ruled from Versailles, away from Paris.
q.how: A mass march forced the king to move.
q.claim: The people's right to bread and to keep watch over the king.
q.winners: Paris radicals, who gained a hold over the king.
q.lasted: Yes: the monarchy never returned to Versailles.

events.bluf: Parisian market women marched on Versailles to get bread and to bring the king back to Paris, where the people could watch him. They got both: French King Louis XVI accepted the August decrees and the Declaration of Rights, and the next day the royal family was moved to the Tuileries. The king lived under the Paris crowd from then on, and the capital's streets rather than the court set the Revolution's pace.
events.lens: Food prices are political: when bread is scarce, governments fall.
events.trig: The reported insult to the tricolour at the royal bodyguards' banquet on 1 October 1789.
events.fact: The crowd escorted the royal family back to Paris chanting that it was bringing 'the baker, the baker's wife and the baker's boy'.

events.hook: The royal family tried to flee France in disguise and was caught, destroying trust in the king.
events.what: The royal family tried to flee France in disguise and was caught, destroying trust in the king.
events.story: On the night of 20 June 1791 French King Louis XVI, Queen Marie Antoinette and their children slipped out of the Tuileries disguised as the household of a Russian baroness, heading for royalist troops under General Bouillé near Montmédy. Postmaster Jean-Baptiste Drouet recognised the king at Sainte-Menehould and rode ahead. The family was stopped at Varennes on 21 June and brought back to Paris under guard on 25 June.
events.why: Louis no longer accepted the Revolution and hoped to recover his power from outside Paris. The Civil Constitution of the Clergy, which he had signed under protest, weighed on his conscience.
events.then: The Assembly suspended the king and then restored him on the fiction that he had been abducted. A republican petition on the Champ de Mars on 17 July 1791 ended with the National Guard firing on the crowd. The monarchy was abolished in September 1792.
events.sig: The Assembly suspended the king and then restored him on the fiction that he had been abducted. A republican petition on the Champ de Mars on 17 July 1791 ended with the National Guard firing on the crowd. The monarchy was abolished in September 1792.
events.now: The flight proved the king would undo the Revolution if he could; the republican movement, a fringe before, became a force within months, and the monarchy fell fourteen months later.

causes.why: Brought to Paris as a virtual prisoner, the king tried to escape.

q.before: A constitutional monarchy was being built around Louis.
q.how: A failed escape exposed the king's real views.
q.claim: The king's claim to rule freely.
q.winners: Republicans; the king lost all trust.
q.lasted: The monarchy fell 15 months later.

events.bluf: French King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette fled Paris in disguise to reach loyal troops near the frontier and recover the king's powers from outside the capital. A postmaster recognised him on the road and the family was stopped at Varennes and brought back under guard. The king was now a suspected traitor; the republican movement grew from a fringe into a force within months, and the monarchy fell fourteen months later.
events.lens: A ruler caught trying to flee loses the claim to lead; legitimacy can collapse in a single night.
events.fact: The king travelled as a valet named Durand, and the heavy coach ran hours behind schedule.

events.what: Enslaved people revolted against French planters.
events.why: Sugar slavery of exceptional brutality came first. Free people of colour were demanding equal rights. The French Revolution's declarations of liberty divided the colony's whites and inspired the enslaved.
events.sig: France abolished slavery in 1794, and Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804. French ruler Napoleon Bonaparte's defeat there led him to sell Louisiana in 1803. Haiti was isolated: the United States withheld recognition until 1862, and France demanded an indemnity of 150 million francs in 1825 in return for recognising it.
events.hook: Enslaved people in the world's richest colony rose up and won their freedom.
events.story: Saint-Domingue produced much of the world's sugar and coffee with the labour of about 500,000 enslaved Africans, worked so hard that planters constantly imported more. In August 1791 the enslaved of the northern plain rose. Under Haitian general Toussaint Louverture and later Jean-Jacques Dessalines they fought off Spanish and British invasions and, in 1802-03, the army French First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte sent to retake the colony.
events.then: France abolished slavery in 1794, and Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804. French ruler Napoleon Bonaparte's defeat there led him to sell Louisiana in 1803. Haiti was isolated: the United States withheld recognition until 1862, and France demanded an indemnity of 150 million francs in 1825 in return for recognising it.
events.now: Haiti paid France's indemnity and the loans taken to service it until 1947, which drained its economy for 122 years; the revolution remains the reference point for Black freedom and anti-colonial movements.
events.fact: Napoleon's failure to retake Haiti is why he gave up on America and sold Louisiana.

sites.d: Vodou ceremony that launched the revolt, August 1791.
Richest colonial city in the Caribbean, burned in the revolt.
Final defeat of Napoleon's army.

causes.why: The Revolution's language of rights, and the political chaos it caused, set off revolt in France's richest colony, Saint-Domingue.

q.why: Enslaved Africans rose against brutal plantation slavery.
q.stakes: Freedom for half a million people.
q.decided: Toussaint's leadership, and yellow fever that destroyed European armies.
q.cost: Perhaps 200,000 or more dead.
q.changed: Slavery ended in Saint-Domingue, and Haiti became independent.

events.bluf: The enslaved of Saint-Domingue rose in August 1791 to end a sugar slavery that killed them faster than planters could import replacements. Under Haitian general Toussaint Louverture and then Jean-Jacques Dessalines they beat Spanish, British and finally French armies and declared independence in 1804. The only slave revolt on record to found a state destroyed the world's most profitable colony, terrified every slaveholding society and pushed Napoleon to sell Louisiana to the United States.
events.trig: A ceremony at Bois Caïman and coordinated uprisings across the northern plain in August 1791.
events.lens: A revolution in one place can redraw maps elsewhere: Haiti's victory is one reason the United States doubled in size.

figs.n: Saint-Domingue produced about a third of all the sugar and coffee traded in the Atlantic world before 1791.

events.what: First 10 amendments guarantee speech, religion, press, trial rights.
events.why: Supporters of the Constitution promised amendments to win over Anti-Federalists who feared central power.
events.sig: At first it limited only the federal government; after the Civil War the 14th Amendment let courts apply it to the states, mostly during the 20th century.
events.hook: Ten amendments spelled out freedoms the government could not take away.
events.story: Opponents of the Constitution feared a powerful central government, and several states ratified only on the promise of amendments. Virginian James Madison introduced amendments in the first Congress in 1789. Ten were ratified by December 1791, protecting speech, religion, the press, the right to bear arms and fair trials.
events.then: At first it limited only the federal government; after the Civil War the 14th Amendment let courts apply it to the states, mostly during the 20th century.
events.now: Free speech, gun rights and police searches are still argued in Bill of Rights terms, and the 14th Amendment of 1868 let courts apply the first ten amendments to the states.

causes.why: Several states ratified the Constitution only after being promised amendments protecting individual rights.

q.before: The Constitution had no list of individual rights.
q.how: Ten amendments ratified by the states.
q.claim: Rights that government may not take away.
q.winners: Citizens, though at first it limited only the federal government.
q.lasted: Yes: courts apply it every day.

events.bluf: Anti-Federalists feared the new central government, and supporters of the Constitution had promised amendments to win ratification. Virginian James Madison drafted them in 1789 and the states ratified ten in 1791, protecting speech, religion, the press, arms and fair trials as limits on federal power. At first the limits bound only the federal government; after the 14th Amendment courts applied them to the states, mostly in the 20th century, and they became the core of American civil liberties.
events.lens: Rights on paper become real only when courts and citizens enforce them.
events.fact: Twelve amendments went to the states; one of the two left unratified, on congressional pay, was finally adopted in 1992 as the 27th Amendment.

events.hook: The Revolution put its king on trial and guillotined him.
events.what: The Revolution put its king on trial and guillotined him.
events.story: The monarchy was overthrown on 10 August 1792 and the republic proclaimed in September. The National Convention tried 'Citizen Louis Capet' for treason in December 1792 and January 1793. Deputies voted almost unanimously that he was guilty; the death sentence passed by a narrow majority. He was guillotined in the Place de la Révolution on 21 January 1793. Queen Marie Antoinette followed in October, as the Terror began.
events.why: The flight to Varennes in 1791 and the king's correspondence with France's enemies, found in an iron cupboard at the Tuileries in November 1792, destroyed trust in him. The Montagnards wanted the Convention bound to the republic by the king's blood.
events.then: Britain, Spain and the Dutch Republic joined the war against France within weeks. Revolt broke out in the Vendée in March 1793. The Revolution, at war with much of Europe and facing revolt at home, turned to the Terror.
events.sig: Britain, Spain and the Dutch Republic joined the war against France within weeks. Revolt broke out in the Vendée in March 1793. The Revolution, at war with much of Europe and facing revolt at home, turned to the Terror.
events.now: It made putting a head of state on trial thinkable, and France's split between republicans and royalists ran through its politics for another century.

causes.why: The king's failed flight in 1791 and war with Austria and Prussia from 1792 radicalised the Revolution.
After Varennes, few trusted the king; he was deposed and tried.

q.before: Louis XVI, deposed in 1792.
q.how: A trial by the National Convention and public execution.
q.lasted: France was a republic until Napoleon became emperor in 1804.

events.bluf: The National Convention tried French King Louis XVI to make the republic irreversible and to settle whether a king could be punished by his people. It found him guilty of conspiring against liberty almost unanimously and voted for death by a narrow margin, and he was guillotined on 21 January 1793. The execution turned the war into one against every monarchy in Europe, and France's split between republicans and royalists ran through its politics for a century.
events.lens: Killing a king closes the door to compromise for both sides.
events.fact: Louis began a speech from the scaffold declaring his innocence; the officer in command ordered the drums to drown him out.

kv: voted for immediate death, a majority of one

events.what: Emperor refused to expand trade.
events.why: China saw itself as the centre of civilisation, receiving foreigners as tribute-bearers. Britain wanted diplomatic equality, more open ports and a resident ambassador.
events.sig: Britain's trade deficit from buying tea kept growing, and it turned to selling Indian opium to China, which led to the Opium Wars after 1839.
events.hook: China's emperor told Britain it had nothing China needed.
events.story: British envoy Lord Macartney sailed to China with about 700 people and gifts including telescopes, clocks and a planetarium, hoping to open more ports, set up a permanent embassy and fix tariffs. He refused to perform the full kowtow and knelt on one knee instead. The Qianlong Emperor received him politely and rejected every request, writing to George III that China possessed all things and had no need of British manufactures.
events.then: Britain's trade deficit from buying tea kept growing, and it turned to selling Indian opium to China, which led to the Opium Wars after 1839.
events.now: It is often taught as China's missed chance to join the industrial age. One reading holds that Qianlong's refusal reflected ignorance of the outside world; the other holds that the Qing understood Britain well enough and judged that open trade and a resident embassy threatened a system that was working for them.

causes.why: A century of Qing prosperity and expansion, under Kangxi and his grandson Qianlong, left the court sure China needed nothing from Europe.

q.before: Foreign trade was confined to Canton under strict rules.
q.how: A diplomatic mission asking for wider trade and an embassy.
q.claim: Britain's wish to be treated as an equal.
q.winners: At the time, the Qing court.
q.lasted: No: Britain later forced trade open with the Opium Wars.

events.bluf: British envoy Lord Macartney went to Beijing in 1793 to win open ports, fixed tariffs and a resident embassy. The Qianlong Emperor received him and refused every request, writing to King George III that China possessed all things and needed no British manufactures. Britain's tea deficit kept growing; it turned to opium and then to force, and the Opium War of 1839 opened China on Britain's terms.
events.lens: Clashes between incompatible ideas of international order, here tribute versus treaty, rarely end in compromise.
events.fact: The only member of the mission who could speak Chinese was a 12-year-old page, George Thomas Staunton, who had learned it on the voyage; the emperor gave him a purse from his own belt.

events.who: Eli Whitney, a young inventor working on a Georgia plantation
events.what: Machine that cleaned cotton fast.
events.why: Short-staple cotton, which grew across the inland South, paid only if its sticky seeds could be removed cheaply, and Britain's mills wanted raw cotton.
events.sig: Enslaved people in the US grew from about 700,000 in 1790 to nearly 4 million by 1860. Cotton became the country's leading export.
events.hook: A simple machine made cotton king and slavery stronger than ever.
events.story: Inventor Eli Whitney's gin pulled seeds from cotton far faster than hands could. Growing short-staple cotton suddenly paid almost anywhere in the South, and planters pushed west into the Deep South with enslaved workers.
events.then: Enslaved people in the US grew from about 700,000 in 1790 to nearly 4 million by 1860. Cotton became the country's leading export.
events.now: The gin revived slavery when it might have declined and bound the South's economy to Britain's mills; the enslaved population rose from about 700,000 in 1790 to nearly 4 million by 1860.
events.fact: Whitney made little money from the gin. He got rich making muskets with interchangeable parts.

q.what: Short-staple cotton, cleaned of its seeds.
q.who: Planters and British mills grew rich; enslaved people paid with their freedom and families.
q.scale: US cotton exports rose from about 500,000 pounds in 1793 to over 80 million by 1810.
q.daily: Enslaved people were forced to pick ever more cotton.
q.system: The 'Cotton Kingdom' of the Deep South.

events.bluf: Inventor Eli Whitney, working on a Georgia plantation, built a machine in 1793 to pull the seeds from short-staple cotton, which paid only if the seeds could be removed cheaply. The gin worked, and short-staple cotton became profitable across the inland South. Planters pushed west with enslaved workers; enslaved people in the United States grew from about 700,000 in 1790 to nearly 4 million by 1860, and cotton became the leading export, tying Southern slavery to Britain's textile mills.
events.lens: Technology that makes a coercive system more profitable can entrench it rather than make it obsolete.

kv: more cotton cleaned per worker per day

events.who: Robespierre; the Committee of Public Safety
events.hook: The Revolution turned on its own people: about 17,000 were officially executed.
events.what: The Revolution turned on its own people: about 17,000 were officially executed.
events.story: By the spring of 1793 France was at war with Austria, Prussia, Britain, Spain and the Dutch Republic and in revolt in the Vendée and the federalist cities of Lyon, Marseille and Toulon. The National Convention gave the Committee of Public Safety executive power, and deputy Maximilien Robespierre joined it in July 1793. The Law of Suspects of September 1793 filled the prisons. About 17,000 people were executed after trial, and many more died in prison or in the crushing of the Vendée. The Terror ended when Robespierre himself was guillotined on 28 July 1794.
events.why: War and fear of invasion came first. Revolt in the Vendée and the federalist cities came second. Jacobin doctrine, which held virtue powerless without terror, supplied the justification.
events.then: The Convention dismantled the Terror's machinery after Thermidor, and a White Terror struck Jacobins in the south in 1795. The Directory governed from 1795 until General Napoleon Bonaparte took power in 1799.
events.sig: The Convention dismantled the Terror's machinery after Thermidor, and a White Terror struck Jacobins in the south in 1795. The Directory governed from 1795 until General Napoleon Bonaparte took power in 1799.
events.now: 'Terror' entered politics as a word for government by fear, and the case that a revolution for liberty ends in dictatorship has been argued from it ever since.

causes.why: Regicide brought Britain and Spain into the war, and with invasion and revolt threatening, the Jacobins turned to terror.

q.before: The National Convention, newly a republic.
q.how: Emergency rule by committees, with revolutionary courts and the guillotine.
q.claim: Saving the Revolution from enemies inside and out.
q.winners: Briefly the Jacobins; no one in the end.
q.lasted: No: it ended in July 1794.

events.bluf: The Committee of Public Safety, with deputy Maximilien Robespierre its leading voice, governed by emergency decree to win a war on every frontier and crush revolt at home. It won the war and crushed the revolts, at the cost of about 17,000 executions after trial and many more deaths in prison and in the Vendée. 'Terror' entered politics as a word for government by fear, and the episode became the standard warning against revolution.
events.lens: Emergencies justify extraordinary powers; watch whether those powers end when the emergency does.
events.fact: Robespierre had argued in 1791 for abolishing the death penalty.

events.who: Maximilien Robespierre; members of the National Convention
events.hook: Fellow revolutionaries turned on Robespierre and sent him to the guillotine, ending the Terror.
events.what: Fellow revolutionaries turned on Robespierre and sent him to the guillotine, ending the Terror.
events.story: French armies had won at Fleurus on 26 June 1794 and the threat of invasion had passed, yet executions in Paris rose. Deputy Maximilien Robespierre told the Convention on 8 Thermidor that unnamed traitors sat among them. On 9 Thermidor, 27 July 1794, deputies shouted him down and voted his arrest. The Paris Commune freed him; troops loyal to the Convention retook the Hôtel de Ville that night. He and about 20 followers were guillotined on 28 July.
events.why: The Terror had grown after the military crisis eased and no deputy felt safe. Robespierre's threat of an unnamed purge united his rivals on the committees with the moderates.
events.then: The Convention cut the Revolutionary Tribunal's powers and closed the Jacobin Club in November 1794. The Directory, a more conservative regime, took power in 1795.
events.sig: The Convention cut the Revolutionary Tribunal's powers and closed the Jacobin Club in November 1794. The Directory, a more conservative regime, took power in 1795.
events.now: 'Thermidor' became shorthand for the moment a revolution turns back toward moderation; Leon Trotsky applied it to Stalin's Russia in the 1930s.

causes.why: The widening Terror turned Robespierre's colleagues against him.

q.before: The Committee of Public Safety, dominated by Robespierre.
q.how: A parliamentary coup and executions.
q.claim: The Convention's authority against a would-be dictator.
q.winners: Moderates and survivors of the Terror.
q.lasted: Yes: the Terror never returned.

events.bluf: Deputies of the National Convention who feared they were next on deputy Maximilien Robespierre's list combined to bring him down. They shouted him down on 9 Thermidor, 27 July 1794, ordered his arrest, and guillotined him and about 20 followers the next day. The Terror ended, the Revolution turned back toward order, and 'Thermidor' became the name for that turn in every later revolution.
events.lens: Revolutionaries who rule by fear eventually unite their colleagues against them.
events.fact: Robespierre's jaw had been shattered by a bullet the night before his execution, and the executioner tore off the bandage on the scaffold.

kv: Robespierre and his followers guillotined within days

events.who: A British naval force under Admiral George Elphinstone
events.what: Seized from the Dutch.

events.sig: British rule, and its abolition of slavery in 1834, angered Dutch-speaking settlers, thousands of whom left the colony in the Great Trek from 1835.

events.story: France conquered the Netherlands in 1795. A British fleet under Admiral George Elphinstone landed troops near Cape Town and took the Dutch colony after a short campaign at Muizenberg. Britain handed it back under the Peace of Amiens in 1803, retook it in 1806 and kept it.

events.now: British rule at the Cape began the conflict between Britain and the Afrikaners, through the Great Trek and the Boer Wars, that shaped Afrikaner nationalism and, in time, apartheid.

q.how: Military occupation.
q.claim: Protecting the colony from France, then permanent possession.
q.lasted: Yes: Britain kept the Cape from 1806.

events.bluf: Britain seized the Cape in 1795 to keep the station on the sea route to India out of French hands after France overran the Netherlands. A fleet under Admiral George Elphinstone landed troops and took the colony after a short campaign at Muizenberg; Britain handed it back in 1803, retook it in 1806 and kept it. Dutch-speaking settlers came under British rule, and British policy, including the abolition of slavery in 1834, drove thousands of them inland in the Great Trek.
events.lens: Strategic bases taken for one reason become colonies with politics of their own.
events.fact: The British carried a letter from the exiled Dutch stadtholder William V ordering the Cape to admit them; the Dutch governor refused to act on it.

events.who: Napoleon Bonaparte; the Mamluk beys; Admiral Nelson
events.hook: Napoleon conquered Egypt with an army and 150 scholars, and found the Rosetta Stone.
events.what: Napoleon conquered Egypt with an army and 150 scholars, and found the Rosetta Stone.
events.story: Egypt in 1798 was an Ottoman province run by Mamluk beys. French General Napoleon Bonaparte landed in July 1798 and defeated the Mamluks at the Battle of the Pyramids. British Rear-Admiral Horatio Nelson destroyed the French fleet at the mouth of the Nile weeks later and stranded the army. The expedition's savants surveyed Egypt, and in 1799 French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, the key to deciphering hieroglyphs.
events.why: France wanted to threaten Britain's route to India and its Mediterranean trade. Napoleon wanted a command far from the politics of Paris.
events.then: Napoleon slipped back to France in 1799 and seized power. The stranded army surrendered in 1801.
events.sig: Napoleon slipped back to France in 1799 and seized power. The stranded army surrendered in 1801.
events.now: Modern Egyptology began with the expedition's 'Description de l'Égypte' and the Rosetta Stone. The invasion was the first large European military intervention in the Middle East since the Crusades and exposed how little the Ottomans could do to stop one.
events.wk: French invasion of Egypt and Syria

q.stakes: Control of Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean.
q.decided: Nelson's destruction of the French fleet at the Nile.
q.cost: Thousands of French and Egyptian dead; the army was stranded.

events.bluf: French General Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Egypt to cut Britain's route to India and to win glory away from Paris. He beat the Mamluks on land, lost his fleet to British Rear-Admiral Horatio Nelson within weeks and abandoned the army in 1799. Mamluk power was broken, which opened the way for Muhammad Ali's state, and the expedition began the European habit of studying the Middle East on the way to dominating it.
events.lens: A failed invasion can still transform a region by destroying its old elite.
events.fact: The Rosetta Stone passed to Britain under the surrender terms of 1801 and has been in the British Museum since 1802.

events.who: Tipu Sultan of Mysore; East India Company forces
events.hook: The East India Company stormed Mysore's capital and killed its sultan, its fiercest Indian enemy.
events.what: The East India Company stormed Mysore's capital and killed its sultan, its fiercest Indian enemy.
events.story: Mysore under Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan fought the Company in four wars from 1767. Tipu, 'the Tiger of Mysore', used iron-cased war rockets, reformed his army on European lines and sent envoys to France. After the third war of 1790-92 he lost half his territory. In May 1799 Company troops under General George Harris stormed Seringapatam and Tipu died in the fighting.
events.why: Governor-General Richard Wellesley feared Tipu's correspondence with France, whose army under Napoleon was in Egypt in 1798, and wanted to destroy the Company's strongest rival in the south.
events.then: The Company restored the Wodeyar dynasty as dependent rulers of a smaller Mysore and annexed the coast. It turned on the Marathas in 1803.
events.sig: The Company restored the Wodeyar dynasty as dependent rulers of a smaller Mysore and annexed the coast. It turned on the Marathas in 1803.
events.now: Mysore's defeat left the Marathas as the Company's only rival in India, beaten in turn by 1818. Tipu's standing is contested in Indian politics: an anti-colonial hero to one side, a persecutor of Hindus and Christians to the other.

causes.why: With Bengal's revenues, the Company fought a series of wars against Mysore, the strongest power in the south.

events.bluf: The East India Company set out to destroy Mysore ruler Tipu Sultan, the strongest Indian power in the south, before his approach to Napoleon's France could bring French help. Company troops stormed Seringapatam on 4 May 1799 and Tipu died defending the breach. Southern India was secure for the Company, and the war showed that an Indian state that had copied European arms still could not match the Company's resources.
events.lens: Alliances with distant powers rarely save a local ruler; they often give the enemy a reason to strike first.
events.fact: Mysore's iron-cased rockets inspired Britain's Congreve rockets, the 'rockets' red glare' of the American national anthem.

events.what: Coup made him First Consul.
events.why: The Directory was corrupt, unpopular and losing the war. Director Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès wanted a new constitution and needed a general; Bonaparte had the reputation.
events.sig: A plebiscite approved the constitution in 1800. Bonaparte made peace with Austria in 1801 and Britain in 1802, became consul for life in 1802 and emperor in 1804. His wars redrew the map of Europe until 1815.
events.hook: A young general took over France in a coup.
events.story: The Directory had governed since 1795 through purges and annulled elections and in 1799 was losing the war against the Second Coalition. General Napoleon Bonaparte returned from Egypt in October 1799 to a hero's welcome. On 18 Brumaire, 9 November, the councils moved to Saint-Cloud on the pretext of a Jacobin plot. On 19 Brumaire the Council of Five Hundred resisted, and soldiers called in by Bonaparte's brother Lucien, the council's president, cleared the chamber. A new constitution in December made Bonaparte First Consul.
events.then: A plebiscite approved the constitution in 1800. Bonaparte made peace with Austria in 1801 and Britain in 1802, became consul for life in 1802 and emperor in 1804. His wars redrew the map of Europe until 1815.
events.now: The coup fixed the pattern of the plebiscitary strongman, ratified by vote in 1800 and copied from Louis-Napoleon in 1851 to the generals of the 20th century: order and civil equality in exchange for political freedom.

causes.why: Years of war, terror and unstable government made a successful general look like a saviour.
Napoleon slipped back from Egypt in 1799 and seized power in Paris a month after landing.
The weak governments after Thermidor opened the way for a general.

q.before: The Directory, a five-man executive.
q.how: A military coup.
q.lasted: He ruled until 1814.

events.bluf: General Napoleon Bonaparte and Director Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès plotted to replace a Directory that was corrupt, unpopular and losing the war with a stronger executive. When the Council of Five Hundred resisted on 19 Brumaire, Bonaparte's soldiers cleared the chamber, and a new constitution made him First Consul. Ten years of experiment in representative government ended; he kept the Revolution's civil gains and ended its political freedom, a template for authoritarian rule with popular backing.
events.lens: When a revolutionary government is weak and at war, a popular general is often the one who takes over.
events.trig: Bonaparte's return from Egypt in October 1799.
events.fact: Bonaparte lost his nerve before the shouting deputies; his brother Lucien saved the coup by calling in the troops.

events.hook: Napoleon's general lured the leader of the Haitian Revolution to a meeting and shipped him to France.
events.what: Napoleon's general lured the leader of the Haitian Revolution to a meeting and shipped him to France.
events.story: French First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte sent an army of tens of thousands under French general Charles Leclerc to retake Saint-Domingue in early 1802. Haitian general Toussaint Louverture submitted in May. On 7 June 1802 he was arrested at a meeting he had been invited to, deported to France and held in the fortress of Joux in the Jura mountains, where he died in April 1803.
events.why: Napoleon wanted French control restored and, as became clear within months, slavery with it. Leclerc judged Toussaint too dangerous to leave at liberty.
events.then: France restored slavery in Guadeloupe in 1802, and when the news reached Saint-Domingue the Haitian officers under Jean-Jacques Dessalines rose again in October. Leclerc died of yellow fever in November 1802.
events.sig: France restored slavery in Guadeloupe in 1802, and when the news reached Saint-Domingue the Haitian officers under Jean-Jacques Dessalines rose again in October. Leclerc died of yellow fever in November 1802.
events.now: The arrest removed the one leader who had kept Saint-Domingue inside the French empire, and the restoration of slavery that followed it turned a colonial war into a war of independence, won in 1803.

causes.why: Toussaint had become ruler of Saint-Domingue, and Napoleon set out to remove him.

q.before: Toussaint governed Saint-Domingue as a near-independent ruler.
q.how: Arrest by trickery and deportation.
q.claim: Napoleon's claim to restore French authority.
q.winners: Briefly France; in the end the Haitian revolutionaries.
q.lasted: No: the French were driven out the next year.

events.bluf: French First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte sent an army under his brother-in-law, French general Charles Leclerc, to retake Saint-Domingue, remove Haitian general Toussaint Louverture and restore slavery. Leclerc seized Toussaint by treachery in June 1802 and shipped him to France, where he died in prison. The arrest backfired: news that France had restored slavery in Guadeloupe convinced the Haitian officers who had submitted to fight on to full independence.
events.lens: Removing a leader rarely ends a movement whose followers fear what defeat would mean.
events.fact: Boarding the ship, Toussaint is reported to have said that France had cut down only the trunk of the tree of liberty in Saint-Domingue, and that it would grow back from roots that were many and deep.

events.who: Chief Justice John Marshall; William Marbury; Secretary of State James Madison
events.hook: The Supreme Court claimed the power to strike down laws that break the Constitution.
events.what: The Supreme Court claimed the power to strike down laws that break the Constitution.
events.story: Outgoing President John Adams had appointed William Marbury a justice of the peace, and the new administration of President Thomas Jefferson withheld his commission. Marbury sued Secretary of State James Madison in the Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Marshall ruled on 24 February 1803 that Marbury was entitled to the commission, and that the law letting him sue directly in the Supreme Court was unconstitutional and therefore void.
events.why: A political fight between the outgoing Federalists, who had filled the courts with their own men, and President Thomas Jefferson's Republicans.
events.then: Judicial review became a pillar of American government, though the Court struck down no further federal law until the Dred Scott case in 1857.
events.sig: Judicial review became a pillar of American government, though the Court struck down no further federal law until the Dred Scott case in 1857.
events.now: Judicial review made the Supreme Court the final interpreter of the Constitution, a power that courts in many countries have since copied.

causes.why: The Constitution's status as supreme law let the Court strike down a statute.

q.before: It was unclear who had the final word on what the Constitution meant.
q.how: A court ruling, not a law or amendment.
q.claim: That the Constitution is the supreme law and judges must apply it.
q.winners: The Supreme Court gained lasting power.
q.lasted: Yes: judicial review is still central to US government.

events.bluf: Chief Justice John Marshall, a Federalist, faced a suit by William Marbury against Secretary of State James Madison for a judgeship the outgoing administration had promised him. Marshall ruled on 24 February 1803 that Marbury had a right to the post and that the law letting him sue in the Supreme Court was unconstitutional and void. The Court had struck down an act of Congress, which established judicial review and made the judiciary the final interpreter of the Constitution.
events.lens: Institutions sometimes gain power by appearing to give it up: Marshall lost a small case to claim a large principle.
events.fact: Marshall had been the secretary of state who failed to deliver Marbury's commission in the first place.

events.bluf: President Thomas Jefferson sent envoys to buy New Orleans, through which western farmers shipped their crops. French ruler Napoleon Bonaparte, his army destroyed in Haiti and needing money for war with Britain, sold the whole of Louisiana: 828,000 square miles for about $15 million. The United States doubled in size and became a continental power, and the question of slavery in the new territories grew over the next half-century into civil war.
events.lens: Distant powers sell territory they cannot defend; the buyer gains land, and new problems.

events.who: Jean-Jacques Dessalines; François Capois; French general Rochambeau
events.hook: Haitian forces won the last battle of their revolution, and the French army left the island.
events.what: Haitian forces won the last battle of their revolution, and the French army left the island.
events.story: Yellow fever had killed much of the French army, and the renewal of war with Britain in May 1803 cut it off from reinforcement. On 18 November 1803 Haitian general Jean-Jacques Dessalines's army attacked the French positions at Vertières outside Cap-Français; Haitian officer François Capois led repeated charges under fire. French general Donatien de Rochambeau agreed to evacuate. Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804.
events.why: Yellow fever had destroyed much of the French army. Renewed war with Britain in 1803 cut off reinforcements and brought a British blockade.
events.then: Haiti became the first state founded after a successful revolt by enslaved people. Rochambeau surrendered to the British blockading squadron rather than to Dessalines.
events.sig: Haiti became the first state founded after a successful revolt by enslaved people. Rochambeau surrendered to the British blockading squadron rather than to Dessalines.
events.now: Vertières made Haiti the second independent state in the Americas and the first founded by the formerly enslaved, a precedent slaveholding powers answered with isolation and France with an indemnity.

causes.why: Toussaint's arrest and France's return to slavery provoked a final war of independence.

q.why: To end French rule and slavery for good.
q.stakes: Whether slavery would return to Saint-Domingue.
q.decided: Haitian determination, French losses to yellow fever, and a British naval blockade.
q.cost: Tens of thousands had died in the war of independence.
q.changed: France lost its richest colony, and Napoleon sold Louisiana.

events.bluf: Haitian general Jean-Jacques Dessalines attacked the last French positions around Cap-Français to finish the war for independence. On 18 November 1803 his army broke the French line at Vertières, and French general Donatien de Rochambeau agreed to evacuate. Napoleon's attempt to retake Saint-Domingue and restore slavery was over, and Haiti declared independence six weeks later, the first state born of a slave revolt.
events.lens: Disease and local knowledge can defeat even the strongest expeditionary armies.
events.fact: Capois's horse was shot from under him during the assault, and Rochambeau is said to have ordered a pause in the firing to salute his courage.

events.who: Napoleon Bonaparte; jurists led by Jean-Étienne-Marie Portalis
events.hook: Napoleon gave France one clear civil law code that spread across Europe and beyond.
events.what: Napoleon gave France one clear civil law code that spread across Europe and beyond.
events.story: Revolutionary France had abolished feudal privilege yet kept hundreds of local legal customs, Roman law in the south and customary law in the north. First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte appointed a commission of four jurists in 1800, with Jean-Étienne-Marie Portalis its leading drafter, and attended many of the Council of State sessions that reviewed its work. The Code was enacted on 21 March 1804. It confirmed equality before the law and secure property and strengthened the power of fathers and husbands over women and children.
events.why: One nation needed one law. Bonaparte wanted the Revolution's gains in property fixed and the family put under paternal authority.
events.then: Napoleon's conquests carried the code to Italy, the Low Countries and western Germany. It was renamed the Code Napoléon in 1807.
events.sig: Napoleon's conquests carried the code to Italy, the Low Countries and western Germany. It was renamed the Code Napoléon in 1807.
events.now: Civil law in countries from Belgium to much of Latin America still rests on it.

causes.why: As First Consul, Napoleon pushed through a single civil code.

q.before: France was a patchwork of hundreds of local laws and customs.
q.how: One written code imposed nationwide.
q.claim: Equality before the law, as the Revolution had promised.
q.winners: Property owners and men; married women lost rights.
q.lasted: Yes: it is still the basis of French civil law.

events.bluf: First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte wanted one law for one nation in place of the hundreds of local customs that had survived the Revolution. A commission of four jurists led by Jean-Étienne-Marie Portalis produced it, and the Civil Code took effect on 21 March 1804: equality before the law, secure property, no feudal privilege, and the authority of fathers and husbands written in. It followed his armies across Europe and is the basis of civil law from Belgium to Latin America.
events.lens: Legal codes outlast the empires that impose them: Napoleon's armies were defeated, but his law stayed.
events.fact: On St Helena Napoleon said that Waterloo would wipe out the memory of his forty victories and that his Civil Code would live for ever.

events.what: Islamic reform jihad built a large state.
events.why: Protest against corrupt Hausa rulers and heavy taxes came first. The reformers' demand for pure Islamic practice gave it a doctrine. The grievances of Fulani herders gave it an army.
events.sig: The caliphate ruled northern Nigeria until British conquest in 1903. Britain then governed through its emirs, in indirect rule, and preserved the old elite.
events.hook: A scholar's holy war built West Africa's largest state.
events.story: The Hausa city-states of today's northern Nigeria were ruled by kings whom reformers accused of mixing Islam with older practice and whose taxes fell on Fulani herders. From 1804 Fulani cleric Usman dan Fodio led a jihad against them. By 1809 his followers had built the Sokoto Caliphate, one of the largest states in 19th-century Africa.
events.then: The caliphate ruled northern Nigeria until British conquest in 1903. Britain then governed through its emirs, in indirect rule, and preserved the old elite.
events.now: The Sultan of Sokoto remains Nigeria's most senior Muslim leader, and Nigeria's north-south divide partly reflects the caliphate's legacy. Boko Haram claims to revive its jihad, though Sokoto's establishment rejects it.

q.belief: A purer Islam and just government.
q.authority: The caliph, Usman dan Fodio, and his successors.
q.believers: Many Hausa and Fulani joined; Islamic learning flourished.
q.fallout: Wars and slave raids on the caliphate's borders.
q.today: The Sultan of Sokoto is the spiritual leader of Nigeria's Muslims.

events.bluf: Fulani cleric Usman dan Fodio launched a jihad in 1804 against the Hausa kings, whom he accused of corruption, heavy taxes and impure Islam. By 1809 his followers had conquered the Hausa city-states and built the Sokoto Caliphate, one of the largest states in 19th-century Africa. Fulani-led Islamic rule united the Hausa lands, survived British conquest in 1903 and still shapes northern Nigeria's politics and religious identity.
events.lens: Religious reform movements can become state-builders, and their institutions often outlast later conquerors.
events.trig: The king of Gobir moved against dan Fodio's community in 1804; dan Fodio withdrew to Gudu and declared the jihad.
events.fact: Dan Fodio's daughter Nana Asma'u, a poet in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa, organised a network of women teachers that still carries her name.

events.what: Crowned himself.
events.why: Napoleon wanted a hereditary throne to secure his rule and his reforms. The plot of 1804 showed that his death would leave France without a succession.
events.sig: His armies carried the Civil Code and the abolition of feudal privilege across Europe. His wars provoked national resistance in Spain from 1808, in Germany and in Russia.
events.hook: Napoleon took the crown from the Pope's hands and put it on his own head.
events.story: A royalist plot to kill First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte was uncovered early in 1804, and the Duc d'Enghien was shot in March. The Senate proclaimed Napoleon Emperor of the French on 18 May, and a plebiscite endorsed the hereditary title. On 2 December 1804 at Notre-Dame, with Pope Pius VII present, he placed the crown on his own head and then crowned Josephine.
events.then: His armies carried the Civil Code and the abolition of feudal privilege across Europe. His wars provoked national resistance in Spain from 1808, in Germany and in Russia.
events.now: Napoleon is the model of a ruler who uses plebiscites and popular appeal to justify concentrated power; the pattern, named Bonapartism, runs from Louis-Napoleon in 1851 to the strongmen of the 20th century.
events.fact: Napoleon was about average height for a Frenchman of his time; British cartoons made him tiny.

causes.why: Napoleon turned his military dictatorship into a hereditary empire, approved by plebiscite.

q.before: Napoleon ruled as First Consul for life.
q.how: A plebiscite and a coronation in Notre-Dame.
q.claim: The will of the people, confirmed by vote.

events.bluf: First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte wanted a hereditary throne to secure his rule and his reforms against assassination and a Bourbon return. He had the Senate proclaim him emperor in May 1804, won a plebiscite, and on 2 December crowned himself at Notre-Dame with Pope Pius VII looking on. The republic became a hereditary empire that kept the Revolution's civil equality, and a ruler who claimed power from the nation and the army rather than from the Church wore a crown.
events.lens: Strongmen often keep a revolution's institutions while discarding its political freedoms.

events.hook: Haiti became the first Black republic and the second independent country in the Americas.
events.story: On 1 January 1804 at Gonaïves, Haitian general Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared the independence of Haiti, taking back the island's Taíno name. He abolished slavery for good. In October 1804 he had himself crowned Emperor Jacques I.
