toll.n: Most of Napoleon's losses came from hunger, cold, disease and desertion rather than battle. Russian civilian deaths are unknown.

events.who: US vs. Britain and Native allies (Tecumseh)
events.where: Great Lakes, Washington DC, New Orleans
events.what: Inconclusive war; Washington burned.
events.why: Britain was seizing American sailors and blocking US trade with France, and many Americans blamed Britain for arming Native resistance and hoped to conquer Canada.
events.sig: The war ended in a draw. Native resistance in the Midwest was crushed with Tecumseh's death, and the Federalist party, which had opposed the war, collapsed.
events.hook: The British burned Washington, and Americans came out more united than ever.
events.story: Britain was seizing American sailors and blocking US trade with France. The United States under President James Madison declared war in June 1812 and tried to invade Canada; the invasions failed. Shawnee leader Tecumseh, allied with Britain, was killed at the Thames in October 1813. British troops burned the White House in August 1814 and failed to take Baltimore in September. The Treaty of Ghent, signed in December 1814, restored the pre-war borders.
events.then: The war ended in a draw. Native resistance in the Midwest was crushed with Tecumseh's death, and the Federalist party, which had opposed the war, collapsed.
events.now: It confirmed American independence and gave Canada a story of resisting the United States, one root of its distinct identity.
events.fact: The Battle of New Orleans was fought after the peace treaty had been signed, because the news had yet to cross the Atlantic. The bombardment of Fort McHenry inspired 'The Star-Spangled Banner'.

q.why: British seizures of US sailors, trade restrictions and support for Native resistance.
q.stakes: US sovereignty and expansion; Canada's survival.
q.decided: Neither side won outright.
q.cost: About 15,000 American and British dead, many from disease.
q.changed: Native resistance in the Old Northwest collapsed.

events.bluf: The United States under President James Madison declared war on Britain in June 1812 over the seizure of American sailors, limits on its trade and British arms to Native resistance, and hoped to conquer Canada. The invasions failed, Britain burned the White House in 1814 and failed at Baltimore, and the Treaty of Ghent restored the pre-war borders. The stalemate confirmed American independence, broke Native resistance in the Old Northwest with Shawnee leader Tecumseh's death, and gave Canada a founding story of resisting the United States.
events.lens: Wars that end in a draw can still have big losers: here, the Native nations.

events.hook: The bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars opened the road to Moscow but did not destroy Russia's army.
events.what: The bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars opened the road to Moscow but did not destroy Russia's army.
events.story: The Russian armies had retreated since June 1812, trading space for time. Russian commander Mikhail Kutuzov, appointed in August, chose to stand at Borodino. On 7 September 1812 about 250,000 men fought west of Moscow, and some 70,000 were killed or wounded. Kutuzov withdrew in good order, and Napoleon entered Moscow a week later.
events.why: Under pressure to defend Moscow, Kutuzov made a stand on prepared ground rather than continuing to retreat. Napoleon needed a decisive battle before winter.
events.then: Moscow burned, Russian Tsar Alexander I refused to negotiate, and in October the French began their retreat.
events.sig: Moscow burned, Russian Tsar Alexander I refused to negotiate, and in October the French began their retreat.
events.now: Russia remembers Borodino as a symbol of national resistance to invaders, invoked again in 1941 and in today's politics.

causes.why: Kutuzov finally stood and fought outside Moscow.

q.why: Napoleon sought a decisive battle; Russia had to defend Moscow.
q.stakes: Moscow, and whether Russia would make peace.
q.decided: Neither side broke; the Russians retreated intact.
q.cost: About 70,000 killed or wounded in one day.
q.changed: Napoleon won Moscow but not the war.

events.bluf: Russian commander Mikhail Kutuzov, under pressure from the tsar and the army to stop retreating, stood on prepared ground west of Moscow; Emperor Napoleon wanted the decisive battle that would end the war. On 7 September 1812 about 250,000 men fought and some 70,000 were killed or wounded, the bloodiest day of the Napoleonic Wars. Napoleon took the field and the road to Moscow; the Russian army withdrew intact, and the war went on.
events.lens: Taking an enemy's capital means little if its army and government survive.
events.fact: Napoleon kept the Imperial Guard out of the battle, refusing to risk his last reserve so far from France.

events.who: Napoleon; the armies of Russia, Prussia, Austria and Sweden
events.hook: The 'Battle of the Nations' broke Napoleon's power in Germany.
events.what: The 'Battle of the Nations' broke Napoleon's power in Germany.
events.story: After the Russian disaster Prussia and Austria joined Russia and Sweden against Napoleon. From 16 to 19 October 1813 about half a million soldiers fought around Leipzig under Austrian Field Marshal Karl Philipp Schwarzenberg's overall allied command, the largest battle in Europe before the First World War. Saxon troops changed sides during the battle. Napoleon was beaten and fell back to France.
events.why: The Russian disaster had cost Napoleon his army and his reputation. Prussia joined Russia in February 1813 and Austria in August, and the allies agreed to fight him only when their combined armies could converge.
events.then: Napoleon's German allies changed sides and the Confederation of the Rhine collapsed. The allies invaded France in January 1814 and Napoleon abdicated in April.
events.sig: Napoleon's German allies changed sides and the Confederation of the Rhine collapsed. The allies invaded France in January 1814 and Napoleon abdicated in April.
events.now: Leipzig broke Napoleon's hold on Germany and made German national feeling a political force; the states that fought him under Prussian and Austrian command were reorganised at Vienna into the Confederation that held until 1866.

causes.why: The ruin of the Grande Armée in Russia encouraged Prussia and Austria to turn on Napoleon.

q.why: The allies set out to free Germany and end Napoleon's empire.
q.stakes: Control of Germany, and Napoleon's survival.
q.decided: Allied numbers, and Saxon troops changing sides mid-battle.
q.cost: Well over 100,000 killed or wounded on both sides.
q.changed: Napoleon's German allies abandoned him.

events.bluf: Russia, Prussia, Austria and Sweden combined to drive Emperor Napoleon out of Germany. Over four days in October 1813 about half a million soldiers fought around Leipzig, the largest battle in Europe before 1914; Napoleon was beaten and fell back across the Rhine. His German allies changed sides, the Confederation of the Rhine collapsed, and the allied invasion of France that followed ended his rule in April 1814.
events.lens: Coalitions defeat a would-be hegemon once enough powers decide that staying out is more dangerous than joining.
events.fact: The Monument to the Battle of the Nations, unveiled for the centenary in 1913, stands 91 m high.

kv: soldiers, the largest battle in Europe before 1914

toll.n: About 30,000 of the French losses were prisoners.

events.who: Napoleon; the allied powers; Louis XVIII
events.hook: Defeated, Napoleon abdicated and was sent to rule a small Mediterranean island.
events.what: Defeated, Napoleon abdicated and was sent to rule a small Mediterranean island.
events.story: The allies entered Paris on 31 March 1814. Emperor Napoleon's marshals, Marshal Michel Ney among them, refused to march on the capital, and he abdicated at Fontainebleau on 6 April. The Treaty of Fontainebleau left him the title of emperor and the island of Elba, with a pension France never paid. French King Louis XVIII, brother of the executed Louis XVI, took the throne.
events.why: The allies had captured Paris and the marshals refused to fight on. The allies and French foreign minister Talleyrand saw the Bourbons as the settlement least likely to restart the war.
events.then: Napoleon left Elba on 26 February 1815 and landed in France on 1 March. He ruled for a hundred days until Waterloo.
events.sig: Napoleon left Elba on 26 February 1815 and landed in France on 1 March. He ruled for a hundred days until Waterloo.
events.now: The escape forced the allies to send Napoleon to St Helena in the South Atlantic in 1815 and to finish the Vienna settlement with his return in mind; a defeated leader with popular support had shown he could come back.

causes.why: After Leipzig the allies invaded France and forced Napoleon to abdicate.

q.before: Napoleon was emperor of the French.
q.how: Abdication forced by defeat.
q.claim: The allies restored the Bourbons by right of victory.
q.lasted: No: Napoleon returned within a year.

events.bluf: With Paris in allied hands and his marshals refusing to fight on, Emperor Napoleon abdicated on 6 April 1814; the allies wanted him out of France and the Bourbons back. The Treaty of Fontainebleau gave him the island of Elba to rule, and French King Louis XVIII took the throne. Elba lay three days' sail from France, and within eleven months Napoleon had escaped and ruled again for a hundred days.
events.lens: Half-measures with a defeated leader invite a comeback: the allies left Napoleon a title, a small army and a base close to France.
events.fact: Napoleon tried to poison himself at Fontainebleau the night after abdicating; the poison had lost its strength.
Most of the fighting was nearer Mont-Saint-Jean; Wellington named the battle after the village where he spent the night.

sites.d: 'Battle of the Nations' breaks Napoleon's power.
First exile; he escaped after 10 months.
Final defeat by Wellington and Blücher.
Remote Atlantic island; Napoleon died there in 1821.

events.hook: Napoleon's final defeat ended 23 years of war.
events.what: Napoleon's final defeat ended 23 years of war.
events.story: Napoleon escaped Elba and retook France in March 1815; the powers at Vienna declared him an outlaw and raised armies. He crossed into Belgium on 15 June and beat the Prussians at Ligny on 16 June. On 18 June, at Waterloo south of Brussels, British commander the Duke of Wellington's army of British, Dutch and German troops held his attacks through the day. Prussian Field Marshal Gebhard von Blücher's army arrived in the evening and the French broke.
events.why: The powers declared Napoleon an outlaw and raised new armies. He struck first in Belgium to beat the British and Prussians before the Austrians and Russians arrived.
events.then: Napoleon abdicated again on 22 June and was exiled to St Helena, where he died in 1821. The Bourbons returned; France paid an indemnity of 700 million francs and accepted an allied occupation army.
events.sig: Napoleon abdicated again on 22 June and was exiled to St Helena, where he died in 1821. The Bourbons returned; France paid an indemnity of 700 million francs and accepted an allied occupation army.
events.now: The order built after Waterloo kept great-power peace in Europe for a century, and 'meeting your Waterloo' still means final defeat.

causes.why: The destruction of the Grande Armée in Russia led to his defeat at Leipzig and exile in 1814; Waterloo ended his comeback.
Napoleon escaped from Elba in 1815 and was beaten at Waterloo.

q.why: Europe refused to accept Napoleon's return.
q.decided: Wellington's defence and the Prussians' arrival.
q.cost: About 50,000 casualties.
q.changed: Napoleon was exiled for good.

events.bluf: Emperor Napoleon struck into Belgium to beat the British and Prussian armies separately before the Austrians and Russians arrived; British commander the Duke of Wellington and Prussian Field Marshal Gebhard von Blücher meant to hold until they could join. On 18 June 1815 Wellington's British, Dutch and German army held its ridge until Blücher's Prussians arrived, and the French army broke. Twenty-three years of war between France and Europe ended, the Vienna settlement held, and no general European war followed for a century.
events.lens: Coalitions win when they hold together: Wellington's stand worked because Blücher kept his word.

events.who: Metternich, Castlereagh, Talleyrand, Tsar Alexander I
events.hook: Europe's diplomats redrew the map to keep the peace, and largely succeeded for a century.
events.what: Europe's diplomats redrew the map to keep the peace, and largely succeeded for a century.
events.story: Delegates met in Vienna from September 1814, and the Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815, nine days before Waterloo. France kept roughly its borders of 1792; Prussia gained the Rhineland and part of Saxony; Russia took most of Poland; Belgium was joined to the Netherlands; a German Confederation of 39 states replaced the Holy Roman Empire. The Concert of Europe that followed held congresses to manage crises together.
events.why: The powers wanted order restored and no single power able to dominate Europe again. They wanted the revolutionary principle of 1789 contained.
events.then: Conservative powers cooperated to crush liberal and nationalist revolts in Naples in 1821 and Spain in 1823. The settlement eroded with the revolutions of 1848 and the unification of Italy and Germany, and no general war broke out until 1914.
events.sig: Conservative powers cooperated to crush liberal and nationalist revolts in Naples in 1821 and Spain in 1823. The settlement eroded with the revolutions of 1848 and the unification of Italy and Germany, and no general war broke out until 1914.
events.now: The Vienna system is the standard model of a peace built by rivals: the great powers agreed to meet and manage crises together, which kept Europe without a general war from 1815 to 1914.

causes.why: Napoleon's defeat after Russia brought the victorious allies to Vienna to redraw Europe's map.

sites.d: Congress redraws Europe.

q.before: Napoleon had redrawn Europe's map.
q.how: Negotiations among the great powers.
q.claim: Legitimate dynasties and a balance of power.
q.lasted: Its system held, with strains, until 1914.

events.bluf: Austrian Foreign Minister Klemens von Metternich, British Foreign Secretary Lord Castlereagh, Russian Tsar Alexander I and French Foreign Minister Talleyrand set out to redraw Europe so that no power could dominate it again and to contain the principles of 1789. They balanced the great powers and created the Concert of Europe to manage crises together. No general European war followed for a century; the suppression of nationalism and liberal revolution produced the revolts of the 1820s, 1830 and 1848 and the national unifications that remade the settlement after 1859.
events.lens: Durable peace settlements bring the defeated power back in: France was included in 1815, unlike Germany in 1919.
events.fact: The Congress never met in full session; business was done in committees and at balls, and the Prince de Ligne quipped that the Congress danced rather than walked.

kv: until the next general European war

events.who: Congress of Tucumán; José de San Martín
events.what: Declared independence from Spain.
events.why: Spain's crisis under Napoleon had let local juntas govern since 1810. Spanish King Ferdinand VII's restoration in 1814 and his reconquest of other colonies made a formal break urgent.
events.sig: Argentina fought civil wars for decades between Buenos Aires, which wanted a strong centre, and provincial strongmen who wanted federalism. A lasting constitution came only in 1853.
events.hook: Argentina declared independence from Spain.
events.story: Local juntas had governed the Río de la Plata since May 1810 in the name of a captive Spanish king. On 9 July 1816 delegates of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata met at Tucumán and declared independence from Spain. In January 1817 Argentine general José de San Martín led an army across the Andes to free Chile and then Peru.
events.then: Argentina fought civil wars for decades between Buenos Aires, which wanted a strong centre, and provincial strongmen who wanted federalism. A lasting constitution came only in 1853.
events.now: The rivalry between Buenos Aires and the provinces, fought out from 1816 to the constitution of 1853, still shapes Argentina's federal politics.

causes.why: Buenos Aires set up its own junta in 1810 after Napoleon's armies overran Spain.

q.before: Spain's Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata.
q.how: A declaration by a congress.
q.claim: The sovereignty of the people of the provinces.
q.winners: Buenos Aires and the independence leaders.
q.lasted: Yes, though civil wars followed.

events.bluf: The delegates at Tucumán wanted to make permanent the self-government the Río de la Plata had exercised since 1810 and to give Argentine general José de San Martín a state to fight for. They declared independence on 9 July 1816, and San Martín's crossing of the Andes the next year carried the war to Chile and Peru. The break with Spain was complete, and decades of civil war between Buenos Aires and the provinces followed, fixing Argentina's divide between port and interior.
events.lens: Independence settles who rules from outside; who rules inside is fought over afterward.
events.fact: San Martín crossed the Andes with about 5,000 men through passes above 3,500 metres and beat the royalists at Chacabuco on 12 February 1817.

events.hook: A stockbroker turned economist showed why countries gain from trade even when one is better at everything.
events.what: A stockbroker turned economist showed why countries gain from trade even when one is better at everything.
events.story: Britain was arguing over the Corn Law of 1815, which kept out foreign grain until the home price was high. London stockbroker David Ricardo, who had made a fortune on the exchange, published 'On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation' in 1817. He used English cloth and Portuguese wine to show that each country gains by specialising in what it produces relatively best, even when one produces both goods more cheaply.
events.why: The Corn Laws raised the price of bread and protected landowners, and Ricardo set out to show why free trade benefited the nation. Rent, he argued, went to landowners at the expense of profit and wages.
events.then: His argument armed the Anti-Corn Law League. The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846, and free trade was British policy for 80 years.
events.sig: His argument armed the Anti-Corn Law League. The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846, and free trade was British policy for 80 years.
events.now: Comparative advantage is still the core argument for free trade, and today's tariff debates turn on how its gains and losses are shared within countries.
events.wk: On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation

causes.why: Ricardo built on Smith's case for free trade.

q.idea: Countries gain from trade by specialising in what they do relatively best.
q.spread: Through economists and free-trade campaigners.
q.critics: Later critics argued that specialisation can trap poorer countries in low-value goods.

events.bluf: London stockbroker David Ricardo wanted to show why the Corn Laws, which taxed imported grain to protect landowners, cost the nation. In 'On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation' of 1817 he showed with English cloth and Portuguese wine that even a country better at producing everything gains by specialising in what it does relatively best and trading for the rest. Comparative advantage became the core case for free trade, armed the campaign that repealed the Corn Laws in 1846 and remains the argument every tariff debate turns on.
events.lens: The gains from trade depend on relative, not absolute, efficiency.
events.fact: Ricardo retired from the Stock Exchange at 42 with a fortune and bought a seat in Parliament in 1819.

kv: countries and goods in his example: England's cloth, Portugal's wine

events.who: Shaka kaSenzangakhona, king of the Zulu
events.what: Military reforms forged a powerful state.
events.why: One reading holds that drought and competition among chiefdoms for land, cattle and water, and for trade at Delagoa Bay, drove the consolidation. The other puts the weight on Shaka's military talent and ambition. Both agree the regiments were his.
events.sig: Peoples fled or were absorbed, and new states such as the Ndebele, the Sotho under Moshoeshoe and the Swazi took shape. Boer trekkers later found some areas depopulated and used that to justify claims to 'empty' land.
events.hook: Shaka forged the Zulu into southern Africa's most powerful kingdom.
events.story: Shaka kaSenzangakhona took power over the small Zulu chiefdom around 1816. He reorganised its men into disciplined regiments armed with short stabbing spears and large shields. He conquered or absorbed neighbouring chiefdoms and built the Zulu kingdom.
events.then: Peoples fled or were absorbed, and new states such as the Ndebele, the Sotho under Moshoeshoe and the Swazi took shape. Boer trekkers later found some areas depopulated and used that to justify claims to 'empty' land.
events.now: The kingdom Shaka built fought Britain at Isandlwana in 1879 and survives as a monarchy with political weight in KwaZulu-Natal. The depopulation of the Mfecane years gave Boer trekkers their claim to 'empty' land in the 1830s.

q.before: Many small Nguni chiefdoms.
q.how: Military reform and conquest.
q.lasted: Shaka was assassinated in 1828, but the kingdom lasted until 1879.

events.bluf: Zulu King Shaka kaSenzangakhona set out from about 1816 to make a small chiefdom the dominant power of its region. He drilled its men into regiments armed with short stabbing spears and large shields and conquered or absorbed its neighbours. The Zulu kingdom became the most powerful state in southern Africa, and the wars and migrations around it, the Mfecane, remade the region's peoples just before European settlers pushed inland.
events.lens: Military reorganization can turn a minor polity into a regional power within a generation.
events.fact: Shaka's half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana stabbed him to death in 1828; Dingane took the throne.

events.who: Ngāpuhi chief Hongi Hika and other Māori iwi
events.where: Bay of Islands and across the North Island
events.hook: Muskets bought from European traders turned old Māori rivalries into devastating wars.
events.what: Muskets bought from European traders turned old Māori rivalries into devastating wars.
events.story: Ships calling at the Bay of Islands after 1800 traded muskets for flax, timber, food and preserved heads. Ngāpuhi chief Hongi Hika led armed raids south from 1818 against iwi that had none. Other iwi rushed to arm, and the fighting spread across the North Island through the 1820s and 1830s. Perhaps 20,000 Māori died in two decades, and many were displaced or enslaved; the wars faded once every iwi held muskets.
events.why: Old grievances between iwi came first; the musket turned them into campaigns of annihilation. Access to European trade decided who struck first.
events.then: Ngāti Toa under chief Te Rauparaha moved south to Kapiti Island and Cook Strait. Missionaries and traders pressed Britain to intervene, and the disorder was one of the Crown's stated reasons for the treaty of 1840.
events.sig: Ngāti Toa under chief Te Rauparaha moved south to Kapiti Island and Cook Strait. Missionaries and traders pressed Britain to intervene, and the disorder was one of the Crown's stated reasons for the treaty of 1840.
events.now: The wars redrew tribal boundaries that still govern land claims in New Zealand, and the disorder they left is why many chiefs saw advantage in a British governor in 1840.
events.fact: Hongi Hika visited England in 1820, met King George IV, and traded many of his gifts for muskets in Sydney on the way home.

q.why: Rival iwi raced to arm themselves with European muskets.
q.stakes: Land, revenge and power among iwi.
q.decided: Who had the most muskets.
q.cost: Perhaps 20,000 Māori killed.
q.changed: Tribal boundaries shifted, and some chiefs sought British protection.

events.bluf: Northern Māori iwi that traded first with European ships armed themselves with muskets to settle old scores with their rivals. Raids led by Ngāpuhi chief Hongi Hika from 1818 set off two decades of war in which perhaps 20,000 Māori died and whole districts were emptied or enslaved. The devastation made some chiefs receptive to British protection, which they accepted in the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840.
events.lens: Arms races set off by uneven access to new weapons are among the deadliest dynamics in history.

events.who: East India Company; Peshwa Baji Rao II
events.hook: The Company defeated the Maratha confederacy and became master of India.
events.what: The Company defeated the Maratha confederacy and became master of India.
events.story: Peshwa Baji Rao II, nominal head of the Maratha confederacy, attacked the Company residency at Pune in November 1817. Company armies under Governor-General the Marquess of Hastings beat the Peshwa, Holkar of Indore and the Bhonsle of Nagpur in a campaign through the winter of 1817-18. The Peshwa surrendered in June 1818 and was pensioned off at Bithur near Kanpur.
events.why: Hastings set out to eliminate rival Indian powers and end raiding by Pindari bands based in Maratha territory. The Maratha chiefs had failed to act together since 1803.
events.then: The Peshwa's office was abolished and his lands annexed to the Bombay Presidency. Much of India was now ruled through princely states bound by treaty to the Company. Nana Sahib, the last Peshwa's adopted heir, was refused his pension and became a leader of the 1857 rebellion.
events.sig: The Peshwa's office was abolished and his lands annexed to the Bombay Presidency. Much of India was now ruled through princely states bound by treaty to the Company. Nana Sahib, the last Peshwa's adopted heir, was refused his pension and became a leader of the 1857 rebellion.
events.now: The paramountcy established in 1818 made the Company and then the Crown the arbiter of every Indian state until 1947, when more than 500 princely states had to be absorbed into India and Pakistan.

causes.why: Panipat broke Maratha power in the north and left the confederacy divided, opening the way for the East India Company.

q.why: The Company was determined to end the last rival Indian power.
q.decided: Company armies defeated the Maratha chiefs one by one.
q.cost: The end of Maratha independence.
q.changed: The Company ruled or controlled most of India.

events.bluf: Governor-General the Marquess of Hastings set out to end the Maratha confederacy as an independent power and to stop Pindari raiding from Maratha lands. Company armies beat Peshwa Baji Rao II and the other Maratha chiefs in the Third Anglo-Maratha War of 1817-18. The Company was now the paramount power in India, ruling directly or through dependent princes, a system that lasted until 1947.
events.lens: Imperial conquest often ends by mopping up rivals already weakened by internal division.
events.fact: The Peshwa's pension of 800,000 rupees a year was among the largest the Company ever paid.

events.what: Decisive victory over Spain.
events.why: Spain's authority had collapsed after Napoleon invaded it in 1808 and Creole elites wanted self-rule. Spain's harsh reconquest after 1815 had turned many against it. Bolívar needed a new strategy after repeated defeats in Venezuela.
events.sig: He created Gran Colombia in December 1819 and helped free Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia. Independence was led by Creole elites, and the colonial social hierarchy, including the exclusion of Indigenous people, largely remained.
events.hook: Bolívar's surprise march over the Andes freed Colombia.
events.story: Spain's authority had collapsed after Napoleon invaded it in 1808, and its reconquest after 1815 had turned many Creoles against it. In 1819 Venezuelan general Simón Bolívar led his army across the flooded plains of the Llanos and over the freezing Andes at the Páramo de Pisba into New Granada. On 7 August at the bridge of Boyacá he defeated the Spanish army under Spanish colonel José María Barreiro. Bogotá fell three days later.
events.then: He created Gran Colombia in December 1819 and helped free Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia. Independence was led by Creole elites, and the colonial social hierarchy, including the exclusion of Indigenous people, largely remained.
events.now: Bolívar's victories from 1819 founded Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia; Venezuela's official name and Hugo Chávez's 'Bolivarian revolution' from 1999 show his continuing political use.
events.fact: Bolivia is named after Bolívar, and so is Venezuela's currency, the bolívar.

sites.d: San Martín crossed the Andes to free Chile.
Bolívar frees New Granada (Colombia).
Sucre frees Quito (Ecuador).
Last major Spanish army defeated.

causes.why: Haiti's president Alexandre Pétion gave Bolívar refuge, weapons and ships in 1815-16, asking only that he free the enslaved.

q.why: To free New Granada and Venezuela from Spain.
q.stakes: Spanish rule in northern South America.
q.decided: Surprise after the Andes crossing.
q.cost: Light at Boyacá; the crossing itself cost many lives.
q.changed: Gran Colombia was founded.

events.bluf: Venezuelan general Simón Bolívar, beaten repeatedly in Venezuela, marched his army across the Llanos and over the Andes to strike Spain where it was weak, in New Granada. He won at Boyacá on 7 August 1819 and took Bogotá three days later. New Granada was freed, the tide turned in northern South America, and Bolívar went on to create Gran Colombia and lead the campaigns that freed five countries.
events.lens: Wars of independence usually transfer power to local elites rather than overturn the social order.

events.what: Spain ceded Florida (Adams-Onís Treaty).
events.why: Spain, weakened by the Napoleonic Wars and independence revolts, could not defend Florida, and Andrew Jackson's raids against the Seminole had already occupied much of it.
events.sig: Florida became a slave territory in 1821 and a state in 1845. The US Army fought long wars to remove the Seminole, many of whom refused to leave.
events.hook: Spain gave up Florida after Andrew Jackson had already invaded it.
events.story: General Andrew Jackson's troops chased Seminole raiders into Spanish Florida in 1818 and seized Spanish forts there. Spain, weak and distracted, ceded Florida in the Adams-Onís Treaty, negotiated by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams and Spanish minister Luis de Onís and signed in February 1819. The treaty also fixed a border between the two powers running to the Pacific.
events.then: Florida became a slave territory in 1821 and a state in 1845. The US Army fought long wars to remove the Seminole, many of whom refused to leave.
events.now: Adams-Onís gave the United States a border to the Pacific and a method, military pressure then purchase from a weakened power, that it repeated through the century.

causes.why: Jackson's raids into Spanish Florida in 1818 showed Spain it could not hold the territory, and it sold it in 1819.

q.before: Spain ruled Florida.
q.how: Military pressure, then a treaty.
q.claim: Purchase, and US claims to restore order.
q.winners: The United States; the Seminole lost.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Secretary of State John Quincy Adams wanted Florida and a defined western border; Spain, weakened by the Napoleonic Wars and revolts across its American empire, could defend neither. General Andrew Jackson's raids against the Seminole had already occupied much of Florida when Spain ceded it in the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819 and fixed a border running to the Pacific. Military pressure followed by purchase from a weakened power became the method of US expansion, and the border gave the United States its first legal claim to the Pacific coast.
events.lens: Facts on the ground often come before the treaties that ratify them.
events.fact: The United States paid Spain nothing; it assumed up to $5 million in claims by its own citizens against Spain.

kv: in Spanish debts the US took on

events.what: Free trading port established.
events.why: Britain wanted to counter Dutch control of the region's trade and secure a base on the route to China. A free port drew the traders the Dutch ports taxed.
events.sig: Singapore grew into the British Empire's key Asian port, the hub for trade between India, China and the Malay world, and a magnet for Chinese immigrants. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 confirmed British possession.
events.hook: A British agent picked a swampy island that became a global hub.
events.story: In 1819 East India Company official Stamford Raffles signed a treaty with a Johor prince and the local Malay chief to set up a trading post on Singapore island. He made it a free port with no import duties. Traders and migrants arrived at once, and the settlement grew rapidly.
events.then: Singapore grew into the British Empire's key Asian port, the hub for trade between India, China and the Malay world, and a magnet for Chinese immigrants. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 confirmed British possession.
events.now: Singapore is now one of the world's richest countries per person and among its busiest ports; its founding as a free port explains its enduring openness.

q.before: The Sultanate of Johor and local Malay chiefs.
q.how: A treaty and a trading post.
q.claim: A deal with a rival claimant to Johor's throne.
q.winners: Britain and merchants of many nations.
q.lasted: British rule lasted until 1963.

events.bluf: East India Company official Stamford Raffles wanted a British base at the southern end of the Strait of Malacca to counter Dutch control of the region's trade and secure the route to China. In 1819 he signed a treaty with a Johor prince and the local Malay chief for a trading post and made it a free port with no import duties. Singapore grew into the British Empire's key Asian port and the base of one of the world's richest city-states.
events.lens: Location plus openness can make a small port a global hub: no duties and free immigration drew trade away from rivals.
events.fact: Raffles founded the Zoological Society of London in 1826, the year he died.

events.what: Missouri admitted as slave state, Maine free; slavery barred north of 36°30'.
events.why: Missouri's admission with slavery would have given slave states a Senate majority. Northern congressmen wanted to stop slavery spreading into the Louisiana Purchase; Southern congressmen held that Congress had no power to set conditions on a new state.
events.sig: The line held for 34 years. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed it and let settlers decide, and the Dred Scott ruling of 1857 declared any such ban unconstitutional.
events.hook: A line across the map kept the Union together, for a while.
events.story: Missouri applied for statehood in 1819 as a slave state while the Senate stood at 11 free and 11 slave states. New York Representative James Tallmadge proposed to bar new slaves from Missouri and free the children of those already there; the House passed it and the Senate refused. Speaker of the House Henry Clay brokered the settlement of 1820: Missouri entered with slavery, Maine entered free, and slavery was barred from the Louisiana Purchase north of 36°30'.
events.then: The line held for 34 years. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed it and let settlers decide, and the Dred Scott ruling of 1857 declared any such ban unconstitutional.
events.now: The compromise set the pattern of admitting slave and free states in pairs, which governed national politics until 1854; its repeal that year and the Dred Scott ruling of 1857 removed the last legal brake on slavery's spread.

causes.why: Cotton's spread made slaveholders determined that new western states allow slavery.
Missouri was the first state carved from the Louisiana Purchase to seek admission, forcing Congress to decide on slavery in the West.

q.before: Equal numbers of slave and free states.
q.how: A congressional compromise.
q.lasted: Until the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854.

events.bluf: Congress wanted to admit Missouri without breaking the balance of 11 free and 11 slave states in the Senate. Speaker of the House Henry Clay's settlement admitted Missouri with slavery and Maine without, and barred slavery from the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of 36°30'. The line held the Union together for 34 years and fixed the principle that Congress would decide where slavery could spread, the question that broke the Union in 1861.
events.lens: Compromises that divide territory instead of settling principles buy time but not peace.
events.fact: Former President Thomas Jefferson wrote that the dispute had woken him 'like a fire bell in the night' and that he took it for the knell of the Union.

kv: free and slave states before Missouri

events.who: Greek rebels; Ottomans; Britain, France, Russia
events.what: Greeks won independence by 1830.
events.why: Greek nationalism, fed by the French Revolution and the classical heritage, against Ottoman rule. The Orthodox merchant diaspora and the secret society Filiki Eteria organised the rising.
events.sig: Greece became independent by the London Protocol of 1830, the first new state from the Ottoman Empire, with Bavarian prince Otto as king from 1832.
events.hook: Greece broke free from the Ottomans, inspiring Europe's romantics.
events.story: Greek rebels rose against Ottoman rule in March 1821. Both sides massacred civilians: Greeks killed the Muslims of Tripolitsa in 1821 and Ottoman forces killed or enslaved most of the population of Chios in 1822. By 1825 Egyptian troops under Ibrahim Pasha, sent by the sultan, were crushing the revolt. European volunteers such as English poet Lord Byron, who died at Missolonghi in 1824, and public sympathy pushed Britain, France and Russia to intervene; their fleet destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian navy at Navarino on 20 October 1827.
events.then: Greece became independent by the London Protocol of 1830, the first new state from the Ottoman Empire, with Bavarian prince Otto as king from 1832.
events.now: Its mix of nationalist revolt and great-power intervention became the pattern for Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria, and the Greek-Turkish rivalry it began still shapes the eastern Mediterranean.

causes.why: After 1683 the empire lost ground to Austria and Russia; its Christian subjects, inspired by nationalism, began to revolt.

q.why: Greek nationalism against Ottoman rule.
q.decided: British, French and Russian intervention at Navarino.
q.cost: Tens of thousands killed, including massacres on both sides.
q.changed: Greece became independent in 1830.

events.bluf: Greek rebels rose in March 1821 to throw off Ottoman rule and found a nation on the model of 1789 and the classical past; the sultan sent Egyptian troops to crush them. By 1825 the revolt was failing, until public sympathy and European volunteers moved Britain, France and Russia to intervene, and their fleet sank the Ottoman-Egyptian navy at Navarino in 1827. Greece became independent in 1830, the first state carved from Ottoman Europe, and the mix of national revolt and great-power intervention became the pattern for Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria.
events.lens: Small nationalist movements succeed when great powers decide it serves their interests.
events.fact: Navarino was the last major battle fought entirely by sailing ships.

kv: killed at Chios in 1822; ~50,000 more enslaved

events.what: Independence won.
events.why: Conservative Creole elites, alarmed by a liberal revolution in Spain that threatened Church and army privileges, decided independence was safer than rule from Madrid.
events.sig: Mexico's first decades brought constant coups and conflict between centralists and federalists, liberals and conservatives. Texas broke away in 1836, and the United States took the north in 1848.
events.hook: Mexico won independence after 11 years of war.
events.story: Royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide, who had fought Mexico's rebels for a decade, switched sides in 1821 and joined insurgent leader Vicente Guerrero. Their Plan of Iguala promised independence, Catholicism and equality between Creoles and Spaniards. Spanish viceroy Juan O'Donojú accepted it in August 1821, and Iturbide entered Mexico City in September. Iturbide made himself emperor in 1822 and was overthrown a year later.
events.then: Mexico's first decades brought constant coups and conflict between centralists and federalists, liberals and conservatives. Texas broke away in 1836, and the United States took the north in 1848.
events.now: Mexico became Latin America's largest Spanish-speaking nation. Arguments over the role of the Church, the army and the regions shaped its politics through the revolution of 1910.

causes.why: Hidalgo's revolt failed, but guerrilla war continued until conservative officers led by Iturbide switched sides in 1821.

q.before: Spain's Viceroyalty of New Spain.
q.how: An alliance of royalists and rebels.
q.claim: The Plan of Iguala's three guarantees.
q.lasted: Independence lasted; Iturbide's empire did not.

events.bluf: Mexico's conservative Creoles, alarmed by the liberal revolution in Spain of 1820, decided that independence was safer for Church and army privileges than rule from Madrid. Royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide joined insurgent leader Vicente Guerrero in the Plan of Iguala, and Spain's last viceroy accepted it in 1821. Mexico was independent on terms that preserved the colonial elite, with a vast, divided territory and fragile institutions, and it lost half of that territory to the United States within a generation.
events.trig: Spain's liberal revolution of 1820, which restored its 1812 constitution.
events.lens: Independence won by conservatives tends to preserve the old social order, postponing conflicts rather than resolving them.
events.fact: Iturbide was shot in 1824 when he returned from exile, unaware that Congress had declared him an outlaw.

kv: territory, far larger than Mexico today

events.who: American Colonization Society; freed Black Americans
events.what: Colony for freed African Americans.
events.why: Abolitionists in the Society believed Black Americans would never be treated equally in the United States. Slaveholders wanted free Black people removed. Most Black Americans rejected the scheme.
events.sig: Liberia became Africa's first republic in 1847, ruled by Americo-Liberians. It and Ethiopia were the only African states to keep their independence through the partition.
events.hook: Freed Black Americans founded Liberia in West Africa.
events.story: The American Colonization Society, founded in 1816, united some abolitionists with slaveholders who wanted free Black people out of the United States. It bought land on the West African coast and sent settlers from 1822. The newcomers, and Africans freed from slave ships, built a colony at Monrovia, often in conflict with the peoples already living there.
events.then: Liberia became Africa's first republic in 1847, ruled by Americo-Liberians. It and Ethiopia were the only African states to keep their independence through the partition.
events.now: Americo-Liberian rule over the indigenous majority ran from 1847 to the coup of 1980, and the resentment it built fed the civil wars of 1989 to 2003.
events.fact: Liberia's capital, Monrovia, is named after US President James Monroe.

causes.why: Britain settled Africans freed by its anti-slavery patrols in Sierra Leone. American reformers copied the idea with Liberia, a colony for free Black Americans.

q.before: Indigenous peoples such as the Kru, Bassa and Vai lived on the coast.
q.how: Land bought, often under pressure, by the American Colonization Society.
q.claim: A refuge for freed African Americans.
q.winners: Americo-Liberian settlers; indigenous peoples were sidelined.
q.lasted: Liberia became independent in 1847.

events.bluf: The American Colonization Society, a coalition of abolitionists who doubted Black Americans would ever be treated as equals and slaveholders who wanted free Black people out of the United States, bought land on the West African coast and sent settlers from 1822. The settlers built a colony at Monrovia, often fighting the peoples already there, and declared Africa's first republic in 1847. Americo-Liberians ruled the indigenous majority for over a century, and that divide fed the coups and civil wars of 1980 to 2003.
events.lens: Colonies founded as refuges can reproduce the hierarchies their founders fled.

events.who: Prince Pedro (Emperor Pedro I); his adviser José Bonifácio
events.what: Prince declared independence.
events.why: Portugal's parliament tried to return Brazil to colonial status after the royal court went home. Brazilian elites rallied behind Prince Pedro to keep their autonomy.
events.sig: Brazil stayed united under a monarchy until 1889 and kept slavery until 1888, the last country in the Americas to abolish it. Portugal recognised independence in 1825 in return for a payment.
events.hook: Brazil declared independence under its own prince.
events.story: Portugal's parliament ordered Brazil back to colonial status in 1821 and recalled Prince Regent Pedro. Advised by Brazilian statesman José Bonifácio de Andrada, he refused in January 1822. On 7 September 1822, by the Ipiranga stream near São Paulo, he declared 'Independence or death!'. He was crowned Emperor Pedro I that December.
events.then: Brazil stayed united under a monarchy until 1889 and kept slavery until 1888, the last country in the Americas to abolish it. Portugal recognised independence in 1825 in return for a payment.
events.now: Independence under a prince kept Brazil one state and one monarchy until 1889 and left the plantation elite in charge, which is why slavery lasted there until 1888, later than anywhere else in the Americas.

causes.why: When the king returned to Lisbon in 1821, his son Pedro stayed and declared Brazil independent the next year.

q.before: Portugal ruled Brazil.
q.how: The heir to Portugal's throne led the break.
q.claim: Brazil's right to self-rule under its own monarch.
q.lasted: Yes; the empire lasted until 1889.

events.bluf: Brazilian elites and Prince Regent Pedro wanted to keep the autonomy Brazil had gained when Portugal's parliament ordered it back to colonial status. Pedro refused the recall, declared independence on 7 September 1822 and was crowned emperor. Brazil stayed united under a monarchy and avoided the wars and fragmentation of Spanish America; it also kept its plantation elite and slavery, which it abolished last in the Americas, in 1888.
events.lens: Smooth transitions preserve existing structures: good for stability, bad for those at the bottom.
events.fact: Pedro I later abdicated, returned to Europe and fought a civil war to put his daughter Maria II on the Portuguese throne.

kv: people, about a third of them enslaved

events.what: Warned Europe not to recolonize the Americas.
events.why: Fear that France or the Holy Alliance would help Spain reconquer its colonies came first. Russia's claim of 1821 to the Pacific coast down to 51 degrees north added a second front. Britain wanted Spain out of American trade, and its navy made the declaration enforceable.
events.sig: President Theodore Roosevelt's corollary of 1904 claimed a right to police Latin American states, and it was used to justify occupations of Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua. Latin American governments came to read the doctrine as a licence for US intervention rather than a shield against Europe.
events.hook: The US told Europe to stay out of the Americas, before it could enforce it.
events.story: Spain's American colonies had won independence by 1823, and a French army had restored absolute monarchy in Spain itself that year. British Foreign Secretary George Canning proposed a joint Anglo-American declaration against reconquest; Secretary of State John Quincy Adams argued for a US statement alone. President James Monroe put it in his annual message to Congress on 2 December 1823: the Americas were closed to new European colonisation, and the United States would stay out of Europe's wars.
events.then: President Theodore Roosevelt's corollary of 1904 claimed a right to police Latin American states, and it was used to justify occupations of Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua. Latin American governments came to read the doctrine as a licence for US intervention rather than a shield against Europe.
events.now: It is still the basis of US policy that treats the Americas as its sphere of influence, and US officials have revived its language in response to Chinese and Russian activity in the region.
events.fact: The United States had no navy able to enforce it. It worked because Britain's Royal Navy also wanted Spain and France kept out.

causes.why: The US warned European powers not to try to reconquer the newly independent Spanish American republics.

q.before: European powers might try to reconquer Latin America.
q.how: A presidential statement.
q.claim: The Americas were closed to new colonisation.
q.winners: At first Britain's navy enforced it; later the US used it.
q.lasted: It is still invoked.

events.bluf: US President James Monroe and Secretary of State John Quincy Adams wanted to keep Europe's monarchies from restoring Spain's rule over the new Latin American republics and Russia from pushing down the Pacific coast. Monroe declared the hemisphere closed to new European colonies in December 1823, with no navy able to enforce it. The claim became the charter for US primacy in the Americas and, after 1904, for a century of interventions.
events.lens: Great powers claim spheres of influence near home; watch how they treat their neighbours' sovereignty.

events.who: East India Company; Burma's Konbaung dynasty
events.hook: Britain's first war with Burma began a 60-year conquest.
events.what: Britain's first war with Burma began a 60-year conquest.
events.story: Burma's Konbaung kings had conquered Arakan, Manipur and Assam, bringing their armies up to the border of British Bengal. Border clashes in Assam and Bengal led to war in 1824. The East India Company landed an army at Rangoon. Disease killed most of the 15,000 Company soldiers who died. Burma lost Assam and its coastal provinces by the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826.
events.why: Burma's expansion had brought it to the border of British Bengal. The Company would tolerate no rival power on that frontier.
events.then: Two more wars, in 1852 and 1885, completed the British conquest. Burma was ruled as a province of British India until 1937.
events.sig: Two more wars, in 1852 and 1885, completed the British conquest. Burma was ruled as a province of British India until 1937.
events.now: The border drawn after this war, between Arakan and Bengal, runs through areas where questions of belonging still drive conflict, including the Rohingya crisis.

causes.why: Bengal became the base from which the Company expanded east into Burma.

q.why: Burmese expansion into Assam clashed with British India.
q.decided: British naval power and persistence, despite disease.
q.cost: About 15,000 Company soldiers dead, mostly from disease.
q.changed: Burma lost Assam and its coastal provinces.

events.bluf: The East India Company went to war to push Burma's Konbaung armies back from the border of British Bengal, where they had arrived after conquering Arakan, Manipur and Assam. The Company won in 1826 at a cost of 15,000 soldiers, most of them killed by disease, and took Assam and Burma's coastal provinces. The war began a 60-year conquest completed in two more wars, and it set the colonial border between Burma and India.
events.lens: Expanding empires collide at their frontiers, and border clashes become wars of conquest.
events.fact: The Company's paddle steamer Diana, which towed boats up the Irrawaddy, was the first steamship used in a war in Asia.

kv: British and Indian soldiers died, most from disease

events.what: Last major Spanish army defeated.
events.why: Spain's last army in South America held the Peruvian highlands. Bolívar and Sucre needed it destroyed to secure the independence of the whole continent.
events.sig: Spain's mainland American empire was over. Upper Peru became Bolivia in 1825, named after Bolívar, with Sucre as its first president.
events.hook: The last major Spanish army in South America surrendered.
events.story: On 9 December 1824, high in the Peruvian Andes, Venezuelan general Antonio José de Sucre's patriot army of about 6,000 defeated the larger royalist army of the last Spanish viceroy, José de La Serna, at Ayacucho. The viceroy was wounded and captured and his army surrendered.
events.then: Spain's mainland American empire was over. Upper Peru became Bolivia in 1825, named after Bolívar, with Sucre as its first president.
events.now: Ayacucho closed Spain's mainland empire in 1824; the republics that replaced it kept the colonial borders, elites and inequalities, which still shape the region's politics.

causes.why: Fear of another Indigenous uprising made Peru's creoles the most reluctant to break with Spain, so independence had to be brought by outside armies.
From liberated New Granada, Bolívar's armies moved south to finish Spanish power in Peru.

q.why: To destroy Spain's last army in South America.
q.decided: Sucre's tactics.
q.cost: About 2,000 royalist casualties.
q.changed: Spain's mainland empire in South America ended.

events.bluf: Venezuelan general Simón Bolívar and his lieutenant, Venezuelan general Antonio José de Sucre, set out to destroy the last royalist army in South America, which held the Peruvian highlands. Sucre beat it at Ayacucho on 9 December 1824 and took the viceroy prisoner. Spain's mainland American empire was over, leaving it Cuba and Puerto Rico, and the new republics inherited colonial borders, elites and inequalities.
events.lens: Empires rarely end with one battle: Ayacucho was the last act of a collapse that began 15 years earlier in Madrid.
events.fact: The capitulation signed at Ayacucho let the Spanish officers sail home at Peru's expense; a Spanish garrison held out at Callao until January 1826.

events.h: Order to fire on foreign ships
events.what: The shogun ordered coastal guards to drive off any foreign ship on sight.
events.why: More Western whalers and warships were appearing off Japan, and the shogunate feared that Christianity and foreign influence would spread.
events.sig: In 1837 coastal guns fired on the US merchant ship Morrison, which was trying to return Japanese castaways. The shogunate replaced the order in 1842 with one allowing foreign ships food, water and fuel.
events.hook: The shogun ordered coastal guards to drive off any foreign ship on sight.
events.story: Western whalers and warships appeared off Japan with growing frequency after 1800. In 1825 the shogunate under Japanese shogun Tokugawa Ienari issued the Edict to Repel Foreign Ships. Guards were to fire without warning, even at ships carrying shipwrecked sailors home.
events.then: In 1837 coastal guns fired on the US merchant ship Morrison, which was trying to return Japanese castaways. The shogunate replaced the order in 1842 with one allowing foreign ships food, water and fuel.
events.now: It shows how isolation was becoming impossible to enforce; within two decades the policy had been abandoned.

causes.why: The Phaeton humiliation convinced the shogunate to be tougher.

q.before: The shogun controlled all foreign contact through Nagasaki.
q.how: A harder isolation policy: no contact at all.
q.lasted: No. News of China's defeat in the Opium War made Japan soften it in 1842.

events.bluf: The Tokugawa shogunate ordered coastal guards in 1825 to fire on any foreign ship without warning, to keep Western whalers and warships, and Christianity with them, away from Japan. Guards obeyed when they could, firing on a US merchant ship in 1837. The order failed to deter the ships and was withdrawn in 1842 after China's defeat by Britain; isolation could no longer be enforced.
events.lens: Rigid policies often peak just before they collapse, hardening when they are already failing.
events.fact: The edict was known as the 'fire without a second thought' order, after the instruction that guards should open fire on sight.

events.what: Locomotive-pulled public railway.
events.why: Mine owners wanted a cheap way to move coal from the Durham pits to the River Tees. Stephenson had built colliery locomotives since 1814.
events.sig: The Liverpool and Manchester line of 1830 proved the intercity passenger railway. Within 25 years Britain had over 6,000 miles of track, and railway building spread across Europe and North America.
events.hook: A steam locomotive pulled the first public railway train.
events.story: Colliery owners in County Durham needed to move coal from the pits to the River Tees. Quaker banker Edward Pease backed the line and engineer George Stephenson built it. On 27 September 1825 Stephenson drove Locomotion No. 1 along the line pulling wagons of coal and passengers. It was the first public railway to use steam locomotives; horses worked much of its traffic for years.
events.then: The Liverpool and Manchester line of 1830 proved the intercity passenger railway. Within 25 years Britain had over 6,000 miles of track, and railway building spread across Europe and North America.
events.now: Railways created standard time and national markets, and rail remains central to moving freight and people, from Chinese high-speed lines to European freight corridors.

causes.why: Decades of improvement after Watt's engine, especially high-pressure steam, made locomotives possible.

q.problem: Moving heavy coal cheaply.
q.how: A steam locomotive on iron rails.
q.replaced: Horses, canals and wagons.
q.spread: Britain had thousands of miles of railway within 25 years.
q.next: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, and railway mania.

events.bluf: Durham colliery owners wanted a cheap way to move coal from the pits to the Tees, and engineer George Stephenson wanted to show that steam locomotives could do the work. On 27 September 1825 Stephenson drove Locomotion No. 1 along the Stockton and Darlington Railway with wagons of coal and passengers, the first public railway to use steam. Railways cut transport costs, created national markets and standard time, and within 25 years Britain had over 6,000 miles of track.
events.lens: Infrastructure that slashes transport costs reshapes where people live and work.
events.fact: A man on horseback carrying a flag rode ahead of the train on the opening day.

events.who: New York State; Gov. DeWitt Clinton
events.what: Connected the Great Lakes to the Atlantic.
events.why: The Appalachians cut the Midwest's farms off from the Atlantic ports, and overland freight cost more than the goods it carried. New York stood to take the trade from Philadelphia, Baltimore and New Orleans.
events.sig: Midwestern grain flowed east through New York, and Rochester, Syracuse and Buffalo grew along the route. Tolls repaid the cost of construction, and other states borrowed for canals of their own, several of which failed in the panic of 1837.
events.hook: A 363-mile ditch made New York City the nation's commercial capital.
events.story: Congress refused federal money for the canal in 1817, and New York Governor DeWitt Clinton persuaded the state legislature to pay. Work began at Rome, New York, in July 1817, mostly by hand. The 584 km canal linked the Hudson River at Albany with Lake Erie at Buffalo and opened in October 1825. Freight costs between the Great Lakes and New York fell by about 90 per cent.
events.then: Midwestern grain flowed east through New York, and Rochester, Syracuse and Buffalo grew along the route. Tolls repaid the cost of construction, and other states borrowed for canals of their own, several of which failed in the panic of 1837.
events.now: The canal tied the Midwest's economy to New York rather than New Orleans, which made New York the country's financial centre and aligned the Northwest with the Northeast when the Union split in 1861.
events.fact: Critics called it 'Clinton's Ditch'. Clinton opened it by pouring a keg of Lake Erie water into New York harbour, the 'wedding of the waters'.

q.what: Grain, timber and goods carried by barge.
q.who: New York City merchants and Midwestern farmers.
q.scale: Freight costs fell by about 90%.
q.daily: Towns like Syracuse, Rochester and Buffalo boomed.
q.system: New York City's rise as the nation's commercial capital.

events.bluf: New York Governor DeWitt Clinton wanted the trade of the Midwest for New York after Congress refused to pay for a canal. The state dug 584 km from the Hudson to Lake Erie in eight years and cut freight costs between the Great Lakes and New York by about 90 per cent. New York City became the country's commercial capital, and the Midwest's trade ran east to the Northeast rather than down the Mississippi to the South, a tie that held in 1861.
events.lens: Transport links shape political alliances: the canal bound the Midwest to the North before the Civil War.

events.who: Prince Diponegoro; the Dutch colonial army
events.hook: A Javanese prince led a five-year revolt against Dutch rule.
events.what: A Javanese prince led a five-year revolt against Dutch rule.
events.story: Javanese Prince Diponegoro, an Islamic mystic, rebelled in 1825 after the Dutch built a road across his family's land. The war killed about 200,000 Javanese and 15,000 colonial soldiers. Diponegoro was captured at peace talks in 1830 and exiled.
events.why: Dutch interference in Javanese courts, land and taxes came first. Resentment of tolls and tax farmers gave the revolt its following. Diponegoro's claim to be a just ruler with a religious mission gave it a leader.
events.then: The war's cost pushed the bankrupt Dutch to introduce the Cultivation System in 1830. Diponegoro died in exile in Makassar in 1855.
events.sig: The war's cost pushed the bankrupt Dutch to introduce the Cultivation System in 1830. Diponegoro died in exile in Makassar in 1855.
events.now: The war's cost drove the Dutch to the Cultivation System of 1830 and to direct rule of Java; Diponegoro's revolt is the founding story of Indonesian resistance to Dutch rule.

causes.why: From Batavia, Dutch power spread across Java, increasingly interfering in its royal courts.

q.why: Javanese resistance to Dutch interference in land, taxes and courts.
q.decided: Dutch fortified posts and Diponegoro's betrayal at peace talks.
q.cost: About 200,000 Javanese dead.
q.changed: The Dutch imposed the Cultivation System.

events.bluf: Javanese Prince Diponegoro rose against Dutch interference in Java's courts, land and taxes, claiming a religious mission as a just ruler. Five years of war killed about 200,000 Javanese and 15,000 colonial soldiers before he was captured at peace talks in 1830 and exiled. The cost pushed the bankrupt Dutch to the Cultivation System, and Diponegoro became a hero of Indonesian independence.
events.lens: The cost of crushing a revolt is often passed on to the colonized through harsher extraction.
events.trig: The Dutch built a road across Diponegoro's family land in 1825.
events.fact: Javanese painter Raden Saleh's 1857 picture of Diponegoro's arrest, painted as an answer to a Dutch version of the scene, is a national icon in Indonesia.

toll.n: Most Javanese deaths came from famine and disease.

events.who: Reform-minded Russian army officers; Tsar Nicholas I
events.hook: Liberal army officers tried to stop Nicholas I becoming tsar and were crushed in a day.
events.what: Liberal army officers tried to stop Nicholas I becoming tsar and were crushed in a day.
events.story: Tsar Alexander I died in December 1825, and his brother Constantine, the heir, had secretly renounced the throne in favour of the younger Nicholas. On 26 December 1825, 14 December in Russia's calendar, about 3,000 soldiers led by reformist officers refused to swear loyalty to Nicholas I and gathered on Senate Square in St Petersburg. Cannon fire scattered them. Five leaders, among them poet Kondraty Ryleyev and Colonel Pavel Pestel, were hanged, and more than 100 were exiled to Siberia.
events.why: Officers who had seen Western Europe in the Napoleonic Wars wanted a constitution and an end to serfdom. The confusion over the succession gave them an opening.
events.then: Russian Tsar Nicholas I ruled as a strict autocrat for 30 years, with censorship and the Third Section secret police from 1826. Serfdom lasted until 1861.
events.sig: Russian Tsar Nicholas I ruled as a strict autocrat for 30 years, with censorship and the Third Section secret police from 1826. Serfdom lasted until 1861.
events.now: The revolt fixed Nicholas I's choice of police rule: the Third Section, his secret police, dates from 1826, and the Decembrists' example gave every Russian revolutionary movement to 1917 its founding martyrs.

causes.why: Officers who had marched to Paris came home wanting the reforms the restored order denied them.

q.before: An autocratic tsar, with serfdom intact.
q.how: An attempted military uprising.
q.claim: Constitutional government and an end to serfdom.
q.lasted: The revolt failed, but its ideas lived on.

events.bluf: Reform-minded officers of the Russian guards wanted a constitution and an end to serfdom, and used the confused succession after Tsar Alexander I's death to try to force them. On 26 December 1825 about 3,000 soldiers on Senate Square refused the oath to Nicholas I; cannon scattered them, five leaders were hanged and more than 100 were exiled to Siberia. Russian Tsar Nicholas I ruled as a strict autocrat for 30 years with censorship and a secret police, and the Decembrists became the martyrs of every later Russian revolutionary movement.
events.lens: Failed elite revolts often bring tighter autocracy, pushing opposition underground and toward radicalism.
events.fact: Three of the five ropes broke at the hanging, and the men were hanged a second time.

events.who: Simón Bolívar; Venezuelan leader José Antonio Páez; Ecuador's Juan José Flores
events.what: Union dissolved.
events.why: Regional elites resented rule from Bogotá. Bolívar's attempt at a strong central government, including his dictatorship of 1828, made enemies among liberals.
events.sig: Latin America stayed divided into many states, often ruled by regional strongmen. Panama remained part of Colombia until 1903.
events.hook: Bolívar's dream of one great nation broke into three.
events.story: Gran Colombia, which Venezuelan general Simón Bolívar had built from today's Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama, came apart in 1830. Venezuela under general José Antonio Páez seceded first, then Ecuador under general Juan José Flores. Bolívar resigned in May 1830 and died of tuberculosis on 17 December 1830 at Santa Marta, having written that he had 'ploughed the sea'.
events.then: Latin America stayed divided into many states, often ruled by regional strongmen. Panama remained part of Colombia until 1903.
events.now: The breakup of 1830 fixed Latin America as a set of mid-sized states rather than one union, a fragmentation that left the region weaker beside the United States; Chávez revived 'Bolivarian' unity as a political programme after 1999.

causes.why: Bolívar's victories created Gran Colombia, a union that regional rivalries pulled apart within a decade.

q.before: Bolívar's union of Gran Colombia, ruled from Bogotá.
q.how: Secession by Venezuela and Ecuador.
q.winners: Regional strongmen such as Páez and Flores.
q.lasted: Yes: the three countries have stayed separate.

events.bluf: Venezuelan general Simón Bolívar had built Gran Colombia to hold Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama in one republic strong enough to stand beside the United States. Regional elites resented rule from Bogotá, and in 1830 Venezuela under general José Antonio Páez and then Ecuador under general Juan José Flores seceded; Bolívar resigned and died that December. His large South American republic was finished, and the continent settled into many states run by regional elites and caudillos.
events.lens: Large states assembled in war often fragment in peace, when regional elites no longer need each other.
events.fact: Bolívar survived an assassination attempt in Bogotá in September 1828 by climbing out of a window while his companion Manuela Sáenz held off the attackers.

events.who: King Charles X's France; the Dey of Algiers, Hussein
events.what: French conquest began.
events.why: Charles X wanted a victory to shore up his regime at home. The insult of 1827 supplied the pretext.
events.sig: Conquest took decades against Emir Abd al-Qadir and others, with massacres and land confiscations. Algeria was divided into French departments, and European settlers took the best land.
events.hook: France invaded Algeria and began 132 years of colonial rule.
events.story: In 1827 Hussein, the Dey of Algiers, struck the French consul with a fly-whisk during a dispute over debts. French King Charles X used the incident as grounds for invasion. French troops landed in June 1830 and took Algiers in July. Conquering the interior took decades against resistance led by Emir Abd al-Qadir.
events.then: Conquest took decades against Emir Abd al-Qadir and others, with massacres and land confiscations. Algeria was divided into French departments, and European settlers took the best land.
events.now: The settler colony France built after 1830 made Algerian independence a war rather than a negotiation. The 1954-62 war still shapes French-Algerian relations.

q.why: Royal prestige, debts owed by France, and a diplomatic insult as pretext.
q.decided: French military power over decades of brutal campaigning.
q.cost: Hundreds of thousands of Algerians died in the conquest.
q.changed: Algeria became a French settler colony for 132 years.

events.bluf: French King Charles X sent an army to Algiers to win military prestige for an unpopular regime, using a three-year-old diplomatic insult as the pretext. Algiers fell in July 1830 and Charles fell three weeks later. France stayed for 132 years, made Algeria legally part of France and settled it with about a million Europeans, which made its war of independence one of the bloodiest of decolonisation.
events.lens: Settler colonies are the hardest to decolonize, because the settlers become a political force of their own.
events.fact: Charles X was overthrown in Paris three weeks after his army took Algiers.

events.what: Authorized forcing Native nations west of the Mississippi.
events.why: Cotton planters wanted the Black Belt lands of Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi. Gold in Cherokee Georgia brought thousands of prospectors. Jackson and the Southern states denied that tribes could be sovereign nations within state borders.
events.sig: About 60,000 Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole people were removed in the 1830s, and thousands died on the journeys, most notoriously on the Cherokee 'Trail of Tears' of 1838. The Seminole fought removal in Florida for seven years from 1835.
events.hook: Congress authorized forcing entire Native nations out of the Southeast.
events.story: Georgia extended its laws over Cherokee territory in 1828 after gold was found there, and the other Southern states followed. US President Andrew Jackson asked Congress for a removal law. The Indian Removal Act passed the House by 102 votes to 97 and Jackson signed it on 28 May 1830. It authorised the president to exchange land west of the Mississippi for tribal lands in the East by treaty. The Choctaw signed first, at Dancing Rabbit Creek in September 1830.
events.then: About 60,000 Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole people were removed in the 1830s, and thousands died on the journeys, most notoriously on the Cherokee 'Trail of Tears' of 1838. The Seminole fought removal in Florida for seven years from 1835.
events.now: Removal made dispossession federal policy and set the precedent that treaty rights yield to settler demand; the term ethnic cleansing is now widely applied to it, and it underlies today's disputes over Native sovereignty and land.

causes.why: The war destroyed Tecumseh's confederacy and the Creek resistance, and made Andrew Jackson a national hero. As president, he pushed removal through Congress.

q.before: The Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole governed their own lands under treaties.
q.how: A law authorising removal treaties, enforced by the army.
q.claim: That Native nations could not remain inside the states.
q.lasted: Yes: most Southeastern nations were forced west.

events.bluf: US President Andrew Jackson and the Southern states wanted the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole off lands prized for cotton and, in Georgia, gold. Congress authorised removal by treaty in 1830, and the treaties were obtained by pressure, fraud and force. Dispossession became federal policy, the Supreme Court's recognition of tribal sovereignty in 1832 went unenforced, and about 60,000 people were moved west in the 1830s.
events.lens: When economic interest and political power align against a minority, legal protections alone rarely save it.
events.fact: Tennessee Congressman Davy Crockett voted against the act and lost his seat the next year; he died at the Alamo six years later.

kv: Native people forced west in the 1830s

events.h: Dutch impose the Cultivation System on Java
events.hook: The Dutch forced Javanese villages to grow export crops for the colonial state.
events.what: The Dutch forced Javanese villages to grow export crops for the colonial state.
events.story: Dutch Governor-General Johannes van den Bosch introduced the Cultivation System in 1830. Villages had to set aside a share of their land, often a fifth, to grow sugar, coffee or indigo for the government at fixed prices. Profits paid off Dutch debts and built Dutch railways. Famine hit some regions of Java in the 1840s.
events.why: The Netherlands was nearly bankrupt after the Java War and Belgium's breakaway in 1830.
events.then: The Dutch novel 'Max Havelaar' of 1860 exposed the system's abuses. The system was wound down from 1870 in favour of private plantations.
events.sig: The Dutch novel 'Max Havelaar' of 1860 exposed the system's abuses. The system was wound down from 1870 in favour of private plantations.
events.now: The system made Java the most profitable colony in the world and paid for the Dutch state's debts and railways, at the cost of Javanese famine; its exposure forced a reform of colonial policy and gave Indonesian nationalism its first grievance.

causes.why: The war's huge cost, on top of Belgium's breakaway, pushed the near-bankrupt Dutch to squeeze more from Java.
Losing Belgium cut Dutch revenues just as the Java War ended, adding pressure to make the colony pay.

q.what: Sugar, coffee and indigo grown by Javanese villagers for the government.
q.who: The Dutch treasury gained enormously; Javanese peasants paid.
q.scale: Colonial profits came to supply a large share of the Dutch state budget.
q.daily: Villagers worked government crops instead of rice, and famine struck some areas.
q.system: An extractive colony that funded its mother country.

events.bluf: Dutch Governor-General Johannes van den Bosch set out to make Java pay for a Netherlands left near bankruptcy by the Java War and Belgium's breakaway. From 1830 villages had to set aside a share of their land, often a fifth, to grow sugar, coffee or indigo for the state at fixed prices. Java became the most profitable colony in the world and paid for Dutch debts and railways, at the cost of famine in parts of Java in the 1840s, and its exposure gave Indonesian nationalism its first grievance.
events.lens: Colonial profit often came from forced production, not trade.
events.fact: 'Max Havelaar', the 1860 novel that exposed it, gave its name to a fair-trade label.

kv: of village land set aside for export crops
of Dutch government revenue in the 1850s

events.who: Parisian crowds; King Charles X; Louis-Philippe
events.hook: Three days of street fighting in Paris overthrew the last Bourbon king.
events.what: Three days of street fighting in Paris overthrew the last Bourbon king.
events.story: French King Charles X, on the throne since 1824, issued four ordinances on 25 July 1830 that dissolved the newly elected chamber, restricted the vote and muzzled the press. Parisians built barricades and fought the troops from 27 to 29 July, the 'Three Glorious Days'. Charles fled to England. The liberal Duke of Orléans became Louis-Philippe, 'King of the French', on 9 August.
events.why: Charles X tried to restore royal absolutism after liberals won the elections of 1830. Unemployment and dear bread in Paris supplied the crowds.
events.then: Belgium rose in August 1830, Poland in November and Italy in 1831. Louis-Philippe's regime rested on the bankers and businessmen who were the only people with the vote.
events.sig: Belgium rose in August 1830, Poland in November and Italy in 1831. Louis-Philippe's regime rested on the bankers and businessmen who were the only people with the vote.
events.now: It showed a revolution could change a regime without ending monarchy; Delacroix's 'Liberty Leading the People' became an emblem of democratic revolution.

causes.why: Vienna restored the Bourbon kings in France; in 1830 Parisians overthrew them for good.

q.before: Charles X, who wanted to restore royal power.
q.how: Three days of street fighting in Paris.
q.claim: The constitutional charter and popular sovereignty.
q.winners: The liberal middle class and Louis-Philippe.
q.lasted: Louis-Philippe ruled until the next revolution, in 1848.

events.bluf: French King Charles X issued ordinances in July 1830 dissolving the chamber, cutting the electorate and muzzling the press to restore royal authority; Parisians built barricades to stop him. After three days of fighting he fled, and the liberal Duke of Orléans took the throne as Louis-Philippe, 'King of the French'. The Vienna settlement had failed to freeze Europe, and revolts followed in Belgium, Poland and Italy within months.
events.lens: Attempts to roll back political gains often provoke the revolution they were meant to prevent.
events.fact: Charles X was the last king of France crowned at Reims, in 1825.

events.who: Belgian liberals and Catholics; the Dutch King William I
events.hook: A riot after an opera in Brussels launched Belgium's independence.
events.what: A riot after an opera in Brussels launched Belgium's independence.
events.story: The Congress of Vienna had joined Belgium to the Netherlands under Dutch King William I. On 25 August 1830 a performance of the opera 'La Muette de Portici' in Brussels ended in riot, and revolt spread across the south. Dutch troops failed to retake Brussels in September, and a provisional government declared independence in October. The great powers recognised Belgium at the London Conference of 1831, Leopold of Saxe-Coburg became king, and in 1839 the Treaty of London guaranteed its neutrality.
events.why: Catholic, largely French-speaking Belgians resented the Protestant king, rules favouring the Dutch language, and taxes and policies that served the north. The July Revolution in Paris a month earlier showed a king could be removed.
events.then: The 1839 guarantee was the 'scrap of paper' that brought Britain into war when Germany invaded Belgium in 1914.
