events.sig: The 1839 guarantee was the 'scrap of paper' that brought Britain into war when Germany invaded Belgium in 1914.
events.now: The 1839 guarantee of neutrality made Belgium the trigger of Britain's entry into the war of 1914; the divide between Dutch and French speakers that the new state inherited still shapes its politics.

causes.why: Vienna joined Belgium to the Netherlands under a Dutch king; in 1830 the Belgians broke away.
News of the Paris revolution helped spark the Brussels uprising a month later.

q.before: The Dutch King William I ruled the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.
q.how: Uprising, then recognition by the great powers.
q.winners: Belgium, with a new king, Leopold I.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Catholic and largely French-speaking Belgians wanted out of the Protestant, Dutch-run kingdom the Congress of Vienna had created; Dutch King William I wanted it kept by force. A riot after an opera in Brussels in August 1830 spread into revolt, the Dutch army failed to retake the city in September, and the great powers recognised Belgian independence and in 1839 guaranteed its neutrality. The map of 1815 had been changed by revolt and accepted by the powers, and the guarantee brought Britain into war in 1914.
events.lens: Guarantees of a small state's neutrality can become triggers for great-power war.
events.fact: The revolt began in the opera house during a duet about love of country.

events.hook: The first intercity railway with timetabled passenger trains pulled entirely by steam opened.
events.what: The first intercity railway with timetabled passenger trains pulled entirely by steam opened.
events.story: The line opened on 15 September 1830 with Prime Minister the Duke of Wellington aboard. At Parkside the Liverpool MP William Huskisson stepped onto the track and was struck by the Stephensons' Rocket; he died that evening, one of the first railway deaths. Within months the line was carrying hundreds of thousands of passengers a year.
events.why: Manchester's cotton mills needed fast, cheap links to the port of Liverpool. The canals charged monopoly rates.
events.then: Britain's 'railway mania' of the 1840s followed, as investors poured money into thousands of miles of track.
events.sig: Britain's 'railway mania' of the 1840s followed, as investors poured money into thousands of miles of track.
events.now: Stephenson's track gauge of 4 ft 8½ in became the world standard, a classic case of an early technical choice locking in for centuries.

causes.why: The Stephensons built on the Stockton and Darlington line.

q.problem: Moving cotton and people quickly between port and mills.
q.how: Steam locomotives on iron rails; the Rocket had won trials in 1829.
q.replaced: Canals and horse-drawn coaches.
q.spread: Railways spread across Europe and America within 20 years.
q.next: Railway mania and a revolution in travel.

events.bluf: Manchester's cotton mills and Liverpool's merchants wanted a fast, cheap link between the port and the mills to break the canal companies' hold. The line that engineers George and Robert Stephenson built opened on 15 September 1830 with timetabled steam trains for passengers and freight, the first modern intercity railway. It carried hundreds of thousands of passengers in its first year, proved that railways could pay, and set off the railway booms of Britain and the world.
events.lens: One successful demonstration can trigger an investment boom.
events.fact: The Rocket won the Rainhill Trials of 1829, held to decide whether locomotives or fixed engines would work the line.

kv: top speed of Stephenson's Rocket at the 1829 trials

events.hook: A strike by enslaved Jamaicans became a huge uprising that hastened the end of slavery in the British Empire.
events.what: A strike by enslaved Jamaicans became a huge uprising that hastened the end of slavery in the British Empire.
events.story: Enslaved Jamaicans believed that freedom had been granted in London and withheld by the planters. Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe planned a peaceful strike after Christmas 1831, and tens of thousands joined. It turned into a revolt across the western parishes. Fourteen white people and about 200 rebels died in the fighting, and over 300 more were executed afterwards, Sharpe among them, in May 1832.
events.why: Rumours that freedom had already been granted in London came first. Conditions on the sugar estates supplied the grievance.
events.then: Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833. Slave owners received £20 million in compensation; the formerly enslaved got nothing and had to work years of unpaid 'apprenticeship', which ended in 1838.
events.sig: Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833. Slave owners received £20 million in compensation; the formerly enslaved got nothing and had to work years of unpaid 'apprenticeship', which ended in 1838.
events.now: The rising, and the planters' reprisals against Baptist missionaries that followed, shifted British opinion in 1832 and brought the Abolition Act of 1833, which freed some 800,000 people across the empire from 1834.

causes.why: With the trade banned, enslaved Jamaicans pressed for freedom itself.

q.why: Enslaved Jamaicans demanded freedom and wages.
q.stakes: Freedom for over 300,000 enslaved people in Jamaica.
q.decided: British troops and militia crushed the revolt.
q.cost: Hundreds of enslaved people killed or executed.
q.changed: It convinced Parliament that slavery could no longer be held in place.

events.bluf: Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe organised the enslaved of western Jamaica to withhold their labour after Christmas 1831 until they were paid wages, on the belief that freedom had already been granted in London. The strike became the largest slave rising in the British Caribbean and was crushed in weeks, with about 200 rebels killed and over 300 executed, Sharpe among them. The rising and its suppression convinced Parliament that slavery could be held only by constant force, and the Abolition Act followed in 1833.
events.lens: Resistance by the oppressed changes the calculations of distant lawmakers.
events.fact: Sharpe is reported to have said on the gallows that he would rather die than live in slavery; he is a National Hero of Jamaica and appears on the $50 note.

events.hook: A young naturalist joined a five-year survey voyage whose observations led to the theory of evolution.
events.what: A young naturalist joined a five-year survey voyage whose observations led to the theory of evolution.
events.story: HMS Beagle left Plymouth on 27 December 1831 under British naval captain Robert FitzRoy to chart South America's coasts. English naturalist Charles Darwin, aged 22, collected fossils and specimens along the way. In the Galápagos in 1835 he noticed that mockingbirds differed from island to island. The ship returned in October 1836.
events.why: FitzRoy wanted a gentleman companion and naturalist for the long voyage. Darwin's Cambridge tutor John Stevens Henslow recommended him.
events.then: Darwin opened his notebooks on the 'transmutation' of species in 1837 and published 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859.
events.sig: Darwin opened his notebooks on the 'transmutation' of species in 1837 and published 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859.
events.now: Darwin's observations of 1831-36 led to 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859, which made common descent the organising idea of biology; the Galápagos remain its living laboratory and a test of conservation.

q.problem: Why do living things differ from place to place?
q.how: Years of collecting and comparing specimens.
q.replaced: The belief that species were created fixed and unchanging.
q.spread: His journal of the voyage was a bestseller in 1839.
q.next: On the Origin of Species.

events.bluf: British naval captain Robert FitzRoy wanted a gentleman naturalist for a survey of South America's coasts, and 22-year-old Charles Darwin took the place. Five years of fossils, geology and island species gave Darwin the observations from which he built the theory of evolution by natural selection. The voyage shows how imperial survey work produced science, and it produced the idea that reorganised biology.
events.lens: Breakthroughs often come from comparing variation across places.
events.fact: FitzRoy nearly rejected Darwin because of the shape of his nose, which he read as a sign of weak character.

events.who: Chief Justice John Marshall; missionary Samuel Worcester; the Cherokee Nation
events.hook: The Supreme Court ruled that Georgia had no power over the Cherokee Nation, and President Jackson ignored it.
events.what: The Supreme Court ruled that Georgia had no power over the Cherokee Nation, and President Jackson ignored it.
events.story: Georgia had extended its laws over Cherokee territory after gold was found there and required white residents to hold a state licence. Missionary Samuel Worcester refused, was convicted and was sentenced to four years' hard labour. On 3 March 1832 Chief Justice John Marshall ruled for the Supreme Court that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community in which Georgia's laws had no force, and that relations with it belonged to the federal government alone. Georgia refused to release Worcester.
events.why: Georgia wanted the land and the gold, and held that no sovereign nation could exist inside a state. The Cherokee had adopted a written constitution in 1827 and chose law over war.
events.then: Worcester was released in 1833 in exchange for dropping further appeals. In December 1835 a faction of about 20 Cherokee signed the Treaty of New Echota ceding all the nation's eastern land, over the protest of Principal Chief John Ross and a petition signed by more than 15,000 Cherokee. The treaty was used to force the whole nation west in 1838.
events.sig: Worcester was released in 1833 in exchange for dropping further appeals. In December 1835 a faction of about 20 Cherokee signed the Treaty of New Echota ceding all the nation's eastern land, over the protest of Principal Chief John Ross and a petition signed by more than 15,000 Cherokee. The treaty was used to force the whole nation west in 1838.
events.now: The ruling remains a foundation of tribal sovereignty in US law and is still cited in cases over tribal jurisdiction.

causes.why: Georgia's attempt to rule Cherokee land under removal policy reached the Supreme Court.

events.myth: Jackson said 'John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it'. The line first appears decades later; what he did was decline to act, which had the same effect.

q.before: The Cherokee governed themselves under treaties with the United States.
q.how: A Supreme Court decision.
q.claim: Native nations' sovereignty under federal treaties.
q.winners: On paper the Cherokee; in practice Georgia.
q.lasted: The legal principle did; Cherokee land in Georgia did not.

events.bluf: Georgia wanted Cherokee land and had extended its laws over the Cherokee Nation; the Cherokee and their missionary allies went to the Supreme Court to stop it. Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Cherokee were a distinct political community in which Georgia's laws had no force. Georgia ignored the ruling and President Andrew Jackson declined to enforce it, which showed that a court's judgment binds only where the executive will act; the Cherokee were removed by force six years later.
events.lens: Courts have no armies: their rulings depend on others to enforce them.
events.fact: Worcester had helped Cherokee editor Elias Boudinot set up the Cherokee Phoenix, the first Native American newspaper, in 1828.

events.who: Parliament; Prime Minister Earl Grey; abolitionists including Thomas Fowell Buxton
events.what: Slavery outlawed; owners compensated.
events.why: Decades of abolitionist campaigning came first. The Jamaican revolt of 1831 showed the cost of holding on. The reformed Parliament of 1832 had fewer seats in the planters' hands.
events.sig: Protests ended apprenticeship early, in 1838, and Caribbean sugar declined. Britain used its navy and diplomacy to press other countries to end slavery, and the owners' compensation was invested in Britain.
events.hook: Britain freed about 800,000 enslaved people across its empire.
events.story: A revolt of tens of thousands of enslaved people in Jamaica at Christmas 1831, led by Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe, was crushed with hundreds of executions. The reformed Parliament elected in 1832 passed the Slavery Abolition Act in August 1833 under Prime Minister Earl Grey. It paid £20 million, about 40 per cent of the national budget, to slave owners and nothing to the enslaved. Freedom came on 1 August 1834 with a period of apprenticeship.
events.then: Protests ended apprenticeship early, in 1838, and Caribbean sugar declined. Britain used its navy and diplomacy to press other countries to end slavery, and the owners' compensation was invested in Britain.
events.now: British taxpayers finished repaying the loan for that compensation only in 2015, and Caribbean governments cite this history in their demands for reparations.

causes.why: Ending the trade did not end slavery itself. That took 26 more years, a mass petition campaign and a huge revolt in Jamaica in 1831.
The Jamaican uprising convinced Parliament slavery could not last.

q.before: About 800,000 people were enslaved in British colonies.
q.how: An act of Parliament, with compensation paid to slave owners.
q.winners: The enslaved, after years of forced 'apprenticeship'; owners got £20 million.
q.lasted: Yes: full freedom came in 1838.

events.bluf: Abolitionists led in the Commons by MP Thomas Fowell Buxton wanted slavery ended across the empire; Prime Minister Earl Grey's Whig government wanted it done without ruining the planters. The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 freed about 800,000 people from 1 August 1834, paid £20 million, about 40 per cent of the national budget, to the owners, and bound the freed to years of unpaid 'apprenticeship'. The world's leading power became an opponent of slavery, and the terms of its abolition remain a grievance.
events.lens: Abolition can be negotiated to protect those who profited: who gets compensated shows where power lies.
events.fact: The £20 million was raised by a loan from banker Nathan Rothschild and his brother-in-law Moses Montefiore.

kv: enslaved people freed across the empire
paid to slave owners, ~40% of the government's yearly budget
the loans raised to pay owners were finally paid off

events.hook: Britain banned textile mills from employing children under nine and appointed inspectors to enforce it.
events.what: Britain banned textile mills from employing children under nine and appointed inspectors to enforce it.
events.story: A parliamentary committee of 1832 under Tory MP Michael Sadler took evidence of children working 12 to 16 hours a day in mills. Tory MP Lord Ashley took up the ten-hour bill after Sadler lost his seat. The Act of 1833 banned children under 9 from textile mills, limited 9- to 13-year-olds to 9 hours a day and 13- to 18-year-olds to 12, required schooling for the younger children, and created the first factory inspectors.
events.why: The inquiries exposed the hours children worked. Evangelical reformers and the workers' short-time committees campaigned for limits.
events.then: The Ten Hours Act of 1847 extended protection to women and young people. Factory regulation spread to other industrial countries.
events.sig: The Ten Hours Act of 1847 extended protection to women and young people. Factory regulation spread to other industrial countries.
events.now: Factory inspection became a model for workplace regulation around the world.

causes.why: Mills relied on child labour, which reformers set out to limit.

q.before: Mill owners set hours as they pleased.
q.how: An act of Parliament, enforced by inspectors.
q.claim: Protecting children who could not protect themselves.
q.lasted: Yes: it was strengthened many times.

events.bluf: Evangelical reformers led by Tory MP Lord Ashley and the factory workers' short-time committees wanted a ten-hour day for all mill workers; the Whig government offered a narrower law. The Factory Act of 1833 banned children under 9 from textile mills, limited 9- to 13-year-olds to 9 hours a day and 13- to 18-year-olds to 12, and created inspectors to enforce it. The state had begun to regulate industrial work to protect the vulnerable, and factory inspection became the model for workplace regulation worldwide.
events.lens: Regulation means little without enforcement; inspectors made this law different.
events.fact: Four inspectors were appointed to cover every textile mill in Britain.

kv: minimum working age in textile mills

events.who: Prussian finance minister Friedrich von Motz (d. 1830); the governments of Prussia, Bavaria, Württemberg, Saxony and the Thuringian states
events.hook: Eighteen German states joined a Prussian-led customs union, uniting the German economy thirty-seven years before Prussia united the German state.
events.what: Eighteen German states joined a Prussian-led customs union, uniting the German economy thirty-seven years before Prussia united the German state.
events.story: On 1 January 1834 the Zollverein came into force, abolishing internal tariffs among eighteen states with about 23 million people. Prussia had built it by absorbing the small states inside its borders after 1818 and then outbidding Austria, which stayed out. Goods moved on one tariff; railways, which began in Germany the following year, followed the customs lines.
events.why: Prussia's lands after 1815 lay in two blocks with small states between them, so its 1818 tariff needed neighbours inside it. Austria's protected industries could not survive a common tariff, so Vienna stayed out.
events.then: Austria's attempts to join in 1849-53 failed. By the 1860s the member states traded mainly with Prussia, and the union survived the Austro-Prussian war of 1866 intact.
events.sig: Austria's attempts to join in 1849-53 failed. By the 1860s the member states traded mainly with Prussia, and the union survived the Austro-Prussian war of 1866 intact.
events.now: It is the standard case for economic integration preceding political union, cited in accounts of the EEC's founding and in arguments about whether a currency union needs a state.

q.before: Thirty-nine German states, each with its own tariffs; a cart from Hamburg to Austria paid duty ten times.
q.how: A treaty on one external tariff, with revenue shared by population.
q.claim: Prussia's: a German market without Austria.
q.winners: Prussian industry and the Prussian treasury.
q.lasted: Until 1919 in form; its map became the Empire's.

events.bluf: Prussian Finance Minister Friedrich von Motz set out to join Prussia's two blocks of territory under one tariff and to draw the small states between them into it, with Austria kept out. The Zollverein came into force on 1 January 1834 with eighteen states and about 23 million people trading on one external tariff. The German economy was united under Prussia thirty-seven years before the German state, and the union decided which of the two German powers would do the uniting.
events.trig: The treaty took effect on 1 January 1834, joining eighteen states and about 23 million people under one external tariff.
events.lens: Markets decided the German question before armies did.
events.fact: The Zollverein issued a common silver coin, the Vereinsthaler, from 1857.

events.what: Boers moved inland to escape British rule.
events.why: Anger at British rule came first: the abolition of slavery in 1834 with what Boers saw as inadequate compensation. Anglicisation of courts and schools and British frontier policy toward the Xhosa added to it.
events.sig: Britain annexed Natal in 1843. It recognised the Transvaal and the Orange Free State in the 1850s and conquered them in the Boer War of 1899-1902.
events.hook: Dutch-speaking settlers trekked inland to escape British rule.
events.story: From 1835 thousands of Boers loaded their families into ox-wagons and moved north and east beyond British rule. They fought the Ndebele and, at Blood River in December 1838, the Zulu. They founded republics in Natal, the Orange Free State and the Transvaal.
events.then: Britain annexed Natal in 1843. It recognised the Transvaal and the Orange Free State in the 1850s and conquered them in the Boer War of 1899-1902.
events.now: The Trek created the Boer republics Britain conquered in 1899-1902 and the founding story Afrikaner nationalism used from the 1930s to justify apartheid; the centenary celebrations of 1938 launched the movement that won power in 1948.

causes.why: British rule, new laws on land and labour and the abolition of slavery drove thousands of Boers north.
Emancipation, with compensation paid only in London, was a leading grievance of the trekkers.
Shaka's wars and the upheavals often called the Mfecane, a concept historians now debate, reshaped the interior the trekkers moved into.

q.before: Britain ruled the Cape; African kingdoms ruled the interior.
q.how: Mass migration and conquest.
q.claim: The Boers' wish to govern themselves, including their racial order.
q.winners: The Boer republics; African peoples lost land.
q.lasted: The republics lasted until the Boer War of 1899-1902.

events.bluf: Thousands of Boers, Dutch-speaking farmers of the Cape, left British rule from 1835 to escape its abolition of slavery, its English-language administration and its frontier policy. They crossed into the interior in ox-wagons, fought the Ndebele and the Zulu, and founded republics in Natal, the Orange Free State and the Transvaal. The Trek became the founding story of Afrikaner nationalism, and the republics it created were the ground of the Boer War and the ideology of apartheid.
events.lens: Groups that leave to escape a state's reforms often build societies that entrench what was reformed.
events.fact: Zulu King Dingane killed trek leader Piet Retief and his party in February 1838 after signing a land treaty with them. The Boers' vow before Blood River gave 16 December a public holiday that was renamed the Day of Reconciliation in 1995.

events.who: Antonio López de Santa Anna; Texan defenders including Jim Bowie and Davy Crockett
events.hook: Mexican troops stormed a mission held by Texan rebels, killing nearly all the defenders.
events.what: Mexican troops stormed a mission held by Texan rebels, killing nearly all the defenders.
events.story: Texan rebels had seized San Antonio in December 1835. Mexican President Antonio López de Santa Anna arrived in February 1836 and besieged the Alamo mission, held by about 200 men under Texan commanders William Travis and Jim Bowie, with former Tennessee congressman Davy Crockett among them. On 6 March 1836, after a 13-day siege, his troops stormed the walls and killed the defenders. Six weeks later, on 21 April, Texan commander Sam Houston's army defeated and captured Santa Anna at San Jacinto, shouting 'Remember the Alamo!'.
events.why: Santa Anna had scrapped Mexico's federal constitution of 1824 and centralised power, which several Mexican states resisted. The American settlers also wanted to keep slaves, which Mexican law restricted.
events.then: Texas declared independence on 2 March 1836, during the siege. Santa Anna signed the Treaties of Velasco in May recognising it, and Mexico repudiated them. The republic was annexed by the United States in 1845.
events.sig: Texas declared independence on 2 March 1836, during the siege. Santa Anna signed the Treaties of Velasco in May recognising it, and Mexico repudiated them. The republic was annexed by the United States in 1845.
events.now: The Alamo remains a contested symbol: one reading holds it as a sacrifice for liberty, the other holds the revolt as partly a fight to keep slavery, which Mexico had abolished in 1829, and the argument shapes how Texas teaches its Mexican past.

q.why: Texan settlers rebelled against Mexico's government.
q.stakes: Whether Texas would stay part of Mexico.
q.decided: Overwhelming Mexican numbers.
q.cost: About 200 defenders and hundreds of Mexican soldiers killed or wounded.
q.changed: The memory of the Alamo rallied Texans to win independence weeks later.

events.bluf: Mexican President Antonio López de Santa Anna marched north to crush a revolt by American settlers in Texas who rejected his centralised rule and Mexico's limits on slavery. He stormed the Alamo after 13 days and killed its roughly 200 defenders. The deaths gave the Texan army its battle cry, and six weeks later Santa Anna was a prisoner; an independent Texas, its annexation in 1845 and the war with Mexico of 1846 followed.
events.lens: Defeats can mobilize more than victories when they become martyrdom stories.
events.fact: Davy Crockett, a three-term congressman, went to Texas after losing his seat and telling his voters they could go to hell.

events.what: ~4,000 Cherokee died on the forced march.
events.why: Georgia had already distributed Cherokee land to white settlers by lottery in 1832. The treaty gave the army a legal basis, and Principal Chief John Ross's petitions to Congress failed.
events.sig: Around 4,000 Cherokee died in the camps and on the march. The nation re-established its government at Tahlequah in 1839, and the signers of the New Echota treaty, including Major Ridge and Elias Boudinot, were killed by other Cherokee that June.
events.hook: The Cherokee won in court and were marched west anyway.
events.story: The Supreme Court had ruled in 1832 that Georgia's laws had no force in Cherokee territory, and President Andrew Jackson declined to enforce it. The Treaty of New Echota of 1835, signed by a minority faction, set May 1838 as the deadline for removal. In May 1838 General Winfield Scott's troops rounded up about 16,000 Cherokee into stockades. Most were marched west in detachments through the autumn and winter of 1838-39 to Indian Territory, now Oklahoma.
events.then: Around 4,000 Cherokee died in the camps and on the march. The nation re-established its government at Tahlequah in 1839, and the signers of the New Echota treaty, including Major Ridge and Elias Boudinot, were killed by other Cherokee that June.
events.now: The Cherokee rebuilt a government in Oklahoma and are today one of the largest Native nations in the United States; the removal is the reference case in every dispute over treaty rights and federal obligations to tribes.
events.fact: The Cherokee had won their case at the Supreme Court in 1832; Jackson ignored the ruling.

causes.why: Under the act, the army forced the Cherokee west in 1838; about 4,000 of some 16,000 died.
Jackson ignored the ruling, and the Cherokee were forced west.

q.why: Georgia and the federal government wanted Cherokee land.
q.stakes: Cherokee survival as a nation in their homeland.
q.decided: The US Army enforcing a disputed treaty.
q.cost: About 4,000 Cherokee died.
q.changed: The Cherokee rebuilt their nation in Indian Territory.

events.bluf: The federal government, under President Martin Van Buren, set out to enforce the Treaty of New Echota and move the Cherokee Nation west of the Mississippi by the deadline of May 1838. The army rounded up about 16,000 people into camps and marched them to Indian Territory; around 4,000 died of disease, cold and hunger. The removal completed the dispossession of the Southeast's nations and became the defining case of a treaty right overridden by settler demand.
events.lens: Legal victories cannot protect a group that lacks political power.

kv: died in the camps and on the march

events.who: Stockmen led by John Fleming; the Wirrayaraay people
events.hook: Colonists massacred at least 28 Aboriginal people, and for the first time seven of the killers were hanged.
events.what: Colonists massacred at least 28 Aboriginal people, and for the first time seven of the killers were hanged.
events.story: Squatters were pushing sheep and cattle onto Aboriginal land in the Gwydir valley. On 10 June 1838 a party of about a dozen stockmen led by John Fleming tied up and killed about 28 Wirrayaraay people, mostly women, children and old men, at Myall Creek station and burned the bodies. New South Wales Governor George Gipps insisted on prosecution; a first jury acquitted the men and a second convicted seven, who were hanged in December 1838. Fleming escaped and was never tried.
events.why: Frontier violence spread with the pastoral expansion of the 1830s. Gipps and Attorney-General John Plunkett wanted a case that would show the law applied to everyone.
events.then: Colonists' outrage at the hangings made later prosecutions rare, and later massacres were covered up. One count, a map of frontier massacres compiled between 2017 and 2022, records more than 400 sites and more than 10,000 Aboriginal dead between 1788 and 1930; critics of the count hold that many entries rest on single or second-hand accounts and that the evidence supports a far lower figure.
events.sig: Colonists' outrage at the hangings made later prosecutions rare, and later massacres were covered up. One count, a map of frontier massacres compiled between 2017 and 2022, records more than 400 sites and more than 10,000 Aboriginal dead between 1788 and 1930; critics of the count hold that many entries rest on single or second-hand accounts and that the evidence supports a far lower figure.
events.now: Myall Creek fixed the rule that Aboriginal people were protected by law in principle and taught the frontier to kill out of sight in practice; the count of later massacres is still argued, and the argument is part of Australian politics.

causes.why: As settlers spread across Aboriginal land for sheep and cattle, frontier violence spread with them.

q.why: Settlers waged a frontier war for Aboriginal land.
q.stakes: Whether colonists would be punished for killing Aboriginal people.
q.decided: A second trial and hangings, unusual for the time.
q.cost: At least 28 Wirrayaraay people killed.
q.changed: Later massacres were more often hidden.

events.bluf: New South Wales Governor George Gipps set out to show that the law protected Aboriginal people after stockmen murdered about 28 Wirrayaraay people at Myall Creek in June 1838. Seven of the killers were convicted and hanged, the only such hangings on the Australian frontier. Colonists' outrage at the verdict taught later killers to leave no witnesses, and the massacres that followed went unpunished and largely unrecorded.
events.lens: Prosecuting atrocities can provoke a backlash that makes future accountability harder.
events.fact: Descendants of the victims and of the perpetrators built a memorial at the site together in 2000.

kv: white men hanged, a first in the colony

events.who: Britain vs. Qing China; Commissioner Lin Zexu
events.what: Britain attacked China.
events.why: Britain bought large quantities of tea while China wanted few British goods, and Britain closed the gap with opium. China tried to suppress the drug trade. Britain also demanded diplomatic equality and open trade.
events.sig: The Treaty of Nanjing in 1842 ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports and imposed an indemnity; later treaties exempted foreigners from Chinese law. Opium imports kept growing, and a Second Opium War in 1856-60 forced further concessions.
events.hook: Britain went to war to keep selling drugs to China.
events.story: The East India Company grew opium in India and smuggled it into China to pay for tea. By the 1830s millions of Chinese were addicted and silver was flowing out. In 1839 Qing Commissioner Lin Zexu seized and destroyed about 20,000 chests of opium at Canton. British Foreign Secretary Lord Palmerston sent warships, which outgunned Chinese forces along the coast and up the Yangtze.
events.then: The Treaty of Nanjing in 1842 ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports and imposed an indemnity; later treaties exempted foreigners from Chinese law. Opium imports kept growing, and a Second Opium War in 1856-60 forced further concessions.
events.now: China calls this the start of its 'century of humiliation', a theme that frames its politics and its foreign policy today.
events.fact: Commissioner Lin Zexu wrote to Queen Victoria asking how Britain would feel if China sold poison to its people. The letter probably never reached her.

sites.d: Only port open to Westerners; Lin destroyed the opium here.
Ceded to Britain in 1842.
Treaty signed aboard a British warship.

causes.why: Britain bought vast amounts of Chinese tea but could sell China little except smuggled Indian opium. When the Qing cracked down on the drug, Britain went to war.

q.why: China destroyed British opium; Britain demanded compensation and open trade.
q.stakes: China's right to control its trade, and Britain's opium profits.
q.decided: British steam warships and modern guns.
q.cost: Thousands of Chinese soldiers killed.
q.changed: China signed the first unequal treaty and gave up Hong Kong.

events.bluf: Britain went to war in 1839 to protect the opium trade that paid for its tea and to force China open to Western commerce on Western terms. Its warships outgunned Qing forces along the coast and up the Yangtze. China lost the ability to set the terms of its foreign relations, and the 'century of humiliation' that Chinese nationalism still invokes began with the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842.
events.trig: Commissioner Lin Zexu's destruction of British opium at Canton in 1839.
events.lens: Trade imbalances can turn into wars when one side uses force to fix them.

kv: chests of opium a year reaching China by 1838
silver dollars China had to pay

events.what: Westernizing legal and military reforms.
events.why: Egypt's armies had shown that the old state could lose to a province. The reformers needed European support and a stronger state to survive.
events.sig: The reforms built a modern bureaucracy and angered Muslims who lost their privileged status. They failed to stop nationalist breakaways or the empire's growing debts to Europe.
events.hook: The Ottoman Empire tried to modernize to survive.
events.story: Muhammad Ali's Egypt had nearly toppled the sultan in 1839 and the empire needed European backing. On 3 November 1839 the 16-year-old Ottoman Sultan Abdülmecid I issued the Edict of Gülhane, drafted by Foreign Minister Mustafa Reşid Pasha, promising all subjects, Muslim and non-Muslim, security of life and property and fair taxation. Over the following decades the Tanzimat, 'reorganisation', reformed the army, courts, schools and administration along European lines.
events.then: The reforms built a modern bureaucracy and angered Muslims who lost their privileged status. They failed to stop nationalist breakaways or the empire's growing debts to Europe.
events.now: The Tanzimat is the template for reform from above across the Middle East, and the tension between westernisation and tradition it opened still shapes Turkey.

causes.why: Losing Greece, and nearly losing Egypt's rebellious governor Muhammad Ali, convinced Ottoman reformers that the state had to modernise.
Muhammad Ali's modernised army nearly toppled the sultan in the 1830s, convincing Ottoman reformers they had to modernise too.

q.before: Islamic law and separate communities defined subjects' status.
q.how: Imperial decrees from the sultan.
q.claim: Equal citizenship for all Ottoman subjects.
q.winners: Reforming officials and many non-Muslim merchants.
q.lasted: Reform continued until Abdulhamid II suspended the constitution in 1878.

events.bluf: Ottoman Sultan Abdülmecid I and his reformers set out to save the empire by rebuilding its army, law and administration on European lines and promising equality to every subject. The reforms built a modern bureaucracy and won European support. They strengthened the central state and failed to stop nationalist breakaways, European interference or the debts that followed.
events.lens: Defensive modernization can strengthen a state but also raise expectations it cannot meet.
events.fact: The edict was read aloud in the Gülhane rose garden below Topkapı Palace before the foreign ambassadors.

events.who: Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson; more than 500 Māori chiefs
events.hook: Britain and Māori chiefs signed New Zealand's founding document, in two versions that said different things.
events.what: Britain and Māori chiefs signed New Zealand's founding document, in two versions that said different things.
events.story: New Zealand in 1839 had about 2,000 European settlers, whalers and traders and no government. Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson arrived in January 1840 with instructions to obtain sovereignty by consent. At Waitangi on 6 February about 40 chiefs signed; copies went round the country and more than 500 chiefs had signed by September. In the English text the chiefs ceded 'sovereignty'; in the Māori text, which nearly all of them signed, they granted 'kāwanatanga' (governorship) and kept 'tino rangatiratanga', full chieftainship over their lands, villages and treasures.
events.why: Britain wanted to control a settler frontier before the New Zealand Company's ships arrived, and to forestall a French claim. The chiefs wanted protection against settlers and the disorder left by the Musket Wars, and trade.
events.then: One reading holds the chiefs ceded sovereignty, as the English text says and as the Crown has acted since 1840; the other holds that the Māori text they signed granted the right to govern settlers and kept chiefly authority intact, so that sovereignty stayed with the chiefs, a finding the Waitangi Tribunal made for the northern chiefs in 2014. Settler demand for land led to the New Zealand Wars of 1845-72 and large confiscations; by 1900 Māori held only a small fraction of their land.
events.sig: One reading holds the chiefs ceded sovereignty, as the English text says and as the Crown has acted since 1840; the other holds that the Māori text they signed granted the right to govern settlers and kept chiefly authority intact, so that sovereignty stayed with the chiefs, a finding the Waitangi Tribunal made for the northern chiefs in 2014. Settler demand for land led to the New Zealand Wars of 1845-72 and large confiscations; by 1900 Māori held only a small fraction of their land.
events.now: Since 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated Crown breaches and settlements have returned land and money to many iwi; what the treaty means for sovereignty is contested in Parliament, where a bill to redefine its principles was introduced in 2024 and voted down in 2025.

causes.why: The devastation of the Musket Wars and lawless European traders led some chiefs to seek British protection.

events.fact: Missionary Henry Williams and his son translated the English draft into Māori overnight on 4-5 February 1840; the day of signing, 6 February, is New Zealand's national day.

q.before: Māori iwi and hapū governed themselves.
q.how: A treaty signed by Britain and hundreds of chiefs.
q.claim: Sovereignty in the English text; only 'governorship' in the Māori text.
q.winners: Britain, at first; Māori lost much land.
q.lasted: Yes: it is New Zealand's founding document, still debated.

events.bluf: Britain wanted authority over a lawless settler frontier and to forestall France; Māori chiefs wanted protection and trade. On 6 February 1840 Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson and the chiefs signed a treaty whose English text ceded sovereignty and whose Māori text granted governorship while preserving chiefly authority. The Crown governed on the English text, settlers took the land, and since 1975 the Māori text has been the basis for redress, which keeps the treaty at the centre of New Zealand politics.
events.lens: When a treaty's two versions disagree, the stronger party's reading prevails, until the weaker party gains the power to contest it.

events.what: Zanzibar becomes the Omani capital.
events.why: Zanzibar's clove plantations and the ivory and slave caravans from the mainland made it far richer than Muscat. The sultan went where the money was.
events.sig: Caravans reached as far as Congo; their routes later guided European explorers and missionaries. After Said's death in 1856 Britain split the empire in 1861 into separate sultanates of Oman and Zanzibar.
events.hook: Oman's sultan moved his capital to Zanzibar, making it East Africa's trading hub.
events.story: Omani Sultan Said bin Sultan moved his court from Muscat to Zanzibar in 1840. He planted cloves across the islands, worked by enslaved Africans. He made Zanzibar the hub of a caravan trade in ivory and captives reaching deep into central Africa.
events.then: Caravans reached as far as Congo; their routes later guided European explorers and missionaries. After Said's death in 1856 Britain split the empire in 1861 into separate sultanates of Oman and Zanzibar.
events.now: The clove plantations and slave caravans built an Arab landowning class over an African labouring majority, a divide that produced the revolution of 1964. The caravan routes opened the interior to European explorers and to the partition that followed from 1884.
events.fact: Zanzibar became the world's leading clove producer. Freddie Mercury was born there in 1946.

causes.why: Omani control of the coast grew until Sultan Said made Zanzibar his capital.

q.before: The sultan ruled from Muscat in Oman.
q.how: The ruler moved his capital to Africa.
q.claim: Omani sovereignty over the Swahili coast.
q.winners: The sultan and Arab and Indian merchants.
q.lasted: Zanzibar split from Oman in 1861 and became a British protectorate in 1890.

events.bluf: Omani Sultan Said bin Sultan moved his court from Muscat to Zanzibar in 1840 to sit at the centre of the trade that was making the island richer than Oman. He planted cloves across Zanzibar and Pemba, worked by enslaved Africans, and organised the caravan trade in ivory and captives that reached deep into central Africa. Zanzibar became the hub of an East African commercial empire, and its caravan routes were the ones European explorers and colonisers later followed inland.
events.lens: Commercial empires follow profit: the sultan moved his capital to where the money was.

kv: enslaved people sold through Zanzibar a year in the 1860s (est.)

events.what: Hong Kong ceded; five ports opened.
events.why: British warships had cut the Grand Canal and threatened Nanjing, which forced the Qing to make peace.
events.sig: France and the United States demanded similar treaties in 1844, and 'most-favoured nation' clauses meant any concession to one power went to all.
events.hook: China gave up Hong Kong and opened its ports to Britain.
events.story: British warships had reached the Yangtze and threatened Nanjing in the summer of 1842. The treaty was signed aboard the warship HMS Cornwallis at Nanjing on 29 August 1842. China agreed to pay 21 million silver dollars, open five ports to British trade and residence and cede Hong Kong Island 'in perpetuity'.
events.then: France and the United States demanded similar treaties in 1844, and 'most-favoured nation' clauses meant any concession to one power went to all.
events.now: Hong Kong's return in 1997 and the 'century of humiliation' narrative make Nanjing a lasting symbol in Chinese politics.
events.fact: Hong Kong was then a barely inhabited rock; British Foreign Secretary Lord Palmerston called it a barren island with hardly a house on it.

causes.why: Defeat forced China to pay an indemnity, open five ports and hand over Hong Kong.

q.before: Trade was restricted to Canton under Qing rules.
q.how: A treaty dictated after military defeat.
q.lasted: Hong Kong returned to China only in 1997.

events.bluf: Britain wanted its opium losses paid, Hong Kong as a base and China's ports open; the Qing wanted British warships off the Yangtze. The treaty signed aboard HMS Cornwallis in August 1842 gave Britain 21 million silver dollars, five ports and Hong Kong Island in perpetuity. It was the first of the 'unequal treaties', and its model of ports, indemnities and privileges set the pattern of Western dominance in China for a century.
events.lens: Treaties signed under duress breed nationalism that later demands their reversal.

events.who: Tokugawa shogunate; senior councillor Mizuno Tadakuni
events.what: Seeing Britain crush China, Japan quietly stopped firing on foreign ships.
events.why: News reached Japan that China, the giant of Asia, had been humbled by a few British warships, and officials feared Japan would be next.
events.sig: Japanese reformers began studying Western gunnery and coastal defence. The shogunate still refused to open the country, and held that line until Perry's arrival in 1853.
events.hook: Seeing Britain crush China, Japan quietly stopped firing on foreign ships.
events.story: News of China's defeat by Britain in the Opium War reached Japan through Dutch and Chinese traders at Nagasaki. Senior councillor Mizuno Tadakuni and his colleagues replaced the 1825 firing order with one allowing foreign ships to receive food, water and fuel.
events.then: Japanese reformers began studying Western gunnery and coastal defence. The shogunate still refused to open the country, and held that line until Perry's arrival in 1853.
events.now: It shows that a neighbour's defeat can change policy faster than one's own experience: China's 'century of humiliation' was Japan's warning.

causes.why: China's defeat showed what Western navies could do to an isolated Asian power.
It replaced the 1825 firing order.

q.before: Fire on sight.
q.how: Foreign ships could now get supplies and leave.
q.claim: Avoiding giving the West an excuse for war.
q.winners: Pragmatists who wanted to avoid China's fate.
q.lasted: It was a stopgap; 11 years later Perry arrived.

events.bluf: Senior councillor Mizuno Tadakuni wanted to spare Japan the fate of China, which a few British warships had just beaten in the Opium War. In 1842 the shogunate replaced its order to fire on foreign ships with one allowing them food, water and fuel, and began studying Western gunnery. The reversal shows the pragmatism that later drove Japan's modernisation, and it came from a neighbour's defeat rather than Japan's own.
events.lens: Watching a neighbour's defeat can teach more than one's own experience.
events.fact: The Dutch at Dejima supplied the shogunate each year with a written summary of world news, the 'fūsetsugaki', which is how word of the Opium War arrived.

events.who: Hōne Heke and other Māori leaders; British and colonial forces
events.hook: Disputes over land and sovereignty led to decades of war between Māori and the colonial government.
events.what: Disputes over land and sovereignty led to decades of war between Māori and the colonial government.
events.story: Ngāpuhi chief Hōne Heke, the first chief to sign at Waitangi in 1840, cut down the British flagstaff at Kororāreka four times between July 1844 and March 1845 in protest at lost trade and authority, and the Northern War followed. Fighting broke out in Taranaki in 1860 over a disputed land sale, and in 1863 colonial and imperial forces on the orders of New Zealand Governor George Grey invaded the Waikato, the territory of the Māori King. Māori fought on both sides. The wars ended by 1872, after the government confiscated millions of acres under the New Zealand Settlements Act of 1863.
events.why: Settlers wanted land faster than Māori would sell it. Disputed sales and the Māori King movement's refusal to sell raised the question of who held authority under the treaty.
events.then: Confiscated land opened the Waikato and Taranaki to settlers, and the iwi concerned were left poor. Waikato-Tainui received a Crown apology and NZ$170 million in 1995, the first large settlement; others followed.
events.sig: Confiscated land opened the Waikato and Taranaki to settlers, and the iwi concerned were left poor. Waikato-Tainui received a Crown apology and NZ$170 million in 1995, the first large settlement; others followed.
events.now: The confiscations impoverished the iwi of Taranaki and Waikato for a century and are the core of the treaty settlements the Crown has negotiated since the 1990s, with apologies and compensation written into law.

causes.why: Disputes over land sales and over who held authority under the treaty led to war.

q.why: Settler demand for land and disputes over authority under the Treaty of Waitangi.
q.decided: Colonial numbers and resources, despite Māori skill in fortified pā.
q.cost: About 2,000 Māori and 800 British and colonial soldiers died.
q.changed: Millions of acres of Māori land were confiscated.

events.bluf: Māori chiefs fought to keep their land and the authority the treaty had promised them; the colonial government fought to open the North Island to settlers. Ngāpuhi chief Hōne Heke's war in the north in 1845 ended in stalemate; the Taranaki and Waikato wars of the 1860s ended in Māori defeat and the confiscation of millions of acres. Settlers rather than Māori would govern New Zealand, and the confiscations are what Crown settlements since 1995 have apologised for.
events.lens: Wars over land often end in confiscation dressed up as punishment.
events.fact: Queen Elizabeth II signed the Waikato-Tainui settlement act in person in 1995, the first Crown apology to an iwi.

toll.n: Estimates.

events.what: Potato blight; ~1M died and ~1M emigrated.
events.why: Over a third of the population depended almost entirely on the potato, grown on tiny plots rented from often absent landlords. Blight destroyed the crop repeatedly from 1845. The British government, holding to free-market principles, limited relief and let food exports continue.
events.sig: Ireland's population fell by about a quarter and kept shrinking until the 20th century, as mass emigration to the United States, Britain and Australia continued. Bitterness toward British rule strengthened nationalist movements.
events.hook: A potato disease and British policy killed a million Irish and drove a million more abroad.
events.story: Blight destroyed the potato, the main food of Irish peasants, in 1845, almost completely in 1846 and again in 1848. British Prime Minister Robert Peel bought maize for relief in 1845-46; Lord John Russell's government from 1846 relied on public works, then soup kitchens, then the poor law. Ireland kept exporting grain and cattle to England throughout. About a million died of hunger and disease, and about a million emigrated.
events.then: Ireland's population fell by about a quarter and kept shrinking until the 20th century, as mass emigration to the United States, Britain and Australia continued. Bitterness toward British rule strengthened nationalist movements.
events.now: The famine made emigration Ireland's demographic norm for a century and gave Irish nationalism, at home and among the diaspora, its charge against British rule; over 30 million Americans claim Irish ancestry.
events.fact: In 1847 the Choctaw Nation, forced down the Trail of Tears sixteen years earlier, sent money to help starving Irish families.

q.what: Potatoes, the staple food of the Irish poor.
q.who: Landowners kept exporting food; tenants starved or were evicted.
q.scale: About a million died and a million or more emigrated.
q.daily: Evictions, soup kitchens and workhouses.
q.system: Mass emigration that built Irish communities in America and Britain.

events.bluf: Potato blight destroyed the crop a third of Ireland lived on, in 1845 and the years after; British Prime Ministers Robert Peel and then Lord John Russell set out to relieve the hunger without disturbing markets or landlords. Relief was slow and limited while grain and cattle still left the country; about a million died and a million emigrated. Ireland's population fell by a quarter and kept falling for a century, and Irish nationalism took the famine as its charge against British rule.
events.lens: Famines are rarely just about food shortage; they are about who has access to food and who decides.

events.what: Texas joined as a slave state.
events.why: Southern politicians wanted another slave state in the Senate. Expansionists wanted the continent and feared Britain would make Texas a client. Texas wanted protection from Mexico and relief from its debts.
events.sig: Mexico broke off diplomatic relations in March 1845. The dispute over whether Texas ended at the Nueces or the Rio Grande gave Polk his occasion for war in 1846, and the Wilmot Proviso of 1846 reopened the fight over slavery in any land taken.
events.hook: A new phrase claimed America was destined to stretch from sea to sea.
events.story: Texas had broken from Mexico in 1836 and sought admission to the United States as a slave state. The Senate rejected an annexation treaty in 1844. Outgoing President John Tyler signed a joint resolution of annexation on 1 March 1845, and President James K. Polk, who had won the election on expansion, signed Texas into the Union on 29 December 1845. That summer New York journalist John O'Sullivan coined 'Manifest Destiny' for the country's claimed right to spread across the continent.
events.then: Mexico broke off diplomatic relations in March 1845. The dispute over whether Texas ended at the Nueces or the Rio Grande gave Polk his occasion for war in 1846, and the Wilmot Proviso of 1846 reopened the fight over slavery in any land taken.
events.now: 'Manifest Destiny' gave American expansion a moral claim that shaped policy from the Pacific coast to the overseas empire of 1898.

causes.why: Mexico invited American settlers into Texas; they rebelled in 1835 over slavery, taxes and central control, and Texas later joined the US.
After winning independence in 1836, Texas joined the US in 1845.

q.before: The independent Republic of Texas.
q.how: Annexation by a joint resolution of Congress.
q.winners: The US and Texas; Mexico protested.
q.lasted: Yes: Texas became a state in December 1845.

events.bluf: Southern politicians and expansionists wanted Texas in the Union as a slave state, and President James K. Polk had won the 1844 election on annexation. Congress admitted Texas by joint resolution in 1845 after the Senate had refused a treaty the year before. Mexico, which still claimed Texas, broke off relations, the border dispute became war within a year, and 'Manifest Destiny' gave expansion a creed that ran to 1898.
events.lens: Ideologies of destiny turn ambitions into perceived rights and make compromise with others' claims harder.
events.fact: Texas entered the Union with the right, written into the resolution, to divide itself into as many as five states.

events.who: Prime Minister Robert Peel; Richard Cobden and the Anti-Corn Law League
events.hook: Britain abolished its tariffs on imported grain and embraced free trade.
events.what: Britain abolished its tariffs on imported grain and embraced free trade.
events.story: The Corn Laws of 1815 taxed imported grain to protect landowners. The Anti-Corn Law League, founded in Manchester in 1838 by manufacturer Richard Cobden and Quaker manufacturer John Bright, campaigned with pamphlets, lectures and voter registration. With famine in Ireland, Conservative Prime Minister Robert Peel carried repeal in 1846 with Whig votes, and his own party split.
events.why: Industrial towns wanted cheap bread and manufacturers wanted foreign markets. Free-trade ideas had spread since Adam Smith. The Irish famine made a tax on food indefensible.
events.then: Peel's government fell within days of repeal, and the Conservatives had no majority again for 28 years. Britain led an era of free trade; cheap grain imports from the 1870s hit British farming.
events.sig: Peel's government fell within days of repeal, and the Conservatives had no majority again for 28 years. Britain led an era of free trade; cheap grain imports from the 1870s hit British farming.
events.now: It remains the textbook case of trade politics as a contest between interests, and today's tariff debates repeat its arguments about who gains and who pays.

causes.why: Ricardo's arguments armed the free-traders.
Famine in Ireland made the case for cheap grain imports urgent.

q.what: Imported grain.
q.who: Workers and manufacturers gained cheaper bread; landowners lost.
q.scale: Grain duties were phased out by 1849.
q.daily: Bread became cheaper.
q.system: Britain's free-trade policy for the rest of the century.

events.bluf: Manchester manufacturer Richard Cobden and Quaker manufacturer John Bright's Anti-Corn Law League wanted the tariffs on imported grain that protected landowners repealed; Prime Minister Robert Peel came to agree, and the Irish famine gave him the occasion. Repeal passed in June 1846 with opposition votes and split his Conservative Party, which turned him out within days. Britain had shifted from protecting landowners to free trade serving industry and consumers, and stayed its champion for 80 years.
events.lens: Trade policy is a contest between interest groups: ask who gains from protection and who pays for it.
events.fact: The Conservative split put the Peelites, among them William Gladstone, on the road to the Liberal Party.

kv: of Conservative MPs voted against their own prime minister

events.what: US invaded and occupied Mexico City.
events.why: Polk wanted California and its ports; Mexico's governments, unstable and in debt, could neither sell nor defend it. 'Manifest Destiny' supplied the public case.
events.sig: Mexico ceded about half its territory, including California and New Mexico, in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of February 1848 for $15 million. The Wilmot Proviso's attempt to bar slavery from the new lands split both parties along sectional lines. Many Civil War generals, including Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee, first fought here.
events.hook: The US invaded Mexico and took half its territory.
events.story: Mexico had never accepted Texas's independence or its annexation, and the two countries disputed whether the border ran along the Nueces or the Rio Grande. US President James K. Polk sent General Zachary Taylor's army into the disputed zone, and after a clash in April 1846 he told Congress that Mexico had 'shed American blood upon American soil'. Congress declared war on 13 May 1846. US forces took California and New Mexico, and General Winfield Scott, after landing at Veracruz in March 1847, captured Mexico City on 14 September 1847.
events.then: Mexico ceded about half its territory, including California and New Mexico, in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of February 1848 for $15 million. The Wilmot Proviso's attempt to bar slavery from the new lands split both parties along sectional lines. Many Civil War generals, including Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee, first fought here.
events.now: The war took half of Mexico's territory and gave the United States its Pacific coast, which settled its continental shape and reopened the slavery question over the new lands; Mexican politics still carries the memory.

sites.d: First major battle, 1846.
Zachary Taylor's victory made him president.
US amphibious landing, 1847.
The 'Niños Héroes' defend Mexico City's castle.

causes.why: Mexico never recognised Texan independence; annexation and a border dispute led to war.

q.why: A border dispute, and President Polk's wish to take California.
q.decided: US armies under Taylor and Scott.
q.cost: About 13,000 US and perhaps 25,000 Mexican dead.
q.changed: Mexico lost California and the Southwest.

events.bluf: US President James K. Polk wanted California and its Pacific ports and Mexico refused to sell; he sent troops into the disputed strip north of the Rio Grande and got his war. US forces took California and New Mexico and captured Mexico City in September 1847. Mexico gave up about half its territory, the United States became a continental power with a Pacific coast, and the fight over slavery in the new lands split its parties along sectional lines.
events.trig: A clash between US and Mexican troops in the disputed land north of the Rio Grande in April 1846.
events.lens: Territorial gains can destabilize the winner: the new land raised the question that tore the United States apart.
events.fact: Grant, who served in it as a lieutenant, later called it one of the most unjust wars ever waged by a stronger against a weaker nation.
1848 is called the 'Springtime of Peoples'; risings hit more than 50 places in a few months.
events.hook: Revolutions swept across Europe in a single spring, and most were crushed within a year.
events.what: Revolutions swept across Europe in a single spring, and most were crushed within a year.
events.story: Bad harvests and an economic slump had left Europe's cities hungry and unemployed. Paris rose in February 1848 and King Louis-Philippe fled; Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest and dozens of other cities followed in March, demanding constitutions, press freedom and national unity. Austrian Chancellor Klemens von Metternich fled Vienna. Most of the risings were crushed within a year.
events.why: Bad harvests, including the potato blight, an economic slump and unemployment came first. Decades of liberal and nationalist frustration with the conservative order of 1815 came second.
events.then: Austria abolished serfdom, Prussia got a constitution, and France got universal male suffrage, then elected Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte president in December 1848; he made himself emperor in 1852. Conservative forces regrouped, and unification came later through Prussian and Piedmontese power politics rather than liberal parliaments.
events.sig: Austria abolished serfdom, Prussia got a constitution, and France got universal male suffrage, then elected Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte president in December 1848; he made himself emperor in 1852. Conservative forces regrouped, and unification came later through Prussian and Piedmontese power politics rather than liberal parliaments.
events.now: '1848' is the template for sudden waves of revolt, such as 1989 or the Arab Spring.

causes.why: Crop failures across Europe in 1845-47, including the potato blight that devastated Ireland, drove up food prices and unrest before 1848.

q.before: Conservative monarchies restored after 1815.
q.how: Street uprisings across Europe.
q.claim: Constitutions, national unity and the rights of citizens.
q.winners: In the short run, the monarchies, which crushed most revolts.
q.lasted: Most gains were reversed, but serfdom's end in Austria lasted.

events.bluf: Liberals, nationalists and workers across Europe rose in 1848 to win constitutions, national unity and relief from slump, after Paris overthrew King Louis-Philippe in February. Within a year the armies of Austria, Prussia and Russia and the French republic's own troops had crushed most of the risings. Serfdom ended in the Habsburg lands, Prussia got a constitution, France got universal male suffrage and then a Bonaparte, and nationalism became the dominant political force; unification would come by Prussian and Piedmontese arms rather than liberal parliaments.
events.trig: The February revolution in Paris, which overthrew King Louis-Philippe.
events.lens: Revolutionary waves spread fast across connected societies but fail when armies stay loyal to rulers.

events.hook: Marx and Engels called on the workers of the world to unite.
events.what: Marx and Engels called on the workers of the world to unite.
events.story: The Communist League, a small group of radical workers, commissioned a programme from German philosopher Karl Marx and his collaborator Friedrich Engels in late 1847. The pamphlet argued that history is a story of class struggle, that the bourgeoisie had created the proletariat that would overthrow it, and that the workers had nothing to lose but their chains. It was published in German in London in February 1848, days before the revolution in Paris. It had little effect at first.
events.why: Industrialisation had created an urban working class in harsh conditions. Capitalism's booms and busts were plain to see. The revolutionary climate of 1848 made radical change seem possible.
events.then: Marx's later work, above all 'Das Kapital' of 1867, shaped socialist and labour movements. The Russian Revolution of 1917 put Marxists in power; reformist socialists turned to democratic politics and the welfare state.
events.sig: Marx's later work, above all 'Das Kapital' of 1867, shaped socialist and labour movements. The Russian Revolution of 1917 put Marxists in power; reformist socialists turned to democratic politics and the welfare state.
events.now: Regimes claiming Marx's inspiration once ruled a third of humanity, and the Manifesto remains one of the most widely read political texts ever written.

causes.why: Marx built on Smith's and Ricardo's economics but argued that capitalism exploited workers and would be overthrown.

q.idea: History is a story of class struggle, and the workers will overthrow capitalism.
q.against: Industrial capitalism and the property-owning middle class.
q.spread: Slowly at first, then through socialist parties in many languages.
q.enabled: Communist and socialist movements and revolutions.
q.critics: Liberals and later critics pointed to the repression of communist states.

events.bluf: German philosopher Karl Marx and his collaborator Friedrich Engels wrote a programme for the Communist League, a small group of radical workers, to explain history as class struggle and to forecast the overthrow of capitalism by the industrial working class. Published in German in London in February 1848, it had little effect on the revolutions of that year. Its doctrine became that of the mass socialist parties after 1870 and, after 1917, of states that ruled a third of humanity.
events.lens: Ideas about inequality win mass followings when economic change produces visible winners and losers.
events.fact: The first English translation appeared in 1850 in a Chartist newspaper, the Red Republican.

events.who: Elected delegates from across the German states
events.hook: Germany's first freely elected parliament tried to unite the country, and failed.
events.what: Germany's first freely elected parliament tried to unite the country, and failed.
events.story: The March revolutions forced the German princes to allow elections. The assembly opened in St Paul's Church, Frankfurt, on 18 May 1848 and wrote a liberal constitution with a list of basic rights. In March 1849 it adopted the constitution and offered the crown of a united Germany to Prussian King Frederick William IV, who refused 'a crown from the gutter'. Troops dispersed the remnant at Stuttgart in June 1849.
events.why: Revolutions across Europe had forced the German princes to allow elections. The assembly had no army and no money of its own and depended on Prussia and Austria accepting its decisions.
events.then: Prussian Minister-President Otto von Bismarck united Germany by war in 1871, under an emperor with a parliament of limited power. Many liberals emigrated, some to the United States.
events.sig: Prussian Minister-President Otto von Bismarck united Germany by war in 1871, under an emperor with a parliament of limited power. Many liberals emigrated, some to the United States.
events.now: Germany's black-red-gold flag and its post-war Basic Law draw on the Frankfurt Parliament.

causes.why: The 1848 revolutions forced the German princes to allow an elected assembly.

q.before: 39 German states loosely joined in the German Confederation.
q.how: An elected assembly wrote a constitution.
q.claim: The sovereignty of the German people.
q.winners: In the end, the princes and Prussia.
q.lasted: No: it broke up in 1849.

events.bluf: Delegates elected across the German states in the spring of 1848 met in Frankfurt to unite Germany as a liberal constitutional state by consent. They wrote a constitution with a list of basic rights and in April 1849 offered the crown to Prussian King Frederick William IV, who refused 'a crown from the gutter'; troops dispersed the remnant in June. Unification by elected assembly had failed, and Germany was united instead by Prussian arms in 1871 under an emperor and a parliament of limited power.
events.lens: Parliaments without armies depend on the rulers who have them.
events.fact: The assembly argued for months over whether Austria belonged in Germany, the 'greater' against the 'smaller' German solution.

events.who: US envoy Nicholas Trist; Mexican commissioners
events.what: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ceded territory.
events.why: US troops occupied Mexico City, and Mexico, divided and bankrupt, could only make peace on American terms. US President James K. Polk had gone to war for California.
events.sig: About 80,000 Mexicans became US residents; their property rights, though promised, were often lost in later land disputes. The Gadsden Purchase of 1853 added the last strip of the border.
events.hook: Mexico lost half its territory to the United States.
events.story: US troops occupied Mexico City in September 1847. Signed on 2 February 1848 at Guadalupe Hidalgo near Mexico City by US envoy Nicholas Trist and Mexican commissioners, the treaty gave the United States about half of Mexico's territory, including California, Nevada, Utah and most of Arizona and New Mexico, for $15 million. Mexicans living there could become US citizens.
events.then: About 80,000 Mexicans became US residents; their property rights, though promised, were often lost in later land disputes. The Gadsden Purchase of 1853 added the last strip of the border.
events.now: The treaty's land and citizenship clauses created the Mexican-American population of the Southwest and the border they live along, and the loss of half the national territory has shaped Mexican attitudes to the United States ever since.

causes.why: The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred California and the Southwest to the US.

q.before: Mexico held the land from Texas to California.
q.how: A treaty after military defeat.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: The United States wanted California and the Southwest and had seized them by force; Mexico, with US troops in its capital, needed peace on any terms it could get. The treaty signed on 2 February 1848 transferred about half of Mexico's territory for $15 million. It fixed most of the modern US-Mexico border and made some 80,000 Mexicans US residents overnight, the origin of the Mexican-American population of the Southwest.
events.lens: Borders move across people as well as people across borders.
events.fact: Trist negotiated the treaty after Polk had recalled him; he ignored the recall, and Polk sent the treaty to the Senate anyway. 'We didn't cross the border, the border crossed us' is a saying in the US Southwest.

events.what: Gold found at Sutter's Mill.
events.why: Gold lay in placer deposits a man with a pan could work, and California had almost no government to control access. Steamships and the press carried the word around the world within months.
events.sig: California entered the Union as a free state in 1850. The easy gold was gone by the mid-1850s and mining passed to companies. The Native population fell from about 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870 through killings, disease and starvation, which California's governor formally acknowledged as genocide in 2019.
events.hook: A flake of gold at a sawmill set off one of the largest migrations in history.
events.story: In January 1848, days before Mexico signed California over to the United States, carpenter James Marshall found gold flakes in the tailrace of a sawmill he was building for Swiss settler John Sutter on the American River. Word spread slowly until US President James K. Polk confirmed the find in his message to Congress in December 1848. About 300,000 people then poured in from the eastern United States, Latin America, Europe, Australia and China. San Francisco grew from about 1,000 people to some 25,000 within two years.
events.then: California entered the Union as a free state in 1850. The easy gold was gone by the mid-1850s and mining passed to companies. The Native population fell from about 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870 through killings, disease and starvation, which California's governor formally acknowledged as genocide in 2019.
events.now: The rush made California a state in 1850 without passing through territorial status, which forced the Compromise of 1850, and it set the Pacific coast's pattern of immigration from Asia and Latin America that shapes its politics still.
events.fact: San Francisco grew from about 1,000 people to around 25,000 in two years. Levi Strauss arrived in 1853 to sell dry goods to miners; the riveted jeans came twenty years later.

causes.why: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill on January 24, 1848, nine days before the treaty that made California American.

q.what: Gold.
q.who: Merchants and a few miners got rich; Native Californians were massacred.
q.scale: About 300,000 people arrived within a few years.
q.daily: Tent cities, high prices and lawlessness.
q.system: California's rapid statehood and a booming Pacific economy.

events.bluf: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill in January 1848, nine days before Mexico ceded California to the United States. About 300,000 people arrived from the eastern states, Latin America, Europe, Australia and China, and California became a state within two years. The rush tied the Pacific coast to the national economy and brought killings, disease and starvation that cut the Native population from about 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870.
events.lens: Resource rushes bring rapid growth, and often catastrophic violence against whoever is already there.

events.what: First women's rights convention.
events.why: Women abolitionists had learned to organise and speak in the anti-slavery movement and were shut out of its leadership. Married women in most states could own no property and had no legal standing apart from their husbands.
events.sig: A national women's rights convention met at Worcester in 1850 and most years after. The movement split in 1869 over the 15th Amendment, which enfranchised Black men and left women out; the two wings reunited in 1890. Women won the national vote in 1920.
events.hook: Three hundred people met in a chapel and declared that 'all men and women are created equal.'
events.story: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott had been refused seats as delegates at the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London in 1840. In July 1848 they called a two-day convention at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York. Stanton's Declaration of Sentiments, modelled on the Declaration of Independence, held that 'all men and women are created equal' and listed women's grievances. The resolution demanding the vote was the only one to pass without unanimity; abolitionist Frederick Douglass spoke for it.
events.then: A national women's rights convention met at Worcester in 1850 and most years after. The movement split in 1869 over the 15th Amendment, which enfranchised Black men and left women out; the two wings reunited in 1890. Women won the national vote in 1920.
events.now: It launched the organised women's rights movement in the United States; its demands, from the vote to property rights, set the agenda until the 19th Amendment in 1920.
events.fact: Of the 100 signers, only one, Charlotte Woodward, lived to see women win the vote in 1920.

causes.why: The Seneca Falls Declaration rewrote Jefferson's words: 'all men and women are created equal'.

q.before: Women could not vote and married women had few property rights.
q.how: A public convention and a Declaration of Sentiments.
q.claim: 'All men and women are created equal.'
q.lasted: Women won the national vote in 1920.

events.bluf: Abolitionists Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, refused seats at an anti-slavery convention in London in 1840 because they were women, called a convention to claim women's rights for themselves. About 300 people met at Seneca Falls in July 1848, and 100 signed a Declaration of Sentiments that demanded equal rights, including the vote. It launched the organised women's rights movement in the United States and set its agenda for the 72 years to the 19th Amendment.
events.lens: Movements gain power by holding a society to its own founding principles.

kv: signed the Declaration of Sentiments: 68 women, 32 men

events.who: Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be Jesus's brother
events.what: Civil war killed ~20 million.
events.why: Population pressure and poverty in the south came first. Qing weakness after the Opium War and ethnic tension between the Hakka and their neighbours gave the movement its recruits. A charismatic religious message promising equality held it together.
events.sig: The Qing relied on regional armies raised by Chinese officials such as Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, and on Western-officered units; these regional power bases later fed warlordism. The devastation of the Yangtze valley set back China's economy for decades.
events.hook: A man who said he was Jesus's brother led a civil war that killed about 20 million.
events.story: Hong Xiuquan failed the civil service examinations, read Christian tracts and came to believe he was the younger brother of Jesus. His movement grew among the poor and the Hakka minority of southern China. In 1853 the Taiping took Nanjing, made it their 'Heavenly Capital' and ruled much of the Yangtze valley. Qing forces retook the city in 1864.
events.then: The Qing relied on regional armies raised by Chinese officials such as Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, and on Western-officered units; these regional power bases later fed warlordism. The devastation of the Yangtze valley set back China's economy for decades.
events.now: The regional armies the Qing raised to survive it became the power bases of warlordism after 1911; both Nationalists and Communists later claimed the Taiping as revolutionary forerunners.
events.fact: Its death toll was comparable to the whole of the First World War, yet it is barely taught in the West.

sites.d: Uprising launched, 1851.
Taiping capital 'Heavenly Capital', fell 1864.

causes.why: Defeat discredited the Qing, and the war's disruption of trade and jobs in south China fed the Taiping uprising.

q.why: Poverty, Qing weakness and Hong Xiuquan's religious movement.
q.decided: Regional Qing armies like Zeng Guofan's, with Western help.
q.cost: Perhaps 20 to 30 million dead.
q.changed: Regional armies grew powerful and the Qing weakened.

events.bluf: Hong Xiuquan, a failed examination candidate who believed himself the younger brother of Jesus, set out to overthrow the Qing and build a Heavenly Kingdom of equality. His armies took Nanjing in 1853 and held the Yangtze valley for eleven years before Qing forces retook it in 1864. The war killed perhaps 20 to 30 million people, and the Qing survived only by relying on regional armies and Western help, which permanently weakened central authority.
events.lens: When a state cannot crush a rebellion with its own forces, the regional armies it relies on become its next problem.

figs.n: One of the deadliest wars in history, almost all of it inside China. Some estimates run higher.

events.what: California free; tough Fugitive Slave Act.
events.why: The Mexican cession reopened the question Missouri had settled. California's admission threatened the balance of 15 slave and 15 free states, and Southern leaders had met at Nashville in June 1850 to discuss secession.
events.sig: Federal marshals seized people who had escaped in Boston, Syracuse and other Northern cities, and crowds fought to free them. Harriet Beecher Stowe's 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' of 1852 sold 300,000 copies in its first year. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 broke the settlement.
events.hook: Another deal kept the Union together, but its slave-catching law radicalized the North.
