events.story: California applied to enter as a free state in 1849, which would have given free states a Senate majority, while Texas claimed half of New Mexico and the South demanded a stronger fugitive slave law. Kentucky Senator Henry Clay proposed an omnibus settlement in January 1850 and Massachusetts Senator Daniel Webster backed it. The omnibus failed in July; Illinois Senator Stephen Douglas passed its parts as separate bills in September. California entered free, New Mexico and Utah were organised with no ban on slavery, Texas gave up its claim for $10 million, the slave trade ended in Washington, and a Fugitive Slave Act put federal commissioners at the service of slaveholders.
events.then: Federal marshals seized people who had escaped in Boston, Syracuse and other Northern cities, and crowds fought to free them. Harriet Beecher Stowe's 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' of 1852 sold 300,000 copies in its first year. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 broke the settlement.
events.now: The compromise bought a decade and used up the material for another; the Fugitive Slave Act put slavery in Northern streets and courtrooms, which turned moderate opinion against it between 1850 and 1860.

causes.why: Land taken from Mexico reopened the question the 1820 line had seemed to settle.
Would California and the Southwest be slave or free? The war's conquests nearly broke the Union in 1850.

q.before: Congress was deadlocked over slavery in the new territories.
q.how: A package of laws passed by Congress.
q.winners: Slaveholders, through the Fugitive Slave Act; California, as a free state.
q.lasted: Only about four years.

events.bluf: Kentucky Senator Henry Clay set out to hold the Union together by settling every dispute raised by the land taken from Mexico in one package. Illinois Senator Stephen Douglas pushed it through in pieces: California entered free, the rest of the Mexican cession was left to its settlers, and the South got a Fugitive Slave Act that made Northerners help return people who had escaped. The compromise bought ten years, and the Fugitive Slave Act turned Northern opinion against slavery faster than any abolitionist had.
events.lens: Concessions that make bystanders complicit can radicalize them.
events.fact: President Zachary Taylor, who opposed the compromise, died in July 1850; his successor Millard Fillmore signed every bill.

kv: paid to Texas to drop its land claims

events.where: Bathurst, New South Wales, and Ballarat, Victoria
events.hook: Gold strikes drew hundreds of thousands of migrants and transformed Australia.
events.what: Gold strikes drew hundreds of thousands of migrants and transformed Australia.
events.story: Prospector Edward Hargraves, back from California, found gold near Bathurst in February 1851; the New South Wales government announced it in May. Finds at Ballarat and Bendigo in Victoria followed within months. Diggers came from Britain, Ireland, Europe, America and China. Australia's population grew from about 430,000 in 1851 to 1.7 million in 1871, and Melbourne became one of the richest cities in the world.
events.why: Prospectors from California recognised the signs. Governments offered rewards because free men were leaving for California and the colonies needed them.
events.then: Victoria taxed Chinese arrivals from 1855 and other colonies followed; miners attacked Chinese camps at Lambing Flat in 1861. The diggers' numbers forced the colonies to widen the franchise within a decade.
events.sig: Victoria taxed Chinese arrivals from 1855 and other colonies followed; miners attacked Chinese camps at Lambing Flat in 1861. The diggers' numbers forced the colonies to widen the franchise within a decade.
events.now: Gold made Victoria rich and populous, filled the colonies with free migrants who demanded the vote, and produced anti-Chinese laws from 1855 that set the pattern for the Immigration Restriction Act of 1901.

causes.why: Edward Hargraves, back from California, recognised similar gold-bearing country near Bathurst.

q.what: Gold, from rivers and deep mines.
q.who: Merchants, lucky diggers and the colonies; Aboriginal people lost more land.
q.scale: Australia's population roughly quadrupled in 20 years.
q.daily: Tent towns, licence hunts and a mix of nationalities.
q.system: Booming colonial cities like Melbourne.

events.bluf: Prospectors who had learned the signs in California went looking for gold in Australia, and the colonial governments, fearing a labour exodus, offered rewards for finding it. Gold was found near Bathurst in February 1851 and in Victoria months later, and Australia's population roughly quadrupled in 20 years. A penal colony became an immigrant society, and hostility to Chinese diggers produced the first of the laws that became the White Australia policy.
events.lens: Immigration booms often bring both prosperity and an exclusionary backlash.
events.fact: The Welcome Stranger nugget, found at Moliagul in Victoria in 1869, weighed about 72 kg and remains the largest alluvial nugget ever found.

events.what: US warships forced Japan to open trade.
events.why: The United States wanted coaling stations for steamships on the route to China, protection for its whalers and new markets. China's defeat by Britain had shown how vulnerable Asian states were.
events.sig: The Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854 and the unequal treaties of 1858 followed. Anger at the shogunate's surrender fed a movement to restore the emperor, and the shogunate fell in 1868.
events.hook: American warships forced Japan to open to the world.
events.story: In July 1853 US Commodore Matthew Perry sailed four ships, two of them steam-powered, into Edo Bay and delivered a letter from President Millard Fillmore demanding trade and good treatment for shipwrecked sailors. He promised to return the next year with a larger fleet. Japan had no navy able to resist.
events.then: The Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854 and the unequal treaties of 1858 followed. Anger at the shogunate's surrender fed a movement to restore the emperor, and the shogunate fell in 1868.
events.now: Japan's transformation into a modern power begins here, and the 'black ships' remain the standard example of an outside shock forcing a closed society to change.
events.fact: Among Perry's gifts was a working miniature steam train that Japanese officials rode around a track.

causes.why: Japan already knew it couldn't fight Western warships.
Perry arrived with China's fate as an unspoken threat.

q.before: The shogun controlled foreign contact; only the Dutch and Chinese could trade.
q.how: Japan was forced into treaties with Western powers.
q.claim: The US claimed the right to trade and to protect its whalers.
q.winners: The US gained ports; the shogun lost prestige.
q.lasted: Yes: Japan never closed again.

events.bluf: US Commodore Matthew Perry sailed into Edo Bay in July 1853 to force Japan to open ports to American ships, under orders to use the threat of his guns. The shogunate, with no navy able to resist, accepted his letter and signed a treaty when he returned in 1854. Two centuries of restricted contact ended, the shogunate's authority was discredited, and the crisis that followed produced the Meiji Restoration of 1868.
events.lens: External shocks expose the weakness of old regimes and empower reformers who can explain how to respond.

events.what: Allies besieged Russia's Sevastopol naval base.
events.why: Russia wanted the Ottoman Balkans and the Straits. Britain and France wanted Russia kept out of the Mediterranean. A quarrel between Russia and France over the protection of Christians in the Holy Land supplied the occasion.
events.sig: The Treaty of Paris of 1856 banned warships from the Black Sea. Russian Tsar Alexander II freed the serfs in 1861 and rebuilt the army. Austria's neutrality cost it Russia's friendship, and it stood alone when Piedmont attacked in 1859 and Prussia in 1866.
events.hook: Britain and France fought Russia to keep it from swallowing the Ottoman Empire.
events.story: Russian Tsar Nicholas I occupied the Ottoman principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia in July 1853, and the Ottomans declared war in October. Britain and France joined in March 1854 after a Russian squadron destroyed an Ottoman flotilla at Sinope. Allied armies landed in Crimea in September 1854 and besieged Russia's Black Sea base at Sevastopol, which fell in September 1855. Supply failures and disease killed far more men than bullets; British nurse Florence Nightingale reorganised the hospitals at Scutari.
events.then: The Treaty of Paris of 1856 banned warships from the Black Sea. Russian Tsar Alexander II freed the serfs in 1861 and rebuilt the army. Austria's neutrality cost it Russia's friendship, and it stood alone when Piedmont attacked in 1859 and Prussia in 1866.
events.now: The war ended the Concert of Europe: the powers that had kept the peace since 1815 fought each other, Austria's neutrality left it isolated, and the wars of Italian and German unification followed within fifteen years. Russia's defeat forced the emancipation of its serfs.
events.fact: The first war covered by telegraph and photography; it gave Britain the Charge of the Light Brigade and Florence Nightingale's reform of nursing.

causes.why: Britain and France went to war to stop Russia from dominating the weakened empire and the route to the Mediterranean.
Victory over Napoleon made Russia the 'gendarme of Europe', and its ambitions against the Ottomans alarmed Britain and France.

q.why: To stop Russian expansion into the Ottoman Empire.
q.stakes: Control of the Black Sea and the Ottoman lands.
q.decided: The fall of Sevastopol after a year-long siege.
q.cost: Perhaps 500,000 dead, mostly from disease.
q.changed: Russia began reforms, and the Concert of Europe weakened.

events.bluf: Britain and France fought Russia to stop it taking Constantinople and the Straits and dominating the eastern Mediterranean. They won, at a cost of about half a million dead, most of them from disease. The war broke the international system established at the Congress of Vienna, and the wars of Italian and German unification followed within fifteen years.
events.trig: Russia's occupation of the Ottoman Danubian principalities, Moldavia and Wallachia, in 1853.
events.lens: Great powers fight to stop a rival from gaining a decisive position as a declining empire weakens.

toll.n: Most died of disease. Estimates vary widely, especially for Russia and the Ottomans.

events.what: Perry returned with a bigger fleet, and Japan signed its first treaty with a Western power.
events.why: Japan had no navy that could resist, and its leaders wanted to avoid China's fate in the Opium War.
events.sig: US consul Townsend Harris arrived in 1856 and pressed for full trade, which led to the unequal treaties of 1858.
events.hook: Perry returned with a bigger fleet, and Japan signed its first treaty with a Western power.
events.story: US Commodore Matthew Perry came back in February 1854 with nine ships. The shogunate agreed to open two small ports, Shimoda and Hakodate, to help shipwrecked sailors and to accept a US consul. The treaty was signed at Kanagawa, now part of Yokohama, on 31 March 1854.
events.then: US consul Townsend Harris arrived in 1856 and pressed for full trade, which led to the unequal treaties of 1858.
events.now: It ended over 200 years of isolation and set off the crisis that brought down the shogunate within 15 years, the starting point of Japan's modernisation.

causes.why: Perry promised to return for an answer, and did.

q.before: Japan had treaties with no Western power except trade with the Dutch.
q.how: Japan entered the Western treaty system.
q.claim: 'Peace and amity' between the US and Japan.
q.winners: The US; Britain, Russia and the Netherlands soon got similar deals.
q.lasted: It was replaced in 1858 by a far harsher trade treaty.

events.bluf: US Commodore Matthew Perry returned to Japan in 1854 with nine ships to get the treaty he had demanded the year before. The shogunate agreed on 31 March to open Shimoda and Hakodate, help shipwrecked sailors and accept a US consul. Japan's first treaty with a Western power ended over 200 years of restricted contact and set off the internal crisis that toppled the shogunate within 15 years.
events.lens: A first concession under pressure invites the next: limited opening in 1854 became full unequal treaties four years later.
events.fact: US consul Townsend Harris opened the first American consulate in Japan in a Buddhist temple at Shimoda.

events.what: Let settlers vote on slavery ('popular sovereignty').
events.why: Douglas wanted a northern railroad route and the organised territory it required. Southern senators would vote for it only with the Missouri ban gone.
events.sig: Anti-slavery Whigs, Democrats and Free Soilers formed the Republican Party in 1854; it carried most of the North in 1856 and elected Abraham Lincoln in 1860. About 55 people died in Kansas by 1859, and the territory entered as a free state in January 1861.
events.hook: Letting settlers vote on slavery turned Kansas into a battlefield.
events.story: Illinois Senator Stephen Douglas introduced a bill in January 1854 to organise the Kansas and Nebraska territories, with slavery to be decided by their settlers under 'popular sovereignty'. The bill repealed the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery north of 36°30', and President Franklin Pierce signed it on 30 May 1854. Pro-slavery Missourians and anti-slavery Northerners poured into Kansas; by 1856 the territory had two rival legislatures and open fighting, 'Bleeding Kansas'.
events.then: Anti-slavery Whigs, Democrats and Free Soilers formed the Republican Party in 1854; it carried most of the North in 1856 and elected Abraham Lincoln in 1860. About 55 people died in Kansas by 1859, and the territory entered as a free state in January 1861.
events.now: The act replaced national parties with sectional ones: it destroyed the Whigs, created the Republican Party and put the first armed fighting over slavery in Kansas, which made a sectional presidential election in 1860 the likely outcome.
events.fact: Abolitionist John Brown and his sons killed five pro-slavery settlers at Pottawatomie Creek in May 1856, days after a South Carolina congressman had beaten Massachusetts Senator Charles Sumner unconscious on the Senate floor.

causes.why: The 1850 idea of letting settlers vote on slavery was extended to Kansas, repealing the Missouri line and setting off 'Bleeding Kansas'.

q.before: The Missouri Compromise banned slavery north of 36°30'.
q.how: An act of Congress.
q.lasted: It deepened the split that led to war.

events.bluf: Illinois Senator Stephen Douglas wanted the Nebraska territory organised for a transcontinental railroad through Chicago and needed Southern votes to do it. He gave them the repeal of the Missouri Compromise line and let settlers vote on slavery. Pro- and anti-slavery settlers fought over Kansas, the Whig Party broke up, the Republican Party was founded to resist slavery's spread, and the sectional politics that produced secession in 1860 took shape within two years.
events.lens: Reopening a settled question can unleash the conflicts the original settlement contained.

events.who: Gold miners led by Peter Lalor; colonial soldiers and police
events.hook: Gold miners rebelled against licence fees and lack of a vote, and about 27 people died.
events.what: Gold miners rebelled against licence fees and lack of a vote, and about 27 people died.
events.story: Victoria's goldfields charged every digger 30 shillings a month for a licence, enforced by police 'digger hunts', and gave him no vote. In October 1854 a hotel keeper was acquitted of killing a miner, and diggers burned his hotel. Under Irish-born digger Peter Lalor the miners swore an oath under the Southern Cross flag and built a stockade at Eureka. Soldiers and police stormed it at dawn on 3 December 1854; about 22 diggers and a handful of soldiers died. A Melbourne jury acquitted all 13 miners tried for treason.
events.why: Heavy licence fees enforced by raids, with no vote to change them, gave the diggers a grievance. The acquittal of a hotel keeper for killing a miner turned grievance into revolt.
events.then: A royal commission replaced the licence with a £1 miner's right in 1855 that carried the vote. Victoria extended the vote to all adult men in 1857. Lalor entered the Victorian Parliament in 1855.
events.sig: A royal commission replaced the licence with a £1 miner's right in 1855 that carried the vote. Victoria extended the vote to all adult men in 1857. Lalor entered the Victorian Parliament in 1855.
events.now: Eureka's acquittals showed the colonial government that juries sided with the diggers, which made manhood suffrage in Victoria in 1857 the path of least resistance; the Southern Cross flag has been a protest symbol since.

causes.why: Miners resented costly gold licences and having no vote.

q.before: Colonial officials and the gold licence system.
q.how: An armed rebellion, quickly crushed.
q.winners: The miners, in the end, through reform.
q.lasted: Its reforms did.

events.bluf: Ballarat's miners wanted the licence fee abolished, the police raids ended and the vote; the Victorian government wanted the licence enforced. Troops stormed the miners' stockade at dawn on 3 December 1854 and killed about 22 diggers. A Melbourne jury acquitted every miner charged with treason, the licence was replaced within a year and Victoria gave men the vote in 1857; the revolt failed in the field and won its demands.
events.lens: Movements that lose the battle can still win the argument, especially when juries and public opinion side with them.
events.trig: The death of digger James Scobie outside Bentley's Eureka Hotel in October 1854 and the acquittal of its owner.
events.fact: Lalor lost an arm at the stockade and served as Speaker of the Victorian Legislative Assembly from 1880 to 1887.

kv: miners tried for treason; all acquitted

events.who: King Mongkut (Rama IV); Sir John Bowring
events.hook: Siam opened its trade to Britain on British terms, and kept its independence.
events.what: Siam opened its trade to Britain on British terms, and kept its independence.
events.story: Siamese King Mongkut (Rama IV) had watched Britain defeat China in the Opium War and Burma in two wars. British envoy Sir John Bowring arrived in Bangkok in 1855. Mongkut agreed to low tariffs, free trade and extraterritorial rights for British subjects.
events.why: Mongkut chose trade concessions rather than giving Britain a pretext for war.
events.then: Siam signed similar treaties with the United States and France in 1856 and with other Western powers after. Rice exports grew and Siam began to modernise.
events.sig: Siam signed similar treaties with the United States and France in 1856 and with other Western powers after. Rice exports grew and Siam began to modernise.
events.now: The treaty set the pattern by which Siam traded concessions for survival, from 1855 to the border cessions of 1893 to 1909; Thailand is the only Southeast Asian country never colonised by a European power.

causes.why: Burma's defeats by Britain, and China's in the Opium War, showed Siam the cost of resisting.
Siam's king had watched Britain force open China and chose to negotiate instead.

q.what: Rice, teak and other Siamese exports for British goods.
q.who: British merchants and Siamese exporters; the royal monopolies lost.
q.scale: Siam's trade grew rapidly.
q.daily: Rice farming for export expanded.
q.system: Free trade that kept Siam independent but limited its sovereignty.

events.bluf: Siamese King Mongkut set out to keep Siam out of a war with Britain after watching Britain defeat China and Burma. He accepted free trade, low tariffs and extraterritorial rights for British subjects on terms brought by British envoy Sir John Bowring in 1855. Siam opened to Western commerce, signed similar treaties with other powers and began to modernise, and it kept its independence while every neighbour was colonised.
events.lens: Small states sometimes preserve their sovereignty by conceding on trade.
events.fact: Mongkut spent 27 years as a Buddhist monk before taking the throne and taught himself English and Latin.

kv: maximum duty Siam could charge on imports

events.who: Supreme Court (Chief Justice Taney); Dred Scott
events.what: Ruled Black Americans weren't citizens; Congress couldn't ban slavery in territories.
events.why: Buchanan and the Court's Southern majority hoped a sweeping ruling would take slavery out of politics. Taney held that the founders had meant no Black person to be part of the political community.
events.sig: Republicans made the ruling their campaign issue; Abraham Lincoln argued in 1858 that it was one step from making slavery lawful in every state. Northern Democrats split from Southern over whether settlers could still bar slavery, and the divided party lost the 1860 election. The 14th Amendment of 1868 overturned the ruling.
events.hook: The Supreme Court ruled that Black Americans could never be citizens.
events.story: Dred Scott, an enslaved man, sued for freedom in 1846 on the ground that his owner had taken him to live in the free state of Illinois and the free Wisconsin Territory. On 6 March 1857 Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled for a 7-2 majority that no Black person, free or enslaved, could be a citizen with standing to sue, and that the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery in the territories had been unconstitutional. President James Buchanan, inaugurated two days earlier, had lobbied a Northern justice to join the majority.
events.then: Republicans made the ruling their campaign issue; Abraham Lincoln argued in 1858 that it was one step from making slavery lawful in every state. Northern Democrats split from Southern over whether settlers could still bar slavery, and the divided party lost the 1860 election. The 14th Amendment of 1868 overturned the ruling.
events.now: The ruling is the standard example of a court entrenching injustice; it was reversed by the 14th Amendment of 1868, whose citizenship clause was written against it.

causes.why: The Supreme Court tried to settle the issue by ruling that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories at all.

q.before: Courts disagreed about slavery in free territories.
q.how: A Supreme Court ruling.
q.claim: That Black Americans could not be citizens and Congress could not ban slavery in territories.
q.lasted: No: the 14th Amendment overturned it in 1868.

events.bluf: Chief Justice Roger Taney and the Supreme Court's Southern majority set out to settle the slavery question by law, with President-elect James Buchanan's encouragement. They ruled that no Black American could be a citizen and that Congress lacked the power to bar slavery from any territory. The ruling declared the Republican Party's whole platform unconstitutional, which made compromise impossible and drove the North to the Republicans in 1860.
events.lens: Court rulings that try to settle a deep political conflict can inflame it instead.
events.fact: Scott was freed by his owners within three months of losing and died of tuberculosis in 1858.

events.what: Large revolt against Company rule.
events.why: Annexations such as Awadh in 1856 and the lost status of landed elites came first. Heavy land taxes, fear of forced Christianisation and sepoy grievances over pay and service overseas added fuel.
events.sig: Britain abolished the Company and ruled India directly through a viceroy from 1858; Bahadur Shah II was exiled to Rangoon. Britain stopped annexing princely states, recruited soldiers from groups it considered loyal, Sikhs, Gurkhas and Punjabi Muslims among them, and kept British society more segregated from Indian.
events.hook: Indian soldiers rose against the British, and Britain took direct rule.
events.story: On 10 May 1857 Indian soldiers, sepoys, of the Bengal army at Meerut mutinied after 85 comrades were jailed for refusing cartridges rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, offensive to Hindus and Muslims alike. They marched to Delhi and proclaimed the aged Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah II their leader. Revolt spread across Awadh and central India; rebels killed British civilians at Kanpur, and British forces killed captured and suspected rebels in large numbers. British forces retook Delhi in September 1857 and Lucknow in March 1858.
events.then: Britain abolished the Company and ruled India directly through a viceroy from 1858; Bahadur Shah II was exiled to Rangoon. Britain stopped annexing princely states, recruited soldiers from groups it considered loyal, Sikhs, Gurkhas and Punjabi Muslims among them, and kept British society more segregated from Indian.
events.now: The rebellion ended Company rule and the policy of reform; the Crown governed India after 1858 through the princes and landlords, kept Indians out of the army's command and treated Hindus and Muslims as separate blocs, a structure that shaped partition ninety years later.

causes.why: A century of Company conquest, annexations and Westernising reforms, plus a rumour that new rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat, set off the 1857 revolt.
The defeat left the Company paramount; Nana Sahib, heir of the last Peshwa, became a leader of the 1857 rebellion.

q.why: Grievances over religion, land and British rule, sparked by the cartridges.
q.decided: British reinforcements and loyal regiments, especially Sikhs.
q.cost: Tens of thousands killed, with massacres on both sides.
q.changed: The Company was abolished and the Crown took over.

events.bluf: Sepoys of the Bengal army mutinied at Meerut over cartridges rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, and princes, landlords and peasants across northern India rose with them to end Company rule. British forces retook Delhi and Lucknow by 1858, with atrocities on both sides. Company rule and the Mughal dynasty ended, and the Crown governed India afterward through princes and landlords, with Hindus and Muslims counted as separate blocs.
events.trig: The cartridge controversy and the jailing of 85 sepoys at Meerut on 9 May 1857 for refusing to use them.
events.lens: Rebellions often begin over a symbolic grievance that crystallizes deeper ones.
events.fact: Indian nationalists call it the First War of Independence; British writers called it the Mutiny.

toll.n: Indian deaths include those from the famine and disease that followed. Estimates vary greatly.

events.what: Crown replaced the East India Company.
events.why: The 1857 rebellion convinced Parliament that a trading company could not govern India.
events.sig: British rule lasted 89 years. Famines in 1876-78 and 1896-1900 killed millions. The English-educated middle class founded the Indian National Congress in 1885, which led the independence movement.
events.hook: The British Crown took direct control of India.
events.story: The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred power from the East India Company to the British Crown. Queen Victoria's proclamation of 1 November 1858 promised religious tolerance and equal treatment under law. A viceroy ruled from Calcutta, from 1911 New Delhi, through a civil service of around 1,000 British officers over a population of some 200 million.
events.then: British rule lasted 89 years. Famines in 1876-78 and 1896-1900 killed millions. The English-educated middle class founded the Indian National Congress in 1885, which led the independence movement.
events.now: India's railways, legal system, civil service and use of English are Raj legacies, and how to weigh them against its famines and extraction is fiercely debated in India and Britain.

causes.why: After crushing the rebellion, Parliament abolished Company rule and the crown governed India directly.

q.before: The East India Company ruled India.
q.how: An act of Parliament.
q.winners: Britain, and princes who kept their states.
q.lasted: Until independence in 1947.

events.bluf: Parliament took India from the East India Company to govern it directly after the rebellion of 1857. A viceroy and a civil service ruled from Calcutta, building railways, courts and an English-educated elite while extracting revenue and presiding over famines. The Raj lasted 89 years, and the elite it created founded the Congress that ended it.
events.lens: Imperial education creates the elite that later demands independence.
events.fact: The Indian Civil Service never had much more than 1,000 officers; by 1900 they administered nearly 300 million people.

kv: British officials of the Indian Civil Service ran it

events.who: US consul Townsend Harris; chief minister Ii Naosuke
events.what: Japan signed treaties that let foreigners live under their own laws and set Japan's tariffs for it.
events.why: US consul Townsend Harris warned that Britain and France, fresh from beating China again, would impose worse terms by force.
events.sig: Opponents rallied around the emperor, and chief minister Ii Naosuke launched the Ansei Purge against them in 1858-59. He was assassinated in 1860.
events.hook: Japan signed treaties that let foreigners live under their own laws and set Japan's tariffs for it.
events.story: Chief minister Ii Naosuke signed the Harris Treaty aboard the USS Powhatan in Edo Bay on 29 July 1858 after Emperor Kōmei refused to approve it. Britain, France, Russia and the Netherlands quickly got the same terms: more open ports, extraterritoriality, with foreigners tried in their own courts, and low fixed tariffs.
events.then: Opponents rallied around the emperor, and chief minister Ii Naosuke launched the Ansei Purge against them in 1858-59. He was assassinated in 1860.
events.now: Undoing these treaties became the central goal of Meiji foreign policy, achieved only in 1899 for extraterritoriality and 1911 for tariffs.

causes.why: Kanagawa opened the door; Harris pushed for full trade.

q.before: Japan controlled its own trade and justice.
q.how: Foreigners became exempt from Japanese law; Japan couldn't set its own tariffs.
q.winners: Western merchants; losers were Japanese sovereignty and the shogun's reputation.
q.lasted: Japan spent 40 years getting them revised, finally succeeding in 1894–1911.

events.bluf: US consul Townsend Harris pressed Japan for a full commercial treaty, warning that Britain and France would impose worse terms by force. Chief minister Ii Naosuke signed in July 1858 without the emperor's approval, and Britain, France, Russia and the Netherlands took the same terms. The treaties gave Western powers extraterritorial rights and control of Japan's tariffs; outrage turned against the shogunate, and revising them became the central goal of Meiji Japan.
events.lens: National humiliation can become the driving force of a modernization programme.
events.fact: US consul Townsend Harris waited two years at Shimoda before being received in Edo; his audience with the shogun in December 1857 was the first granted to a foreign diplomat.

events.what: Published theory of evolution by natural selection.
events.why: Darwin had the evidence for decades and feared the reaction. Wallace's independent discovery of the same theory in 1858 forced his hand.
events.sig: Religious leaders attacked the book at once. Most scientists accepted evolution within decades; natural selection as the mechanism stayed disputed until genetics confirmed it in the 1930s and 1940s. 'Survival of the fittest' was applied to societies and races and fed eugenics and imperial ideology.
events.hook: Darwin showed that all life evolved by natural selection.
events.story: English naturalist Charles Darwin had worked on the problem since the Beagle voyage, for more than twenty years. In 1858 naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace sent him a paper setting out the same theory. Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species' in November 1859. He argued that individuals vary, more are born than can survive, and those with helpful traits leave more offspring, so species change over long periods.
events.then: Religious leaders attacked the book at once. Most scientists accepted evolution within decades; natural selection as the mechanism stayed disputed until genetics confirmed it in the 1930s and 1940s. 'Survival of the fittest' was applied to societies and races and fed eugenics and imperial ideology.
events.now: Evolution is the foundation of modern biology and medicine, from vaccines to genetics.
events.fact: The first printing of 1,250 copies sold out to the trade on the day of publication.

causes.why: What Darwin saw on the voyage started his thinking about species.

q.problem: Why are there so many species, and why do they fit their environments?
q.how: Natural selection: small variations that help survival are passed on.
q.replaced: The belief that each species was created separately and never changes.
q.spread: Scientists accepted evolution within about 20 years.
q.next: Genetics, and the modern study of life.

events.bluf: English naturalist Charles Darwin set out to explain how species arise from evidence gathered over twenty years, and published when Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea. He showed that variation, competition and inheritance produce new species over long periods, with no design required. Biology got its organising theory, religious accounts of creation lost their standing among the educated, and a misapplied 'survival of the fittest' served racism and empire.
events.lens: Scientific ideas get borrowed for political ends: separate what a theory says from what people claim it justifies.

kv: copies in the first printing, sold out on day one

events.h: Chief minister assassinated in the snow
events.who: Ii Naosuke; samurai from Mito domain
events.what: Samurai killed the shogun's chief minister outside Edo Castle for signing the treaties.
events.why: Rage at the treaties and the purge, and a belief that the shogun had betrayed the emperor.
events.sig: Attacks on foreigners and officials multiplied, and the shogunate's authority visibly crumbled.
events.hook: Samurai killed the shogun's chief minister outside Edo Castle for signing the treaties.
events.story: Chief minister Ii Naosuke had signed the unequal treaties of 1858 and purged his critics in the Ansei Purge. On a snowy morning in March 1860, 18 samurai, 17 from Mito and one from Satsuma, ambushed his procession at the Sakurada Gate of Edo Castle and cut off his head.
events.then: Attacks on foreigners and officials multiplied, and the shogunate's authority visibly crumbled.
events.now: It is a turning point: the regime's authority visibly cracked, and assassination became a recurring feature of Japanese politics into the 1930s.

causes.why: Ii had signed the treaties without the emperor's consent.

q.before: The shogun's government looked untouchable.
q.how: Political murder became a tool; 'sonnō jōi' (revere the emperor, expel the barbarians) spread.
q.claim: Loyalty to the emperor over the shogun.
q.lasted: The shogunate never recovered its authority.

events.bluf: Samurai from Mito domain set out to kill chief minister Ii Naosuke for signing the unequal treaties and purging their allies. Eighteen of them ambushed his procession in the snow outside Edo Castle's Sakurada Gate in March 1860 and took his head. The shogunate had shown it could neither protect its own leaders nor control samurai anger, and a cycle of political violence began that ended in the regime's fall in 1868.
events.lens: When a regime cannot protect its own top officials, its authority is collapsing.
events.fact: The shogunate concealed Ii's death for weeks, reporting him wounded, while it arranged the succession to his domain.

events.what: Imperial palace looted and burned.
events.why: Revenge for the torture and killing of envoys, and pressure on the emperor to accept Allied terms.
events.sig: China legalised opium, opened more ports and ceded Kowloon to Britain. Russia used the moment to take China's Pacific coast north of Korea in the Treaty of Peking of 1860.
events.hook: British and French troops looted and burned the emperor's Summer Palace.
events.story: British and French troops reached Beijing in October 1860 during the Second Opium War, and the Xianfeng Emperor fled to Jehol. Qing officials had tortured and killed members of an Allied negotiating party. British envoy Lord Elgin ordered the Yuanmingyuan palace gardens, the Summer Palace, looted and burned.
events.then: China legalised opium, opened more ports and ceded Kowloon to Britain. Russia used the moment to take China's Pacific coast north of Korea in the Treaty of Peking of 1860.
events.now: The burning of the palace at the end of the Second Opium War forced the Qing to open Beijing to foreign legations and the interior to trade and missionaries; it is the act China's government cites as the start of its century of humiliation.
events.fact: The ruins are a national memorial, and China asks for the looted treasures back.

causes.why: With the Qing fighting the Taiping, Britain and France pressed new demands in the Second Opium War and burned the emperor's Summer Palace in 1860.

q.why: Britain and France forced China to accept wider trade and diplomacy.
q.stakes: China's sovereignty and the Allies' treaty demands.
q.decided: Allied troops occupied Beijing.
q.cost: Hundreds of buildings and countless treasures destroyed.
q.changed: China signed the Convention of Peking, opening more ports.

events.bluf: British and French commanders in the Second Opium War wanted the Qing court punished for the torture and killing of their envoys and forced to accept their terms. In October 1860 British envoy Lord Elgin had the Yuanmingyuan palace gardens looted and burned. The Qing signed the Convention of Peking within days, legalising opium and opening Beijing and the interior, and the burning became China's defining symbol of Western humiliation.
events.lens: Cultural destruction can leave deeper grievances than military defeat.

kv: British troops set the fires, burning for 3 days

events.hook: A bishop and 'Darwin's bulldog' clashed over evolution before a packed hall.
events.what: A bishop and 'Darwin's bulldog' clashed over evolution before a packed hall.
events.story: At the British Association meeting in the Oxford University Museum on 30 June 1860, Bishop of Oxford Samuel Wilberforce spoke against Darwin's book. He is reported to have asked biologist Thomas Huxley whether it was through his grandfather or his grandmother that he claimed descent from an ape. Huxley is said to have replied that he would rather have an ape for a grandfather than a man who used his gifts to obscure the truth. No full record of the exchange was taken.
events.why: Darwin's book, published seven months earlier, had provoked argument across educated England. Wilberforce had been briefed by anatomist Richard Owen, Huxley's rival.
events.then: Most scientists accepted evolution within about 20 years. Natural selection as its mechanism stayed disputed until the 1930s.
events.sig: Most scientists accepted evolution within about 20 years. Natural selection as its mechanism stayed disputed until the 1930s.
events.now: The retold debate set the rule in England that a scientific claim answers to evidence rather than to bishops; the professional, secular science of the later 1800s was built on that standing.

causes.why: The book's publication set off public argument.

q.problem: Was evolution by natural selection good science?
q.how: A public argument at a scientific meeting.
q.replaced: Unquestioned religious accounts of creation within science.
q.spread: Newspapers and retellings made it famous.
q.next: Scientific acceptance of evolution.

events.bluf: Bishop of Oxford Samuel Wilberforce attacked Darwin's book at the British Association meeting to defend scripture and the fixity of species; biologist Thomas Huxley answered to establish that science owed the Church no deference. Neither side won on the day, and the accounts that made it a rout were written years later. The legend outlived the exchange, and it marked the point at which English scientists stopped answering to bishops.
events.lens: Public debates matter more for the stories told about them than for what was actually said.
events.fact: Royal Navy officer Robert FitzRoy, Darwin's captain on the Beagle, stood up in the audience holding a Bible and begged the room to believe God rather than man.
At unification only a small minority of Italians, by some estimates under 10 per cent, spoke standard Italian.
events.who: Cavour, Garibaldi, King Victor Emmanuel II
events.hook: Cavour's diplomacy and Garibaldi's Redshirts made Italy one kingdom.
events.what: Cavour's diplomacy and Garibaldi's Redshirts made Italy one kingdom.
events.story: Piedmontese Prime Minister Camillo Cavour won French help to drive Austria out of Lombardy in 1859. Nationalist general Giuseppe Garibaldi landed in Sicily with about a thousand volunteers in May 1860 and took Sicily and Naples by the autumn. Plebiscites joined the central and southern states to Piedmont. On 17 March 1861 Piedmontese King Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of Italy.
events.why: Nationalism had a following among the educated and in the towns. Cavour's Piedmont had the army and the diplomacy. Austria stood alone after its neutrality in the Crimean War.
events.then: Venice joined in 1866 and Rome in 1870, after French troops left; the papacy refused to recognise the Italian state until 1929. The south rose in a brigands' war that the army put down through the 1860s.
events.sig: Venice joined in 1866 and Rome in 1870, after French troops left; the papacy refused to recognise the Italian state until 1929. The south rose in a brigands' war that the army put down through the 1860s.
events.now: Italy's north-south economic divide dates from unification and still shapes its politics, from regional parties to arguments over how taxes are shared.

causes.why: Piedmont joined Britain and France in the Crimean War and won French backing for its 1859 war against Austria.
1848's failure taught Italian nationalists that they needed Piedmont's army and French help, not just popular uprisings.

q.before: Italy was divided among Austria, the Pope, and several kingdoms and duchies.
q.how: Wars, revolution and plebiscites.
q.claim: Italian national unity under the House of Savoy.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Piedmontese Prime Minister Camillo Cavour set out to unite northern Italy under the House of Savoy with French help; nationalist general Giuseppe Garibaldi's volunteers took the south and handed it over. A Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in March 1861 and counted as a great power in name. A richer north absorbed a poorer south in two years, and the divide between them has shaped Italian politics ever since.
events.lens: National unification often means one region absorbing the others on its own terms.

events.hook: Russia freed 23 million serfs, two years before Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.
events.what: Russia freed 23 million serfs, two years before Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.
events.story: Defeat in the Crimean War convinced Russian Tsar Alexander II that Russia needed to modernise. His Emancipation Manifesto of 3 March 1861, 19 February in the Russian calendar, freed the privately owned serfs. The peasants received allotments and paid redemption dues for them over 49 years; the plots were often smaller than the land they had farmed before.
events.why: Military defeat came first. Fear of revolt came second: 'better to abolish serfdom from above than wait for it to abolish itself from below', the tsar told the Moscow nobility in 1856.
events.then: Redemption payments, debt and land hunger kept the villages poor. Peasant unrest ran through the decades and erupted in 1905 and 1917; the payments were cancelled in 1907.
events.sig: Redemption payments, debt and land hunger kept the villages poor. Peasant unrest ran through the decades and erupted in 1905 and 1917; the payments were cancelled in 1907.
events.now: Emancipation left peasants paying for land they had farmed as their own; the land question it left open drove rural revolt in 1905 and 1917, and it remains the standing case for whether reform from above can hold without political freedom.

causes.why: Defeat in Crimea convinced Alexander II that Russia had to modernise, and serfdom had to go first.

q.before: About 23 million privately owned serfs were bound to their masters.
q.how: An imperial decree.
q.claim: The tsar's authority to modernise from above.
q.winners: Serfs gained freedom but heavy debts; nobles kept much land.
q.lasted: Yes, though land hunger fed revolution.

events.bluf: Russian Tsar Alexander II freed 23 million privately owned serfs to modernise a state defeated in Crimea before revolt did it for him. Legal bondage ended; the peasants paid for their allotments over 49 years and often got less land than they had farmed. Rural poverty and land hunger fed the unrest of 1905 and 1917.
events.lens: Reforms from above that leave the core grievance unresolved can deepen instability.
events.fact: Many peasants refused to believe the terms and held that the true decree, giving them the land free, had been hidden by the landlords.

events.what: Confederates fired on a federal fort.
events.why: Decades of conflict over slavery's expansion came first. The South's economy rested on the labour of about 4 million enslaved people, and the free-labour North had the population and the votes to outgrow it.
events.sig: Some 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers died. The Union's advantages in industry and manpower, emancipation and the enlistment of about 180,000 Black soldiers brought victory in April 1865. The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments ended slavery, defined citizenship and protected the vote, and Southern states nullified much of the last two after 1877.
events.hook: Southern guns fired on Fort Sumter, and America went to war with itself.
events.story: Republican Abraham Lincoln won the election of November 1860 without carrying a single Southern state. South Carolina seceded in December and six more states followed by February 1861, forming the Confederate States with Mississippi Senator Jefferson Davis as president. On 12 April 1861 Confederate batteries fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour, and the garrison surrendered the next day. Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers, and four more states, Virginia among them, joined the Confederacy.
events.then: Some 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers died. The Union's advantages in industry and manpower, emancipation and the enlistment of about 180,000 Black soldiers brought victory in April 1865. The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments ended slavery, defined citizenship and protected the vote, and Southern states nullified much of the last two after 1877.
events.now: The war ended slavery, settled that the Union could not be left, and created a federal state with an income tax, a national currency and a standing claim on its citizens that the republic of 1789 lacked.

sites.d: First shots, April 12, 1861.
Bloodiest single day in US history; gave Lincoln the win he needed to announce emancipation.
Lee's invasion of the North fails.
Union takes control of the Mississippi.
Sherman's capture helped re-elect Lincoln.
Lee surrenders to Grant.

causes.why: Fury over the act created the Republican Party; its victory in 1860 led the Deep South to secede.
Canals and then railroads tied the Midwest's farms to New York's markets rather than to the South's river trade, one reason the Northwest stood with the Union in 1861.

q.why: Southern states seceded to protect slavery.
q.stakes: The Union's survival and slavery's future.
q.decided: Union manpower, industry and finally Grant's strategy.
q.cost: About 620,000 to 750,000 dead.
q.changed: Slavery ended and the Union was preserved.

events.bluf: Eleven Southern states seceded to protect slavery after Abraham Lincoln won the presidency on a pledge to stop its spread; Lincoln fought to hold the Union together. Four years of war killed 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers and ended with the Confederacy destroyed and slavery abolished. The Union's victory fixed the supremacy of the national government, and the collapse of Reconstruction left the question of Black citizenship unsettled for another century.
events.trig: Lincoln's election in November 1860 and the Confederate attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861.
events.lens: When a political system can no longer compromise over a core economic and moral question, secession or war follows.
events.fact: No one was killed in the 34-hour bombardment of Fort Sumter; the war's first death came when a gun exploded during the surrender salute.

toll.n: Two-thirds died of disease. Recent estimates put total deaths at 620,000–750,000, about as many as all other US wars combined.

events.what: France tried to install an empire; lost at Puebla (Cinco de Mayo).
events.why: Mexico suspended its debt payments. Napoleon III wanted a French-backed empire while the United States was busy with its civil war, and Mexican conservatives beaten in the Reform War invited him.
events.sig: France took Mexico City in 1863 and made Austrian archduke Maximilian emperor in 1864, but faced continuing guerrilla resistance and the hostility of the United States once its civil war ended in 1865.
events.hook: France invaded Mexico, and Mexicans beat them at Puebla.
events.story: In 1861 Mexico under President Benito Juárez suspended payments on its foreign debts. Britain, France and Spain landed troops at Veracruz; Britain and Spain soon withdrew, but French Emperor Napoleon III's forces marched inland, seeking a Catholic monarchy friendly to France. Mexican forces under general Ignacio Zaragoza beat the French at Puebla on 5 May 1862. France took Mexico City in June 1863.
events.then: France took Mexico City in 1863 and made Austrian archduke Maximilian emperor in 1864, but faced continuing guerrilla resistance and the hostility of the United States once its civil war ended in 1865.
events.now: The collapse of the French-backed empire in 1867 discredited monarchy in Mexico for good and fixed the liberal republic under Juárez, with the Church's power limited by the reform laws.
events.fact: Cinco de Mayo, the 1862 victory at Puebla, is now celebrated more in the United States than in Mexico.

causes.why: War, debt and a civil war left Mexico bankrupt. When Juárez suspended debt payments, France invaded.

q.why: Napoleon III wanted a French-backed empire in Mexico.
q.decided: French reinforcements after the defeat at Puebla.
q.cost: Tens of thousands dead over five years.
q.changed: Maximilian was made emperor of Mexico.

events.bluf: French Emperor Napoleon III invaded Mexico to install a Catholic monarchy under French protection while the United States was absorbed by its civil war. His army lost at Puebla on 5 May 1862, took Mexico City in 1863 and placed Austrian archduke Maximilian on a throne that fell in 1867. The scheme failed against Mexican resistance and US pressure, and it strengthened Mexican nationalism and the republic under President Benito Juárez.
events.lens: Great powers exploit their rivals' distractions, and the window closes when the rival recovers.

events.what: Declared enslaved people in rebel states free.
events.why: Lincoln wanted to weaken the Confederacy's labour force, recruit Black soldiers and make it politically impossible for Britain and France to back the South. Enslaved people fleeing to Union lines had already made slavery a war issue.
events.sig: About 180,000 Black soldiers fought for the Union, Britain and France stayed out, and the 13th Amendment abolished slavery nationwide in December 1865.
events.hook: Lincoln turned a war to save the Union into a war to end slavery.
events.story: Enslaved people had been fleeing to Union lines since 1861, and Congress had declared them confiscated property. US President Abraham Lincoln issued a preliminary proclamation on 22 September 1862, five days after the Union stopped Lee at Antietam. On 1 January 1863 the final proclamation declared enslaved people in areas still in rebellion 'forever free' and opened the army and navy to Black men. It left the loyal slave states and Union-held districts untouched, so it freed few people at once; every Union advance thereafter brought freedom.
events.then: About 180,000 Black soldiers fought for the Union, Britain and France stayed out, and the 13th Amendment abolished slavery nationwide in December 1865.
events.now: The proclamation turned the war into a war against slavery, kept Britain and France out of it, and brought 180,000 Black soldiers into the Union army, which made emancipation irreversible before the amendment of 1865.
events.fact: Juneteenth, a federal holiday since 2021, marks the day the news reached the last enslaved Texans.

causes.why: As the war dragged on, Lincoln turned emancipation into a war aim, weakening the South and keeping Britain and France out.

q.before: Slavery was legal in the rebel states.
q.how: A presidential war order.
q.winners: Enslaved people in Union-held areas, and the Union cause.
q.lasted: Yes: made permanent by the 13th Amendment.

events.bluf: US President Abraham Lincoln wanted to strip the Confederacy of its labour, recruit Black soldiers and make it impossible for Britain or France to recognise the South. On 1 January 1863 he declared enslaved people in the rebel states 'forever free' under his war powers. The Union's war became a war against slavery, about 180,000 Black men joined its army, and emancipation was irreversible before the 13th Amendment made it law in 1865.
events.lens: Wars change their purposes: what begins as a fight to preserve a state can become a fight to transform it.

kv: enslaved people in Confederate areas it declared free
Black soldiers who then served in the Union army

events.what: Biggest battle of the war; Lee's invasion of the North failed.
events.why: Lee wanted to feed his army off Northern farms, draw Union forces out of Virginia and win a victory that would strengthen the Northern peace movement. Chancellorsville had convinced him his army could beat any force it met.
events.sig: Lee retreated to Virginia on 4 July, the day Vicksburg surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant and gave the Union the Mississippi. The South never invaded the North again. Lincoln dedicated the cemetery on 19 November 1863 with a 270-word address.
events.hook: Three days in Pennsylvania ended the South's last invasion of the North.
events.story: After his victory at Chancellorsville in May 1863, Confederate General Robert E. Lee led about 75,000 men into Pennsylvania. The armies met at Gettysburg on 1 July 1863, and Union General George Meade, in command for three days, held the ridges south of the town. On 3 July Lee sent about 12,500 men against the Union centre in Pickett's Charge; half of them fell. About 50,000 men were killed, wounded or captured over the three days.
events.then: Lee retreated to Virginia on 4 July, the day Vicksburg surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant and gave the Union the Mississippi. The South never invaded the North again. Lincoln dedicated the cemetery on 19 November 1863 with a 270-word address.
events.now: With Vicksburg's fall the next day, Gettysburg ended the Confederacy's capacity for offensive war; Lincoln's address there in November 1863 redefined the Union's purpose as equality and government by the people, the terms in which American democracy has described itself since.
events.fact: Lincoln's address ran about 270 words and took two minutes; orator Edward Everett, the main speaker before him, talked for two hours.

sites.d: Union line held on the far left on day two.
Failed Confederate assault on day three: the 'high-water mark' of the Confederacy.
Surrendered the next day, July 4, 1863.

q.why: Lee hoped a victory in the North would force peace.
q.decided: Union defences on high ground, and the failure of Pickett's Charge.
q.cost: About 50,000 casualties.
q.changed: The South never invaded the North again.

events.bluf: Confederate General Robert E. Lee invaded Pennsylvania to win a battle on Northern soil that would break Northern will and bring peace. Union General George Meade's army held the high ground for three days and broke Pickett's Charge on the third; about 50,000 men on both sides were killed, wounded or captured. Lee never invaded again, Vicksburg fell the next day, and the Confederacy's chance of winning by arms was gone.
events.lens: Words can define a war's meaning as much as battles decide its outcome.

toll.n: The bloodiest battle of the war.

events.h: Blackbirding: Pacific Islanders brought to Queensland
events.who: Labour recruiters; Pacific Islanders; Queensland sugar planters
events.hook: About 62,000 Pacific Islanders were brought, many by deception or force, to work Queensland's sugar fields.
events.what: About 62,000 Pacific Islanders were brought, many by deception or force, to work Queensland's sugar fields.
events.story: Queensland's planters began importing labour in 1863, when Sydney merchant Robert Towns brought the first shipload to his cotton plantation. From 1863 to 1904 recruiters took about 62,000 workers from Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands and other islands to Queensland on three-year contracts. Many were tricked or kidnapped, a practice called 'blackbirding', and thousands died of disease and overwork. The Commonwealth's Pacific Island Labourers Act of 1901 ordered their deportation.
events.why: Planters wanted cheap tropical labour. Recruiters were paid per head, and the islands lay beyond effective law.
events.then: Deportations ran from 1906, and the sugar industry was reserved for white labour under bounties. A minority won exemptions and stayed; their descendants were recognised in 1994.
events.sig: Deportations ran from 1906, and the sugar industry was reserved for white labour under bounties. A minority won exemptions and stayed; their descendants were recognised in 1994.
events.now: The trade fixed the pattern by which Australia imported non-white labour and then expelled it; the descendants of those who stayed were recognised as a distinct community, Australian South Sea Islanders, in 1994.

q.what: Labour for Queensland's sugar plantations.
q.who: Planters profited; Islanders were exploited and many died.
q.scale: About 62,000 contracts over 40 years.
q.daily: Long hours in the cane fields for low pay.
q.system: Indentured labour, ended by the White Australia policy.

events.bluf: Queensland sugar planters wanted cheap labour for tropical plantations they believed white men would refuse. Recruiters brought tens of thousands of Pacific Islanders to Queensland between 1863 and 1904 on fixed contracts, many by deception or force, and thousands died. The new Commonwealth deported most of them after 1906 under the White Australia policy, so that labour exploitation and racial exclusion followed one another.
events.lens: Societies import cheap labour when they need it and exclude the labourers when politics turns against them.
events.fact: Townsville is named after Robert Towns, who brought the first Islander labourers to Queensland.

events.what: British warships shelled Satsuma's capital, and Satsuma decided to learn from Britain instead of fighting it.
events.why: Britain demanded punishment for Richardson's killing.
events.sig: Satsuma paid the indemnity, bought warships from Britain and sent students to Britain in 1865. Chōshū learned the same lesson when Western fleets bombarded Shimonoseki in 1863-64.
events.hook: British warships shelled Satsuma's capital, and Satsuma decided to learn from Britain instead of fighting it.
events.story: In September 1862 Satsuma samurai killed British merchant Charles Richardson, who had failed to give way to the procession of Satsuma regent Shimazu Hisamitsu, in what became known as the Namamugi Incident. Britain demanded compensation and the killers. When Satsuma refused, a Royal Navy squadron bombarded Kagoshima in August 1863 and burned much of the town.
events.then: Satsuma paid the indemnity, bought warships from Britain and sent students to Britain in 1865. Chōshū learned the same lesson when Western fleets bombarded Shimonoseki in 1863-64.
events.now: Defeat taught Japan's most anti-foreign domains that they had to modernise rather than 'expel the barbarians'.

causes.why: Anti-foreign violence was spreading among samurai.

q.why: Revenge and enforcing Western treaty rights.
q.stakes: Whether a Japanese domain could defy a Western power.
q.decided: British naval guns, though Satsuma's shore batteries damaged several ships.
q.cost: Much of Kagoshima burned; casualties on both sides were relatively small.
q.changed: Satsuma paid, then bought British ships and sent students to Britain.

events.bluf: Britain sent a squadron to Kagoshima in August 1863 to force Satsuma domain to pay for the killing of merchant Charles Richardson and hand over his killers. The ships burned much of the town and lost 13 men; Satsuma paid and then bought British warships. One of Japan's most anti-foreign domains concluded it had to learn from the West rather than fight it, and Satsuma and Chōshū went on to lead Meiji modernisation.
events.lens: Defeat can turn the most resistant into the most effective reformers.
events.fact: Satsuma's shore guns killed 13 British sailors, among them the captain of the flagship.
events.btt: Japan: The fall of the Tokugawa

toll.n: Much of the town burned.

events.what: Deadliest war in Latin American history.
events.why: López intervened against Brazil's ally in Uruguay, then invaded Brazilian and Argentine territory, which united his neighbours against him. Brazil and Argentina wanted the Paraguay river open and a weaker Paraguay.
events.sig: Paraguay may have lost over half its population, including most of its men; estimates range widely. Brazil and Argentina took border territory, and Brazilian troops occupied Paraguay until 1876.
events.hook: Paraguay fought Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay at once, and was devastated.
events.story: In 1864 Paraguayan President Francisco Solano López intervened in a Uruguayan civil war against Brazil's ally and invaded Brazilian Mato Grosso, then crossed Argentine territory to attack Brazil. Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay signed the Triple Alliance in May 1865. The war dragged on until López was killed at Cerro Corá on 1 March 1870.
events.then: Paraguay may have lost over half its population, including most of its men; estimates range widely. Brazil and Argentina took border territory, and Brazilian troops occupied Paraguay until 1876.
events.now: The losses of 1864-70, perhaps over half of Paraguay's people, and the territory ceded to Brazil and Argentina fixed Paraguay's standing as the region's weak state and its wariness of its larger neighbours.
events.fact: In the last campaigns López's army was made up of boys and old men; at Acosta Ñu in August 1869 Brazilian troops fought a Paraguayan force largely of children, and Paraguay marks the date as Children's Day.

q.why: López intervened in Uruguay and invaded his neighbours.
q.stakes: Paraguay's survival and control of the River Plate basin.
q.decided: The allies' far larger population and resources.
q.cost: Paraguay may have lost over half its population.
q.changed: Paraguay was devastated for generations.

events.bluf: Paraguayan President Francisco Solano López intervened in Uruguay's civil war in 1864 to check Brazil and then invaded Brazilian and Argentine territory. Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay allied against him and fought until he was killed in 1870. Paraguay lost a large share of its population and territory in the deadliest war in Latin American history, and Brazil and Argentina were confirmed as the region's powers.
events.lens: A small state that takes on bigger neighbours at once risks annihilation.

kv: of Paraguay's people died (estimates vary widely)
figs.n: The deadliest war in Latin American history. Paraguay's adult male population was almost wiped out.

events.fact: The surrender was signed in the parlour of Wilmer McLean, who had moved to Appomattox from Manassas after the war's first battle was fought across his farm.
events.who: Ulysses S. Grant; Robert E. Lee
events.hook: Lee surrendered, and the Civil War was effectively over.
events.what: Lee surrendered, and the Civil War was effectively over.
events.story: After a ten-month siege at Petersburg, Confederate General Robert E. Lee abandoned the city and Richmond on 2 April 1865 and marched west, hoping to turn south to join General Joseph Johnston's army in North Carolina. Union cavalry under General Philip Sheridan got ahead of him at Appomattox Court House. On 9 April 1865 Lee surrendered his roughly 28,000 men to Union General Ulysses S. Grant in the parlour of Wilmer McLean's house. Grant paroled the men and let them keep their horses.
events.why: The Confederacy was outnumbered and outproduced; Sherman's march had wrecked its heartland, and the Petersburg siege had stretched Lee's army to breaking point. Desertion emptied his ranks over the final winter.
events.then: Johnston surrendered to Sherman on 26 April, and the last Confederate forces in the field gave up in June. Lincoln was shot on 14 April, five days after Appomattox. The war's dead are estimated at 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers, the most of any American conflict.
events.sig: Johnston surrendered to Sherman on 26 April, and the last Confederate forces in the field gave up in June. Lincoln was shot on 14 April, five days after Appomattox. The war's dead are estimated at 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers, the most of any American conflict.
events.now: Appomattox fixed the terms of reunion: no treason trials, officers paroled, the Confederate army dissolved into the civilian population; the leniency made reconciliation between white North and South possible and left the former Confederates in place to resist Reconstruction.

causes.why: Gettysburg and the fall of Vicksburg in July 1863 turned the war decisively against the Confederacy.

q.why: Lee's army was trapped after the fall of Richmond.
q.decided: Union numbers and supplies.
q.cost: The war as a whole killed 620,000 to 750,000.
q.changed: The Confederacy collapsed.

events.bluf: Union General Ulysses S. Grant set out to destroy the Army of Northern Virginia, and Confederate General Robert E. Lee tried to break away to join the Confederacy's last army in North Carolina. Grant's cavalry cut off Lee's starving column at Appomattox and Lee surrendered on 9 April 1865. The surrender ended the war in all but name, and Grant's terms, which sent the men home with their horses and no prosecutions, set the pattern of a peace built on reunion ahead of justice for the freed people.
events.lens: Generous surrender terms speed peace but can leave the losers' social order intact.

events.hook: Five days after Lee's surrender, a Confederate sympathiser shot Lincoln at the theatre.
events.what: Five days after Lee's surrender, a Confederate sympathiser shot Lincoln at the theatre.
events.story: On the night of 14 April 1865, five days after Lee's surrender, actor John Wilkes Booth entered the presidential box at Ford's Theatre in Washington and shot Abraham Lincoln in the back of the head. Lincoln died at 7.22 the next morning in a boarding house across the street. The same night Booth's accomplice Lewis Powell stabbed Secretary of State William Seward, who survived; the man assigned to kill Vice President Andrew Johnson lost his nerve. Booth was shot dead in a Virginia barn on 26 April, and four accomplices were hanged in July.
events.why: Booth believed killing the Union's leaders would throw its government into chaos and give the South a last chance. Lincoln's speech of 11 April endorsing limited Black suffrage had enraged him.
events.then: Andrew Johnson became president, pardoned most former Confederates and let Southern states pass Black Codes restricting the freed people. Congress overrode his vetoes, passed the 14th Amendment and impeached him in 1868; he survived removal by one vote.
events.sig: Andrew Johnson became president, pardoned most former Confederates and let Southern states pass Black Codes restricting the freed people. Congress overrode his vetoes, passed the 14th Amendment and impeached him in 1868; he survived removal by one vote.
events.now: Lincoln's death put Reconstruction in the hands of a president who pardoned Confederates wholesale and vetoed civil rights bills, which produced the clash between Congress and the executive of 1866-68 and weakened protection of the freed people from the start.

causes.why: Booth struck five days after Lee's surrender, hoping to throw the victorious Union into chaos.

events.fact: On the day he was shot, Lincoln signed the law creating the Secret Service, originally to fight counterfeit money.

q.before: Lincoln led the Union to victory.
q.how: Assassination.
q.winners: No one; the South lost a moderate president.
q.lasted: Andrew Johnson's lenient policies were overturned by Congress.

events.bluf: Actor and Confederate sympathiser John Wilkes Booth planned to kill the president, vice president and secretary of state in one night to throw the Union government into chaos and revive the Confederate cause. He shot Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre on 14 April 1865; Lincoln died the next morning, Secretary of State William Seward survived a stabbing, and the attack on the vice president never came. Andrew Johnson, a Tennessee Democrat hostile to Black rights, took charge of Reconstruction and tilted the peace toward the defeated South.
events.lens: Assassinations change policy when the successor holds very different views.

events.hook: The Constitution was changed to end slavery everywhere in the United States.
events.what: The Constitution was changed to end slavery everywhere in the United States.
events.story: The Emancipation Proclamation was a war measure that covered only rebel areas. The Senate passed an abolition amendment in April 1864; the House fell short of two thirds in June. After his re-election US President Abraham Lincoln pressed wavering Democrats, and the House passed it on 31 January 1865 by 119 votes to 56. Georgia's ratification on 6 December 1865 made it law: slavery and involuntary servitude were abolished 'except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted'. About four million people were freed.
events.why: The proclamation rested on war powers that would lapse with peace, and the courts might have ruled against it. Lincoln wanted abolition settled before the Southern states returned to Congress.
events.then: The 14th Amendment of 1868 defined citizenship and equal protection, and the 15th of 1870 barred denial of the vote by race. Southern states leased convicts to mines, railways and plantations from the 1870s, and most of the convicts were Black men convicted under vagrancy laws.
events.sig: The 14th Amendment of 1868 defined citizenship and equal protection, and the 15th of 1870 barred denial of the vote by race. Southern states leased convicts to mines, railways and plantations from the 1870s, and most of the convicts were Black men convicted under vagrancy laws.
events.now: The exception for punishment of crime was the legal basis of convict leasing from the 1870s to the 1920s and is the subject of today's argument over prison labour.
events.wk: Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

causes.why: The proclamation was a war measure covering only rebel areas; the 13th Amendment made the end of slavery permanent and nationwide.

q.before: Slavery was legal in the border states and protected by the Constitution.
q.how: A constitutional amendment.
q.claim: Freedom for all, except as punishment for crime.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: US President Abraham Lincoln and the Republicans wanted abolition written into the Constitution so that no court or peace settlement could undo the Emancipation Proclamation. The Senate passed the amendment in April 1864 and the House, after Lincoln's lobbying, in January 1865; ratification came in December. Slavery ended by law for about four million people, and the exception for punishment of crime was used after Reconstruction to lease convicts as forced labour across the South.
events.lens: Watch the exceptions in landmark laws: they often become the loopholes.
events.fact: Mississippi's legislature rejected the amendment in 1865 and ratified it only in 1995; the paperwork reached the federal register in 2013.

events.h: Satsuma and Chōshū unite against the shogun
events.who: Saigō Takamori (Satsuma), Kido Takayoshi (Chōshū), go-between Sakamoto Ryōma
events.what: Two rival domains, both humbled by Western guns, secretly allied to overthrow the shogun.
events.why: Both had learned they needed modern weapons and a new government that could stand up to the West.
events.sig: Chōshū defeated the shogun's punitive expedition in 1866, which showed the shogunate's weakness.
events.hook: Two rival domains, both humbled by Western guns, secretly allied to overthrow the shogun.
events.story: Satsuma and Chōshū had fought each other in Kyoto in 1864. Sakamoto Ryōma, a former Tosa samurai, brokered a secret alliance in Kyoto in 1866 between Satsuma leader Saigō Takamori and Chōshū leader Kido Takayoshi. Satsuma would help Chōshū buy Western weapons and would resist the shogun's attacks on it.
events.then: Chōshū defeated the shogun's punitive expedition in 1866, which showed the shogunate's weakness.
events.now: The alliance built the coalition that overthrew the shogunate in 1868 and supplied the men who ran the Meiji government; Sakamoto Ryōma, who brokered it, remains a national model of pragmatic coalition-building.

causes.why: Both domains had learned from Western bombardments that they needed modern arms.

q.before: Domains were divided, and the shogun could play them off against each other.
q.how: A united front against the shogun, in the emperor's name.
q.winners: Satsuma and Chōshū leaders would dominate Japan for decades.
q.lasted: Yes: 'Satchō' men ran the Meiji government.

events.bluf: Satsuma and Chōshū, long enemies, wanted modern weapons and a government able to stand up to the West; Tosa go-between Sakamoto Ryōma brokered a secret alliance between them in Kyoto in 1866. Satsuma would supply Chōshū with Western arms and back it against the shogun. Japan's two most powerful anti-shogunate domains now acted together, which made the overthrow of the shogunate possible, and their leaders ran the Meiji government.
events.lens: Former enemies unite when they share a bigger threat and a common goal.
events.fact: Go-between Sakamoto Ryōma was assassinated in Kyoto in December 1867 at 31, a year before the restoration he had worked for.

events.what: Empire split into a dual monarchy.
events.why: Defeat by Prussia in 1866 left Austria weak. Hungarian nationalists demanded autonomy as the price of their loyalty.
events.sig: The Czechs demanded the same standing and were refused in 1871. Croatia received limited autonomy under Hungary in 1868. The Slav question and the Magyarisation of Hungary's minorities ran to 1918.
events.hook: Austria shared its empire with Hungary to hold it together.
events.story: Defeated by Prussia in 1866 and shut out of Germany, Habsburg Emperor Franz Joseph struck a deal with Hungarian leaders Ferenc Deák and Gyula Andrássy, the Compromise of 1867. The empire became Austria-Hungary: two states with their own parliaments and governments, sharing a monarch, an army, a foreign policy and the finances to pay for them. Franz Joseph was crowned King of Hungary in Buda on 8 June 1867.
events.then: The Czechs demanded the same standing and were refused in 1871. Croatia received limited autonomy under Hungary in 1868. The Slav question and the Magyarisation of Hungary's minorities ran to 1918.
events.now: The Compromise gave Hungary equal standing and left the Slavs of both halves without it, a structure that could satisfy neither nationalism nor reform; its collapse in 1918 drew the modern map of Central Europe.

causes.why: Defeats by France and Piedmont in 1859 and by Prussia in 1866 forced the Habsburgs to share power with Hungary.

q.before: The Austrian Empire, ruled centrally from Vienna.
q.how: A compromise (Ausgleich) with Hungarian leaders.
q.claim: Franz Joseph as Emperor of Austria and King of Hungary.
q.winners: Austrians and Hungarians; other nationalities lost out.
q.lasted: Until 1918.

events.bluf: Habsburg Emperor Franz Joseph, defeated by Prussia and shut out of Germany, bought Hungary's loyalty with self-government. The Compromise of 1867 made a dual monarchy with two parliaments under one crown, army and foreign policy. Hungary was satisfied; the Czechs, Croats, Romanians and other Slavs were left without equal standing, and their claims pulled the empire apart in 1918.
events.lens: Concessions to one national group in a multinational empire raise demands from all the others.
events.fact: The economic terms of the Compromise came up for renewal every ten years, and the two halves fought over the shared budget at each renewal.

events.what: French puppet emperor shot.
events.why: Napoleon III pulled out his troops under US pressure and because Prussia's rise demanded them in Europe, which left Maximilian without protection.
events.sig: Juárez restored the republic and the liberal reforms that limited the Church's power. He died in office in 1872.
events.hook: Mexico executed the emperor France had imposed.
events.story: After the US Civil War the United States pressed France to leave Mexico, and French Emperor Napoleon III withdrew his troops in 1866-67. Emperor Maximilian stayed on. Mexican President Benito Juárez's republican forces besieged him at Querétaro and captured him in May 1867. He was shot on 19 June 1867 with his generals Miguel Miramón and Tomás Mejía.
events.then: Juárez restored the republic and the liberal reforms that limited the Church's power. He died in office in 1872.
events.now: The execution ended European attempts to rule Mexico and fixed the liberal, secular republic; Juárez, a Zapotec lawyer, became the symbol of Mexican sovereignty that every later government has claimed.
events.fact: Édouard Manet painted the execution as a criticism of Napoleon III, and the painting was banned in France.

causes.why: When the US Civil War ended and France withdrew its troops, Maximilian's regime collapsed.

q.before: Emperor Maximilian, installed by France.
q.how: Defeat, capture and execution.
q.lasted: Yes: Mexico has been a republic ever since.

events.bluf: Mexican President Benito Juárez set out to end the French-imposed empire once French Emperor Napoleon III withdrew his troops under US pressure in 1866-67. Republican forces captured Emperor Maximilian at Querétaro in May 1867 and shot him on 19 June despite appeals from European courts. The execution ended the last European attempt to rule Mexico and confirmed the liberal republic and Juárez as the symbol of Mexican sovereignty.
events.lens: Rulers installed by foreign armies rarely survive their patrons' departure.

events.who: Secretary of State William Seward; Russia
events.what: Bought for $7.2 million.
events.why: Russia needed cash after the Crimean War, could not defend Alaska, and preferred selling it to the United States to seeing Britain take it.
events.sig: Gold strikes in the Yukon and at Nome in the 1890s brought the first rush of settlers. Alaska became a state in 1959, oil was found at Prudhoe Bay in 1968, and its bases faced the Soviet Union across the Bering Strait through the Cold War.
events.hook: The US bought Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million, and people called it folly.
