events.story: Russia had held Alaska since the 1700s through a fur company whose profits were falling. After the Crimean War of 1853-56 Russian Tsar Alexander II concluded the colony could never be defended against Britain and offered it to the United States. US Secretary of State William Seward and Russian minister Eduard de Stoeckl signed the treaty on 30 March 1867 for $7.2 million, about 2 cents an acre. The Senate ratified it in April and the transfer took place at Sitka in October.
events.then: Gold strikes in the Yukon and at Nome in the 1890s brought the first rush of settlers. Alaska became a state in 1959, oil was found at Prudhoe Bay in 1968, and its bases faced the Soviet Union across the Bering Strait through the Cold War.
events.now: Alaska gives the United States an Arctic coastline and a Pacific position 55 miles from Russia, which made it the front line of air defence in the Cold War and makes it the country's stake in Arctic shipping and resources now.
events.fact: Critics mocked the purchase as 'Seward's Folly' and 'Andrew Johnson's polar bear garden'. It cost about 2 cents an acre.

causes.why: After the Crimean War, Russia feared Britain could seize Alaska and needed money; selling it to the US seemed better than losing it.

q.before: Russia owned Alaska; Native Alaskans lived there.
q.how: A purchase for $7.2 million.
q.lasted: Yes: Alaska became a state in 1959.

events.bluf: Russian Tsar Alexander II wanted cash after the Crimean War and feared losing an indefensible Alaska to Britain; US Secretary of State William Seward wanted the territory and the Pacific position. The United States paid $7.2 million, about 2 cents an acre, in 1867. Russia left North America, and a purchase mocked as 'Seward's Folly' yielded gold from the 1890s, oil from the 1960s and a Cold War frontier facing the Soviet Union.
events.lens: Sellers undervalue territory they cannot defend; buyers may see its value only decades later.

events.h: Last shogun hands power to the emperor
events.what: The last shogun gave up power, hoping to keep it in a new form.
events.why: Shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu hoped to avoid civil war and keep the Tokugawa family on top.
events.sig: The Satsuma-Chōshū coup of 3 January 1868 proclaimed 'imperial restoration' and stripped the Tokugawa of lands and office.
events.hook: The last shogun gave up power, hoping to keep it in a new form.
events.story: Under pressure from the Satsuma-Chōshū alliance, Japanese shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu announced at Nijō Castle in Kyoto in November 1867 that he was returning governing authority to the 15-year-old Emperor Meiji. He expected to lead a council of lords under the throne.
events.then: The Satsuma-Chōshū coup of 3 January 1868 proclaimed 'imperial restoration' and stripped the Tokugawa of lands and office.
events.now: It ended nearly 700 years of rule by military shoguns and returned formal power to the emperor, the foundation on which the modern Japanese state was built.

causes.why: The alliance made the shogun's position impossible.

q.before: The Tokugawa shoguns had ruled for 264 years.
q.how: Power formally returned to the imperial court.
q.claim: The emperor as Japan's true sovereign.
q.winners: The Satsuma-Chōshū leaders, who wanted the Tokugawa out completely.
q.lasted: No: weeks later they staged a coup.

events.bluf: Japanese shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu returned governing authority to the emperor in November 1867 to avoid civil war and keep his house at the head of a new council of lords. The surrender ended nearly 700 years of rule by military shoguns. His rivals in Satsuma and Chōshū moved within weeks to shut the Tokugawa out entirely, and the coup of January 1868 followed.
events.lens: Leaders who give up power in order to keep it often find their rivals won't let them.
events.fact: Tokugawa Yoshinobu lived until 1913, longer than any other shogun, and was made a duke by the government that had deposed him.

events.who: Imperial forces (Satsuma, Chōshū) vs. Tokugawa loyalists
events.what: A short civil war decided whether Japan's future would be imperial or Tokugawa.
events.why: The Tokugawa refused to be shut out of the new government entirely, and northern domains feared the dominance of Satsuma and Chōshū.
events.sig: The capital moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo, 'eastern capital', in 1868. The new government abolished the domains in 1871.
events.hook: A short civil war decided whether Japan's future would be imperial or Tokugawa.
events.story: Tokugawa forces clashed with imperial troops from Satsuma and Chōshū at Toba-Fushimi near Kyoto in January 1868 and lost. Edo surrendered peacefully in May after talks between Satsuma leader Saigō Takamori and Tokugawa retainer Katsu Kaishū. Northern domains led by Aizu fought on and fell that autumn. Loyalists under naval commander Enomoto Takeaki made a last stand at Hakodate in Hokkaido in 1869.
events.then: The capital moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo, 'eastern capital', in 1868. The new government abolished the domains in 1871.
events.now: The war destroyed the shogunate and the domains that fought for it, and put the Meiji government in sole control of Japan, which let it abolish the samurai order within a decade.

causes.why: The coup excluded the Tokugawa from power.

q.why: Who would rule the new Japan.
q.stakes: The future of the whole political system.
q.decided: Imperial forces had the emperor's banner and more modern weapons.
q.cost: About 8,200 killed.
q.changed: The Tokugawa were finished; the new government was free to reform.

events.bluf: The new imperial government fought to destroy the Tokugawa as a power, and Tokugawa loyalists fought to keep a place in the new order. Imperial troops won at Toba-Fushimi in January 1868, took Edo without a fight and crushed the northern domains and a last stand in Hokkaido in 1869. The war was short and limited, which let the Meiji state consolidate quickly and abolish the samurai order within a decade.
events.lens: Short civil wars with decisive results allow faster state-building than long ones.
events.fact: Aizu's defeat is still remembered in Fukushima, where the losers keep their own version of the war.
events.btt: Japan: The fall of the Tokugawa

events.hook: Britain sent its last convicts to Australia, ending 80 years of penal transportation.
events.what: Britain sent its last convicts to Australia, ending 80 years of penal transportation.
events.story: New South Wales stopped receiving convicts in 1840 and Van Diemen's Land in 1853, after campaigns by colonists. Western Australia, short of labour, asked for convicts in 1850. The Hougoumont reached Fremantle in January 1868 with 280 convicts, among them 62 Irish Fenian rebels. About 162,000 convicts had been transported to Australia since 1788.
events.why: The eastern colonies had refused convicts for a generation and British prisons had changed. Transportation was costly, and the colonists' objection was loud.
events.then: Six Fenians escaped from Fremantle in 1876 aboard the American whaler Catalpa. Western Australia's convict-built roads and public buildings remained.
events.sig: Six Fenians escaped from Fremantle in 1876 aboard the American whaler Catalpa. Western Australia's convict-built roads and public buildings remained.
events.now: The end of transportation closed the penal era and left the colonies to govern themselves as free societies; the shame attached to convict ancestry lasted a century and has since reversed into pride.

causes.why: Transportation continued for 80 years and sent about 162,000 convicts to Australia.

q.before: Britain shipped convicts to Australia for 80 years.
q.how: The last voyage of a policy being wound down.
q.claim: Transportation as punishment under British law.
q.winners: Free settlers who had campaigned against convict labour.
q.lasted: Yes: transportation ended for good.

events.bluf: Britain wanted to keep transporting convicts; the eastern colonies, wanting free immigrants and self-government, had refused them since 1840, and only Western Australia still took them. The Hougoumont landed 280 convicts at Fremantle in January 1868, the last of about 162,000 sent since 1788. Transportation ended, and Australia's self-governing colonies went on as free settler societies with a convict past to live down.
events.lens: Colonies outgrow their founding purpose once settlers have the political voice to reject it.
events.fact: Perhaps one in five Australians descends from a convict.

events.what: The new government promised to seek knowledge 'throughout the world'.
events.why: The new regime, installed by a coup and still fighting the Tokugawa, needed to win over the domains and show that it would rule by consensus and reform.
events.sig: The government began dismantling the feudal order: the domains were abolished in 1871, and class restrictions on jobs and marriage were lifted.
events.hook: The new government promised to seek knowledge 'throughout the world'.
events.story: On 6 April 1868 Emperor Meiji swore an oath before the court nobles and lords in Kyoto. It set out five principles: deliberative assemblies, unity of all classes, freedom to pursue careers, abandoning 'evil customs of the past' and seeking knowledge worldwide. Reformers Yuri Kimimasa and Fukuoka Takachika drafted it, and Chōshū leader Kido Takayoshi revised it.
events.then: The government began dismantling the feudal order: the domains were abolished in 1871, and class restrictions on jobs and marriage were lifted.
events.now: The oath put the emperor's name on reform, which let the government dismantle the feudal order without a constitution; after the Second World War Emperor Hirohito cited it to argue that democracy had Japanese roots.

causes.why: The new government needed a statement of purpose.

q.idea: Japan would learn from the world to strengthen the empire.
q.spread: It became the guiding statement of Meiji reform.
q.enabled: Students and officials sent abroad; Western-style institutions.
q.critics: Its promise of assemblies was slow to arrive; a parliament came only in 1890.

events.bluf: The new Meiji government, installed by a coup and still fighting the Tokugawa, needed to win over the domains and show it would rule by consensus and reform. In April 1868 Emperor Meiji swore five principles: deliberative assemblies, unity of all classes, freedom to pursue careers, an end to 'evil customs of the past' and the search for knowledge worldwide. The oath gave sweeping change the emperor's authority, and the government used it to dismantle the feudal order within three years.
events.lens: Reformers often wrap radical change in traditional authority to make it acceptable.
events.fact: Emperor Hirohito's New Year rescript of 1946, renouncing his divinity, opened by quoting the oath in full.

events.what: Shogun overthrown; rapid Western-style modernization.
events.why: Fear of being colonised like China came first. The shogunate's humiliation by the unequal treaties discredited it. Ambitious samurai from the outer domains had learned that Western technology was the key to power.
events.sig: Japan revised the unequal treaties by 1911, defeated China in 1895 and Russia in 1905, and annexed Taiwan and Korea. Modernisation concentrated power in a small oligarchy and a military answerable only to the emperor, a structure militarists later exploited.
events.hook: Japan's samurai overthrew the shogun and turned Japan into a modern power in one generation.
events.story: In January 1868 reformist samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū seized the palace in Kyoto and proclaimed the restoration of direct rule by the 15-year-old Emperor Meiji. Over the following decades the new government abolished the feudal domains and the samurai class, built railways, factories and a conscript army, and introduced universal schooling. In 1889 it adopted a constitution modelled on Prussia's.
events.then: Japan revised the unequal treaties by 1911, defeated China in 1895 and Russia in 1905, and annexed Taiwan and Korea. Modernisation concentrated power in a small oligarchy and a military answerable only to the emperor, a structure militarists later exploited.
events.now: Japan became the first non-Western industrial nation, and its state-led development became a model for East Asia's later 'tiger' economies.
events.fact: In about 40 years Japan went from samurai with swords to a navy that sank Russia's fleet.

causes.why: The shogun's resignation opened the way for the coup.
The shogun's failure to resist the West destroyed his legitimacy.

q.before: The shogun ruled; the emperor was a figurehead in Kyoto.
q.how: A central government in the emperor's name, run by young samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū.
q.claim: Restoring ancient imperial rule; in practice, modernizing to resist the West.
q.winners: Reformist samurai; losers were the Tokugawa and eventually the samurai class itself.
q.lasted: Yes: it built modern Japan.

events.bluf: Reformist samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū seized the Kyoto palace in January 1868 to replace the shogunate with rule in the emperor's name and build a state that could resist the West. Within a generation their government had abolished the domains and the samurai, built railways, factories, schools and a conscript army, and adopted a constitution. Japan became the first non-Western industrial and imperial power; the same structure concentrated power in an oligarchy and a military answerable only to the emperor.
events.lens: Defensive modernization works when elites agree that the external threat outweighs their own privileges.

events.hook: A reforming king abolished slavery, modernised the state and kept Siam independent.
events.what: A reforming king abolished slavery, modernised the state and kept Siam independent.
events.story: Siamese King Chulalongkorn (Rama V) reigned from 1868 to 1910. He abolished slavery and the prostration of subjects before the king, and built railways, schools and a modern civil service. He gave up Laos and western Cambodia to France and the northern Malay states to Britain to keep the core of Siam free.
events.why: Britain held Burma and Malaya and France held Indochina. A state with modern administration and fixed borders gave neither a pretext.
events.then: Siam stayed independent as a buffer between British Burma and French Indochina. It gave up Laos to France in 1893, western Cambodia in 1907 and four northern Malay states to Britain in 1909.
events.sig: Siam stayed independent as a buffer between British Burma and French Indochina. It gave up Laos to France in 1893, western Cambodia in 1907 and four northern Malay states to Britain in 1909.
events.now: Chulalongkorn's centralised state, built between 1868 and 1910, is the Thai state of today, and his reputation as the king who kept Siam independent underpins the monarchy's prestige.

causes.why: Opening to the West brought the pressure that pushed Mongkut's son Chulalongkorn into sweeping reform.

q.before: An absolute monarchy with slavery and court rituals of prostration.
q.how: Reforms from the throne.
q.winners: The monarchy and a new bureaucracy; Siam stayed independent.
q.lasted: His reforms shaped Thailand until the 1932 revolution and beyond.

events.bluf: Siamese King Chulalongkorn set out to make Siam strong and 'civilised' enough that no colonial power would have an excuse to take it. Over a reign of 42 years he abolished slavery, built railways, schools and a modern civil service, and ceded border territories to France and Britain. Siam became a centralised nation-state and survived as a buffer between British Burma and French Indochina, the only country in the region never colonised.
events.lens: Buffer states survive by being useful to both neighbouring powers and too costly for either to take.
events.fact: Chulalongkorn was tutored as a boy by Anna Leonowens, the governess of 'The King and I'.

events.what: Linked the Mediterranean and Red Sea.
events.why: A shorter route between Europe and Asia promised large profits to investors. Said Pasha's friendship with de Lesseps supplied the concession.
events.sig: Egypt's ruler Ismail Pasha sold his canal shares to Britain in 1875 and the country went bankrupt. Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 to protect the canal and its investments. The canal sped European trade with Asia and East Africa and the conquest of both.
events.hook: The Suez Canal linked the Mediterranean and Red Sea.
events.story: Egypt's ruler Said Pasha granted a concession to his friend, French promoter Ferdinand de Lesseps, whose Suez Canal Company built the 164 km waterway between 1859 and 1869, at first largely with forced Egyptian labour. The canal joined the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and cut the sea voyage between Europe and India by thousands of kilometres.
events.then: Egypt's ruler Ismail Pasha sold his canal shares to Britain in 1875 and the country went bankrupt. Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 to protect the canal and its investments. The canal sped European trade with Asia and East Africa and the conquest of both.
events.now: About 12 per cent of world trade passes through the canal. Its nationalisation in 1956 set off the Suez Crisis, and the Ever Given blockage of 2021 and Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping since 2023 show how exposed the route remains.
events.fact: Egypt's ruler commissioned Verdi's opera Aida around the canal opening; it premiered in Cairo in 1871.

causes.why: His successors, especially his son Said, granted the French engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps the canal concession.

q.what: Passage for ships between Europe and Asia.
q.who: Shareholders and shipping firms gained; Egypt's labourers and treasury paid.
q.scale: Tens of thousands of workers dug it over a decade.
q.daily: Faster mail and cheaper goods between Europe and Asia.
q.system: A strategic waterway that drew Britain into Egypt.

events.bluf: French promoter Ferdinand de Lesseps and Egypt's ruler Said Pasha wanted a canal that would shorten the route between Europe and Asia and make Egypt its toll gate. The canal opened in 1869 and did both. Building it put Egypt into debts that brought British occupation in 1882, and the waterway became a strategic prize fought over for a century.
events.lens: Infrastructure built with foreign money can cost a country its independence when the debts come due.

of world trade passes through it today

events.who: Union Pacific & Central Pacific; Chinese and Irish laborers
events.what: Linked East and West coasts by rail.
events.why: Congress wanted to bind California to the Union and open the West to settlement and markets, and offered railroad companies land grants and loans to do it. Private capital alone would have left the empty interior unbuilt.
events.sig: Crossing the country fell from months to about a week. Railways brought settlers and hunters to the Plains; the bison herds were shot out by the mid-1880s and the Plains nations confined to reservations. The Crédit Mobilier scandal of 1872 exposed Union Pacific insiders who had paid congressmen in shares.
events.hook: A golden spike tied the US together coast to coast.
events.story: The Pacific Railway Act of 1862, passed with the South out of Congress, chartered the Union Pacific to build west from Omaha and the Central Pacific to build east from Sacramento, with government loans and alternate sections of public land along the route. The Central Pacific hired thousands of Chinese workers, who cut the line through the Sierra Nevada; the Union Pacific hired Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans. The two met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on 10 May 1869, where a golden spike was driven.
events.then: Crossing the country fell from months to about a week. Railways brought settlers and hunters to the Plains; the bison herds were shot out by the mid-1880s and the Plains nations confined to reservations. The Crédit Mobilier scandal of 1872 exposed Union Pacific insiders who had paid congressmen in shares.
events.now: Its mix of public subsidy and private profit set the pattern for American infrastructure, and the time zones adopted for the railways in 1883 still govern daily life.
events.fact: Railroads were the reason the United States adopted standard time zones in 1883; before that every town kept its own time.

causes.why: California's sudden growth made a rail link to the East a national priority.
Railways spread from Britain worldwide; by 1869 one crossed North America.

q.what: A rail link across the continent.
q.who: Railroad owners grew rich on land grants; Chinese workers and Plains nations paid.
q.scale: About 3,000 km of track built in six years.
q.daily: Coast-to-coast travel in about a week.
q.system: A national market, and the settlement of the West.

events.bluf: Congress wanted California bound to the Union and the West opened to settlement, and it paid two companies in land grants and loans to build the line. The Central Pacific, with thousands of Chinese workers, and the Union Pacific, with Irish labourers and Civil War veterans, met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on 10 May 1869. A crossing of months fell to about a week, a national market followed, and the Plains nations and the bison herds they lived on were destroyed within two decades.
events.lens: Infrastructure picks winners and losers: the railroad empowered settlers and doomed nomadic peoples.

Chinese workers on the Central Pacific line

events.who: Bismarck's Prussia vs. Napoleon III's France
events.what: Prussia crushed France in months.
events.why: Bismarck wanted a war with France to bring the south German states into a Prussian-led Germany. Napoleon III wanted prestige and took a Prussian candidate for the Spanish throne as a threat.
events.sig: The German Empire was proclaimed in January 1871. France lost Alsace-Lorraine and paid an indemnity of five billion francs; Napoleon III's empire fell and the Third Republic was born. Italy took Rome as French troops left.
events.hook: Prussia crushed France in months and used the victory to create Germany.
events.story: In July 1870 France declared war on Prussia after Prussian Minister-President Otto von Bismarck released the edited Ems telegram. Prussia and its south German allies mobilised fast by railway, encircled one French army at Metz and captured French Emperor Napoleon III with another at Sedan in September. Paris was besieged and surrendered in January 1871.
events.then: The German Empire was proclaimed in January 1871. France lost Alsace-Lorraine and paid an indemnity of five billion francs; Napoleon III's empire fell and the Third Republic was born. Italy took Rome as French troops left.
events.now: French resentment and German power shaped Europe's alliances until 1914, and the Franco-German rivalry ended only with European integration after 1945.

causes.why: France declared war six days after Bismarck published the edited telegram.

q.why: Bismarck wanted war to unite Germany; France wanted to check Prussia.
q.stakes: German unity and the balance of power.
q.decided: Faster German mobilisation and better artillery.
q.cost: About 180,000 dead, including civilians.
q.changed: Germany was united; France lost Alsace-Lorraine.

events.bluf: Prussian Minister-President Otto von Bismarck wanted a war that would bring the south German states into a Prussian-led Germany; French Emperor Napoleon III fought to keep Prussia from dominating the continent. Prussia won in six weeks of field battles and a four-month siege of Paris. A united German Empire replaced France as the strongest power on the continent, and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine kept France looking for allies and for revenge until 1914.
events.trig: Bismarck's release of the edited Ems telegram on 13 July 1870.
events.lens: Wars that humiliate the loser and take its territory plant the seeds of the next war.
events.fact: The French chassepot rifle outranged the Prussian needle gun; Prussia won with its steel Krupp artillery.

kv: people in Alsace-Lorraine, annexed by Germany

toll.n: Estimates.

events.who: Otto von Bismarck; King Wilhelm I; French ambassador Vincent Benedetti
events.hook: Bismarck edited a royal telegram to insult France and provoke a war.
events.what: Bismarck edited a royal telegram to insult France and provoke a war.
events.story: At the spa town of Ems on 13 July 1870 French ambassador Vincent Benedetti asked Prussian King Wilhelm I to promise that no Hohenzollern would ever again be a candidate for the Spanish throne. Wilhelm declined with courtesy and sent Prussian Minister-President Otto von Bismarck a report by telegram. Bismarck cut the report so that it read as a snub on both sides and released it to the press that evening. France declared war on 19 July.
events.why: Bismarck wanted a war with France to bring the south German states into a united Germany. France's government wanted a public victory over Prussia after the Spanish candidacy had been withdrawn.
events.then: The south German states joined Prussia. French Emperor Napoleon III was captured at Sedan on 2 September, and the German Empire was proclaimed in January 1871.
events.sig: The south German states joined Prussia. French Emperor Napoleon III was captured at Sedan on 2 September, and the German Empire was proclaimed in January 1871.
events.now: The edited telegram provoked France into declaring war on Prussia with the south German states on Prussia's side, the condition Bismarck needed for unification.

q.before: Germany was split between the Prussian-led north and independent southern states.
q.how: A deliberate provocation that led to war.
q.winners: Bismarck, who got the war he wanted.
q.lasted: Its result, a united Germany, did.

events.bluf: Prussian Minister-President Otto von Bismarck wanted a war that France would declare, so that the south German states would join Prussia and the other powers would stand aside. He cut the king's report of a meeting with the French ambassador so it read as a snub and gave it to the press. France declared war within six days, the south joined Prussia, and Germany was united within six months.
events.lens: Make the other side fire the first shot, and your allies will rally to you.
events.fact: Bismarck said the shortened text would have the effect of a red rag on the Gallic bull.

kv: from its publication to France's declaration of war

events.who: Prussian chief of staff Helmuth von Moltke; Emperor Napoleon III
events.hook: Prussia surrounded a French army and captured the French emperor himself.
events.what: Prussia surrounded a French army and captured the French emperor himself.
events.story: On 1 September 1870 German armies under Prussian chief of staff Helmuth von Moltke encircled French Marshal Patrice de MacMahon's army at Sedan near the Belgian border. French Emperor Napoleon III, who was with the army, surrendered the next day with about 100,000 men. On 4 September crowds in Paris proclaimed a republic.
events.why: Germany mobilised faster by railway and planned better through its general staff. Its steel breech-loading artillery outgunned the French. French commanders hesitated into encirclement.
events.then: Paris was besieged from 19 September. Germany was united under the Prussian king in January 1871, and Paris surrendered the same month.
events.sig: Paris was besieged from 19 September. Germany was united under the Prussian king in January 1871, and Paris surrendered the same month.
events.now: The defeat gave birth to the Third Republic, and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine became a lasting grievance that fed French support for war in 1914.

causes.why: The war's decisive battle came within six weeks.

q.why: France tried to relieve its army trapped at Metz.
q.stakes: France's main field army, and the emperor.
q.decided: German encirclement and artillery.
q.cost: About 17,000 French killed or wounded and over 100,000 taken prisoner.
q.changed: The French Second Empire collapsed.

events.bluf: Prussian chief of staff Helmuth von Moltke wanted to destroy the French field army before it could fall back on Paris. He encircled Marshal Patrice de MacMahon's army at Sedan and took it whole, with French Emperor Napoleon III inside. The Second Empire fell within two days, and every European army copied the railway mobilisation and general-staff planning that had done it.
events.lens: Military methods proven decisive in one war are copied by everyone, shaping the next war.
events.fact: Napoleon III went into exile in England and died at Chislehurst in Kent in 1873.

kv: French troops surrendered with the emperor

toll.n: Plus about 104,000 French captured.

events.fact: Germany proclaimed its empire inside the French palace of Versailles, a deliberate humiliation France repaid in the same hall in 1919.
events.hook: Germany was proclaimed an empire in the palace of the defeated French kings.
events.what: Germany was proclaimed an empire in the palace of the defeated French kings.
events.story: With Paris under siege, the German princes proclaimed Prussian King Wilhelm I German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 18 January 1871. France gave up Alsace and much of Lorraine and paid an indemnity of five billion francs.
events.why: Prussia's victories over Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870 let Prussian Minister-President Otto von Bismarck unite Germany on Prussia's terms.
events.then: Germany became continental Europe's strongest economy and army. Bismarck spent twenty years building alliances to keep France isolated and reassure everyone else.
events.sig: Germany became continental Europe's strongest economy and army. Bismarck spent twenty years building alliances to keep France isolated and reassure everyone else.
events.now: A united Germany with the largest army and soon the largest economy on the continent replaced the balance of 1815 with a problem every other power needed to answer; the alliance systems of 1879 to 1907 were the answers.

causes.why: After liberals failed to unify Germany by parliament in 1848, Bismarck did it, as he put it, by 'iron and blood'.
Victory over France let Bismarck proclaim the German Empire, and annex Alsace-Lorraine, which France never accepted.
Victory at Sedan opened the way to Paris and German unification.
Where elected liberals failed, Prussian arms succeeded.

q.before: Germany was split into many states.
q.how: Proclamation by the German princes after victory.
q.claim: The Prussian king as German Emperor.
q.lasted: Until 1918.

events.bluf: Prussian Minister-President Otto von Bismarck wanted the German princes to offer the imperial crown to Prussian King Wilhelm I while the victory over France was fresh. They did, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, and a united Germany under Prussian leadership came into being. The continent now held a single state stronger than any neighbour, and the alliances built to contain or to use it set up 1914.
events.lens: The arrival of a new great power is the hardest test of any international order.

events.who: Paris workers and National Guard; French government troops
events.hook: Paris rose in a radical revolt, and the French army crushed it in a week of slaughter.
events.what: Paris rose in a radical revolt, and the French army crushed it in a week of slaughter.
events.story: After France's defeat and the siege, the government under French head of state Adolphe Thiers tried to seize the National Guard's cannon on 18 March 1871 and lost the city. Paris elected the Commune, which separated church and state and banned night work in bakeries. In the 'Bloody Week' of 21 to 28 May government troops retook the city street by street and killed perhaps 10,000 or more Communards.
events.why: Humiliation in the war and the hardships of the siege came first. Anger at a conservative national government that had moved to Versailles came second.
events.then: France stayed a republic, the Third Republic. Its left and right stayed divided by the memory of the week.
events.sig: France stayed a republic, the Third Republic. Its left and right stayed divided by the memory of the week.
events.now: The Commune's suppression killed about 20,000 and settled the Third Republic as a conservative state; its example gave the socialist movement a model of workers' government and a lesson, drawn by Lenin, that a revolution must hold the army.

causes.why: Defeat, a four-month siege and harsh peace terms set off the radical revolt in Paris.

q.before: The national government had just signed a humiliating peace.
q.how: An uprising and a city council elected by Parisians.
q.claim: Self-government for Paris and social reform.
q.winners: The national government, which crushed it.
q.lasted: About two months.

events.bluf: Paris radicals and the National Guard set up their own government to defend the republic and the city against a conservative national assembly they expected to restore the monarchy. The French army, under the government at Versailles, retook Paris in a week in May and killed perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 Communards. The Third Republic was secured as a conservative state, and the socialist left gained its founding example and its lesson that a revolution must hold the army.
events.lens: Revolutionary experiments crushed by force often become more powerful as myths.
events.fact: German writer Karl Marx, in London, hailed it as the first workers' government.

events.who: Meiji government (Ōkubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi, Saigō Takamori)
events.what: In one decree, Japan's 260-plus feudal domains were replaced by modern prefectures.
events.why: A modern state needed central control of taxes, armies and law, and many domains were deep in debt. Leaders from Satsuma, Chōshū and Tosa backed abolition with troops.
events.sig: Conscription and a national land tax, both in 1873, and the end of samurai privileges followed, which concentrated power in Tokyo.
events.hook: In one decree, Japan's 260-plus feudal domains were replaced by modern prefectures.
events.story: Lords had already returned their lands to the emperor in 1869 and stayed on as governors. In August 1871 the government, led by Ōkubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi and Saigō Takamori, abolished the domains entirely. Lords were pensioned off to Tokyo, and governors appointed from the capital took over.
events.then: Conscription and a national land tax, both in 1873, and the end of samurai privileges followed, which concentrated power in Tokyo.
events.now: It is one of the fastest dismantlings of feudalism anywhere, and Japan's centralised, prefecture-based state still follows its design.

causes.why: Victory gave the government power to impose sweeping change.

q.before: About 270 lords ran their own domains, taxes and armies.
q.how: A centralized state with prefectures run from Tokyo.
q.claim: All land and people belonged to the emperor.
q.winners: The central government; losers were the lords and, soon, the samurai.
q.lasted: Yes: Japan's 47 prefectures today descend from it.

events.bluf: The Meiji leaders from Satsuma, Chōshū and Tosa wanted central control of taxes, armies and law, and many domains were too deep in debt to resist. In August 1871 a single decree abolished the domains, pensioned the lords off to Tokyo and put governors appointed from the capital in their place, with the three domains' troops behind it. Rule by hereditary lords ended in a day, and Japan became a centralised state on the prefecture design it still uses.
events.lens: Centralization succeeds when the losers are bought off (the lords were pensioned) rather than crushed.
events.fact: Over 300 prefectures replaced the domains at first; they were merged to 75 by the end of 1871 and to today's 47 by 1888.

events.what: 'Dr. Livingstone, I presume?': a newspaper stunt that made Europe obsessed with Africa's interior.
events.why: The story sold newspapers. Livingstone's fame as an anti-slavery hero made his fate a public question.
events.sig: Livingstone's death in 1873 raised British anti-slavery pressure on Zanzibar. Stanley returned to Africa in 1874 to cross the continent.
events.hook: 'Dr. Livingstone, I presume?': a newspaper stunt that made Europe obsessed with Africa's interior.
events.story: Scottish missionary and explorer David Livingstone, campaigning against the East African slave trade, had been out of contact in the interior for years. The New York Herald sent journalist Henry Morton Stanley to find him. Stanley reached him at Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika in November 1871. Livingstone refused to leave and died in the interior in 1873.
events.then: Livingstone's death in 1873 raised British anti-slavery pressure on Zanzibar. Stanley returned to Africa in 1874 to cross the continent.
events.now: Livingstone's accounts of the slave caravans, carried to a mass readership by Stanley, built the public pressure that forced Zanzibar to close its slave market in 1873 and gave British intervention in East Africa its justification for the rest of the century.

causes.why: The canal brought East Africa much closer to Europe.

q.what: Newspaper adventure stories about 'darkest Africa'.
q.new: Explorers became celebrities and newspapers created news to sell it.
q.audience: Millions of readers in Britain and the US.
q.reveals: Europeans saw Africa as empty land to be discovered, ignoring the people who guided them.
q.today: Ujiji has a Livingstone memorial; the phrase is still a cliché.

events.bluf: The New York Herald sent journalist Henry Morton Stanley to find Scottish missionary and explorer David Livingstone, out of contact in the interior for years, for the sake of the story. Stanley found him at Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika in November 1871, and the report was a sensation on two continents. The meeting made Africa's interior a public obsession and joined exploration, the anti-slavery cause and mass newspapers into the opinion that later backed colonial expansion.
events.lens: Media spectacles can create the public appetite for political ventures.
events.fact: 'Dr Livingstone, I presume?' appears in Stanley's book; the page of his diary for that day was torn out, and Livingstone's own account omits the line.

events.who: Iwakura Tomomi, Ōkubo Toshimichi, Itō Hirobumi and about 100 others
events.where: San Francisco, Washington, London, Berlin and more
events.what: Half of Japan's government spent nearly two years touring America and Europe to learn how the West worked.
events.why: Japan's leaders wanted to renegotiate the unequal treaties and to understand the West well enough to catch up with it.
events.sig: Returning members blocked a plan to invade Korea in 1873, which split the government and sent Saigō Takamori into opposition.
events.hook: Half of Japan's government spent nearly two years touring America and Europe to learn how the West worked.
events.story: Court noble Iwakura Tomomi led about 100 officials and students, among them Ōkubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi and Itō Hirobumi, from Yokohama in December 1871. The mission hoped to renegotiate the unequal treaties. Western governments refused, so the delegates studied factories, schools, parliaments and armies in the United States, Britain, Germany and elsewhere. It returned in 1873.
events.then: Returning members blocked a plan to invade Korea in 1873, which split the government and sent Saigō Takamori into opposition.
events.now: It is a model of a country systematically studying others to modernise, an approach later echoed by South Korea, Singapore and China.

causes.why: Revising the unequal treaties was a main goal.

q.idea: Japan should adopt the best institutions from each Western country.
q.against: The idea that Japan could stay as it was.
q.spread: Mission members became Japan's top leaders.
q.enabled: German-style constitution and army, British-style navy, American-style schools.
q.critics: Some at home wanted to invade Korea instead of reforming.

events.bluf: Half of Japan's leadership, under court noble Iwakura Tomomi, sailed in December 1871 to renegotiate the unequal treaties and to study the states that had imposed them. The Western powers refused to renegotiate, so for 18 months the mission studied factories, schools, parliaments and armies. Its members came home convinced that domestic modernisation must come before foreign adventures, and blocked the plan to invade Korea in 1873.
events.lens: States that study their rivals systematically catch up faster.
events.fact: The mission took five girls to be educated in America; the youngest, Tsuda Umeko, was six and later founded a women's college in Tokyo.

events.who: Meiji government; British engineer Edmund Morel
events.what: Japan opened its first railway just 19 years after Perry's arrival.
events.why: Railways were the symbol and engine of Western power, and Meiji leaders saw them as essential to unify the country and move goods and troops.
events.sig: Railways, telegraphs and factories spread fast, built by the state and later sold to private firms close to the government.
events.hook: Japan opened its first railway just 19 years after Perry's arrival.
events.story: Japan's first railway opened on 14 October 1872, running 29 km, 18 miles, between Shimbashi in Tokyo and Yokohama, the main port for foreign trade. It was built with a British loan under British engineer Edmund Morel, and Emperor Meiji rode it on opening day. Some officials had opposed borrowing abroad, fearing that foreign debt would bring foreign control.
events.then: Railways, telegraphs and factories spread fast, built by the state and later sold to private firms close to the government.
events.now: Japan's rail network, from the shinkansen to dense commuter lines, is among the world's best, rooted in this early state commitment.

causes.why: The government was committed to Western technology.

q.problem: Moving goods and people between Tokyo and its port.
q.how: British-built locomotives and track.
q.replaced: Walking, horses and palanquins on the Tōkaidō road.
q.spread: Japan had nearly 5,000 miles of track by 1907.
q.next: Japan later built the world's first high-speed rail line, the Shinkansen, in 1964.

events.wk: History of rail transport in Japan
events.bluf: Meiji leaders wanted a railway to unify the country, move goods and troops and show the West Japan's commitment to its technology. The first line, 29 km from Shimbashi in Tokyo to the port of Yokohama, opened in October 1872, built with a British loan under British engineer Edmund Morel. The state went on to build a national network that knit the economy together, then sold lines to firms close to the government.
events.lens: Early infrastructure projects signal a state's direction and attract investment.
events.fact: British engineer Edmund Morel chose a narrow gauge of 1,067 mm, which Japan's conventional lines still use; he died of tuberculosis in 1871, a year before the line opened.

events.what: Peasants were drafted into a national army, ending the samurai's monopoly on fighting.
events.why: A modern army needed mass conscripts rather than a hereditary warrior class, and Yamagata Aritomo saw national service as a way to build loyalty to the emperor.
events.sig: Angry samurai, and peasants who resented the 'blood tax', rose in revolts that culminated in the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877.
events.hook: Peasants were drafted into a national army, ending the samurai's monopoly on fighting.
events.story: Army reformer Yamagata Aritomo, drawing on Prussian and French models, introduced universal military service for men in January 1873. Samurai lost their stipends in 1876 and the right to wear swords the same year.
events.then: Angry samurai, and peasants who resented the 'blood tax', rose in revolts that culminated in the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877.
events.now: The Imperial Army it created dominated Japan until 1945, one reason post-war Japan's constitution renounced war.

causes.why: Central government made a national army possible.

q.why: Japan needed an army that could match Western ones.
q.stakes: The samurai class's whole reason for existing.
q.decided: Government determination and the example of Prussia.
q.cost: Peasant riots against the draft, and bitter samurai.
q.changed: Japan had a modern national army within a decade.

events.bluf: Army reformer Yamagata Aritomo wanted a mass army of commoners loyal to the emperor in place of a hereditary warrior class. The Conscription Ordinance of January 1873 made military service universal for men, on the Prussian and French model. Samurai lost their stipends and their swords by 1876, and the Imperial Army the ordinance created became a pillar of the Meiji state and later the engine of Japanese militarism.
events.lens: Mass armies tie citizens to the state, and the military that leads them gains political power.
events.fact: The ordinance called conscription a 'blood tax', translating a French phrase; peasants took it literally, and rumours that conscripts' blood would be drawn fed the riots.

events.what: Ended the main East African slave market.
events.why: Britain's campaign against the slave trade had public support at home, strengthened by Livingstone's reports. Zanzibar's dependence on British naval protection gave the threat force.
events.sig: Slavery itself was abolished in Zanzibar only in 1897. Britain's role as enforcer drew the sultanate steadily under British control, and it became a protectorate in 1890.
events.hook: Britain forced Zanzibar to close East Africa's biggest slave market.
events.story: Zanzibar's market was the largest in East Africa, and the clove plantations and caravan trade depended on it. British envoy Sir Bartle Frere arrived in early 1873 to demand a treaty and was refused. Under the threat of a naval blockade, Zanzibar Sultan Barghash signed a treaty in June 1873 closing the market and banning the seaborne slave trade. The trade continued by land and by smuggling.
events.then: Slavery itself was abolished in Zanzibar only in 1897. Britain's role as enforcer drew the sultanate steadily under British control, and it became a protectorate in 1890.
events.now: The treaty made Britain the enforcer on the coast, and enforcement became control: the protectorate of 1890, the bombardment of 1896 and abolition in 1897 followed from it.
events.fact: An Anglican cathedral stands on the site of the market; its altar is where the whipping post used to be.

causes.why: Clove plantations and ivory caravans made Zanzibar East Africa's biggest slave market until British pressure closed it in 1873.
Britain used its navy and diplomacy to pressure other slave-trading states, including Zanzibar.
Livingstone's campaign and death built pressure on Britain to act.

q.before: Zanzibar's market was the hub of the East African slave trade.
q.how: A treaty forced by British pressure.
q.claim: Britain's campaign to end the slave trade.
q.lasted: Slavery itself ended in Zanzibar only in 1897.

events.bluf: Britain set out to end the seaborne slave trade of East Africa and threatened a naval blockade to make Zanzibar comply. Zanzibar Sultan Barghash signed a treaty in June 1873 closing the island's slave market, the largest in East Africa, and banning the trade by sea; the trade went on by land and by smuggling. Anti-slavery became the standing justification for British intervention in East Africa and drew the sultanate under British control over the next twenty years.
events.lens: Humanitarian causes can become justifications for expanding control.

events.h: The 'invade Korea' debate splits the government
events.what: Japan's leaders nearly went to war with Korea in 1873, and the split led to civil war.
events.why: Korea refused to recognise the new Meiji government, and samurai who had lost their privileges were looking for a cause.
events.sig: Saigō Takamori and his allies left the government, and Saigō later led the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877. Japan forced Korea open by gunboat diplomacy instead, in 1876.
events.hook: Japan's leaders nearly went to war with Korea in 1873, and the split led to civil war.
events.story: Korea refused to recognise the new Meiji government. Councillor Saigō Takamori proposed to go to Korea as an envoy and provoke a war that would give unemployed samurai a purpose. Councillor Ōkubo Toshimichi and the leaders returning from the Iwakura Mission argued that Japan must reform first, and they prevailed in October 1873.
events.then: Saigō Takamori and his allies left the government, and Saigō later led the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877. Japan forced Korea open by gunboat diplomacy instead, in 1876.
events.now: It shows that Korea was in Japan's sights from the start of the Meiji era; the debate was over timing rather than the goal.

causes.why: Returning mission leaders argued Japan wasn't ready.
Samurai had lost their role and were looking for one.

q.before: Leaders shared power after the Restoration.
q.how: Reformers won; Saigō and others resigned.
q.winners: Ōkubo's reformers; Saigō went home to Satsuma.
q.lasted: The idea of expanding into Korea didn't go away; Japan forced Korea open three years later.

events.bluf: Councillor Saigō Takamori wanted a war with Korea to give displaced samurai a purpose and to punish Korea's refusal to recognise the Meiji government; councillor Ōkubo Toshimichi and the Iwakura Mission returnees insisted Japan reform first. The reformers won in October 1873 and Saigō left the government. Korea stayed a target, and Japan forced it open by gunboat in 1876.
events.lens: Expansionist ideas defeated once often return when conditions change.
events.fact: Saigō Takamori offered to go to Korea without an escort and get himself killed, to give Japan its pretext.

events.h: Stanley crosses Africa down the Congo
events.who: Henry Morton Stanley; hundreds of African porters
events.what: Stanley's brutal 999-day expedition traced the Congo River, and caught the eye of King Leopold.
events.why: Stanley, sponsored by the New York Herald and the Daily Telegraph, wanted the geography solved and his name made.
events.sig: Belgian King Leopold II founded his International African Association in 1876 and hired Stanley in 1878 to build stations on the Congo.
events.hook: Stanley's brutal 999-day expedition traced the Congo River, and caught the eye of King Leopold.
events.story: Starting from Zanzibar in 1874, journalist Henry Morton Stanley led about 350 people across the continent, circled Lake Victoria and Lake Tanganyika by boat and followed the Congo to its mouth, which he reached in 1877. He fought his way through. Fewer than half survived.
events.then: Belgian King Leopold II founded his International African Association in 1876 and hired Stanley in 1878 to build stations on the Congo.
events.now: Stanley's route gave Leopold II the map and the method for the Congo Free State of 1885. The violence of the expedition set the pattern of the colony's rule.

causes.why: The Livingstone story made Stanley famous.

q.what: Geographic knowledge that showed a navigable river into the heart of Africa.
q.who: Leopold II, who hired Stanley; the cost was paid by porters and communities he attacked.
q.scale: About 7,000 miles in 999 days.
q.daily: Not yet, but it opened the Congo basin to trade in ivory and later rubber.
q.system: It laid the ground for Leopold's private colony.

events.bluf: Journalist Henry Morton Stanley set out from Zanzibar in 1874 to settle the geography of the great lakes and the Congo River, and to win fame. He led about 350 people across the continent and down the Congo, fighting his way through; fewer than half survived. The river proved a waterway into the heart of central Africa, and Belgian King Leopold II hired Stanley to claim it.
events.lens: Explorers' maps became instruments of conquest: knowing a river opened it to a king's ambitions.
events.fact: Congolese called Stanley 'Bula Matari', breaker of rocks; the name later attached to the colonial state itself.

kv: from Zanzibar to the Congo's mouth

events.who: Japan's Meiji government; Korea's Joseon court
events.what: Unequal treaty imposed.
events.why: Meiji Japan copied Western gunboat diplomacy to win influence in Korea, which China claimed as a tributary.
events.sig: Japan competed with China and Russia for control of Korea and fought both of them, in 1894-95 and 1904-05.
events.hook: Japan used Western-style gunboat diplomacy on Korea.
events.story: In 1875 the Japanese warship Un'yō provoked a clash with Korean forts on Ganghwa Island. Early the next year Japan sent warships and forced Korea's Joseon court to sign the Treaty of Ganghwa, opening three ports and giving Japanese residents extraterritorial rights.
events.then: Japan competed with China and Russia for control of Korea and fought both of them, in 1894-95 and 1904-05.
events.now: It opened Korea on unequal terms, beginning the Japanese pressure that ended in annexation in 1910 and the grievances that still shape Korea-Japan relations.

causes.why: Japan chose to pressure Korea without full war.
Japan used the same gunboat tactics on Korea that Perry used on Japan.

q.before: Korea was closed to most foreign trade and looked to China.
q.how: Gunboat diplomacy and an unequal treaty.
q.claim: That Korea was an independent state, not a Chinese tributary.
q.lasted: It led to Japanese domination and annexation in 1910.

events.bluf: Meiji Japan wanted influence in Korea, which China claimed as a tributary, and used the gunboat diplomacy the West had used on Japan. After a warship provoked a clash at Ganghwa Island in 1875, Japan forced Korea in February 1876 to open three ports and grant Japanese residents extraterritorial rights. Korea was opened on unequal terms, and Japan's contest with China and Russia for control of it ended in annexation in 1910.
events.lens: Victims of imperialism can become imperialists once they gain power.
events.fact: The treaty's first article declared Korea an independent state, wording aimed at cutting China's claim to it.

events.what: Ruled 35 years.
events.why: Díaz led a revolt against President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada's bid for re-election. Mexico's elites wanted an end to decades of coups and foreign intervention.
events.sig: Peasants lost their land to haciendas and foreign companies. Díaz's rigged re-election of 1910 brought Francisco Madero's call to arms, and Díaz resigned and sailed into exile in May 1911.
events.hook: Díaz ruled Mexico for 35 years, modernizing it for the few.
events.story: Mexican general Porfirio Díaz led a revolt in 1876 against President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada's bid for re-election and took the presidency. He ruled from 1876 to 1911 with one four-year break. Railways grew from under 1,000 km to some 19,000 km, mines and foreign investment boomed, and peasants and Indigenous villages lost their land to haciendas.
events.then: Peasants lost their land to haciendas and foreign companies. Díaz's rigged re-election of 1910 brought Francisco Madero's call to arms, and Díaz resigned and sailed into exile in May 1911.
events.now: The Porfiriato's land concentration and political closure produced the revolution of 1910-20 and the constitution of 1917; 'order and progress' remains the model development dictatorships cite.

causes.why: Díaz, a hero of the war against France, seized power in 1876.

q.before: President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada.
q.how: An armed revolt, then rigged elections.
q.lasted: 35 years, until the Revolution.

events.bluf: Mexican general Porfirio Díaz seized power in 1876 under the slogan 'no re-election' and set out to give Mexico order and growth. He ruled almost continuously until 1911, bringing railways, mines and foreign investment and concentrating land and wealth in a few hands. The inequality and the closed politics of 35 years produced the revolution of 1910.
events.lens: Growth without broadly shared gains or political openness builds pressure for revolt.
events.fact: The line 'Poor Mexico, so far from God and so close to the United States' is attributed to Díaz.

events.who: Lakota and Cheyenne (Sitting Bull, Crazy Horse) vs. Custer
events.what: Custer's 7th Cavalry wiped out.
events.why: The United States broke the 1868 treaty once gold was found and had no intention of removing the miners. The order to come in by January was issued in midwinter, when travel was impossible, and the bands treated it as a declaration of war.
events.sig: Within a year Crazy Horse had surrendered, Sitting Bull had fled to Canada and Congress had taken the Black Hills by an act of February 1877. The Supreme Court ruled in 1980 that the taking was unlawful and awarded compensation that the Lakota have refused.
events.hook: Lakota and Cheyenne warriors wiped out Custer's command.
events.story: The Treaty of Fort Laramie of 1868 had guaranteed the Black Hills to the Lakota. Gold was found there in 1874 by an expedition under Lieutenant Colonel George Custer, prospectors poured in, and the government ordered all Lakota onto reservations by 31 January 1876. Three army columns went after the bands that stayed out. On 25 June 1876 Custer divided his 7th Cavalry and attacked a camp of several thousand Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho on the Little Bighorn in Montana; the warriors, with Crazy Horse among their leaders, killed Custer and about 210 men with him.
events.then: Within a year Crazy Horse had surrendered, Sitting Bull had fled to Canada and Congress had taken the Black Hills by an act of February 1877. The Supreme Court ruled in 1980 that the taking was unlawful and awarded compensation that the Lakota have refused.
events.now: The Lakota have refused payment for the Black Hills to this day; a 1980 Supreme Court ruling awarded compensation that, with interest, now exceeds $1 billion.
events.fact: Comanche, a cavalry horse found wounded on the field, was the army's only survivor of Custer's column and lived on as a regimental mascot.

causes.why: Railroads, and gold found in the Black Hills in 1874, brought settlers and soldiers into Lakota lands guaranteed by treaty.

q.why: The US invaded the Black Hills after gold was found.
q.decided: Lakota and Cheyenne numbers and Custer's rash attack.
q.cost: Custer and about 268 soldiers killed.
q.changed: The US answered with overwhelming force.

events.bluf: The United States wanted the Black Hills after gold was found there in 1874 and ordered every Lakota onto a reservation by January 1876; Lakota chief Sitting Bull and war leader Crazy Horse gathered the bands that refused. On 25 June 1876 their warriors destroyed Lieutenant Colonel George Custer's column of about 210 men on the Little Bighorn. The victory brought overwhelming retaliation: within a year Congress had seized the Black Hills, Crazy Horse had surrendered and Sitting Bull had fled to Canada.
events.lens: A victory can provoke a stronger enemy into total mobilization.

events.who: Saigō Takamori vs. the Imperial Army
events.what: Japan's most famous samurai led a doomed revolt against the government he helped create.
events.why: Samurai resented reforms that took away their stipends, swords and status, and Saigō Takamori had left the government after losing the 1873 debate over Korea.
events.sig: Opposition turned to politics, in a movement for a constitution and a parliament that won an imperial promise of a Diet in 1881.
events.hook: Japan's most famous samurai led a doomed revolt against the government he helped create.
events.story: Samurai in Satsuma, furious at losing their stipends and swords, rose under Saigō Takamori in January 1877. The government's conscript army, with modern rifles and artillery, besieged them for months. Saigō died at Shiroyama in September 1877.
events.then: Opposition turned to politics, in a movement for a constitution and a parliament that won an imperial promise of a Diet in 1881.
events.now: The conscript army's victory settled that the Meiji state could enforce its reforms; Saigō remains a beloved tragic hero, and the rebellion's memory shapes Japanese ideas of loyalty and sacrifice.

causes.why: Conscription and the end of samurai stipends drove the revolt.
Saigō had left the government after the Korea debate.

q.why: Samurai rejected the end of their privileges.
q.stakes: Whether the new state could control the old warrior class.
q.decided: Peasant conscripts with modern weapons beat elite swordsmen.
q.cost: About 13,000 killed in total, roughly half on each side.
q.changed: It was the last armed challenge to the Meiji state.

events.bluf: Satsuma samurai, stripped of stipends, swords and status, rose under Saigō Takamori in January 1877 to reverse the Meiji reforms by force. The government's conscript army, with modern rifles and artillery, wore them down over eight months, and Saigō died at Shiroyama in September. The samurai ended as a political force, and opposition moved into the movement for a constitution and a parliament.
events.lens: When armed opposition fails, dissent moves into politics: after 1877 critics of the government fought with newspapers and petitions, not swords.
events.fact: The government pardoned Saigō Takamori posthumously in 1889, and his statue stands in Tokyo's Ueno Park.

events.what: Federal troops withdrawn from the South.
events.why: Northern voters had tired of occupying the South, and the depression after 1873 moved politics to money and labour. White paramilitaries had already overturned Mississippi's Republican government by violence in 1875. The disputed election gave both parties a reason to deal.
events.sig: Southern states used poll taxes, literacy tests and violence to strip Black citizens of the vote; Mississippi's constitution of 1890 set the model. The Supreme Court upheld segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896. Thousands of Black Americans were lynched over the following decades.
events.hook: A backroom deal pulled federal troops out of the South, and Black rights collapsed.
events.story: Democrat Samuel Tilden won the popular vote in November 1876, and the returns from South Carolina, Louisiana and Florida were disputed. A congressional commission awarded every contested elector to Republican Rutherford B. Hayes by 8 votes to 7. Southern Democrats accepted the result on the understanding that Hayes would withdraw the troops guarding the Republican governments in South Carolina and Louisiana; he did so in April 1877, and those governments fell. Southern Democrats, the 'Redeemers', then held every former Confederate state.
events.then: Southern states used poll taxes, literacy tests and violence to strip Black citizens of the vote; Mississippi's constitution of 1890 set the model. The Supreme Court upheld segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896. Thousands of Black Americans were lynched over the following decades.
events.now: The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 60s was a fight to undo this, and the balance between federal and state control of voting is still contested.
events.fact: 'Jim Crow' came from a minstrel-show character of the 1830s played by white performer Thomas Rice in blackface.

causes.why: Lincoln's death, Southern terror and Northern fatigue undermined Reconstruction; federal troops left the South in 1877.

q.before: Federal troops protected Black voting in the South.
q.how: A political deal to resolve a disputed election.
q.lasted: Jim Crow lasted until the 1960s.

events.bluf: Republicans wanted the presidency after a disputed 1876 election, and Southern Democrats wanted the last federal troops out of their statehouses. The deal gave Rutherford B. Hayes the White House and withdrew the troops from South Carolina and Louisiana in April 1877. Federal protection of Black Southerners ended, white-supremacist governments stripped them of the vote by 1900 and built segregation under law, and the settlement held until the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 60s.
events.trig: The Compromise of 1877, which gave Republican Rutherford B. Hayes the presidency in exchange for removing federal troops from the South.
events.lens: Rights depend on enforcement: when the national government stops protecting a minority, local majorities can reverse its gains.

events.what: Title proclaimed.
events.why: Disraeli wanted to tie India's princes to the Crown and match the prestige of the German and Russian emperors. Victoria wanted the title.
events.sig: The famine of 1876-78 killed millions while the celebrations went on; estimates range from about 5 million to 10 million. Indian critics such as Dadabhai Naoroji argued that British rule was draining India's wealth. Durbars followed in 1903 and 1911.
events.hook: Queen Victoria became Empress of India.
events.story: Under the Royal Titles Act of 1876, British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli made Queen Victoria 'Empress of India'. Viceroy Lord Lytton proclaimed the title at a Delhi Durbar on 1 January 1877 attended by the Indian princes, while famine spread across the Deccan and the Madras Presidency.
events.then: The famine of 1876-78 killed millions while the celebrations went on; estimates range from about 5 million to 10 million. Indian critics such as Dadabhai Naoroji argued that British rule was draining India's wealth. Durbars followed in 1903 and 1911.
events.now: The title bound the princes to the Crown as feudatories, the structure through which Britain ruled about a third of India's territory until 1947.

causes.why: Disraeli gave Victoria the new title to bind India's princes to the crown and to assert British prestige.

q.before: Victoria ruled India as queen after 1858.
q.how: An act of Parliament and a ceremonial durbar.
q.lasted: The title ended in 1947.

events.bluf: British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli wanted to bind India's princes to the Crown and give Queen Victoria a title to match the emperors of Germany and Russia. The Royal Titles Act of 1876 made her Empress of India, proclaimed at a Delhi Durbar on 1 January 1877 while famine spread across southern India. The Raj presented itself as an imperial court of princes for the next 70 years, and the gap between its pageantry and the famine dead fed Indian criticism of British rule.
events.lens: Imperial pageantry is a tool of legitimacy, and often coincides with neglect.
events.fact: Victoria never visited India; she learned Urdu from her Indian attendant Abdul Karim.

events.what: Redrew the Balkans after a Russo-Turkish war.
events.why: Russia's victory over the Ottomans had created a large Bulgaria under Russian influence, which alarmed Britain and Austria-Hungary.
events.sig: Serbian anger at Austria-Hungary's control of Bosnia festered, and Austria annexed it outright in 1908. Russia blamed Germany for its losses, and Bismarck's Dual Alliance with Austria followed in 1879.
events.hook: Europe's powers redrew the Balkans, leaving everyone unsatisfied.
events.story: Russia beat the Ottomans in 1877-78 and imposed the Treaty of San Stefano, which created a large Bulgaria. German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck hosted the powers in Berlin in June and July 1878. Bulgaria was cut back; Serbia, Romania and Montenegro became independent; Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia; Britain took Cyprus.
events.then: Serbian anger at Austria-Hungary's control of Bosnia festered, and Austria annexed it outright in 1908. Russia blamed Germany for its losses, and Bismarck's Dual Alliance with Austria followed in 1879.
events.now: It set up the tensions that exploded in Sarajevo in 1914, and Bosnia's place between Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks remains unresolved.

causes.why: Russia, humiliated in Crimea, fought the Ottomans again in 1877-78. Europe's powers met in Berlin to cut back its gains.
Bismarck, leading Europe's strongest new power, hosted the congress as an 'honest broker' to keep the peace among the other powers.

q.before: Russia had just won a war against the Ottomans.
q.how: A congress of the great powers.
q.winners: Austria-Hungary and Britain; Russia felt cheated.
q.lasted: Its Balkan settlement unravelled by 1914.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck called the powers to Berlin to cut back Russia's gains from its war with the Ottomans before Britain and Austria-Hungary fought over them. The congress shrank the Russian-sponsored Bulgaria, recognised Serbia, Romania and Montenegro as independent and gave Austria-Hungary Bosnia to occupy. Every Balkan nationalism left dissatisfied, Russia felt cheated by Germany, and the quarrels ran to Sarajevo in 1914.
events.lens: Settlements imposed by great powers over the heads of local peoples store up future conflicts.
events.fact: Bismarck called himself the 'honest broker' of the congress; Russia left convinced he had brokered for Austria.

events.what: Zulus won at Isandlwana, then lost.
events.why: Britain wanted southern Africa in a confederation under its control. High Commissioner Sir Bartle Frere saw the Zulu army as the obstacle and acted without London's approval.
events.sig: Britain destroyed the Zulu kingdom and split it into 13 chiefdoms that fought one another. Cetshwayo was exiled, restored in 1883 and died in 1884. Zululand was annexed in 1887.
events.hook: The Zulu crushed a British army at Isandlwana, then lost the war.
events.story: In January 1879 British forces invaded Zululand after Zulu King Cetshwayo refused an ultimatum to disband his army. At Isandlwana on 22 January a Zulu army killed over 1,300 British and allied soldiers. The same night a small garrison held out at Rorke's Drift. Britain sent reinforcements and burned the royal homestead at Ulundi in July.
events.then: Britain destroyed the Zulu kingdom and split it into 13 chiefdoms that fought one another. Cetshwayo was exiled, restored in 1883 and died in 1884. Zululand was annexed in 1887.
events.now: The destruction of the kingdom in 1879 and the civil wars among the 13 chiefdoms broke Zulu independence. Annexation in 1887 and incorporation into Natal in 1897 put the Zulu under the settler rule that led to apartheid.

sites.d: Zulu army wiped out a British column, Jan 1879.
~150 British defended a mission station the same day.
Final British victory; royal kraal burned.

causes.why: The kingdom Shaka built was still the region's strongest African power, an obstacle to British plans for a South African confederation.

q.why: Britain wanted to remove an independent African power.
q.decided: British reinforcements and firepower after Isandlwana.
q.cost: Thousands of Zulu and over 1,700 British-side dead.
q.changed: The Zulu kingdom was broken up.

events.bluf: British High Commissioner Sir Bartle Frere wanted southern Africa in a confederation under British control and the independent Zulu kingdom removed as an obstacle. He sent Zulu King Cetshwayo an ultimatum to disband his army and invaded in January 1879; the Zulu destroyed a British column at Isandlwana on 22 January, and Britain returned with more troops and burned Ulundi in July. The Zulu kingdom was broken into 13 chiefdoms that fought one another, and Zululand was annexed in 1887.
events.lens: Colonial wars often follow a pattern: an early shock defeat, then overwhelming retaliation.
events.fact: Isandlwana was among the heaviest defeats of a colonial army by an African force. Eleven Victoria Crosses were awarded for Rorke's Drift, the most for a single action.

events.hook: An Egyptian colonel led a nationalist movement against foreign control of Egypt's finances.
events.what: An Egyptian colonel led a nationalist movement against foreign control of Egypt's finances.
events.story: Egypt's debts had handed Britain and France control of its finances, and Egyptian-born officers resented the Turkish-speaking elite that held the senior posts. In September 1881 Egyptian Colonel Ahmed Urabi led troops to Khedive Tewfik's palace to demand a constitution and limits on European influence. He became war minister in 1882.
events.why: Foreign control of the treasury and a closed officer corps gave the army and the notables a shared grievance. Khedive Tewfik had no force of his own to resist.
events.then: Britain bombarded Alexandria in July 1882 and defeated Urabi at Tel el-Kebir in September, then occupied Egypt for over 70 years.
events.sig: Britain bombarded Alexandria in July 1882 and defeated Urabi at Tel el-Kebir in September, then occupied Egypt for over 70 years.
events.now: The revolt gave Britain its reason to occupy Egypt in 1882, an occupation that lasted over 70 years and made Egyptian nationalism anti-British from its start.

causes.why: Canal debts and European control fuelled Egyptian nationalism.

q.before: Khedive Tewfik ruled under European financial control.
q.how: Military pressure for constitutional government.
q.lasted: No: it was crushed in 1882.

events.bluf: Egyptian Colonel Ahmed Urabi led the army to demand a constitution and an end to European control of Egypt's finances and to Turkish-speaking monopoly of senior posts. He became war minister, and Britain and France read the movement as a threat to their loans and to the Suez Canal. Britain invaded in 1882 and stayed for over 70 years, which made Egyptian nationalism anti-British from its start.
events.lens: Nationalist revolts against debt control give creditors a pretext for intervention.
events.fact: Urabi was exiled to Ceylon and allowed home in 1901; he is remembered as an early hero of Egyptian nationalism.

events.what: Defensive military alliance.
events.why: German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck wanted to keep France isolated. Italy was angry that France had taken Tunisia in 1881.
events.sig: France answered by allying with Russia in 1894 and reaching an entente with Britain in 1904. Italy, never fully committed, switched sides in 1915.
events.hook: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy formed an alliance against France.
events.story: In May 1882 Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy signed a secret defensive alliance. Each promised help if another was attacked by two great powers, and Germany and Italy pledged to aid each other against a French attack.
events.then: France answered by allying with Russia in 1894 and reaching an entente with Britain in 1904. Italy, never fully committed, switched sides in 1915.
events.now: It is the standard example of rigid alliance blocs turning a local crisis into a general war, a lesson still cited whenever alliances are debated.

causes.why: Bismarck built alliances to keep a vengeful France isolated.
Russia's anger at the Berlin settlement pushed Bismarck into a firm alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, which Italy joined in 1882.

q.before: Germany and Austria-Hungary had allied in 1879.
q.how: A secret treaty.
q.lasted: Italy switched sides in 1915.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck wanted France isolated and Austria-Hungary covered; Italy wanted a counter to France after losing Tunisia. The three signed a secret defensive alliance in May 1882 and renewed it to 1914. France answered with Russia in 1894 and Britain in 1904, and the two armed camps turned the Balkan crisis of 1914 into a general war.
events.lens: Defensive alliances can make wars larger by linking local disputes to great powers.
events.fact: Italy attached a declaration that the alliance could never be directed against Britain, and in 1915 it joined Britain's side.

events.what: British troops crushed Urabi's revolt and occupied Egypt.
events.why: The canal was Britain's route to India and European investors held Egypt's debt. Urabi's movement threatened both.
events.sig: Britain called the occupation temporary and stayed. Egypt was formally independent from 1922, and British troops held the canal zone until 1956.
events.hook: Britain took over Egypt to control the Suez Canal.
events.story: Egypt's bankruptcy had put its finances under British and French control, and nationalists led by Egyptian Colonel Ahmed Urabi took power. In July 1882 British warships bombarded Alexandria. In September British General Sir Garnet Wolseley's army defeated Urabi at Tel el-Kebir and occupied Cairo.
events.then: Britain called the occupation temporary and stayed. Egypt was formally independent from 1922, and British troops held the canal zone until 1956.
events.now: The occupation helped set off the Scramble for Africa and made the Suez Canal a lasting symbol of Egyptian sovereignty.

causes.why: Protecting the canal was Britain's main reason.
Britain invaded to crush Urabi and protect its interests.

q.before: Khedive Tewfik under European financial control, challenged by Urabi.
q.how: Military invasion.
q.claim: Restoring order and protecting the canal.
q.lasted: British troops stayed until 1956.

events.bluf: Britain invaded Egypt to protect the Suez Canal and European bondholders after Egypt's bankruptcy and the Urabi revolt. It won in one battle and announced a temporary occupation that lasted until 1956. Egypt became the base of British power in the Middle East, and the occupation drew Britain deeper into Africa and helped set off the Scramble for Africa.
events.lens: 'Temporary' occupations to protect investments often become permanent.
events.fact: British Prime Minister William Gladstone, who had campaigned against imperial adventures, ordered the invasion.

events.what: Banned Chinese labor immigration.
events.why: Chinese workers on the West Coast were blamed for low wages during the depression of the 1870s, and politicians of both parties courted anti-Chinese voters in a closely divided electorate.
events.sig: The Geary Act of 1892 renewed the ban and required Chinese residents to carry papers; the exclusion was made permanent in 1902. The Immigration Act of 1924 barred all Asian immigration and set national quotas. Congress repealed exclusion in 1943, when China was a wartime ally, with a quota of 105 a year.
events.hook: The US banned immigrants by nationality for the first time.
events.story: Chinese workers had come to the West Coast since the gold rush and had built the Central Pacific railway. The depression of the 1870s brought anti-Chinese riots and the Workingmen's Party in California under the slogan 'The Chinese must go'. Congress passed a 20-year ban that President Chester A. Arthur vetoed in April 1882; he signed a 10-year ban on 6 May 1882. It barred Chinese labourers from entering and Chinese residents from naturalising.
events.then: The Geary Act of 1892 renewed the ban and required Chinese residents to carry papers; the exclusion was made permanent in 1902. The Immigration Act of 1924 barred all Asian immigration and set national quotas. Congress repealed exclusion in 1943, when China was a wartime ally, with a quota of 105 a year.
events.now: It is the root of US laws that decide who may enter by origin; Congress formally expressed regret for it in 2011 and 2012.

causes.why: Thousands of Chinese labourers built the Central Pacific. When the work ended, anti-Chinese agitation led to the first federal law banning immigration by nationality.

q.before: Chinese immigration was largely unrestricted.
q.how: An act of Congress.
q.lasted: Until 1943.

events.bluf: West Coast politicians and labour leaders wanted Chinese workers out, blaming them for low wages in a depression, and both parties wanted the votes. Congress barred Chinese labourers from entering for ten years and President Chester A. Arthur signed it in May 1882. For the first time the United States excluded immigrants by nationality, which set the template for the race-based quotas of 1924, and the ban held until 1943.
events.lens: Laws aimed at one group often become templates for wider restrictions.
events.fact: The Supreme Court ruled in 1898 that a man born in San Francisco to Chinese parents was a citizen, which fixed birthright citizenship for everyone born in the country.
