events.who: 14 European powers and the US; no Africans present
events.what: Set rules for claiming African land ('effective occupation').
events.why: European rivals wanted to avoid war among themselves while racing for colonies. Industrial demand for raw materials and national prestige drove the race; quinine against malaria, machine guns and river steamers made conquest feasible.
events.sig: By 1914 European powers controlled about 90 per cent of Africa; only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed independent. Leopold's Congo Free State became notorious for atrocities.
events.hook: European powers met in Berlin to divide Africa, with no Africans present.
events.story: German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck hosted 14 states, including the United States, in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885. No Africans were present. The powers agreed rules for claiming African coastline, declared free trade and navigation on the Congo and Niger rivers, and recognised Belgian King Leopold II's claim to the Congo basin. The partition itself was carried out over the next 20 years through bilateral treaties and conquest.
events.then: By 1914 European powers controlled about 90 per cent of Africa; only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed independent. Leopold's Congo Free State became notorious for atrocities.
events.now: Most of Africa's borders date from the partition and cut across ethnic and political communities. In 1964 African states agreed to keep them anyway, fearing endless wars if they were reopened.
events.fact: Many of Africa's borders are straight lines drawn in European capitals by men who had never been there.

causes.why: Darwin's theory was twisted into 'Social Darwinism', which imperialists used to present conquest as the 'survival of the fittest', a phrase coined by Herbert Spencer, not Darwin.
Britain's move sparked a rush by France and Germany.
Leopold's Congo claims needed to be settled.
Bismarck, now Europe's leading statesman, hosted the conference that set the rules for dividing Africa.

q.before: Africans ruled almost all of Africa; Europeans held coastal footholds.
q.how: Rules for claiming African land: 'effective occupation' and notice to other powers.
q.claim: Spreading 'civilization', Christianity and free trade, and ending slavery.
q.winners: European powers; no African was invited.
q.lasted: The borders drawn mostly survive today.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck convened 14 states to set rules for claiming African territory so that the European race for colonies would end in treaties rather than a European war. The conference recognised Belgian King Leopold II's Congo, declared free trade on the Congo and Niger and made 'effective occupation' the test of a coastal claim; no African was present. It set off a scramble in which European powers seized almost the whole continent within 30 years and drew borders with little regard for the societies inside them.
events.lens: Rules made by outsiders for dividing a region shape it long after the outsiders leave.
events.myth: The conference carved up Africa on a map. It set rules for claims and recognised the Congo; the borders were drawn over the next 20 years in bilateral treaties and by conquest.

kv: countries at the conference; no Africans
African states independent by 1914: Ethiopia and Liberia

events.h: Carl Peters' treaties found German East Africa
events.who: Carl Peters; local chiefs in Usagara
events.what: A German adventurer got chiefs to sign treaties they couldn't read, and Germany claimed East Africa.
events.why: Germany's leaders, under pressure from colonial lobbyists, wanted colonies to match Britain and France. Peters wanted fame and a chartered company of his own.
events.sig: Germany and Britain divided the East African mainland in 1886 and left the Sultan of Zanzibar a coastal strip.
events.hook: A German adventurer got chiefs to sign treaties they couldn't read, and Germany claimed East Africa.
events.story: German adventurer Carl Peters travelled inland from the coast with a few companions in November 1884 and collected 'treaties' from chiefs in Usagara in weeks, often by trickery. The chiefs signed away sovereignty over land the Sultan of Zanzibar claimed. In February 1885 Kaiser Wilhelm I granted Peters' company an imperial charter.
events.then: Germany and Britain divided the East African mainland in 1886 and left the Sultan of Zanzibar a coastal strip.
events.now: The treaties gave Germany the claim on which it partitioned the mainland with Britain in 1886. The colony became Tanganyika under British rule from 1919 and Tanzania in 1964.

causes.why: The conference set the rules Peters exploited.

q.before: Inland peoples were independent; the coast belonged to the Sultan of Zanzibar.
q.how: A private company claimed sovereignty under German protection.
q.winners: Peters' German East Africa Company; losers were local people and the Sultan.
q.lasted: Until 1919.

events.bluf: German adventurer Carl Peters went inland from the coast in late 1884 to collect treaties with chiefs in Usagara that would give his Society for German Colonisation a claim to East Africa. He gathered them in weeks, often by trickery, and in February 1885 Kaiser Wilhelm I granted his company an imperial charter. The treaties became the legal basis of German East Africa and a claim German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck used in the partition.
events.lens: Colonial 'treaties' often served as legal cover for conquest.
events.fact: Germany dismissed Peters in 1897 for his brutality; Africans called him 'Mkono wa Damu', the bloody hand.

events.what: The Berlin Conference recognised Belgium's king as the personal owner of a territory 76 times the size of Belgium.
events.why: Leopold wanted a colony that Belgium would not give him. He won recognition at the Berlin Conference by promising free trade and an end to the slave trade. The rubber boom of the 1890s made forced labour pay.
events.sig: Campaigners E.D. Morel, Roger Casement and George Washington Williams exposed the abuses. The scandal forced Belgium to annex the colony in 1908. Belgian rule kept extracting resources and left very few Congolese with higher education at independence in 1960.
events.hook: The Berlin Conference recognised Belgium's king as the personal owner of a territory 76 times the size of Belgium.
events.story: Belgian King Leopold II had posed as a humanitarian and promised to end the slave trade. His agents forced Congolese to collect rubber and ivory, held families hostage and cut off hands as punishment for missed quotas.
events.then: Campaigners E.D. Morel, Roger Casement and George Washington Williams exposed the abuses. The scandal forced Belgium to annex the colony in 1908. Belgian rule kept extracting resources and left very few Congolese with higher education at independence in 1960.
events.now: The Free State fixed the Congo as a state organised to extract rather than govern, a pattern Belgian rule to 1960 and Mobutu's regime to 1997 repeated. The campaign against it, organised from 1904, was the model for later human rights movements.
events.fact: King Leopold II ran Congo as his private property for 23 years and never once visited it.

causes.why: The conference recognised Leopold's Congo Free State as his personal domain.

q.before: Many African kingdoms and peoples in the Congo basin.
q.how: Recognition at the Berlin Conference of Leopold's private colony.
q.lasted: Until 1908, when Belgium took over.

events.bluf: Belgian King Leopold II wanted a colony that Belgium's parliament would not give him and won the powers' recognition of a private state in the Congo basin by promising free trade and an end to the slave trade. His agents forced Congolese to collect rubber and ivory, held families hostage and cut off hands for missed quotas; the population fell by millions. The atrocities provoked the first international human rights campaign, forced Belgium to annex the colony in 1908 and left Congo a state built for extraction.
events.lens: Humanitarian rhetoric can mask extraction: follow the commodity to see what a regime really does.

events.what: Nationalist political party founded.
events.why: Western-educated Indians wanted a voice in how India was governed. The European backlash of 1883 against the Ilbert Bill, which would have let Indian judges try Europeans, showed them a discrimination they could organise against.
events.sig: Congress split between moderates and extremists in 1907 and reunited in 1916. Under Mohandas Gandhi from 1920 and Jawaharlal Nehru it became a mass movement and led India to independence in 1947.
events.hook: Educated Indians formed the party that would lead India to independence.
events.story: In December 1885, 72 delegates, mostly lawyers, teachers and journalists, met in Bombay to found the Indian National Congress, with retired civil servant Allan Octavian Hume as organiser and Calcutta barrister W. C. Bonnerjee as president. The early resolutions asked for more Indians in the civil service and the legislative councils.
events.then: Congress split between moderates and extremists in 1907 and reunited in 1916. Under Mohandas Gandhi from 1920 and Jawaharlal Nehru it became a mass movement and led India to independence in 1947.
events.now: It ruled India for most of its first 50 years, and its decline since the 1990s has reshaped Indian politics around the Hindu-nationalist BJP.

causes.why: British schools and universities produced an Indian professional class that began organising to demand a voice in government.

q.before: Indians had little voice in British-run government.
q.how: A political association meeting yearly.
q.winners: Educated Indians, in the long run.
q.lasted: Yes: it led India to independence.

events.bluf: Western-educated Indians wanted a national body to ask for a larger Indian role in government, and retired British official Allan Octavian Hume helped them found one. Seventy-two delegates met in Bombay in December 1885 and petitioned for reform within British rule. Under Mohandas Gandhi the Congress became the mass movement that won independence in 1947, and it governed India for most of its first 50 years.
events.lens: Movements often begin moderate and elite before becoming mass and radical.
events.fact: Hume, the British founder, was an ornithologist whose collection of Indian birds went to the Natural History Museum in London.

events.hook: A bomb at a Chicago labour rally gave the world May Day.
events.what: A bomb at a Chicago labour rally gave the world May Day.
events.story: About 300,000 workers struck across the country on 1 May 1886 for the eight-hour day. On 3 May Chicago police fired on strikers at the McCormick reaper works and killed at least two. Anarchist leaders called a protest at Haymarket Square on 4 May; as police moved to disperse it, someone threw a bomb that killed one officer at once and six more from wounds, and the police fired into the crowd. Eight anarchists were tried for murder; the bomber was never identified. Four were hanged on 11 November 1887, one killed himself in his cell, and three were pardoned by Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld in 1893.
events.why: Workers were fighting for an eight-hour day amid violent clashes with police and employers. Chicago's anarchist press had called for arms, which the prosecution used in place of evidence.
events.then: Fear of immigrant radicals spread, employers broke the eight-hour strikes, and the Knights of Labor fell from about 700,000 members in 1886 to a remnant within a decade. The American Federation of Labor, founded that December, took its place. The Second International named 1 May the workers' day in 1889.
events.sig: Fear of immigrant radicals spread, employers broke the eight-hour strikes, and the Knights of Labor fell from about 700,000 members in 1886 to a remnant within a decade. The American Federation of Labor, founded that December, took its place. The Second International named 1 May the workers' day in 1889.
events.now: May 1 became International Workers' Day in honour of the Haymarket martyrs, almost everywhere except the United States; at home the backlash moved labour from the Knights' broad crusade to the AFL's craft unionism, the pattern until the 1930s.

causes.why: Railroads created giant corporations and national labour markets; the Great Railroad Strike of 1877 began decades of labour conflict.

q.before: Workers often worked 10-12 hour days.
q.how: Strikes and rallies, then a bombing and trials.
q.lasted: May Day became a global workers' holiday.

events.bluf: Chicago's workers struck for an eight-hour day on 1 May 1886, and anarchists called a rally in Haymarket Square after police killed strikers at the McCormick works. Someone threw a bomb at the police; seven officers and at least four civilians died, eight anarchists were convicted on evidence that tied none of them to the bomb, and four were hanged. In the United States the affair fed fear of immigrant radicals and broke the Knights of Labor; abroad it made 1 May the workers' day.
events.lens: One violent incident can discredit a whole movement and justify repression.
events.fact: The police statue erected in Haymarket Square was blown up twice, in 1969 and 1970, by the Weathermen; the martyrs' monument in a Chicago cemetery draws unions from around the world.

events.who: Spain's government; Cuban abolitionists and the enslaved
events.what: Slavery abolished.
events.why: The Ten Years' War, in which rebels freed enslaved people who joined them, made slavery a liability. Abolitionist pressure in Spain and from Britain grew. The end of slavery in the United States in 1865 removed Cuba's last large slaveholding neighbour.
events.sig: Formerly enslaved Cubans joined the independence war of 1895-98 in large numbers. Brazil abolished slavery in 1888, the last state in the Americas to do so.
events.hook: Spain finally abolished slavery in Cuba, its richest remaining colony.
events.story: Cuba's sugar boom had depended on enslaved Africans. In the Ten Years' War of 1868-78 rebels freed enslaved people who joined them. Spain's Moret Law of 1870 freed the newborn and the elderly, the patronato of 1880 turned the rest into bound 'apprentices', and a royal decree of October 1886 ended the system two years early.
events.then: Formerly enslaved Cubans joined the independence war of 1895-98 in large numbers. Brazil abolished slavery in 1888, the last state in the Americas to do so.
events.now: Afro-Cuban soldiers' part in the wars of 1868-98, above all under general Antonio Maceo, tied Black freedom to Cuban nationhood, a link that Afro-Cuban music, religion and culture carry at the heart of Cuban identity.

causes.why: With US slavery ended, and Cuban rebels in the Ten Years' War (1868-78) freeing enslaved people who joined them, Spain began a gradual abolition completed in 1886.

q.before: About 200,000 people were enslaved in Cuba in the 1870s.
q.how: Gradual abolition laws, completed in 1886.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Spain's government ended slavery in Cuba in stages to keep the island, under pressure from the Ten Years' War, in which the enslaved had fought for independence, and from abolitionists at home and abroad. The patronato system of 1880 was abolished in 1886 and the last patrocinados were freed. One of the largest and last slave economies in the Americas ended, and Afro-Cubans' role in the independence wars tied racial freedom to Cuban nationalism.
events.lens: Wars that arm enslaved people make slavery impossible to restore.
events.fact: Cuba was the second-to-last place in the Americas to abolish slavery; only Brazil, in 1888, came later.
events.btt: Cuba: Sugarcane and the growth of slavery

events.h: Britain and Germany divide East Africa
events.what: Diplomats drew the line between future Kenya and Tanzania, with Kilimanjaro going to Germany.
events.why: Britain and Germany wanted no conflict over overlapping claims. They settled their spheres without consulting Africans.
events.sig: Germany leased the Sultan's coastal strip in 1888, which set off the Abushiri revolt. Britain took over the northern coast.
events.hook: Diplomats drew the line between future Kenya and Tanzania, with Kilimanjaro going to Germany.
events.story: German adventurer Carl Peters' treaties of 1884 had given Germany claims that overlapped Britain's and Zanzibar's. In 1886 Britain and Germany drew a line from the coast to Lake Victoria, bending to put Kilimanjaro on the German side. Britain took the zone to the north, which became Kenya; Germany took the south, mainland Tanzania. Zanzibar Sultan Barghash, who claimed the whole coast, was left his islands and a 10-mile coastal strip, and no African ruler inland was consulted.
events.then: Germany leased the Sultan's coastal strip in 1888, which set off the Abushiri revolt. Britain took over the northern coast.
events.now: The 1886 line is still the Kenya-Tanzania border. The Sultan's coastal strip, leased and then bought by the European powers, became the coast of both colonies and the ground of the Abushiri revolt of 1888.

causes.why: Rival British and German claims needed settling.

q.before: The Sultan claimed the coast and influence inland.
q.how: Two European spheres, drawn without asking the people.
q.lasted: It's essentially the Kenya-Tanzania border today.

events.bluf: Britain and Germany set out to settle their overlapping claims on the East African mainland before they collided. In 1886 they drew a line from the coast to Lake Victoria, bending to put Kilimanjaro on the German side, and left Zanzibar Sultan Barghash, who claimed the whole coast, his islands and a 10-mile strip. The line became the Kenya-Tanzania border, and no African ruler inland was consulted.
events.lens: Borders drawn in European capitals reflect diplomatic trade-offs, not local realities.
events.myth: Queen Victoria 'gave' Kilimanjaro to her grandson the Kaiser as a birthday present. The bend came from the 1886 negotiations, and Wilhelm became Kaiser two years later.
events.fact: The border runs almost straight from the coast to the lake except for the bend around Kilimanjaro.

kv: the coastal strip left to the Sultan

events.hook: Skilled workers' unions formed the federation that would dominate American labour.
events.what: Skilled workers' unions formed the federation that would dominate American labour.
events.story: The Knights of Labor, which organised skilled and unskilled workers together, was collapsing after Haymarket. Delegates from craft unions met at Columbus, Ohio, on 8 December 1886 and elected cigar maker Samuel Gompers president of the new American Federation of Labor. Gompers set its course on 'bread-and-butter' goals, wages, hours and conditions, won by strikes and contracts with employers, and kept it from endorsing any party.
events.why: After the Haymarket backlash weakened the more radical Knights of Labor, craft unions wanted a stronger national organisation of their own. Skilled workers had bargaining power the unskilled lacked and wanted to use it without carrying them.
events.then: The AFL reached about 2 million members by 1914 and more than 4 million by 1920. Gompers led it until his death in 1924. It merged with the industrial unions of the CIO in 1955.
events.sig: The AFL reached about 2 million members by 1914 and more than 4 million by 1920. Gompers led it until his death in 1924. It merged with the industrial unions of the CIO in 1955.
events.now: The AFL's focus on wages and conditions rather than socialism shaped American unions, which remain more pragmatic and less tied to a political party than many in Europe.

causes.why: The Haymarket backlash weakened the more radical Knights of Labor, leaving the craft unions of the new AFL to lead American labour.

q.what: Organised labour: wages, hours and working conditions.

events.bluf: Craft union leaders, with cigar maker Samuel Gompers at their head, wanted a national federation that would bargain for wages and hours and leave politics and revolution alone. They founded the American Federation of Labor at Columbus, Ohio, in December 1886, weeks after Haymarket. Its 'business unionism' became the pattern of American labour, which never built a mass socialist party on the European model.
events.lens: Labor movements that seek gains within the system tend to survive; revolutionary ones attract repression.
events.fact: Gompers, asked what labour wanted, answered 'More'.

events.who: The French Third Republic; Vietnamese, Cambodian and Lao rulers

events.then: French rule rested on forced labour on rubber plantations and heavy taxes and was resisted from the start. Vietnamese revolutionary Ho Chi Minh founded the Indochinese Communist Party in 1930.
events.now: French Indochina's borders created modern Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, and the struggle against French rule led directly into the Vietnam wars.

q.how: Conquest and protectorate treaties.
q.winners: French colonists and rubber and rice companies.

events.bluf: France's Third Republic set out to build an Asian empire for markets, prestige against Britain and a route into southern China. It conquered southern Vietnam from 1858, made Cambodia a protectorate in 1863, took northern and central Vietnam after a war with China in 1883-85 and combined them into the Indochinese Union in 1887, adding Laos in 1893. The colony's borders made modern Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, and resistance to it produced Vietnamese nationalism, communism and three decades of war.
events.lens: Colonies assembled from distinct peoples often split apart after independence.
events.fact: Hanoi's opera house, finished in 1911, was modelled on the Palais Garnier in Paris.

events.what: Last country in the Americas to end slavery.
events.why: Mass flight from the plantations made slavery unworkable by 1887, and the army's refusal to recapture runaways removed the means of enforcing it. A national abolitionist movement had made slavery a liability for the crown. The laws of 1871 and 1885 had already set a closing date in all but name.
events.sig: Planters who had lost their workforce without compensation backed the officers who overthrew Brazilian Emperor Pedro II in November 1889. The freed received no land. The state subsidised European immigration to replace them, in part with the stated aim of 'whitening' the population.
events.hook: Brazil became the last country in the Americas to end slavery.
events.story: Brazil had received more enslaved Africans than any other country and still held about 700,000 people in slavery in 1888. A law of 1871 had freed children born to enslaved mothers, and a law of 1885 freed the elderly. Through the 1880s enslaved people left the plantations in large numbers and the army declined to hunt them. On 13 May 1888 Princess Isabel, acting as regent for Brazilian Emperor Pedro II, signed the Lei Áurea, the Golden Law, abolishing slavery without compensation.
events.then: Planters who had lost their workforce without compensation backed the officers who overthrew Brazilian Emperor Pedro II in November 1889. The freed received no land. The state subsidised European immigration to replace them, in part with the stated aim of 'whitening' the population.
events.now: Abolition without land or schooling left Black Brazilians at the bottom of the labour market from 1888, and state subsidies for European immigrants kept them there. Brazil has the largest population of African descent outside Africa, and racial gaps in income, education and policing remain wide.
events.fact: Brazil received about 4.9 million enslaved Africans, more than any other country and roughly 40 per cent of the whole transatlantic trade.

causes.why: With slavery ended in the United States and ending in Cuba, Brazil was isolated as the last slave society in the Americas.

q.before: Brazil had the largest enslaved population in the Americas.
q.how: A short law signed by the regent.
q.winners: The formerly enslaved, though without land or support.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Brazilian abolitionists, enslaved people fleeing the plantations and Regent Princess Isabel set out to end slavery in the last country in the Americas that kept it. The Golden Law of 13 May 1888 freed about 700,000 people at once, with no compensation for owners and no land for the freed. Planters withdrew their support from the monarchy, which fell eighteen months later, and Black Brazilians entered freedom at the bottom of the social order.
events.lens: Emancipation without land or resources leaves freed people dependent: look at what accompanies a legal change.

events.hook: Britain handed East Africa to a private company, as Germany had done.
events.story: Scottish shipping magnate William Mackinnon's Imperial British East Africa Company received a royal charter in 1888 to trade and govern the British sphere from Mombasa to Uganda. It sent Captain Frederick Lugard to Buganda in 1890. It made no profit.
events.then: The company went nearly bankrupt. Britain took over Uganda in 1894 and Kenya in 1895 directly.
events.now: Company failure made the British state the direct ruler of Uganda from 1894 and Kenya from 1895, and the railway it then built to justify the cost shaped both colonies.

q.what: Trade in ivory and plans for a railway to Uganda.
q.who: Investors hoped for profit; the company soon went broke.

q.daily: Little for most people.
q.system: 'Company rule', which Britain replaced with protectorates in 1894–95.

events.bluf: Britain wanted influence from Mombasa to Uganda without the cost of direct rule and let a company carry the risk. Shipping magnate William Mackinnon's Imperial British East Africa Company received a royal charter in 1888 to trade and govern the British sphere; it made no profit and was near bankruptcy within five years. The British government took over Uganda in 1894 and Kenya in 1895 directly, and the colonial state replaced the company.
events.lens: Empire on the cheap fails when costs exceed profits, and the state then takes over.
events.fact: Mackinnon had made his fortune with the British India Steam Navigation Company, whose mail steamers had linked Aden and Zanzibar since 1872.

events.h: Abushiri revolt on the Swahili coast

events.story: In August 1888 the German East Africa Company took over the coastal towns under its lease from the Sultan and imposed taxes and land registration. Coastal traders, Arab and African leaders and inland allies, led by Pangani trader Abushiri ibn Salim al-Harthi, drove the Germans out of almost every town. Germany sent commander Hermann von Wissmann with an army of African mercenaries. Abushiri was captured and hanged in December 1889.
events.then: The German state took direct control of German East Africa in 1891 and ended company rule.
events.now: The revolt ended company rule in German East Africa in 1891 and put the colony under a military administration. Abushiri is honoured in Tanzania as an early resistance leader, and the revolt is an early case of coastal and inland Africans uniting against colonial rule.

q.decided: A naval blockade and Wissmann's mercenary force.

q.changed: Germany took the colony from the company and ruled it directly from 1891.

events.bluf: The German East Africa Company took over the Sultan's coastal towns in August 1888 and imposed taxes and land registration; coastal traders, Arab and African leaders and inland allies under Pangani trader Abushiri ibn Salim al-Harthi rose to throw it out. They drove the Germans from almost every town, and Germany sent commander Hermann von Wissmann with an army of African mercenaries to crush them; Abushiri was hanged in December 1889. Company rule had failed, and the German state took direct control of the colony in 1891.
events.lens: Private companies can claim colonies but often need their governments to hold them.
events.fact: Wissmann recruited his army in Egypt from Sudanese veterans and added Zulu from Mozambique; it became the colony's Schutztruppe.

events.hook: Japan became the first Asian country with a Western-style constitution and parliament.
events.story: After studying constitutions in Europe, statesman Itō Hirobumi chose Prussia's model, with a strong emperor and a limited parliament. Emperor Meiji promulgated the constitution as a 'gift' to his people on 11 February 1889. The Diet first met in 1890.
events.then: Western powers began agreeing to revise the unequal treaties, starting with Britain in 1894, and the elected Diet slowly gained influence through its power over budgets.
events.now: Its weakness, the army answering only to the emperor, helped militarists take over in the 1930s.

After the rebellion, opposition shifted to demanding a parliament.

events.bluf: Statesman Itō Hirobumi wanted a constitution that would satisfy demands for a parliament and prove to the West that Japan was 'civilised' enough to end the unequal treaties, while keeping power with the emperor and his ministers. The constitution of February 1889, on the Prussian model, gave Japan a parliament and a strong emperor. Asia had its first constitutional state; a military answerable only to the emperor, outside cabinet control, let militarists take charge in the 1930s.
events.lens: Constitutional details about who controls the military can decide a nation's fate.
events.fact: The promulgation date, 11 February, was the legendary founding day of Japan by Emperor Jimmu, then a national holiday.

events.who: Marshal Manuel Deodoro da Fonseca; Emperor Pedro II
events.what: Emperor overthrown.
events.why: Planters who had lost their slaves without compensation in 1888 withdrew their loyalty to the crown. Army officers resented civilian governments that had slighted them since the Paraguayan War. Republican and positivist ideas had spread among junior officers and urban professionals.
events.sig: Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca became the first president and resigned in 1891 under military and congressional pressure. Power settled with the coffee oligarchies of São Paulo and Minas Gerais until 1930. The military intervened in politics repeatedly for the next century.
events.hook: Brazil's army overthrew Emperor Pedro II and declared a republic.
events.story: Brazilian Emperor Pedro II had reigned since 1831, and his heir, Princess Isabel, had lost the planters' loyalty by signing abolition in 1888. On 15 November 1889 Marshal Manuel Deodoro da Fonseca led troops in Rio de Janeiro against the cabinet, and a republic was proclaimed the same day. The imperial family left for Europe within two days.
events.then: Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca became the first president and resigned in 1891 under military and congressional pressure. Power settled with the coffee oligarchies of São Paulo and Minas Gerais until 1930. The military intervened in politics repeatedly for the next century.
events.now: The officers who founded the republic treated the army as guardian of the nation, and that claim justified military interventions from 1889 to the dictatorship of 1964-85. The flag's motto, 'Order and Progress', comes from the positivist philosophy many of them held.

causes.why: The war made Brazil's army a political force; officers overthrew the emperor in 1889.
Planters angry at abolition without compensation withdrew their support from the monarchy, which fell the next year.

q.before: Emperor Pedro II.
q.how: A military coup.
q.lasted: Yes: Brazil has been a republic since.

events.bluf: Army officers led by Marshal Manuel Deodoro da Fonseca, with planters angry at uncompensated abolition behind them, set out to replace Brazil's monarchy with a republic. They deposed Brazilian Emperor Pedro II in a nearly bloodless coup on 15 November 1889, and he sailed into exile. The army established itself as the arbiter of Brazilian politics, a role it claimed again in 1930, 1945 and 1964.
events.lens: Coups that succeed easily become precedents: Brazil's army learned that it could remake the state.
events.fact: Pedro II died in exile in Paris in 1891; he had kept a box of Brazilian soil to be buried with him.

events.who: Kaiser Wilhelm II; Chancellor Otto von Bismarck
events.hook: The new Kaiser forced out the chancellor who had kept France isolated for twenty years, and within four years France and Russia were allies.
events.what: The new Kaiser forced out the chancellor who had kept France isolated for twenty years, and within four years France and Russia were allies.
events.story: German Kaiser Wilhelm II, 31 and on the throne for twenty months, demanded Chancellor Otto von Bismarck's resignation on 18 March 1890 after disputes over social policy and the chancellor's right to see ministers alone. Three months later Berlin let the secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapse. Russia turned to France; the Franco-Russian alliance was signed in 1894.
events.why: The alliance system rested on contradictions only Bismarck managed: Germany was allied to Austria and secretly pledged to Russia at once. Wilhelm II wanted to govern himself and had been told the Russian treaty was disloyal to Austria.
events.then: Russia turned to France and the two signed a military alliance in 1894. German planning for a two-front war became the Schlieffen Plan.
events.sig: Russia turned to France and the two signed a military alliance in 1894. German planning for a two-front war became the Schlieffen Plan.
events.now: It is the clearest modern case of a structural shift caused by a personnel decision, and a standing argument against systems that depend on one person.

q.before: Three emperors' league, then the Reinsurance Treaty: Russia and Germany pledged neutrality.
q.how: The Kaiser demanded resignation; the chancellor complied.
q.claim: Wilhelm's: the monarch, not the chancellor, would set policy.
q.lasted: The two-front problem lasted until 1945.

events.bluf: German Kaiser Wilhelm II, 31 and twenty months on the throne, wanted to govern in his own name and forced Chancellor Otto von Bismarck out. Bismarck's alliance system, which had kept France isolated through contradictions only he managed, lapsed within months when Berlin dropped the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia. Russia allied with France in 1894, and Germany spent the next generation planning the two-front war that resulted.
events.trig: Wilhelm demanded Bismarck's resignation on 18 March 1890; in June Berlin let the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapse.
events.lens: A system that only its author could run ended when he left.
events.fact: Punch marked the dismissal with the cartoon 'Dropping the Pilot': Bismarck climbing down a ship's ladder while the young Kaiser watches from the rail.

events.what: ~250 Lakota killed; Census declared frontier closed.
events.why: The army feared the Ghost Dance, a movement promising the return of the old world, and reservation agents had called for troops. The killing of Sitting Bull days earlier had sent Lakota bands fleeing across the reservations.
events.sig: The Dawes Act of 1887 was pushed through the reservations, breaking tribal land into private plots and selling the 'surplus' to settlers; Native landholding fell by about two thirds by 1934. Children were sent to boarding schools to strip them of language and culture.
events.hook: The massacre of Lakota families marked the end of armed Native resistance.
events.story: The Ghost Dance, a religious movement promising the return of the bison and the dead, spread through the Lakota reservations in 1890, and the army moved in. Lakota chief Sitting Bull was killed by reservation police on 15 December during an attempt to arrest him. Chief Spotted Elk led his band toward the Pine Ridge agency and surrendered to the 7th Cavalry, which surrounded the camp at Wounded Knee Creek with four Hotchkiss guns. On 29 December 1890, as soldiers searched for weapons, a rifle went off and the troops opened fire; about 250 Lakota and 25 soldiers died. The same year the Census Bureau declared the frontier closed.
events.then: The Dawes Act of 1887 was pushed through the reservations, breaking tribal land into private plots and selling the 'surplus' to settlers; Native landholding fell by about two thirds by 1934. Children were sent to boarding schools to strip them of language and culture.
events.now: Wounded Knee closed the Plains wars and opened the assimilation era; the American Indian Movement occupied the site for 71 days in 1973 to protest broken treaties, and the massacre remains the reference point in debates over Native sovereignty and land.
events.fact: The army awarded 20 Medals of Honor for Wounded Knee, which Lakota descendants have campaigned to have rescinded.

causes.why: After Custer's defeat, the army forced the Lakota onto reservations; Wounded Knee was the last major massacre.

q.why: The army feared the Ghost Dance movement.
q.decided: Soldiers fired on a camp being disarmed.
q.cost: About 250 Lakota killed.
q.changed: Armed Native resistance on the Plains ended.

events.bluf: The army set out to disarm a band of about 350 Lakota under Chief Spotted Elk whose Ghost Dance observance it feared, two weeks after Sitting Bull was killed in an arrest attempt. A rifle went off during the search for weapons on 29 December 1890, and the 7th Cavalry's rifles and Hotchkiss guns killed about 250 people, many of them women and children. Armed Native resistance in the United States ended there, and decades of allotment, boarding schools and forced assimilation followed unopposed.
events.lens: Fear of a religious revival can lead armed forces to massacre.

events.what: Germany swapped its claims to Zanzibar for a small North Sea island.
events.why: Britain wanted control of the Nile's sources and Zanzibar. Germany wanted Heligoland to protect its naval coast and the Kiel Canal then under construction.
events.sig: Britain's grip on Zanzibar led to the 1896 bombardment. Germany turned Heligoland into a naval fortress.
events.hook: Germany swapped its claims to Zanzibar for a small North Sea island.
events.story: British Prime Minister Lord Salisbury and German Chancellor Leo von Caprivi concluded the treaty on 1 July 1890. Britain got Zanzibar as a protectorate, and Germany dropped claims in Uganda and Witu. Germany got the island of Heligoland and the Caprivi Strip in Namibia.
events.then: Britain's grip on Zanzibar led to the 1896 bombardment. Germany turned Heligoland into a naval fortress.
events.now: The treaty fixed the sphere Britain turned into Uganda and Kenya and the protectorate it used to govern Zanzibar until 1963. Heligoland became the fortress guarding the Kiel Canal and the German fleet.

causes.why: Germany needed stability on the coast.
Britain wanted to secure the route to Uganda.

q.before: Zanzibar was independent, with Germany and Britain competing for influence.
q.how: Zanzibar became a British protectorate.
q.winners: Britain and Germany; nobody asked Zanzibar.
q.lasted: Zanzibar was a protectorate until 1963.

events.bluf: Britain wanted the sources of the Nile in Uganda and a protectorate over Zanzibar; Germany wanted the North Sea island of Heligoland to guard its naval coast. In 1890 they traded: Germany dropped its claims to Uganda and Witu, and Britain got Zanzibar, gave up Heligoland and conceded the Caprivi Strip. Africa's borders were set by a bargain over unrelated interests, and Britain's hold on Zanzibar led to the bombardment of 1896.
events.lens: In great-power bargains, distant territories become trading chips.
events.fact: The Caprivi Strip's odd shape on Namibia's map comes from this treaty; Germany wanted a corridor to the Zambezi.

events.h: Mkwawa's Hehe destroy a German column at Lugalo
events.who: Chief Mkwawa's Hehe army vs. Emil von Zelewski's Schutztruppe
events.what: The Hehe ambushed and nearly wiped out a German army, the Germans' worst early defeat in Africa.
events.why: Germany wanted Hehe control of the trade routes broken. Mkwawa refused to submit.
events.sig: Germans stormed Mkwawa's fortress at Kalenga in 1894. He fought a guerrilla war until 1898.
events.hook: The Hehe ambushed and nearly wiped out a German army, the Germans' worst early defeat in Africa.
events.story: The Hehe under Chief Mkwawa were the strongest power in the southern highlands and controlled the caravan routes. On 17 August 1891 about 3,000 Hehe warriors ambushed German commander Emil von Zelewski's force of about 320 askari plus officers and porters at Lugalo. Zelewski was killed.
events.then: Germans stormed Mkwawa's fortress at Kalenga in 1894. He fought a guerrilla war until 1898.
events.now: The defeat forced Germany to fight a seven-year war against the Hehe and to garrison the interior, which made German East Africa a military colony; Mkwawa's resistance became a founding story of Tanzanian nationalism.

causes.why: Once the coast was crushed, Germany pushed inland.

q.why: Hehe independence vs. German expansion inland.
q.stakes: Control of the southern highlands and caravan routes.
q.decided: A well-planned ambush in tall grass.
q.cost: Most of the German column killed.
q.changed: It began seven years of Hehe resistance.

events.bluf: German commander Emil von Zelewski marched into the southern highlands to break Hehe control of the caravan routes after Hehe Chief Mkwawa refused to submit. On 17 August 1891 about 3,000 Hehe warriors ambushed his column of about 320 askari plus officers and porters at Lugalo and killed him. It was the heaviest early defeat of colonial forces in German East Africa, and it forced Germany into a seven-year war that made the colony a military one.
events.lens: Early defeats often lead colonial powers to escalate rather than withdraw.
events.fact: The Hehe carried off the column's rifles and guns. Lugalo is celebrated in Tanzania as a symbol of resistance.

toll.n: The commander, Emil von Zelewski, was among the dead.

events.who: Queen Liliʻuokalani; American and European planters; US Minister John Stevens
events.hook: American planters, backed by US Marines, overthrew Hawaii's queen.
events.what: American planters, backed by US Marines, overthrew Hawaii's queen.
events.story: The 1887 'Bayonet Constitution' had stripped the Hawaiian monarch of most power and limited the vote by wealth. Hawaiian Queen Liliʻuokalani moved in January 1893 to proclaim a new constitution restoring royal authority and Hawaiian voting rights. A Committee of Safety of mostly American businessmen declared a provisional government on 17 January 1893 under Sanford Dole; US Minister John Stevens had Marines landed from USS Boston the day before. The queen yielded under protest to avoid bloodshed.
events.why: Sugar planters wanted annexation to secure duty-free access to the American market after the 1890 US tariff ended their advantage. The queen's constitution threatened their control.
events.then: US President Grover Cleveland withdrew the annexation treaty, called the overthrow an 'act of war' and declined to restore the queen by force. The Republic of Hawaii was declared in 1894; Congress annexed it in 1898.
events.sig: US President Grover Cleveland withdrew the annexation treaty, called the overthrow an 'act of war' and declined to restore the queen by force. The Republic of Hawaii was declared in 1894; Congress annexed it in 1898.
events.now: The overthrow is the legal grievance on which Native Hawaiian sovereignty claims rest, acknowledged by the 1993 apology resolution and unresolved since.

causes.why: The kingdom Kamehameha founded lasted until American planters overthrew it in 1893.

q.before: Queen Liliʻuokalani ruled the Hawaiian Kingdom.
