q.lasted: Yes: the US annexed Hawaii in 1898.

events.bluf: American sugar planters in Hawaii wanted annexation by the United States and duty-free access to its market; Hawaiian Queen Liliʻuokalani wanted a new constitution restoring royal power. A Committee of Safety of mostly American businessmen seized power on 17 January 1893 with US Marines landed by US Minister John Stevens. The monarchy was gone, annexation followed in 1898, and the US Congress acknowledged the overthrow as illegal in 1993 without reversing it.
events.lens: Economic interests can drive regime change, with official forces providing cover.
events.fact: Liliʻuokalani composed 'Aloha ʻOe', the best-known Hawaiian song, in 1878.

events.h: New Zealand gives women the vote
events.who: Kate Sheppard and the Women's Christian Temperance Union
events.hook: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections.
events.what: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections.
events.story: The Women's Christian Temperance Union, with suffrage campaigner Kate Sheppard as its organiser, gathered petitions in 1891, 1892 and 1893; the last carried nearly 32,000 signatures, about a quarter of the colony's adult women. Premier Richard Seddon opposed the bill. The Legislative Council passed it by 20 votes to 18, and Governor Lord Glasgow signed the Electoral Act on 19 September 1893. Māori and Pākehā (European) women voted in the general election ten weeks later.
events.why: The temperance movement gave the campaign its organisation and a motive, since women were expected to vote against drink. Two opponents in the Council voted for the bill in anger at Seddon's tactics.
events.then: Australia granted women the federal vote in 1902 and Finland in 1906; Britain and the United States followed after the First World War. New Zealand women could stand for Parliament from 1919, and the first woman MP was elected in 1933.
events.sig: Australia granted women the federal vote in 1902 and Finland in 1906; Britain and the United States followed after the First World War. New Zealand women could stand for Parliament from 1919, and the first woman MP was elected in 1933.
events.now: New Zealand's precedent gave suffrage campaigners elsewhere a working democracy to point to: Australia followed in 1902, Finland in 1906, Britain and the United States after the First World War.

q.before: Only men could vote.
q.how: Petitions and an act of Parliament.
q.winners: New Zealand women, Māori and Pākehā.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Suffrage campaigner Kate Sheppard and the Women's Christian Temperance Union set out to win New Zealand women the vote, over Premier Richard Seddon's opposition. Three petitions, the last signed by about a quarter of the colony's adult women, and a two-vote margin in the upper house carried the Electoral Act on 19 September 1893. New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the national vote, Māori women included, and other democracies followed over the next 30 years.
events.lens: Small, newer democracies can adopt reforms faster than older, larger ones.
events.fact: The 1893 petition was glued into a single roll about 270 metres long and unrolled on the floor of the House; Sheppard appears on New Zealand's $10 note.

q.before: Company rule.
q.how: Direct British administration.
q.lasted: Until independence in 1962–63.

events.hook: After its chartered company went broke, Britain took Uganda under direct rule.
events.what: After its chartered company went broke, Britain took Uganda under direct rule.
events.story: The Imperial British East Africa Company could not afford to hold Uganda and announced its withdrawal in 1892. Missionary lobbies and Nile strategists in Britain campaigned to stay. The British government declared a protectorate in 1894, with Buganda's king and chiefs as its partners.
events.why: Control of the source of the Nile protected Britain's position in Egypt. Missionary and anti-slavery opinion wanted Buganda's Protestants protected.
events.then: Britain built a railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria to hold it. It ruled largely through the Buganda kingdom's chiefs, whose position the Uganda Agreement of 1900 confirmed.
events.sig: Britain built a railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria to hold it. It ruled largely through the Buganda kingdom's chiefs, whose position the Uganda Agreement of 1900 confirmed.
events.now: Britain's Nile strategy governed East Africa to 1956: Uganda, Kenya and Sudan were held to secure Egypt's water. The Nile still shapes the region's politics, including the dispute over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
events.bluf: The British government declared a protectorate over Uganda in 1894 to keep the source of the Nile, and with it Egypt's water, out of another power's hands after the Imperial British East Africa Company could no longer afford to hold it. Buganda's kingdom became the core of a British colony. Strategic worry about water drove the colonisation of a whole region and tied Uganda's fate to Egypt's for the rest of the century.
events.lens: Control of rivers and water sources drives strategy across borders.
events.fact: Uganda takes its name from Buganda, the kingdom at its centre, as Swahili speakers rendered it.

events.what: Japan won easily.
events.why: Rivalry over Korea came first: China treated it as a tributary and Japan's planners saw it as a dagger pointed at Japan's heart. Japan's Meiji reforms had produced a conscript army and a modern fleet while Qing self-strengthening had produced ships without a unified command.
events.sig: China ceded Taiwan and the Pescadores and paid 200 million taels. Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to return the Liaodong Peninsula within a week and took Chinese leases for themselves from 1897. Chinese reformers concluded that the Qing system had failed; the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 and the revolution of 1911 followed.
events.hook: Japan crushed China and became Asia's leading power.
events.story: Korea was a Qing tributary in which Japan had built commercial and political influence since 1876. The Donghak peasant rebellion of 1894 brought Chinese troops at the Korean court's request and Japanese troops in answer. Japanese Prime Minister Itō Hirobumi's government declared war on 1 August 1894. Japan's army beat Qing forces at Pyongyang in September, its navy won at the Yalu the same month, and its troops took Port Arthur in November 1894 and Weihaiwei in February 1895. Qing viceroy Li Hongzhang signed peace at Shimonoseki in April 1895.
events.then: China ceded Taiwan and the Pescadores and paid 200 million taels. Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to return the Liaodong Peninsula within a week and took Chinese leases for themselves from 1897. Chinese reformers concluded that the Qing system had failed; the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 and the revolution of 1911 followed.
events.now: The war moved leadership in East Asia from China to Japan, gave Japan Taiwan and a free hand in Korea, and exposed the Qing to the scramble for concessions that followed; it began fifty years of Japanese expansion that ended in 1945.
events.fact: It was the first time an Asian state beat China with Western methods. The Qing fleet lost five ships at the Yalu and Japan lost none.

causes.why: After 1860 the Qing tried 'self-strengthening', buying modern ships and guns. In 1894 Japan's more thorough modernisation destroyed them.
Japan and China had competed over Korea since 1876.
Japan went to war two weeks after Britain agreed to treaty revision.

q.why: Control of Korea; Japan saw it as 'a dagger pointed at the heart of Japan'.
q.stakes: Who would dominate Korea and East Asia.
q.decided: Japan's modern army and navy crushed China's forces on land and at the Yalu River.
q.cost: About 35,000 Chinese and 13,000 Japanese dead, most from disease.
q.changed: Japan replaced China as East Asia's leading power.

events.bluf: Japan fought Qing China in 1894 to end Chinese control of Korea and take China's place as the leading power in East Asia. Its modernised army and navy won every major engagement in nine months, and the Treaty of Shimonoseki gave Japan Taiwan, an indemnity of 200 million taels and a free hand in Korea. Leadership of East Asia passed from China to Japan, and the exposed weakness of the Qing set off a European scramble for concessions in China.
events.trig: The Donghak peasant rebellion in Korea, which led both China and Japan to send troops in 1894.
events.lens: Wars between neighbours often reveal which has adapted faster to new technologies.

toll.n: Most Japanese deaths came from disease.

events.what: Military alliance against Germany.
events.why: Germany let its Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapse in 1890. France, seeking to end its own isolation, offered Russia loans and an alliance.
events.sig: Germany now faced possible war on two fronts and planned for it with the Schlieffen Plan: beat France fast, then turn on Russia.
events.hook: France and Russia joined against Germany, creating a two-front threat.
events.story: After Germany let its Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapse in 1890, France offered Russia loans and friendship. A secret military convention, agreed in 1892 and ratified in 1894, pledged each to fight Germany if it attacked the other.
events.then: Germany now faced possible war on two fronts and planned for it with the Schlieffen Plan: beat France fast, then turn on Russia.
events.now: That plan's march through neutral Belgium brought Britain into World War I, a lesson in how military plans can drive political decisions.

causes.why: France, determined to recover Alsace-Lorraine, found an ally once Germany let its treaty with Russia lapse in 1890.

q.before: Bismarck had kept France isolated.
q.how: A secret military convention.
q.lasted: Until 1917.

events.bluf: France wanted out of the isolation Bismarck had built around it; Russia wanted loans and a counterweight to Germany after Berlin let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse. A secret military convention agreed in 1892 and ratified in 1894 bound each to fight Germany if it attacked the other. Germany now faced war on two fronts, and the plan it drew to win one, through Belgium, brought Britain in when it was used in 1914.
events.lens: When one power's diplomacy lapses, rivals fill the gap: alliances form against the strongest.
events.fact: French savers lent Russia the money that built its railways; by 1914 about a quarter of French foreign investment was in Russia.

events.what: Britain became the first Western power to give up special legal rights in Japan.
events.why: Japan had a constitution and modern legal codes. Britain wanted Japan as a partner against Russia.
events.sig: Two weeks later Japan went to war with China, confident of Britain's goodwill. Japan recovered full control of its tariffs in 1911.
events.hook: Britain became the first Western power to give up special legal rights in Japan.
events.story: Japanese Foreign Minister Mutsu Munemitsu negotiated the Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation, signed in London on 16 July 1894. It agreed that foreigners in Japan would face Japanese courts from 1899. The other powers followed.
events.then: Two weeks later Japan went to war with China, confident of Britain's goodwill. Japan recovered full control of its tariffs in 1911.
events.now: Treaty revision made Japan the first non-Western state admitted to the European order as a legal equal, which licensed its own imperial expansion from 1895 and its alliance with Britain in 1902.

causes.why: Modern laws and a constitution persuaded Britain.
It began undoing the 1858 treaties.

q.before: Foreigners were exempt from Japanese law.
q.how: Japan regained full legal sovereignty over foreigners.
q.lasted: Yes; Japan regained full tariff control in 1911.

events.wk: Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation
events.bluf: Japanese Foreign Minister Mutsu Munemitsu set out to end the unequal treaties that put foreigners in Japan beyond Japanese courts; Britain wanted a modernising partner against Russia. The Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of July 1894 ended extraterritoriality from 1899, and the other powers followed. Japan became the first non-Western state to leave the unequal treaty system, and went to war with China two weeks later confident of Britain's goodwill.
events.lens: Recognition as an equal often comes when a rising power becomes useful to an established one.
events.fact: Japan had built the Rokumeikan, a Western-style ballroom in Tokyo, in 1883 to show foreign diplomats that it was civilised by their standards.

kv: Japan regained control of its tariffs

events.what: China paid a huge indemnity and handed Japan Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula.
events.why: China had been beaten on land and at sea and feared a Japanese march on Beijing. Japan wanted its gains fixed before the European powers intervened.
events.sig: Within six days Russia, France and Germany demanded that Japan give back Liaodong. Japan complied for a further 30 million taels and spent the combined indemnity on its navy.
events.hook: China paid a huge indemnity and handed Japan Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula.
events.story: Talks opened at Shimonoseki in March 1895 between Japanese Prime Minister Itō Hirobumi and Qing viceroy Li Hongzhang. On 24 March a Japanese nationalist shot Li in the face; he survived, and Japan softened its terms. The treaty signed on 17 April 1895 recognised Korea's 'independence', ending China's influence there; ceded Taiwan, the Pescadores and the Liaodong Peninsula; opened ports; and set an indemnity of 200 million taels of silver.
events.then: Within six days Russia, France and Germany demanded that Japan give back Liaodong. Japan complied for a further 30 million taels and spent the combined indemnity on its navy.
events.now: The indemnity funded Japan's naval expansion after 1896 and its move to the gold standard in 1897, which gave it access to London capital for the war against Russia in 1904.

causes.why: China sued for peace after its defeats.

q.before: China was Korea's protector and Asia's great power.
q.how: Japan gained colonies and influence over Korea.
q.winners: Japan; losers were China and, soon, Korea.
q.lasted: Taiwan was Japanese until 1945; within weeks Japan was forced to agree to hand Liaodong back.

events.bluf: Japanese Prime Minister Itō Hirobumi set out to turn victory over China into territory, money and a free hand in Korea. Qing viceroy Li Hongzhang conceded Taiwan, the Pescadores, the Liaodong Peninsula, 200 million taels and Korea's 'independence'. Japan became an imperial power with a treasury to fund a navy and the gold standard, and the Qing court's exposed weakness opened the reform crisis of 1898 and the foreign scramble for Chinese ports.
events.lens: Indemnities can finance the winner's next round of expansion.
events.fact: Li Hongzhang finished the talks with the assassin's bullet still lodged below his left eye.

events.h: Triple Intervention: Japan forced to give back its prize
events.who: Russia, France and Germany vs. Japan
events.what: Three European powers forced Japan to return the Liaodong Peninsula, and Japan never forgot it.
events.why: Russian Tsar Nicholas II's government wanted a warm-water port in Manchuria. France was Russia's ally under the treaty of 1894. German Kaiser Wilhelm II wanted Russia's attention on Asia and away from Germany's eastern border.
events.sig: Japan adopted the slogan 'gashin shōtan', enduring hardship for revenge, and built up its navy in British yards. Russia leased Port Arthur in 1898, Britain allied with Japan in 1902 and Japan attacked Russia in 1904.
events.hook: Three European powers forced Japan to return the Liaodong Peninsula, and Japan never forgot it.
events.story: On 23 April 1895, six days after the Treaty of Shimonoseki, the ministers of Russia, France and Germany in Tokyo 'advised' Japan to give up the Liaodong Peninsula, including Port Arthur. Britain refused to join them. Japanese Prime Minister Itō Hirobumi's cabinet, facing three great powers with a fleet worn by war, gave the peninsula back for an extra 30 million taels.
events.then: Japan adopted the slogan 'gashin shōtan', enduring hardship for revenge, and built up its navy in British yards. Russia leased Port Arthur in 1898, Britain allied with Japan in 1902 and Japan attacked Russia in 1904.
events.now: The intervention turned Japanese policy toward armament against Russia from 1895 to 1904 and is the standard case of a humiliation setting a state's foreign policy; Russia's seizure of the same port in 1898 made the war of 1904 likelier.

causes.why: Russia didn't want Japan in Manchuria.

q.before: Japan thought victory had made it a great power.
q.how: European powers showed they still decided the fate of East Asia.
q.winners: Russia, which leased Port Arthur itself in 1898.
q.lasted: Japan took Port Arthur back from Russia in 1905.

events.myth: The intervening powers are often given as Britain and France, or the dispute placed in Korea. The powers were Russia, France and Germany, the territory was the Liaodong Peninsula, and Britain stayed out and became Japan's ally.
events.bluf: Russia, with France and Germany, set out to stop Japan holding the Liaodong Peninsula, which Russia wanted for its own warm-water port. Japan, unable to fight three European powers, returned the peninsula for 30 million taels. Tokyo drew the lesson that only armed strength would bring respect, and ten years of naval building aimed at Russia followed.
events.lens: Diplomatic humiliation can drive a nation's foreign policy for a generation.
events.fact: 'Gashin shōtan' comes from a Chinese tale of a king who slept on firewood and tasted gall each day to keep his hunger for revenge fresh.

kv: extra taels Japan got for handing back Liaodong

events.who: Japan; the short-lived Republic of Formosa
events.what: China ceded Taiwan.
events.why: Japan wanted a southern base facing Fujian and the Philippines, a colony to prove great-power rank, and the island's sugar and camphor.
events.sig: Japan crushed armed resistance over seven years at a cost of thousands of Taiwanese lives, then built railways, ports, schools and sugar mills to make Taiwan a model colony. From 1937 it pressed Japanese names and language on the population. In 1945 the island passed to Chiang Kai-shek's Republic of China.
events.hook: Taiwan became Japan's first colony.
events.story: Under the Treaty of Shimonoseki of April 1895 Qing China ceded Taiwan and the Pescadores to Japan. Qing governor Tang Jingsong and local gentry declared a Republic of Formosa in May 1895 to resist the transfer. Japanese troops landed in late May, entered Taipei in June and took Tainan in October; the republic was gone within months. Armed resistance continued for years, and from 1898 Japanese Governor-General Kodama Gentarō and civil administrator Gotō Shinpei ran the colony.
events.then: Japan crushed armed resistance over seven years at a cost of thousands of Taiwanese lives, then built railways, ports, schools and sugar mills to make Taiwan a model colony. From 1937 it pressed Japanese names and language on the population. In 1945 the island passed to Chiang Kai-shek's Republic of China.
events.now: Fifty years of Japanese rule from 1895 to 1945 gave Taiwan railways, schools and a legal order separate from the mainland's. That separate experience, followed by Nationalist rule from 1945, is one root of a Taiwanese identity that Beijing reads as a provincial variation of Chinese identity and that many in Taiwan read as national.

causes.why: Taiwan was ceded in the treaty.

q.before: Taiwan was a Qing province.
q.how: Cession by treaty, then military occupation.
q.lasted: Until 1945.

events.bluf: Japan demanded Taiwan at Shimonoseki to gain a southern base and a colony that would mark it as a great power. Qing officials on the island declared a Republic of Formosa in May 1895; Japanese troops entered Taipei in June and took the last resisting city in October, and fifty years of colonial rule followed. Taiwan's development ran on a separate track from mainland China's, which is one root of the identity question that divides the strait today.
events.lens: Different colonial histories create different national memories, even among neighbours.
events.fact: The Republic of Formosa lasted about five months and is often called Asia's first republic.

events.what: Final war against Spain.
events.why: Cubans wanted the independence the Ten Years' War of 1868-78 had failed to win. A fall in sugar prices and a US tariff of 1894 ruined planters and workers alike.
events.sig: US newspapers publicised the camps, and after USS Maine exploded in Havana in February 1898 the United States declared war on Spain in April. Spain gave up Cuba in December 1898. The Platt Amendment of 1901 gave the United States a right to intervene in independent Cuba.
events.hook: Cubans rose once more against Spain, led by the poet José Martí.
events.story: Cuban poet and organiser José Martí, after years of exile in New York, launched the war in February 1895 with General Antonio Maceo and General Máximo Gómez. Martí was killed at Dos Ríos on 19 May 1895, weeks after landing. From 1896 Spanish Captain-General Valeriano Weyler forced rural civilians into fortified towns, where many died of hunger and disease. Maceo was killed in December 1896.
events.then: US newspapers publicised the camps, and after USS Maine exploded in Havana in February 1898 the United States declared war on Spain in April. Spain gave up Cuba in December 1898. The Platt Amendment of 1901 gave the United States a right to intervene in independent Cuba.
events.now: Independence on terms written in Washington made sovereignty against the United States the core of Cuban nationalism from 1902. Both the Cuban government and Cuban exiles in Miami claim José Martí as their national hero.

causes.why: With slavery gone, Black and white Cubans fought side by side in an independence army led by José Martí and Antonio Maceo.

q.why: Cubans fought for independence from Spain.
q.decided: US intervention in 1898.
q.cost: Hundreds of thousands died, many in Spanish camps.
q.changed: Spain lost Cuba, but the US took control.

events.bluf: Cuban nationalists led by poet José Martí and General Antonio Maceo rose in 1895 to end Spanish rule after the Ten Years' War had failed to win it. By 1898 they had Spain's army confined to the towns, at the cost of mass civilian deaths in Spanish detention camps. The United States intervened and took the victory, and Cuba gained independence under US supervision, a grievance that fed Cuban nationalism up to 1959.
events.lens: Outside powers that intervene in independence wars often claim the victory for themselves.
events.fact: Martí wrote the verses later set to the song 'Guantanamera'.

events.hook: Britain took over the bankrupt company's coastal territory: the future Kenya.
events.what: Britain took over the bankrupt company's coastal territory: the future Kenya.
events.story: In July 1895 Britain took over the company's territory between the coast and Uganda as the East Africa Protectorate, with its capital at Mombasa. The capital moved to Nairobi in 1905. The territory became Kenya Colony in 1920.
events.why: Britain wanted the route between the coast and Uganda secured, and with it the headwaters of the Nile.
events.then: The railway and white settlers in the highlands followed. Africans were pushed into reserves.
events.sig: The railway and white settlers in the highlands followed. Africans were pushed into reserves.
events.now: The land alienated for settlers from 1902 was the grievance behind the Mau Mau uprising of 1952-60 and the land politics of independent Kenya.

causes.why: When the company went bankrupt, Britain took over its territory directly.

q.before: The Imperial British East Africa Company ran the territory.
q.how: The British government took over directly.
q.lasted: It became Kenya Colony in 1920.

events.bluf: Britain took over the Imperial British East Africa Company's territory between the coast and Uganda in July 1895 to secure the route to the Nile. The East Africa Protectorate, run from Mombasa, moved its capital to Nairobi in 1905 and became Kenya Colony in 1920. A railway and white settlement in the highlands shaped the colony, and the land taken for settlers became the central grievance of Kenyan nationalism.
events.lens: Land seized for settlers fuels later anticolonial revolts, and land remains the hardest issue to settle after independence.
events.fact: Kenya is named after its mountain, which the Kikuyu call Kirinyaga.

events.who: Japanese agents and Korean allies; Queen Min (Empress Myeongseong)
events.what: Japanese agents broke into Korea's royal palace and killed the queen who was turning Korea toward Russia.
events.why: Miura feared Korea would slide into Russia's sphere after the Triple Intervention. Queen Min and her clan were the pro-Russian and anti-Japanese centre of the court.
events.sig: King Gojong fled to the Russian legation in February 1896 and ruled from it for a year; Russian advisers and concessions followed, and the rivalry between Japan and Russia sharpened. In 1897 Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire and buried Min as Empress Myeongseong.
events.hook: Japanese agents broke into Korea's royal palace and killed the queen who was turning Korea toward Russia.
events.story: After Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to return the Liaodong Peninsula in April 1895, Korean Queen Min, consort of King Gojong, turned to Russia to balance Japanese power. Japanese minister Miura Gorō organised an attack on Gyeongbok Palace in the early hours of 8 October 1895. Japanese agents and Korean soldiers trained by Japan broke in, killed the queen and burned her body.
events.then: King Gojong fled to the Russian legation in February 1896 and ruled from it for a year; Russian advisers and concessions followed, and the rivalry between Japan and Russia sharpened. In 1897 Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire and buried Min as Empress Myeongseong.
events.now: The murder pushed Korea toward Russia from 1896 and turned the contest for Korea into the direct Russo-Japanese rivalry that ended in war in 1904. In Korea-Japan relations it stands first in the list of grievances from the colonial period.

causes.why: The Intervention showed Korea's court that Russia could check Japan.

q.before: Korea's court balanced Japan, China and Russia.
q.how: Korea's king fled to the Russian legation for a year.
q.claim: Japan claimed it was protecting Korea's 'independence'.
q.winners: In the short term, Russia gained influence in Korea.
q.lasted: It poisoned Korean views of Japan for good.

events.bluf: Japanese minister in Seoul Miura Gorō organised the murder of Korean Queen Min to remove the court's leading advocate of leaning on Russia against Japan. Japanese agents and Korean allies killed her in Gyeongbok Palace on 8 October 1895 and burned her body. The killing drove King Gojong into the Russian legation instead of securing Japan's hold, and the Russo-Japanese rivalry over Korea sharpened toward the war of 1904.
events.lens: Removing a leader who favours a rival can backfire by pushing the country further toward that rival.
events.fact: A Japanese court in Hiroshima released Miura and his accomplices in January 1896 for want of evidence.

kv: until King Gojong fled to the Russian legation
Japanese tried in Hiroshima, all acquitted

events.what: Britain built a railway from the coast to Lake Victoria, and built Kenya around it.
events.why: Britain wanted Uganda and the Nile secured. It wanted the inland slave caravans ended and the colony paying for itself.
events.sig: White settlers took fertile highlands along the line. Indian traders and workers settled in towns along its route.
events.hook: Britain built a railway from the coast to Lake Victoria, and built Kenya around it.
events.story: Begun in 1896 at Mombasa, the railway reached Lake Victoria at Kisumu in 1901. Over 30,000 labourers came from British India; several thousand died. In 1898 two lions at Tsavo killed at least 28 workers. Nairobi grew from a railway camp.
events.then: White settlers took fertile highlands along the line. Indian traders and workers settled in towns along its route.
events.now: The line decided where Kenya's capital, settler farms and towns would be. Nairobi exists because of the railway, Kenya's Indian community descends partly from its workers, and the settler economy it was built to pay for created the land grievance of 1952.

causes.why: To hold Uganda and the Nile's source, Britain needed a railway from the coast.
The railway ran from Mombasa across the new protectorate to Lake Victoria.

q.what: A 600-mile railway across Kenya.
q.who: Indian laborers and Africans whose land it crossed paid; British settlers later profited.
q.scale: About £5.5 million, enormous at the time.
q.daily: It brought settlers, cash crops and new towns.
q.system: A settler colony based on export farming.

events.myth: Critics in Parliament mocked it as 'the Lunatic Line' because it seemed to go from nowhere to nowhere.
events.bluf: Britain built the Uganda Railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria to hold Uganda and the Nile's headwaters, end the inland slave caravans and make the colony pay. Begun in 1896 with over 30,000 labourers from British India, several thousand of whom died, it reached the lake in 1901. It fixed Kenya's geography: Nairobi, white settlement in the highlands and the Indian community all grew from it.
events.lens: Railways built for strategy create cities and societies along their routes.
events.fact: Critics in Parliament mocked it as 'the Lunatic Line' because it ran from nowhere to nowhere; it cost over £5 million.

events.what: Ethiopian army crushed an Italian invasion force.
events.why: Italy wanted Ethiopia as the hinterland of its colony of Eritrea. Menelik had united Ethiopia's regional lords and built a large army with modern rifles, many bought from France and Russia.
events.sig: Ethiopia and Liberia were the only African states to keep their independence through the partition. Italy invaded again under Mussolini in 1935.
events.hook: Ethiopia crushed an Italian invasion and stayed independent.
events.story: Italy claimed a protectorate under a clause of the 1889 Treaty of Wuchale whose Amharic and Italian versions differed. On 1 March 1896 Ethiopian Emperor Menelik II's army of around 100,000 men, armed with modern rifles, destroyed an Italian invasion force under General Oreste Baratieri at Adwa. Empress Taytu led her own contingent. About 7,000 Italian soldiers were killed. Italy recognised Ethiopia's independence that October.
events.then: Ethiopia and Liberia were the only African states to keep their independence through the partition. Italy invaded again under Mussolini in 1935.
events.now: Adwa kept Ethiopia independent until 1936 and made it the reference point of pan-Africanism. Ethiopia's colours appear on many African flags, and Addis Ababa hosts the African Union.
events.fact: Ethiopia's green, yellow and red were later adopted by many newly independent African states as pan-African colours.

sites.d: March 1, 1896: Italy loses ~7,000 killed.
Italy's Red Sea base, later colony of Eritrea.
Menelik's new capital.

causes.why: Italy was racing to claim its share of Africa.

q.why: Italy tried to make Ethiopia a protectorate.
q.decided: Menelik's large, well-armed army and Italian blunders.
q.cost: About 7,000 Italians and several thousand Ethiopians killed.
q.changed: Ethiopia stayed independent.

events.bluf: Italy claimed a protectorate over Ethiopia under the Treaty of Wuchale and invaded to enforce it; Ethiopian Emperor Menelik II raised about 100,000 men armed with modern rifles to stop it. At Adwa on 1 March 1896 his army destroyed the Italian force, killing about 7,000, and Italy recognised Ethiopia's independence that October. Ethiopia stayed free while almost all of Africa was colonised, and Adwa became the proof that an African state could beat a European army.
events.lens: Where African states combined unity among regional rulers with modern weapons, colonization failed.

toll.n: About 3,000 Italians were also captured. It was the worst defeat of a European army in Africa in the colonial era.

events.who: Britain vs. Sultan Khalid bin Barghash
events.what: Shortest war in history (~40 minutes).
events.why: Khalid seized the palace without British approval. Britain, which claimed the right to approve the sultan under the 1890 protectorate, chose to make an example.
events.sig: Britain installed Hamoud bin Mohammed as sultan. He abolished slavery in 1897. Zanzibar remained a British protectorate until 1963.
events.hook: Britain bombarded Zanzibar in the shortest war in history.
events.story: Zanzibar Sultan Hamad died on 25 August 1896. His cousin Khalid bin Barghash seized the palace without British approval. On 27 August British warships shelled the palace for about 40 minutes until Khalid's flag came down. About 500 of his defenders were killed or wounded.
events.then: Britain installed Hamoud bin Mohammed as sultan. He abolished slavery in 1897. Zanzibar remained a British protectorate until 1963.
events.now: The bombardment installed a sultan who did as Britain asked, ended Zanzibar's independence and forced the abolition of slavery in 1897; British control of the coast and the Swahili interior followed.
events.fact: At about forty minutes, it is the shortest recorded war. Khalid fled to the German consulate and was carried out to a German warship.

causes.why: Zanzibar was a British protectorate.

q.why: Britain rejected a sultan who took power without its approval.
q.decided: Naval gunfire.
q.cost: About 500 Zanzibari casualties.
q.changed: A pro-British sultan was installed.

events.bluf: Britain claimed the right to approve Zanzibar's sultan, and when Khalid bin Barghash seized the palace on Sultan Hamad's death in August 1896 it chose to make an example. On 27 August British warships shelled the palace for about 40 minutes until Khalid's flag came down; about 500 of his defenders were killed or wounded. Britain installed a sultan who did as it asked, and the sultanate's independent authority ended.
events.lens: Protectorates are colonies in all but name: watch who approves the ruler.

events.what: Upheld 'separate but equal' segregation.
events.why: Southern states were rolling back the rights of Reconstruction, and the committee wanted a federal ruling before segregation hardened. The Court's majority read the 14th Amendment as guaranteeing legal rather than social equality.
events.sig: Segregation spread by law through schools, trains, restaurants and hospitals across the South, and the 'equal' half of the formula was ignored. Southern states stripped Black citizens of the vote in the same decade. Brown v. Board of Education overturned the doctrine for schools in 1954.
events.hook: The Supreme Court blessed 'separate but equal' and legalized segregation.
events.story: Louisiana's Separate Car Act of 1890 required railways to seat Black and white passengers apart. The Comité des Citoyens of New Orleans arranged for shoemaker Homer Plessy, one-eighth Black and able to pass as white, to buy a first-class ticket and sit in a whites-only car on 7 June 1892; he was arrested by prior arrangement. On 18 May 1896 the Supreme Court ruled 7-1 that the law was constitutional under the 14th Amendment provided facilities were equal. Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented alone: 'Our Constitution is colour-blind'.
events.then: Segregation spread by law through schools, trains, restaurants and hospitals across the South, and the 'equal' half of the formula was ignored. Southern states stripped Black citizens of the vote in the same decade. Brown v. Board of Education overturned the doctrine for schools in 1954.
events.now: 'Separate but equal' governed American law for 58 years until Brown v. Board overturned it in 1954, a reminder that courts can entrench injustice as well as end it.

causes.why: The Supreme Court upheld segregation as 'separate but equal', giving Jim Crow constitutional cover.

q.before: Southern states were passing segregation laws.
q.how: A Supreme Court ruling.
q.lasted: Until Brown v. Board of Education in 1954.

events.bluf: A committee of New Orleans Creoles of colour set out to test Louisiana's railway segregation law by having shoemaker Homer Plessy, who was one-eighth Black, arrested in a whites-only car. The Supreme Court ruled 7-1 in 1896 that separate facilities were lawful if 'equal'. Segregation gained constitutional approval, spread through every public institution in the South and stood for 58 years, until Brown v. Board of Education in 1954.
events.lens: Legal doctrines that pretend unequal treatment is equal entrench hierarchy.
events.fact: Plessy pleaded guilty in 1897 and paid a $25 fine; Louisiana pardoned him posthumously in 2022.

events.hook: Spain executed the Philippines' most famous writer, turning him into a martyr of the revolution.
events.what: Spain executed the Philippines' most famous writer, turning him into a martyr of the revolution.
events.story: Filipino writer José Rizal's novels exposed the abuses of Spanish friars and officials. He advocated reform within the empire. When the Katipunan secret society launched an uprising in August 1896, Spain arrested him, tried him for rebellion and shot him in Manila on 30 December.
events.why: Spain blamed Rizal's writings for inspiring the Katipunan revolt and wanted to make an example of him.
events.then: The revolution spread. Filipino forces under Emilio Aguinaldo declared independence in June 1898, and the United States conquered the islands in the war that followed.
events.sig: The revolution spread. Filipino forces under Emilio Aguinaldo declared independence in June 1898, and the United States conquered the islands in the war that followed.
events.now: Rizal's execution turned a reform movement into a revolution within two years and gave the Philippines a national hero whose method was writing rather than arms.

q.before: Spain ruled the Philippines through officials and friars.
q.how: Arrest, trial and execution.
q.claim: Spain blamed his writings for the revolt.
q.winners: No one: his death fuelled the revolution.
q.lasted: Spanish rule ended in 1898.

events.bluf: Spanish colonial authorities executed Filipino writer José Rizal to make an example of the man they blamed for inspiring the Katipunan uprising. Rizal had argued for reform rather than revolution, and the firing squad in Manila on 30 December 1896 turned him into a martyr. The revolution spread, Filipino forces declared independence in 1898, and the Philippines gained a national hero whose weapon had been the pen.
events.lens: Killing moderates leaves only radicals to lead: Spain turned a reformer into the revolution's martyr.
events.fact: Rizal, trained as an eye doctor, wrote his novels in Spanish; 'Noli Me Tangere' was printed in Berlin in 1887.

events.who: Sultan of Zanzibar under British pressure
events.what: Slavery itself was abolished in Zanzibar, 24 years after the market closed.
events.why: British pressure after the 1896 bombardment came first. Britain needed to justify its protectorate as an anti-slavery mission.
events.sig: Slavery on the mainland lingered for years. Kenya's coast ended it only in 1907, and German East Africa never fully abolished it.
events.hook: Slavery itself was abolished in Zanzibar, 24 years after the market closed.
events.story: In April 1897 Zanzibar Sultan Hamoud bin Mohammed, under British pressure, abolished the legal status of slavery on Zanzibar and Pemba. Enslaved people had to apply to a court for freedom, owners were compensated and concubines were excluded until 1909. Relatively few applied at first, because freedom brought no land or income. Many stayed on the clove plantations as low-paid workers or squatters.
events.then: Slavery on the mainland lingered for years. Kenya's coast ended it only in 1907, and German East Africa never fully abolished it.
events.now: Zanzibar's 1964 revolution, which overthrew the Arab-dominated government, was rooted partly in the inequalities left by slavery.

causes.why: Britain installed a compliant sultan.
The market had closed in 1873.

q.what: Clove plantations depended on enslaved labor.
q.who: Owners got compensation; the formerly enslaved got little.

q.daily: Freedom on paper; poverty in practice.

events.bluf: Britain pressed Zanzibar to abolish slavery to justify the protectorate as an anti-slavery mission. In April 1897 Zanzibar Sultan Hamoud bin Mohammed abolished the legal status of slavery on Zanzibar and Pemba in a cautious decree: enslaved people had to apply to a court, owners were compensated and concubines were excluded until 1909. Few applied at first, since freedom brought no land or income, and the inequality between Arab landowners and African labourers that remained fed the revolution of 1964.
events.lens: Abolition that preserves landownership preserves inequality.
events.fact: The decree came 24 years after the market closed and 90 years after Britain banned its own slave trade.

events.who: US Navy; Spanish authorities in Cuba
events.hook: A US battleship blew up in Havana harbour, and American newspapers blamed Spain.
events.what: A US battleship blew up in Havana harbour, and American newspapers blamed Spain.
events.story: The Maine anchored in Havana harbour on 25 January 1898. On the night of 15 February it exploded and sank, killing 266 of its crew. A US naval court of inquiry in March concluded that an external mine had set off the forward magazines, without naming who laid it. 'Remember the Maine! To hell with Spain!' became a newspaper slogan, and Congress declared war in April.
events.why: Washington sent the ship after riots in Havana in January 1898 threatened Americans there. Newspaper publishers William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer, competing for readers, had run Spanish atrocity stories for two years.
events.then: The United States defeated Spain in under four months and took Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. A second inquiry in 1911 also blamed an external explosion; the 1976 study reversed it.
events.sig: The United States defeated Spain in under four months and took Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. A second inquiry in 1911 also blamed an external explosion; the 1976 study reversed it.
events.now: The Maine set the pattern of an incident blamed on an enemy before the evidence was in supplying the case for war. A 1976 US Navy study found the likely cause was a fire in a coal bunker igniting the ship's own magazine.

causes.why: The Maine was sent to Havana to protect Americans during the Cuban revolt.

q.why: Americans sympathised with Cuba's rebels and blamed Spain for the explosion.
q.stakes: Cuba's future and US power in the Caribbean.

q.changed: The United States went to war with Spain.

events.bluf: The United States sent the battleship Maine to Havana in January 1898 to protect American lives and interests during Cuba's war of independence. It exploded on 15 February, killing 266 of its crew, and a US naval inquiry blamed a mine. Newspapers blamed Spain, Congress declared war in April, and the explosion became the standard case of an unexplained incident carrying a country into war.
events.lens: Be wary of incidents that conveniently justify a war many people already want.
events.fact: The wreck was raised in 1911 and sunk again in deep water in 1912 with military honours.

events.sig: Russian troops occupied Manchuria during the Boxer Rebellion in 1900 and stayed. Japan formed an alliance with Britain in 1902 and, after talks on spheres of influence failed, attacked Port Arthur in February 1904.
events.hook: Three years after forcing Japan out, Russia leased the same peninsula for itself.
events.story: In March 1898 Russian Tsar Nicholas II's government forced the Qing court to lease it the tip of the Liaodong Peninsula, with Port Arthur (Lüshun) and Dalian, for 25 years, and began a railway linking the ports to its Trans-Siberian line across Manchuria. It was the territory Russia, France and Germany had made Japan hand back three years earlier. Germany had just taken Qingdao, and Britain answered by taking Weihaiwei.
events.then: Russian troops occupied Manchuria during the Boxer Rebellion in 1900 and stayed. Japan formed an alliance with Britain in 1902 and, after talks on spheres of influence failed, attacked Port Arthur in February 1904.
events.now: The lease put a Russian fleet and railway in southern Manchuria from 1898 and turned the insult of 1895 into a standing threat; it set the ground and the object of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05.

causes.why: Russia had pushed Japan out of the same place.

q.lasted: Until 1905, when Japan captured it.

events.bluf: Russian Tsar Nicholas II's government forced Qing China to lease it the tip of the Liaodong Peninsula, the ground it had made Japan return three years earlier, to gain an ice-free naval base on the Pacific. It got Port Arthur and Dalian for 25 years and a railway linking them to the Trans-Siberian line. Japanese resentment became direct strategic rivalry, and war between the two within a decade became likelier.
events.lens: Taking a prize you denied a rival guarantees enmity and turns resentment into a strategic threat.
events.fact: Russia held Port Arthur for less than seven years; its garrison surrendered to Japan in January 1905.

events.hook: In four months the US defeated Spain and became an overseas empire.
events.what: In four months the US defeated Spain and became an overseas empire.
events.story: Congress declared war in April 1898, after USS Maine exploded in Havana harbour in February. US Commodore George Dewey destroyed the Spanish Pacific squadron at Manila Bay on 1 May. Theodore Roosevelt, who had resigned as assistant navy secretary to lead the volunteer Rough Riders, fought at San Juan Hill on 1 July, and the US Navy destroyed the Spanish Atlantic squadron off Santiago de Cuba on 3 July. An armistice followed in August.
events.why: Sympathy for Cuban rebels, stoked by sensational newspapers, gave the war its public support. Investors in Cuban sugar wanted order, and naval strategists wanted bases and coaling stations.
events.then: The United States took Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, made Cuba a protectorate and annexed Hawaii the same year. Filipinos who had fought Spain then fought the United States from 1899 to 1902, a war that killed about 4,200 US soldiers and, by estimates that start at 200,000, far more Filipino civilians.
events.sig: The United States took Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, made Cuba a protectorate and annexed Hawaii the same year. Filipinos who had fought Spain then fought the United States from 1899 to 1902, a war that killed about 4,200 US soldiers and, by estimates that start at 200,000, far more Filipino civilians.
events.now: The war made the United States a Caribbean and Pacific power from 1898, and the argument it opened over whether a republic should hold colonies runs through every later US debate on intervention. Puerto Rico and Guam remain US territories.

causes.why: With the frontier declared closed in 1890, influential voices argued America needed new frontiers and markets overseas.
US sympathy for Cuban rebels, sensational newspapers and the explosion of the USS Maine led to war with Spain.

q.changed: The US became an overseas empire.

events.bluf: US President William McKinley went to war with Spain in April 1898 to end the Cuban war on US terms, with the press, sugar interests and naval strategists pressing him. The United States destroyed two Spanish fleets and won in under four months. It became an overseas empire in the Caribbean and the Pacific and began its first counter-insurgency war abroad, in the Philippines.
events.trig: The explosion of USS Maine in Havana harbour in February 1898.
events.lens: Rising powers often move from continental expansion to overseas empire once their home territory is secure.
events.fact: More US soldiers died of disease, mainly typhoid and yellow fever, than of Spanish fire.

events.what: Navy Laws launched a battleship fleet.
events.why: Wilhelm II wanted 'a place in the sun' for Germany as a world power, which he believed required a great navy.
events.sig: Britain launched the Dreadnought in 1906 and settled its differences with France in 1904 and Russia in 1907.

events.story: German Kaiser Wilhelm II and Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz pushed Navy Laws through the Reichstag in 1898 and 1900 to build a battle fleet that could challenge Britain's. Britain answered with HMS Dreadnought in 1906, which made every earlier battleship obsolete, and a naval arms race followed.
events.then: Britain launched the Dreadnought in 1906 and settled its differences with France in 1904 and Russia in 1907.
events.now: The Anglo-German naval race is a standard example of a security dilemma and is often cited in debates over China's naval build-up and US power in the Pacific.

q.before: Britain ruled the seas unchallenged.
q.how: Navy Laws passed by the Reichstag.
q.winners: No one: it pushed Britain toward France and Russia.
q.lasted: The arms race lasted until 1914.

events.bluf: German Kaiser Wilhelm II and Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz set out to build a battle fleet strong enough to make Britain treat Germany as a world power. The Navy Laws of 1898 and 1900 began it; Britain answered with Dreadnought in 1906 and outbuilt Germany. The race ended Britain's isolation, pushing it to settle with France in 1904 and Russia in 1907, and made Anglo-German hostility a fixed condition before 1914.
events.lens: When a rising power challenges an established power's core security interest, alignment against it follows.
events.fact: Tirpitz's 'risk theory' held that a fleet two-thirds the size of Britain's would deter it; by August 1914 Britain had 29 dreadnoughts to Germany's 17.

kv: battleships planned by the 1900 Navy Law
HMS Dreadnought launched, restarting the race

events.what: Spain's empire ended in the Americas.
events.why: Spain had lost both its fleets and could not defend its colonies. US President William McKinley wanted coaling stations and bases for a navy operating in two oceans.
events.sig: US troops occupied Cuba until 1902 and returned in 1906-09 and 1917-22. The United States fought Filipino nationalists from 1899 to 1902. The Platt Amendment stood until 1934.
events.hook: Spain lost the last of its American empire, and the US took its place.
events.story: The treaty was signed in Paris on 10 December 1898. Spain relinquished Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States, which paid $20 million. Cuba became independent in 1902 after accepting the Platt Amendment, which gave the United States a right to intervene and a naval base at Guantánamo Bay.
events.then: US troops occupied Cuba until 1902 and returned in 1906-09 and 1917-22. The United States fought Filipino nationalists from 1899 to 1902. The Platt Amendment stood until 1934.
events.now: Puerto Rico and Guam have been US territories since 1898; their residents hold US citizenship and cannot vote for president. The Guantánamo lease of 1903 still stands over the Cuban government's objection.

causes.why: The war ended Spain's American empire; the US took Puerto Rico and made Cuba a protectorate.

q.before: Spain ruled Cuba and Puerto Rico.
q.how: A peace treaty.
q.lasted: Puerto Rico is still a US territory.

events.bluf: The United States, having beaten Spain in four months, set out to take Spain's remaining colonies and secure naval bases in the Caribbean and the Pacific. By the Treaty of Paris Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, the last for $20 million. Spain's American empire of four centuries ended, and the United States became an overseas colonial power with Cuba as its protectorate.
events.lens: One empire's collapse is often another's expansion: the US inherited Spain's islands and its colonial wars.
events.fact: Spain called 1898 'the Disaster', and a generation of Spanish writers took the name the Generation of '98.

events.what: Cornered after years of guerrilla war, Mkwawa shot himself, and the Germans sent his skull to Germany.

events.hook: Cornered after years of guerrilla war, Mkwawa shot himself, and the Germans sent his skull to Germany.
events.story: Hehe Chief Mkwawa had fought a guerrilla war since his fortress at Kalenga fell in 1894. Surrounded at Mlambalasi near Iringa, he took his own life on 19 July 1898. German soldiers cut off his head as a trophy and sent the skull to Germany.
events.then: His skull was held in Bremen. It was returned in 1954 and is in a memorial museum at Kalenga.
events.now: Mkwawa is a national hero in Tanzania, and the return of his skull is an early landmark in debates over restitution of colonial-era remains and objects.

causes.why: Mkwawa had resisted since Lugalo.

q.why: Hehe independence.
q.decided: Years of German pursuit and scorched earth.
q.cost: The Hehe lost their leader and much of their land.
q.changed: German control of the southern highlands.

events.myth: The Treaty of Versailles (1919) actually ordered Germany to hand over 'the skull of the Sultan Mkwawa'. It was finally returned in 1954.
events.bluf: German forces had hunted Hehe Chief Mkwawa for four years after his fortress at Kalenga fell in 1894. Surrounded at Mlambalasi on 19 July 1898, he took his own life rather than surrender, and German soldiers cut off his head as a trophy. The Hehe resistance, one of the longest against German rule, ended, and the return of his skull from Germany in 1954 became an early case of colonial restitution.
events.lens: Resistance leaders become national heroes long after their defeat.
events.fact: Article 246 of the Treaty of Versailles of 1919 ordered Germany to hand over 'the skull of the Sultan Mkwawa'. It took 35 years.

events.who: US Congress; the Republic of Hawaii (set up by the 1893 coup)
events.hook: Five years after American planters overthrew Hawaii's queen, the US annexed the islands.
events.what: Five years after American planters overthrew Hawaii's queen, the US annexed the islands.
events.story: The Republic of Hawaii, run by the planters who had overthrown Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893, sought annexation from the day it was formed. A treaty failed to find two-thirds in the Senate. During the war with Spain, with the Philippines the next objective, Congress passed the Newlands Resolution in July 1898 and US President William McKinley signed it. The American flag went up over ʻIolani Palace on 12 August 1898.
events.why: The navy wanted a coaling and repair base at Pearl Harbor on the route to the Philippines. Sugar interests wanted the market secured for good.
events.then: Hawaii became a US territory in 1900. Pearl Harbor became the Pacific Fleet's main base, the target of Japan's attack in 1941, and Hawaii became a state in 1959.
events.sig: Hawaii became a US territory in 1900. Pearl Harbor became the Pacific Fleet's main base, the target of Japan's attack in 1941, and Hawaii became a state in 1959.
events.now: Annexation made the United States a Pacific power and Pearl Harbor the base Japan struck in 1941; the US Congress apologised in 1993 for the overthrow that preceded it, and the apology is the basis of sovereignty claims.

causes.why: The planters' government sought annexation, which Congress granted during the war with Spain.

q.before: The Republic of Hawaii, set up by the 1893 coup.
q.how: A joint resolution of Congress.
q.winners: Sugar planters and the US Navy.
q.lasted: Yes: Hawaii became a state in 1959.

events.bluf: US President William McKinley and the Senate's expansionists wanted Hawaii as a mid-Pacific naval base, sugar planters wanted its market secured, and the Republic of Hawaii set up by the 1893 coup wanted in. Congress annexed Hawaii by joint resolution in July 1898, during the war with Spain. The United States became a Pacific power with a base at Pearl Harbor, and Native Hawaiians lost their country without a vote.
events.lens: Strategic value often overrides questions of legitimacy: a war gave Congress the reason to annex what it had earlier rejected.
events.fact: Annexation went through by simple majorities in both houses because a treaty could not get two-thirds of the Senate.
