q.why: Control of the Nile.
q.stakes: Britain's grip on Egypt and the Nile.
q.decided: Maxim machine guns; France's weakness at sea.
q.cost: About 10,000 Sudanese killed at Omdurman.
q.changed: Britain controlled Sudan; Britain and France settled their rivalry by 1904.

events.who: Kitchener's British-Egyptian army vs. the Mahdist state
events.hook: British machine guns killed about 10,000 Sudanese soldiers in a morning.
events.what: British machine guns killed about 10,000 Sudanese soldiers in a morning.
events.story: Mahdist Sudan under Khalifa Abdallahi had ruled since the fall of Khartoum in 1885. British commander Herbert Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army, with Maxim guns and artillery, faced about 50,000 Mahdist troops outside Omdurman on 2 September 1898. About 10,000 Sudanese were killed; fewer than 50 British troops died.
events.why: Britain wanted the Nile valley secured against France. Gordon's death in 1885 gave the campaign its public cause.
events.then: Britain and Egypt ruled Sudan jointly as the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan until 1956. Kitchener marched on to Fashoda to face the French.
events.sig: Britain and Egypt ruled Sudan jointly as the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan until 1956. Kitchener marched on to Fashoda to face the French.
events.now: Anglo-Egyptian rule from 1899 governed Sudan's north and south as separate worlds, which deepened the division that produced the civil wars of 1955 to 2005 and South Sudan's secession in 2011.

causes.why: Holding Egypt meant controlling the Nile.

events.bluf: British commander Herbert Kitchener led an Anglo-Egyptian army up the Nile to destroy the Mahdist state, secure the Nile valley and avenge General Charles Gordon's death at Khartoum in 1885. Outside Omdurman on 2 September 1898 his Maxim guns and artillery killed about 10,000 of some 50,000 Mahdist troops for fewer than 50 British dead. The Mahdist state was destroyed, and Britain and Egypt ruled Sudan jointly until 1956.
events.lens: When one side has industrial weapons and the other does not, battles become slaughter and conquest becomes cheap.
events.fact: Winston Churchill rode in the charge of the 21st Lancers at Omdurman and wrote it up in 'The River War'.

toll.n: About 13,000 Mahdists were also wounded. Machine guns did most of the killing.

events.hook: Britain and France nearly went to war over a mud fort on the Nile.
events.what: Britain and France nearly went to war over a mud fort on the Nile.
events.story: French Major Jean-Baptiste Marchand's small expedition had crossed Africa over two years to plant the flag at Fashoda on the White Nile in July 1898. British commander Herbert Kitchener arrived in September with a much larger force after Omdurman. After weeks of tension France backed down.
events.why: France wanted a belt of territory across Africa from west to east. Britain wanted the whole Nile. France's navy could not fight Britain's.
events.then: France ordered Marchand to withdraw in November 1898. The two settled their colonial disputes in the Entente Cordiale of 1904.
events.sig: France ordered Marchand to withdraw in November 1898. The two settled their colonial disputes in the Entente Cordiale of 1904.
events.now: Fashoda settled that France would leave the Nile to Britain, which cleared the way for the Entente Cordiale of 1904 and the alliance that fought Germany ten years later.

causes.why: Fresh from Omdurman, Kitchener steamed up the Nile and confronted the French at Fashoda.

q.before: Both France and Britain claimed the upper Nile.
q.how: A tense standoff, then a French withdrawal.
q.claim: Britain's claim to the Nile valley.
q.lasted: Sudan stayed Anglo-Egyptian until 1956.

events.bluf: France sent Major Jean-Baptiste Marchand across Africa to plant its flag on the Upper Nile and claim a belt of territory from west to east; Britain wanted the whole Nile from Cairo to Uganda. Marchand reached Fashoda in July 1898 and British commander Herbert Kitchener arrived with a far larger force after Omdurman; after weeks of tension France, with the weaker navy, backed down. The Nile went to Britain, and the two rivals settled their colonial disputes in the Entente Cordiale of 1904.
events.lens: A crisis that ends with one side backing down can lead to settlement when both face a bigger threat.
events.fact: 'Fashoda syndrome' is still used for French wariness of British influence in Africa.

kv: British and Egyptian troops under Kitchener

events.what: The US bought the Philippines from Spain and fought a brutal war to keep it.
events.why: The US wanted a Pacific base and Asian markets. US President William McKinley said Filipinos were unready to govern themselves.
events.sig: US rule built schools and institutions and promised eventual self-government. The Philippines became a commonwealth in 1935 and independent in 1946.
events.hook: The US bought the Philippines from Spain and fought a brutal war to keep it.
events.story: After defeating Spain in 1898, the United States paid $20 million for the islands under the Treaty of Paris. Filipino forces under Emilio Aguinaldo, who had declared independence, fought the Americans from February 1899. The US declared the war over in July 1902. At least 200,000 Filipino civilians died, mostly from famine and disease.
events.then: US rule built schools and institutions and promised eventual self-government. The Philippines became a commonwealth in 1935 and independent in 1946.
events.now: Largely forgotten in the United States, the war is central to Philippine history; today's US-Philippine alliance, including bases facing China in the South China Sea, grew from this relationship.

causes.why: The peace treaty gave the US the Philippines, which it then held in a bloody war against Filipino independence fighters.
The revolution Rizal's execution helped inspire declared independence in 1898, then fought the US to keep it.

q.before: The Philippine Republic had declared independence from Spain.
q.how: Military conquest.
q.lasted: Until independence in 1946.

events.bluf: The United States fought to hold the Philippines, bought from Spain for $20 million, as a Pacific base and gateway to Asian markets; Filipino forces under Emilio Aguinaldo fought for the independence they had declared. The US won after three years of war in which at least 200,000 Filipino civilians died, mostly of famine and disease. America became a colonial power in Asia, and the relationship it built produced the alliance that still ties the two countries.
events.lens: Liberators become occupiers when they decide the liberated are not ready to rule themselves.
events.fact: Aguinaldo was captured in March 1901 by American officers who entered his camp posing as prisoners of Filipino scouts in US service.

toll.n: Many civilian deaths came from disease and famine. Some estimates are far higher.

events.who: Britain vs. Boer republics (Transvaal, Orange Free State)
events.what: Britain won using scorched earth and concentration camps.
events.why: Control of the Witwatersrand gold fields came first. British demands for rights for foreign miners in the Transvaal gave a cause. Imperial ambition to unite southern Africa under British rule set the goal.
events.sig: Britain won at Vereeniging in May 1902. In 1910 it created the Union of South Africa, a white-ruled dominion that excluded Black Africans from power.
events.hook: Britain fought the Boer republics for gold, using concentration camps.
events.story: Gold had been found on the Witwatersrand in 1886 and Britain wanted it. War began in October 1899 after Transvaal President Paul Kruger's ultimatum. Boer guerrillas fought on after the republics' capitals fell in 1900; Britain burned farms and held about 100,000 civilians in camps where tens of thousands died.
events.then: Britain won at Vereeniging in May 1902. In 1910 it created the Union of South Africa, a white-ruled dominion that excluded Black Africans from power.
events.now: The camps and farm-burning of 1900-02 were an early case of 20th-century warfare against civilians, and the bitterness they left fed the Afrikaner nationalism that won power in 1948 and built apartheid.

sites.d: Diamond town besieged; Cecil Rhodes trapped inside.
118-day siege.
Siege led by Baden-Powell, founder of the Scouts.
Peace signed here, 1902.

causes.why: The Boer republics founded by the trekkers sat on the world's richest gold field after 1886, and Britain wanted control.

q.why: Britain wanted the Transvaal's gold and control of South Africa.
q.decided: British numbers and scorched-earth tactics.
q.cost: About 22,000 British soldiers, 7,000 Boer fighters and over 40,000 civilians in camps died.
q.changed: The Boer republics became British colonies.

events.bluf: Britain went to war with the Transvaal and the Orange Free State to control the Witwatersrand gold fields and bring southern Africa under its rule. It won in 1902 after burning farms and holding about 100,000 civilians in camps where about 26,000 Boer civilians, most of them children, and at least 14,000 Black Africans died. The Union of South Africa of 1910 reconciled British and Boer whites at the expense of Black South Africans.
events.lens: Wars against insurgents tend to escalate into wars against civilians.
events.trig: Transvaal President Paul Kruger's ultimatum of 9 October 1899 demanding that British troops withdraw from the Transvaal border.
events.fact: Welsh campaigner Emily Hobhouse's report on the camps in 1901 forced a government inquiry and a change of camp administration.

toll.n: Estimates. The camps' death toll became a scandal in Britain.

events.who: Queen Mother Yaa Asantewaa; British colonial forces
events.hook: When the British governor demanded to sit on the sacred Golden Stool, the Asante rose in revolt.
events.what: When the British governor demanded to sit on the sacred Golden Stool, the Asante rose in revolt.
events.story: Britain had exiled Asantehene Prempeh I in 1896. In March 1900 Gold Coast Governor Frederick Hodgson demanded the Golden Stool, the symbol of the Asante nation. Queen Mother Yaa Asantewaa of Ejisu led Asante fighters, who besieged the British fort at Kumasi for months. A relief force broke the revolt.
events.why: Britain wanted complete control after exiling the king. The demand for the Stool struck at the one bond above all Asante chiefs.
events.then: Asante was annexed to the Gold Coast colony in 1901. Yaa Asantewaa was exiled to the Seychelles, where she died in 1921. The Stool stayed hidden.
events.sig: Asante was annexed to the Gold Coast colony in 1901. Yaa Asantewaa was exiled to the Seychelles, where she died in 1921. The Stool stayed hidden.
events.now: The Stool's survival let Asante keep its identity under colonial rule. Britain restored the Asantehene in 1926 and the Asante Confederacy in 1935, and the Asantehene remains the strongest traditional authority in Ghana.

causes.why: Britain's push for full control of Asante led to the last Asante war.

q.why: The British demand for the Golden Stool.
q.stakes: Asante independence and its sacred symbol.
q.decided: British reinforcements and firepower.
q.cost: Around 1,000 British and allied casualties and perhaps 2,000 Asante dead.
q.changed: Asante became a British colony, but the Stool stayed hidden.

events.bluf: Gold Coast Governor Frederick Hodgson demanded in March 1900 to sit on the Golden Stool, the seat of Asante's soul, to complete the control Britain had taken by exiling the Asantehene in 1896. Queen Mother Yaa Asantewaa of Ejisu led Asante fighters in a siege of the British fort at Kumasi for months before a relief force broke the revolt. Britain annexed Asante to the Gold Coast in 1901, the Stool stayed out of its hands, and the sovereignty it stood for outlived the conquest.
events.lens: Symbols of sovereignty can matter more to a people than territory.
events.fact: Yaa Asantewaa is a national heroine in Ghana and a symbol of women's leadership in anti-colonial resistance. The Stool was kept from the British and is still never sat on, even by the king.

events.what: Anti-foreign uprising; foreign troops crushed it.
events.why: Resentment of missionaries, foreign concessions and the legal privileges of Chinese Christians came first. Drought and hardship across north China supplied recruits. The court saw a chance to turn popular anger against the powers that had taken leases in 1898.
events.sig: The Boxer Protocol of September 1901 imposed an indemnity of 450 million taels of silver and stationed foreign troops in Beijing. Russian troops stayed in Manchuria, which set up the war of 1904. The Qing fell in 1911.
events.hook: An anti-foreign uprising besieged Beijing's embassies, and eight nations crushed it.
events.story: The Boxers, a militia movement in north China whose martial-arts rituals they believed made them immune to bullets, killed missionaries and thousands of Chinese Christians in 1899-1900. In June 1900 Qing Empress Dowager Cixi backed them and declared war on the foreign powers. Boxers and Qing troops besieged the foreign legations in Beijing for 55 days. An eight-nation force, mostly Japanese and Russian, relieved the siege on 14 August 1900 and looted the capital; the court fled to Xi'an.
events.then: The Boxer Protocol of September 1901 imposed an indemnity of 450 million taels of silver and stationed foreign troops in Beijing. Russian troops stayed in Manchuria, which set up the war of 1904. The Qing fell in 1911.
events.now: The Boxer Protocol of 1901 put foreign troops in Beijing and a 39-year indemnity on Chinese revenue, which discredited the Qing and fed the nationalism behind the revolution of 1911. The episode is a fixed part of the 'century of humiliation' narrative the Communist Party uses to argue that only a strong state keeps foreign powers out.
events.fact: 'Boxers' was a Western nickname for the martial-arts rituals the rebels believed made them bulletproof.

causes.why: The 1897-98 scramble for concessions, including Germany's seizure of Qingdao and Russia's of Port Arthur, inflamed anti-foreign anger in north China.

q.why: Resentment of missionaries and foreign control.
q.decided: An eight-nation army took Beijing.
q.cost: Tens of thousands dead, including many Chinese Christians.
q.changed: China paid huge reparations.

events.bluf: The Boxers, a militia movement in north China, set out to drive foreigners and Christians from the country, and Qing Empress Dowager Cixi backed them with a declaration of war on the powers in June 1900. An eight-nation army relieved the besieged legations in Beijing in August, looted the capital and imposed an indemnity of 450 million taels. The dynasty's authority was discredited at home and abroad, and the revolution that ended it came within eleven years.
events.lens: A government that sponsors a xenophobic uprising against powers it cannot defeat ends up weakening itself most.

toll.n: Tens of thousands of Boxers, Qing soldiers and civilians were then killed by foreign troops in reprisals.

events.who: Six British colonies; Prime Minister Edmund Barton
events.hook: Six British colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia.
events.what: Six British colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia.
events.story: The colonies of New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania negotiated a constitution at conventions in 1891 and 1897-98, and voters approved it in referendums between 1898 and 1900. The British Parliament enacted it in 1900. The Commonwealth was proclaimed in Centennial Park, Sydney, on 1 January 1901, with Governor-General Lord Hopetoun and Prime Minister Edmund Barton. Parliament sat in Melbourne until 1927.
events.why: Defence against Germany and France in the Pacific, trade without internal tariffs, and a growing sense of being Australian rather than six colonies.
events.then: The Immigration Restriction Act of 1901 created the White Australia policy. The Franchise Act of 1902 gave women the federal vote and excluded Aboriginal Australians, Asians, Africans and Pacific Islanders unless already enrolled in a state.
events.sig: The Immigration Restriction Act of 1901 created the White Australia policy. The Franchise Act of 1902 gave women the federal vote and excluded Aboriginal Australians, Asians, Africans and Pacific Islanders unless already enrolled in a state.
events.now: The 1901 constitution still governs Australia and the British monarch is still head of state; a referendum on a republic failed in 1999 and one on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament failed in 2023.

q.before: Six separate British colonies.
q.how: Referendums and an act of the British Parliament.
q.claim: A federal constitution approved by voters.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Six colonies wanted common defence, a single market without internal tariffs and a national identity. After a decade of conventions and referendums they united on 1 January 1901 as the Commonwealth of Australia, a self-governing federation within the British Empire under Prime Minister Edmund Barton. The new democracy gave white men and, from 1902, white women the vote, and founded itself on racial exclusion: White Australia and the denial of the federal vote to most Aboriginal people.
events.lens: New nations define themselves by whom they include and exclude.
events.fact: Melbourne served as the federal capital until Parliament moved to Canberra in 1927.

events.what: Became president after McKinley's assassination.
events.why: President McKinley was shot by an anarchist in Buffalo in September 1901 and died eight days later. Roosevelt believed that unregulated corporate power would bring socialism unless government curbed it.
events.sig: The Progressive Era brought the income tax in 1913, direct election of senators in 1913 and women's suffrage in 1920. Roosevelt won the 1904 election outright, declined to run in 1908 and split the Republicans in 1912.
events.hook: A young, energetic president took on big business.
events.story: Anarchist Leon Czolgosz shot President William McKinley at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo on 6 September 1901; McKinley died eight days later and Vice President Theodore Roosevelt was sworn in. Roosevelt sued to break up the Northern Securities railway combine in 1902 and won in 1904, mediated the anthracite coal strike of 1902, and signed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act in 1906. He created five national parks, 18 national monuments and some 150 national forests.
events.then: The Progressive Era brought the income tax in 1913, direct election of senators in 1913 and women's suffrage in 1920. Roosevelt won the 1904 election outright, declined to run in 1908 and split the Republicans in 1912.
events.now: Antitrust law, food safety rules and national parks are his lasting legacy, and debates over breaking up today's tech giants revive his arguments.

causes.why: Labour violence, urban poverty and the power of big trusts pushed reformers to demand regulation.

q.before: President William McKinley.
q.how: Succession after an assassination.
q.lasted: He won his own term in 1904.

events.bluf: Theodore Roosevelt became president at 42 when William McKinley died of an assassin's bullet in September 1901, and he set out to make the federal government the referee between big business and the public. He broke up the Northern Securities railway trust, regulated food and medicine, settled a coal strike and put about 230 million acres under federal protection. Washington's role in the economy grew, and the Progressive Era that followed brought the income tax, direct election of senators and women's suffrage.
events.lens: Industrial concentration eventually produces a political response; the question is when, not whether.
events.fact: Party boss Mark Hanna had put Roosevelt in the vice presidency to get him out of New York politics, and on McKinley's death is reported to have said that 'that damned cowboy' was now president.

events.hook: Australia's new parliament passed a law designed to keep out non-European immigrants.
events.what: Australia's new parliament passed a law designed to keep out non-European immigrants.
events.story: The Immigration Restriction Act, one of the first laws of the Commonwealth Parliament sitting in Melbourne, passed in December 1901 under Prime Minister Edmund Barton. It let officials give any arrival a 50-word dictation test in a European language of the officer's choosing; the test was given to those the government wished to exclude, and nearly all of them failed it. A separate act provided for deporting Pacific Islander workers.
events.why: Fear of cheap Asian labour undercutting wages came first, and the labour movement and employers' parties agreed on it. A belief in a white nation ran through all of them, and London asked only that the law avoid naming race, to spare Japan's feelings.
events.then: Non-European migration stayed near zero for 60 years. The Holt government loosened the rules in 1966, and the Whitlam government removed race from immigration law in 1973.
events.sig: Non-European migration stayed near zero for 60 years. The Holt government loosened the rules in 1966, and the Whitlam government removed race from immigration law in 1973.
events.now: White Australia kept the country British in population until the 1960s and strained its relations with Asia; its removal between 1966 and 1973 produced the Australia in which about 30 per cent of residents were born overseas.

causes.why: Hostility to Chinese gold diggers produced the first anti-Chinese laws in the 1850s, the roots of White Australia.
A companion law of 1901 provided for deporting most Pacific Islander workers.
One of the new federal parliament's first laws was the Immigration Restriction Act.

q.before: Each colony had its own immigration laws.
q.how: Federal legislation.
q.winners: Labour unions and nationalists of the time.
q.lasted: It was dismantled between 1949 and 1973.

events.bluf: The new federal parliament wanted to keep Australia white and its wages high, a goal shared across the main parties. The Immigration Restriction Act of 1901 let officials give any arrival a dictation test in a European language and so exclude Asian and other non-white migrants without naming race. The policy shaped Australia's population and its relations with Asia for 70 years, until governments dismantled it from 1966 and ended it in 1973.
events.lens: Immigration laws reveal a nation's idea of itself, and changing them changes that idea.
events.fact: Czech journalist Egon Kisch, barred in 1934, was given the test in Scottish Gaelic, failed it, and won in the High Court, which ruled that Gaelic fell outside the act's meaning of a European language.

kv: words in the dictation test, in any European language the officer chose

events.what: The world's greatest naval power made Japan its ally, the first equal alliance between Europe and Asia.
events.why: Both feared Russian expansion in Manchuria and Korea. Britain also wanted to end its isolation and share the naval burden in the Pacific, and British yards had built most of Japan's battleships.
events.sig: Two years later Japan attacked Russia, confident no European power would intervene. The alliance was renewed in 1905 and 1911 and ended at the Washington Conference of 1921-22.
events.hook: The world's greatest naval power made Japan its ally, the first equal alliance between Europe and Asia.
events.story: British Foreign Secretary Lord Lansdowne and Japanese minister in London Hayashi Tadasu signed the treaty on 30 January 1902. It committed each side to stay neutral if the other went to war with one power, and to join in if a second power entered. It was Britain's first formal alliance in decades, ending its 'splendid isolation', and the first alliance on equal terms between a Western power and an Asian state.
events.then: Two years later Japan attacked Russia, confident no European power would intervene. The alliance was renewed in 1905 and 1911 and ended at the Washington Conference of 1921-22.
events.now: The alliance let Japan fight Russia in 1904 without fear of a second enemy and ran until 1923. It is the model for a global power partnering with a regional one to balance a shared rival.

causes.why: Russia's advance threatened both British and Japanese interests.
Britain had refused to join the Intervention.

q.before: Japan was isolated after the Triple Intervention.
q.how: Japan gained a great-power partner.
q.claim: Mutual interests in China and Korea.
q.winners: Japan; it guaranteed France wouldn't join Russia in a war.
q.lasted: Until 1923.

events.bluf: Britain wanted a partner to check Russia in East Asia without adding to its own naval burden; Japan wanted assurance that no second European power would join Russia in a war. The treaty signed in London on 30 January 1902 bound each to neutrality if the other fought one power and to join in if a second entered. Japan could now fight Russia alone, and a Western power had taken an Asian state as an equal ally for the first time.
events.lens: An alliance that isolates a rival can give a smaller power room to strike.
events.fact: The Mikasa, Admiral Tōgō's flagship at Tsushima, was built at Barrow-in-Furness in England.

events.what: Independence backed by US warships.
events.why: The United States wanted a canal under its own control. Colombia's Senate wanted better terms. Panamanians had revolted against rule from Bogotá several times in the 1800s.
events.sig: The United States controlled the Canal Zone for most of the 20th century. In 1921 it paid Colombia $25 million in what amounted to compensation.
events.hook: The US backed Panama's independence so it could build a canal.
events.story: Colombia's Senate rejected the Hay-Herrán canal treaty in August 1903. Panamanian separatists, in contact with French engineer Philippe Bunau-Varilla, rose on 3 November 1903. The gunboat USS Nashville prevented Colombian troops from reaching Panama City. Washington recognised Panama within days, and Bunau-Varilla, as Panama's envoy, signed a treaty on 18 November giving the United States a canal zone in perpetuity.
events.then: The United States controlled the Canal Zone for most of the 20th century. In 1921 it paid Colombia $25 million in what amounted to compensation.
events.now: Panama took full control of the canal on 31 December 1999. In 2025 US pressure over Chinese-linked operators at ports near the canal showed it remains a strategic flashpoint between great powers.

causes.why: The war showed the US Navy needed a canal to move ships between oceans; when Colombia balked at the terms, the US backed Panama's secession.

q.before: Panama was a province of Colombia.
q.how: A revolt protected by US warships.
q.winners: The United States and Panama's elite.
q.lasted: Yes: Panama has been independent since.

events.bluf: US President Theodore Roosevelt wanted a canal across the Isthmus of Panama, and the Colombian Senate rejected his treaty in August 1903. Panamanian separatists declared independence on 3 November and US warships kept Colombian troops from landing. Panama signed the canal treaty Colombia had refused within weeks, and the United States held a zone across a sovereign country until 1999.
events.lens: Great powers will create new states when existing ones block their strategic projects.
events.trig: The Colombian Senate's rejection of the Hay-Herrán Treaty in August 1903.
events.fact: Panama's treaty with the United States was signed by a Frenchman, Philippe Bunau-Varilla, before Panama's own delegation reached Washington.

kv: paid to Panama, plus $250,000 a year

events.what: First powered, controlled airplane flight.
events.why: Earlier builders had chased lift and power; the Wrights treated control as the problem and solved it with wing-warping and a movable rudder. Lighter petrol engines and decades of glider data made the rest possible.
events.sig: The Wrights flew for the US Army in 1908 and sold it a plane in 1909. Within 15 years planes were fighting in the First World War. Air power reshaped war, from strategic bombing to aircraft carriers, and jet airliners from the 1950s made mass travel possible.
events.hook: Twelve seconds over a beach in North Carolina began the age of flight.
events.story: Orville and Wilbur Wright, bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, had tested gliders at Kitty Hawk since 1900 and built their own wind tunnel to correct the published lift tables. Their 1903 Flyer had a 12-horsepower engine they built themselves and controls for pitch, roll and yaw. On 17 December 1903 Orville flew it 120 feet in 12 seconds; the fourth flight that day, with Wilbur, covered 852 feet in 59 seconds.
events.then: The Wrights flew for the US Army in 1908 and sold it a plane in 1909. Within 15 years planes were fighting in the First World War. Air power reshaped war, from strategic bombing to aircraft carriers, and jet airliners from the 1950s made mass travel possible.
events.now: Aviation shrank every distance within half a century, made air power the decisive arm of war from 1940 and now carries about 4 billion passenger trips a year, with emissions that are part of the climate argument.
events.fact: The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet, less than the wingspan of a Boeing 747.

q.problem: How to control a powered aircraft in the air.
q.how: Wing-warping for control, a light engine and efficient propellers.
q.replaced: Gliders and failed powered attempts.
q.spread: Within a decade, planes flew across Europe.
q.next: Military aviation, then airlines.

events.bluf: Bicycle makers Orville and Wilbur Wright of Dayton, Ohio, set out to solve the problem that had killed the glider pioneers: control. They built a powered machine with wing-warping and a movable rudder, and on 17 December 1903 at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, it flew 120 feet in 12 seconds. Powered flight became an engineering fact; within 15 years aircraft were fighting over the Western Front, and within fifty, air travel and air power had shrunk every distance.
events.lens: The decisive breakthrough often comes from solving the control problem, not just the power problem.

events.who: German colonial army under Gen. Lothar von Trotha
events.what: Tens of thousands killed or driven into the desert.
events.why: German settlers seized Herero and Nama land and cattle. Abuse and debt schemes drove the Herero to revolt, and the Nama followed.
events.sig: Up to 80 per cent of the Herero and about half of the Nama died. Survivors were held in camps, and their land and cattle were confiscated. Berlin rescinded the order in December 1904, after most of the killing.
events.hook: Germany carried out the first genocide of the 20th century in Namibia.
events.story: German settlers had seized Herero and Nama land and cattle. The Herero under Chief Samuel Maharero rose in January 1904, and the Nama under Hendrik Witbooi followed in October. German General Lothar von Trotha issued an extermination order in October 1904 after the battle of Waterberg. Survivors were driven into the desert or concentration camps.
events.then: Up to 80 per cent of the Herero and about half of the Nama died. Survivors were held in camps, and their land and cattle were confiscated. Berlin rescinded the order in December 1904, after most of the killing.
events.now: Germany acknowledged it as genocide in 2021 and offered development aid; many Herero and Nama groups rejected the deal as inadequate, and the land question it left is still open in Namibia.
events.fact: Germany formally acknowledged it as genocide in 2021. Skulls of the dead sent to Germany for racial research were returned in 2011 and 2018.

q.why: The Herero and Nama rose against land and cattle seizures.
q.decided: General von Trotha's order to destroy the Herero, and the desert.
q.cost: Perhaps 65,000 Herero and 10,000 Nama died.
q.changed: Their land went to German settlers.

events.bluf: German settlers in South West Africa had taken Herero and Nama land and cattle, and the Herero rose in January 1904, the Nama after them. German General Lothar von Trotha ordered the Herero exterminated, drove survivors into the Omaheke desert and held the rest in concentration camps; up to 80 per cent of the Herero and about half of the Nama died. It is widely recognised as the first genocide of the 20th century, and its extermination order, camps and racial science reappeared in the atrocities that followed.
events.lens: Colonial wars can turn genocidal when settlers want the land, not the labor.

toll.n: Estimates. Many died of thirst in the Omaheke desert or in camps.

events.what: Settled colonial disputes.
events.why: Both feared Germany's growing power and navy. Settling their quarrels over Egypt and Morocco freed them to cooperate.
events.sig: Germany tested the Entente in Morocco in 1905 and 1911, which drew Britain and France closer. Russia joined in 1907, forming the Triple Entente.
events.hook: Old enemies Britain and France settled their quarrels.
events.story: In April 1904 Britain and France signed a set of agreements settling old colonial quarrels: France accepted British control of Egypt, and Britain accepted French influence in Morocco. The agreements carried no military obligation.
events.then: Germany tested the Entente in Morocco in 1905 and 1911, which drew Britain and France closer. Russia joined in 1907, forming the Triple Entente.
events.now: The Anglo-French partnership forged here fought two world wars together and remains the core of European defence cooperation, including on Ukraine.

causes.why: Germany's challenge at sea pushed Britain to settle its colonial quarrels with France.
Having backed down at Fashoda, France chose to settle its colonial quarrels with Britain rather than fight.

q.before: Britain and France had been colonial rivals for centuries.
q.how: Agreements on colonial disputes.
q.lasted: They fought as allies in both world wars.

events.bluf: Britain and France set out to settle the colonial quarrels, over Egypt and Morocco above all, that had brought them close to war at Fashoda in 1898. The agreements of April 1904 traded British control of Egypt for French influence in Morocco. An arrangement that began as colonial bookkeeping became, under German pressure, the core of the coalition that fought Germany in two world wars.
events.lens: Old enemies reconcile when a new threat looms larger; settling small disputes clears the way for a big alignment.
events.fact: British King Edward VII's state visit to Paris in May 1903, where he won over a hostile crowd, prepared the ground.

events.what: US claimed right to intervene.
events.why: European navies had used force over debts in the hemisphere, and Germany's part in the Venezuela blockade alarmed Washington. The United States was building a canal in Panama and wanted no European base near it.
events.sig: US Marines occupied Nicaragua for most of 1912-33, Haiti from 1915 to 1934 and the Dominican Republic from 1916 to 1924. US President Franklin Roosevelt renounced armed intervention under the Good Neighbor policy in 1933.
events.hook: The US declared itself the policeman of the Western Hemisphere.
events.story: British, German and Italian warships blockaded Venezuela in 1902-03 over unpaid debts. In his annual message to Congress in December 1904, US President Theodore Roosevelt said 'chronic wrongdoing' in the Americas might force the United States to exercise 'an international police power'. In 1905 the United States took over customs collection in the Dominican Republic to pay its creditors.
events.then: US Marines occupied Nicaragua for most of 1912-33, Haiti from 1915 to 1934 and the Dominican Republic from 1916 to 1924. US President Franklin Roosevelt renounced armed intervention under the Good Neighbor policy in 1933.
events.now: The corollary fixed Latin American suspicion of US power from 1904, and that suspicion revives whenever Washington threatens force in the region, as against Venezuela in 2025.

causes.why: Roosevelt claimed a right to police the hemisphere, turning Monroe's warning to Europe into a justification for US intervention.

q.before: The Monroe Doctrine warned Europe off the Americas.
q.how: A presidential statement of policy.
q.claim: The US as the hemisphere's policeman.
q.winners: The United States and US banks.
q.lasted: It was replaced by FDR's 'Good Neighbor' policy in the 1930s.

events.bluf: US President Theodore Roosevelt wanted to keep European powers from collecting debts by force in the Americas, after their navies blockaded Venezuela in 1902-03. He claimed a US right to act as 'an international police power' in the hemisphere. The Monroe Doctrine became a licence for US intervention, used to justify occupations of Nicaragua, Haiti and the Dominican Republic over the next three decades.
events.lens: Doctrines meant to keep others out often become justifications for going in.
events.fact: Roosevelt's favourite proverb, 'speak softly and carry a big stick', gave the policy its popular name, the Big Stick.

events.who: Ngoni, Matumbi and other peoples vs. German colonial rule
events.what: Mass uprising against forced cotton growing.
events.why: Forced cotton labour, a hut tax and the whip came first. The maji cult gave scattered peoples a single cause and a promise of protection.
events.sig: Famine followed the burning; estimates of the dead run from 75,000 to 300,000, most from hunger. Berlin created a Colonial Office in 1907 and shifted to African cash crops. In November 2023 German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier asked forgiveness in Tanzania for the German crimes of the war.
events.hook: Southern Tanganyika rose against German rule, armed with belief in sacred water.
events.story: German East Africa forced villagers in the south to grow cotton for export on communal plots under corporal punishment. In July 1905 Matumbi villagers uprooted cotton, and the rising spread to the Ngoni and some twenty other peoples behind the prophet Kinjikitile Ngwale, whose 'maji', or water, was said to turn German bullets to water. German forces hanged Kinjikitile in August 1905 and burned crops and villages across the south until 1907.
events.then: Famine followed the burning; estimates of the dead run from 75,000 to 300,000, most from hunger. Berlin created a Colonial Office in 1907 and shifted to African cash crops. In November 2023 German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier asked forgiveness in Tanzania for the German crimes of the war.
events.now: The rising forced the German reforms of 1907 and gave Tanzania a shared anti-colonial memory that cut across its 120 ethnic groups, which Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere used to build a single national identity after 1961.
events.fact: 'Maji' is Swahili for water. Fighters sprinkled it on their bodies before battle in the belief that German bullets would turn to water.

sites.d: Uprising began here, July 1905.
Home of the prophet Kinjikitile, source of the 'maji'.
Failed attack on a German fort with machine guns.
Ngoni leaders hanged here, 1906.

causes.why: Earlier resistance had been crushed one group at a time; Maji Maji united many.
German rule had relied on force since the coastal revolt.

q.why: Forced cotton growing for export, harsh taxes and abuse by German agents.
q.stakes: Survival and freedom across southern Tanganyika.
q.decided: Machine guns, then a deliberate scorched-earth famine.
q.cost: Estimates range from about 75,000 to 300,000 dead, mostly from famine.
q.changed: Germany reformed colonial policy; southern Tanzania took decades to recover.

events.bluf: Peoples of southern Tanganyika rose to end German forced cotton growing, taxes and corporal punishment, trusting a prophet's water to turn bullets to water. Germany crushed the rising within two years with a scorched-earth campaign, and famine killed somewhere between 75,000 and 300,000 people. The disaster drove Germany to reform its colonial administration, and the rising later became the founding story of Tanzanian unity across ethnic lines.
events.lens: Shared spiritual beliefs can unite different groups against a common oppressor.
events.trig: Matumbi villagers uprooted the cotton at Nandete in July 1905.

toll.n: The Germans burned crops and villages to starve the rising out.

events.what: Asian power beat a European empire.
events.why: Rivalry over Korea and Manchuria: Russia's lease of Port Arthur and its railways threatened Japan's ambitions, and the Anglo-Japanese Alliance kept other powers out.
events.sig: The Treaty of Portsmouth in September 1905 gave Japan the Port Arthur lease and southern Sakhalin. Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910. Defeat sparked the Revolution of 1905 in Russia.
events.hook: An Asian nation beat a European empire for the first time in modern war.
events.story: In February 1904 Japan attacked the Russian fleet at Port Arthur before declaring war on Russian Tsar Nicholas II's government. After a siege that cost tens of thousands of casualties it took the port in January 1905 and won the land battle of Mukden in March. At Tsushima on 27-28 May 1905 Japanese Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō destroyed Russia's Baltic Fleet, which had sailed halfway around the world.
events.then: The Treaty of Portsmouth in September 1905 gave Japan the Port Arthur lease and southern Sakhalin. Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910. Defeat sparked the Revolution of 1905 in Russia.
events.now: The victory made Japan the dominant power in Korea and southern Manchuria from 1905 to 1945, weakened Russian Tsar Nicholas II's regime enough to set off the Revolution of 1905, and showed nationalists from India to Egypt that a European empire could be beaten in the field. Its opening surprise attack prefigured Pearl Harbor.
events.fact: Russia's Baltic Fleet sailed 18,000 miles around Africa to be sunk in one afternoon at Tsushima. On the way it fired on British fishing boats, taking them for Japanese torpedo boats.

sites.d: Russian naval base besieged and taken.
Largest land battle before WWI.
Russian fleet annihilated, May 1905.
Peace brokered by Theodore Roosevelt.

causes.why: Britain's alliance kept other powers out.
Russia held the port Japan had been forced to give up.

q.why: Control of Korea and Manchuria.
q.stakes: Whether Russia or Japan would dominate Northeast Asia.
q.decided: Japan's surprise attack on Port Arthur and the destruction of Russia's Baltic Fleet at Tsushima.
q.cost: About 130,000–170,000 total dead.
q.changed: Japan took Port Arthur, southern Sakhalin and control of Korea.

events.bluf: Japan fought Russia to keep it out of Korea and push it back in Manchuria after talks on spheres of influence failed. It took Port Arthur, won at Mukden and destroyed Russia's Baltic Fleet at Tsushima in May 1905, at a cost that left its treasury near empty. An Asian power had beaten a European great power in a major war for the first time; Japan gained Korea and a foothold in Manchuria, Russia got the Revolution of 1905, and anti-colonial nationalists across Asia and Africa took note.
events.trig: The breakdown of talks over spheres of influence in Korea and Manchuria.
events.lens: A surprise attack followed by a short, decisive war can work once; Japan tried to repeat it in 1941.

kv: Russian ships sunk at Tsushima; 7 more captured

toll.n: Estimates. Tsushima, in May 1905, destroyed most of Russia's Baltic Fleet in a day.

events.what: Uprising forced the tsar to allow a parliament.
events.why: Defeat by Japan exposed the regime's incompetence. Industrial workers and peasants lived in deep poverty. The Bloody Sunday massacre destroyed faith in the tsar.
events.sig: Nicholas II curtailed the Duma's powers in the Fundamental Laws of 1906 and dissolved the first two Dumas. His prime minister Pyotr Stolypin had more than a thousand rebels executed by field courts-martial, and the anger stayed unresolved.
events.hook: Defeat by Japan and a massacre of protesters forced the tsar to share power.
events.story: On 22 January 1905 troops fired on a peaceful procession led by priest Georgy Gapon to the Winter Palace in St Petersburg; hundreds died. Strikes, peasant risings and a mutiny on the battleship Potemkin spread through the year. In October a general strike forced Russian Tsar Nicholas II to issue the October Manifesto, which granted a parliament, the Duma, and civil liberties.
events.then: Nicholas II curtailed the Duma's powers in the Fundamental Laws of 1906 and dissolved the first two Dumas. His prime minister Pyotr Stolypin had more than a thousand rebels executed by field courts-martial, and the anger stayed unresolved.
events.now: Lenin called it the 'dress rehearsal' for 1917: a regime that grants reforms only under pressure and then takes them back can lose its legitimacy.

causes.why: Emancipation left peasants with heavy redemption payments and too little land, fuelling decades of unrest.
Defeat by Japan humiliated the regime; after troops fired on peaceful marchers on 'Bloody Sunday', revolution spread.

q.before: An autocratic tsar with no parliament.
q.how: Mass strikes, mutinies and uprisings.
q.winners: Briefly the liberals, with a Duma.
q.lasted: Partly: the Duma survived but with little power.

events.bluf: Workers, peasants and liberals pressed Russian Tsar Nicholas II for a constitution after defeat by Japan and the shooting of marchers on Bloody Sunday. He conceded a parliament, the Duma, and civil liberties in the October Manifesto and took much of it back once the army held. The regime survived with its legitimacy spent, and the next crisis, in 1917, finished it.
events.lens: Concessions withdrawn once a crisis passes leave a regime with less legitimacy than before.
events.fact: The hangman's noose became known as 'Stolypin's necktie'.

q.before: Russia dominated Manchuria.
q.how: Japan took over Russia's position in southern Manchuria and Korea.
q.winners: Japan and Roosevelt, who won the Nobel Peace Prize.
q.lasted: Japan's gains lasted until 1945.

events.hook: Theodore Roosevelt brokered peace between Japan and Russia, and won the Nobel Peace Prize.
events.what: Theodore Roosevelt brokered peace between Japan and Russia, and won the Nobel Peace Prize.
events.story: US President Theodore Roosevelt brought the two sides together at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, where Japanese Foreign Minister Komura Jutarō and Russian chief minister Sergei Witte negotiated. Under the treaty signed on 5 September 1905, Russia recognised Japan's dominance in Korea and handed over the Port Arthur lease, the southern Manchurian railway and the southern half of Sakhalin, and paid no indemnity. Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for his mediation.
events.why: Both sides were exhausted: Russia faced revolution at home, and Japan, though victorious, was close to bankruptcy and out of reserves.
events.then: Months later Japan made Korea a protectorate, while Tokyo crowds rioted over the lack of an indemnity.
events.sig: Months later Japan made Korea a protectorate, while Tokyo crowds rioted over the lack of an indemnity.
events.now: The treaty confirmed Japan as a great power with Korea and southern Manchuria in its hands, and left Japan's public convinced it had been cheated of an indemnity, a grievance that fed militarism.

causes.why: Japan's victories forced Russia to negotiate.

events.bluf: US President Theodore Roosevelt mediated to end a war both sides could no longer afford and to keep either from dominating East Asia. Russia conceded Japan's dominance in Korea, the Port Arthur lease, the southern Manchurian railway and the southern half of Sakhalin, and paid no indemnity. Japan became a recognised great power; its public, told to expect more, rioted, and the grievance fed later resentment of the United States.
events.lens: Peace brokers can earn the resentment of the side that expected more.
events.fact: It was the first time a US president mediated a peace between great powers.

events.hook: Japanese crowds who expected more from victory burned police stations in Tokyo.
events.what: Japanese crowds who expected more from victory burned police stations in Tokyo.
events.story: Japan's government had hidden how close the war had brought it to bankruptcy, and the press had promised an indemnity and territory. When the Portsmouth terms arrived, crowds gathered in Hibiya Park on 5 September 1905 and rioted until 7 September. They burned police stations and churches and attacked the home minister's residence and the pro-government newspaper Kokumin Shimbun. Seventeen people died, and the government declared martial law.
events.why: The government had hidden how close Japan was to bankruptcy, so the public expected an indemnity and new territory on the scale of 1895.
events.then: Prime Minister Katsura Tarō's cabinet fell in January 1906. Popular nationalism became a force Japanese governments had to reckon with.
events.sig: Prime Minister Katsura Tarō's cabinet fell in January 1906. Popular nationalism became a force Japanese governments had to reckon with.
events.now: The riots fixed a pattern from 1905 to 1945 in which Japanese governments feared being outflanked by nationalist opinion, and they planted the resentment of the United States as the power that short-changed Japan.

causes.why: News that the treaty brought Japan no indemnity set off riots in Tokyo.

q.before: The government had promised a glorious victory.
q.how: Riots and martial law.
q.claim: That Japan had been cheated of its rightful gains.
q.winners: No one; the cabinet fell months later.
q.lasted: The anger fed Japanese nationalism.

events.bluf: Tokyo crowds, told for months of great victories, gathered in Hibiya Park on 5 September 1905 to protest a peace with no indemnity. Three days of rioting killed 17 people, burned police boxes and churches and brought martial law to the capital. Popular nationalism had shown it could turn on the government that fed it, and later cabinets had to reckon with a street that punished any sign of weakness abroad.
events.lens: Governments that oversell victories create expectations they cannot meet.
events.fact: Hibiya was the first of a series of crowd protests in Tokyo over the following decade; one of them toppled Katsura's third cabinet in 1913.
events.btt: Empire of Japan: the Russo-Japanese War

events.h: Nandi leader killed at a peace meeting
events.who: Koitalel Arap Samoei; British officer Richard Meinertzhagen
events.what: The Nandi resisted the railway for a decade, until their leader was shot at a truce meeting.
events.why: Britain wanted the railway, the telegraph and the highlands secure for settlement. The Nandi had held out longer than any other people in Kenya.
events.sig: Nandi resistance ended within weeks. The Nandi were moved to a reserve in 1906, and the Uasin Gishu plateau was opened to white settlers.
events.hook: The Nandi resisted the railway for a decade, until their leader was shot at a truce meeting.
events.story: The Uganda Railway and its telegraph crossed Nandi land in western Kenya, and Nandi fighters raided both for about ten years. Britain mounted five expeditions against them. On 19 October 1905 British officer Richard Meinertzhagen met the Nandi orkoiyot, or spiritual leader, Koitalel Arap Samoei under a flag of truce and shot him dead with his escort.
events.then: Nandi resistance ended within weeks. The Nandi were moved to a reserve in 1906, and the Uasin Gishu plateau was opened to white settlers.
events.now: The killing cleared the Uasin Gishu plateau for white settlement between 1906 and 1920 and fixed the reserve system that separated Kenya's land into African and settler zones until independence in 1963.

causes.why: The railway ran through Nandi country.

q.why: Defending Nandi land from the railway and settlers.
q.decided: Treachery at a truce.
q.cost: Hundreds of Nandi killed, cattle seized.
q.changed: Nandi resistance collapsed; land was taken for settlers.

events.bluf: Britain wanted the Uganda Railway and its telegraph secure across Nandi land after a decade of raids; the Nandi wanted the line and the soldiers gone. British officer Richard Meinertzhagen shot the Nandi orkoiyot Koitalel Arap Samoei at a meeting arranged as a truce in October 1905, and Nandi resistance collapsed within weeks. The Nandi were confined to a reserve and the Uasin Gishu plateau went to white settlers, the pattern for the Kenya highlands.
events.lens: Truce meetings have often been traps; trust was a resource colonizers spent freely.
events.trig: The truce meeting at Ket-ny-barak on 19 October 1905.
events.fact: Meinertzhagen was sent home over the killing after an inquiry, and later became a noted ornithologist whose bird specimens were found to include stolen museum skins.
events.btt: Kenya: The British East Africa Company

events.hook: Britain split Bengal in two, and Indians answered with a boycott of British goods.
events.what: Britain split Bengal in two, and Indians answered with a boycott of British goods.
events.story: Viceroy Lord Curzon divided Bengal on 16 October 1905, creating a province of Eastern Bengal and Assam with its capital at Dhaka and a Muslim majority. Bengali Hindus saw divide-and-rule and launched the Swadeshi movement, boycotting British cloth and burning it in public, founding national schools and Indian-owned mills. Some turned to bombs; Bengal's revolutionary societies date from these years.
events.why: Officially administrative efficiency in a province of 78 million. Nationalists read an attempt to split Bengal's Hindu political class from its base.
events.then: Britain reversed the partition at the Delhi Durbar of December 1911 and moved the capital to Delhi. Separate Muslim electorates, granted in 1909, kept the communal divide in the political system. Muslim leaders, who had gained a province and lost it, founded the Muslim League at Dhaka in 1906.
events.sig: Britain reversed the partition at the Delhi Durbar of December 1911 and moved the capital to Delhi. Separate Muslim electorates, granted in 1909, kept the communal divide in the political system. Muslim leaders, who had gained a province and lost it, founded the Muslim League at Dhaka in 1906.
events.now: The partition and its reversal set both communities' politics: Hindu Bengalis learned that mass protest worked, Muslim leaders learned that Congress would resist a Muslim province, and the 1905 line roughly anticipated the border of East Pakistan in 1947.

causes.why: Curzon's partition was widely seen as an attempt to weaken Bengal's Congress-led nationalists.

q.before: Bengal was one huge province ruled from Calcutta.
q.how: An administrative decree.
q.winners: At first the British; in the end, the nationalists.
q.lasted: No: it was reversed in 1911.

events.bluf: Viceroy Lord Curzon divided Bengal, a province of some 78 million people, into a Hindu-majority west and a Muslim-majority east, for administrative efficiency in his account and to weaken Bengali politics in his critics' account. Bengali Hindus answered with the Swadeshi boycott of British goods, India's first mass nationalist campaign. Britain reversed the partition in 1911, which showed that protest could change policy, and the Hindu-Muslim line it drew reappeared in 1947.
events.lens: Administrative boundaries can become political weapons, and redrawing them can create identities that outlast the map.
events.fact: Rabindranath Tagore wrote 'Amar Shonar Bangla' for the anti-partition movement in 1905; it is now Bangladesh's national anthem.

events.what: Japanese troops surrounded the palace while Korea signed away control of its foreign policy.
events.why: Japan wanted Korea as a secure base on the mainland, and its victory over Russia removed the last power able to stop it.
events.sig: Korean 'righteous armies' rose against Japan. Gojong sent envoys to the Hague peace conference of 1907 and was forced to abdicate in favour of his son Sunjong; Japan annexed Korea in 1910.
events.hook: Japanese troops surrounded the palace while Korea signed away control of its foreign policy.
events.story: In November 1905, with Japanese troops surrounding the palace in Seoul, Japanese elder statesman Itō Hirobumi pressed Korea's cabinet to sign a treaty handing control of its foreign affairs to Japan. Korean Emperor Gojong refused to approve it; five ministers signed on 17 November, and Koreans call them the 'Eulsa traitors'. The United States and Britain had already accepted Japan's control of Korea. Itō became Resident-General.
events.then: Korean 'righteous armies' rose against Japan. Gojong sent envoys to the Hague peace conference of 1907 and was forced to abdicate in favour of his son Sunjong; Japan annexed Korea in 1910.
events.now: The protectorate stripped Korea of its diplomacy in 1905 and led to the loss of its sovereignty in 1910. The memory of ministers who signed under duress still shapes Korean politics, in which the charge of pro-Japanese collaboration remains a disqualification.

causes.why: The peace gave Japan a free hand in Korea.

q.before: Korea was formally independent.
q.how: Japan controlled Korea's foreign affairs, then more and more of its government.
q.winners: Japan; the US and Britain accepted it in exchange for Japan accepting their colonies.
q.lasted: It led to full annexation in 1910.

events.bluf: Japanese elder statesman Itō Hirobumi set out to take control of Korea's foreign relations by treaty rather than outright conquest. With troops around the palace in November 1905, five Korean ministers signed; Emperor Gojong withheld his approval. Korea became a protectorate under a Japanese Resident-General, the last step before annexation in 1910, and the signatories became the standing symbol of collaboration in Korean politics.
events.lens: Protectorates are often stepping stones to annexation: control of foreign policy comes first, the rest follows.
events.fact: Gojong's envoys to the Hague in 1907 were refused a hearing because the powers accepted that Korea's diplomacy belonged to Japan.

events.who: Muslim notables including Aga Khan III
events.hook: Muslim leaders formed their own party, which would later demand Pakistan.
events.what: Muslim leaders formed their own party, which would later demand Pakistan.
events.story: On 30 December 1906 Muslim notables meeting at Dhaka, among them Aga Khan III and Nawab Salimullah of Dhaka, founded the All-India Muslim League. The Morley-Minto reforms of 1909 gave Muslims separate electorates. Muhammad Ali Jinnah, a Congress member who joined the League in 1913, led it from the 1930s, and at Lahore in March 1940 it resolved that Muslim-majority areas should form independent states.
events.why: Muslim elites feared domination by the Hindu-majority Congress. The Hindu campaign against the 1905 partition of Bengal, which had given them a Muslim-majority province, alarmed them. A deputation to Viceroy Lord Minto at Simla in October 1906 had already won a promise of separate representation.
events.then: Congress accepted separate electorates in the Lucknow Pact of 1916. The League won most Muslim seats in the 1946 elections and Pakistan in August 1947.
events.sig: Congress accepted separate electorates in the Lucknow Pact of 1916. The League won most Muslim seats in the 1946 elections and Pakistan in August 1947.
events.now: Its argument that India's Muslims formed a separate nation led to Pakistan's creation in 1947, and the 'two-nation' idea still divides India and Pakistan.

causes.why: Muslim leaders, many of whom supported the partition, formed their own party to protect Muslim interests.

q.before: Congress claimed to speak for all Indians.
q.how: A political party founded by Muslim notables.
q.winners: Muslim elites, and later the Pakistan movement.
q.lasted: Yes: it led the creation of Pakistan.

events.bluf: Muslim notables led by Aga Khan III and Nawab Salimullah of Dhaka wanted a body to defend Muslim interests against a Hindu-majority Congress and to secure a Muslim share of power. They founded the All-India Muslim League at Dhaka in December 1906 and won separate Muslim electorates in 1909. Under Muhammad Ali Jinnah the League demanded a Muslim state in 1940 and won Pakistan in 1947.
events.lens: Separate electorates harden communal identities and make partition more likely.
events.fact: Jinnah, who led the League to Pakistan, had been called the 'ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity' by Congress leader Sarojini Naidu in the 1910s.

events.h: Germany reforms its colonies after Maji Maji
events.who: Colonial Secretary Bernhard Dernburg; Governor Rechenberg
events.what: The shock of Maji Maji and the Herero genocide forced Germany to change how it ran its colonies.
events.why: The wars had made force expensive and unpopular at home. Dernburg and Rechenberg believed African farmers would produce more and cost less than settler estates.
events.sig: The Central Line reached Lake Tanganyika at Kigoma in 1914. Cotton, coffee and sisal exports grew. One reading holds the programme was real reform, citing the end of forced cotton and the peasant policy; the other holds it was exploitation by other means, citing the hut tax that still drove Africans into wage labour.
events.hook: The shock of Maji Maji and the Herero genocide forced Germany to change how it ran its colonies.
events.story: The colonial wars in East and South-West Africa cost hundreds of millions of marks and became scandals in the Reichstag, and the January 1907 election was fought over colonial policy. Banker Bernhard Dernburg became the first German Colonial Secretary in May 1907 and argued that colonies should be run as businesses resting on African farmers. In Dar es Salaam, Governor Albrecht von Rechenberg favoured African peasant production over settler plantations.
events.then: The Central Line reached Lake Tanganyika at Kigoma in 1914. Cotton, coffee and sisal exports grew. One reading holds the programme was real reform, citing the end of forced cotton and the peasant policy; the other holds it was exploitation by other means, citing the hut tax that still drove Africans into wage labour.
events.now: The railways and cash-crop economy built between 1907 and 1914 became the base of Tanganyika's economy under British rule and after independence, which is why Tanzania's export crops and transport lines still follow the German map.

causes.why: The rebellion shocked Germany.
Both wars caused scandal in Germany.

q.before: Rule by military force and forced labor.
q.how: More focus on African cash crops and fewer settler demands.
q.winners: Some African farmers; settlers were angry.
q.lasted: Until WWI.

events.bluf: German Colonial Secretary Bernhard Dernburg wanted colonies that paid their way after the Maji Maji and Herero wars had cost Berlin money and scandal. He created a Colonial Office in 1907, built railways and promoted African cash crops in place of rule by the whip. German East Africa gained the Central Line to Lake Tanganyika and a cotton and coffee economy; one reading calls it reform, the other a more efficient extraction.
events.lens: Colonial reforms tend to follow scandals that threaten the colonizer's politics at home.
events.fact: The 1907 Reichstag vote became known as the 'Hottentot election' after the Nama people Germany had just fought in South-West Africa.

events.who: William Knox D'Arcy's company (later Anglo-Persian Oil, now BP)
events.hook: A British venture struck oil in Persia, the first big oil find in the Middle East.
events.what: A British venture struck oil in Persia, the first big oil find in the Middle East.
events.story: British investor William Knox D'Arcy had won a 60-year concession over most of Persia from the Shah in 1901. After years of failure and nearly out of money, his drillers struck oil at Masjed Soleyman in May 1908. The Anglo-Persian Oil Company was formed in 1909. In 1914 the British government bought a controlling stake to fuel the Royal Navy.
events.why: The concession of 1901 gave one company most of a country for 60 years. The Royal Navy's conversion from coal to oil gave the British state a reason to own it.
events.then: Oil made the region strategically vital, and Britain's need to protect it shaped its Middle East policy for half a century.
events.sig: Oil made the region strategically vital, and Britain's need to protect it shaped its Middle East policy for half a century.
events.now: The company became BP. Iranian anger over its terms led to nationalisation in 1951 and the coup of 1953, which Iran's leaders still cite against Britain and the United States.

q.what: Crude oil.
q.who: The company and the British government profited; Persia got a small share.
q.scale: Masjed Soleyman became the first big oil field in the Middle East.
q.daily: A company town of oil workers grew in the desert.
q.system: Western oil concessions across the Middle East.

events.bluf: British investor William Knox D'Arcy's drillers wanted oil before his money ran out, and the British government wanted fuel for a navy switching from coal. The strike at Masjed Soleyman in May 1908 gave both, and in 1914 the government bought control of the company. The Middle East became strategically vital to Western energy, and Persian resentment of the concession's terms led to nationalisation in 1951, a coup in 1953 and lasting distrust of Britain and the United States.
events.lens: Resources controlled by foreigners become the focus of nationalist politics.
events.fact: D'Arcy never set foot in Persia.

events.who: Belgian parliament; reformers E.D. Morel, Roger Casement
events.what: Congo became a Belgian state colony.
events.why: Casement's report gave the atrocities official standing, and Morel's campaign made Leopold's rule a diplomatic liability for Belgium.
events.sig: Belgium ruled the Congo until 1960, with regulated labour and company concessions in place of Leopold's rubber terror. In June 2020 Belgian King Philippe expressed his 'deepest regrets' for the wounds of the colonial period.
events.hook: International outrage forced Leopold to give up Congo.
events.story: Belgian King Leopold II had ruled the Congo Free State as personal property since 1885 and ran it on forced rubber collection enforced by mutilation and hostage-taking. British consul Roger Casement's report of 1904 documented the system, and journalist E. D. Morel's Congo Reform Association campaigned in Britain and the United States. On 15 November 1908 the Belgian parliament annexed the territory as the Belgian Congo.
events.then: Belgium ruled the Congo until 1960, with regulated labour and company concessions in place of Leopold's rubber terror. In June 2020 Belgian King Philippe expressed his 'deepest regrets' for the wounds of the colonial period.
events.now: The campaign established the model of international pressure through documented atrocity. Belgian rule left Congo with fewer than twenty African university graduates at independence in 1960, which shaped the state's collapse that followed.

causes.why: Leopold's Congo began with Stanley.
International outrage over atrocities forced Belgium to take the colony from its king in 1908.

q.before: King Leopold's personal colony.
q.how: Annexation by the Belgian state.
q.winners: Reformers; Congolese suffered less extreme but continued exploitation.
q.lasted: Belgian rule lasted until 1960.

events.bluf: British consul Roger Casement and journalist E. D. Morel set out to end Belgian King Leopold II's personal rule over the Congo Free State by exposing its rubber regime of mutilation, hostage-taking and mass death. The Belgian parliament annexed the Congo as a state colony in November 1908. One of the first modern human-rights campaigns had removed a sovereign from his private empire; Belgian rule stayed extractive until 1960.
events.lens: International publicity can force change, but often only in who rules, not how.
events.fact: Casement, knighted for his Congo and Amazon reports, was hanged by Britain in 1916 for seeking German help for the Irish rising.

events.what: Restored the constitution.
events.why: The officers wanted a modern state able to hold the empire together. Losses to Balkan nationalists and European powers had discredited the sultan's rule.
events.sig: The CUP led the empire into the First World War on Germany's side in 1914 and lost almost all its remaining Arab lands.
events.hook: Reformist officers forced the sultan to restore the constitution.
events.story: In July 1908 officers of the Committee of Union and Progress, the 'Young Turks', mutinied in Macedonia. Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II restored the constitution of 1876 and elections followed. A counter-coup in April 1909 failed, and the Young Turks deposed Abdülhamid.
events.then: The CUP led the empire into the First World War on Germany's side in 1914 and lost almost all its remaining Arab lands.
events.now: Mustafa Kemal came from this movement, and the Young Turks' turn to Turkish nationalism led both to the Armenian genocide and to the founding of modern Turkey.

causes.why: Continued losses in the Balkans persuaded army officers that only a revolution could save the empire.

q.before: Sultan Abdulhamid II ruled as an autocrat.
q.how: A military revolt.
q.winners: The Committee of Union and Progress.
q.lasted: They ruled until 1918.

events.bluf: Officers of the Committee of Union and Progress mutinied to restore the constitution and to stop the empire losing territory to Balkan nationalists and European powers. They forced Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II to restore the constitution of 1876 and deposed him a year later. The constitutional regime turned into a nationalist, centralising one that took the empire into the First World War and carried out the Armenian genocide.
events.lens: Reformist revolutions can turn nationalist and authoritarian under the pressure of war and territorial loss.
events.fact: Abdülhamid was exiled to Salonica, the city where the revolt against him had begun.

events.who: Henry Ford and the Ford Motor Company
events.what: Affordable mass-produced car.
events.why: Ford wanted a car ordinary people could afford, and standardised parts and the moving assembly line made it possible. Rising wages and cheap steel and petrol gave him the market.
events.sig: By 1927 Ford had sold 15 million Model Ts. Mass car ownership created suburbs, highways and dependence on oil. General Motors overtook Ford in the late 1920s by offering styles and annual models.
events.hook: Henry Ford put the world on wheels with a car ordinary workers could buy.
events.story: Ford Motor Company put the Model T on sale in October 1908 at $850, a simple car built from interchangeable parts. In 1913 its Highland Park plant in Detroit introduced the moving assembly line, which cut the time to build a chassis from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes. In January 1914 Henry Ford doubled his workers' pay to $5 a day, which cut turnover and let them afford the car. The price fell to about $260 by the mid-1920s.
events.then: By 1927 Ford had sold 15 million Model Ts. Mass car ownership created suburbs, highways and dependence on oil. General Motors overtook Ford in the late 1920s by offering styles and annual models.
events.now: Fordism, high-volume production with wages high enough to buy the output, became the model of industrial economies from the 1920s to the 1970s; mass car ownership built the suburbs and highways and made oil a matter of national security.
events.fact: Ford said customers could have it 'any colour, as long as it's black'. Black was chosen because it dried fastest on the line.

q.what: A cheap, sturdy car for ordinary families.
q.who: Ford grew rich; workers got high wages for repetitive work.
q.scale: 15 million sold by 1927.
q.daily: Farmers and workers could drive.
q.system: Mass production on the moving assembly line.

events.bluf: Henry Ford wanted a car that a working family could afford, built from standard parts by unskilled labour. The Model T of 1908 and the moving assembly line of 1913 cut build time from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes and the price from $850 to about $260. Mass production and mass consumption became the model of industry, and the car reshaped cities, suburbs and the politics of oil.
events.lens: Making a product affordable to the workers who build it creates a mass market.

events.hook: A French aviator flew from France to England in 37 minutes, and Britain realised it was no longer safely an island.
events.what: A French aviator flew from France to England in 37 minutes, and Britain realised it was no longer safely an island.
events.story: On 25 July 1909 French aviator Louis Blériot flew his monoplane about 36 km across the English Channel from near Calais to Dover in some 37 minutes, winning the Daily Mail's £1,000 prize. British commentators warned that the country could no longer count on the sea and its navy to keep it safe.
events.why: Newspapers offered prizes to promote aviation. Engines and aircraft were improving fast after the Wright brothers' first flights in 1903.
events.then: Military interest in aircraft grew. Planes fought in World War I five years later.
events.sig: Military interest in aircraft grew. Planes fought in World War I five years later.
events.now: Air power soon erased Britain's island security, a shift that shaped British strategy in both world wars.

causes.why: Within six years of the Wrights, planes could cross the sea.

q.problem: Crossing open sea by air.
q.how: A light monoplane with a 25-horsepower engine.
q.replaced: The sense of Britain as protected by the sea.
q.spread: Air shows and flying clubs boomed across Europe.
q.next: Military aviation in World War I.

events.bluf: French aviator Louis Blériot flew the Channel to win the Daily Mail's £1,000 prize and prove his monoplane. He crossed from near Calais to Dover in about 37 minutes on 25 July 1909. The sea no longer guaranteed Britain's safety, and the air entered British strategy from then on.
events.lens: New technologies can erase old geographic advantages: the Channel stopped Napoleon but could not stop an aircraft.
events.fact: A granite outline of the aircraft marks the landing spot on Northfall Meadow behind Dover Castle.

events.what: A Korean independence fighter shot the architect of modern Japan at a railway station.
events.why: An Jung-geun sought revenge for Japan's takeover of Korea, of which Itō had been the chief architect. At his trial he listed fifteen charges against Itō, from the murder of Queen Min to the Eulsa treaty.
events.sig: Japan annexed Korea in August 1910, ten months later, and ruled it until 1945.
events.hook: A Korean independence fighter shot the architect of modern Japan at a railway station.
events.story: Japanese statesman Itō Hirobumi, four times prime minister and chief drafter of the Meiji constitution, had served as Korea's first Resident-General until mid-1909. On 26 October 1909, as he arrived at Harbin station in Manchuria to meet Russian Finance Minister Vladimir Kokovtsov, Korean independence fighter An Jung-geun shot him dead. An was executed in March 1910. Itō had been among the more cautious Japanese leaders on outright annexation, though he had accepted it by then.
events.then: Japan annexed Korea in August 1910, ten months later, and ruled it until 1945.
events.now: The killing removed a cautious voice in Tokyo and sped annexation in August 1910. An's status, hero in Seoul and criminal in Tokyo, is a standing point of friction; Japan protested when a memorial hall to him opened at Harbin in 2014.

causes.why: Itō had run the protectorate.

q.before: Itō, ironically, had been cautious about full annexation.
q.how: Hardliners pushed annexation through.
q.claim: An said he acted for Korean independence and peace in East Asia.
q.lasted: Korea was annexed less than a year later.

events.bluf: Korean independence activist An Jung-geun shot Itō Hirobumi, Japan's four-time prime minister and first Resident-General of Korea, at Harbin station on 26 October 1909 to punish the architect of Japan's takeover. Itō died within minutes; An was executed in March 1910. Japan annexed Korea ten months later, and the shooting became a patriot's act in Korean memory and a founding statesman's murder in Japan's, a divide that still separates the two countries' histories.
events.lens: The same person can be a terrorist to one nation and a patriot to another.
events.fact: An had cut off the last joint of his ring finger early in 1909 as a blood pledge to kill Itō; his handprint with the missing joint is a national emblem in Korea.

events.what: Self-governing dominion created.
events.why: Britain wanted a loyal white dominion and the gold mines running. Boer leaders accepted union on condition that the vote stayed white outside the Cape.
events.sig: Black leaders founded the South African Native National Congress in January 1912, renamed the African National Congress in 1923. The land act forced African tenant farmers off white-owned land into reserves and wage labour.
events.hook: Britain merged its colonies and the defeated Boer republics into one white-ruled country.
events.story: Britain had defeated the Boer republics in 1902. In 1910 it merged the Cape, Natal, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State into the Union of South Africa, a self-governing dominion. Only white men could vote except in the Cape, which kept a qualified franchise. The Natives Land Act of 1913 restricted African land ownership to about 7 per cent of the country.
events.then: Black leaders founded the South African Native National Congress in January 1912, renamed the African National Congress in 1923. The land act forced African tenant farmers off white-owned land into reserves and wage labour.
events.now: The 1913 land law confined African ownership to about 7 per cent of the country, later 13 per cent, and the dispute over who owns South Africa's land runs through its politics into the 2020s.

causes.why: After the war, Britain united its colonies and the defeated republics, leaving power in white hands to reconcile the Boers.

q.before: Four separate British colonies.
q.how: An act of the British Parliament.
q.lasted: It became a republic in 1961.

events.bluf: Britain wanted to reconcile British and Boer whites eight years after the Boer War and hand them a self-governing dominion. The Union of South Africa was created on 31 May 1910 on terms that reserved the vote to white men in three of its four provinces. White unity was bought by excluding Black Africans from power, and the 1913 Natives Land Act that followed fixed the racial land map that apartheid later completed.
events.lens: Peace between rival elites can be built at the expense of the excluded majority.
events.fact: The Union's two former Boer generals, Louis Botha and Jan Smuts, became its first prime ministers.
