events.who: Japan's government; Korean Emperor Sunjong and Prime Minister Ye Wanyong
events.what: Korea made a colony.
events.why: Japan wanted to secure Korea as a strategic buffer and colony after defeating Russia.
events.sig: Korean protests such as the March 1st Movement of 1919 were crushed. In the 1930s and 1940s Japan mobilised Koreans for its wars through forced labour, conscription and the sexual slavery of 'comfort women'. Korea was liberated in 1945, then divided by the United States and the Soviet Union.
events.hook: Korea became a Japanese colony for 35 years.
events.story: Under a treaty signed on 22 August 1910 by Korean Prime Minister Ye Wanyong, Korea was annexed to Japan and Emperor Sunjong lost his throne. Japanese Governor-General Terauchi Masatake ruled with the army and police. Koreans' land was surveyed and much of it taken; later Korean was banned in schools and Koreans were pressed to adopt Japanese names.
events.then: Korean protests such as the March 1st Movement of 1919 were crushed. In the 1930s and 1940s Japan mobilised Koreans for its wars through forced labour, conscription and the sexual slavery of 'comfort women'. Korea was liberated in 1945, then divided by the United States and the Soviet Union.
events.now: Colonial rule ran from 1910 to 1945, and its wartime mobilisation produced the forced-labour and 'comfort women' claims that Japan holds were settled by the treaty of 1965 and that Korean courts have ruled open since 2018. The dispute shapes relations between two US allies and the way history is taught in both.

causes.why: Itō's assassination gave hardliners their excuse.
The protectorate had already stripped Korea of control.

q.before: Korea had been a Japanese protectorate since 1905.
q.how: An annexation treaty signed under pressure.
q.claim: The treaty, which Korea considers invalid.
q.lasted: Until 1945.

events.bluf: Japan set out to make Korea a colony and strategic buffer after beating Russia. The treaty of 22 August 1910, signed by Korean Prime Minister Ye Wanyong, annexed Korea and placed it under a governor-general backed by the army and police. Thirty-five years of rule developed Korea for Japan's benefit, confiscated land and in its last decade tried to erase the Korean language and names; forced labour and the 'comfort women' system of those years still poison relations between Tokyo and Seoul.
events.lens: Colonial rule that tries to erase a people's identity produces lasting nationalism and grievance.
events.fact: The treaty was signed on 22 August and announced on 29 August 1910, which Koreans mark as the Day of National Humiliation.

events.what: Decade of civil war.
events.why: Land had concentrated in haciendas under Mexican President Porfirio Díaz, and most rural Mexicans owned none. Rigged elections had closed every legal route to power. Foreign capital owned much of the mines, oil and railways.
events.sig: The 1917 constitution promised land reform and national ownership of oil and minerals. Zapata was assassinated in 1919 and Villa in 1923. Mexican President Lázaro Cárdenas redistributed land and nationalised oil in the 1930s. The ruling party, later the PRI, held power until 2000.
events.hook: Mexico's revolution was the first great social revolution of the 20th century.
events.story: Mexican President Porfirio Díaz had ruled since 1876 with one interruption. After his fraudulent re-election in 1910, Francisco Madero called for revolt on 20 November. Díaz resigned in May 1911 and Madero became president; General Victoriano Huerta overthrew him and had him murdered in February 1913. Constitutionalists under Venustiano Carranza, northern forces under Pancho Villa and southern peasants under Emiliano Zapata, whose cry was 'land and liberty', fought Huerta and then each other. Estimates of the dead from fighting, disease and hunger run from 1 to 2 million.
events.then: The 1917 constitution promised land reform and national ownership of oil and minerals. Zapata was assassinated in 1919 and Villa in 1923. Mexican President Lázaro Cárdenas redistributed land and nationalised oil in the 1930s. The ruling party, later the PRI, held power until 2000.
events.now: The revolution produced Mexico's communal landholdings, the ejidos, and its doctrine of national ownership of oil, and the ruling party it created governed from 1929 to 2000.
events.fact: Revolutionary general Pancho Villa signed a contract with the Mutual Film Company in 1914 to film his battles.

sites.d: Pancho Villa's base in the north.
Zapata's peasant army: 'Land and Liberty'.
Changed hands repeatedly.

causes.why: Opposition to Díaz's long rule exploded in 1910.

q.why: Inequality and Díaz's long dictatorship.
q.stakes: Land, power and the future of Mexico.
q.decided: Shifting alliances; Carranza and then Obregón won.
q.cost: Perhaps 1 to 2 million dead.
q.changed: A new constitution and, eventually, one-party rule.

events.bluf: Mexican landowner Francisco Madero called a revolt in 1910 to end Mexican President Porfirio Díaz's 35-year rule, and peasant armies under Emiliano Zapata and Pancho Villa joined to win land. Díaz fell in 1911, and a decade of civil war killed an estimated 1 to 2 million people. The 1917 constitution promised land, labour rights and national ownership of resources, and the party the winners built ruled Mexico for 71 years.
events.trig: Díaz's fraudulent re-election in 1910 and Francisco Madero's call to revolt.

events.what: Republic of China founded.
events.why: Defeats by foreign powers and the Boxer indemnity came first, then failed reforms and the court's 1911 plan to nationalise provincial railways, which turned provincial elites against it. Sun Yat-sen's revolutionary alliance supplied the ideology and the network.
events.sig: General Yuan Shikai arranged the abdication and became president, then tried to make himself emperor in 1915. After his death in 1916 China split among warlords, and Nationalists and Communists competed to reunify it.
events.hook: China's last dynasty fell, ending 2,000 years of emperors.
events.story: On 10 October 1911 an army mutiny in Wuchang spread as province after province declared independence from the Qing. Revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen became provisional president on 1 January 1912. On 12 February 1912 the six-year-old Qing emperor Puyi abdicated, ending over 2,000 years of imperial rule.
events.then: General Yuan Shikai arranged the abdication and became president, then tried to make himself emperor in 1915. After his death in 1916 China split among warlords, and Nationalists and Communists competed to reunify it.
events.now: The fall left China without a central authority strong enough to hold it together from 1916 to 1928 and opened the contest between Nationalists and Communists over what should replace the empire. Both Beijing and Taipei honour Sun Yat-sen as the founder of modern China.
events.fact: The last emperor, Puyi, ended his life working as a gardener and archivist in Communist Beijing.

events.bluf: Revolutionaries led by Sun Yat-sen and provincial elites angered by the court's railway nationalisation set out to end Manchu rule. A mutiny at Wuchang on 10 October 1911 spread province by province, and in February 1912 the six-year-old emperor Puyi abdicated, ending over 2,000 years of imperial rule. The republic had no army of its own and passed within a year to General Yuan Shikai; warlordism, Japanese invasion and civil war followed before the Communists won in 1949.

events.bluf: Italy invaded the Ottoman provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica to gain a colony on the coast opposite it while the Young Turk government was weak. It won the provinces in 1912 and spent two decades subduing Libyan resistance. Ottoman defeat invited the Balkan states to attack in 1912, and Italian rule, with concentration camps in the 1930s, left Libya a lasting grievance.
events.lens: One great power's grab encourages others to grab too, and exposed weakness invites the next attack.
events.fact: On 1 November 1911 an Italian pilot dropped grenades by hand on Ottoman troops, the first aerial bombing in history.

events.hook: A constitutional amendment let Washington tax incomes.
events.what: A constitutional amendment let Washington tax incomes.
events.story: The Supreme Court had struck down an income tax in 1895 as a direct tax that had to be apportioned among the states by population. Congress passed the amendment in July 1909 under President William Howard Taft, and Delaware's ratification on 3 February 1913 completed it. The Revenue Act of October 1913 set rates of 1 to 7 per cent on incomes above $3,000, which exempted all but about 1 per cent of households.
events.why: Progressive reformers wanted revenue that fell on the wealthy rather than tariffs that raised prices for everyone. Conservatives in Congress proposed the amendment expecting the states to reject it.
events.then: Rates rose to 77 per cent on the highest incomes to pay for the First World War. The tax paid for the New Deal and the Second World War, when withholding from wages made most workers taxpayers, and became the government's main source of revenue.
events.sig: Rates rose to 77 per cent on the highest incomes to pay for the First World War. The tax paid for the New Deal and the Second World War, when withholding from wages made most workers taxpayers, and became the government's main source of revenue.
events.now: The individual income tax is still the largest single source of federal revenue, which is why fights over its rates are the central fight of American fiscal politics.
events.wk: Sixteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

q.scale: Today it is the largest source of federal revenue.
q.daily: Annual tax returns became part of American life.

events.bluf: Progressive reformers in both parties wanted federal revenue that fell on the wealthy rather than on tariffs that raised everyone's prices, after the Supreme Court had struck down an income tax in 1895. Congress proposed the amendment in 1909 and the states ratified it in February 1913. The federal government gained a revenue source that could grow without limit, which financed two world wars, the New Deal and the modern American state.
events.lens: A state's capacity depends on what it can tax: the income tax turned Washington into a power that could fund world wars and welfare.
events.fact: The first Form 1040 ran to four pages, including the instructions.

events.hook: After repeated bank panics, the US created a central bank.
events.what: After repeated bank panics, the US created a central bank.
events.story: Bank panics in 1873, 1893 and 1907 had closed banks and businesses across the country, and in 1907 banker J. P. Morgan locked the leading financiers in his library until they agreed to a rescue. A National Monetary Commission under Senator Nelson Aldrich proposed a central bank; Democrats rejected its banker-run design. President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act on 23 December 1913: twelve regional reserve banks owned by member banks, overseen by a board appointed by the president, with power to issue currency and lend to banks.
events.why: Repeated banking panics, ending in 1907, and the lack of any lender of last resort, which left the system depending on private bankers. Wilson's Democrats wanted public control, the banks wanted private, and the act split the difference.
events.then: The Fed's failure to stop bank collapses after 1929 deepened the Great Depression. The Banking Act of 1935 centralised power in the Washington board, and the 1951 accord with the Treasury established its independence in setting rates.
events.sig: The Fed's failure to stop bank collapses after 1929 deepened the Great Depression. The Banking Act of 1935 centralised power in the Washington board, and the 1951 accord with the Treasury established its independence in setting rates.
events.now: The Fed sets interest rates that move markets worldwide, and its independence from political pressure is a recurring battle, intensified in 2025.

causes.why: After the Panic of 1907, Progressive-era reformers created a central bank.

q.what: Money, credit and banking reserves.
q.who: Banks gained a lender of last resort.
q.scale: Twelve regional banks under a board in Washington.
q.daily: Interest rates on loans and mortgages.
q.system: American central banking.

events.bluf: President Woodrow Wilson and Congress wanted a lender of last resort after the Panic of 1907 had been stopped only by banker J. P. Morgan's private rescue. The Federal Reserve Act of December 1913 created twelve regional reserve banks under a board in Washington. The United States gained a central bank; its failure to stop bank collapses after 1929 deepened the Depression, and its later authority over interest rates made it the most powerful economic institution in the world.
events.lens: Financial crises create the institutions that manage the next ones.
events.fact: The plan was drafted in secret in November 1910 at a club on Jekyll Island, Georgia, by bankers who travelled there using first names only.

events.who: German Gen. Lettow-Vorbeck vs. British Empire
events.what: Four-year guerrilla war across East Africa.
events.why: Germany wanted British forces held away from Europe, and Britain wanted the colony and its coast. Neither side could feed an army in the bush without conscripted carriers.
events.sig: Hundreds of thousands of porters and civilians died of disease, hunger and exhaustion; the British Carrier Corps alone recorded over 40,000 deaths. Famine and influenza followed the armies across the region in 1918-19.
events.hook: World War I was fought across East Africa for four years, mostly by Africans.
events.story: The war reached East Africa in August 1914. German commander Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck led a force that peaked at about 3,000 Germans and 12,000 askari on a four-year chase through Tanganyika, Kenya and Mozambique against British, Indian, South African, Belgian and Portuguese forces. Both sides moved supplies on the backs of more than a million African porters. He surrendered on 25 November 1918 after learning of the armistice in Europe.
events.then: Hundreds of thousands of porters and civilians died of disease, hunger and exhaustion; the British Carrier Corps alone recorded over 40,000 deaths. Famine and influenza followed the armies across the region in 1918-19.
events.now: The campaign tied down 150,000 Allied troops for four years, killed perhaps 100,000 African porters and transferred Tanganyika from Germany to Britain, which fixed the map of East Africa until independence.

events.bluf: Britain wanted German East Africa taken and Germany wanted British troops tied down far from Europe. German commander Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck's force of German officers and African askari evaded far larger armies across Tanganyika, Kenya and Mozambique for four years and surrendered only after the armistice. The campaign held some 150,000 Allied troops, consumed more than a million African porters, of whom perhaps 100,000 died, and transferred Tanganyika from Germany to Britain.
events.lens: Wars between empires are fought on colonized land with colonized labor.
events.fact: The porters who died are the least recorded dead of the war; most have no name in any register.

toll.n: Estimates vary widely. Most deaths came from disease, hunger and exhaustion.

events.who: Central Powers vs. Russia, France, Britain
events.what: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand triggered alliances.
events.why: Rival alliance blocs, an arms race and mobilisation plans that rewarded striking first came first. Nationalism in the Balkans and among the great powers came second. Austria-Hungary's fear of collapse and Germany's sense of encirclement came third.
events.sig: About 20 million soldiers and civilians died. The German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires collapsed; the Bolsheviks took Russia; new states emerged in Eastern Europe; Britain and France divided the Arab Middle East; the United States emerged as the world's creditor.
events.hook: An assassination in Sarajevo dragged Europe's empires into a catastrophic war.
events.story: On 28 June 1914 Bosnian Serb nationalist Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, sent Serbia an ultimatum; Russia mobilised to support Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia and France and invaded Belgium, which brought in Britain. Machine guns, artillery and trenches turned the Western Front into a stalemate of mass slaughter.
events.then: About 20 million soldiers and civilians died. The German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires collapsed; the Bolsheviks took Russia; new states emerged in Eastern Europe; Britain and France divided the Arab Middle East; the United States emerged as the world's creditor.
events.now: Today's Middle East and Eastern European borders, and the causes of World War II, come from this war. Analysts still study 1914 to understand how a crisis between great powers could spiral into a war nobody wanted.
events.fact: Franz Ferdinand's driver took a wrong turn and stopped right in front of the assassin, Gavrilo Princip.

None got the short war each had planned. Four years killed about 20 million people, four empires fell, communism took Russia, and the settlement left the grievances that produced the next war.
events.trig: The assassination in Sarajevo and the July Crisis of ultimatums and mobilisations that followed.
events.lens: Alliances and war plans that make striking first look necessary can turn a local crisis into a world war.

events.what: Linked Atlantic and Pacific.
events.why: The United States wanted a fast route between its coasts for trade and for its navy. In 1898 the battleship Oregon had needed 67 days to sail round South America to reach Cuba.
events.sig: The United States governed a 10-mile-wide Canal Zone through Panama. Riots over the right to fly Panama's flag in the zone killed more than 20 people in January 1964. The 1977 treaties signed by US President Jimmy Carter and Panamanian leader Omar Torrijos returned the canal on 31 December 1999.
events.hook: The Panama Canal joined the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
events.story: A French company led by diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps began a canal in 1881 and abandoned it after about 22,000 workers died, mostly of malaria and yellow fever. The United States took over in 1904. US Army physician William Gorgas cut the mosquito populations that carried both diseases, and US Army engineer George Goethals built locks that lift ships 26 metres to an artificial lake. The canal opened on 15 August 1914.
events.then: The United States governed a 10-mile-wide Canal Zone through Panama. Riots over the right to fly Panama's flag in the zone killed more than 20 people in January 1964. The 1977 treaties signed by US President Jimmy Carter and Panamanian leader Omar Torrijos returned the canal on 31 December 1999.
events.now: About 5 per cent of world seaborne trade passes through the canal. Drought cut transits in 2023, and US pressure on Panama over Chinese influence in 2025 reopened the question of who controls it.
events.fact: Ships pay tolls by weight; US writer Richard Halliburton paid 36 cents to swim the canal in 1928.

causes.why: The new Panamanian government granted the US a canal zone; the canal took ten years to build.

It opened the canal on 15 August 1914, cutting the sea route from New York to San Francisco by about 8,000 miles. The United States became a two-ocean naval power, and the Canal Zone became the most visible symbol of US dominance in Latin America until 1999.

events.who: French commander Joseph Joffre; the British Expeditionary Force; German armies under Helmuth von Moltke the Younger
events.hook: France and Britain stopped the German advance short of Paris, ending hopes of a quick war.
events.what: France and Britain stopped the German advance short of Paris, ending hopes of a quick war.
events.story: German armies under chief of staff Helmuth von Moltke the Younger swept through Belgium toward Paris. From 6 September 1914 French forces under commander Joseph Joffre and the British Expeditionary Force counter-attacked into a gap between two German armies; some French reinforcements were rushed from Paris in taxis. The Germans fell back to the Aisne River and dug in.
events.why: Germany's Schlieffen Plan required defeating France in about six weeks. The German right wing had turned east of Paris and exposed its flank.
events.then: Both sides dug trenches from the Channel to Switzerland, and the war became a stalemate.
events.sig: Both sides dug trenches from the Channel to Switzerland, and the war became a stalemate.
events.now: The Marne stopped Germany short of Paris and destroyed its plan for a short war; the trench stalemate that followed turned the conflict into four years of attrition that broke four empires.

q.stakes: Paris, and the course of the war.

q.cost: About half a million casualties on both sides.

events.bluf: German chief of staff Helmuth von Moltke the Younger sought to finish France in six weeks by swinging his right wing round Paris; French commander Joseph Joffre set out to stop it. From 6 September 1914 French and British forces struck into a gap between two German armies and drove them back to the Aisne. Germany lost the short war its whole plan depended on, and four years of trench war followed that broke four empires.

events.fact: The 'taxis of the Marne' became a French legend of mobilisation.

events.h: Battle of Tanga: the 'Battle of the Bees'
events.what: A British force eight times larger was routed by Germans, askari, and swarms of angry bees.
events.why: Britain wanted the colony taken quickly before it could threaten Kenya. The landing force was untrained and its commander gave the Germans warning by delaying.
events.sig: Lettow-Vorbeck's force took 16 machine guns, hundreds of rifles and 600,000 rounds. The East Africa campaign ran until two weeks after the armistice.
events.hook: A British force eight times larger was routed by Germans, askari, and swarms of angry bees.
events.story: Indian Expeditionary Force B, about 8,000 men, landed near Tanga on 2 November 1914 to seize German East Africa's northern railhead. German commander Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck brought about 1,000 German officers and African askari by rail and counterattacked on 4 November. Bees disturbed by gunfire stung both sides and broke up British units. The British re-embarked on 5 November and left their equipment behind.
events.then: Lettow-Vorbeck's force took 16 machine guns, hundreds of rifles and 600,000 rounds. The East Africa campaign ran until two weeks after the armistice.
events.now: The captured rifles, machine guns and ammunition from Tanga supplied the German force for months and made possible the campaign that kept some 150,000 Allied troops in East Africa until November 1918.

causes.why: War in Europe spread to Africa.

q.why: WWI spread to the colonies.

q.cost: About 360 British killed vs. about 70 German and askari.

events.bluf: Britain landed about 8,000 Indian Army troops at Tanga in November 1914 to take German East Africa's northern port in a single stroke. German commander Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck's force of about 1,000 counterattacked, bee swarms disturbed by gunfire broke up British units, and the British re-embarked after three days leaving their weapons on the beach. A four-year campaign followed in which a small mobile force tied down armies many times its size.
events.lens: Small, mobile forces can tie down much larger ones in vast terrain.
events.fact: British propaganda later claimed the Germans had used the bees on purpose; the swarms stung both sides and there is no evidence of a plan.

events.who: British and German soldiers on the Western Front

events.what: Soldiers on both sides stopped fighting, sang carols and met in no man's land.
events.story: On Christmas Eve and Christmas Day 1914, along parts of the front, mostly in Belgium, British and German troops called unofficial truces. They buried their dead, swapped food and cigarettes, and in a few places kicked a football about.
events.why: Exhaustion and cold came first. A sense that the enemy was much like themselves came second.
events.then: Commanders forbade fraternising. The war grew more brutal, with poison gas used from April 1915; later truces were rare.
events.sig: Commanders forbade fraternising. The war grew more brutal, with poison gas used from April 1915; later truces were rare.
events.now: The truce showed commanders that hostility between conscript armies needed discipline and propaganda to maintain, and both sides ordered against repetition; the war's brutalisation followed.

causes.why: Within three months both armies were dug into trenches facing each other.

q.new: Enemies openly meeting between the trenches.
q.audience: The soldiers themselves; their letters home spread the story.
q.reveals: How little many soldiers hated the men opposite them.

events.bluf: British and German soldiers along parts of the Flanders front stopped fighting at Christmas 1914 to bury their dead and, with that done, met in no man's land. The truces held for a day or two and ended when commanders on both sides ordered fire resumed. Armies learned that hostility between conscript soldiers needed discipline and propaganda to maintain, and the war that followed was fought with gas and without such pauses.
events.lens: Wars depend on keeping the enemy abstract; contact erodes it.
events.fact: German troops set candle-lit Christmas trees on their parapets, and the carol both sides knew was 'Silent Night'.

events.who: The Young Turk government (Committee of Union and Progress); Ottoman Armenians
events.where: Eastern Anatolia and the Syrian desert
events.hook: The Ottoman government deported and killed most of its Armenian subjects.
events.what: The Ottoman government deported and killed most of its Armenian subjects.
events.story: Armenians had suffered massacres in the Ottoman Empire in 1894-96. On 24 April 1915 the government arrested Armenian leaders in Constantinople. Ottoman Interior Minister Talat Pasha's ministry then ordered the deportation of Armenians from Anatolia on marches to the Syrian desert. Massacres, starvation and disease killed most of the deportees; counts range from about 600,000 to 1.5 million dead.
events.why: The Young Turk regime read the Armenians as allies of Russia after its defeats in the Caucasus. Its leaders pursued a Turkish-Muslim Anatolia.
events.then: Survivors scattered into a diaspora in Lebanon, France and the United States, and Anatolia's ethnic map was remade. Polish lawyer Raphael Lemkin coined the word 'genocide' in 1944 partly with this case in mind.
events.sig: Survivors scattered into a diaspora in Lebanon, France and the United States, and Anatolia's ethnic map was remade. Polish lawyer Raphael Lemkin coined the word 'genocide' in 1944 partly with this case in mind.
events.now: Armenia, the diaspora and more than 30 states, including the United States in 2021, call the killings genocide. Turkey's government holds that Armenians died in a wartime relocation amid famine, disease and intercommunal fighting, with no plan to destroy them, and disputes the figures; the disagreement shapes its relations with Armenia and the West.

causes.why: The Young Turks' radical wing, ruling the empire in wartime, pursued a Turkish-Muslim Anatolia and organised the deportations.
At war with Russia, the regime accused Armenians of siding with the enemy and used the war as cover for the deportations.

q.why: The regime accused Armenians of disloyalty and sought a Turkish-Muslim Anatolia.
q.stakes: The survival of the Armenian people in their homeland.
q.decided: State-organised deportation and killing.
q.cost: About 600,000 to 1.5 million dead.
q.changed: Armenian life in Anatolia was largely destroyed.

events.bluf: At war with Russia and after heavy defeats, the Young Turk government set out to remove the Armenian population from Anatolia, which it branded a disloyal fifth column. Deportations and massacres from April 1915 killed most of the deportees; counts range from about 600,000 to 1.5 million. An ancient community in Anatolia was destroyed, the survivors became a global diaspora, and the question of what to call the killing remains a dispute between Turkey, Armenia and the states that have recognised it as genocide.
events.lens: Wartime fear of an internal 'enemy' can turn a state against its own minorities; watch for leaders branding a group as traitors.
events.fact: Talat Pasha was shot dead in Berlin in 1921 by Armenian survivor Soghomon Tehlirian, whom a German jury acquitted.

events.who: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC), British and French forces; Ottoman army (Mustafa Kemal)
events.hook: Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli; the failed campaign became a founding story for both nations.
events.what: Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli; the failed campaign became a founding story for both nations.
events.story: Britain and France tried to force the Dardanelles by sea in March 1915 and lost three battleships to mines. British commander General Ian Hamilton then landed troops on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April 1915; the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps came ashore at what became Anzac Cove, British and French forces at Cape Helles. Ottoman Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Kemal's 19th Division held the heights above the Anzac beach. After eight months of trench warfare the Allies withdrew in December 1915 and January 1916. About 8,700 Australians and 2,700 New Zealanders died, along with far larger numbers of British, French and Ottoman soldiers.
events.why: The Western Front was deadlocked and Churchill wanted a way round it. Taking Constantinople would have knocked the Ottomans out of the war and opened the Black Sea to Russia.
events.then: Churchill lost the Admiralty in May 1915. Kemal's reputation carried him to command of the Turkish national movement after 1919. The Allies shifted their effort to the Western Front, Salonika and Mesopotamia.
events.sig: Churchill lost the Admiralty in May 1915. Kemal's reputation carried him to command of the Turkish national movement after 1919. The Allies shifted their effort to the Western Front, Salonika and Mesopotamia.
events.now: Gallipoli gave Australia and New Zealand a national story independent of Britain and made the man who founded the Turkish Republic in 1923; both countries date their sense of nationhood from it.

causes.why: Fourteen years after federation, Australian soldiers went to war under a national flag for the first time.
With the Western Front deadlocked, Britain and France tried to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war.

q.why: To knock the Ottomans out of the war and reach Russia.
q.decided: Ottoman defenders holding the high ground.
q.cost: Over 100,000 dead on both sides.
q.changed: The Allies withdrew; Mustafa Kemal rose to fame.

events.bluf: First Lord of the Admiralty Winston Churchill wanted to force the Dardanelles, take Constantinople and open a sea route to Russia. Allied troops, Australians and New Zealanders among them, landed on 25 April 1915, held a few square miles for eight months and withdrew; about 8,700 Australians and 2,700 New Zealanders died, with far larger numbers of British, French and Ottoman soldiers. The campaign failed, gave Australia and New Zealand a founding story of sacrifice, and made the reputation of Ottoman Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Kemal.
events.lens: Nations often build their identity around sacrifices in defeat, not only victories.
events.fact: The evacuation was the campaign's one success: more than 100,000 men were taken off the beaches with almost no losses.

events.who: German submarine U-20; the Cunard liner Lusitania
events.where: Off the Old Head of Kinsale, Ireland
events.hook: A German submarine sank a British liner, killing nearly 1,200 people, 128 of them American.
events.what: A German submarine sank a British liner, killing nearly 1,200 people, 128 of them American.
events.story: On 7 May 1915 the German submarine U-20 torpedoed the British liner Lusitania off southern Ireland without warning, and it sank in 18 minutes. Of 1,959 people aboard, 1,198 died, including 128 Americans. Germany had placed notices in New York newspapers warning that ships in the war zone could be sunk, and the liner was carrying rifle ammunition, which Germany cited to justify the attack.
events.why: Germany had declared the waters around Britain a war zone. The ship was also carrying rifle ammunition.
events.then: American outrage forced Germany to limit submarine attacks until 1917. When it resumed unrestricted warfare in 1917, the United States entered the war.
events.sig: American outrage forced Germany to limit submarine attacks until 1917. When it resumed unrestricted warfare in 1917, the United States entered the war.
events.now: The sinking made submarine warfare the issue on which American neutrality turned from 1915 to 1917; every later argument over attacks on civilians and neutral opinion starts here.

q.stakes: Freedom of the seas, and American neutrality.
q.decided: A single torpedo and a fast sinking.
q.cost: 1,198 dead, including 128 Americans.
q.changed: American opinion turned sharply against Germany.

events.bluf: Germany had declared the waters around Britain a war zone to cut its supplies; the submarine U-20 sank the Cunard liner Lusitania without warning on 7 May 1915. Of 1,959 people aboard, 1,198 died, 128 of them Americans. American opinion turned against Germany, Berlin restricted its submarines until 1917, and the resumption of unrestricted sinking that year brought the United States into the war.
events.lens: Attacks on civilians can cost more politically than they gain militarily.
events.fact: A German medallist struck a satirical medal of the sinking; Britain copied it in large numbers and sold it as propaganda.

events.hook: China's president tried to make himself emperor and lasted 83 days.
events.what: China's president tried to make himself emperor and lasted 83 days.
events.story: Chinese President Yuan Shikai had pushed Sun Yat-sen aside in 1912 and dissolved parliament in 1914. He accepted the throne in December 1915 as the Hongxian Emperor, after petitions his own officials had arranged. General Cai E raised Yunnan against him and other provinces followed. Yuan abandoned the monarchy on 22 March 1916 and died on 6 June.
events.why: Yuan wanted to secure his personal power and believed China needed a monarch to hold it together. Flatterers and fake petitions told him the country agreed.
events.then: China broke apart among regional warlords, and Japan used the chaos to extend its influence.
events.sig: China broke apart among regional warlords, and Japan used the chaos to extend its influence.
events.now: Yuan's death opened the warlord era, which lasted until the Nationalists reunified most of China in 1928 and which Japan used to extend its hold on Manchuria and Shandong.

causes.why: Yuan took the presidency of the new republic and then reached for the throne.

q.before: Yuan ruled as president of the new republic.
q.how: A staged vote to restore the monarchy.
q.lasted: 83 days.

events.bluf: Chinese President Yuan Shikai set out to secure his personal power by making himself emperor, convinced China needed a monarch to hold it together. He took the throne as the Hongxian Emperor in December 1915; provinces rebelled from Yunnan outward, he gave up the monarchy in March 1916 and died in June. The republic was left with no central authority, and China broke into warlord domains until 1928.
events.lens: Strongmen who try to revive an old form of legitimacy often find the old order cannot be restored.
events.fact: The Hongxian reign lasted 83 days.

events.who: German Fifth Army; French army under Philippe Pétain and Robert Nivelle
events.hook: Germany tried to 'bleed France white' at Verdun; the battle lasted ten months.
events.what: Germany tried to 'bleed France white' at Verdun; the battle lasted ten months.
events.story: From 21 February 1916 German forces attacked the fortress city of Verdun. France rotated most of its army through the battle under General Philippe Pétain and then General Robert Nivelle, with the slogan 'They shall not pass'. By December the front was back near where it started.
events.why: German chief of staff Erich von Falkenhayn wanted to wear down France's army on ground it could never give up.
events.then: Verdun made Pétain a national hero, which later helped him lead Vichy France. France built the Maginot Line in the 1930s on the lesson of fixed defence.
events.sig: Verdun made Pétain a national hero, which later helped him lead Vichy France. France built the Maginot Line in the 1930s on the lesson of fixed defence.
events.now: Verdun became the symbol of French endurance and of the futility of attrition; Kohl and Mitterrand chose it in 1984 to stage Franco-German reconciliation.

causes.why: The failure of the war of movement led to battles of attrition.

q.why: Germany sought to exhaust France's army.
q.stakes: A symbolic fortress city, and French morale.
q.decided: French endurance, and the Allied offensive on the Somme.
q.cost: About 700,000 casualties, around 300,000 of them dead.
q.changed: Both armies were exhausted; neither gained ground.

events.bluf: German chief of staff Erich von Falkenhayn attacked Verdun to bleed the French army white on ground France would defend at any cost. France held under General Philippe Pétain, and ten months of fighting cost the two sides about 700,000 casualties between them for a front back where it began. Verdun became France's symbol of endurance, made Pétain a national hero and fixed French faith in fixed defences.
events.lens: Attrition strategies often exhaust the attacker as much as the defender.
events.fact: Fort Douaumont, the strongest fort at Verdun, fell on 25 February to a small German party that found it almost unmanned.

kv: February–December 1916, the longest battle of the war

events.h: Pancho Villa raids Columbus, New Mexico
events.who: Pancho Villa; US general John J. Pershing
events.hook: Villa raided a US border town, and the US sent an army into Mexico after him.
events.what: Villa raided a US border town, and the US sent an army into Mexico after him.
events.story: The United States had recognised Venustiano Carranza's government in October 1915 and let his troops cross US territory to defeat Villa at Agua Prieta. Before dawn on 9 March 1916 several hundred Villistas attacked Columbus, New Mexico, burned part of the town and killed 18 Americans. President Woodrow Wilson sent General John J. Pershing with a force that grew to more than 10,000 men into Chihuahua. Carranza's troops fought Pershing's at Carrizal in June, and the expedition withdrew in February 1917 without finding Villa.
events.why: Villa was angry that the United States had recognised his rival, Venustiano Carranza, and had helped Carranza's army against him. A US intervention would show Carranza as a weak defender of Mexican soil.
events.then: Tension with Mexico made Germany's Zimmermann Telegram of January 1917, offering Mexico its lost territory, all the more alarming when it was published in March. Pershing commanded the American Expeditionary Force in France within months of returning.
events.sig: Tension with Mexico made Germany's Zimmermann Telegram of January 1917, offering Mexico its lost territory, all the more alarming when it was published in March. Pershing commanded the American Expeditionary Force in France within months of returning.
events.now: The expedition fixed US military intervention in Mexico as a standing grievance in Mexican politics, and Villa remains a folk hero there, a symbol of defiance toward US power.

causes.why: Villa turned on the US after it backed his rival.

q.why: Villa retaliated against US support for Carranza.
q.decided: Villa escaped into the mountains.
q.cost: 18 Americans and dozens of raiders killed.
q.changed: US troops spent 11 months inside Mexico.

events.bluf: Mexican revolutionary general Pancho Villa wanted to punish the United States for recognising his rival Venustiano Carranza and to provoke a crisis that would discredit Carranza's government. His men attacked Columbus, New Mexico, on 9 March 1916 and killed 18 Americans. President Woodrow Wilson sent General John J. Pershing and more than 10,000 troops into Mexico for eleven months without catching him, which brought the two countries close to war as Germany was courting Mexico.
events.lens: Punitive expeditions against elusive enemies often fail and inflame nationalism.
events.fact: The expedition was the US Army's first to use aircraft and motor trucks in the field; its eight planes were all wrecked or worn out within weeks.
events.btt: Mexico: The Mexican Revolution and its aftermath

events.what: Secret plan to divide Ottoman Arab lands.
events.why: Britain and France wanted to secure routes to India, oil and influence before the Ottoman collapse. Each made overlapping promises to win allies.
events.sig: The Bolsheviks published the agreement in 1917 and embarrassed Britain. Through the League of Nations mandates of 1920, Britain took Iraq, Palestine and Transjordan and France took Syria and Lebanon, and Arab revolts followed.
events.hook: Britain and France secretly split up the Middle East.
events.story: In May 1916 British diplomat Sir Mark Sykes and French diplomat François Georges-Picot secretly agreed how to divide the Ottoman Empire's Arab provinces: France would get Syria and Lebanon, Britain southern Mesopotamia and influence across to the Gulf, with Palestine under international administration. At the same time Britain was promising Sharif Hussein of Mecca an independent Arab kingdom in return for revolt against the Ottomans. In 1917 it promised a Jewish national home in Palestine.
events.then: The Bolsheviks published the agreement in 1917 and embarrassed Britain. Through the League of Nations mandates of 1920, Britain took Iraq, Palestine and Transjordan and France took Syria and Lebanon, and Arab revolts followed.
events.now: Sykes-Picot remains the symbol of Western betrayal in the Arab world. ISIS staged the 'end of Sykes-Picot' in 2014 by bulldozing the Iraq-Syria border, though the actual borders came from later deals rather than the 1916 lines.

causes.why: The Young Turks took the empire into World War I on Germany's side, and Britain and France planned how to divide it.

q.before: The Ottoman Empire ruled the Arab lands.
q.how: A secret Anglo-French agreement.
q.claim: Spheres of influence after Ottoman defeat.
q.lasted: Its lines shaped Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Jordan.

events.bluf: Britain and France, expecting the Ottomans to lose, wanted the Arab provinces divided between them before anyone else could claim them. British diplomat Sir Mark Sykes and French diplomat François Georges-Picot drew the spheres in secret in May 1916 while Britain was promising Sharif Hussein of Mecca an Arab kingdom. The mandates that followed produced Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine, and the agreement became the standing Arab symbol of Western betrayal.
events.lens: Contradictory wartime promises come due after the war, and someone is always betrayed.
events.fact: Tsarist Russia was the third party to the deal and was assigned eastern Anatolia; the Bolsheviks found the text in its archives and published it.

the secret deal exposed by the Bolsheviks

events.who: British and French armies; the German army
events.hook: On its first day the British army suffered 57,000 casualties, the worst day in its history.
events.what: On its first day the British army suffered 57,000 casualties, the worst day in its history.
events.story: On 1 July 1916, after a week of bombardment, British troops advanced and were cut down by German machine guns. The battle went on until November, saw the first use of tanks, and gained about 10 km.
events.why: British commander Douglas Haig attacked to relieve pressure on the French at Verdun and to break the German line.
events.then: Commanders learned costly lessons in artillery, infantry tactics and tanks that helped the Allies break the German lines in 1918.
events.sig: Commanders learned costly lessons in artillery, infantry tactics and tanks that helped the Allies break the German lines in 1918.
events.now: The Somme shapes British memory of World War I as futile slaughter and is studied as a lesson in adapting tactics to new technology.

causes.why: The Somme offensive was brought forward to relieve the French at Verdun.

q.why: To relieve Verdun and break through.
q.stakes: A breakthrough on the Western Front.
q.decided: German defences held, and the Allies gained little.
q.cost: Over a million casualties on all sides.
q.changed: Tanks appeared, and Britain's volunteer army was shattered.

events.bluf: British commander Douglas Haig attacked on the Somme to relieve the French at Verdun and break the German line. The first day cost 57,000 British casualties; by November both sides had lost more than a million men for about 10 km of ground. The British army learned the artillery and infantry methods it used to win in 1918, and the first day became the British image of the whole war.
events.lens: Old tactics against new technology produce massacres until doctrine catches up.
events.fact: The British fired about 1.5 million shells in the opening bombardment; many were duds, and farmers still plough them up every year.

kv: British casualties on the first day, ~19,240 killed

toll.n: About 10 km of ground was gained.

events.hook: Mexico adopted a radical constitution that gave the nation ownership of land and minerals and protected workers.
events.what: Mexico adopted a radical constitution that gave the nation ownership of land and minerals and protected workers.
events.story: The Constitutional Congress met at Querétaro and proclaimed the constitution on 5 February 1917. Article 27 gave the nation ownership of land and subsoil resources and allowed land reform. Article 123 guaranteed an eight-hour day and the right to strike. Other articles limited the Church's property and role in education.
events.why: The winning faction under Constitutionalist First Chief Venustiano Carranza needed the peasants and workers who had fought. Radicals in the congress pushed for land and labour rights beyond Carranza's own draft.
events.then: Carranza was overthrown and killed in 1920. Article 27 became the legal basis for land redistribution, which peaked under Mexican President Lázaro Cárdenas in the 1930s, and for nationalising oil in 1938.
events.sig: Carranza was overthrown and killed in 1920. Article 27 became the legal basis for land redistribution, which peaked under Mexican President Lázaro Cárdenas in the 1930s, and for nationalising oil in 1938.
events.now: It is still Mexico's constitution, much amended. Article 27's claim of national ownership of land and minerals underpinned the oil nationalisation of 1938 and every later dispute over foreign investment in Mexican energy.

causes.why: The winning faction wrote the revolution's demands into law.

q.before: The 1857 liberal constitution, ignored under Díaz.
q.how: A constitutional congress of the winning faction.
q.claim: The revolution's promises of land and labour rights.
q.lasted: Yes: it is still in force.

events.bluf: Constitutionalist First Chief Venustiano Carranza called a congress to legalise his victory, and the radicals in it set out to give peasants and workers what they had fought for. The constitution proclaimed on 5 February 1917 gave the nation ownership of land and subsoil, licensed land reform and guaranteed labour rights. It became the legal basis for land redistribution and the oil nationalisation of 1938, and a model for social constitutions elsewhere.
events.lens: Constitutions that redefine property rights redefine the economy.
events.fact: It wrote social rights such as the eight-hour day into a national constitution before the Soviet constitution of 1918 and the Weimar constitution of 1919.

events.who: Nicholas II; Petrograd workers and soldiers; the Provisional Government
events.hook: Bread riots in Petrograd turned into revolution, and the last tsar abdicated within a week.
events.what: Bread riots in Petrograd turned into revolution, and the last tsar abdicated within a week.
events.story: Strikes and food protests began in Petrograd on International Women's Day, 8 March 1917, 23 February in Russia's calendar. When soldiers joined the crowds, Russian Tsar Nicholas II's generals advised him to go, and he abdicated on 15 March. A Provisional Government took over, alongside workers' councils called soviets.
events.why: Millions of war dead and food shortages in the cities came first. A monarchy discredited by defeat and by Rasputin's influence came second. When the capital's garrison refused to fire, the regime fell.
events.then: The Provisional Government kept fighting the war. The Bolsheviks seized power in November.
events.sig: The Provisional Government kept fighting the war. The Bolsheviks seized power in November.
events.now: It ended more than 300 years of Romanov rule, and the failure of the new government to end the war or build stable institutions opened the way for the Bolsheviks.

q.before: Tsar Nicholas II, an autocrat.
q.how: Mass protest and a mutiny of the capital's garrison.
q.claim: Popular sovereignty, to be settled by an elected assembly.
q.lasted: No: the Bolsheviks overthrew them eight months later.

events.bluf: Petrograd workers struck for bread and the garrison refused to fire on them; Russian Tsar Nicholas II's generals told him to go. He abdicated on 15 March 1917, and three centuries of Romanov rule ended in a week. Power split between a Provisional Government and the soviets, and the government's choice to fight on gave the Bolsheviks their opening.
events.lens: Revolutions that remove a ruler but continue his unpopular war rarely last.
events.fact: Nicholas abdicated for his son as well as himself; his brother Michael refused the crown the next day.

events.who: German foreign minister Arthur Zimmermann; British codebreakers of Room 40
events.hook: Germany secretly offered Mexico Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if it joined a war against the United States.
events.what: Germany secretly offered Mexico Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if it joined a war against the United States.
events.story: On 16 January 1917 German Foreign Minister Arthur Zimmermann cabled Germany's minister in Mexico City, proposing an alliance if the United States entered the war and offering Mexico its lost territory in Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. Britain's Room 40 intercepted and decoded it. To hide the source Britain obtained a copy from the Mexico City telegraph office and gave it to US Ambassador Walter Hines Page on 24 February. President Woodrow Wilson released it to the press on 28 February and it was published on 1 March. Zimmermann confirmed it was genuine on 3 March.
events.why: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917 and expected the United States to join the war within months. A Mexican front would keep American troops at home.
events.then: With U-boats sinking American ships, Wilson asked Congress for war on 2 April and Congress declared it on 6 April 1917. Mexico declined the offer.
events.sig: With U-boats sinking American ships, Wilson asked Congress for war on 2 April and Congress declared it on 6 April 1917. Mexico declined the offer.
events.now: It is one of the most consequential intelligence coups in history, and Britain hid how it had broken the code, a model of protecting sources while using what they reveal.

causes.why: Germany hoped to exploit US-Mexican tension.

q.before: The United States was neutral.
q.how: A secret diplomatic offer, exposed.
q.claim: Germany promised Mexico the lands it lost in 1848.
q.winners: Britain, which wanted America in the war.
q.lasted: Mexico declined; the United States entered the war.

events.bluf: German Foreign Minister Arthur Zimmermann wanted Mexico to tie down the United States if it entered the war that Germany's unrestricted submarine campaign was about to provoke. British codebreakers in Room 40 read his telegram offering Mexico Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, and Britain passed it to Washington while hiding how it had been obtained. Published on 1 March 1917, it turned American opinion, and Congress declared war five weeks later.
events.lens: Intelligence changes wars when it is revealed at the right moment.
events.fact: Many Americans assumed the telegram was a British forgery until Zimmermann himself confirmed it at a press briefing.

kv: from its publication to the US declaration of war

events.what: Tsar abdicated; Bolsheviks seized power in October.
events.why: War losses, food shortages and a discredited autocracy came first. Peasant hunger for land came second. The Provisional Government's decision to stay in the war came third.
events.sig: The Bolsheviks made peace with Germany, won the civil war and founded the USSR in 1922. Under Stalin the state collectivised agriculture, industrialised by force and imprisoned and killed millions.
events.hook: Russia overthrew its tsar, and Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power.
events.story: In February 1917, March in the Western calendar, strikes and bread riots in Petrograd, joined by soldiers, forced Russian Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate. A Provisional Government kept fighting the war while workers' and soldiers' councils, the soviets, competed for power. In October, November in the West, Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin's party seized the capital promising 'peace, land and bread', shut down the elected Constituent Assembly and fought a civil war against its opponents.
events.then: The Bolsheviks made peace with Germany, won the civil war and founded the USSR in 1922. Under Stalin the state collectivised agriculture, industrialised by force and imprisoned and killed millions.
events.now: The 20th century's great ideological struggle, communism against capitalism, starts here, and Russia's later authoritarianism draws on Soviet habits of rule.
events.fact: The 'October Revolution' happened in November by the Western calendar; Russia still used the old Julian calendar.

causes.why: The tsar granted a parliament in 1905 but kept real power; the unresolved conflict exploded in wartime.
Military disasters, food shortages and millions of casualties destroyed support for the tsar.
Lenin adapted Marx's ideas, arguing that a disciplined party could lead a revolution in a mostly peasant country.
The Provisional Government's failures opened the way for the Bolsheviks.

q.before: Tsar Nicholas II, then a Provisional Government.
q.how: Mass revolution in February, then a Bolshevik seizure of power in October.
q.claim: Power to the soviets: 'peace, land and bread'.
q.lasted: The Soviet state lasted until 1991.

events.bluf: Petrograd's workers and soldiers brought down the tsar in March 1917; Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin then set out to take power from the Provisional Government that fought on. The Bolsheviks seized the capital in November, shut the elected assembly and won a civil war. The first communist state produced the century's central ideological conflict, inspired revolutionaries worldwide and became a one-party dictatorship that killed millions.
events.trig: Bread riots and strikes in Petrograd in February 1917; in October, the collapse of the Provisional Government's authority and Lenin's decision to seize power.
events.lens: Revolutions are won by the best-organized minority when the old regime collapses, not necessarily by the most popular movement.

events.what: US declared war on Germany.
events.why: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1917 and sank American ships. The Zimmermann Telegram revealed it had offered Mexico US territory. The United States also had heavy loans to Britain and France at stake.
events.sig: Two million US troops reached France and helped force Germany to seek an armistice.
events.hook: America's entry tipped the Great War and made it a world power.
events.story: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917 and sank American ships. The Zimmermann Telegram, published in March, showed Germany offering Mexico US territory for joining its side. US President Woodrow Wilson asked Congress for war on 2 April, and Congress declared it on 6 April 1917.
events.then: Two million US troops reached France and helped force Germany to seek an armistice.
events.now: American entry decided the war and set the pattern of 1917 to 1945: a United States that intervenes decisively and then argues over whether it should have.

causes.why: German submarine warfare against shipping, and the Zimmermann Telegram's offer to Mexico, brought the US into the war in 1917.
The sinking turned American opinion against Germany.
The telegram's publication pushed Congress toward war.

events.wk: American entry into World War I

q.why: German submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram.
q.stakes: Allied victory and freedom of the seas.
q.decided: Fresh American troops and resources in 1918.
q.cost: About 116,000 American dead.
q.changed: The US became a world power.

events.bluf: US President Woodrow Wilson asked Congress for war to stop German submarine attacks on American ships and, as he put it, to make the world safe for democracy. Two million American troops and American credit tipped the war to the Allies by late 1918. The United States arrived as a decisive power and then rejected the League of Nations, and the argument between engagement and isolation has run through its foreign policy since.
events.lens: Rising powers often enter a war late and decisively, and gain the most from it.
events.fact: The Zimmermann Telegram was intercepted and decoded by British naval intelligence, which passed it to Washington.

kv: US military deaths, about half from disease

events.who: British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour; Zionist leaders
events.hook: Britain promised a 'national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine.
events.what: Britain promised a 'national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine.
events.story: Zionist leaders, among them Chaim Weizmann, had lobbied the British government through the war. On 2 November 1917 British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour wrote to Lord Rothschild declaring British support for 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine, provided nothing was done to prejudice the rights of its 'existing non-Jewish communities', who were about 90 per cent of the population.
events.why: Britain wanted Jewish support for the war in the United States and Russia and a strategic position near the Suez Canal. Zionist lobbying supplied the text.
events.then: Britain ruled Palestine under a League of Nations mandate that incorporated the declaration from 1920.
events.sig: Britain ruled Palestine under a League of Nations mandate that incorporated the declaration from 1920.
events.now: Israelis read the declaration as the first international recognition of Zionism; Palestinians read it as the root of their dispossession. Both readings shape how each side argues its case today.

causes.why: Britain was making overlapping wartime promises about the Ottoman Arab lands to France, to Arab leaders and to Zionists.

q.before: Ottoman rule; Arabs were the large majority in Palestine.
q.how: A letter from the British foreign secretary.
q.claim: British support for a Jewish national home.
q.lasted: It shaped British rule and the conflict that followed.

events.bluf: Britain wanted Jewish support for the war effort and a foothold near the Suez Canal, and Zionist leaders wanted a great power's backing. British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour's letter of 1917 promised a 'national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine and protection of the rights of its other communities, about 90 per cent of the population. Written into Britain's mandate, the two promises pulled against each other, and the conflict between them has run for a century.
events.lens: Promises made to two peoples over the same land store up conflict.
events.fact: The declaration's operative sentence runs to 67 words.

kv: of Palestine's people were Jewish in 1917 (est.)

events.hook: Wilson promised a peace based on self-determination and a League of Nations.
events.what: Wilson promised a peace based on self-determination and a League of Nations.
events.story: The Bolsheviks had published the Allies' secret treaties in November 1917 and called for peace without annexations. US President Woodrow Wilson answered in a speech to Congress on 8 January 1918 with fourteen points: open covenants, freedom of the seas, free trade, disarmament, impartial settlement of colonial claims, the evacuation of occupied territory, self-determination for the peoples of Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire, an independent Poland, and a general association of nations. Britain and France accepted them as a basis for armistice in November 1918 with reservations on the seas and on reparations.
events.why: Wilson wanted to define Allied war aims and answer Bolshevik calls for peace after the Russian Revolution. He also wanted a settlement that would avoid the next war.
events.then: Germany asked for an armistice on the basis of the Fourteen Points in October 1918 and held the Treaty of Versailles a betrayal of them. Egyptian, Korean and Vietnamese petitioners were turned away at Paris in 1919, and the Senate rejected the League in November 1919.
events.sig: Germany asked for an armistice on the basis of the Fourteen Points in October 1918 and held the Treaty of Versailles a betrayal of them. Egyptian, Korean and Vietnamese petitioners were turned away at Paris in 1919, and the Senate rejected the League in November 1919.
events.now: Colonised peoples from Egypt to Korea and Vietnam took up Wilson's language of self-determination in 1919, were refused, and turned to other means; the League of Nations and its successor the UN descend from the fourteenth point.

causes.why: Once in the war, Wilson set out American war aims for the peace.

q.before: Secret treaties and balance-of-power diplomacy.
q.how: A speech setting out war aims.
q.claim: Self-determination and a league of nations.
q.winners: Ideas of self-determination; few of the points were fully applied.
q.lasted: The League was created, but failed.

events.bluf: US President Woodrow Wilson wanted to state Allied war aims that would answer the Bolsheviks' call for a peace without annexations and hold the Allied publics behind the war. On 8 January 1918 he gave Congress fourteen points: open diplomacy, free trade, freedom of the seas, self-determination for Europe's peoples and a League of Nations. Germany sought an armistice on their basis in October 1918, Versailles applied them unevenly, and colonised peoples who had taken up the language of self-determination were refused it.
events.lens: Universal principles applied selectively breed resentment among those left out.
events.fact: French Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau is reported to have remarked that God himself had been content with ten commandments.

events.who: Lenin's Bolshevik government; Germany and its allies
events.hook: Lenin's government gave up a huge slice of the old empire to get out of the war.
events.what: Lenin's government gave up a huge slice of the old empire to get out of the war.
events.story: Signed on 3 March 1918, the treaty took Russia out of World War I. Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic lands, Finland and Ukraine, with about a third of its population and much of its industry and farmland.
events.why: The Bolsheviks needed peace to hold on to power. The army had collapsed.
events.then: Germany moved troops west for a last offensive. The treaty was cancelled after Germany's defeat in November.
events.sig: Germany moved troops west for a last offensive. The treaty was cancelled after Germany's defeat in November.
events.now: Several of the lost lands, from Finland and the Baltic states to Poland, became independent, and Russia's view of them as lost borderlands still shapes its policy.

causes.why: The Bolsheviks had promised peace and paid a heavy price for it.

q.before: The Russian Empire stretched from Poland to the Pacific.
q.how: A peace treaty forced on a defeated government.
q.claim: German victory on the Eastern Front.
q.winners: Germany, briefly; new nations in the longer run.
q.lasted: No: it was annulled after Germany lost the war.

events.bluf: Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin wanted peace at any price to hold power with an army that had dissolved; Germany wanted its eastern troops free for the west. The treaty of 3 March 1918 gave up Poland, the Baltic lands, Finland and Ukraine, with about a third of Russia's population and much of its industry and farmland. Germany got a short-lived eastern empire, and the Bolsheviks showed they would trade land for power.
events.lens: Revolutionary regimes often trade territory for survival, betting that they can recover it later; the Bolsheviks retook much of it within three years.
events.fact: Soviet Foreign Commissar Leon Trotsky's first answer at the talks was 'neither war nor peace'; the Germans resumed their advance and the Bolsheviks signed worse terms.

events.who: The Bolshevik Red Army under Leon Trotsky; White armies; Allied interventions
events.hook: Reds and Whites fought a brutal civil war, which the Bolsheviks won by 1921.
events.what: Reds and Whites fought a brutal civil war, which the Bolsheviks won by 1921.
events.story: From 1918, anti-Bolshevik White armies, nationalist forces and Allied troops fought the Red Army built by War Commissar Leon Trotsky. Fighting, terror on both sides, famine and disease killed perhaps 7 to 12 million people.
events.why: The Bolsheviks' seizure of power came first. Their closing of the elected Constituent Assembly came second.
events.then: The Bolsheviks won through central control, terror and their enemies' disunity, and founded the Soviet Union in 1922.
events.sig: The Bolsheviks won through central control, terror and their enemies' disunity, and founded the Soviet Union in 1922.
events.now: The war shaped the Soviet state's militarised, one-party character, and the Allied intervention fed a Russian narrative of Western hostility that is still invoked.

causes.why: Opponents of Bolshevik rule took up arms.

q.why: Who would rule Russia after the revolution.
q.decided: Red control of the central cities and railways, and divided White leadership.
q.cost: Millions dead from fighting, terror, famine and disease.
q.changed: A one-party communist state was established.

events.bluf: The Bolsheviks fought to hold the state they had seized; White generals, national movements and Allied expeditions fought to remove them. Three years of war, terror on both sides, famine and disease killed perhaps 7 to 12 million people and ended in Bolshevik victory. The Soviet state came out militarised and one-party, with a memory of foreign intervention it has invoked since.
events.lens: Regimes forged in civil war often keep its habits (centralization, terror, secrecy) in peacetime.
events.fact: The Czechoslovak Legion, some 40,000 former prisoners of war trying to leave Russia by the Trans-Siberian Railway, seized the line in 1918 and opened the war in Siberia.

events.what: Fighting stopped on 11 November.
events.why: Germany was exhausted and its allies had collapsed. Revolution was breaking out at home.
events.sig: The German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires fell. New countries followed, among them Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia.
events.hook: At 11 a.m. on 11 November, the guns stopped, and four empires were gone.
events.story: With its army retreating, its allies collapsing and revolution breaking out at home, Germany sent delegates to meet Allied commander Ferdinand Foch in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne. The armistice took effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918.
events.then: The German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires fell. New countries followed, among them Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia.
events.now: An armistice signed with the army still abroad let German nationalists claim from 1919 that it had been stabbed in the back at home; the claim carried the Nazi case against the republic.

causes.why: Fresh American troops and resources tipped the balance on the Western Front in 1918.

q.why: Germany could no longer fight.
q.decided: Allied offensives, the blockade and German collapse at home.
q.cost: About 20 million dead in the war.
q.changed: The fighting stopped; peace terms followed at Versailles.

events.bluf: Germany's high command sought an armistice before the army broke and before revolution at home finished the state; the Allies set terms that made resumption impossible. The guns stopped at 11 am on 11 November 1918 with the German army still on foreign soil. Four empires fell, and the way the war ended let German nationalists claim the army had been stabbed in the back at home.
events.lens: How a war ends shapes the myths that follow: a defeat without invasion can be denied.
events.myth: Germany's army was undefeated in the field. Its high command asked for an armistice in October because the front was giving way under the Allied offensives of August to October.
events.fact: Remembrance Day at 11 am on 11 November marks the hour the guns stopped.

events.story: With White forces approaching Yekaterinburg, the Ural Regional Soviet, with Moscow's approval, had Russian Tsar Nicholas II, Empress Alexandra, their five children and four servants shot in the night of 16-17 July 1918. events.then: Rumours that a daughter, Anastasia, had survived lasted for decades until DNA disproved them.
events.sig: Rumours that a daughter, Anastasia, had survived lasted for decades until DNA disproved them.
events.now: The Russian Orthodox Church canonised the family in 2000, part of post-Soviet Russia's embrace of its tsarist past alongside its Soviet one.

q.how: A secret execution.
q.winners: The Bolsheviks, who removed a possible rallying point.
q.lasted: Yes: the monarchy was never restored.

events.bluf: The Ural Regional Soviet, with Moscow's approval, shot Russian Tsar Nicholas II and his family to deny the approaching Whites a rallying point. Eleven people died in the cellar of the Ipatiev House on the night of 16-17 July 1918. The killing marked the Bolsheviks' readiness to use terror, and the family's canonisation in 2000 marked post-Soviet Russia's recovery of its tsarist past.
events.lens: Revolutionaries kill deposed rulers to remove alternatives, not just to punish them.
events.fact: The remains were reburied in the Peter and Paul Cathedral in St Petersburg in July 1998, with Russian President Boris Yeltsin present.
