events.hook: An influenza pandemic killed tens of millions of people, more than the war itself.
events.what: An influenza pandemic killed tens of millions of people, more than the war itself.
events.story: Influenza spread with troops and ships in 1918, in waves. The deadliest wave struck almost at once in August and September at Brest in France, Freetown in Sierra Leone and Boston. It killed many healthy young adults; estimates of the dead range from about 17 to 50 million or more.
events.why: Crowded camps, troop ships and wartime hunger helped a new flu virus spread.
events.then: It faded by 1920. Many countries built up their public health services.
events.sig: It faded by 1920. Many countries built up their public health services.
events.now: It remains the benchmark for pandemic planning; scientists reconstructed the virus in 2005 to study how pandemics spread.

causes.why: Troop camps and transports spread the flu around the world.

events.fact: It was called 'Spanish' only because neutral Spain's newspapers reported it freely while warring countries censored the news.

q.problem: A new flu that spread fast and killed young adults.
q.how: It spread by coughs in crowded camps and ships; there were no flu vaccines or antibiotics.
q.replaced: Quarantines, masks and closures were the only tools available.
q.spread: Around the world within months.
q.next: Governments created health ministries and disease surveillance.

events.bluf: A new influenza strain spread with the troop movements of 1918 in waves, the second of them lethal to healthy young adults. It killed between about 17 and 50 million people or more, more than the war itself. Governments built up their public health services, and the pandemic remains the benchmark for pandemic planning.
events.lens: Pandemics follow transport networks, and war moves people fastest.

events.h: Last German army in WWI surrenders in Africa
events.what: Lettow-Vorbeck's army surrendered two weeks after the war ended in Europe, undefeated in the field.
events.why: The armistice of 11 November had ended the war, and Lettow-Vorbeck learned of it two weeks late from a captured message.
events.sig: The Allies divided Germany's colonies among themselves as League of Nations mandates. Lettow-Vorbeck was paraded through Berlin in March 1919 as the one undefeated German general.
events.hook: Lettow-Vorbeck's army surrendered two weeks after the war ended in Europe, undefeated in the field.
events.story: German commander Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck's force of German officers and African askari had evaded far larger British forces for four years, living off the land and moving through Mozambique into Northern Rhodesia. He learned of the armistice from a captured British dispatch and surrendered at Abercorn, now Mbala in Zambia, on 25 November 1918, two weeks after the war ended in Europe. His campaign cost hundreds of thousands of African lives, most of them porters and civilians, through disease, famine and forced labour.
events.then: The Allies divided Germany's colonies among themselves as League of Nations mandates. Lettow-Vorbeck was paraded through Berlin in March 1919 as the one undefeated German general.
events.now: The surrender ended German rule in Africa, and the Allies divided the colonies as League of Nations mandates in 1919-22, which drew the borders of today's Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Namibia, Togo and Cameroon.

causes.why: The campaign had dragged on four years.
The war ended in Europe.

q.why: He kept fighting until officially told the war was over.
q.decided: The armistice in Europe.
q.cost: East Africa devastated.
q.changed: German East Africa passed to the Allies.

events.bluf: German commander Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck wanted to keep his force in the field and Allied troops occupied until Germany won in Europe. He learned of the armistice from a captured British dispatch and surrendered at Abercorn in Northern Rhodesia on 25 November 1918, the last German force of the war, unbeaten in battle. Germany made him a hero; the hundreds of thousands of Africans who died carrying his and his enemies' supplies went unrecorded.
events.lens: Military 'heroes' of colonial campaigns are often celebrated without counting the cost to the colonized.
events.fact: His campaign is still taught in military colleges as a model of guerrilla war; the porters who carried it are absent from most of the lessons.

events.hook: British troops fired into a peaceful crowd, killing hundreds, and turned moderates against British rule.
events.what: British troops fired into a peaceful crowd, killing hundreds, and turned moderates against British rule.
events.story: Unrest over the Rowlatt Acts and the arrest of two local leaders had led to riots in Amritsar on 10 April 1919 in which five Europeans were killed. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer banned gatherings. On 13 April, the Baisakhi festival, thousands gathered in Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden with narrow exits. Dyer marched in about 50 riflemen and ordered them to fire without warning; they fired about 1,650 rounds in ten minutes. The official count was 379 dead; Indian estimates ran to around 1,000.
events.why: Unrest over the Rowlatt Acts, which extended wartime detention without trial, came first. Dyer meant to terrorise the Punjab into order, and Punjab Governor Michael O'Dwyer backed him.
events.then: The Hunter Committee censured Dyer in 1920 and he was retired; the House of Lords voted in his favour and a public subscription raised £26,000 for him. Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood. Mohandas Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920, and moderates who had trusted British promises turned to demanding independence.
events.sig: The Hunter Committee censured Dyer in 1920 and he was retired; the House of Lords voted in his favour and a public subscription raised £26,000 for him. Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood. Mohandas Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920, and moderates who had trusted British promises turned to demanding independence.
events.now: The massacre moved Congress from petitioning to mass non-cooperation within a year. Britain has expressed regret, in 1997, 2013 and 2019, and declined a formal apology, which keeps Amritsar central to the argument over how Britain remembers its empire.

q.before: British rule with wartime emergency powers.
q.how: A massacre by troops.
q.winners: No one: it turned Indians against British rule.
q.lasted: It hardened the independence movement.

events.bluf: Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer set out to make an example of a crowd that had defied his ban on gatherings during unrest over the Rowlatt Acts. His troops fired without warning on thousands in Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919, killing 379 by the official count and around 1,000 by Indian estimates. Moderate Indians who had trusted British promises turned to demanding independence, and Gandhi's mass campaign of 1920 had its cause.
events.lens: State violence against a peaceful crowd can destroy a regime's legitimacy in a single afternoon.
events.fact: Udham Singh, who had been in Amritsar in 1919, shot Michael O'Dwyer dead in London in 1940.

events.what: Germany's colony was handed to Britain as 'Tanganyika', with Rwanda and Burundi going to Belgium.
events.why: The Allies wanted the colonies, and US President Woodrow Wilson's principles obliged them to call the arrangement trusteeship under League oversight.
events.sig: Tanganyika became a UN trust territory in 1946, which gave its nationalists a hearing in New York. Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere's party used that forum on the road to independence in 1961.
events.hook: Germany's colony was handed to Britain as 'Tanganyika', with Rwanda and Burundi going to Belgium.
events.story: The Treaty of Versailles of 1919 stripped Germany of its colonies. Britain received most of German East Africa as a League of Nations mandate, renamed Tanganyika, with the mandate formally conferred in 1922. Belgium received Ruanda-Urundi. Britain ruled through chiefs under 'indirect rule' with far less white settlement than in Kenya.
events.then: Tanganyika became a UN trust territory in 1946, which gave its nationalists a hearing in New York. Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere's party used that forum on the road to independence in 1961.
events.now: The mandate's borders are today's Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi, and the idea of international trusteeship shaped the UN's later push for decolonisation.

causes.why: Germany lost its colonies.
Versailles stripped Germany of colonies.

q.before: German rule.
q.how: British rule under League supervision.
q.claim: 'A sacred trust of civilization' to prepare people for self-rule.
q.lasted: Tanganyika became independent in 1961.

events.bluf: The Allies wanted Germany's colonies and US President Woodrow Wilson wanted them held in trust rather than annexed. The Treaty of Versailles gave most of German East Africa to Britain as a League of Nations mandate, confirmed in 1922, and Ruanda-Urundi to Belgium. The mandate was colonial rule in practice, and its reporting duty to the League, then the UN, gave Tanganyikans an international forum they used to press for independence by 1961.
events.lens: Even weak international oversight gives colonized people a platform.
events.fact: Germany's East African colony had been larger than Germany itself.

events.what: Mass protest against Versailles treaty.
events.why: The Versailles conference handed Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan rather than back to China, which had joined the Allies and sent 140,000 labourers to the Western Front. Japan's Twenty-One Demands of 1915 had already made it the target of Chinese nationalism.
events.sig: The movement spread new ideas of science, democracy and writing in everyday Chinese. Veterans of it founded the Chinese Communist Party in 1921.
events.hook: Students protested in Beijing, and modern Chinese nationalism was born.
events.story: On 4 May 1919 about 3,000 students marched in Beijing against the decision at Versailles to hand Germany's rights in Shandong province to Japan. Strikes and boycotts of Japanese goods spread to other cities, and China's delegation declined to sign the treaty. The movement became a wider call for science, democracy and a new culture.
events.then: The movement spread new ideas of science, democracy and writing in everyday Chinese. Veterans of it founded the Chinese Communist Party in 1921.
events.now: The movement moved the reform generation from faith in Western liberalism to nationalism and, for leaders such as Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, to Marxism, which produced the Communist Party in 1921. Communists, Nationalists and liberals all claim its legacy.

causes.why: The new republic collapsed into warlord rule. When the Versailles conference gave Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan, students rose in protest.
News that the Allies had handed Shandong to Japan, not back to China, sparked the protests of May 4, 1919.

q.idea: China needed 'Mr Science and Mr Democracy' to survive.
q.spread: Student unions, new magazines and strikes.
q.enabled: Chinese nationalism and the Communist Party.

events.bluf: Beijing students set out to stop their government accepting the Versailles decision that gave Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan. About 3,000 marched on 4 May 1919; strikes and boycotts spread across the cities, and China's delegates withheld their signature from the treaty. The movement turned a generation of Western-educated reformers toward nationalism and, for some, toward Marxism, and its veterans founded the Chinese Communist Party in 1921.
events.lens: Betrayal by Western powers drove many Asian nationalists toward communism.
events.fact: China marks 4 May as Youth Day.

events.what: Harsh peace terms imposed on Germany.
events.why: France, invaded twice in 50 years, wanted security and reparations. Britain wanted German naval and colonial power curbed. US President Woodrow Wilson wanted a League of Nations and self-determination. The compromise satisfied no one.
events.sig: Germans called it a 'dictated peace'. The US Senate rejected it, reparations were repeatedly rescheduled and largely unpaid, and Britain and France failed to enforce its limits when Hitler rearmed.
events.hook: A harsh peace punished Germany, and planted the seeds of the next war.
events.story: Signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the treaty blamed Germany for the war, took its colonies and about 13 per cent of its European territory, limited its army to 100,000 men and required reparations later set at 132 billion gold marks.
events.then: Germans called it a 'dictated peace'. The US Senate rejected it, reparations were repeatedly rescheduled and largely unpaid, and Britain and France failed to enforce its limits when Hitler rearmed.
events.now: The treaty's terms fixed German politics for twenty years: every party demanded revision, the republic that signed it carried the blame, and the settlement was harsh enough to be hated and too weakly enforced to prevent rearmament. The 1945 settlement was designed as its opposite.
events.fact: It was signed in the Hall of Mirrors, where Germany had proclaimed its empire in 1871, on the fifth anniversary of Franz Ferdinand's assassination.

causes.why: The victors met in Paris to impose terms on Germany and redraw Europe's map.
Germany asked for an armistice on the basis of the Fourteen Points; the treaty fell well short of them.

q.before: Germany was a defeated great power.
q.how: A treaty dictated by the victors.
q.winners: France, Britain and new states like Poland.
q.lasted: Hitler tore it up in the 1930s.

events.bluf: French Premier Georges Clemenceau wanted security against Germany, British Prime Minister David Lloyd George wanted its navy and colonies gone, and US President Woodrow Wilson wanted a League of Nations. The treaty they signed on 28 June 1919 blamed Germany for the war, took its colonies and about 13 per cent of its European territory, capped its army at 100,000 and set reparations. Harsh enough to be hated and too weakly enforced to hold, it fixed German politics on revision for twenty years.

events.h: Senate rejects the Treaty of Versailles
events.who: The Senate (Henry Cabot Lodge); Woodrow Wilson
events.hook: America designed the League of Nations, then refused to join it.
events.what: America designed the League of Nations, then refused to join it.
events.story: President Woodrow Wilson returned from Paris in July 1919 with a treaty that bound members of the League to defend one another's territory under Article X. Massachusetts Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, drafted fourteen reservations, chief among them that Congress alone could commit the United States to action. Wilson toured the country for the treaty in September, collapsed and suffered a stroke on 2 October 1919 that left him an invalid. The Senate rejected the treaty with reservations and without them on 19 November 1919, and a final vote on 19 March 1920 fell seven short of two thirds.
events.why: Fear of foreign entanglements, party rivalry after the Republicans won Congress in 1918, and Wilson's refusal to compromise, worsened by his stroke. Lodge and Wilson detested each other.
events.then: The United States made a separate peace with Germany in 1921 and stayed out of the League, which failed to stop Japan in Manchuria in 1931 or Italy in Ethiopia in 1935. The United Nations of 1945 was designed with the United States at its centre and a veto for the great powers.
events.sig: The United States made a separate peace with Germany in 1921 and stayed out of the League, which failed to stop Japan in Manchuria in 1931 or Italy in Ethiopia in 1935. The United Nations of 1945 was designed with the United States at its centre and a veto for the great powers.
events.now: The UN, founded in 1945 with the US at its centre, was designed to avoid the League's mistakes.

causes.why: The US Senate refused to ratify the treaty, keeping the US out of Wilson's own League of Nations.

q.before: Wilson wanted the US to lead the League of Nations.
q.how: Senate votes against ratification.
q.lasted: The US never joined the League.

events.bluf: President Woodrow Wilson wanted the Senate to ratify the Treaty of Versailles and the League of Nations covenant without changes; Republicans under Massachusetts Senator Henry Cabot Lodge demanded reservations to keep Congress's power to decide on war. Wilson refused every reservation, suffered a stroke in October 1919 and ordered his party to vote against Lodge's version. The treaty failed in November 1919 and March 1920, the United States stayed out of the League it had designed, and the League faced the aggressions of the 1930s without it.
events.lens: International institutions are only as strong as the great powers willing to back them.
events.fact: Wilson's wife Edith screened every paper that reached him for the rest of his term, and the extent of his incapacity was hidden from the public.

events.who: Woodrow Wilson's idea; 42 founding member states
events.hook: The first worldwide organisation for keeping the peace opened, without the United States.
events.what: The first worldwide organisation for keeping the peace opened, without the United States.
events.story: Created by the Treaty of Versailles, the League came into being on 10 January 1920. It settled some small disputes and ran mandates and refugee work. The US never joined, and the League could not stop Japan, Italy or Germany in the 1930s.
events.why: Horror at the slaughter of World War I came first. US President Woodrow Wilson's belief that open diplomacy and collective security could replace the balance of power came second.
events.then: Japan and Germany left in 1933 and Italy in 1937, and the League could not stop the aggressions that led to World War II.
events.sig: Japan and Germany left in 1933 and Italy in 1937, and the League could not stop the aggressions that led to World War II.
events.now: The United Nations replaced it in 1945-46, with a Security Council where the great powers hold vetoes, designed to keep them inside the system that the League had lost.

q.how: An international body based on collective security.
q.claim: That states would act together against any aggressor.
q.winners: Smaller states gained a forum; great powers ignored it when they chose.

events.bluf: US President Woodrow Wilson wanted a permanent body in which open diplomacy and collective security replaced the balance of power. The League came into being in January 1920 with 42 members and without the United States. It settled small disputes and ran mandates and refugee work, failed against Japan, Italy and Germany in the 1930s, and its failures shaped the design of the United Nations.
events.lens: Collective security works only if the strongest members are willing to act.
events.fact: The United States, whose president designed it, never joined; the Senate rejected the treaty in November 1919 and again in March 1920.

events.who: Suffragists: Alice Paul, Carrie Chapman Catt
events.what: Women gained the right to vote.
events.why: Seven decades of organisation gave the movement lawyers, lobbyists and a press. Western states from Wyoming onward had shown women voting without disorder. Women's war work made the denial of the vote harder to defend.
events.sig: Women's votes split along the same lines as men's rather than forming the bloc both parties expected. Southern states kept Black women from the polls through poll taxes, literacy tests and intimidation until the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The League of Women Voters, founded in 1920, took up the work of registering and informing new voters.
events.hook: After 72 years of struggle, American women won the right to vote.
events.story: The campaign for women's votes dated from the Seneca Falls convention of 1848, and several Western states, Wyoming first, already let women vote. National Woman's Party founder Alice Paul led pickets outside the White House and hunger strikes in prison; National American Woman Suffrage Association president Carrie Chapman Catt lobbied state by state. Women's work in the war industries of 1917-18 widened support. Congress passed the amendment in 1919 and Tennessee's ratification completed it in August 1920.
events.then: Women's votes split along the same lines as men's rather than forming the bloc both parties expected. Southern states kept Black women from the polls through poll taxes, literacy tests and intimidation until the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The League of Women Voters, founded in 1920, took up the work of registering and informing new voters.
events.now: Women now vote at higher rates than men in US elections, and the gender gap between the parties has become one of the largest divides in American politics.
events.fact: Tennessee ratified by a single vote: legislator Harry Burn switched after a letter from his mother.

events.bluf: American suffragists, led by National Woman's Party founder Alice Paul and National American Woman Suffrage Association president Carrie Chapman Catt, set out to win the vote for women by constitutional amendment after 72 years of campaigning. The 19th Amendment was ratified in August 1920 and roughly doubled the electorate. It joined a wave of women's enfranchisement after the First World War; Black women in the South stayed largely barred from the polls until 1965.
events.lens: Rights movements win in stages, and often at first only for some members of the group.

events.story: A nationwide revolt in 1919, led by Egyptian nationalist Saad Zaghloul's Wafd party, made British rule costly. On 28 February 1922 Britain declared Egypt independent. Egypt got a king, Fuad I, and a parliament. Britain kept control of defence, Sudan, the Suez Canal and the protection of foreign interests.

events.now: Egypt's limited independence, with Britain keeping defence and Suez, set up the grievances that led to the 1952 revolution and Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser's Arab nationalism.

events.bluf: Britain wanted to end a nationwide revolt without giving up the Suez Canal, Sudan or Egypt's defence; Egyptian nationalist Saad Zaghloul's Wafd wanted full independence. Britain declared Egypt independent in 1922 and kept the four matters it cared about. The half-measure satisfied no one, and 30 years of frustrated nationalism ended in the revolution of 1952 and Nasser's Arab nationalism.
events.lens: Half-independence breeds full-scale nationalism: a foreign power that keeps the key levers becomes the target of every grievance.

events.now: Fascism remains the benchmark for movements that use democratic institutions to win power and then dismantle them, and arguments over the label run through politics today.

events.hook: Atatürk built a secular Turkish republic from the Ottoman ruins.
events.story: After the Ottoman defeat the Allies planned to partition Anatolia under the Treaty of Sèvres of 1920. events.now: Atatürk's image is still everywhere in Turkey, and its politics since the 2000s under Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan have been partly a contest over his secular legacy.

events.bluf: Turkish nationalist leader Mustafa Kemal set out to build a secular nation-state from the Ottoman ruins and to keep Anatolia out of Allied hands. He won the war of independence, proclaimed the republic in 1923 and abolished the sultanate and the caliphate, Islamic law and the Arabic script. Turkey became the model of top-down modernisation in the Muslim world, and the suppression of religious and Kurdish identities that came with it still shapes its politics.
events.lens: Top-down modernization can transform a society quickly but leaves suppressed identities that return later.

events.what: The Allies recognised the new Turkey, replacing the far harsher Treaty of Sèvres.
events.story: Turkish nationalists under Mustafa Kemal had won their war against Greece in 1922. Turkey's negotiator İsmet Pasha, later İsmet İnönü, faced the Allied powers at Lausanne. The treaty signed on 24 July 1923 set Turkey's borders and ended Allied claims in Anatolia. An agreement reached during the talks arranged a population exchange: about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians left Turkey and about 400,000 Muslims left Greece.
events.why: Turkey had won on the ground and the Allies had no appetite for another war. Both sides accepted the exchange as the price of a stable frontier.
events.then: The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed three months later. The exchange uprooted communities that had lived together for centuries.
events.sig: The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed three months later. The exchange uprooted communities that had lived together for centuries.
events.now: Lausanne's borders still define Turkey, and its silence on Kurdish self-rule is the root of the Kurdish question in Turkey, Iraq and Syria.

q.winners: Kemal's Turkey; Greek and Armenian hopes in Anatolia were lost.

Lausanne gave Turkey its borders and sovereignty and endorsed a compulsory exchange of about 1.6 million Greeks and Turks. Modern Turkey's frontiers date from it, and so does the practice of unmixing peoples by treaty.
events.lens: Military victory can overturn a treaty imposed in defeat: Turkey replaced Sèvres by winning a war.
events.fact: The exchange ran by religion, so Turkish-speaking Christians of Anatolia went to Greece and Greek-speaking Muslims of Crete went to Turkey.

events.what: Germany's money collapsed: by November 1923 one US dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks.
events.story: Printing money to pay its bills and to support workers resisting the French occupation of the Ruhr, the German government lost control of prices. Prices doubled every few days, workers were paid twice a day, and savings were wiped out. By November 1923 one US dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks.

events.sig: A new currency, the Rentenmark, ended it in late 1923. The middle class kept the memory.

Prices lost all meaning by the autumn of 1923, and middle-class savings vanished. The Rentenmark ended it in November, and a German fear of inflation that shaped policy and the design of the European Central Bank dates from it.
events.lens: Wiping out the middle class's savings destroys its faith in the political system.
events.fact: Workers spent their pay at midday before prices rose again, and banknotes were used as wallpaper and fuel.

events.what: Turkey's parliament abolished the caliphate, the office that had claimed leadership of the Muslim world for 1,300 years.
events.story: The sultanate had been abolished in 1922 and the caliphate left to the last caliph, Abdulmejid II, as a religious office. On 3 March 1924 Turkey's Grand National Assembly abolished the caliphate and exiled the Ottoman family. Religious courts and schools were closed. Over the following years Turkey adopted European law codes, the Latin alphabet and votes for women.
events.why: Mustafa Kemal saw the caliphate as a rival centre of power and an obstacle to a secular state.
events.then: Attempts to revive the caliphate elsewhere came to nothing. Turkey's secularisation went further, banning religious dress for officials and replacing the Arabic script.
events.sig: Attempts to revive the caliphate elsewhere came to nothing. Turkey's secularisation went further, banning religious dress for officials and replacing the Arabic script.
events.now: Islamist movements, including ISIS in 2014, have claimed to restore the caliphate; its absence is part of the argument they make.

events.bluf: Mustafa Kemal wanted no rival centre of authority in the new republic, and the caliphate was the last one. Turkey's Grand National Assembly abolished it on 3 March 1924 and exiled the Ottoman family. An office that had claimed leadership of the Muslim world since the 7th century ended, and the vacuum it left has been claimed by Islamist movements ever since.
events.lens: Abolishing a symbol does not abolish the yearning for it: the empty office became a goal for later movements.
events.fact: Abdulmejid II, a painter, died in exile in Paris in 1944 and was buried in Medina.

events.what: Won the power struggle after Lenin died.

events.sig: Forced collectivisation, famine and purges killed millions. The USSR also industrialised fast.
events.hook: Stalin outmaneuvered rivals and became the Soviet Union's dictator.
events.story: After Lenin died in January 1924, Joseph Stalin used his post as the party's General Secretary to fill it with loyalists. He allied with rivals to defeat Leon Trotsky, then turned on them; by 1929 he was undisputed leader.
events.then: Forced collectivisation, famine and purges killed millions. The USSR also industrialised fast.
events.now: Russia's ambivalence about Stalin, as victor in World War II and as mass murderer, and Ukraine's memory of the Holodomor are both rooted in his rule.

q.how: Control of the party machine.

events.bluf: Joseph Stalin set out to succeed Lenin by controlling the party's appointments rather than winning its arguments. By 1929 he had used the General Secretary's office to defeat Leon Trotsky and every other rival. He turned the Soviet Union into a personal dictatorship that industrialised by force at the cost of famine, terror and millions of deaths, and built the state that beat Germany in 1945.
events.lens: Control of appointments can matter more than charisma: the bureaucrat can beat the revolutionary hero.
events.fact: Lenin's last testament asked the party to remove Stalin as General Secretary; it was read to delegates and then suppressed.

events.who: Teacher John Scopes; lawyer Clarence Darrow; prosecutor William Jennings Bryan
events.hook: A Tennessee teacher was tried for teaching evolution, in a trial followed across the country.
events.what: A Tennessee teacher was tried for teaching evolution, in a trial followed across the country.
events.story: Tennessee's Butler Act of March 1925 banned the teaching of human evolution in public schools. The American Civil Liberties Union offered to defend any teacher who broke it, and Dayton teacher John Scopes agreed to be charged. In July 1925 defence lawyer Clarence Darrow faced prosecutor William Jennings Bryan, three times a Democratic candidate for president, and called him to the stand as an expert on the Bible. Scopes was found guilty and fined $100. The Tennessee Supreme Court overturned the fine in 1927 on a technicality and declined to rule on the law.
events.why: Fundamentalist Protestants held that evolution undermined the Bible and public morality, and had won laws in several states. The ACLU wanted a case that would reach the Supreme Court. Dayton's businessmen wanted the attention.
events.then: Bryan died in Dayton five days after the verdict. The law stayed on the books until 1967. In 1968 the Supreme Court struck down Arkansas's similar ban in Epperson v. Arkansas.
events.sig: Bryan died in Dayton five days after the verdict. The law stayed on the books until 1967. In 1968 the Supreme Court struck down Arkansas's similar ban in Epperson v. Arkansas.
events.now: Arguments over teaching evolution continue in some US states and have broadened into fights over what schools may teach about religion, race and sexuality.

causes.why: Sixty years on, evolution was still contested in American schools.

q.belief: Whether teaching evolution undermined the Bible.
q.authority: State legislatures and the courts.
q.believers: Many rural Americans supported the ban.
q.fallout: Fundamentalists were mocked in the national press.
q.today: Evolution is taught in US public schools, though controversy lingers.

events.bluf: The American Civil Liberties Union wanted a test case against Tennessee's new ban on teaching human evolution, and Dayton teacher John Scopes agreed to be it. He was convicted and fined $100, a verdict overturned on a technicality, and the law stood for another 42 years. The trial, carried live on radio, made the contest between fundamentalist Protestantism and modern science a permanent fixture of American politics.
events.lens: Culture-war trials are fought for public opinion more than for verdicts.
events.fact: The trial was the first in the United States broadcast live on radio, by WGN of Chicago.

events.hook: Lindbergh flew alone, non-stop from New York to Paris, in 33 and a half hours.
events.what: Lindbergh flew alone, non-stop from New York to Paris, in 33 and a half hours.
events.story: American aviator Charles Lindbergh took off from Roosevelt Field on 20 May 1927 in the Spirit of St. Louis and landed at Le Bourget the next evening before a crowd of tens of thousands. He won a $25,000 prize.
events.why: Hotelier Raymond Orteig had offered a prize for the first non-stop flight between New York and Paris.
events.then: Interest in flying boomed, investment in aviation surged, and airlines began carrying passengers across the United States.
events.sig: Interest in flying boomed, investment in aviation surged, and airlines began carrying passengers across the United States.
events.now: Lindbergh later led the 'America First' campaign against entering World War II, making him a symbol of America's prewar debate over intervention.

causes.why: Rapid improvements in engines and aircraft made ocean crossings possible.

q.problem: Flying non-stop across the Atlantic.
q.how: A single-engine plane carrying extra fuel instead of a co-pilot.
q.replaced: In time, week-long ocean liner crossings.
q.spread: Regular passenger flights across the Atlantic began in 1939.
q.next: The age of long-distance air travel.

events.bluf: American aviator Charles Lindbergh flew alone from New York to Paris to win the $25,000 Orteig Prize for the first non-stop flight between the two cities. He landed at Le Bourget on 21 May 1927 after 33 and a half hours before a crowd of tens of thousands. Aviation became a mass enthusiasm, investment poured into airlines, and the oceans stopped guaranteeing distance between continents.
events.lens: Celebrated feats can trigger investment booms in new technologies.
events.fact: Lindbergh carried no radio and no parachute, and saw ahead through a periscope because the fuel tank blocked the windscreen.

events.who: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists vs. Mao's Communists
events.what: Nationalists purged Communist allies.

events.then: The war paused in 1937 for an uneasy alliance against Japan, resumed in 1946 and ended with Communist victory in 1949.
events.now: It is why there are two Chinese governments today, in Beijing and Taipei, and the unfinished civil war is the root of the Taiwan question.

events.bluf: Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek set out to destroy his Communist allies before they could take over the united front that was reconquering China from the warlords. On 12 April 1927 his forces and Shanghai gangsters killed thousands of Communists and unionists in the city. The Communists fled to the countryside, and a civil war began that paused for the Japanese invasion and ended in 1949 with Communists in Beijing and Nationalists in Taipei.
events.lens: Allies of convenience often turn on each other once their common enemy is weakened.
events.fact: The Communist uprising at Nanchang on 1 August 1927, four months after the purge, is counted as the founding of the People's Liberation Army.

events.what: Market collapsed on 'Black Tuesday'.
events.why: Buying on borrowed money had pushed prices far above earnings. Weak bank regulation let failures spread. Overproduction in farming and industry, and the war debts and reparations that distorted world payments, made the slump deeper and wider.
events.sig: The Federal Reserve let the money supply shrink and thousands of banks fail. Governments raised tariffs and defended the gold standard, which spread the slump worldwide. By 1933 a quarter of American workers were unemployed, and mass unemployment in Germany fed the Nazi vote.
events.hook: Black Tuesday wiped out fortunes and began the Great Depression.
events.story: Stock prices rose through the 1920s, much of the buying financed by brokers' loans. On 'Black Thursday', 24 October 1929, and 'Black Tuesday', 29 October, prices collapsed on record volumes. President Herbert Hoover assured the country that business was sound. Over the next three years thousands of banks failed and the economy shrank by about a quarter.
events.then: The Federal Reserve let the money supply shrink and thousands of banks fail. Governments raised tariffs and defended the gold standard, which spread the slump worldwide. By 1933 a quarter of American workers were unemployed, and mass unemployment in Germany fed the Nazi vote.
events.now: It led to deposit insurance and stock market rules still in force, and its lessons (save the banks, keep spending up) shaped responses to the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic.
events.fact: Shoeshine boys giving stock tips were a famous warning sign that the bubble had gone too far.

causes.why: Mass production and consumer credit fuelled the 1920s boom that ended in the crash.

q.what: Shares bought largely on borrowed money.
q.who: Investors and then ordinary workers lost.
q.scale: Stock prices fell about 89% by 1932.
q.daily: Unemployment reached 25%.
q.system: The Great Depression.

events.bluf: Investors had bid stocks up on borrowed money through the 1920s in the expectation that prices would keep rising. In October 1929 prices collapsed, and the losses, through margin calls, bank failures and policy errors, became the Great Depression: output shrank by about a quarter and a quarter of workers were idle by 1933. The slump discredited unmanaged capitalism, produced the New Deal and fed the rise of extremists in Europe.
events.trig: Panic selling on 'Black Thursday', 24 October, and 'Black Tuesday', 29 October 1929.
events.lens: Crashes become depressions when policymakers let the financial system collapse and cut spending.

events.story: The Depression collapsed coffee prices in 1929, and São Paulo's candidate, Júlio Prestes, won the March 1930 presidential election. Getúlio Vargas, the losing candidate, led a revolt from the south in October 1930 and took power. He imposed the Estado Novo dictatorship in 1937. His government created a minimum wage in 1940, a labour code in 1943 and a national steel company.
events.then: The army removed Vargas in October 1945. He won the presidency in 1950 and founded the oil company Petrobras in 1953. Facing a military ultimatum, he shot himself in the presidential palace on 24 August 1954.
events.now: Vargas built the Brazilian state that still exists: labour law, state industry, a centralised bureaucracy and a politics of the urban poor; his model governed Brazil through dictatorship and democracy alike.

causes.why: The collapse of coffee prices broke the power of Brazil's old ruling elites; Vargas took power in a revolt in 1930.

q.before: Rule by the coffee elites of São Paulo and Minas Gerais.
q.how: A revolt, then a dictatorship.
q.lasted: He ruled 1930-45 and again 1951-54.

events.bluf: Rio Grande do Sul Governor Getúlio Vargas led a revolt in 1930 after the Depression wrecked coffee prices and he lost a disputed election. He took power, ruled for 15 years, as dictator from 1937, and built a centralised state with steel mills, labour law and a minimum wage. His model of state-led industry and appeal to urban workers governed Brazil through dictatorship and democracy alike.
events.lens: Economic crisis in commodity-exporting countries often brings state-led industrialization and populism.
events.fact: He is remembered as 'the father of the poor', and his suicide letter ends 'I leave life to enter history'.

events.who: Senator Reed Smoot; Representative Willis Hawley; President Herbert Hoover
events.hook: The US raised tariffs on thousands of imports, other countries retaliated, and world trade shrank.
events.what: The US raised tariffs on thousands of imports, other countries retaliated, and world trade shrank.
events.story: Farm prices had fallen through the 1920s. Utah Senator Reed Smoot and Oregon Representative Willis Hawley sponsored a bill to raise farm tariffs, and industries added their own products as it moved through Congress. President Herbert Hoover signed it on 17 June 1930 despite a petition signed by 1,028 teachers of economics. It raised duties on more than 20,000 goods. Canada, European countries and others retaliated, and world trade fell by about two-thirds between 1929 and 1934.
events.why: Farm prices had collapsed and Hoover had promised farmers relief. Once the bill was in Congress, every industry with a lobbyist asked for its own protection, and vote-trading carried the whole.
events.then: Canada raised its own tariffs within months and signed preferential trade deals with Britain in 1932. The Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934 let the president negotiate tariff cuts with other countries, which moved trade policy from Congress to the executive for the rest of the century.
events.sig: Canada raised its own tariffs within months and signed preferential trade deals with Britain in 1932. The Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934 let the president negotiate tariff cuts with other countries, which moved trade policy from Congress to the executive for the rest of the century.
events.now: It is invoked in every debate over tariffs, including the sweeping US tariffs of 2025, as a warning of retaliation and shrinking trade.

causes.why: As the economy fell, Congress tried to protect American producers.

q.what: Duties on imported goods, from farm produce to manufactures.
q.who: Protected producers gained briefly; exporters and consumers paid.
q.scale: Duties on taxed imports rose to around half their value.
q.daily: Fewer imports, and lost export markets for American farmers.
q.system: A wave of trade wars that deepened the Depression.

events.bluf: Utah Senator Reed Smoot and Oregon Representative Willis Hawley set out to protect American farmers, and then every industry with a lobbyist, with higher duties. President Herbert Hoover signed the act in June 1930 over a petition from 1,028 teachers of economics; Canada and European governments retaliated, and world trade fell by about two-thirds between 1929 and 1934. The act became the standard warning against protectionism and the reason Congress handed tariff-making to the president in 1934.
events.lens: Tariffs invite retaliation, and in a downturn everyone protecting themselves can make everyone poorer.
events.myth: Smoot-Hawley caused the Great Depression. The slump was a year old when Hoover signed; one reading holds the tariff deepened it through retaliation, the other holds that trade was too small a share of output to matter beside the banking collapse.
events.fact: Both sponsors lost their seats in the 1932 election.

events.what: 240-mile march to make salt illegally.
events.why: Gandhi chose the salt tax as a simple injustice that every Indian understood. Congress had resolved on full independence at Lahore in December 1929 and needed a campaign.
events.sig: More than 60,000 people were arrested, Gandhi among them in May. Viceroy Lord Irwin negotiated the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931, and Gandhi attended the Round Table Conference in London that year as Congress's sole delegate.
events.hook: Gandhi walked 240 miles to make salt, and shook the British Empire.
events.story: On 12 March 1930 Mohandas Gandhi set out from Sabarmati ashram near Ahmedabad with 78 followers and walked about 385 km (240 miles) to the sea at Dandi. On 6 April he picked up a lump of natural salt, breaking the law that made salt a government monopoly. Millions followed by making or buying illegal salt, boycotting British cloth and refusing taxes. At the Dharasana salt works in May police beat unresisting marchers, and American journalist Webb Miller's report reached newspapers worldwide.
events.then: More than 60,000 people were arrested, Gandhi among them in May. Viceroy Lord Irwin negotiated the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931, and Gandhi attended the Round Table Conference in London that year as Congress's sole delegate.
events.now: The march made non-violent mass disobedience the method of the Indian movement to 1947 and the template Martin Luther King Jr. and later movements adopted.
events.fact: Time magazine named Gandhi its Man of the Year for 1930.

causes.why: Gandhi turned the Congress from an elite debating society into a mass movement of civil disobedience.
The massacre turned Gandhi and millions of moderates against British rule; mass non-cooperation began in 1920.

q.before: British rule, taxing a basic necessity.
q.how: Nonviolent civil disobedience.
q.lasted: India won independence in 1947.

events.bluf: Mohandas Gandhi chose the salt tax, which every Indian paid, as the issue on which to launch civil disobedience against British rule. He walked 240 miles to the sea at Dandi and broke the salt law on 6 April 1930; millions followed with illegal salt, cloth boycotts and tax refusal, and more than 60,000 were jailed. Indian independence became a mass movement, and Britain negotiated with Gandhi as an equal in 1931.
events.lens: Pick a grievance everyone understands, and nonviolent protest can expose a regime's injustice.

events.who: Chancellor Heinrich Brüning; President Paul von Hindenburg
events.hook: American loans stopped, unemployment doubled, and in the September 1930 election the Nazis went from 12 seats to 107.
events.what: American loans stopped, unemployment doubled, and in the September 1930 election the Nazis went from 12 seats to 107.
events.story: Germany's recovery after 1924 ran on short-term American credit. After the 1929 crash the loans were called in; unemployment rose from 1.3 million in 1929 to 3 million by September 1930 and 6 million by early 1932. German Chancellor Heinrich Brüning governed by presidential decree from July 1930 with the backing of President Paul von Hindenburg and cut wages and benefits to defend the currency. On 14 September 1930 the NSDAP took 18.3 per cent of the vote, up from 2.6 per cent in 1928.
events.why: German recovery after the 1924 Dawes Plan was financed by short-term loans from New York, and when the crash called them in German banks and employers had no reserve. Brüning's answer, deflation by presidential decree, deepened the slump to protect the currency and the reparations settlement.
events.then: Deflation continued into 1932 and unemployment reached 6 million. The Reichstag was bypassed by decree. The NSDAP took 37.3 per cent in July 1932.
events.sig: Deflation continued into 1932 and unemployment reached 6 million. The Reichstag was bypassed by decree. The NSDAP took 37.3 per cent in July 1932.
events.now: Germany's political collapse was deflationary, in 1930-32, which is why German policy since 1949 fears both inflation and mass unemployment and why the European Central Bank's mandate was written the way it was.

q.before: The 'golden twenties' after the 1924 Dawes Plan, financed from New York.
q.how: Credit withdrawal, then austerity by decree.
q.claim: Brüning's: the currency and the reparations settlement came first.
q.winners: The parties of the extremes; the NSDAP above all.
q.lasted: Until the Nazi state spent its way out after 1933.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Heinrich Brüning set out to ride out the Depression by deflation, defending the currency and the reparations settlement while American credit drained away. Unemployment rose from 1.3 million in 1929 to 6 million by early 1932 and the Reichstag was bypassed by decree. The slump turned the Nazi party from a 2.6 per cent fringe into the second party in Germany within a year and hollowed out parliamentary government before Hitler touched it.
events.trig: Unemployment passed 3 million in September 1930; on 14 September the NSDAP won 107 seats, up from 12.
events.lens: The vote for the extremes tracked the dole queue, month by month.
events.fact: Brüning earned the nickname 'Hunger Chancellor'; he later said he had been a hundred metres from the finish when Hindenburg dismissed him in May 1932.

events.what: Set up puppet state Manchukuo.
events.why: Army officers wanted Manchuria's land, coal and iron and a buffer against the Soviet Union. The Depression had cut Japan's exports and discredited party government. The cabinet in Tokyo lacked the authority to stop its own army.
events.sig: The League of Nations condemned the invasion, and Japan left the League in 1933. The army's success emboldened militarists at home.
events.hook: Japan's army staged a bombing to seize Manchuria.
events.story: On 18 September 1931 Kwantung Army staff officers Ishiwara Kanji and Itagaki Seishirō had a small bomb set off on a railway near Mukden and blamed Chinese troops. The Japanese army then occupied all of Manchuria and in 1932 set up the puppet state of Manchukuo with the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as its head.
events.then: The League of Nations condemned the invasion, and Japan left the League in 1933. The army's success emboldened militarists at home.
events.now: The seizure showed between 1931 and 1933 that the League could not stop a great power, and it moved control of Japan's foreign policy from the cabinet to the army, the first step toward the war with China in 1937 and the Pacific war of 1941.

causes.why: A China divided among warlords could not resist when Japanese officers staged the Mukden Incident in 1931.
The Depression hit Japanese farmers and exporters hard and strengthened militarists who saw Manchuria as an economic lifeline.
Korea gave Japan a land bridge to Manchuria, where its Kwantung Army guarded the railway won from Russia in 1905.

q.why: Japan's army wanted Manchuria's resources.
q.decided: Japanese military power and Chinese weakness.
q.cost: Thousands of Chinese troops and civilians killed.
q.changed: Japan left the League of Nations.

events.bluf: Officers of Japan's Kwantung Army set out to seize Manchuria's land and resources without waiting for Tokyo's approval. They blew up a section of their own railway near Mukden on 18 September 1931, blamed Chinese troops and occupied the whole region within months; in 1932 they installed the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as head of the puppet state of Manchukuo. The League of Nations condemned the seizure and Japan left the League; the army had taken control of Japanese foreign policy, and the lesson that aggression paid travelled to Europe.
events.lens: When a military acts without civilian control and is rewarded, it will do so again.
events.fact: The explosion did so little damage that a train passed over the track minutes later.

events.what: Stalin's grain seizures caused a famine that killed about 3.5 to 5 million people in Ukraine.
events.story: Forced collectivisation and impossible grain quotas brought famine across the USSR in 1932-33. events.now: Ukraine and many other countries recognise the Holodomor as a genocide; Russia denies that Ukrainians were singled out. The dispute is one of the memory conflicts behind the war since 2014.

events.bluf: Soviet leader Joseph Stalin set out to collectivise farming and pay for industry with grain, and to break Ukrainian peasant resistance and the nationalism he suspected behind it. Grain quotas and a sealed border starved millions of Ukrainians to death in 1932-33 while exports continued. The famine broke the Ukrainian countryside as a political force, and the denial that followed became a foundation of Ukrainian national identity against Moscow.
events.lens: Famines can be political weapons: watch who controls food and who is prevented from leaving.
events.fact: Welsh journalist Gareth Jones reported the famine in 1933 after walking through Ukrainian villages; Moscow correspondents, led by Walter Duranty of the New York Times, denied it in print.

events.sig: The Nazis and their allies won a majority on 5 March 1933 with the communist deputies in custody. The Enabling Act followed on 23 March.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler used the burning of the Reichstag to claim a communist uprising and win emergency powers before the election a week away. President Paul von Hindenburg signed a decree the next day suspending civil liberties, and the police arrested thousands of communists. The decree stayed in force until 1945 and is the standard case of a leader using an emergency to end a constitution.
events.lens: Be wary when a crisis conveniently gives a leader powers he already wanted.
events.myth: The Nazis set the fire themselves. Van der Lubbe's sole responsibility was accepted by the Nazi-era court and remains the reading with the most evidence; the question stays open because the regime destroyed what it could.

q.how: A law passed under intimidation.

q.lasted: Until 1945.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler asked the Reichstag to vote its own powers to his cabinet so that he could rule without further elections or decrees from the president. With communist deputies in custody and SA men in the hall, every party except the Social Democrats voted yes. Parliamentary government in Germany ended in one vote, and the Act is the case every postwar constitution was written to make impossible.
events.lens: Legal forms can be used to dismantle the legal order: authoritarians prefer to take power lawfully when they can.
events.fact: Otto Wels told Hitler to his face that 'you can take our lives and our freedom, but not our honour'; he died in exile in Paris in 1939.

events.story: In 1933 few farms in the Tennessee valley had electricity, floods were regular and much of the land was worn out. President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the act creating the Authority on 18 May 1933, with Nebraska Senator George Norris as its champion in Congress. events.then: Within a decade most of the valley's farms had electricity. The Authority's power fed aluminium plants and, from 1943, the uranium-enrichment plant at Oak Ridge.
events.sig: Within a decade most of the valley's farms had electricity. The Authority's power fed aluminium plants and, from 1943, the uranium-enrichment plant at Oak Ridge.
events.now: The TVA still supplies power to about 10 million people as the largest public utility in the United States, and its model of federal investment in a poor region is the reference for every later regional development scheme.

causes.why: The TVA was one of the New Deal's first and largest projects.

events.bluf: President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Congress set up the Tennessee Valley Authority to bring electricity, flood control and work to one of the poorest regions of the United States through public investment. It built dams across the valley, cut power prices and brought electricity to farms that had none. It became the model for state-led regional development that governments from India to Colombia copied.
events.lens: Public infrastructure can transform regions that markets ignore.
events.fact: Private utilities fought the TVA to the Supreme Court and lost in 1936 and 1939.

events.now: It is the standard case of a democracy dismantled from within by legal means, and the reason the Federal Republic's constitution of 1949 bars parties that work against the democratic order.

events.bluf: The conservatives around German President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Nazi leader Adolf Hitler chancellor to harness his mass following for their own authoritarian aims. Hitler used the office to dismantle German democracy within months, and the men who meant to control him were sidelined or killed. The regime that resulted made a European war and the murder of Europe's Jews its policy, and its rise is the defining case of a democracy dismantled from inside.

The New Deal coalition of workers, farmers, urban immigrants, Southern whites and Black voters dominated elections for decades. events.hook: Roosevelt remade the federal government to fight the Depression.
events.story: A quarter of the workforce was unemployed and banks were closing when President Franklin D. Roosevelt took office in March 1933. In his first hundred days Congress passed laws that closed and reopened the banks, insured deposits, regulated the stock market and set up public works. Later acts protected workers' right to organise and, in 1935, created Social Security. Millions worked on federal roads, dams and schools.

The New Deal coalition of workers, farmers, urban immigrants, Southern whites and Black voters dominated elections for decades. Many programmes excluded farm and domestic workers, who were disproportionately Black, especially in the South.
events.now: It established the expectation, which no later administration has reversed, that the federal government answers for economic security, and it built the Democratic coalition that held Congress for most of the years to 1994.

events.bluf: President Franklin D. Roosevelt set out to end a banking collapse and put a quarter of the workforce back to work through federal action. His programmes regulated banks and markets, employed millions, protected unions and built a safety net; recovery was slow and full employment came only with the war. The New Deal made economic security a federal responsibility and built a coalition that governed for a generation.
events.lens: Deep crises can permanently expand what citizens expect government to do.
events.fact: The Supreme Court struck down two of the main early programmes in 1935 and 1936, and Roosevelt's plan to enlarge the Court in 1937 failed in Congress.

From 30 June to 2 July 1934 German Chancellor Adolf Hitler had the SS under Heinrich Himmler kill Röhm, the SA leadership and old enemies including former Chancellor Kurt von Schleicher. The dead numbered at least 85 by the regime's count and several hundred by other reckonings.
events.then: Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934. Hitler merged the offices of president and chancellor as Führer and the army swore an oath of loyalty to him by name. A law of 3 July declared the killings legal.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler decided to destroy the SA leadership to win the army's loyalty before President Paul von Hindenburg died. The SS shot SA chief Ernst Röhm and dozens of others, along with old enemies, over three days in June and July 1934. The army accepted murder as policy, and when Hindenburg died a month later it swore an oath to Hitler personally.
events.lens: Dictators often purge their own early supporters to reassure the institutions they need.

events.bluf: The Chinese Communists broke out of their Jiangxi base in October 1934 to escape Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek's encirclement. About 86,000 set out; after a year's march across mountains and rivers perhaps 8,000 reached Shaanxi. The retreat cost nine in ten of the army, but it saved the party, made Mao Zedong its leader at Zunyi in January 1935 and put it in a northern base from which it grew during the war with Japan.

events.story: Wheat prices in the First World War and the 1920s had drawn farmers to plough the shortgrass prairie of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas and Colorado. A reporter's account of 'Black Sunday' coined the term 'Dust Bowl'.
events.why: Ploughing removed the roots that held the soil. Years of drought dried it. Wind did the rest.

events.now: The Dust Bowl made soil conservation a federal responsibility from 1935 and remains the reference case for farming that outruns its climate.

events.bluf: Spain's generals rose to overthrow an elected Republic they saw as the enemy of the Church, the army and property; the Republic fought to survive. Germany and Italy armed General Francisco Franco, the Soviet Union armed the Republic, and Franco won after three years and perhaps half a million dead. Spain got 36 years of dictatorship, and the war became the rehearsal ground for the weapons and alliances of the Second World War.

events.bluf: Japan's army sought resources and a sphere of control in China; Chinese Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek, pressed by nationalist opinion, could concede nothing more. A clash at the Marco Polo Bridge on 7 July 1937 became a full war within weeks. Eight years of fighting killed 15 to 20 million Chinese, drained the Nationalists while the Communists grew, and drew the United States into sanctions that led to Pearl Harbor; the Second World War in Asia began here, two years before Europe's.
events.trig: A night-time clash at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing on 7 July 1937.
events.lens: Wars of conquest against large countries often become quagmires that drain the invader.
events.fact: Chiang Kai-shek's government moved its capital twice, to Wuhan and then to Chongqing, where it stayed until 1945 under years of Japanese bombing.

The NKVD under Nikolai Yezhov arrested more than 1.5 million people in 1936-38 and shot about 680,000. Terror became the Soviet state's governing method, and the Red Army lost most of its high command three years before the German invasion.
events.lens: Purges secure a dictator but weaken the institutions he needs in a crisis.

Estimates of the dead range from tens of thousands to 300,000: the post-war Tokyo tribunal of 1948 put it at over 200,000; China's official figure, set by the Nanjing war crimes tribunal of 1947 and carried by the Nanjing memorial, is 300,000; Japanese estimates run from the tens of thousands to around 200,000.
events.why: Japan expected China to collapse quickly after Shanghai, and commanders let exhausted, poorly supplied troops loose on the city to terrorise China into surrender.
events.then: China's government moved inland, first to Wuhan and then to Chongqing, and fought on. Matsui was hanged by the Tokyo tribunal in 1948; Prince Asaka was exempted from prosecution as a member of the imperial family.
events.sig: China's government moved inland, first to Wuhan and then to Chongqing, and fought on. Matsui was hanged by the Tokyo tribunal in 1948; Prince Asaka was exempted from prosecution as a member of the imperial family.
events.now: The massacre is the event through which China and Japan still argue over the war. Beijing holds the toll at 300,000 and treats denial as a national insult; Tokyo acknowledges the killing of many non-combatants and holds that the number cannot be fixed, while some Japanese nationalists deny the scale or the event.

q.changed: China fought on, and world opinion turned against Japan.

events.bluf: Japanese commanders, expecting China to collapse after the fall of Shanghai, let their troops loose on the captured capital to terrorise the Nationalist government into surrender. From 13 December 1937 soldiers killed surrendered Chinese troops and civilians and raped tens of thousands of women over six weeks; China's official count is 300,000 dead, the Tokyo tribunal of 1948 found over 200,000, and Japanese estimates run from tens of thousands upward. The government fought on from inland, and the massacre became the central wound in Chinese memory of Japan.
events.lens: How a nation remembers its atrocities shapes its relations with its neighbours.
events.fact: German businessman John Rabe, a Nazi party member, led the international Safety Zone that sheltered some 200,000 Chinese during the killing.

events.story: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler, Austrian-born, pressured Austrian Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg in February 1938 to admit Nazis to his government. Schuschnigg called a plebiscite on independence for 13 March; Hitler demanded its cancellation and his resignation. German troops entered Austria on 12 March 1938 without resistance, and a staged vote in April recorded 99 per cent for union.
events.then: Vienna's Jews were attacked and humiliated in the streets within days, and the Nuremberg Laws applied from May. Hitler turned at once to the Sudetenland in Czechoslovakia, now surrounded by German territory on three sides.
events.now: Austria long called itself 'Hitler's first victim', a claim it revised from the 1980s to acknowledge Austrians' share in the regime.

q.how: Austria became a province of Germany.
q.winners: Hitler; Austrian Jews were immediately persecuted.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler set out to bring Austria into the Reich, by pressure if he could and by force if he had to. Austrian Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg called a plebiscite to resist, was forced to resign, and German troops entered on 12 March 1938 without resistance and to cheering crowds. Germany gained seven million people and the position to surround Czechoslovakia, and the absence of any Western response set up the Sudeten crisis.
events.lens: Expansion presented as national unification is hard for outsiders to oppose.
events.fact: Schuschnigg spent the war in Nazi custody, including Dachau; he later taught in the United States.

events.bluf: Saudi King Abdulaziz ibn Saud needed money after the Depression cut pilgrimage income, and Standard Oil of California wanted a concession on ground no one else had tested. The gamble paid in March 1938 when Dammam No. 7 flowed in commercial quantities on the edge of the world's largest reserves. The kingdom became central to the world economy, and the US-Saudi exchange of oil for security has shaped Middle East politics since.
events.lens: Energy dependence creates strategic alliances that outlast changes in ideology.
events.fact: US President Franklin Roosevelt met Ibn Saud aboard the cruiser USS Quincy in the Suez Canal in February 1945.

events.what: Britain and France let Germany take the Sudetenland.

events.story: At Munich on 29-30 September 1938 British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and French Premier Édouard Daladier agreed with German Chancellor Adolf Hitler and Italian leader Benito Mussolini that Germany could annex the Sudetenland, the German-speaking border regions of Czechoslovakia, within ten days. Czechoslovakia, which had an alliance with France and strong fortifications along that border, was not invited. Chamberlain flew home promising 'peace for our time'.
events.then: Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939 and invaded Poland in September. Britain and France rearmed faster after Munich than before it.
events.now: 'Munich' is invoked in almost every debate about confronting aggression, sometimes misleadingly.

events.bluf: British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and French Premier Édouard Daladier set out to avoid a war over the Sudetenland that they were unready to fight. They gave German Chancellor Adolf Hitler the German-speaking border regions of Czechoslovakia, with its fortifications, without consulting Prague. Hitler took the rest of the country six months later, and 'Munich' became the name for the danger of conceding to an aggressor.
events.lens: Concessions to an aggressor with unlimited aims buy time, not peace.
events.myth: Munich simply bought Britain a year to rearm. The year also gave Germany the Czech army's equipment and the Škoda works, and the balance of the twelve months is argued both ways.

events.bluf: Mexican President Lázaro Cárdenas set out to enforce Mexican law on foreign oil companies that had defied the Supreme Court over workers' wages. Pemex became the emblem of Mexican sovereignty, and the expropriation set the precedent for resource nationalism from Iran to Venezuela and Bolivia.
events.lens: Control of natural resources is a core test of sovereignty, and a nationalization's success depends on whether the great powers choose to fight it.

Persecution by law became persecution by violence, and few countries opened their doors to the refugees it produced.

He bullied Czech President Emil Hácha into 'requesting' German protection and marched into Prague on 15 March 1939. The Munich deal stood exposed as a sham, Britain and France guaranteed Poland, and the line that brought war in September was drawn.
events.lens: When an aggressor goes beyond his stated grievances, his real aims are revealed.

events.who: Germany (with USSR) vs. Poland, Britain, France

events.hook: Germany invaded Poland, and the deadliest war in history began.
events.story: Having secured a secret deal with Soviet leader Joseph Stalin to divide eastern Europe, German Chancellor Adolf Hitler invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France declared war two days later. Over the next six years the war spread to western Europe, the Soviet Union, North Africa, the Atlantic and, after Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the Pacific.
events.then: Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August. The Holocaust murdered six million Jews and millions of others. Europe was divided between the US and Soviet spheres, nuclear weapons were used, and the European empires began to dissolve.
events.now: The postwar world, from the UN and NATO to the Cold War and decolonisation, grew from its ruins.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler invaded Poland to win living space in the east and racial domination, after securing a deal with Soviet leader Joseph Stalin to divide eastern Europe. Six years of war killed 70-85 million people, including six million Jews in the Holocaust, and ended with Germany and Japan in ruins. The United States and the Soviet Union emerged as superpowers, Europe was divided between them, the United Nations was founded, and the European empires began to dissolve.
events.trig: Germany's invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939.
events.lens: Expansionist regimes with unlimited aims can only be stopped by force; the question is how early.

events.hook: Sworn enemies Hitler and Stalin made a deal, and secretly agreed to split Eastern Europe.
events.story: On 23 August 1939 German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop and Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov signed a ten-year non-aggression pact in Moscow, stunning a world that saw the two states as ideological enemies. A secret protocol, whose existence the USSR denied until 1989, divided eastern Europe: Germany would take western Poland; the Soviets eastern Poland, Latvia, Estonia, Finland and Bessarabia, with Lithuania added a month later.

events.now: Its secret protocol still shapes Baltic and Polish memory of the war, and Russia's defence of the pact is a sore point in its relations with its western neighbours.

q.how: Germany could invade Poland without fear of Soviet attack.
q.winners: Hitler, for 22 months; Stalin gained territory.
q.lasted: Until Hitler invaded the USSR in June 1941.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler wanted to invade Poland without a two-front war; Soviet leader Joseph Stalin wanted time to rearm and territory on his western border. Their foreign ministers signed a non-aggression pact in Moscow on 23 August 1939 with a secret protocol dividing eastern Europe between them. Germany invaded Poland nine days later, the Soviet Union took eastern Poland, the Baltic states and Bessarabia, and the pact's memory still divides Russia from its western neighbours.
events.lens: Ideological enemies cooperate when their immediate interests align.
events.fact: Stalin toasted Hitler's health at the signing; the Soviet parliament condemned the secret protocol as void in December 1989.

events.what: Tiny Finland humiliated the Red Army in the snow, and Hitler took note.

events.hook: Tiny Finland humiliated the Red Army in the snow, and Hitler took note.
events.story: When Finland refused to cede land near Leningrad, the Soviet Union invaded on 30 November 1939, expecting victory within weeks. Outnumbered Finnish troops under Marshal Carl Gustaf Mannerheim, fighting on skis in temperatures far below freezing, destroyed Soviet columns in the forests, and the League of Nations expelled the USSR. Weight of numbers broke the Finnish defences on the Karelian Isthmus in February 1940, and in March Finland ceded about a tenth of its territory but kept its independence.
events.then: The Red Army's poor showing convinced Hitler the USSR would be easy to defeat, while Stalin began reforming his army. Finland joined Germany's attack on the USSR in 1941.
events.now: It is a source of Finnish national pride and shaped its strong defence tradition; after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Finland joined NATO in 2023.

q.decided: Soviet numbers eventually won, but at great cost.

q.changed: Finland kept its independence; the Red Army looked weak.

events.bluf: Soviet leader Joseph Stalin wanted a buffer around Leningrad and invaded Finland when it refused to cede the land. Finland's army held the Red Army for three months at a cost far below its own, then gave up about a tenth of its territory and kept its independence. The Red Army's showing convinced German Chancellor Adolf Hitler that the USSR could be beaten quickly, and it gave Finland the defence tradition that carried it into NATO in 2023.
events.lens: Small nations defending home terrain can make invasion very costly.
events.fact: The Molotov cocktail got its name in this war; Finnish troops named the petrol bomb after the Soviet foreign minister.

The Commons debate on the failure brought down Chamberlain, and Churchill became prime minister on 10 May 1940.

events.bluf: Germany set out to secure Swedish iron ore shipped through Narvik and to win naval bases on the Atlantic before Britain could mine the route. It took Denmark in hours and Norway in two months in April to June 1940, at the cost of half its destroyer fleet. The botched Allied response brought down British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and put Winston Churchill in power on the day Germany attacked France.
events.lens: Military failures change governments, and the right leader arriving at a crisis can change history.
events.fact: Norwegian Nazi Vidkun Quisling seized the radio to declare himself prime minister on the day of the invasion; his name became the word for a collaborator.
