q.cost: Britain left behind almost all its heavy equipment.
q.changed: Britain could keep fighting.

events.bluf: Britain set out to save its army after German tanks reached the Channel and cut the Allied forces in two. A German pause, the Royal Navy and hundreds of small civilian boats brought over 338,000 British and French troops off the beaches between 26 May and 4 June 1940. Britain kept an army with which to fight on, and a defeat became the national story of resilience.
events.lens: Saving an army to fight another day can matter more than holding ground.
events.fact: The 'little ships' included Thames pleasure boats, fishing smacks and lifeboats; about 700 took part.

kv: vessels, many of them small civilian boats

events.what: France defeated in six weeks.
events.why: German tactics of concentrated tanks and aircraft coordinated by radio beat a French army spread along a static line. French defensive doctrine and command failures left no reserve to meet the breakthrough.
events.sig: France was split between German occupation and the collaborationist Vichy regime under Marshal Philippe Pétain. Britain, under Prime Minister Winston Churchill, fought on, and General Charles de Gaulle launched the Free French from London.
events.hook: France collapsed in six weeks.
events.story: On 10 May 1940 Germany invaded the Netherlands and Belgium. The main thrust came through the wooded Ardennes, bypassing France's Maginot Line; German tanks reached the Channel in ten days, trapping the Allied armies, of which over 338,000 men were evacuated from Dunkirk. Paris fell on 14 June, and France signed an armistice on 22 June.
events.then: France was split between German occupation and the collaborationist Vichy regime under Marshal Philippe Pétain. Britain, under Prime Minister Winston Churchill, fought on, and General Charles de Gaulle launched the Free French from London.
events.now: France's defeat and collaboration shaped its postwar politics and its determination, with Germany, to build European unity.
events.fact: Hitler had the 1940 armistice signed in the same railway carriage at Compiègne used for the German surrender of 1918, then took the carriage to Berlin.

causes.why: The Allied armies had been split and driven back.

q.why: Hitler wanted to knock France out before Britain or the USSR could act.
q.decided: A surprise tank thrust through the Ardennes forest bypassed the Maginot Line.
q.cost: About 90,000 French soldiers killed; nearly 2 million taken prisoner.
q.changed: Germany dominated Western Europe; Vichy France collaborated.

events.bluf: Germany set out to knock France out of the war in one campaign by striking through the Ardennes rather than through Belgium as in 1914. The thrust reached the Channel in ten days, trapped the Allied armies, and France signed an armistice on 22 June 1940, six weeks after the attack began. Britain stood alone, the Vichy regime collaborated with the occupier, and the defeat shaped French politics and the drive for European unity for the rest of the century.
events.lens: Defensive plans built for the last war fail against new methods.

events.what: The RAF stopped Germany's air force from clearing the way for an invasion.
events.why: Britain refused to make peace after France fell, and Hitler needed control of the air before he could invade across the Channel.
events.sig: Germany's bombing of cities, the Blitz, killed about 43,000 British civilians by May 1941. Hitler turned to planning the invasion of the Soviet Union.
events.hook: The RAF stopped Germany's air force from clearing the way for an invasion.
events.story: In summer 1940 the Luftwaffe under Hermann Göring set out to destroy the Royal Air Force as a prelude to invasion. RAF Fighter Command under Air Chief Marshal Hugh Dowding, guided by a chain of radar stations and a central control system, inflicted heavy losses. In September Germany switched from attacking airfields to bombing London, which gave the RAF time to recover, and on 17 September Hitler postponed the invasion indefinitely.
events.then: Germany's bombing of cities, the Blitz, killed about 43,000 British civilians by May 1941. Hitler turned to planning the invasion of the Soviet Union.
events.now: Britain's survival kept a base in western Europe for the later American and British return, and radar-guided integrated air defence remains the model for modern air defence.

causes.why: Britain stood alone.

q.why: Hitler's invasion plan depended on it.
q.decided: Radar, the Spitfire and Hurricane, and a German switch to bombing cities.
q.cost: About 1,500 RAF aircrew killed; Germany lost more planes and crews.
q.changed: Hitler shelved the invasion and turned east.

events.bluf: The Luftwaffe set out to destroy the Royal Air Force so that Germany could invade across the Channel; the RAF set out to deny it. Radar, a central control system and the switch of German bombing from airfields to London in September 1940 let Fighter Command hold, and Hitler postponed the invasion indefinitely on 17 September. Britain stayed in the war as the base from which western Europe was later liberated.
events.lens: Defensive technology plus organization can defeat a stronger attacker.
events.fact: About a fifth of Fighter Command's pilots were from outside Britain; the Polish 303 Squadron claimed the highest score of any squadron in the battle.

toll.n: About 544 RAF aircrew and some 2,500 German aircrew were killed.

events.what: The US became 'the arsenal of democracy' before it entered the war.
events.why: Roosevelt judged that Britain's survival was America's first line of defence. Isolationist opinion ruled out troops; supply was what he could sell.
events.sig: The Soviet Union received about 400,000 trucks, along with aircraft, locomotives and food. American industry converted to war production before Pearl Harbor.
events.hook: The US became 'the arsenal of democracy' before it entered the war.
events.story: By late 1940 Britain had nearly run out of dollars to pay for American arms. President Franklin D. Roosevelt proposed in December to lend equipment as one lends a neighbour a garden hose. Congress passed the Lend-Lease Act on 11 March 1941 after two months of debate. Aid went first to Britain and China, and after the German invasion of June 1941 to the Soviet Union. Deliveries came to about $50 billion by 1945.
events.then: The Soviet Union received about 400,000 trucks, along with aircraft, locomotives and food. American industry converted to war production before Pearl Harbor.
events.now: It became the model for supplying allies without sending troops, and its name was revived for aid to Ukraine in 2022.

causes.why: Britain survived but was broke.

q.what: Planes, tanks, trucks, food and fuel.
q.who: US industry boomed; Britain and later the USSR got supplies.
q.scale: About $50 billion in aid (roughly $700 billion today).
q.daily: US factories switched to war production.
q.system: It tied the Allies' economies together.

events.bluf: President Franklin D. Roosevelt wanted Britain to keep fighting Germany without the United States sending troops, at a time when most Americans opposed entering the war. The Lend-Lease Act of March 1941 let him supply weapons, food and vehicles to any country whose defence he judged vital, payment deferred or waived. It made the United States the 'arsenal of democracy', tied its economy to the Allied cause and sustained Britain and, from late 1941, the Soviet Union.
events.lens: Economic support can sustain an ally's war long before a country fights directly.
events.fact: Roosevelt sold the idea at a press conference with the image of lending a garden hose to a neighbour whose house is on fire.

events.what: Operation Barbarossa, largest invasion ever.
events.why: Hitler's goals of 'living space' in the east and the destruction of 'Jewish Bolshevism' came first. The grain of Ukraine and the oil of the Caucasus were the material prize.
events.sig: After Stalingrad in 1942-43 and Kursk in 1943 the Red Army pushed west to Berlin. The USSR lost about 27 million people, and about three-quarters of German military deaths came on the Eastern Front.
events.hook: Hitler launched the largest invasion in history, and it decided the war.
events.story: On 22 June 1941 over three million Axis troops invaded the USSR on a front from the Baltic to the Black Sea. They encircled Soviet armies at Minsk, Smolensk and Kyiv, reached the outskirts of Moscow and besieged Leningrad, and were stopped by Soviet counterattacks in December. Behind the lines SS killing squads murdered Jews and others in mass shootings.
events.then: After Stalingrad in 1942-43 and Kursk in 1943 the Red Army pushed west to Berlin. The USSR lost about 27 million people, and about three-quarters of German military deaths came on the Eastern Front.
events.now: The invasion turned the war into the largest in history, cost the Soviet Union about 27 million dead, and brought the Red Army to the Elbe, which decided the division of Europe for forty-five years.
events.fact: Russia remembers it as the Great Patriotic War; Victory Day is its largest holiday and the memory is used to justify policy, including the war in Ukraine.

sites.d: 872-day siege; ~1M civilians died.
Germans stopped at the gates, December 1941.
Turning point; German 6th Army surrendered, 1943.
Largest tank battle in history, 1943.

causes.why: Unable to beat Britain, Hitler turned east.
The Red Army's poor performance convinced Hitler it would collapse.
Hitler broke the pact.

q.why: Hitler's goal of 'living space', destroying communism and enslaving the Slavs.
q.decided: Russian winter, Soviet sacrifice and the failure to take Moscow.
q.cost: About 27 million Soviet dead over the war.
q.changed: Most German losses in the war came on this front.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler invaded the Soviet Union to win living space in the east, destroy 'Jewish Bolshevism' and take Ukraine's grain and the Caucasus's oil. The largest invasion in history reached the outskirts of Moscow by December 1941 and was stopped there. The war became a four-year contest that killed about 27 million Soviet citizens and three-quarters of Germany's military dead, and the Red Army's march to the Elbe fixed the division of Europe for forty-five years.
events.lens: Ideological wars of annihilation provoke total resistance: Germany's brutality turned potential collaborators into enemies.

kv: front, from the Baltic to the Black Sea

toll.t: Military deaths on the Eastern Front, 1941–45
toll.n: Soviet civilian deaths were higher still, about 13–19 million (est.).

events.who: Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto's carrier fleet; US Pacific Fleet
events.what: Surprise Japanese attack killed ~2,400.
events.why: Japan needed oil for its war in China and judged the Dutch East Indies the source. The Pacific Fleet was the one force that could stop a southern advance, and Yamamoto believed a knockout blow would buy time to build a defensible perimeter.
events.sig: Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on 11 December. American output, which exceeded that of all the Axis powers combined, tipped the war on both fronts. Japan's conquest of Southeast Asia ran to May 1942 and stopped at Midway in June.
events.hook: A surprise attack on a Sunday morning brought the US into World War II.
events.story: The United States froze Japanese assets and cut off oil in July 1941 after Japan occupied southern Indochina. Japanese Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto planned a carrier strike on the Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor; Vice Admiral Chūichi Nagumo's six carriers crossed the North Pacific undetected. On the morning of 7 December 1941 two waves of aircraft sank or damaged eight battleships and killed about 2,400 Americans. The three US carriers were at sea. Congress declared war the next day.
events.then: Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on 11 December. American output, which exceeded that of all the Axis powers combined, tipped the war on both fronts. Japan's conquest of Southeast Asia ran to May 1942 and stopped at Midway in June.
events.now: The attack brought American industry into the war on both fronts, which decided it, and fixed the surprise attack as the scenario American defence planning has organised itself against ever since.
events.fact: The sunken USS Arizona still leaks a few drops of oil every day, more than 80 years later.

sites.d: December 7, 1941.
June 1942: US sinks four Japanese carriers; turning point.
First major US offensive, 1942–43.
Flag-raising photo, 1945.
Bloodiest Pacific battle, 1945.

causes.why: To end the China war and secure oil, Japan moved into French Indochina. The US answered with an oil embargo, and Japan chose war.
Annexation gave the US Pearl Harbor, home of its Pacific Fleet from 1940.

q.why: Japan wanted to cripple the US Pacific Fleet.
q.decided: Surprise, though US carriers were away.
q.cost: About 2,400 Americans killed.
q.changed: The US entered the war.

events.bluf: Japan, at war in China and cut off from American oil, set out to seize Southeast Asia's resources and to cripple the US Pacific Fleet so that it could not interfere. Japanese Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto's carriers struck Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, sank or damaged eight battleships and killed about 2,400 Americans, and missed the carriers and the fuel stores. The attack brought the United States into the war with a united public, Germany declared war four days later, and the European and Asian wars became one.
events.trig: The US oil embargo and the failure of negotiations in November 1941, when Washington demanded that Japan withdraw from China.
events.lens: A tactical success can be a strategic disaster if it awakens a far stronger enemy.

kv: US ships sunk or damaged, 8 of them battleships

events.who: Japan vs. Britain, the US and the Netherlands
events.where: Malaya, Singapore, the Philippines and the Dutch East Indies
events.what: Within hours of Pearl Harbor, Japan attacked Malaya, the Philippines and Hong Kong; within five months it held Southeast Asia.
events.why: Japan wanted the region's oil, rubber and tin after the US oil embargo.
events.sig: Japan ruled the region until 1945, using forced labour on projects such as the Burma Railway. It armed local nationalists who later fought the returning Europeans.
events.hook: Within hours of Pearl Harbor, Japan attacked Malaya, the Philippines and Hong Kong; within five months it held Southeast Asia.
events.story: The United States embargoed oil exports to Japan in August 1941. Japan's offensive of 8 December 1941 (7 December across the date line in Hawaii) struck Malaya, Hong Kong and the Philippines. Singapore fell on 15 February 1942, the Dutch East Indies in March and the Philippines by May.
events.then: Japan ruled the region until 1945, using forced labour on projects such as the Burma Railway. It armed local nationalists who later fought the returning Europeans.
events.now: Four years of Japanese occupation, 1941 to 1945, broke the colonial administrations and armed the nationalists who fought the returning Dutch, French and British; most of the region was independent within twelve years of 1945.

causes.why: Britain's great naval base at Singapore fell to Japan in February 1942; Churchill called it the worst disaster in British military history.
Bogged down in China and cut off from US oil, Japan struck south for the resources of Southeast Asia.

events.wk: South-East Asian theatre of World War II

q.why: Japan wanted Southeast Asia's oil, rubber and tin.
q.decided: Japanese speed and air power.
q.cost: Hundreds of thousands of prisoners and civilians died under Japanese occupation.
q.changed: European colonial prestige collapsed.

events.bluf: Japan set out to seize the oil, rubber and tin of Southeast Asia after the US oil embargo of 1941 cut its supply. Its offensive of 8 December 1941 struck Malaya, Hong Kong and the Philippines; Singapore fell on 15 February 1942, the Dutch East Indies in March and the Philippines by May. Japan held the region until 1945, and the collapse of European authority made the return of the empires after the war far harder to sustain.
events.lens: When colonial powers are seen to lose, their authority rarely recovers.
events.fact: The Burma Railway killed more than 12,000 Allied prisoners and tens of thousands of Asian labourers in sixteen months of construction.

events.what: Germany besieged Leningrad for 872 days, and about a million civilians died, mostly of hunger.
events.why: Hitler wanted to wipe out the city of Lenin and chose starvation over the cost of street fighting. Finland's advance from the north closed the ring.
events.sig: The siege lasted until January 1944. About a million civilians died, most of them from starvation.
events.hook: Germany besieged Leningrad for 872 days, and about a million civilians died, mostly of hunger.
events.story: German Army Group North cut the last land route to Leningrad on 8 September 1941 and Hitler ordered the city starved rather than stormed. In the first winter the bread ration fell to 125 grams a day and people ate wallpaper paste and pets. Supplies came over the frozen Lake Ladoga, the 'Road of Life'. The siege ended on 27 January 1944.
events.then: The siege lasted until January 1944. About a million civilians died, most of them from starvation.
events.now: The siege is central to Russia's memory of the war, and St Petersburg marks the end of the blockade every 27 January.

causes.why: German armies reached the city in weeks.

q.why: Leningrad was the cradle of the Bolshevik Revolution.
q.decided: The city held; the siege was broken in January 1944.
q.cost: About 800,000 to 1 million civilians died.
q.changed: It became a symbol of Soviet endurance.

events.bluf: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler chose to starve Leningrad rather than storm it, intending to erase the city of Lenin. The siege ran 872 days from September 1941 to January 1944 and killed about a million civilians, most of them from hunger in the first winter. The city held, and its survival became the central symbol of Soviet endurance and of Russian war memory since.
events.lens: Starvation as a weapon targets civilians first, and is now a war crime under international law.
events.fact: Dmitri Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony was performed in the besieged city in August 1942 by an orchestra of survivors, broadcast by loudspeaker toward the German lines.

figs.rec: Among the deadliest sieges in history

events.h: Hitler declares war on the United States
events.what: Four days after Pearl Harbor, Hitler declared war on America, a choice that doomed Germany.
events.why: Hitler underestimated American power and judged that war was coming anyway. The declaration freed his submarines to attack American shipping.
events.sig: Roosevelt adopted a 'Germany first' strategy. US troops were fighting in North Africa by November 1942.
events.hook: Four days after Pearl Harbor, Hitler declared war on America, a choice that doomed Germany.
events.story: Four days after Pearl Harbor, on 11 December 1941, German Chancellor Adolf Hitler declared war on the United States in a speech to the Reichstag, and Italian leader Benito Mussolini followed. Germany's alliance with Japan was defensive and did not require it, and Japan had not consulted Germany before attacking. Hitler held that the US was already waging an undeclared naval war in the Atlantic and that Japan would tie it down in the Pacific.
events.then: Roosevelt adopted a 'Germany first' strategy. US troops were fighting in North Africa by November 1942.
events.now: It brought the world's largest economy into the war against Germany without Roosevelt having to ask Congress for it, and let the Allies put Germany's defeat before Japan's.

causes.why: Japan's attack brought the US into the war against Japan.

q.why: Hitler believed war with the US was inevitable.
q.stakes: Whether the US would fight in Europe.
q.decided: Hitler's own choice.
q.cost: It brought the world's largest economy against Germany.
q.changed: The US adopted a 'Germany first' strategy.

events.wk: German declaration of war on the United States
events.bluf: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler declared war on the United States four days after Pearl Harbor, though no treaty required it, in the belief that war with America was coming anyway and Japan would tie it down in the Pacific. The declaration let President Franklin Roosevelt commit America's economy to Europe first. Germany now faced the United States, Britain and the USSR together, and its defeat became a matter of time.
events.lens: Ideology and contempt for an enemy can lead to catastrophic strategic choices.
events.fact: German submarines sank hundreds of ships off the American coast in the first half of 1942 while American cities kept their lights on.

events.who: Reinhard Heydrich, Adolf Eichmann and 13 officials
events.what: In a lakeside villa, Nazi officials coordinated the murder of Europe's 11 million Jews.
events.why: The Nazi leadership had already decided to exterminate Europe's Jews. Wannsee coordinated the government agencies involved and settled the SS's authority over them.
events.sig: Deportations to the death camps accelerated across Europe through 1942. By 1945 about six million Jews had been murdered.
events.hook: In a lakeside villa, Nazi officials coordinated the murder of Europe's 11 million Jews.
events.story: Mass shootings in the occupied USSR had already killed hundreds of thousands of Jews by the end of 1941. On 20 January 1942 SS General Reinhard Heydrich chaired a meeting of fifteen officials from the SS, the party and the ministries at a villa on the Wannsee in Berlin, with SS Lieutenant Colonel Adolf Eichmann taking the minutes. Heydrich set out the 'Final Solution': deporting Jews from across Europe to the east, where those fit for work would be worked to death and the rest killed.
events.then: Deportations to the death camps accelerated across Europe through 1942. By 1945 about six million Jews had been murdered.
events.now: Wannsee turned the murder of Europe's Jews from an SS operation into a programme of the whole state, which is why the Holocaust is read as a crime of administrators as much as of fanatics.

causes.why: Persecution had escalated step by step.
Mass shootings of Jews began behind the Eastern Front.

q.belief: Jews, as a people and a faith, were targeted for total destruction.
q.authority: The German state bureaucracy.
q.believers: Six million Jews would be murdered.
q.fallout: Death camps like Auschwitz, Treblinka and Sobibor ran at full scale.
q.today: The villa is now a Holocaust memorial and education center.

events.bluf: SS General Reinhard Heydrich called fifteen senior officials to a villa at Wannsee to put every ministry behind the murder of Europe's Jews, which the Nazi leadership had already decided on. In ninety minutes they settled the division of labour for deporting 11 million people to the east. The Holocaust ran from then on as a state project of administrators, and the minutes are the clearest surviving record of it.
events.lens: Genocide requires bureaucracy: ordinary administration can be turned to mass murder.
events.fact: One copy of the minutes, out of thirty, survived in a Foreign Office file and was found by American prosecutors in 1947.

kv: Jews listed, country by country, for 'the final solution'

events.who: Franklin D. Roosevelt; about 120,000 Japanese Americans
events.where: Manzanar, California, one of ten camps
events.hook: The US government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese descent, most of them citizens, into camps.
events.what: The US government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese descent, most of them citizens, into camps.
events.story: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 on 19 February 1942, letting the army exclude anyone from military areas; Lieutenant General John DeWitt applied it to all people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast. Families had days to sell homes and businesses before being sent to ten camps, from Manzanar in California to Jerome in Arkansas. Many stayed until 1945.
events.why: Fear of invasion and sabotage after Pearl Harbor came first. Decades of anti-Asian agitation on the West Coast supplied the prejudice. Farm interests wanted the land, and politicians wanted to be seen acting.
events.then: The Supreme Court upheld the exclusion in Korematsu v. United States in December 1944 by six votes to three. Not one Japanese American was convicted of espionage. In 1988 Congress apologised and paid $20,000 to each surviving internee.
events.sig: The Supreme Court upheld the exclusion in Korematsu v. United States in December 1944 by six votes to three. Not one Japanese American was convicted of espionage. In 1988 Congress apologised and paid $20,000 to each surviving internee.
events.now: Congress apologised and paid $20,000 to each surviving internee in 1988, and the Supreme Court repudiated Korematsu in 2018; the case is cited whenever a government proposes to detain or exclude a group on grounds of origin.

causes.why: Wartime fear after Pearl Harbor led to mass removal.

q.before: Japanese Americans lived as citizens and residents on the West Coast.
q.how: An executive order carried out by the army.
q.winners: No one; some neighbours bought farms and businesses cheaply.
q.lasted: The camps closed in 1945-46; the apology came in 1988.

events.bluf: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, under pressure from the army and West Coast politicians after Pearl Harbor, ordered the removal of about 120,000 Japanese Americans, two-thirds of them US citizens, from the Pacific coast. They were held in ten remote camps, many until 1945, and lost homes and businesses; none was ever convicted of espionage. The internment stands as the reference case in American law and politics for what wartime fear can do to civil liberties.
events.lens: In wartime, fear can override constitutional rights for groups seen as foreign.
events.fact: The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, recruited from the camps and from Hawaii, became the most decorated unit of its size in US army history.

events.hook: Japanese planes bombed Darwin, the largest attack ever on Australia.
events.what: Japanese planes bombed Darwin, the largest attack ever on Australia.
events.story: Singapore surrendered on 15 February 1942. On 19 February, 188 aircraft from four Japanese carriers under Vice Admiral Chūichi Nagumo, led by Commander Mitsuo Fuchida, and 54 land-based bombers attacked Darwin in two raids. They sank eight ships, wrecked the airfields and killed at least 235 people; many residents and servicemen fled south in the days after. Raids on northern Australia continued until November 1943.
events.why: Japan wanted Darwin out of action before its landings on Timor and Java. The carriers were available between operations.
events.then: Curtin, who had declared in December 1941 that Australia 'looks to America', brought Australian divisions home from the Middle East and accepted US General Douglas MacArthur as supreme commander in the South-West Pacific in March 1942. Australia became the main US base in the South Pacific.
events.sig: Curtin, who had declared in December 1941 that Australia 'looks to America', brought Australian divisions home from the Middle East and accepted US General Douglas MacArthur as supreme commander in the South-West Pacific in March 1942. Australia became the main US base in the South Pacific.
events.now: Darwin fixed Australia's shift from Britain to the United States as guarantor, announced by Prime Minister John Curtin in December 1941; the US alliance, formalised in the ANZUS treaty of 1951, has been the core of Australian defence policy since.

causes.why: Four days after Singapore fell, Japan struck Darwin to protect its invasion of the Dutch East Indies.

q.why: Japan wanted to stop Darwin being used as an Allied base.
q.decided: Surprise and air power.
q.cost: At least 235 killed.
q.changed: Australia turned to the US for defence.

events.bluf: Japan wanted to stop Darwin serving as a base against its invasion of the Dutch East Indies and Timor. On 19 February 1942, four days after Singapore fell, 242 aircraft from four of the carriers that had struck Pearl Harbor and from bases in the Dutch East Indies hit Darwin's harbour and airfields and killed at least 235 people. The attack confirmed that Britain could no longer defend Australia, and Australia built its security on the United States from then on.
events.lens: Smaller powers realign toward whichever great power can actually protect them.
events.fact: Commander Mitsuo Fuchida led the first wave at Pearl Harbor and the raid on Darwin; the Australian government announced a far lower death toll at the time.

events.who: General Tomoyuki Yamashita; Lieutenant-General Arthur Percival
events.hook: Britain's 'impregnable fortress' surrendered to a smaller Japanese army; about 80,000 troops became prisoners.
events.what: Britain's 'impregnable fortress' surrendered to a smaller Japanese army; about 80,000 troops became prisoners.
events.story: Japanese General Tomoyuki Yamashita's army raced down the Malay Peninsula in two months and crossed the Johor Strait to Singapore. On 15 February 1942 Lieutenant-General Arthur Percival surrendered about 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops. British Prime Minister Winston Churchill called it the worst disaster in British military history.
events.why: Singapore's defences faced the sea. Japan came by land with control of the air.
events.then: Many prisoners died building the Burma Railway. Japanese troops massacred tens of thousands of Chinese Singaporeans in the Sook Ching purge.
events.sig: Many prisoners died building the Burma Railway. Japanese troops massacred tens of thousands of Chinese Singaporeans in the Sook Ching purge.
events.now: The surrender ended the belief in British invincibility on which colonial rule in Asia rested; Malaya was independent within fifteen years and Singapore a state within 23.

causes.why: Japan's drive south took Singapore within ten weeks.

q.why: Japan needed Southeast Asia's oil and rubber, and Singapore guarded the route.
q.decided: Japanese speed and air power, and British mistakes.
q.cost: About 80,000 troops taken prisoner.
q.changed: European prestige in Asia collapsed.

events.bluf: Japanese General Tomoyuki Yamashita set out to take Singapore, Britain's main base in Asia, by land down the Malay Peninsula while its guns faced the sea. On 15 February 1942 Lieutenant-General Arthur Percival surrendered about 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops, the largest surrender in British military history. Belief in British power in Asia collapsed, and the empire never recovered its standing in the East.
events.lens: Prestige is a form of power; when it collapses, so does authority.
events.fact: Yamashita's roughly 30,000 men took the surrender of a garrison more than twice their size.

events.who: The Japanese army; American and Filipino prisoners

events.what: After surrendering on Bataan, about 75,000 American and Filipino troops were force-marched to prison camps; thousands died.
events.story: US and Filipino forces on Bataan surrendered on 9 April 1942 after months of siege. Japanese troops marched the prisoners about 100 km in the heat with little food or water. Those who fell were often beaten or killed. Thousands of Filipinos and several hundred Americans died on the march.
events.why: Japan was unprepared for so many prisoners. Its army treated surrender with contempt.
events.then: Thousands more died in the prison camps that followed. News of the march, released in 1944, hardened American attitudes toward Japan. Japanese General Masaharu Homma, who had commanded the invasion, was tried and executed in 1946.
events.sig: Thousands more died in the prison camps that followed. News of the march, released in 1944, hardened American attitudes toward Japan. Japanese General Masaharu Homma, who had commanded the invasion, was tried and executed in 1946.
events.now: The march made the treatment of prisoners an American war aim and gave the US-Philippine alliance a shared memory of suffering that both governments still invoke.

q.why: Japan invaded the Philippines, then a US territory.
q.decided: The besieged troops ran out of food and medicine.
q.cost: Thousands of prisoners died on the march.
q.changed: Its story hardened American resolve; the Japanese commander was executed after the war.

events.bluf: Japan's army set out to move some 75,000 American and Filipino prisoners off Bataan after their surrender on 9 April 1942, with no plan for so many. It marched them about 100 km in the heat with little food or water and beat or killed those who fell; thousands of Filipinos and several hundred Americans died. News of the march, released in 1944, hardened American attitudes toward Japan, and it remains central to Philippine memory of the war.
events.lens: The treatment of prisoners shapes how wars are remembered and how harsh the peace becomes.
events.fact: 9 April is the Day of Valour, Araw ng Kagitingan, a national holiday in the Philippines.

toll.n: Estimates. Thousands more died later in the camps.

events.who: US Navy (Chester Nimitz) vs. the Japanese navy (Yamamoto)
events.hook: US code-breakers let the navy ambush Japan's carriers, and four were sunk in a day.
events.what: US code-breakers let the navy ambush Japan's carriers, and four were sunk in a day.
events.story: Navy code-breakers at Pearl Harbor under Commander Joseph Rochefort read enough of Japan's naval code to identify Midway as the target and the date. US Admiral Chester Nimitz placed three carriers north-east of the atoll. On 4 June 1942, after torpedo squadrons had attacked at heavy loss, dive bombers from Enterprise and Yorktown found the carriers Akagi, Kaga and Sōryū with aircraft refuelling and rearming on deck and set all three ablaze within minutes; Hiryū was sunk that evening. The US lost the Yorktown.
events.why: Yamamoto wanted the US carriers destroyed before American shipyards could outbuild him. Nimitz knew the plan and accepted the odds.
events.then: Japan lost four fleet carriers and many of its best aircrew. The United States commissioned more than a dozen new fleet carriers by 1945 against Japan's handful, and went on the offensive at Guadalcanal in August 1942.
events.sig: Japan lost four fleet carriers and many of its best aircrew. The United States commissioned more than a dozen new fleet carriers by 1945 against Japan's handful, and went on the offensive at Guadalcanal in August 1942.
events.now: Midway destroyed four Japanese carriers and ended Japan's offensive in the Pacific six months after Pearl Harbor; from then the United States chose where to fight.

causes.why: Six months after Pearl Harbor, US code-breakers let the navy ambush the carriers that had attacked it.

q.why: Japan hoped to destroy the US carrier fleet.
q.decided: US code-breaking and dive bombers striking at the right moment.
q.cost: Japan lost four carriers and about 3,000 men; the US about 300.
q.changed: Japan lost the initiative in the Pacific.

events.bluf: Japanese Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto wanted to seize Midway and draw the remaining US carriers into a decisive battle; US Admiral Chester Nimitz, told by code-breakers where and when, set an ambush. On 4 June 1942 American dive bombers caught four Japanese carriers with aircraft refuelling on deck and sank all four, for the loss of one US carrier. Japan's offensive power in the Pacific was gone six months after Pearl Harbor, and the United States chose where to fight from then on.
events.lens: Intelligence advantages can decide battles between evenly matched forces.
events.fact: The code-breakers confirmed the target by having Midway radio in clear that its water plant had failed; Japanese traffic soon reported that 'AF' was short of water.

toll.n: Japan also lost about 250 aircraft and many experienced pilots.

events.who: Australian troops vs. the Japanese South Seas Force
events.hook: Australian soldiers stopped Japan's overland advance on Port Moresby in New Guinea's mountains.
events.what: Australian soldiers stopped Japan's overland advance on Port Moresby in New Guinea's mountains.
events.story: Japanese forces landed at Gona on Papua's north coast on 21 July 1942 and pushed up the Kokoda Track across the Owen Stanley Range. Australian militia of the 39th Battalion, then regulars back from the Middle East, fought a retreat to Ioribaiwa Ridge, within 50 km of Port Moresby, in September. Horii's force, starving at the end of its supply line, was ordered back; the Australians retook Kokoda on 2 November and the fighting ended at Buna and Gona in January 1943. Papuan carriers, the 'Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels', carried supplies up the track and the wounded down it.
events.why: Port Moresby would have given Japan an airbase within range of northern Australia and the Coral Sea. The Coral Sea battle in May had turned back the seaborne attempt.
events.then: Australian and US forces took Buna and Gona in January 1943 at heavy cost. Japan's land advance in the South Pacific was over; Milne Bay in August-September 1942 had already been its first defeat in a landing.
events.sig: Australian and US forces took Buna and Gona in January 1943 at heavy cost. Japan's land advance in the South Pacific was over; Milne Bay in August-September 1942 had already been its first defeat in a landing.
events.now: Kokoda, with Milne Bay and Guadalcanal, ended Japan's advance in the South Pacific; it marks the point at which Australia's defence rested on its own troops and the United States rather than Britain.

causes.why: Japan pushed into New Guinea to cut Australia off from the US.

q.why: Japan wanted Port Moresby as a base against Australia.
q.stakes: New Guinea and Australia's northern approaches.
q.decided: Australian resistance in brutal terrain, and Japanese supply failures.
q.cost: Over 600 Australians and thousands of Japanese killed.
q.changed: Japan's advance on Port Moresby was stopped.

events.bluf: Japan's South Seas Force under Major General Tomitarō Horii set out to take Port Moresby overland across the Owen Stanley Range after the sea route was blocked at the Coral Sea. Outnumbered Australian militia and then regular units fought a retreat along the Kokoda Track from July 1942, stopped the advance within 50 km of Port Moresby in September and drove the Japanese back to the north coast by November. Japan lost its last chance of bases within bombing range of Australia, and the campaign joined Gallipoli as a founding story.
events.lens: Fights close to home become national myths, and defending one's own territory builds identity.
events.fact: Horii drowned in the Kumusi River during the retreat in November 1942.

s: ~2,050, plus many deaths from disease and hunger
toll.n: About 4,000 more Australians fell sick, mostly with malaria and dysentery.

events.what: The bloodiest battle in history destroyed a German army and turned the war.
events.why: Stalingrad guarded the route to the oil of the Caucasus and bore Stalin's name. Hitler's refusal to let the Sixth Army withdraw turned a defeat into its destruction.
events.sig: Germany's last big offensive in the east failed at Kursk in July 1943. Romania, Hungary and Italy began looking for a way out of the war.
events.hook: The bloodiest battle in history destroyed a German army and turned the war.
events.story: German forces under General Friedrich Paulus reached Stalingrad in August 1942 and fought for it street by street and building by building. On 19 November the Soviets launched Operation Uranus, smashing through the Romanian armies on the flanks and encircling about 300,000 men of the German Sixth Army. Hitler forbade a breakout; supplied by air with a fraction of what it needed, the army starved, and its last troops surrendered on 2 February 1943. About 91,000 were taken prisoner, and only a few thousand ever returned home.
events.then: Germany's last big offensive in the east failed at Kursk in July 1943. Romania, Hungary and Italy began looking for a way out of the war.
events.now: Stalingrad destroyed a German army and ended the Wehrmacht's offensive capacity in the east; from February 1943 Germany was retreating, and the Soviet claim to have carried the war rests on it.

causes.why: Germany had failed to take Moscow and turned south for oil.

q.why: Oil, and prestige for both dictators.
q.stakes: Germany's chance to win in the East.
q.decided: The Soviet encirclement, Operation Uranus.
q.cost: About 2 million total casualties; of 91,000 Germans captured, only about 5,000 returned.
q.changed: Germany was on the defensive in the East from now on.

events.bluf: Germany set out to take Stalingrad to cover its drive for the Caucasus oil and to hold a city that bore Stalin's name. The Red Army broke through the Romanian flanks in November 1942, trapped about 300,000 men of the German Sixth Army and starved them into surrender by 2 February 1943. Germany lost an army and the initiative in the east, and its allies began looking for a way out of the war.
events.lens: Battles become turning points when they destroy forces that cannot be replaced.
events.fact: Hitler promoted Paulus to field marshal the day before he surrendered, on the reasoning that no German field marshal had ever been taken alive; Paulus surrendered anyway.

figs.rec: Among the bloodiest battles in history

toll.n: Estimates. Tens of thousands of civilians also died.

events.who: US Marines and Navy vs. Japan
events.hook: In the first major Allied offensive of the Pacific War, US forces took Guadalcanal after six months of fighting.
events.what: In the first major Allied offensive of the Pacific War, US forces took Guadalcanal after six months of fighting.
events.story: Japanese forces began an airfield on Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands in July 1942. US Marines under Major General Alexander Vandegrift landed on 7 August, took it and named it Henderson Field. Japan sent troops in by night, the 'Tokyo Express', and fought seven naval battles in the surrounding waters; so many ships sank that the strait became Ironbottom Sound. Solomon Islander scouts and Allied coastwatchers reported Japanese movements. Japan evacuated its surviving troops in the first week of February 1943.
events.why: The airfield would have put Japanese bombers over the convoy routes between the United States and Australia. The United States had the carriers left after Midway to cover a landing.
events.then: Japan lost two battleships, a carrier and hundreds of aircraft and pilots it could not replace. The Allies advanced up the Solomons and along New Guinea toward the Philippines.
events.sig: Japan lost two battleships, a carrier and hundreds of aircraft and pilots it could not replace. The Allies advanced up the Solomons and along New Guinea toward the Philippines.
events.now: Guadalcanal showed that the Pacific War would be decided by shipyards, aircraft plants and pilot training, where the United States outproduced Japan many times over; from February 1943 the Allies chose where to fight, and Solomon Islanders who scouted for them were part of the reason.

causes.why: With Japan's carrier force weakened at Midway, the Allies could go on the offensive.

q.why: Both sides wanted the island's airfield.
q.stakes: The sea lanes between the US and Australia.
q.decided: US persistence and control of the air by day.
q.cost: About 7,000 Allied and 30,000 Japanese dead.
q.changed: The Allies went on the offensive.

events.bluf: The United States wanted to take the airfield Japan was building on Guadalcanal before it could cut the sea lanes to Australia; Japan wanted it back. US Marines under Major General Alexander Vandegrift landed on 7 August 1942 and held the field through six months of jungle fighting and night naval battles until Japan evacuated in February 1943. The attrition drained Japan's ships, aircraft and trained pilots, and the Allies took the initiative in the Pacific.
events.lens: Wars of attrition favour the side with greater industrial capacity.
events.fact: Solomon Islander Sergeant Major Jacob Vouza, captured, tied to a tree and bayoneted, freed himself and warned the Marines of an attack; he was knighted in 1979.

events.hook: Gandhi demanded that Britain 'Quit India' at once, and Britain jailed the Congress leadership.
events.what: Gandhi demanded that Britain 'Quit India' at once, and Britain jailed the Congress leadership.
events.story: After the Cripps mission of March 1942 offered dominion status after the war and Congress rejected it, Congress met in Bombay and passed the Quit India resolution on 8 August 1942, with Mohandas Gandhi's call to 'do or die'. Within hours Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru and the leadership were arrested. Strikes, sabotage of railways and attacks on police stations followed; the government used troops and arrested tens of thousands.
events.why: Britain had declared India at war in 1939 without consulting Indians. The Cripps offer gave too little, and Japan's advance to Burma made Gandhi want Britain out before an invasion.
events.then: Congress leaders stayed in prison until 1945. The Muslim League, which opposed the movement, grew in membership and won most Muslim seats in the 1946 elections, strengthening its demand for Pakistan.
events.sig: Congress leaders stayed in prison until 1945. The Muslim League, which opposed the movement, grew in membership and won most Muslim seats in the 1946 elections, strengthening its demand for Pakistan.
events.now: The movement showed that Britain could hold India only by force, which it would not have after the war; independence and partition followed within five years.

causes.why: After a decade of civil disobedience, Gandhi demanded immediate British withdrawal in 1942.

q.before: British rule, with India at war without its consent.
q.how: Mass civil disobedience, crushed by arrests.
q.winners: In the short term the British; in the long term the nationalists.
q.lasted: Britain left five years later.

events.bluf: Mohandas Gandhi and the Congress demanded that Britain leave India at once, with Japan on the border, to force a settlement before the war ended. Britain jailed the leadership within hours of the resolution of 8 August 1942 and crushed the protests. Congress sat in prison until 1945 while the Muslim League organised, which made partition more likely when Britain did leave five years later.
events.lens: Absence from politics at a crucial moment can cost a movement its leverage.
events.fact: Gandhi's wife Kasturba died in detention at the Aga Khan Palace in Pune in 1944.

kv: killed by police and army fire (est.)

events.who: Montgomery's Eighth Army vs. Rommel's Afrika Korps
events.what: Britain won its first big land victory and saved Egypt and the Suez Canal.
events.why: Control of Egypt, the canal and the oil beyond was the prize. Montgomery had the numbers, the supplies and the decrypts.
events.sig: US and British troops landed in Morocco and Algeria days later. The Axis forces in North Africa surrendered in Tunisia in May 1943.
events.hook: Britain won its first big land victory and saved Egypt and the Suez Canal.
events.story: In summer 1942 German Field Marshal Erwin Rommel's German and Italian army drove deep into Egypt and was stopped at El Alamein, about 100 km from Alexandria. On 23 October British General Bernard Montgomery's Eighth Army attacked with more than twice as many tanks and guns and with intelligence from decoded German messages. After about twelve days the Axis lines broke and Rommel retreated across Libya.
events.then: US and British troops landed in Morocco and Algeria days later. The Axis forces in North Africa surrendered in Tunisia in May 1943.
events.now: The victory ended the Axis threat to the Suez Canal and Middle Eastern oil, which became central to Western strategy in the region after the war.

causes.why: Italy joined the war and fighting spread to North Africa.

q.why: The Suez Canal and oil.
q.stakes: Britain's route to India and the Middle East.
q.decided: Allied numbers, supplies and air power.
q.cost: About 30,000 Axis prisoners.
q.changed: Axis forces were driven out of North Africa by May 1943.

events.bluf: German Field Marshal Erwin Rommel drove into Egypt to take the Suez Canal and the oil beyond it; British General Bernard Montgomery's Eighth Army fought to stop him 100 km from Alexandria. Montgomery attacked on 23 October 1942 with more than twice Rommel's tanks and guns and broke the Axis line in twelve days. Egypt, the canal and Middle Eastern oil stayed Allied, and with the landings in Morocco and Algeria days later the Axis was driven out of Africa.
events.lens: Protecting critical supply routes can matter more than winning territory.
events.fact: Britain's church bells, silent since 1940 as an invasion alarm, were rung to mark the victory.

toll.n: Second battle, 23 October to 11 November 1942.

events.who: Jewish fighters (ŻOB, led by Mordechai Anielewicz) vs. SS
events.what: Knowing they faced death camps, Jewish fighters in Warsaw rose up against the SS.
events.why: Facing deportation to Treblinka, the fighters chose to resist and die fighting.
events.sig: The SS destroyed the ghetto, and its survivors were sent to death camps. The uprising inspired revolts at Treblinka and Sobibor later that year.
events.hook: Knowing they faced death camps, Jewish fighters in Warsaw rose up against the SS.
events.story: Most of the ghetto's people had already been sent to Treblinka in the summer of 1942. When the SS entered to clear the remaining 50,000 or so on 19 April 1943, several hundred fighters of the Jewish Combat Organisation under Mordechai Anielewicz and the Jewish Military Union opened fire. SS General Jürgen Stroop burned the ghetto block by block. Resistance ended on 16 May 1943 when Stroop blew up the Great Synagogue.
events.then: The SS destroyed the ghetto, and its survivors were sent to death camps. The uprising inspired revolts at Treblinka and Sobibor later that year.
events.now: It became a lasting symbol of Jewish resistance and dignity in the face of annihilation, central to Israeli and Polish memory of the Holocaust.

causes.why: Deportations to death camps were in full swing.

q.why: To resist the destruction of the ghetto.
q.stakes: Dignity and resistance in the face of genocide.
q.decided: Overwhelming German force.
q.cost: About 13,000 Jews killed; the rest deported.
q.changed: It was the largest Jewish revolt of the war and inspired others.

events.bluf: The Jewish fighters of the Warsaw ghetto, under Mordechai Anielewicz, chose to fight the final deportation to Treblinka and die on their own terms rather than in the gas chambers. Several hundred lightly armed fighters held the SS for nearly a month from 19 April 1943 before the ghetto was burned block by block. The largest Jewish armed revolt of the Holocaust became the central symbol of resistance against annihilation in Israeli and Polish memory.
events.lens: Resistance can matter morally even when it cannot win militarily.
events.fact: Anielewicz died in the command bunker at Mila 18 on 8 May 1943, aged 24; Stroop was hanged in Warsaw in 1952.

kv: Jews captured; most were killed on the spot or sent to death camps

events.what: Germany's last great offensive in the East ended in the largest tank battle in history.
events.why: Hitler wanted to regain the initiative after Stalingrad and shorten the front. He delayed the attack by two months to wait for new tanks, which gave the Soviets time to prepare.
events.sig: The Soviets advanced steadily west and held the initiative for the rest of the war. Germany shifted troops to Italy after the Allied landing in Sicily.
events.hook: Germany's last great offensive in the East ended in the largest tank battle in history.
events.story: On 5 July 1943 Germany launched Operation Citadel, a pincer attack on a Soviet bulge in the front around Kursk, with new Tiger and Panther tanks. Forewarned by intelligence, the Soviets under Marshal Georgy Zhukov had built belts of minefields and anti-tank defences many kilometres deep and massed reserves behind them. The German attack stalled within a week; Hitler called it off as the Allies landed in Sicily, and Soviet counteroffensives retook Orel, Kharkiv and Kyiv by November.
events.then: The Soviets advanced steadily west and held the initiative for the rest of the war. Germany shifted troops to Italy after the Allied landing in Sicily.
events.now: Kursk ended Germany's capacity to attack in the east; from July 1943 the Red Army chose where and when to fight, which carried it to Berlin in under two years.

causes.why: Germany needed to recover from Stalingrad.

q.why: To destroy Soviet forces and regain momentum.
q.stakes: Who would hold the initiative in the East.
q.decided: Soviet intelligence, defenses and reserves.
q.cost: Huge losses on both sides in tanks and men.
q.changed: Germany never launched another major offensive in the East.

events.bluf: Germany set out to regain the initiative after Stalingrad by pinching off the Soviet bulge around Kursk with its new Tiger and Panther tanks. Forewarned, the Red Army built defences many kilometres deep, stopped the attack within a week and counterattacked. Germany had launched its last major offensive in the east, and the Red Army held the initiative for the rest of the war.
events.lens: Attacking prepared defences that the enemy knows are coming is ruinously costly.
events.myth: Prokhorovka on 12 July was the largest tank battle in history and a Soviet victory. The Soviet tank army lost several times as many tanks as the Germans there; the battle was won by the defensive belts and the reserves, over weeks.

figs.rec: Often called the largest tank battle in history

toll.n: Includes the Soviet counteroffensives that followed. Soviet tank losses were several times Germany's.

q.why: To knock Italy out of the war.
q.decided: Allied landings and Italian war-weariness.
q.cost: A slow, bloody campaign up the peninsula until 1945.
q.changed: Italy switched sides; Mussolini was later killed by partisans.

events.hook: The Allies landed in Sicily, their first major landing in Europe.
events.what: The Allies landed in Sicily, their first major landing in Europe.
events.story: On 10 July 1943 about 160,000 US, British and Canadian troops under American General Dwight Eisenhower landed in Sicily. They took the island in 38 days. German forces escaped across the Strait of Messina with their equipment.
events.why: British Prime Minister Winston Churchill called Italy the 'soft underbelly' of Axis Europe. Knocking Italy out of the war would tie down German troops while the Allies prepared the invasion of France.
events.then: Mussolini fell two weeks after the landings. The Allies landed on the Italian mainland in September 1943 and fought up the peninsula until May 1945.
events.sig: Mussolini fell two weeks after the landings. The Allies landed on the Italian mainland in September 1943 and fought up the peninsula until May 1945.
events.now: The Italian campaign dragged on until May 1945, a lesson in how costly it is to fight up a narrow, mountainous peninsula against a determined defender.

causes.why: Victory in North Africa opened the way to Sicily.

events.bluf: The Allies invaded Sicily to knock Italy out of the war and tie down German troops while the invasion of France waited. About 160,000 US, British and Canadian troops took the island in 38 days, Mussolini fell within two weeks, and Italy surrendered in September. Germany then occupied the peninsula and turned it into a front that cost the Allies twenty months of fighting and delayed nothing on the German side.
events.lens: Peripheral campaigns can bring political wins without decisive military results.
events.fact: General George Patton slapped two shell-shocked soldiers in Sicilian field hospitals and was removed from command for nearly a year.

kv: Axis troops escaped across the Strait of Messina

events.who: Fascist Grand Council; King Victor Emmanuel III; Mussolini
events.hook: Italy's own leaders voted Mussolini out and arrested him.
events.what: Italy's own leaders voted Mussolini out and arrested him.
events.story: On 25 July 1943, two weeks after the Allied landing in Sicily, the Fascist Grand Council voted against Italian leader Benito Mussolini and King Victor Emmanuel III had him arrested. Marshal Pietro Badoglio's government surrendered on 8 September. Germany occupied the north and centre, freed Mussolini from a mountain hotel and set him up as ruler of a puppet republic at Salò.
events.why: Military defeat, Allied bombing of Italian cities and the invasion of Sicily convinced Fascist leaders and the king that Mussolini had to go.
events.then: Italy fought a civil war alongside the Allied campaign. Partisans shot Mussolini on 28 April 1945 and hung his body in a Milan square.
events.sig: Italy fought a civil war alongside the Allied campaign. Partisans shot Mussolini on 28 April 1945 and hung his body in a Milan square.
events.now: Italy marks 25 April as Liberation Day, and the anti-fascist resistance is a founding myth of the Italian Republic.
events.wk: Fall of the Fascist regime in Italy

causes.why: Two weeks after the landings, Italy's own leaders turned on Mussolini.

q.before: Mussolini had ruled Italy for 21 years.
q.how: A vote by his own Fascist Grand Council and the king's arrest order.
q.winners: The king and Marshal Badoglio, briefly.
q.lasted: Mussolini returned as a German puppet until 1945.

events.bluf: Italy's Fascist Grand Council and King Victor Emmanuel III removed Benito Mussolini to get Italy out of a war it was losing. Italy surrendered in September 1943, Germany occupied the north and centre and set Mussolini up as a puppet, and the country became a battleground and a civil war at once. A dictatorship had collapsed from inside when defeat loomed, and the resistance that followed became the founding myth of the Italian Republic.
events.lens: Elites abandon a dictator when he becomes a liability; the institutions that served him can also remove him.
events.fact: Mussolini was freed from the Gran Sasso by German glider troops under Otto Skorzeny in a raid that cost no lives on either side.

kv: Fascist Grand Council vote against Mussolini

events.what: The 'Big Three' met for the first time and agreed on D-Day.
events.why: The Allies needed to coordinate the final defeat of Germany. Roosevelt wanted Soviet entry into the war against Japan and Stalin's support for a postwar United Nations.
events.sig: D-Day was set for spring 1944. Stalin agreed to join the war against Japan after Germany's defeat.
events.hook: The 'Big Three' met for the first time and agreed on D-Day.
events.story: US President Franklin Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met together for the first time in Tehran, from 28 November to 1 December 1943. Stalin, whose armies had borne most of the fighting, pressed for a second front in France; Churchill preferred operations in the Mediterranean, and Roosevelt sided with Stalin. They committed to invade France in May 1944 and agreed in principle to move Poland's borders west.
events.then: D-Day was set for spring 1944. Stalin agreed to join the war against Japan after Germany's defeat.
events.now: It began the great-power bargains that shaped postwar Europe, including Poland's new borders, decided over the heads of the Poles.

causes.why: Soviet victories gave Stalin leverage.

q.before: The Allies argued over strategy.
q.how: A unified plan for 1944.
q.lasted: The alliance held until victory, then split.

events.bluf: Soviet leader Joseph Stalin wanted a firm date for a second front in France; British Prime Minister Winston Churchill wanted to keep operating in the Mediterranean; US President Franklin Roosevelt wanted Soviet help against Japan and a postwar order. Roosevelt sided with Stalin, and the three committed to invade France in May 1944 and agreed in principle to move Poland's borders west. The bargains that shaped postwar Europe began here, over the heads of the Poles.
events.lens: Wartime allies negotiate the peace while still fighting, and whoever holds territory has the strongest hand.
events.fact: Roosevelt stayed in the Soviet embassy compound after reports of a German plot; Soviet listening devices recorded his conversations.

kv: the target date set for the invasion of France

events.what: Largest seaborne invasion in history.
events.why: Stalin had demanded a second front since 1941. The Western Allies needed to defeat Germany and reach central Europe before the Red Army did.
events.sig: Paris was freed in August 1944. Germany was squeezed between the Western Allies and the Red Army until its surrender in May 1945.
events.hook: The largest seaborne invasion ever opened the Western front.
events.story: On 6 June 1944, after months of deception about where they would land, about 156,000 American, British, Canadian and other Allied troops under American General Dwight Eisenhower crossed the Channel to five Normandy beaches, supported by airborne troops and thousands of ships. They suffered about 10,000 casualties on the first day. The beachhead held and a million men were ashore within a month.
events.then: Paris was freed in August 1944. Germany was squeezed between the Western Allies and the Red Army until its surrender in May 1945.
events.now: The line where Western and Soviet armies met became the Iron Curtain; D-Day anniversaries remain major moments of Western alliance remembrance.
events.fact: The Allies used a fake army with inflatable tanks to convince Germany the main landing would come at Calais.

sites.d: Heaviest US casualties of the landings.
Taken by British gliders in the first minutes.
Battle of the Bulge, Germany's last offensive in the West, Dec 1944.

causes.why: The Big Three agreed the date.

q.why: To open a Western front and liberate France.
q.decided: Overwhelming air and sea power, deception about the landing site, and the courage of the first waves.
q.cost: About 4,400 Allied dead on the first day.
q.changed: Germany faced a two-front war on land.

events.bluf: The Western Allies set out to open the second front in France that Stalin had demanded since 1941 and to reach central Europe before the Red Army. About 156,000 troops landed on five Normandy beaches on 6 June 1944 at a cost of about 10,000 casualties on the first day and held. Western Europe was liberated by the Western Allies rather than the Soviets, and the line where the armies met became the Cold War border.
events.lens: Where armies stand when a war ends determines the political map of the peace.

figs.rec: The largest seaborne invasion in history

toll.n: In the whole Normandy campaign each side suffered over 200,000 casualties.

events.who: Red Army vs. German Army Group Centre
events.what: Weeks after D-Day, the Soviets destroyed an entire German army group.
events.why: The Soviets aimed to drive Germany out of the USSR and reach Poland. They timed the offensive to follow D-Day, when German reserves were committed in the west.
events.sig: Poland's Home Army rose in Warsaw on 1 August 1944, hoping to free the city before the Soviets arrived. The Red Army halted on the Vistula until January 1945.
events.hook: Weeks after D-Day, the Soviets destroyed an entire German army group.
events.story: On 22 June 1944, three years to the day after Germany's invasion, the Red Army attacked German Army Group Centre in Belarus. Deceived about where the blow would fall and forbidden by Hitler to retreat, German forces were encircled at Vitebsk, Bobruisk and Minsk. In five weeks the Soviets advanced about 500 km toward the Vistula and East Prussia, destroying some 28 German divisions, a worse defeat for Germany than Stalingrad.
events.then: Poland's Home Army rose in Warsaw on 1 August 1944, hoping to free the city before the Soviets arrived. The Red Army halted on the Vistula until January 1945.
events.now: Bagration put the Red Army in Poland and decided that eastern Europe would be Soviet-occupied; it is overlooked in the West next to D-Day though it destroyed more German divisions, and the gap in memory still shapes politics between Russia and the West.

causes.why: Stalin promised an offensive to coincide with D-Day.

q.why: To liberate Belarus and push toward Germany.
q.stakes: The German front in the East.
q.decided: Soviet deception, mass and speed.
q.cost: Germany's single greatest defeat; hundreds of thousands lost.
q.changed: The Red Army reached Warsaw's outskirts.

events.bluf: The Red Army set out to destroy German Army Group Centre in Belarus and reach Poland, timing the blow to follow D-Day. In five weeks from 22 June 1944 it advanced about 500 km and destroyed some 28 German divisions, a worse defeat for Germany than Stalingrad. The Red Army stood on the Vistula and the border of East Prussia, in position to settle eastern Europe's future by occupation.
events.lens: Western memory often overlooks the decisive battles of the Eastern Front.
events.fact: Some 57,000 German prisoners from Bagration were marched through Moscow on 17 July 1944, followed by water trucks washing the streets.

figs.rec: Germany's worst military defeat of the war

events.who: Polish Home Army vs. German forces
events.what: Poland's resistance rose up to free Warsaw before the Soviets arrived, and Stalin let it be crushed.
events.why: The Home Army aimed to liberate Warsaw and give Poland's government-in-exile a claim to rule. Stalin had no interest in a Polish government he did not control.
events.sig: The Soviets took the ruined city in January 1945 and installed a communist government. Home Army veterans were persecuted under it for decades.
events.hook: Poland's resistance rose up to free Warsaw before the Soviets arrived, and Stalin let it be crushed.
events.story: On 1 August 1944 the Polish Home Army, loyal to the government-in-exile in London, rose in Warsaw as the Red Army approached. The Soviets halted across the Vistula, and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin at first refused to let Western supply planes use Soviet airfields. After 63 days the insurgents surrendered on 2 October; between 150,000 and 200,000 civilians had been killed, and Hitler ordered the city razed.
events.then: The Soviets took the ruined city in January 1945 and installed a communist government. Home Army veterans were persecuted under it for decades.
events.now: Warsaw stops for a minute every 1 August, a sign of how central the uprising is to Polish identity and its distrust of Russia.

causes.why: The Soviet advance reached Warsaw.

q.why: To free Warsaw under Polish, not Soviet, control.
q.decided: German force and Soviet inaction.
q.cost: About 150,000–200,000 civilians killed; the city about 85% destroyed.
q.changed: Communists took over Poland after the war.

events.bluf: The Polish Home Army rose to free Warsaw before the Red Army arrived and give the government-in-exile in London a claim to rule Poland. The Soviets halted across the Vistula while German forces crushed the rising over 63 days, killed between 150,000 and 200,000 civilians and razed the city. Poland's chance of a non-communist government died with it, and the memory fixed Polish distrust of Russia.
events.lens: Allies of convenience may let your forces be destroyed if it serves their postwar interest.
events.fact: By the time the Red Army entered, about 85 per cent of Warsaw's buildings had been destroyed, much of it by demolition squads after the surrender.

kv: of the city destroyed by January 1945

toll.n: German losses are disputed, from about 2,000 to 17,000 killed.

events.what: Hitler's last gamble in the West caught US troops by surprise in the winter forest.

events.hook: Hitler's last gamble in the West caught US troops by surprise in the winter forest.
events.story: On 16 December 1944 Germany attacked through the Ardennes in fog and snow, as it had in 1940, with about 200,000 men against a thinly held American sector. The advance made a bulge 100 km deep in the Allied line. US troops held the road junction at Bastogne until the weather cleared on 23 December and Allied aircraft returned. By late January 1945 the line was back where it had started, and the largest battle fought by the US Army in the war had cost it about 75,000 casualties.
events.then: Allied armies crossed the Rhine in March 1945 and Germany collapsed; its last armoured reserves had been spent in the Ardennes.
events.now: It shows how surprise can briefly overturn a lost strategic position and cannot reverse it; the reserves spent in the Ardennes were the ones Germany lacked on the Rhine and the Oder.

Germany had spent its last armour, and the Allies crossed the Rhine in March 1945 against an army with nothing left.
events.lens: Last-ditch offensives by a losing side often hasten its collapse.
events.fact: Asked to surrender at Bastogne, US General Anthony McAuliffe replied with one word, 'Nuts', which the German envoys had to have explained.

events.story: German Chancellor Adolf Hitler killed himself in his Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945 as Soviet troops fought through the city. His successor, Grand Admiral Karl Dönitz, sought a surrender to the Western Allies alone and was refused. events.now: 8 May is marked across Europe as Victory in Europe Day, and the total defeat it marked is why Germany, unlike after 1918, had no stab-in-the-back myth and rebuilt as a democracy that confronts its crimes.

events.hook: Fifty nations signed a charter to prevent another world war.
events.story: The League of Nations had failed to stop the war. Delegates from 50 nations met in San Francisco from 25 April to 26 June 1945 and drafted the Charter; Poland signed later as the 51st founder. It created a General Assembly of all members, a Secretariat and a Security Council in which the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China hold permanent seats and a veto. The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945.
events.then: The veto paralysed the Council through most of the Cold War. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in December 1948. Membership grew with decolonisation from 51 to 193, and armed peacekeeping began in 1956.
events.now: The UN has 193 members. The veto has blocked Council action on Syria, Ukraine and Gaza, and Security Council reform is debated every year without result.

Within three weeks the bomb destroyed two Japanese cities, within four years the Soviet Union had its own, and great-power relations have been conducted under the threat since.
events.lens: Once a technology is proven, others race to acquire it, and secrecy only delays them.

events.bluf: Japanese Emperor Hirohito intervened to end a war his cabinet could not agree to stop, after the atomic bombs and the Soviet declaration of war. His broadcast of 15 August 1945 told the nation to 'endure the unendurable', and the formal surrender followed aboard USS Missouri on 2 September. A US occupation under General Douglas MacArthur remade Japan into a pacifist democracy and American ally, and keeping the emperor on the throne eased the whole process.
events.lens: Preserving a defeated nation's symbols can make occupation and reform easier.
events.fact: The broadcast was the first time most Japanese had heard the emperor's voice. Army officers had tried to seize the recording the night before and failed.

events.hook: For the first time, a country's leaders were tried for 'crimes against humanity'.
events.story: From November 1945 the International Military Tribunal, with judges from the US, Britain, France and the USSR, tried 22 leading Nazis for conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and the new charge of crimes against humanity. Using the regime's own documents and film from the camps, American chief prosecutor Robert Jackson and his colleagues laid out the Holocaust in court. Twelve were sentenced to death on 1 October 1946, Reichsmarschall Hermann Göring killed himself before he could be hanged, and three were acquitted.

events.bluf: The Allies set out to punish the Nazi leaders by law rather than by summary execution, to document their crimes for history, and to establish that waging aggressive war and mass murder were crimes. The International Military Tribunal tried 22 leaders from November 1945, sentenced twelve to death and acquitted three. Leaders could now be held personally responsible for crimes against peace and humanity, the foundation of international criminal law.
events.lens: Accountability for atrocities depends on who wins the war, but trials that follow fair procedures can still build lasting law.
events.myth: Nuremberg was simply victors' justice. Only the losers were tried, and the Soviet judges sat over crimes their own state had committed; the tribunal still acquitted three defendants and rested its verdicts on the regime's own documents.

events.hook: Churchill warned that an 'iron curtain' had come down across Europe.

events.story: Soviet forces held Eastern Europe and pro-Soviet governments were taking power there. Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill spoke at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, on 5 March 1946, with President Harry Truman on the stage. From Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic, he said, an iron curtain had descended across the continent. He called for a fraternal association of the English-speaking peoples. Soviet leader Joseph Stalin replied in Pravda that Churchill was a warmonger.
events.why: Soviet control of Eastern Europe was hardening while Western opinion still hoped for cooperation with Moscow. Churchill wanted the United States committed to Europe before Britain's weakness showed.
events.then: The Truman Doctrine of March 1947 committed the United States to containing communism. The Marshall Plan followed in June 1947 and NATO in 1949.
events.sig: The Truman Doctrine of March 1947 committed the United States to containing communism. The Marshall Plan followed in June 1947 and NATO in 1949.
events.now: The speech named the division of Europe and marked the Western turn from alliance with Moscow to containment; the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan followed within fifteen months.

events.bluf: Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, out of office and with President Harry Truman beside him, set out to warn Western publics that the Soviet Union had closed off Eastern Europe and to call for an Anglo-American alliance. The speech at Fulton, Missouri, on 5 March 1946 was attacked as warmongering at the time and adopted as policy within a year. It gave the Cold War its defining phrase and framed the Western turn from alliance with Moscow to containment.
events.lens: Naming a conflict shapes how publics understand it and which policies they will support.
events.fact: Churchill had used 'iron curtain' in a telegram to Truman in May 1945; the Fulton speech made it public.

events.story: Argentine Colonel Juan Perón joined the military government of 1943 and, as secretary of labour, raised wages and backed unions. Rivals in the army arrested him in October 1945.
