Eight years of war with 400,000 French troops, torture and mass detention ended in independence in 1962. The war toppled the Fourth Republic, brought Charles de Gaulle back to power and left a legacy of trauma and migration that still shapes French and Algerian politics.
events.trig: Coordinated FLN attacks across Algeria on 1 November 1954.
events.lens: Settler colonies produce the bloodiest decolonization wars, because settlers resist leaving.
events.fact: France called the fighting 'events' and recognised it as a war in law only in 1999.

kv: European settlers left for France in 1962

toll.n: Thousands of European civilians and harkis (Algerians who served France) were also killed.

events.what: School segregation ruled unconstitutional.
events.why: The NAACP had spent two decades building cases against segregated graduate and law schools before attacking elementary schools. Warren wanted unanimity so the South could find no dissent to shelter behind.
events.sig: A second ruling in 1955 ordered desegregation 'with all deliberate speed', which Southern states read as licence to delay. Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus blocked Little Rock Central High in 1957 and President Dwight Eisenhower sent paratroopers. Most Southern schools stayed segregated until the courts and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 forced the issue.
events.hook: The Supreme Court ruled that segregated schools are unconstitutional.
events.story: Plessy v. Ferguson of 1896 had allowed separate facilities for Black and white Americans if they were equal. NAACP Legal Defense Fund chief Thurgood Marshall argued five consolidated cases, led by that of Topeka schoolgirl Linda Brown, that segregation harmed Black children whatever the facilities. Chief Justice Earl Warren, appointed in 1953, assembled a unanimous court. The ruling of 17 May 1954 held that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal'.
events.then: A second ruling in 1955 ordered desegregation 'with all deliberate speed', which Southern states read as licence to delay. Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus blocked Little Rock Central High in 1957 and President Dwight Eisenhower sent paratroopers. Most Southern schools stayed segregated until the courts and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 forced the issue.
events.now: Brown removed the legal basis of segregation and made the federal courts the engine of civil rights for two decades; schools segregated by income and neighbourhood remain the unfinished part of its work.
events.fact: Thurgood Marshall, who argued the case, became the first Black Supreme Court justice in 1967.

causes.why: The Supreme Court unanimously overturned Plessy's 'separate but equal' rule for public schools.

q.before: 'Separate but equal' segregated schools.
q.how: A unanimous Supreme Court ruling.
q.lasted: Yes, though desegregation took decades.

events.bluf: NAACP lawyers led by Thurgood Marshall set out to overturn the 'separate but equal' doctrine that had licensed school segregation since 1896. On 17 May 1954 the Supreme Court under Chief Justice Earl Warren ruled unanimously that segregated schools are inherently unequal. The ruling gave the civil rights movement constitutional backing; enforcing it took federal troops and two decades of litigation.
events.lens: Court rulings can change the law faster than society, and enforcement sets the pace.
events.btt: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka

kv: of Black students in the South attended school with white students by 1964

events.who: France, Viet Minh, Britain, USSR, China and the US
events.where: Geneva (signed); Vietnam split at the 17th parallel
events.hook: Vietnam was split at the 17th parallel, supposedly until elections in 1956.
events.what: Vietnam was split at the 17th parallel, supposedly until elections in 1956.
events.story: At Geneva, France agreed to leave Indochina. Vietnam was temporarily divided at the 17th parallel, with Vietnamese leader Ho Chi Minh's communists in the North and a French-backed state in the South. Nationwide elections were promised for 1956. The United States took note of the accords without signing them.
events.why: France had lost at Dien Bien Phu. The great powers wanted to avoid a wider war, and China pressed Ho to accept partition.
events.then: The US-backed South under Ngo Dinh Diem refused to hold the elections. A communist insurgency grew in the South from the late 1950s.
events.sig: The US-backed South under Ngo Dinh Diem refused to hold the elections. A communist insurgency grew in the South from the late 1950s.
events.now: Vietnam was reunified only by war, in 1975; the elections promised at Geneva never happened, a reminder that peace deals without enforcement often fail.

causes.why: Dien Bien Phu fell the day before the Geneva conference took up Indochina, and France negotiated its exit.

sites.d: Temporary line dividing North and South.
Conference that split Vietnam.

q.before: French Indochina.
q.how: An international conference.
q.winners: The Viet Minh in the North.
q.lasted: No: the division became permanent until war ended it.

events.bluf: France wanted out of Indochina after Dien Bien Phu, and Britain, the Soviet Union, China and the United States wanted to avoid a wider war. At Geneva in July 1954 Vietnam was divided at the 17th parallel, with Vietnamese leader Ho Chi Minh's communists in the North and a French-backed state in the South, and nationwide elections were promised for 1956. The US-backed South refused to hold them, and the temporary line became the front of the Vietnam War.
events.lens: Temporary partitions tend to become permanent, or become wars.
events.fact: Close to a million people, most of them Catholics, moved from North to South in the 300 days of free movement the accords allowed.

kv: northerners moved south, most of them Catholics

events.who: 29 Asian and African countries: Sukarno, Nehru, Zhou Enlai, Nasser
events.hook: Leaders of newly independent Asian and African nations met to chart a path between the superpowers.
events.what: Leaders of newly independent Asian and African nations met to chart a path between the superpowers.
events.story: The Asian-African Conference met at Bandung in April 1955 with 29 countries representing over half the world's people. Indonesian President Sukarno hosted; Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai and Egyptian leader Gamal Abdel Nasser led the main delegations. They condemned colonialism 'in all its manifestations' and called for peaceful coexistence and economic cooperation.
events.why: Newly independent states wanted to complete decolonisation. They refused to be forced to choose between the American and Soviet blocs.
events.then: It inspired the Non-Aligned Movement, founded at Belgrade in 1961, and African independence movements.
events.sig: It inspired the Non-Aligned Movement, founded at Belgrade in 1961, and African independence movements.
events.now: Bandung created the Afro-Asian bloc that drove the UN General Assembly's decolonisation agenda from 1960 and the Non-Aligned Movement of 1961; its vocabulary is the one the Global South still uses.

causes.why: Sukarno's Indonesia hosted the first great gathering of newly independent Asian and African states.

q.before: Colonial powers and Cold War blocs dominated world affairs.
q.how: A conference of newly independent states.
q.claim: Solidarity of Asia and Africa against colonialism.
q.winners: Leaders like Nehru, Sukarno and Nasser.
q.lasted: It inspired the Non-Aligned Movement.

events.bluf: Indonesian President Sukarno, Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai and Egyptian leader Gamal Abdel Nasser gathered 29 Asian and African states to complete decolonisation and refuse a choice between the American and Soviet blocs. The conference condemned colonialism 'in all its manifestations' and called for peaceful coexistence. It founded the idea of a 'Third World' and led to the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961.
events.lens: Newly independent states seek a collective voice to avoid being pawns of great powers.
events.fact: A chartered plane carrying Chinese delegates to the conference was bombed in flight; Premier Zhou Enlai had changed his route and survived.

events.who: Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr.
events.what: Year-long boycott of segregated buses.
events.why: Parks's arrest gave an organised community its case. Montgomery's Black churches, the Women's Political Council and the NAACP had the networks to sustain a year without buses.
events.sig: Buses were integrated on 21 December 1956. King's home had been bombed in January 1956; he founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference in 1957 and carried the method to Birmingham and Selma.
events.hook: A seamstress refused to give up her seat, and a city's bus system went broke.
events.story: Montgomery, Alabama, required Black passengers to give up seats to whites. On 1 December 1955 NAACP branch secretary Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing. The Women's Political Council and NAACP activist E. D. Nixon called a one-day boycott, and Black residents formed the Montgomery Improvement Association with 26-year-old Baptist minister Martin Luther King Jr. as president. The boycott ran for 381 days, sustained by car pools and walking. The Supreme Court affirmed in November 1956 that bus segregation was unconstitutional.
events.then: Buses were integrated on 21 December 1956. King's home had been bombed in January 1956; he founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference in 1957 and carried the method to Birmingham and Selma.
events.now: The boycott established the method, mass nonviolent action with economic pressure and a legal case behind it, that the civil rights movement used for the next decade, and it produced the movement's leader.
events.fact: It lasted 381 days, and King was 26 when it began.

causes.why: Brown energised activists. A year later, Rosa Parks's arrest launched the bus boycott and made Martin Luther King Jr. a national figure.

q.before: Segregated buses enforced by law.
q.how: A 381-day boycott and a lawsuit.
q.lasted: Yes: bus segregation ended.

events.bluf: Montgomery's Black residents set out to end segregated seating on the city's buses by refusing to ride them. The boycott, led by 26-year-old Baptist minister Martin Luther King Jr., lasted 381 days until the Supreme Court struck down bus segregation in November 1956. It showed that organised nonviolent economic pressure could beat Jim Crow and made King the leader of a national movement.
events.lens: Boycotts give the powerless leverage when they control demand.

events.what: Revolt crushed by Soviet tanks.
events.why: Soviet control itself was the grievance. Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin in February had loosened the fear that held the bloc together, and Poland had won a partial relaxation in October without invasion.
events.sig: The West, divided by the Suez crisis the same week, confined itself to protest. Moscow installed János Kádár, who had Nagy executed and later allowed a softer 'goulash communism'. Western communist parties lost members over the invasion.
events.hook: Hungarians rose up against Soviet rule, and Soviet tanks crushed them.
events.story: On 23 October 1956 a student demonstration in Budapest grew into a nationwide uprising. Reform communist Imre Nagy became prime minister, promised free elections and, on 1 November, announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact and become neutral. On 4 November Soviet tanks entered Budapest and crushed the revolt; about 2,500 Hungarians were killed and 200,000 fled. Nagy was tried in secret and hanged in 1958.
events.then: The West, divided by the Suez crisis the same week, confined itself to protest. Moscow installed János Kádár, who had Nagy executed and later allowed a softer 'goulash communism'. Western communist parties lost members over the invasion.
events.now: The crushing of the uprising showed that the West would not intervene behind the Iron Curtain and that Moscow would use force to hold its bloc; the rule held until 1989.

causes.why: Khrushchev's 1956 'Secret Speech' denouncing Stalin encouraged reformers in Eastern Europe. When Hungary tried to leave the Warsaw Pact, Soviet tanks crushed it.

q.why: Hungarians demanded freedom from Soviet control.
q.decided: Soviet tanks.
q.cost: About 2,500 Hungarians and 700 Soviet soldiers killed.
q.changed: Soviet control of Eastern Europe was reaffirmed.

events.bluf: Hungarians rose to end Soviet control, and reform communist Imre Nagy as prime minister promised free elections and neutrality. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev sent in tanks and crushed the rising in a week, at a cost of about 2,500 Hungarian dead and 200,000 refugees. Moscow had shown it would use force to hold its bloc, the West had shown it would stay out, and the division of Europe held on those terms until 1989.
events.lens: Spheres of influence are enforced by force and tacitly accepted by rivals unwilling to risk war.
events.fact: Hungary marks 23 October as a national holiday.

toll.n: Imre Nagy was executed in 1958.

events.who: Nasser; Britain, France, Israel; US & USSR
events.what: Britain, France and Israel invaded after Nasser nationalized the canal.
events.why: Nasser nationalised the canal to pay for the Aswan Dam after the United States and Britain withdrew funding. British Prime Minister Anthony Eden read him as a dictator to be removed.
events.sig: Nasser became the hero of the Arab world, Eden resigned, and the UN sent its first armed peacekeeping force.
events.hook: Egypt took control of the Suez Canal and broke the last of Britain's imperial power.
events.story: In July 1956 Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the British- and French-owned Suez Canal Company. Britain, France and Israel secretly agreed that Israel would invade Sinai and the two European powers would intervene as 'peacekeepers' to seize the canal. When they attacked in October and November, US President Dwight Eisenhower threatened to sink the British pound, the Soviets threatened rocket attacks, and the invaders withdrew.
events.then: Nasser became the hero of the Arab world, Eden resigned, and the UN sent its first armed peacekeeping force.
events.now: The crisis marked the moment the United States replaced Britain and France as the dominant Western power in the Middle East.
events.fact: Eisenhower forced Britain to retreat by threatening to dump US holdings of British pounds.

sites.d: British and French paratroopers landed.
Israel's invasion route.

causes.why: Nasser's 1952 revolution ended British influence; when he nationalised the canal in 1956, Britain, France and Israel invaded.
Israel joined Britain and France in 1956, seeking to stop raids from Egyptian-held Gaza and to reopen its shipping lanes.
Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956 to pay for the Aswan Dam and to assert Egyptian sovereignty.

q.before: Britain and France owned the canal company.
q.how: Nationalisation, then an invasion forced back by US pressure.
q.lasted: Yes: Egypt kept the canal.

events.bluf: Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal to pay for the Aswan Dam; Britain, France and Israel invaded to take it back and to bring him down. The United States forced them out within days by threatening the pound. Britain and France lost the capacity to act as independent imperial powers, and the United States and the Soviet Union stood confirmed as the arbiters of the Middle East.
events.trig: Nasser's nationalisation of the canal in July 1956.
events.lens: Middle powers that act against their superpower patron's wishes discover how dependent they are.

events.who: Fidel Castro, Raúl Castro, Che Guevara and 79 other rebels
events.hook: Castro sailed from Mexico with 82 men to start a guerrilla war; only a few dozen survived the first days.
events.what: Castro sailed from Mexico with 82 men to start a guerrilla war; only a few dozen survived the first days.
events.story: The overcrowded yacht Granma left Tuxpan, Mexico, with 82 men and landed at Playa Las Coloradas on 2 December 1956, two days late. Cuban President Fulgencio Batista's army ambushed the rebels at Alegría de Pío on 5 December. About 20 survivors, including Fidel Castro, his brother Raúl Castro and Argentine doctor Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, regrouped in the Sierra Maestra mountains.
events.why: Cuban revolutionary Fidel Castro had sworn to overthrow Batista after his failed attack on the Moncada barracks in 1953 and his release in an amnesty in 1955.
events.then: The guerrillas grew into an army as Batista's repression alienated Cubans, and Batista fled on 1 January 1959.
events.sig: The guerrillas grew into an army as Batista's repression alienated Cubans, and Batista fled on 1 January 1959.
events.now: The landing began the guerrilla war that took Havana in two years and put a Soviet ally ninety miles from Florida; the Cuban revolution's method was copied across Latin America for three decades.

q.why: To overthrow the dictator Fulgencio Batista.
q.decided: Guerrilla endurance in the mountains.
q.cost: Most of the 82 were killed or captured in the first days.
q.changed: A small band grew into a revolutionary army.

events.bluf: Cuban revolutionary Fidel Castro sailed from Mexico with 81 others to start a guerrilla war against Cuban President Fulgencio Batista, in power since a 1952 coup. The landing went badly: the Granma arrived two days late and the army scattered the force within days. The survivors regrouped in the Sierra Maestra and built an army that took power on 1 January 1959, and the landing became the founding act of the Cuban state.
events.lens: Small guerrilla groups can grow when the regime they fight has lost popular legitimacy.
events.fact: The Cuban Communist Party's daily newspaper is named Granma, and so is the province where the boat landed.

events.who: The FLN; French paratroopers under General Jacques Massu
events.hook: French paratroopers broke the FLN in Algiers using torture, winning the battle but losing the argument.
events.what: French paratroopers broke the FLN in Algiers using torture, winning the battle but losing the argument.
events.story: In 1956-57 the FLN bombed cafés and called a general strike in Algiers. From January 1957 French General Jacques Massu's 10th Parachute Division took control of the city and arrested thousands; torture and disappearances were widespread. By October the FLN network in the city had been destroyed.
events.why: The FLN wanted the war in the capital where the world press could see it. The French government wanted it crushed and gave the army the powers to do so.
events.then: Revelations of torture turned French and world opinion against the war, and Algeria won independence in 1962.
events.sig: Revelations of torture turned French and world opinion against the war, and Algeria won independence in 1962.
events.now: France won the battle with torture and lost the argument: the methods discredited the war at home and abroad, and Algeria was independent five years later.

causes.why: The FLN brought the war into the capital.

q.why: The FLN fought for independence; France to keep Algeria French.
q.stakes: Control of Algiers, and international opinion.
q.decided: Mass arrests and torture by French troops.
q.cost: Thousands of civilians killed or disappeared.
q.changed: France won the battle but lost the moral argument.

events.bluf: The FLN brought the war into Algiers to win world attention; France handed French General Jacques Massu's paratroopers police powers to crush it. The paratroopers destroyed the FLN network in the city by October 1957 using systematic torture. France won the battle and lost the argument, and Algiers became the standard case of counterinsurgency's moral costs.
events.lens: Torture can win tactical battles while losing the political war.
events.fact: The 1966 film of the battle is still studied by armies; the Pentagon screened it in 2003 before the occupation of Iraq.

events.what: First sub-Saharan colony to win independence.
events.why: Nkrumah's mass movement won elections Britain could ignore only by force, and a weakened Britain saw a gradual handover as the best way to keep influence.
events.sig: Nkrumah championed pan-Africanism and backed independence movements across the continent. He made Ghana a one-party state in 1964 and was overthrown by the army in February 1966.
events.hook: Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence.
events.story: Ghanaian nationalist Kwame Nkrumah founded the Convention People's Party in 1949 and called a campaign of strikes and boycotts. Britain jailed him in 1950; his party won the 1951 election while he was in prison, and Britain released him to lead the government. On 6 March 1957 the Gold Coast became independent Ghana, named after a medieval West African empire, with Nkrumah as prime minister.
events.then: Nkrumah championed pan-Africanism and backed independence movements across the continent. He made Ghana a one-party state in 1964 and was overthrown by the army in February 1966.
events.now: Ghana's independence opened the floodgates of African decolonisation, and its return to stable democracy since 1992 has made it a regional model.
events.fact: Nkrumah named the country after the medieval Ghana Empire, which lay hundreds of miles away in today's Mali and Mauritania.

q.before: British colonial rule.
q.how: Elections and negotiations.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Ghanaian Prime Minister Kwame Nkrumah's Convention People's Party set out to win self-government from Britain through strikes, boycotts and elections. Britain conceded, and the Gold Coast became Ghana on 6 March 1957, the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence from European rule. The example set off a wave of independence across the continent, and Nkrumah became the leading voice of pan-Africanism before his rule turned authoritarian.
events.lens: The first success in a wave of independence inspires and accelerates the rest.

events.what: Common market created.
events.why: The founders wanted war between France and Germany made impractical by shared industry and trade. They also wanted a market large enough to compete with the United States and a voice between the superpowers.
events.sig: Britain joined in 1973. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the European Union and set the path to a single currency. The Union had 27 members after Britain's departure in 2020.
events.hook: Six countries started the common market that became the European Union.
events.story: The European Coal and Steel Community of 1951 had pooled the six countries' war industries. On 25 March 1957 France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg signed the treaty in Rome creating the European Economic Community, with a common market, a customs union and a commission in Brussels. It came into force on 1 January 1958.
events.then: Britain joined in 1973. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the European Union and set the path to a single currency. The Union had 27 members after Britain's departure in 2020.
events.now: The six founders and the states that joined them have fought no war among themselves since 1957; the euro crisis of 2010 and Brexit in 2016 showed where pooled sovereignty strains.

causes.why: Marshall aid required European countries to plan their recovery together, an early step toward integration.

q.before: Separate national economies in Western Europe.
q.how: A treaty creating a common market.
q.lasted: Yes: it grew into the EU.

events.bluf: France, West Germany, Italy and the Benelux countries set out to tie their economies together so that war among them became impractical and to give Europe weight between the superpowers. The treaty created a common market with a customs union and shared institutions. It grew into the European Union of 27 states, the furthest any group of states has gone in pooling sovereignty.
events.lens: Economic interdependence can make war between former enemies unthinkable.
events.fact: The Commission the treaty created had nine members; today's has 27, one per member state.

events.who: The Soviet space programme, led by chief designer Sergei Korolev
events.what: Soviets launched the first satellite.
events.why: The Soviets had built the R-7 and could prove it with a satellite. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev wanted the prestige of beating the United States.
events.sig: The United States created NASA in 1958 and passed the National Defense Education Act the same year. The Advanced Research Projects Agency, also founded in 1958, funded the work that led to the internet.
events.hook: A beeping Soviet ball in orbit panicked the US into the space race.
events.story: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a 58 cm metal sphere that beeped radio signals as it circled the Earth every 96 minutes. The launcher was the R-7, the first intercontinental ballistic missile, built by chief designer Sergei Korolev's team. Americans grasped that a rocket able to orbit a satellite could carry a nuclear warhead across the world.
events.then: The United States created NASA in 1958 and passed the National Defense Education Act the same year. The Advanced Research Projects Agency, also founded in 1958, funded the work that led to the internet.
events.now: The space race the launch set off produced the satellites that carry GPS, television and weather forecasting, and the research funding, through NASA and DARPA, from which the internet grew.
events.fact: Sputnik was a polished ball that only beeped, and amateur radio operators around the world could hear it pass overhead.

causes.why: The nuclear arms race drove the rocket race: Sputnik's launcher was a missile designed to carry hydrogen bombs.

q.problem: Could a rocket put an object into orbit?
q.how: The R-7 missile, adapted to carry a small satellite.
q.replaced: American confidence in its technological lead.
q.spread: The US launched its first satellite four months later.
q.next: NASA, the space race and the Moon landing.

events.bluf: The Soviet space programme under chief designer Sergei Korolev launched the first artificial satellite to prove the R-7 missile and to beat the United States into orbit. It succeeded. Americans read it as proof that Soviet rockets could reach them with nuclear warheads, and the United States answered with NASA, a surge in science funding and the research agency whose work later produced the internet.
events.lens: Technological shocks from a rival can spur massive public investment.

events.hook: Malaya became independent from Britain while a communist insurgency was still being fought.
events.what: Malaya became independent from Britain while a communist insurgency was still being fought.
events.story: Malayan leader Tunku Abdul Rahman's Alliance of Malay, Chinese and Indian parties won the elections of 1955. Britain granted independence on 31 August 1957 with the Tunku as prime minister. The Malayan Emergency against communist guerrillas, declared in 1948, lasted until 1960.
events.why: Britain wanted to hand power to moderate leaders who would protect its rubber and tin interests. An inter-ethnic alliance offered a stable partner while the communist insurgency was being defeated.
events.then: Malaya joined with Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak to form Malaysia in 1963. It expelled Singapore two years later amid ethnic tensions.
events.sig: Malaya joined with Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak to form Malaysia in 1963. It expelled Singapore two years later amid ethnic tensions.
events.now: The 1957 bargain, Malay political primacy with citizenship for Chinese and Indians, is the constitution Malaysia still governs under; its politics turn on relations between the ethnic communities.

q.before: British colonial rule.
q.how: Negotiated independence.
q.lasted: Yes; Malaysia was formed in 1963.

events.bluf: Britain set out to hand Malaya to moderate leaders who would protect its rubber and tin interests while British forces fought a communist insurgency; Malayan leader Tunku Abdul Rahman set out to win independence by negotiation with an alliance of Malay, Chinese and Indian parties. Independence came on 31 August 1957. The model of Malay political dominance with ethnic power-sharing still defines Malaysian politics, and the Emergency ended in 1960.
events.lens: Power-sharing between ethnic communities can secure independence but freeze ethnic politics.
events.fact: The Tunku shouted 'Merdeka', freedom, seven times at the independence ceremony in the stadium built for it.

events.what: Forced collectivization and industrialization.
events.why: Mao's belief that mass mobilisation could leap past economic limits came first, then rivalry with the Soviet Union, and a political system in which no one dared report failure.
events.sig: The famine of 1959-61 killed tens of millions; most estimates range from 15 to 45 million. Mao stepped back from day-to-day management, and pragmatists such as Chinese President Liu Shaoqi and party secretary-general Deng Xiaoping restored some private farming.
events.hook: Mao's push to industrialize overnight caused the deadliest famine in history.
events.story: In 1958 Chinese Chairman Mao Zedong launched a campaign to overtake Britain's industrial output within 15 years. Peasants were herded into vast communes with communal kitchens and ordered to make steel in backyard furnaces, often melting down their own tools. Local officials, afraid of punishment, reported impossible harvests, and the state took grain on the basis of those false figures, even exporting it, while villages starved.
events.then: The famine of 1959-61 killed tens of millions; most estimates range from 15 to 45 million. Mao stepped back from day-to-day management, and pragmatists such as Chinese President Liu Shaoqi and party secretary-general Deng Xiaoping restored some private farming.
events.now: The famine was hidden for decades and remains politically sensitive in China, where the party's official verdict speaks of 'mistakes' and protects Mao's standing; the leap is the standard case of a system in which fear of reporting failure turns error into catastrophe.
events.fact: Villagers melted pots and tools in backyard furnaces to meet steel quotas, producing mostly useless iron.

causes.why: Confident after land reform and the first five-year plan, Mao tried to overtake Britain's industrial output in fifteen years through mass mobilisation.

q.before: Peasants farmed in small cooperatives.
q.how: Mass campaigns and giant communes.
q.lasted: Abandoned by 1961 after famine.

events.bluf: Chinese Chairman Mao Zedong launched the Great Leap Forward in 1958 to overtake Britain's industrial output within 15 years by mass mobilisation into communes and backyard furnaces. Officials falsified harvests, the state requisitioned grain on the false figures and exported it while villages starved, and the famine of 1959-61 killed between 15 and 45 million people, the deadliest on record. Mao's standing fell, pragmatists restored private farming, and his bid to recover power became the Cultural Revolution.
events.lens: When officials are punished for bad news, the state flies blind, and bad policy becomes catastrophe.

figs.rec: Likely the deadliest famine in history
kv: famine deaths, 1959–61 (most estimates fall between 15 and 45 million)

events.what: Batista overthrown.
events.why: Batista's dictatorship had closed the electoral route after 1952. Inequality between Havana and the countryside was wide, and US companies owned much of the sugar, utilities and mines. Batista's army lost the will to fight in 1958.
events.sig: Cuban leader Fidel Castro nationalised US businesses in 1960, and the United States imposed an embargo and broke relations. Cuba allied with the Soviet Union, which led to the missile crisis of 1962. Cuba backed guerrillas in Latin America and sent troops to Angola and Ethiopia, and more than a million Cubans emigrated over the following decades.
events.hook: Fidel Castro's guerrillas took power in Cuba, creating a communist state 90 miles from the US.
events.story: After a failed attack on the Moncada barracks in 1953 and a near-disastrous landing in 1956, Cuban revolutionary Fidel Castro, his brother Raúl Castro and Argentine doctor Ernesto 'Che' Guevara built a guerrilla army in the Sierra Maestra. Cuban President Fulgencio Batista's army lost ground, the United States stopped selling him arms in 1958, and Batista fled on New Year's Day 1959. Castro had promised elections and held none.
events.then: Cuban leader Fidel Castro nationalised US businesses in 1960, and the United States imposed an embargo and broke relations. Cuba allied with the Soviet Union, which led to the missile crisis of 1962. Cuba backed guerrillas in Latin America and sent troops to Angola and Ethiopia, and more than a million Cubans emigrated over the following decades.
events.now: Cuba remains a one-party state in economic crisis, losing population to emigration. The Cuban government and its supporters hold that the revolution delivered universal health care and literacy under a US siege; its opponents hold that it delivered political prisoners, poverty and exile under one-party rule.
events.fact: Cuban intelligence claims there were more than 600 plots to kill Castro. He died of old age in 2016.

sites.d: Castro's guerrilla base.
Che's victory that made Batista flee.
Castro entered January 8, 1959.

causes.why: Che Guevara was in Guatemala during the coup; it convinced him and other radicals that reform required armed revolution.
The Granma survivors became the core of Castro's rebel army.

q.before: Fulgencio Batista's dictatorship.
q.how: Guerrilla war.
q.claim: A revolution for Cuban independence and social justice.
q.lasted: Yes: the Communist Party still rules.

events.bluf: Cuban revolutionary Fidel Castro's movement set out to overthrow Cuban President Fulgencio Batista, who had taken power in a 1952 coup. Batista fled on 1 January 1959, and Castro built a one-party socialist state allied with the Soviet Union 90 miles from Florida. Cuba became a Cold War flashpoint and the model for guerrilla movements across Latin America, and the US embargo imposed in 1960-62 remains in force.
events.lens: US-backed dictatorships that block reform can produce revolutions hostile to the United States.

events.hook: When Defence Minister Peng Dehuai criticised the Great Leap, Mao purged him, and the famine grew worse.
events.what: When Defence Minister Peng Dehuai criticised the Great Leap, Mao purged him, and the famine grew worse.
events.story: At a party meeting at the mountain resort of Lushan in July 1959, Chinese Defence Minister Peng Dehuai wrote Chairman Mao Zedong a letter about the Great Leap's failures. Mao denounced him as anti-party and replaced him with Lin Biao. Officials stopped reporting bad news, and grain was still taken from starving villages.
events.why: Mao treated criticism of the Great Leap as an attack on his authority, and no one in the leadership dared defend Peng.
events.then: Officials, terrified of being labelled 'rightists', kept inflating harvest figures, and the famine of 1959-61 killed an estimated 15 to 45 million people.
events.sig: Officials, terrified of being labelled 'rightists', kept inflating harvest figures, and the famine of 1959-61 killed an estimated 15 to 45 million people.
events.now: Peng was cleared after Mao's death, in 1978; the purge is the standard case of one-man rule silencing warnings, and the Great Leap famine went on to kill tens of millions.

causes.why: Peng Dehuai's criticism of the Leap led to his purge.

q.before: Mao led the party, but senior leaders could still speak up.
q.how: A purge at a party meeting.
q.winners: Mao and loyalists such as Lin Biao.
q.lasted: The famine continued until 1961.

events.bluf: Chinese Chairman Mao Zedong purged Defence Minister Peng Dehuai at Lushan in July 1959 for a letter criticising the Great Leap, to stop criticism of the leap from becoming criticism of himself. Peng lost his post to Lin Biao and the leadership closed ranks. Officials stopped reporting bad news, grain was still taken from starving villages, and the famine of 1959-61 went on to kill an estimated 15 to 45 million people.
events.lens: Punishing those who report bad news guarantees that more goes unreported.
events.fact: Peng died in 1974 after years of persecution in the Cultural Revolution and was rehabilitated in 1978.

events.hook: Hawaii became the 50th US state.
events.what: Hawaii became the 50th US state.
events.story: Hawaii had been a US territory since 1898, five years after American businessmen overthrew its queen, and had sought statehood since the 1930s. Southern Democrats in Congress blocked it, fearing two more senators for civil rights. Alaska was admitted in January 1959. US President Dwight Eisenhower signed the Hawaii Admission Act in March 1959; in a June referendum 94 per cent voted yes, and Hawaii became the 50th state on 21 August 1959. The ballot offered statehood or continued territorial status, with no option of independence.
events.why: Hawaii's place as the Pacific Fleet's base and its growing population of US citizens made continued territorial status hard to defend. Admitting Alaska first balanced the parties' fears about new senators.
events.then: Statehood brought full representation in Congress and a boom in jet-age tourism and migration from the mainland. The United Nations struck Hawaii from its list of non-self-governing territories in 1959.
events.sig: Statehood brought full representation in Congress and a boom in jet-age tourism and migration from the mainland. The United Nations struck Hawaii from its list of non-self-governing territories in 1959.
events.now: Statehood settled Hawaii's place in the United States for most of its people and left the sovereignty question open: Native Hawaiian movements contest the annexation that preceded it, and the 1993 apology resolution acknowledged their claim without acting on it.

causes.why: After 61 years as a territory, Hawaii became a state.

q.before: Hawaii was a US territory.
q.how: An act of Congress and a referendum.
q.winners: Hawaii's voters and the tourism industry.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Hawaii's territorial leaders wanted statehood and the full representation that went with it; Southern Democrats in Congress had blocked it for years, in part because the islands' people were mostly Asian and Hawaiian. After Alaska's admission in January 1959 Congress passed the Admission Act, 94 per cent of voters said yes in June, and Hawaii became the 50th state on 21 August 1959. Statehood brought full citizenship and a jet-age tourism boom, and left unanswered the question Native Hawaiians were given no chance to vote on, independence.
events.lens: Referendums that offer limited choices can legitimize outcomes some groups never accepted.
events.fact: Daniel Inouye, a decorated Japanese-American veteran, became the state's first congressman in 1959 and sat in the Senate from 1963 until his death in 2012.

events.who: South African police; Pan Africanist Congress protesters
events.hook: Police fired on a crowd protesting against the pass laws, killing 69 people.
events.what: Police fired on a crowd protesting against the pass laws, killing 69 people.
events.story: On 21 March 1960 thousands gathered at Sharpeville police station south of Johannesburg to protest against the laws forcing Black South Africans to carry passes. Police opened fire and killed 69 people, many of them shot in the back; about 180 were wounded.
events.why: PAC leader Robert Sobukwe had launched a campaign of mass arrest against the pass laws, and the police at Sharpeville faced a crowd many times their number.
events.then: The government declared a state of emergency and banned the ANC and PAC in April 1960. Both formed armed wings in 1961, and the UN Security Council condemned South Africa for the first time.
events.sig: The government declared a state of emergency and banned the ANC and PAC in April 1960. Both formed armed wings in 1961, and the UN Security Council condemned South Africa for the first time.
events.now: Sharpeville ended the hope of peaceful change inside South Africa: the ANC and PAC were banned, turned to armed struggle in 1961 and stayed banned for thirty years, and the UN began its campaign against apartheid.

causes.why: Protests against apartheid's pass laws were met with gunfire.

q.before: Apartheid laws controlled where Black people could live and work.
q.how: Police violence against a peaceful protest.
q.winners: The apartheid state, in the short term.
q.lasted: Apartheid lasted three more decades.

events.bluf: The Pan Africanist Congress called Black South Africans to leave their passes at home and present themselves for arrest to break the pass laws. On 21 March 1960 police at Sharpeville fired on a crowd of thousands and killed 69, many shot in the back. The government banned the ANC and PAC, both turned to armed struggle in 1961, and apartheid became a target of worldwide condemnation.
events.lens: When peaceful protest is met with massacre, movements turn to arms.
events.trig: The PAC's anti-pass campaign of 21 March 1960.
events.fact: 21 March is Human Rights Day in South Africa and the UN's International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.

events.who: 17 newly independent nations incl. Nigeria, Congo, Senegal
events.what: 17 countries became independent in a single year.
events.why: World War II had weakened the European powers and the United States and the UN pressed them to leave. Nationalist movements were strong. France chose rapid independence to keep influence through cooperation agreements.
events.sig: Military coups swept the continent from the mid-1960s. France kept political, military and monetary ties with its former colonies, including the CFA franc.
events.hook: Seventeen African countries became independent in a single year.
events.story: In 1960 seventeen African countries won independence, among them Nigeria, Congo, Senegal, Madagascar, Somalia, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire and most of French West and Central Africa. In February British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan told South Africa's parliament that a 'wind of change' was blowing through the continent. Congo's crisis began within days of its independence on 30 June.
events.then: Military coups swept the continent from the mid-1960s. France kept political, military and monetary ties with its former colonies, including the CFA franc.
events.now: Most of Africa's map, and many of its political challenges, date from this moment; the recent expulsion of French troops from the Sahel shows those post-independence ties are still contested.

causes.why: Suez showed that Britain and France could no longer act as imperial powers without US approval, and decolonisation accelerated.
Nkrumah's Ghana showed independence was possible and championed pan-Africanism.
Bandung's condemnation of colonialism encouraged African independence movements.

q.before: Most of Africa was ruled by European colonial powers.
q.how: Negotiated independence, mostly peaceful.
q.lasted: Yes, though many democracies soon gave way to one-party rule or coups.

events.bluf: France, Britain and Belgium each decided in 1960 that handing over power was cheaper than holding on, and seventeen African colonies became states in a single year. The new states inherited colonial borders, export economies built around raw materials and few trained administrators, and within months Congo was in crisis. Africa's map was fixed, and Cold War rivalry, coups and conflict followed alongside the building of new national identities and institutions.
events.lens: Independence transfers sovereignty, but economic structures and borders inherited from empire shape what comes next.
events.fact: The UN admitted sixteen new African members in a single session in 1960, the largest intake in its history.

events.who: Patrice Lumumba; Katangan secessionists, with Belgian officers present
events.hook: Congo's first elected prime minister was murdered seven months after independence.
events.what: Congo's first elected prime minister was murdered seven months after independence.
events.story: Congolese Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba had denounced Belgian colonialism at the independence ceremony of 30 June 1960. Within weeks the army mutinied and Katanga seceded with Belgian support. Congolese President Joseph Kasa-Vubu dismissed Lumumba in September, Colonel Joseph Mobutu's soldiers arrested him, and he was flown to Katanga and shot on 17 January 1961 with Belgian officers present. The CIA had earlier plotted to poison him.
events.why: Belgium and the United States feared Lumumba would turn to the Soviet Union. Congolese rivals in Léopoldville and Katanga wanted him gone.
events.then: Congo slid into civil war. Mobutu seized power in 1965 and ruled for 32 years with Western support while looting the state.
events.sig: Congo slid into civil war. Mobutu seized power in 1965 and ruled for 32 years with Western support while looting the state.
events.now: The killing cleared the way for Congolese President Mobutu Sese Seko's 32-year rule and fixed the pattern of outside powers choosing Congo's rulers. Belgium apologised in 2022 and returned his only remains, a tooth, to his family.

causes.why: Congo's rushed independence in June 1960 collapsed into mutiny and secession within weeks; Lumumba was murdered in January 1961.

q.before: Lumumba was Congo's elected prime minister.
q.how: Dismissal, arrest and murder.
q.claim: His enemies called him a communist threat.
q.winners: Mobutu, Katangan secessionists and their foreign backers.
q.lasted: Mobutu ruled from 1965 to 1997.

events.bluf: Belgium, the United States and Congolese rivals wanted Congolese Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba gone, fearing he would bring the Soviet Union into Congo. Katangan secessionists shot him on 17 January 1961 with Belgian officers present, after Colonel Joseph Mobutu's soldiers had delivered him. Congo's elected government lost its leader seven months after independence, Mobutu ruled from 1965 to 1997 with Western backing, and Lumumba became the symbol of betrayed African independence.
events.lens: Cold War powers often preferred reliable dictators to unpredictable democrats.

events.hook: A Soviet pilot orbited the Earth once, becoming the first person in space.
events.what: A Soviet pilot orbited the Earth once, becoming the first person in space.
events.story: On 12 April 1961 cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin's Vostok 1 lifted off from Baikonur and circled the Earth once in 108 minutes. He ejected during the descent, as planned, and parachuted down near Saratov. He was 27.
events.why: The Soviet Union had a lead in heavy rockets from its missile programme. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev wanted Cold War prestige.
events.then: On 25 May 1961 US President John F. Kennedy committed the United States to landing a man on the Moon before the decade ended. The space race became a central front of the Cold War. Gagarin died in a training flight in 1968.
events.sig: On 25 May 1961 US President John F. Kennedy committed the United States to landing a man on the Moon before the decade ended. The space race became a central front of the Cold War. Gagarin died in a training flight in 1968.
events.now: Gagarin's flight made manned spaceflight the measure of a superpower; the contest it started is run again today between the United States and China, with the Moon once more the goal.

causes.why: The Soviet lead in rockets let them put the first man in space.

q.problem: Could a human survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry?
q.how: A rocket put a capsule in orbit; it re-entered and Gagarin parachuted out.
q.replaced: Flights carrying only animals or instruments.
q.spread: Alan Shepard flew three weeks later, and John Glenn orbited in 1962.
q.next: The race to the Moon.

events.bluf: The Soviet programme under chief designer Sergei Korolev put cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin into orbit to claim the first human spaceflight and the prestige that went with it. He circled the Earth once in 108 minutes and landed safely. The United States answered within six weeks with President John F. Kennedy's commitment to land on the Moon, and the space race became a central contest of the Cold War.
events.lens: Prestige contests between rivals can drive enormous technological investment.
events.fact: Soviet officials concealed for years that Gagarin had parachuted, because the record rules required a pilot to land with his craft.

events.hook: Kennedy asked Congress to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out.
events.what: Kennedy asked Congress to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out.
events.story: Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth on 12 April 1961, and the Bay of Pigs invasion failed five days later. On 25 May President John F. Kennedy told a joint session of Congress that the nation should commit itself to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the decade was out. NASA's budget rose more than fivefold between 1961 and 1966.
events.why: The Soviet Union led in rockets and in prestige. Kennedy's advisers, Vice President Lyndon Johnson among them, chose a goal far enough off that American industry could overtake.
events.then: Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969. At its peak the programme took more than 4 per cent of the federal budget and employed about 400,000 people.
events.sig: Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969. At its peak the programme took more than 4 per cent of the federal budget and employed about 400,000 people.
events.now: 'Moonshot' became the word for any goal with a deadline and the resources to match, and NASA's Artemis programme aims to return astronauts to the Moon in a new race with China.

causes.why: Gagarin's flight pushed Kennedy to set a bold goal.

q.problem: How to overtake the Soviets in space.
q.how: A huge national programme: Mercury, Gemini, then Apollo.
q.replaced: Piecemeal US space efforts.
q.spread: At its peak, about 400,000 people worked on Apollo, most for contractors.
q.next: Apollo 11.

events.bluf: President John F. Kennedy, six weeks after Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin's flight and five after the Bay of Pigs, wanted a contest the United States could win. On 25 May 1961 he asked Congress to commit to landing a man on the Moon by the end of the decade. Congress paid, NASA's budget rose to more than 4 per cent of federal spending, and Apollo 11 landed in July 1969.
events.lens: Clear, ambitious goals with deadlines can mobilize governments and industry.
events.fact: Kennedy told NASA chief James Webb in a taped meeting in 1962 that he was 'not that interested in space', only in beating the Soviets to the Moon.

events.what: Wall sealed off West Berlin.
events.why: The exodus was draining the state's workforce. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev wanted the Berlin crisis closed without war.
events.sig: At least 140 people died trying to cross. Berlin became the front line of the Cold War, and the wall stood until 9 November 1989.
events.hook: East Germany sealed off West Berlin with a wall overnight.
events.story: About 3 million East Germans had fled west through Berlin since 1949, many of them young and skilled. In the early hours of 13 August 1961 East German police and workers strung barbed wire along the sector border, with Soviet approval. Concrete followed within days.
events.then: At least 140 people died trying to cross. Berlin became the front line of the Cold War, and the wall stood until 9 November 1989.
events.now: The wall stopped the drain of skilled workers and let East Germany survive 28 more years; its opening on 9 November 1989 marked the end of the Cold War in Europe.
events.fact: East German leader Walter Ulbricht told a press conference on 15 June 1961 that nobody intended to build a wall; the wire went up two months later.

causes.why: Millions fled East Germany through Berlin until the regime sealed the border in 1961.

q.before: Berliners could cross between sectors.
q.how: Overnight barbed wire, then a concrete wall.
q.claim: An 'anti-fascist protection rampart', East Germany said.
q.winners: The East German regime, which stopped the exodus.
q.lasted: Until 1989.

events.bluf: East German leader Walter Ulbricht, with Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev's consent, sealed the border in Berlin to stop an exodus that had taken about 3 million people west and threatened the state's survival. The wall stopped the flight. The communist state stabilised behind it and became known as the regime that walled in its own people, and Berlin stayed the front line of the Cold War until the wall opened in 1989.
events.lens: A state that must wall its people in has lost the argument about its legitimacy.

events.what: Failed invasion.
events.why: Washington wanted Cuban leader Fidel Castro removed after he nationalised US property and moved toward Moscow. Planners assumed a landing would spark a popular uprising, and Kennedy wanted US involvement deniable.
events.sig: Castro declared the revolution socialist on 16 April, the eve of the landing, and himself a Marxist-Leninist in December 1961. The prisoners were ransomed in December 1962 for $53 million in food and medicine. The Soviet Union placed nuclear missiles in Cuba in 1962.
events.hook: A CIA-backed invasion of Cuba collapsed in three days.
events.story: Brigade 2506, about 1,400 Cuban exiles trained by the CIA in Guatemala, landed at the Bay of Pigs on 17 April 1961. Air strikes two days earlier had left part of Cuba's air force intact, and US President John F. Kennedy cancelled a second strike and refused direct air support. Cuban leader Fidel Castro's forces sealed the beachhead, and by 19 April most of the brigade had been captured.
events.then: Castro declared the revolution socialist on 16 April, the eve of the landing, and himself a Marxist-Leninist in December 1961. The prisoners were ransomed in December 1962 for $53 million in food and medicine. The Soviet Union placed nuclear missiles in Cuba in 1962.
events.now: The invasion made Castro's rule secure and his Soviet alliance open from 1961, and it is the standard case of a covert action that strengthens its target and pushes it toward a rival.

causes.why: The CIA trained Cuban exiles to overthrow Castro; the invasion collapsed in three days.

q.why: To overthrow Castro.
q.decided: Poor planning, no air support and no popular uprising.
q.cost: About 100 exiles killed and 1,100 captured.
q.changed: Castro moved closer to the Soviet Union.

events.bluf: The CIA, under plans approved by US President Dwight Eisenhower and carried out under US President John F. Kennedy, landed about 1,400 Cuban exiles to overthrow Cuban leader Fidel Castro. Castro's forces defeated them in three days and captured most of them. Castro emerged stronger, Cuba moved openly into the Soviet camp, and the Soviet decision to place missiles in Cuba followed the next year.
events.lens: Half-hearted covert operations can produce the worst of both worlds: failure plus blame.
events.fact: Kennedy said afterwards that 'victory has a hundred fathers and defeat is an orphan'.

events.who: Julius Nyerere; the Tanganyika African National Union (TANU)
events.hook: Nyerere led Tanganyika to independence without a shot fired.
events.what: Nyerere led Tanganyika to independence without a shot fired.
events.story: Tanzanian nationalist Julius Nyerere founded the Tanganyika African National Union in 1954 and built a mass party across the trust territory's 120 ethnic groups. TANU won the elections of 1958-59 and 1960. Tanganyika became independent on 9 December 1961 with Nyerere as prime minister; he became president of a republic in 1962.
events.why: TANU's mass support left Britain no alternative partner, and Britain accepted that the UN trust territory would become independent.
events.then: Tanganyika united with Zanzibar in April 1964 to form Tanzania. Nyerere's 1967 Arusha Declaration launched African socialism and, from 1973, forced villagisation.
events.sig: Tanganyika united with Zanzibar in April 1964 to form Tanzania. Nyerere's 1967 Arusha Declaration launched African socialism and, from 1973, forced villagisation.
events.now: Nyerere's choice of Swahili and a single national party made Tanzania one of the few African states without a major ethnic conflict since independence, a cohesion that still holds.

causes.why: The mandate set the stage for independence.

q.before: A British-run UN trust territory.
q.how: Peaceful negotiation and elections.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Tanzanian nationalist Julius Nyerere's Tanganyika African National Union set out to win independence from Britain by mass organising rather than arms. Britain agreed to a timetable, and the UN trust territory became independent on 9 December 1961 with Nyerere as prime minister. Nyerere built one of Africa's most unified states around Swahili and a single party, with economic results that stayed poor under his socialism.
events.lens: Peaceful, mass-based independence movements tend to produce more stable states.
events.fact: Nyerere is known in Tanzania as 'Mwalimu', Swahili for teacher, his profession before politics.

events.hook: Samoa became the first Pacific Islands country to win independence in the 20th century.
events.what: Samoa became the first Pacific Islands country to win independence in the 20th century.
events.story: New Zealand took Western Samoa from Germany in August 1914 and ruled it under a League of Nations mandate and then a UN trusteeship. The nonviolent Mau movement campaigned for self-rule from the 1920s; on 28 December 1929, 'Black Saturday', New Zealand police fired on a Mau procession in Apia and killed its leader Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III and about ten others. After the Second World War New Zealand moved the territory toward self-government in stages. Western Samoa became independent on 1 January 1962 under Prime Minister Fiamē Mataʻafa Mulinuʻu II.
events.why: The Mau's long campaign kept the demand alive. The UN Trusteeship Council pressed New Zealand to set a date, and New Zealand wanted to leave on good terms.
events.then: Fiji became independent in 1970, Tonga ended its British protectorate the same year and Papua New Guinea followed in 1975. Western Samoa took the name Samoa in 1997. New Zealand Prime Minister Helen Clark apologised in 2002 for the 1918 influenza epidemic and Black Saturday.
events.sig: Fiji became independent in 1970, Tonga ended its British protectorate the same year and Papua New Guinea followed in 1975. Western Samoa took the name Samoa in 1997. New Zealand Prime Minister Helen Clark apologised in 2002 for the 1918 influenza epidemic and Black Saturday.
events.now: Samoa's independence set the pattern for a Pacific of small sovereign states, which is why the region today holds a dozen UN votes and is courted by Australia, China and the United States.

q.before: New Zealand rule under a UN trusteeship.
q.how: A constitution and a UN-supervised vote.
q.winners: Samoan chiefs and the Mau's heirs.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Samoans under the Mau movement wanted New Zealand's rule, imposed in 1914, to end; New Zealand, under UN pressure after 1945, wanted an orderly exit. Western Samoa became independent on 1 January 1962, the first Pacific island state to do so. It showed that small island nations could win sovereignty and opened a wave of decolonisation across the Pacific that ran to Fiji in 1970 and Papua New Guinea in 1975.
events.lens: Persistent nonviolent movements can win independence even from distant powers.
events.fact: A New Zealand-administered ship carrying influenza was allowed to dock in 1918, and the epidemic killed about a fifth of Samoa's population; American Samoa, which imposed quarantine, lost no one.

events.who: The French government; the FLN's provisional government
events.hook: France and the FLN agreed a ceasefire and a vote on independence, ending eight years of war.
events.what: France and the FLN agreed a ceasefire and a vote on independence, ending eight years of war.
events.story: French President Charles de Gaulle's government and the FLN's provisional government signed the accords at Évian-les-Bains on 18 March 1962. Algerians voted overwhelmingly for independence in a referendum on 1 July, and Algeria became independent on 5 July. Nearly a million European settlers left for France.
events.why: De Gaulle had concluded that Algeria could not be held at an acceptable cost. The FLN had the population and the world's sympathy.
events.then: The settler terror group OAS fought on. Algerians who had served France, the harkis, faced deadly reprisals.
events.sig: The settler terror group OAS fought on. Algerians who had served France, the harkis, faced deadly reprisals.
events.now: The memory of the war still shapes relations between France and Algeria, French debates on immigration and the legitimacy of Algeria's ruling elite.

causes.why: Torture revelations and endless war led de Gaulle to negotiate.

q.before: Algeria had been ruled as part of France since 1830.
q.how: A negotiated ceasefire and a referendum.
q.winners: The FLN, which ruled Algeria for decades.
q.lasted: Yes: Algeria has been independent ever since.

events.bluf: French President Charles de Gaulle had concluded that Algeria could be held only at an unacceptable cost; the FLN's provisional government wanted independence recognised. The accords of March 1962 ended the war and led to independence on 5 July. Nearly a million settlers left for France, Algerians who had served France faced reprisals, and the memory still shapes relations between the two states.
events.lens: Peace deals in colonial wars often leave unprotected those who chose the losing side.
events.fact: Algeria chose 5 July for independence, the date French troops had taken Algiers in 1830.

events.what: Nuclear standoff.
events.why: Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev wanted to protect Cuban leader Fidel Castro after the Bay of Pigs. He also wanted to offset US missiles in Turkey and Italy and the US lead in long-range missiles.
events.sig: Both sides set up a hotline and signed a partial test-ban treaty in 1963. The Soviet Union began a nuclear build-up to end its inferiority. Khrushchev was ousted in 1964.
events.hook: For 13 days, the world came closer to nuclear war than ever before.
events.story: In October 1962 US spy planes found Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba. US President John F. Kennedy declared a naval 'quarantine' of the island on 22 October. A US spy plane was shot down over Cuba on 27 October, and a Soviet submarine came close to firing a nuclear torpedo. On 28 October Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret promise to remove US missiles from Turkey.
events.then: Both sides set up a hotline and signed a partial test-ban treaty in 1963. The Soviet Union began a nuclear build-up to end its inferiority. Khrushchev was ousted in 1964.
events.now: The crisis produced the first instruments of arms control, the hotline and the test-ban treaty of 1963, and it is the reference case for nuclear crisis diplomacy from Ukraine to Taiwan.
events.fact: The Moscow-Washington hotline set up in 1963 was a teletype link, never a red telephone.

causes.why: After the invasion, Castro sought Soviet protection, and Khrushchev secretly sent nuclear missiles.

q.why: Soviet missiles in Cuba.
q.decided: A naval 'quarantine' and secret diplomacy.
q.cost: One US pilot killed; the world came close to catastrophe.
q.changed: A hotline and arms control followed.

events.bluf: Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev placed nuclear missiles in Cuba to protect Cuban leader Fidel Castro and offset US missiles in Turkey; US President John F. Kennedy set out to remove them without war. After 13 days of blockade and bargaining, Khrushchev withdrew them for a public US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret promise to remove the missiles in Turkey. Both powers then built tools for managing the nuclear rivalry, and détente followed.
events.trig: US U-2 photographs of the missile sites, taken on 14 October 1962.
events.lens: In a nuclear crisis, giving the other side a face-saving way out can prevent catastrophe.

events.where: Himalayan border (Aksai Chin and Arunachal Pradesh)
events.hook: China defeated India in a short Himalayan border war.
events.what: China defeated India in a short Himalayan border war.
events.story: Disputes had run for years over Aksai Chin, where China had built a road to Tibet in the 1950s, and over the McMahon Line in the east, and India had sheltered the Dalai Lama since 1959. Chinese forces attacked on 20 October 1962 in Ladakh and across the McMahon Line. They routed Indian forces and reached the foothills of Assam, then declared a unilateral ceasefire on 21 November, withdrawing in the east and keeping Aksai Chin.
events.why: China had rejected the McMahon Line, drawn by Britain in 1914, and India had rejected China's hold on Aksai Chin, through which the road to Tibet ran. India's 'forward policy' of 1961 pushed patrols into contested areas. China's reading is of a defensive strike against encroachment; India's is of unprovoked aggression.
events.then: Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru's standing never recovered, and he died in 1964. India enlarged its army and turned to the Soviet Union for arms. China tested a nuclear bomb in October 1964, and India followed in 1974.
events.sig: Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru's standing never recovered, and he died in 1964. India enlarged its army and turned to the Soviet Union for arms. China tested a nuclear bomb in October 1964, and India followed in 1974.
events.now: The border has never been agreed; troops killed each other in the Galwan valley in June 2020, the first deaths there since 1975.

causes.why: China's takeover of Tibet in 1950 created a long, disputed frontier with India.

q.why: Disputed borders and tension over Tibet.
q.decided: China's well-prepared offensive.
q.cost: About 1,400 Indian and 700 Chinese soldiers killed.
q.changed: China kept Aksai Chin.

events.bluf: China set out to end Indian patrols pushing into territory it held in Aksai Chin and to settle the Himalayan border by force; India's leaders had bet that China would not attack. Chinese forces attacked on 20 October 1962, routed the Indian army in both sectors and declared a ceasefire a month later, keeping Aksai Chin. India's leadership was humiliated, the border stayed undefined, and the two largest countries in Asia have faced each other across it since.
events.lens: Unresolved colonial-era borders between rising powers are long-term flashpoints.
events.fact: The war fell in the same weeks as the Cuban missile crisis, and the United States airlifted arms to India while Washington and Moscow faced off over Cuba.

events.fact: The OAU, and later the African Union, chose Addis Ababa because Ethiopia had kept its independence through the colonial era.
events.who: Haile Selassie, Kwame Nkrumah and 30 other heads of state
events.hook: Newly independent African states created a continental union.
events.what: Newly independent African states created a continental union.
events.story: Thirty-two states founded the Organisation of African Unity in Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963, with Ethiopian Emperor Haile Selassie as host. Ghanaian President Kwame Nkrumah had argued for a union government; the majority chose a looser body of sovereign states. The charter committed members to non-interference and the end of colonial rule.
events.why: New states wanted their sovereignty defended, colonial rule ended in the rest of Africa and border disputes contained.

The hotline became the standing tool, and symbol, of crisis management between nuclear rivals and the model for every later one.
events.lens: Rivals need reliable channels to talk, above all in a crisis.

events.bluf: The Arab League created the PLO in 1964 to give Palestinians a voice it could control; after 1967 Yasser Arafat's Fatah took it over and made it an independent national movement built on armed struggle. The PLO moved from guerrilla war to recognising Israel in 1993 and gained self-rule in parts of the West Bank and Gaza. It has yet to achieve a state, and its Fatah faction now governs the West Bank's Palestinian Authority.
events.lens: National movements without a state often begin with armed struggle and move toward diplomacy.
events.fact: Arafat addressed the UN General Assembly in 1974 carrying, in his words, an olive branch and a freedom fighter's gun.

In 2025 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro, who had praised the dictatorship, of plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election; his supporters call the case political persecution, and his opponents call it the first time Brazil has punished a coup plot.

events.bluf: US President Lyndon Johnson wanted congressional authority to escalate in Vietnam. A clash on 2 August 1964 between the destroyer USS Maddox and North Vietnamese torpedo boats, and a reported second attack on 4 August, gave him the occasion, and Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution almost unanimously. No second attack had occurred; the resolution became the legal basis for an American war that peaked at over 500,000 troops.
events.lens: Ambiguous incidents can be used to justify decisions already made.

events.bluf: US President Lyndon Johnson set out to stop South Vietnam falling to communism, which he feared would spread across Asia. events.bluf: Civil rights marchers led by Baptist minister Martin Luther King Jr. and SNCC chairman John Lewis set out to force federal protection for Black voters in the South; President Lyndon Johnson wanted a law that would do it. events.bluf: Malaysian Prime Minister Tunku Abdul Rahman set out to end two years of race riots and political clashes with Lee Kuan Yew's mostly Chinese People's Action Party by expelling Singapore from the federation. Singapore became independent on 9 August 1965, a city-state with no natural resources and a prime minister who wept as he announced it. Under Lee it became one of the world's richest countries through trade, foreign investment and an efficient, authoritarian government.
events.lens: Small states without resources can thrive through openness and effective institutions.
events.fact: Singapore is often described as the only country to have gained independence against its own wish.

events.who: The Indonesian army (Suharto) and allied militias; suspected communists
events.hook: After a failed coup attempt, the army and militias killed about half a million suspected communists.
events.what: After a failed coup attempt, the army and militias killed about half a million suspected communists.
events.story: On the night of 30 September 1965 a group calling itself the 30 September Movement killed six army generals in Jakarta. The army under Major General Suharto blamed the Communist Party (PKI). Over the following months the army and allied civilian groups killed an estimated 500,000 to 1 million people in Java, Bali, Sumatra and elsewhere. Hundreds of thousands more were imprisoned without trial. Estimates of the dead range from 78,000, the figure of a commission President Sukarno appointed in early 1966, to the 500,000 to 1 million most widely cited since.
events.why: Cold War fears came first. Rivalry between the army and the PKI gave the army its target, and local religious and social conflicts gave the killings their footsoldiers. One reading holds that the PKI planned the coup and that the killings were a popular response the army channelled; the other holds that the army organised and directed the killings and that the PKI leadership's role in the 30 September Movement remains unproven.
events.then: Suharto pushed Sukarno aside in March 1966 and ruled for 31 years with Western support. He built an economy open to foreign investment and an army-dominated state.
events.sig: Suharto pushed Sukarno aside in March 1966 and ruled for 31 years with Western support. He built an economy open to foreign investment and an army-dominated state.
events.now: The killings founded Suharto's New Order, which ruled from 1966 to 1998 on anti-communism and the army's claim to guard the state; the ban on the PKI and on communist ideas remains law, and no one has been prosecuted.

events.bluf: Indonesia's army under Major General Suharto set out to destroy the Communist Party (PKI), the world's third largest, after an attempted coup on 30 September 1965 that the army blamed on the party. Over the following months the army and allied militias killed an estimated 500,000 to 1 million suspected communists and imprisoned hundreds of thousands more. Suharto pushed President Sukarno aside and ruled for 31 years with Western backing; no one has been prosecuted for the killings.
events.lens: Cold War alignments led Western powers to tolerate mass atrocities by their allies.
events.fact: The PKI had about 3 million members in 1965, the largest communist party outside the Soviet Union and China.

events.what: Purges and persecution.
events.why: Mao, sidelined after the Great Leap's failure, wanted to reassert control and revive revolutionary zeal.
events.sig: Schools and universities closed for years and hundreds of thousands to millions died. Mao used the turmoil to purge rivals including Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping. The movement ended with Mao's death in September 1976 and the arrest of the Gang of Four.
events.hook: Mao unleashed students to attack 'old ideas', and China descended into chaos.
events.story: In 1966 Chinese Chairman Mao Zedong launched the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution to purge 'capitalist roaders' from the party. Millions of teenage Red Guards humiliated and beat teachers and officials, destroyed temples and relics, and fought one another. Schools closed and millions of young people were sent to the countryside.
events.then: Schools and universities closed for years and hundreds of thousands to millions died. Mao used the turmoil to purge rivals including Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping. The movement ended with Mao's death in September 1976 and the arrest of the Gang of Four.
events.now: Xi Jinping and many of China's current leaders were 'sent down' to the countryside during it, and the party discourages open discussion of the period.

causes.why: Sidelined after the famine, Mao launched the Cultural Revolution partly to destroy rivals who had reversed his policies.
Mao's later campaign against party leaders echoed the purge of Peng.

q.before: Leaders such as Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping ran the state after the Great Leap.
q.how: Mass mobilisation of youth against the party establishment.
q.winners: Mao and the radical 'Gang of Four', until his death.
q.lasted: It ended with Mao's death in 1976.

events.bluf: Chinese Chairman Mao Zedong launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966 to purge 'capitalist roaders' from the party and recover the authority he had lost after the Great Leap. Millions of teenage Red Guards attacked teachers, officials, temples and one another; schools closed and millions of young people were sent to the countryside. Hundreds of thousands to millions died over ten years, education and cultural heritage were wrecked, and the generation that now rules China was formed by it.
events.lens: Leaders who bypass their own institutions to mobilize the masses can unleash chaos.
events.fact: Mao swam the Yangtze at Wuhan in July 1966, aged 72, to show he had the strength for the fight ahead.

events.hook: Tanzania launched African socialism, Ujamaa: self-reliance and village collectives.
events.what: Tanzania launched African socialism, Ujamaa: self-reliance and village collectives.
events.story: On 5 February 1967 Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere issued the Arusha Declaration committing Tanzania to Ujamaa, Swahili for 'familyhood'. The state nationalised banks, insurance and major industries and barred party leaders from holding shares or renting property. From 1973 the government moved millions of rural people into collective villages, often by force.
events.why: Nyerere believed an African socialism rooted in village life would build a united, self-reliant nation free of the dependence he saw in Kenya's model.
events.then: Ujamaa villages produced less than the farms they replaced, and food imports rose. Tanzania accepted IMF terms and market reforms in 1986, the year after Nyerere stepped down.
events.sig: Ujamaa villages produced less than the farms they replaced, and food imports rose. Tanzania accepted IMF terms and market reforms in 1986, the year after Nyerere stepped down.
events.now: Ujamaa's emphasis on Swahili and national unity helped make Tanzania one of Africa's most cohesive nations.

causes.why: Three years after union with Zanzibar, Nyerere set out the new nation's socialist path.

events.fact: Nyerere translated Shakespeare's 'Julius Caesar' and 'The Merchant of Venice' into Swahili.

q.idea: African socialism based on village life and self-reliance.
q.against: Capitalism and dependence on foreign aid.
q.spread: Through TANU, schools and the Swahili language.
q.enabled: A strong national identity in Tanzania.
q.critics: Economists pointed to failed collective farms and forced relocations.

events.bluf: Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere wanted a self-reliant socialist nation built on village life rather than foreign capital or a private elite. The Arusha Declaration of February 1967 nationalised banks and industries, bound party leaders to a code against private wealth and, from 1973, moved millions into collective villages by force. The programme built national unity and a literate population and failed as an economy; Tanzania turned to market reforms in the 1980s.
events.lens: Ideological development models can fail economically and still leave lasting social effects.
