events.h: Australians vote to include Aboriginal people
events.who: Australian voters; Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal campaigners
events.hook: Over 90% of Australians voted to change the constitution so the federal government could act for Aboriginal people.
events.what: Over 90% of Australians voted to change the constitution so the federal government could act for Aboriginal people.
events.story: Australia's constitution excluded 'aboriginal natives' from the census count and barred the Commonwealth from making laws for them. A decade of campaigning by activists including Faith Bandler, Jessie Street and Charles Perkins, and the Freedom Ride through New South Wales towns in 1965, built support. Prime Minister Harold Holt's government put the amendment to a referendum on 27 May 1967. It passed with 90.77 per cent of the vote and carried every state.
events.why: A decade of campaigning by Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal activists came first. Australia was dismantling White Australia, and its treatment of Aboriginal people was an embarrassment abroad.
events.then: The Commonwealth legislated for Aboriginal people from the 1970s, including the Northern Territory land-rights act of 1976. The 2023 referendum on a Voice to Parliament failed with about 60 per cent voting no; its supporters held that a constitutional advisory body would give Indigenous Australians a say in the laws made about them, and its opponents held that it would divide citizens by race, that its design was left undefined and, for some Indigenous critics, that it offered too little.
events.sig: The Commonwealth legislated for Aboriginal people from the 1970s, including the Northern Territory land-rights act of 1976. The 2023 referendum on a Voice to Parliament failed with about 60 per cent voting no; its supporters held that a constitutional advisory body would give Indigenous Australians a say in the laws made about them, and its opponents held that it would divide citizens by race, that its design was left undefined and, for some Indigenous critics, that it offered too little.
events.now: The referendum made Indigenous affairs a Commonwealth responsibility, the base of every land-rights and native-title law since; in 2023 Australians rejected a proposal for an Indigenous Voice to Parliament in another referendum.
events.myth: The referendum gave Aboriginal people citizenship and the vote. They were already citizens and could vote in federal elections from 1962; the vote changed the census and the Commonwealth's law-making power.

q.before: The constitution excluded Aboriginal people from the census and from federal laws.
q.how: A national referendum.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal campaigners wanted the Commonwealth empowered to make laws for Aboriginal people and to count them in the census, and Prime Minister Harold Holt's government agreed to put it to a vote. On 27 May 1967, 90.77 per cent of voters said yes, the largest majority in any Australian referendum. The federal government could now legislate on Indigenous affairs, which produced the land-rights laws of the 1970s and made Indigenous policy a national question.
events.lens: Symbolic reforms can matter as much for what they signal as for what they change in law.
events.fact: Faith Bandler, the campaign's best-known organiser, was the daughter of a man taken from Vanuatu to Queensland's cane fields in the blackbirding trade.

kv: voted yes, the largest yes vote in an Australian referendum

events.what: Guevara executed.
events.why: Che believed a small guerrilla band could create the conditions for revolution. Bolivia's peasants had received land in the 1953 reform and had little reason to join foreign insurgents.
events.sig: The Bolivian army displayed his body to the press in Vallegrande and buried it in secret. His remains were found in 1997 and reburied in Santa Clara, Cuba. Cuba shifted from sponsoring guerrillas to sending its own troops, especially to Angola.
events.hook: Che Guevara was captured and executed in the Bolivian jungle.
events.story: Argentine-born revolutionary Ernesto 'Che' Guevara left Cuba in 1965, fought in the Congo and arrived in Bolivia in November 1966 with a small band of Cuban and Bolivian fighters. Bolivian peasants gave him little support, and the Bolivian Communist Party declined to back him. Bolivian Rangers trained by US advisers captured him at Quebrada del Yuro on 8 October 1967. He was executed the next day in the schoolhouse at La Higuera on the Bolivian government's orders.
events.then: The Bolivian army displayed his body to the press in Vallegrande and buried it in secret. His remains were found in 1997 and reburied in Santa Clara, Cuba. Cuba shifted from sponsoring guerrillas to sending its own troops, especially to Angola.
events.now: Che's failure in Bolivia discredited the rural guerrilla model in South America after 1967, and Cuba turned to sending its own troops abroad, above all to Africa from 1975.

causes.why: Che left Cuba to spread revolution, first to the Congo and then to Bolivia, where he was captured and executed.

q.why: Che wanted to spread revolution across South America.
q.stakes: Revolution in Bolivia, and Che's life.
q.decided: Peasants did not join, and Bolivian troops trapped his band.
q.cost: Che was captured and executed on October 9, 1967.
q.changed: He became a global icon.

events.bluf: Argentine-born revolutionary Ernesto 'Che' Guevara went to Bolivia in 1966 to start a guerrilla war that would spread across South America. Bolivian peasants stayed away, and Bolivian troops advised by the CIA captured him on 8 October 1967 and shot him the next day. His strategy failed, and his death made him the most reproduced revolutionary image of the century.
events.lens: Revolutionary strategies that worked in one place often fail elsewhere.
events.fact: Cuban photographer Alberto Korda's portrait of Che, taken in 1960, is often called the most reproduced photograph in the world.

events.what: Israel took the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai, Golan.
events.why: Tension with Syria and Soviet reports of Israeli troop movements led Nasser to mobilise. The closure of the Straits was the step Israel had long said it would treat as war.
events.sig: UN Resolution 242 set out the formula of 'land for peace'. Israel began building settlements, and Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza came under Israeli military rule. Secular Arab nationalism was discredited and Islamist movements gained ground.
events.hook: Israel defeated three Arab armies in six days.
events.story: In May 1967 Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser expelled UN peacekeepers from Sinai, mobilised his army there and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. On 5 June Israel struck first and destroyed most of Egypt's air force on the ground. In six days it took Sinai and Gaza from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan and the Golan Heights from Syria.
events.then: UN Resolution 242 set out the formula of 'land for peace'. Israel began building settlements, and Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza came under Israeli military rule. Secular Arab nationalism was discredited and Islamist movements gained ground.
events.now: Israel still holds the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, and settlements are at the heart of today's disputes.
events.fact: The war ran from 5 to 10 June; most of Egypt's air force was destroyed in the first three hours.

causes.why: Suez made Nasser the hero of Arab nationalism. In 1967 he expelled UN peacekeepers and closed the Straits of Tiran, and Israel struck first.

q.why: Rising tension, Egypt's blockade and troop build-up.
q.stakes: Israel's security and the Arab states' standing.
q.decided: Israel's surprise air strike.
q.cost: About 800 Israelis and many thousands of Arab soldiers killed.
q.changed: Israel occupied large new territories.

events.bluf: Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser mobilised in Sinai and closed the Straits of Tiran to force Israel back; Israeli Prime Minister Levi Eshkol's government struck first to break the encirclement. In six days Israel took Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, tripling the land it controlled. The occupation of Palestinian territories, settlements and 'land for peace' became the central questions of the conflict.
events.trig: Egypt's closure of the Straits of Tiran in May 1967.
events.lens: Sweeping military victories can create long-term political problems the victor must manage.

kv: the territory Israel held, by area

toll.n: Estimates. About 300,000 Palestinians fled or were displaced.

events.fact: Médecins Sans Frontières was founded in 1971 by French doctors who had worked in Biafra.
events.who: Nigerian federal government vs. Biafra (Odumegwu Ojukwu)
events.hook: Nigeria went to war to stop Biafra breaking away, and a blockade caused famine.
events.what: Nigeria went to war to stop Biafra breaking away, and a blockade caused famine.
events.story: Two coups in 1966 and massacres of Igbo in northern Nigeria drove Igbo back to the southeast. On 30 May 1967 Biafran leader Odumegwu Ojukwu declared the region independent as Biafra. Nigerian federal forces under General Yakubu Gowon blockaded it, and images of starving children went round the world. Biafra surrendered on 15 January 1970.
events.why: Ethnic and regional rivalry in a federation built by British rule came first. The oil of the southeast made secession intolerable to Lagos.
events.then: Estimates of the dead range from about 500,000 to over 2 million, mostly from famine. Gowon declared 'no victor, no vanquished', and oil revenue centralised power in the federal government.
events.sig: Estimates of the dead range from about 500,000 to over 2 million, mostly from famine. Gowon declared 'no victor, no vanquished', and oil revenue centralised power in the federal government.
events.now: Biafra fixed the rule that Africa's colonial borders would be defended by force, and Igbo complaints of marginalisation and a revived separatist movement still shape Nigerian politics.

causes.why: Nigeria, independent in 1960, was a federation of rival regions created by British rule; after two coups in 1966, the southeast seceded as Biafra.
Britain ruled the former caliphate through its emirs, preserving a Muslim north very different from the south. That divide shaped Nigeria's crises after independence.

q.why: Biafra sought independence after massacres of Igbo people.
q.decided: Federal blockade and military superiority.
q.cost: Perhaps 500,000 to 2 million dead, mostly from famine.
q.changed: Nigeria stayed united.

events.bluf: Nigeria's federal government under General Yakubu Gowon fought to prevent the Igbo southeast seceding as Biafra, and Biafran leader Odumegwu Ojukwu fought to keep it independent after massacres of Igbo in the north. The federal blockade starved Biafra into surrender in January 1970; estimates of the dead run from about 500,000 to more than two million, most from famine. Nigeria stayed whole, and Africa's colonial borders had been defended by force.
events.lens: Federations of rival ethnic regions built by colonial rule can break into civil war over power and resources.
events.trig: The declaration of Biafran independence on 30 May 1967.

events.who: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand
events.hook: Five Southeast Asian states formed an association to keep the peace among themselves.
events.what: Five Southeast Asian states formed an association to keep the peace among themselves.
events.story: The foreign ministers of Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand signed the ASEAN Declaration in Bangkok on 8 August 1967. It aimed to promote regional cooperation and stability, partly as a bulwark against communism.
events.why: Ending the Indonesia-Malaysia confrontation of 1963-66 came first. Fear of communist expansion as the Vietnam War grew gave the five a shared interest.
events.then: Brunei joined in 1984. Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia joined in the 1990s, and Timor-Leste became the eleventh member in 2025.
events.sig: Brunei joined in 1984. Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia joined in the 1990s, and Timor-Leste became the eleventh member in 2025.
events.now: ASEAN's members have about 680 million people, and the bloc tries to balance between the United States and China.

causes.why: Suharto's anti-communist Indonesia ended its confrontation with Malaysia, making regional cooperation possible.

q.before: Rivalries between neighbours, such as Indonesia's confrontation with Malaysia.
q.how: A regional declaration.
q.lasted: Yes: it has ten members.

events.bluf: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand set out to manage their own disputes after the Indonesia-Malaysia confrontation and to stand together against communist expansion. Their foreign ministers signed the ASEAN Declaration in Bangkok in August 1967. The body grew to ten members by 1999 and eleven in 2025, and it became the forum through which Southeast Asia balances between the United States and China.
events.lens: Regional groups built on consensus and non-interference can keep peace among very different states.
events.fact: The founding declaration ran to two pages; the charter that gave ASEAN a legal personality came into force only in 2008.

events.who: North Vietnamese army and Viet Cong; US and South Vietnamese forces
events.hook: A surprise communist offensive across South Vietnam failed on the battlefield but turned Americans against the war.
events.what: A surprise communist offensive across South Vietnam failed on the battlefield but turned Americans against the war.
events.story: During the Lunar New Year truce at the end of January 1968, about 80,000 North Vietnamese and Viet Cong troops attacked more than 100 towns and cities, including the grounds of the US embassy in Saigon. US and South Vietnamese forces beat them back with heavy losses. Hue was held for a month. Americans who had been told victory was near were shocked.
events.why: Hanoi hoped surprise attacks across the South would spark a popular uprising and break the South Vietnamese government.
events.then: US President Lyndon Johnson halted most bombing of the North on 31 March 1968 and announced he would not run again. Peace talks began in Paris in May.
events.sig: US President Lyndon Johnson halted most bombing of the North on 31 March 1968 and announced he would not run again. Peace talks began in Paris in May.
events.now: Tet turned American opinion from 1968 onward, making the war one to exit rather than win; every later government has feared the gap between official optimism and televised fact that Tet exposed.

causes.why: With 500,000 US troops in Vietnam, Hanoi struck everywhere at once.

q.why: North Vietnam sought a decisive blow.
q.stakes: South Vietnam's survival and US public support for the war.
q.decided: US firepower won the battles; television coverage shifted opinion.
q.cost: Tens of thousands killed, including thousands of civilians in Huế.
q.changed: The United States began looking for a way out.

events.bluf: North Vietnam's leaders set out to break the South Vietnamese government with surprise attacks across the South during the Lunar New Year truce, hoping to spark a popular uprising. About 80,000 troops struck more than 100 towns and cities at the end of January 1968 and were beaten back with heavy losses, though they held Hue for a month. The uprising never came; the fighting convinced many Americans the war was unwinnable, and US President Lyndon Johnson halted most bombing, declined to run again and opened talks.
events.lens: Wars are won in politics as well as on battlefields; a military defeat can be a political victory.
events.myth: Tet was a North Vietnamese battlefield victory. It was a military defeat for the North, with the Viet Cong's southern cadres largely destroyed; the political effect in the United States was the victory.
events.fact: Viet Cong sappers blew a hole in the wall of the US embassy compound in Saigon and held the grounds for six hours.

toll.n: Communist forces killed about 2,800–6,000 civilians in Huế.

events.who: US Army Charlie Company; the villagers of Sơn Mỹ
events.where: Sơn Mỹ, Quảng Ngãi province, Vietnam
events.hook: American soldiers killed hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese villagers, mostly women, children and old people.
events.what: American soldiers killed hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese villagers, mostly women, children and old people.
events.story: On 16 March 1968 soldiers of US Army Charlie Company searching for the Viet Cong killed between 347 and 504 villagers of Son My; the lower figure is the US Army's count, the higher the figure on the Vietnamese memorial. Helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson landed between soldiers and villagers to stop the killing. The army covered it up until journalist Seymour Hersh exposed it in November 1969.
events.why: Frustration over casualties from mines and snipers came first. Poor leadership and orders to destroy a village suspected of sheltering the Viet Cong turned a sweep into killing.
events.then: Only Lieutenant William Calley was convicted. He served three and a half years, mostly under house arrest, after US President Richard Nixon ordered him released from the stockade.
events.sig: Only Lieutenant William Calley was convicted. He served three and a half years, mostly under house arrest, after US President Richard Nixon ordered him released from the stockade.
events.now: The massacre and its cover-up, exposed in November 1969, deepened American opposition to the war and made the duty to refuse unlawful orders a fixed part of military training.

causes.why: Six weeks after Tet began, US soldiers massacred villagers at My Lai.

q.why: A search-and-destroy mission against a suspected Viet Cong base.
q.stakes: How US soldiers conducted the war.
q.decided: Officers who ordered or allowed the killing.
q.cost: Up to 504 civilians killed.
q.changed: Americans confronted war crimes committed by their own soldiers.

events.bluf: US soldiers of Charlie Company set out to destroy a village suspected of sheltering the Viet Cong, under orders and after weeks of casualties from mines and snipers. On 16 March 1968 they killed between 347 and 504 unarmed villagers at Son My. The army covered it up until journalist Seymour Hersh exposed it in 1969; the revelation deepened American opposition to the war, and only one officer was convicted.
events.lens: Atrocities exposed by a free press can shift public opinion on a war.
events.fact: Hugh Thompson received the Soldier's Medal for his actions in 1998, thirty years after the massacre.

kv: he served, mostly under house arrest

events.who: James Earl Ray; Martin Luther King Jr.
events.hook: The leader of the civil rights movement was shot in Memphis.
events.what: The leader of the civil rights movement was shot in Memphis.
events.story: Baptist minister Martin Luther King Jr. had turned to fighting poverty and opposing the Vietnam War and was planning a Poor People's Campaign for Washington. He went to Memphis to support striking Black sanitation workers. On 4 April 1968, the evening after his 'I've Been to the Mountaintop' speech, he was shot dead on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel. He was 39.
events.why: James Earl Ray, an escaped convict and segregationist, pleaded guilty in 1969 and was sentenced to 99 years; he recanted within days. King's family later questioned whether he acted alone.
events.then: Riots broke out in more than 100 cities, about 40 people died and federal troops were deployed in Washington, Chicago and Baltimore. Congress passed the Fair Housing Act on 10 April and President Lyndon Johnson signed it the next day. The Poor People's Campaign went ahead in May without him and faded.
events.sig: Riots broke out in more than 100 cities, about 40 people died and federal troops were deployed in Washington, Chicago and Baltimore. Congress passed the Fair Housing Act on 10 April and President Lyndon Johnson signed it the next day. The Poor People's Campaign went ahead in May without him and faded.
events.now: King's murder set off riots in a hundred cities, pushed the Fair Housing Act through Congress within a week, and ended the phase of the civil rights movement that had worked through nonviolent mass protest.
events.wk: Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.

causes.why: After the Voting Rights Act, King turned to poverty and opposing the Vietnam War; he was killed in Memphis in 1968 while supporting striking sanitation workers.

q.before: King was the leading figure of the civil rights movement.
q.how: Assassination.
q.winners: No one; riots swept the country.
q.lasted: King's influence endures.

events.bluf: Escaped convict James Earl Ray shot Baptist minister Martin Luther King Jr. dead on a Memphis motel balcony on 4 April 1968, as King was turning the movement toward poverty and the Vietnam War. The murder set off riots in more than 100 cities and pushed the Fair Housing Act through Congress within a week. It ended the phase of the civil rights movement that worked through nonviolent mass protest.
events.lens: The assassination of a movement's leader can trigger both unrest and reform.
events.fact: His birthday became a federal holiday in 1986, and his words are claimed across the political spectrum.

kv: until the Fair Housing Act passed

events.who: Students and workers; President Charles de Gaulle
events.hook: Student protests in Paris grew into a general strike of millions of workers.
events.what: Student protests in Paris grew into a general strike of millions of workers.
events.story: Clashes between students and police in the Latin Quarter in early May 1968 spread to the factories. A general strike of perhaps 10 million workers followed, the largest in French history. President Charles de Gaulle flew to a French base in Germany on 29 May, returned, dissolved the National Assembly and won a landslide in June.
events.why: An overcrowded, authoritarian university system came first. A conservative society under a ten-year presidency and the worldwide student mood of 1968 supplied the rest.
events.then: The Grenelle agreements raised the minimum wage by about a third. Universities were reformed. De Gaulle resigned in April 1969 after losing a referendum.
events.sig: The Grenelle agreements raised the minimum wage by about a third. Universities were reformed. De Gaulle resigned in April 1969 after losing a referendum.
events.now: The protests brought France to a general strike and de Gaulle's departure within a year; the social liberalisation they demanded arrived in the following decade, in law and in custom.

q.before: De Gaulle's conservative Fifth Republic.
q.how: Student protests and a general strike.
q.claim: Freedom, and an end to authoritarian institutions.
q.winners: Workers won wage rises; de Gaulle won the election.
q.lasted: Its cultural changes lasted.

events.bluf: Students in Paris wanted a freer university and a freer society; the workers who joined them wanted higher wages and a say at work. Together they produced a strike of perhaps 10 million, the largest in French history, and forced President Charles de Gaulle to call elections, which he won. The institutions held, and the liberalisation of law and custom the protesters demanded arrived over the following decade.
events.lens: Cultural revolutions can succeed even when political ones fail.
events.fact: The slogan 'under the paving stones, the beach' came from the cobbles students pulled up for barricades.
events.btt: Charles de Gaulle president of France

events.hook: Robert Kennedy was shot moments after winning the California primary.
events.what: Robert Kennedy was shot moments after winning the California primary.
events.story: New York Senator Robert F. Kennedy entered the Democratic race in March 1968 as an opponent of the Vietnam War. On 5 June 1968, after claiming victory in the California primary at the Ambassador Hotel, he was shot in the kitchen passage; he died on 6 June, aged 42. Sirhan Sirhan was seized at the scene.
events.why: Sirhan Sirhan, a Palestinian-born Jordanian, said he was angered by Kennedy's support for Israel; the shooting fell on the first anniversary of the Six-Day War.
events.then: Vice President Hubert Humphrey won the nomination at a Chicago convention marked by street violence. Republican Richard Nixon won the presidency in November on a 'law and order' platform. The Secret Service began protecting presidential candidates.
events.sig: Vice President Hubert Humphrey won the nomination at a Chicago convention marked by street violence. Republican Richard Nixon won the presidency in November on a 'law and order' platform. The Secret Service began protecting presidential candidates.
events.now: Kennedy's murder removed the one candidate who might have united the anti-war and civil rights coalitions, opened the way for Nixon, and shifted American politics toward 'law and order' for a generation.

causes.why: Kennedy ran for president in 1968 as an opponent of the war.

q.before: RFK was a leading presidential candidate.
q.how: Assassination.
q.lasted: Nixon won the election.

events.bluf: Sirhan Sirhan, a Palestinian-born Jordanian angered by New York Senator Robert F. Kennedy's support for Israel, shot Kennedy in a Los Angeles hotel kitchen on 5 June 1968, minutes after he had won the California Democratic primary. Kennedy died the next day. The killing removed the leading anti-war candidate, deepened the sense that the country was coming apart and helped Richard Nixon win in November on 'law and order'.
events.lens: Political violence in a polarized year can redirect a nation's course.
events.fact: Sirhan's death sentence became life when California abolished the death penalty in 1972; parole was granted in 2021 and reversed by Governor Gavin Newsom in 2022.

events.hook: Czechoslovakia tried 'socialism with a human face' until Soviet tanks rolled in.
events.what: Czechoslovakia tried 'socialism with a human face' until Soviet tanks rolled in.
events.story: From January 1968 Czechoslovak Communist Party leader Alexander Dubček eased censorship and allowed open debate, 'socialism with a human face'. On the night of 20-21 August about 250,000 Warsaw Pact troops from the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and East Germany entered the country. The government ordered no resistance. Dubček was flown to Moscow and signed a protocol reversing the reforms.
events.why: Moscow feared the reforms would spread to Poland and Ukraine and pull Czechoslovakia out of the bloc. Dubček had kept the party in control of everything except the press.
events.then: Brezhnev declared in November 1968 that the Soviet Union would intervene wherever socialism was threatened, the 'Brezhnev Doctrine'. Dubček was removed in April 1969 and 'normalisation' purged the party. Student Jan Palach burned himself to death in protest in January 1969.
events.sig: Brezhnev declared in November 1968 that the Soviet Union would intervene wherever socialism was threatened, the 'Brezhnev Doctrine'. Dubček was removed in April 1969 and 'normalisation' purged the party. Student Jan Palach burned himself to death in protest in January 1969.
events.now: Many Western communists broke with Moscow after the invasion, and its logic, that Moscow will not let a neighbour drift west, resurfaced in Georgia in 2008 and Ukraine from 2014.

causes.why: Like Hungary in 1956, Czechoslovakia learned that Moscow would use force to keep its bloc together.

q.before: Hard-line communist rule.
q.how: Reform from within, crushed by invasion.
q.lasted: No: hard-liners ruled until 1989.

events.bluf: Czechoslovak party leader Alexander Dubček set out to reform communism from within, with open debate and an end to censorship; Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev sent the Warsaw Pact's armies to stop it. About 250,000 troops ended the experiment in a night. Moscow then declared a right to intervene in any socialist country, and reform in the bloc stayed off the table until Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev dropped that doctrine in 1989.
events.lens: Empires enforce the limits of reform at their edges: what Moscow tolerated depended on whether the bloc stayed intact.
events.fact: Dubček ended his career as a forestry official and returned as speaker of parliament after the Velvet Revolution in 1989.

kv: Warsaw Pact troops on day one

events.who: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins; NASA
events.what: First humans on the Moon (Apollo 11).
events.why: Kennedy had committed the United States in 1961 to a goal far enough off to win. Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin's flight had made space a test of which system was superior, and Congress paid for the answer.
events.sig: Twelve men walked on the Moon by December 1972, and no one has been back since. The Soviet lunar programme was cancelled after four failures of its N1 rocket. The rivalry wound down into cooperation, from the Apollo-Soyuz mission of 1975 to the International Space Station.
events.hook: Humans walked on another world for the first time.
events.story: Apollo 11 launched from Florida on 16 July 1969 with commander Neil Armstrong, lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin and command module pilot Michael Collins. The lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquillity on 20 July with under a minute of fuel to spare. Armstrong stepped onto the surface and Aldrin followed; they spent about two and a half hours outside. About 600 million people watched on television.
events.then: Twelve men walked on the Moon by December 1972, and no one has been back since. The Soviet lunar programme was cancelled after four failures of its N1 rocket. The rivalry wound down into cooperation, from the Apollo-Soyuz mission of 1975 to the International Space Station.
events.now: Apollo spun off advances in computing and materials, and NASA's Artemis programme and China's lunar plans have revived a race to the Moon.
events.fact: The Apollo guidance computer had about 4 KB of memory, far less than a modern calculator.

Apollo achieved Kennedy's goal with five months to spare.

q.spread: Six landings by 1972.
q.next: Space shuttles and space stations.

events.bluf: NASA set out to meet President John F. Kennedy's 1961 pledge to land a man on the Moon before the decade ended and to beat the Soviet Union there. Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969, and astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface while Michael Collins orbited. The United States won the prestige contest of the space race, and the programme showed what concentrated public investment in engineering could achieve.
events.lens: Geopolitical rivalry can drive science further and faster than curiosity alone.

events.who: Bengali nationalists (Sheikh Mujibur Rahman); Pakistan's army; India
events.hook: East Pakistan broke away to become Bangladesh after a brutal crackdown and an Indian intervention.
events.what: East Pakistan broke away to become Bangladesh after a brutal crackdown and an Indian intervention.
events.story: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's Awami League won 160 of 300 seats in Pakistan's December 1970 election. Pakistani President Yahya Khan and West Pakistani leader Zulfikar Ali Bhutto postponed the assembly. On the night of 25 March 1971 the army launched Operation Searchlight in Dhaka and arrested Mujib. Guerrillas of the Mukti Bahini fought through the year with Indian support, and about 10 million refugees crossed into India. Deaths over the nine months are put at 3 million by the Bangladesh government, at 26,000 by Pakistan's Hamoodur Rahman Commission of 1974 and in the hundreds of thousands by most outside estimates. Indian forces invaded on 3 December after Pakistani air strikes on Indian airfields, and Pakistan's eastern command surrendered in Dhaka on 16 December with about 93,000 prisoners.
events.why: West Pakistan dominated politics, the army and the economy, and the attempt to make Urdu the national language had provoked Bengali resistance since the Language Movement of 1952. The two wings were 1,600 km apart with India between them.
events.then: Bangladesh became independent and Pakistan lost more than half its population. The United States and China backed Pakistan while the Soviet Union backed India under a treaty signed in August 1971. Pakistani Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto launched a nuclear weapons programme in 1972. Mujib was assassinated in a coup in August 1975.
events.sig: Bangladesh became independent and Pakistan lost more than half its population. The United States and China backed Pakistan while the Soviet Union backed India under a treaty signed in August 1971. Pakistani Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto launched a nuclear weapons programme in 1972. Mujib was assassinated in a coup in August 1975.
events.now: The war fixed India's primacy in South Asia and set off Pakistan's drive for a nuclear weapon from 1972. In Bangladesh the count of the dead and the trials of collaborators since 2010 remain the dividing line of its politics.

causes.why: Partition created a Pakistan of two wings 1,600 km apart, divided by language and political power.

q.why: Bengalis demanded rights after West Pakistan refused to let them govern.
q.decided: Indian military intervention.
q.cost: Hundreds of thousands to millions killed, and 10 million refugees.
q.changed: Bangladesh became independent.

events.bluf: Bengali nationalists under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman set out to govern Pakistan after winning its 1970 election and, when West Pakistan's rulers refused, to leave it. Pakistan's army launched a crackdown in March 1971 that drove about 10 million refugees into India and killed, by Bangladesh's count, 3 million people and by most outside estimates hundreds of thousands; India invaded in December and Pakistan surrendered in two weeks. Pakistan lost more than half its population, India became the dominant power in South Asia, and a state built on religion had split along language.
events.trig: The army's crackdown, Operation Searchlight, from 25 March 1971, after Pakistan's leaders refused to let the election winners govern.
events.lens: Shared religion cannot hold a state together if one region dominates another's language, power and wealth.
events.fact: The surrender at Dhaka of about 93,000 men was the largest since the Second World War.

events.what: Ended converting dollars to gold.
events.why: US inflation and Vietnam War spending had put far more dollars abroad than gold to back them. Nixon wanted growth before the 1972 election, and Treasury Secretary John Connally wanted the burden put on other countries.
events.sig: Currencies floated. US inflation rose through the 1970s and passed 13 per cent in 1979. The dollar stayed the world's reserve currency and oil was priced in it.
events.hook: Nixon cut the dollar's link to gold, creating today's money system.
events.story: Under the Bretton Woods system of 1944 the dollar was convertible into gold at $35 an ounce and other currencies were fixed to the dollar. By 1971 dollars held abroad far exceeded US gold reserves, and foreign governments were converting them. On 15 August 1971 President Richard Nixon announced on television the suspension of convertibility, a 10 per cent import surcharge and a 90-day freeze on wages and prices. Fixed rates were patched at the Smithsonian in December 1971 and abandoned by March 1973.
events.then: Currencies floated. US inflation rose through the 1970s and passed 13 per cent in 1979. The dollar stayed the world's reserve currency and oil was priced in it.
events.now: Every major currency since 1973 has rested on trust in its government rather than on gold, which gave states freedom to print in a crisis and made inflation a political choice.

q.what: Dollars and gold.
q.who: US exports gained; holders of dollars lost.
q.scale: It ended the world's postwar monetary system.
q.daily: Inflation rose through the 1970s.
q.system: Floating exchange rates and paper money backed by trust.

events.bluf: President Richard Nixon set out to stop foreign governments draining US gold and to fight inflation before the 1972 election. On 15 August 1971 he suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold and imposed wage and price controls. The Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates collapsed within two years, currencies floated, and money has rested on trust in governments since.
events.lens: Monetary systems rest on credibility; when it is spent, the system changes.
events.fact: Nixon made the decision at a weekend meeting at Camp David and announced it before the markets opened on Monday; in Japan it is remembered as the 'Nixon shock'.

events.hook: The Paris Peace Accords took US troops out of Vietnam after eight years of war.
events.story: US envoy Henry Kissinger and North Vietnamese negotiator Le Duc Tho reached terms in Paris. The accords, signed on 27 January 1973, led to the withdrawal of the last US combat troops in March and the return of American prisoners of war. More than 58,000 Americans had died. Fighting between North and South went on.
events.then: Congress cut American aid to Saigon. Without US troops or air support, South Vietnam fell to a North Vietnamese offensive in April 1975.
events.now: The 'Vietnam syndrome' kept the United States out of large ground wars from 1973 to the Gulf War of 1991 and shaped the all-volunteer army that replaced the draft the same year.

Rising casualties and protests at home led the US to negotiate its way out; the Paris Peace Accords were signed in 1973.

q.stakes: US withdrawal and the return of prisoners.

q.cost: Over 58,000 Americans dead by then.

events.bluf: US President Richard Nixon set out to withdraw from a war that had become deeply unpopular while claiming 'peace with honour'. The Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 took the last US combat troops out by March and returned American prisoners of war; more than 58,000 Americans had died. Fighting between North and South continued, Saigon fell in April 1975, and the United States emerged with a lasting reluctance to fight long foreign wars.
events.lens: Peace deals that let the stronger side leave without settling the conflict usually just delay the outcome.
events.fact: Kissinger and Le Duc Tho were awarded the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize; Tho refused it.

events.what: Allende overthrown.
events.why: Allende's supporters hold that US economic pressure and covert funding of the opposition, ordered by US President Richard Nixon from 1970, wrecked the economy; his opponents hold that his own expropriations, price controls and money printing did. Cold War fears in Washington and in Chile's officer corps turned the crisis into a coup.
events.sig: Official commissions of 1991 and 2011 counted about 3,200 killed or disappeared and more than 38,000 tortured or imprisoned for political reasons. From 1975 Chilean officials trained at the University of Chicago privatised pensions and state firms and opened trade. Pinochet lost a plebiscite in 1988 and handed power to an elected president in 1990. He was arrested in London in 1998 on a Spanish warrant and died in 2006 without being convicted.
events.hook: Chile's army overthrew elected socialist Salvador Allende on September 11, 1973.
events.story: Chilean President Salvador Allende, a socialist, won the 1970 election with 36.6 per cent of the vote. His government nationalised copper in 1971 and expropriated farms and firms; by 1973 inflation ran in the hundreds of per cent and goods were short. In August 1973 the Chamber of Deputies passed a resolution accusing the government of breaking the constitution. On 11 September 1973 the armed forces under General Augusto Pinochet bombed La Moneda palace, and Allende died inside, by his own hand, as a forensic inquiry confirmed in 2011.
events.then: Official commissions of 1991 and 2011 counted about 3,200 killed or disappeared and more than 38,000 tortured or imprisoned for political reasons. From 1975 Chilean officials trained at the University of Chicago privatised pensions and state firms and opened trade. Pinochet lost a plebiscite in 1988 and handed power to an elected president in 1990. He was arrested in London in 1998 on a Spanish warrant and died in 2006 without being convicted.
events.now: The 1980 constitution written under Pinochet still governs Chile; voters rejected replacement drafts in 2022 and 2023. Pinochet's defenders hold that the coup stopped a Marxist government and that his reforms made Chile one of Latin America's richest countries; his opponents hold that it destroyed a democracy and that the growth rested on repression and inequality.
events.fact: The coup took place on 11 September 1973, and Chileans call it their own 9/11.

causes.why: Fearing 'another Cuba', the Nixon administration worked to undermine Chile's elected socialist president, Salvador Allende.

q.before: President Salvador Allende, elected in 1970.
q.how: A military coup.
q.lasted: Until 1990.

events.bluf: Chilean General Augusto Pinochet and the armed forces, with US encouragement, set out to remove Chilean President Salvador Allende's elected socialist government amid economic crisis and political deadlock. They bombed the presidential palace on 11 September 1973, and Allende died inside. Seventeen years of military rule followed, in which official commissions counted more than 3,000 killed or disappeared, and Chile became a laboratory for free-market reform.
events.lens: Coups often claim to save a nation from chaos and then impose radical projects of their own.

events.hook: Australia removed race from its immigration rules.
events.what: Australia removed race from its immigration rules.
events.story: The Holt government in 1966 had let non-Europeans with skills settle and shortened their wait for citizenship. Prime Minister Gough Whitlam's government, with Immigration Minister Al Grassby, ended the remaining racial criteria in 1973 and ratified international conventions against racial discrimination. The Racial Discrimination Act became law in 1975.
events.why: Trade with Japan and Asia had outgrown trade with Britain, which joined the European Community in 1973. Asian governments and Australia's own public had turned against the policy.
events.then: Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser's government took in Vietnamese refugees from 1976. Migration from Asia grew through the 1980s and 1990s.
events.sig: Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser's government took in Vietnamese refugees from 1976. Migration from Asia grew through the 1980s and 1990s.
events.now: The removal of race from immigration law produced the population Australia has now: about 30 per cent born overseas, one of the highest shares in the world, with India and China the largest sources after Britain.

causes.why: After 70 years, changing attitudes and Asian ties ended racial immigration rules.

q.before: Immigration was restricted by race.
q.how: Government policy and new laws.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Prime Minister Gough Whitlam's government wanted race removed from immigration law to match Australia's trade with Asia and its standing abroad. In 1973 it ended the last racial criteria for entry, and the Racial Discrimination Act followed in 1975. Large-scale Asian migration began with Vietnamese refugees under the Fraser government in the late 1970s, and Australia became a country in which about 30 per cent of residents were born overseas.
events.lens: Changing economic and strategic ties drive changes in immigration policy.
events.fact: Grassby introduced the word 'multiculturalism' into Australian policy in a 1973 speech.

events.where: Suez Canal and the Golan Heights
events.hook: Egypt and Syria surprised Israel on Judaism's holiest day.
events.what: Egypt and Syria surprised Israel on Judaism's holiest day.
events.story: On 6 October 1973, Yom Kippur, Egyptian troops crossed the Suez Canal and Syrian forces attacked on the Golan Heights. Israeli Prime Minister Golda Meir's government had read the mobilisation as a bluff. After heavy early losses, Israel, resupplied by a US airlift, counterattacked and crossed the canal before a ceasefire.
events.why: Egypt and Syria wanted their land back and an end to the diplomatic stalemate. Sadat planned limited gains that would force talks.
events.then: US diplomacy led to the Camp David Accords of 1978 and an Egypt-Israel peace treaty in 1979.
events.sig: US diplomacy led to the Camp David Accords of 1978 and an Egypt-Israel peace treaty in 1979.
events.now: Israel's intelligence failure of 1973 is still debated and was compared to the failure of 7 October 2023.

causes.why: Egypt and Syria attacked in 1973 to win back land lost in 1967; Arab oil producers used an embargo as a weapon.

q.why: Egypt and Syria wanted back the land lost in 1967.
q.decided: Israel's counter-offensive with US supplies.
q.cost: Thousands killed on all sides.
q.changed: It opened the way to Egypt-Israel peace.

events.bluf: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Syrian President Hafez al-Assad attacked on 6 October 1973 to regain the land lost in 1967 and to force negotiations; Sadat aimed for limited gains rather than victory. Early Arab advances broke Israel's sense of invincibility before Israel, resupplied by a US airlift, counterattacked across the canal. Egyptian pride was restored, the Arab oil embargo followed, and the path to a separate Egyptian-Israeli peace opened.
events.lens: Limited wars can achieve political goals without military victory.
events.fact: The war fell in Ramadan as well as on Yom Kippur; Egypt calls it the October War or the Ramadan War.

toll.n: Estimates.

events.who: Arab oil producers, led by Saudi Arabia
events.hook: Arab states cut oil to the US and others, and prices quadrupled.
events.what: Arab states cut oil to the US and others, and prices quadrupled.
events.story: Days after the October war began, Arab oil producers led by Saudi King Faisal cut production and embargoed shipments to the United States and other backers of Israel. OPEC raised prices at the same time. Oil went from about 3 dollars a barrel to about 12 by early 1974.
events.why: The producers wanted to pressure Israel's backers. They also wanted to assert control over their own oil after decades of company pricing.
events.then: Queues at petrol stations, inflation and recession hit the West. Oil wealth transformed the Gulf states.
events.sig: Queues at petrol stations, inflation and recession hit the West. Oil wealth transformed the Gulf states.
events.now: The embargo showed how far the world depended on Middle Eastern oil and drove energy-saving rules such as fuel-economy standards.

causes.why: The dollar's fall cut oil exporters' real income; Arab producers used the 1973 war to cut supplies and quadruple prices.
Arab oil producers cut supplies to punish the US and others for backing Israel during the war.
By 1973 Saudi Arabia was the world's leading oil exporter, able to lead an embargo.

q.what: Crude oil.
q.who: Oil producers gained; Western consumers paid.
q.scale: Oil prices roughly quadrupled.
q.daily: Petrol queues and rationing.
q.system: Oil as a political weapon.

events.bluf: Arab oil producers led by Saudi Arabia cut output and embargoed shipments to punish the United States and others for backing Israel in the October war, and to assert control over their own oil. With OPEC raising prices, oil went from about 3 to about 12 dollars a barrel by early 1974. Inflation and recession hit the West, wealth shifted to the producers, and energy security became a core strategic concern.
events.lens: Control of a critical commodity is a powerful weapon, as long as the market cannot easily replace it.
events.fact: The United States imposed a national 55 mph speed limit in 1974 to save fuel.

events.hook: India tested a nuclear device, which it called a 'peaceful nuclear explosion'.
events.what: India tested a nuclear device, which it called a 'peaceful nuclear explosion'.
events.story: Code-named 'Smiling Buddha', the test of 18 May 1974 at Pokhran in Rajasthan used plutonium from the Canadian-supplied CIRUS reactor. The Indian Atomic Energy Commission under chairman Homi Sethna and physicist Raja Ramanna ran it. India called it a peaceful nuclear explosion; it made India the first nation outside the five permanent Security Council members to explode a nuclear device.
events.why: China's nuclear weapons, tested from 1964, two years after it defeated India, came first. Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi wanted a demonstration of standing after the victory of 1971.
events.then: Canada and the United States cut nuclear cooperation. Supplier states formed the Nuclear Suppliers Group in 1975 to control nuclear exports. Pakistan's programme, begun in 1972, accelerated. India tested again only in 1998.
events.sig: Canada and the United States cut nuclear cooperation. Supplier states formed the Nuclear Suppliers Group in 1975 to control nuclear exports. Pakistan's programme, begun in 1972, accelerated. India tested again only in 1998.
events.now: India and Pakistan both openly tested weapons in 1998, and South Asia now has two nuclear-armed rivals that have fought a limited war and several crises since.

causes.why: Defeat by China, which tested a bomb in 1964, pushed India toward nuclear weapons.

q.problem: Could India build a nuclear device?
q.how: A plutonium device exploded underground.
q.replaced: India's purely civil nuclear image.
q.spread: Pakistan accelerated its own programme.
q.next: Open nuclear tests by both in 1998.

events.bluf: Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government set out to show that India could build a nuclear device, ten years after China's first test. The device exploded under the Rajasthan desert at Pokhran on 18 May 1974, which India called a 'peaceful nuclear explosion'. India became the first state outside the five recognised nuclear powers to test, supplier states formed the Nuclear Suppliers Group to tighten exports, and Pakistan's own programme gained urgency.
events.lens: A rival's nuclear weapons push neighbours to acquire their own.
events.fact: The test fell on Buddha's birthday, hence the codename; the message to Indira Gandhi read 'the Buddha has smiled'.

events.what: Emperor deposed after 44 years.
events.why: The hidden famine discredited the court. Price rises and unpaid soldiers gave the mutinies their numbers.
events.sig: The emperor died in custody in August 1975. Derg leader Mengistu Haile Mariam took sole power in 1977, and the Red Terror of 1977-78 killed tens of thousands.
events.hook: Ethiopia's emperor was deposed, ending one of the world's oldest monarchies.
events.story: Ethiopian Emperor Haile Selassie had ruled since 1930. A famine in Wollo in 1972-74 killed tens of thousands while the court concealed it, and rising fuel and food prices set off strikes and army mutinies in early 1974. A committee of junior officers, the Derg, took control of the army and deposed the emperor on 12 September 1974.
events.then: The emperor died in custody in August 1975. Derg leader Mengistu Haile Mariam took sole power in 1977, and the Red Terror of 1977-78 killed tens of thousands.
events.now: The Derg's fall in 1991 brought a system of ethnic federalism that still shapes Ethiopia's politics and conflicts.

q.before: Emperor Haile Selassie.
q.how: A creeping military takeover.
q.lasted: The Derg ruled until 1991.

events.bluf: Ethiopian army officers formed the Derg in 1974 to force reform on a court that had hidden a famine and let prices rise. They deposed Emperor Haile Selassie on 12 September 1974, ended a monarchy that claimed descent from Solomon and turned to Marxism under Mengistu Haile Mariam. The Derg's Red Terror, its wars in Eritrea and Tigray and the famine of 1984 devastated Ethiopia until its fall in 1991.
events.lens: Regimes that hide a crisis lose legitimacy fast when the truth comes out.
events.trig: A television film of the Wollo famine, shown in Addis Ababa in September 1974 beside footage of the imperial court.
events.fact: Haile Selassie was driven from his palace in the back seat of a Volkswagen Beetle.

events.what: First president to resign.
events.why: Nixon's campaign organised the break-in. Nixon ordered the FBI investigation blocked and hush money paid, and the cover-up became the crime.
events.sig: President Gerald Ford pardoned Nixon on 8 September 1974. Congress passed campaign finance limits in 1974 and curbs on presidential war and spending powers. Trust in government, above 70 per cent in 1964, fell below 30 per cent by 1980 (Pew series).
events.hook: For the first and only time, a US president resigned.
events.story: Five men linked to President Richard Nixon's re-election campaign were arrested inside the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex on 17 June 1972. Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein traced the money to the campaign. The Senate Watergate Committee learned in July 1973 that Nixon taped his office. The Supreme Court ordered the tapes released on 24 July 1974; one recorded Nixon directing the cover-up six days after the break-in. He resigned on 9 August 1974 ahead of certain impeachment.
events.then: President Gerald Ford pardoned Nixon on 8 September 1974. Congress passed campaign finance limits in 1974 and curbs on presidential war and spending powers. Trust in government, above 70 per cent in 1964, fell below 30 per cent by 1980 (Pew series).
events.now: Watergate remains the benchmark for abuse of executive power, and '-gate' became the suffix for every scandal.

causes.why: Watergate grew out of the Nixon White House's campaign against leaks, such as the Pentagon Papers on Vietnam, and against political opponents.

q.before: President Richard Nixon.
q.how: Resignation under threat of impeachment.
q.claim: The rule of law over the president.
q.lasted: Yes: Gerald Ford took over.

events.bluf: President Richard Nixon's re-election campaign broke into the Democratic headquarters at the Watergate complex in June 1972, and Nixon set out to cover it up. Investigations by the press, the Senate and a special prosecutor, and his own tapes, exposed the cover-up, and he resigned on 9 August 1974, the only president to do so. Congress limited executive power and campaign money, and trust in government fell for a generation.
events.lens: Courts, Congress and a free press can hold even a president accountable, if they act independently.
events.fact: The source Woodward called 'Deep Throat' was FBI Deputy Director Mark Felt, who admitted it in 2005.

sites.d: Site of the 1968 Tet Offensive's fiercest fighting.
Fell April 30, 1975; helicopter evacuation from the US embassy.

events.hook: North Vietnamese tanks crashed through the gates of Saigon's presidential palace, and Vietnam was unified.
events.what: North Vietnamese tanks crashed through the gates of Saigon's presidential palace, and Vietnam was unified.
events.story: North Vietnam's spring offensive of March 1975 collapsed the South's army in weeks. As helicopters evacuated the last Americans from the US embassy, North Vietnamese tanks entered Saigon on 30 April 1975. South Vietnamese President Duong Van Minh surrendered. The city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.
events.why: South Vietnam depended on US support, which had ended. Corruption undermined its state, and the North was determined.
events.then: Communists also took power in Laos and Cambodia in 1975. Vietnam's re-education camps and economic failure drove hundreds of thousands of 'boat people' to flee over the next decade.
events.sig: Communists also took power in Laos and Cambodia in 1975. Vietnam's re-education camps and economic failure drove hundreds of thousands of 'boat people' to flee over the next decade.
events.now: The fall of Saigon ended thirty years of war and American intervention in Southeast Asia, reunified Vietnam under the Communist Party, and left a United States that avoided ground wars for fifteen years.

causes.why: Without US forces, South Vietnam fell to the North's offensive in April 1975.

q.why: North Vietnam's final offensive to reunify the country.
q.decided: The collapse of the South Vietnamese army.
q.cost: Thousands killed in the final offensive.
q.changed: Vietnam was reunified under communist rule.

events.bluf: North Vietnam's leaders set out to finish the war by conventional offensive once US troops and aid were gone. Their spring offensive collapsed the South's army in weeks, and tanks entered Saigon on 30 April 1975 as helicopters lifted the last Americans out. Thirty years of war ended with Vietnam unified under the Communist Party; the United States avoided ground wars for fifteen years, and the predicted 'domino' collapse stopped at Indochina.
events.lens: Governments sustained by foreign support often collapse quickly once that support ends.
events.fact: The United States and Vietnam restored diplomatic relations in 1995, twenty years after the fall.

events.hook: The Khmer Rouge emptied Cambodia's cities and began a genocide that killed up to 2 million people.
events.what: The Khmer Rouge emptied Cambodia's cities and began a genocide that killed up to 2 million people.
events.story: On 17 April 1975 the Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot took Phnom Penh and forced its entire population into the countryside. They abolished money, schools and religion. Roughly a quarter of Cambodia's people were killed or died of starvation and overwork by 1979. Estimates of the dead run from 1.5 to 2 million, the range the UN-backed tribunal worked with, to 3.3 million, the figure of the Vietnamese-installed government of the 1980s.
events.why: The spread of the Vietnam War into Cambodia helped the Khmer Rouge grow, and the US-backed government of Lon Nol collapsed. One reading holds that American bombing of 1969-73 drove peasants to the Khmer Rouge; the other holds that the party's growth came from North Vietnamese backing and from Prince Sihanouk's call to join it after the 1970 coup against him. Pol Pot's aim of total agrarian revolution set the scale of the killing.
events.then: Vietnam invaded in December 1978 and drove the Khmer Rouge from power in January 1979. China, the United States and others kept recognising the Khmer Rouge at the UN for years.
events.sig: Vietnam invaded in December 1978 and drove the Khmer Rouge from power in January 1979. China, the United States and others kept recognising the Khmer Rouge at the UN for years.
events.now: The Khmer Rouge killed about a quarter of Cambodia's people in four years, the most intense genocide of the century in proportion to population; Vietnam's invasion to end it isolated both countries for a decade.

causes.why: With US forces gone from Indochina, Cambodia's US-backed government collapsed to the Khmer Rouge in April 1975.

sites.d: Emptied by the Khmer Rouge within days, April 1975.

q.why: The Khmer Rouge sought total power and an agrarian utopia.
q.decided: The collapse of the US-backed government.
q.cost: About 1.5 to 2 million Cambodians died by 1979.
q.changed: Cities were emptied and a genocide began.

events.bluf: Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge set out to build an agrarian communist society from nothing. After taking Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975 they emptied the cities, abolished money, schools and religion, and killed or starved roughly a quarter of Cambodia's people by 1979. Vietnam's invasion ended the regime in January 1979; a UN-backed tribunal convicted the surviving leaders of genocide in 2018, and the toll remains the century's most intense in proportion to population.
events.lens: Utopian ideologies that try to remake society from scratch can kill on a massive scale.
events.fact: A UN-backed tribunal convicted the surviving leaders of genocide in 2018.

events.hook: Mozambique won independence after a decade of guerrilla war against Portugal.
events.what: Mozambique won independence after a decade of guerrilla war against Portugal.
events.story: FRELIMO under Mozambican leader Samora Machel had fought Portuguese rule since 1964. After Portugal's Carnation Revolution of April 1974 the new government in Lisbon agreed to withdraw. Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975 with Machel as president.
events.why: Portugal's colonial wars had exhausted its army, which overthrew the dictatorship in 1974.
events.then: Rhodesia and then South Africa armed RENAMO against FRELIMO's Marxist state. The civil war killed about a million people before the Rome peace accord of October 1992.
events.sig: Rhodesia and then South Africa armed RENAMO against FRELIMO's Marxist state. The civil war killed about a million people before the Rome peace accord of October 1992.
events.now: FRELIMO has governed Mozambique since independence, and its disputed 2024 election win set off deadly protests.

q.before: Portuguese colonial rule.
q.how: Independence after guerrilla war and a revolution in Portugal.
q.lasted: Yes, though civil war followed.

events.bluf: FRELIMO under Samora Machel had fought Portugal since 1964 to end colonial rule in Mozambique. Portugal's own revolution of April 1974 ended the war, and Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975 under Machel. The new state became a target of Rhodesia and South Africa, which armed RENAMO rebels in a civil war that killed about a million people before peace in 1992.
events.lens: A revolution at the imperial centre can free colonies overnight.
events.fact: Machel died in a 1986 plane crash on South African territory that many Mozambicans still blame on Pretoria.

events.who: 35 nations including the US, USSR and Canada
events.hook: Cold War rivals accepted Europe's borders and pledged to respect human rights.
events.what: Cold War rivals accepted Europe's borders and pledged to respect human rights.
events.story: Thirty-five states, including the United States, the Soviet Union and Canada, signed the Final Act in Helsinki on 1 August 1975. The Soviet Union won recognition of its postwar borders. In return it signed commitments to human rights and freedom of movement. Dissident groups, Charter 77 in Czechoslovakia and the Moscow Helsinki Group, cited the promises against their governments.
events.why: Détente came first: Brezhnev wanted the borders of 1945 recognised and the West wanted lower tensions. Western Europeans insisted on the human-rights basket as the price.
events.then: The Moscow Helsinki Group formed in 1976 and Charter 77 in 1977. Violations were aired at follow-up conferences in Belgrade and Madrid. The process became the OSCE in 1995.
events.sig: The Moscow Helsinki Group formed in 1976 and Charter 77 in 1977. Violations were aired at follow-up conferences in Belgrade and Madrid. The process became the OSCE in 1995.
events.now: The human-rights commitments gave dissidents from Moscow to Prague a text their governments had signed, and the follow-up conferences a forum to cite it; the OSCE that grew from the process monitors elections and conflicts in Europe today.

q.before: Cold War tension over borders and rights.
q.how: An agreement signed by 35 states.
q.winners: In the long run, dissidents in the East.

On 31 August the government signed the Gdańsk Agreement recognising Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc; it grew to about 10 million members. General Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law on 13 December 1981 and interned its leaders.
events.then: Martial law drove the union underground. Round-table talks in 1989 produced semi-free elections on 4 June 1989, which Solidarity swept; Tadeusz Mazowiecki became the bloc's first non-communist prime minister in August. Wałęsa was president from 1990 to 1995.
events.now: Solidarity's survival underground and its victory in the elections of June 1989 gave the bloc its first non-communist government and the method, negotiation at a round table, that Hungary and Czechoslovakia followed within months.

events.bluf: President Ronald Reagan set out to shrink government at home, rebuild the military and press the Soviet Union abroad. Conservatism became the governing creed of American politics for a generation, and the Cold War ended on his successor's watch.

Defeat brought down the junta and restored democracy in Argentina, and victory secured Thatcher's re-election in 1983.
events.lens: Military regimes that gamble on nationalist wars risk everything if they lose.

events.story: Oil exporters deposited their surpluses in Western banks in the 1970s, and the banks lent heavily to Latin American governments. Banks stopped lending across the region, and country after country turned to the IMF for loans conditioned on austerity.

events.hook: A gas leak at a pesticide plant killed thousands in the world's worst industrial disaster.
events.what: A gas leak at a pesticide plant killed thousands in the world's worst industrial disaster.
events.story: On the night of 2-3 December 1984 about 40 tonnes of methyl isocyanate gas escaped from a storage tank at the Union Carbide India Limited pesticide plant and spread over sleeping neighbourhoods. The official immediate death toll was about 3,800; later estimates of total deaths run to 15,000 or more, and hundreds of thousands were injured. Union Carbide chairman Warren Anderson was arrested on arrival in Bhopal and released on bail.
events.why: Safety systems at a loss-making plant, including the tank's refrigeration and the gas scrubber, had been shut down or neglected, and a dense neighbourhood had grown up around it. Union Carbide holds that a worker's sabotage put water in the tank; Indian investigators found that water entered through poor maintenance.
events.then: Union Carbide paid $470 million in a 1989 settlement with the Indian government that victims called inadequate. Anderson never returned to face Indian charges and died in 2014. Seven Indian managers were convicted of negligence in 2010 and sentenced to two years. Dow Chemical bought Union Carbide in 2001 and denies liability.
events.sig: Union Carbide paid $470 million in a 1989 settlement with the Indian government that victims called inadequate. Anderson never returned to face Indian charges and died in 2014. Seven Indian managers were convicted of negligence in 2010 and sentenced to two years. Dow Chemical bought Union Carbide in 2001 and denies liability.
events.now: Bhopal produced the US Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act of 1986 and India's Environment Protection Act of 1986; the site remains contaminated and claims are still in litigation.

events.bluf: A Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, running at a loss with safety systems shut down, stood beside densely settled neighbourhoods. On the night of 2-3 December 1984 about 40 tonnes of methyl isocyanate escaped and killed about 3,800 people by the official immediate count, with later estimates of total deaths far higher, and injured hundreds of thousands. The world's worst industrial accident became the test case for holding multinational companies to account in poor countries, and the company settled for $470 million in 1989.
events.lens: When safety costs are cut where regulation is weak, the poor pay the price.

events.what: Launched glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring).
events.why: The Soviet economy was stagnating and the arms race was a burden it could no longer carry. The old leaders had died one after another, and the Politburo chose a younger man.

events.hook: A reformer took over the Soviet Union and accidentally helped end it.
events.story: Three Soviet leaders had died in office between 1982 and 1985. On 11 March 1985 the Politburo chose Mikhail Gorbachev, aged 54, as general secretary. He introduced glasnost, openness, and perestroika, restructuring, to revive the economy and society. He withdrew from Afghanistan by 1989, signed the INF Treaty with US President Ronald Reagan in 1987 and declined to use force to hold Eastern Europe.
events.then: Communist governments fell across Eastern Europe in 1989. Germany reunified in October 1990. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991 and Gorbachev resigned.
events.now: Gorbachev is admired in the West and widely blamed in Russia, where Russian President Vladimir Putin's view of the Soviet collapse as a catastrophe shapes policy toward the former republics.

events.bluf: The Politburo chose Mikhail Gorbachev to revive a stagnant economy and a rigid state. His reforms, glasnost and perestroika, loosened the controls that held the system together, and his refusal to use force let Eastern Europe leave. Within six years the Cold War had ended peacefully, communism in Europe had collapsed and the Soviet Union had dissolved, the reverse of what he had set out to do.
events.lens: Reforming a system built on coercion can loosen the very controls that held it together.
events.fact: Gorbachev won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990; in Russia's 1996 presidential election he took about 0.5 per cent of the vote.

events.hook: The world's worst nuclear accident exposed the Soviet system's lies.
events.story: In the early hours of 26 April 1986 operators running a safety test on Reactor 4 at Chernobyl, in Soviet Ukraine, triggered a power surge that blew the reactor apart and set its graphite core on fire. Two workers died in the blast and about 30 firefighters and staff within months from radiation. Authorities evacuated nearby Pripyat only the next day and admitted the accident only after Swedish monitors detected the fallout. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev spoke about it on television 18 days later.
events.then: About 350,000 people were evacuated, and a 30 km exclusion zone remains. Fallout spread across Belarus, Ukraine and much of Europe. Gorbachev later called the accident a turning point that pushed glasnost forward.
events.now: The accident froze nuclear construction across much of Europe for two decades and gave glasnost its first test; Russian forces occupied the site for five weeks in 2022.
events.fact: The 30 km exclusion zone has become an accidental wildlife refuge with wolves, bison and wild horses.

q.problem: Running a test on a reactor with a dangerous design.
q.how: A power surge blew the reactor apart.
q.replaced: Trust in Soviet nuclear safety.
q.spread: Radiation spread across Europe.
q.next: Glasnost, and debates about nuclear power.

events.bluf: Operators at Chernobyl's Reactor 4 ran a safety test on a reactor with a known design flaw, with its safety systems disabled. The reactor exploded, its graphite core burned for days, and fallout spread across Belarus, Ukraine and Europe; about 30 workers and firefighters died within months and about 350,000 people were evacuated. The cover-up exposed the Soviet state's secrecy, pushed Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost forward and set back nuclear power worldwide.
events.lens: Disasters handled with secrecy destroy trust in the state: Chernobyl turned many Soviet citizens against their leaders.

events.who: The CIA; Pakistan's intelligence service; Afghan mujahideen
events.hook: US-supplied Stinger missiles began shooting down Soviet helicopters.
events.what: US-supplied Stinger missiles began shooting down Soviet helicopters.
events.story: Through Operation Cyclone the CIA channelled billions of dollars of weapons through Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence to Afghan rebels from 1979. On 25 September 1986 mujahideen fired the first Stingers near Jalalabad airfield and brought down Soviet helicopters. The United States supplied some 2,000 of the missiles over the rest of the war.
events.why: The United States wanted to make Afghanistan the Soviet Union's Vietnam. Congress, led by Representative Charlie Wilson, pushed a reluctant CIA to supply advanced missiles.
events.then: Soviet helicopter and transport losses mounted. One reading holds that the Stingers made the war unwinnable; the other holds that Gorbachev had told the Politburo in 1985 that he wanted out, before the first missile was fired. Soviet forces left in February 1989. Many Stingers were never recovered, and the CIA ran a buy-back programme in the 1990s.
events.sig: Soviet helicopter and transport losses mounted. One reading holds that the Stingers made the war unwinnable; the other holds that Gorbachev had told the Politburo in 1985 that he wanted out, before the first missile was fired. Soviet forces left in February 1989. Many Stingers were never recovered, and the CIA ran a buy-back programme in the 1990s.
events.now: The flood of weapons and foreign volunteers shaped the Afghan wars that followed, and hundreds of unrecovered Stingers worried air forces for a decade.

causes.why: The US armed the resistance to make the war costly.

q.decided: Portable missiles blunted Soviet air power.
q.cost: About 15,000 Soviet soldiers and perhaps a million Afghans died in the war.
q.changed: The Soviets began looking for a way out.

events.bluf: The CIA, pushed by Congress, set out to raise the cost of the Soviet war in Afghanistan by giving the mujahideen a weapon against helicopter gunships. Stinger missiles fired near Jalalabad in September 1986 brought down Soviet helicopters and forced Soviet aircraft to fly higher and less often. The war's cost to Moscow rose as Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev was deciding to leave, and the weapons and fighters the programme created shaped the Afghan wars that followed.
events.lens: Weapons supplied to proxies outlive the war they were meant for.
events.fact: The CIA spent tens of millions of dollars in the 1990s buying back missiles it had given away.

events.hook: Reagan and Gorbachev came close to agreeing to abolish all their nuclear weapons.
events.what: Reagan and Gorbachev came close to agreeing to abolish all their nuclear weapons.
events.story: US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met at Höfði House in Reykjavík on 11-12 October 1986. They discussed eliminating all ballistic missiles and then all nuclear weapons within ten years. The talks collapsed over Reagan's refusal to confine his Strategic Defense Initiative, the 'Star Wars' missile shield, to the laboratory.
events.why: Gorbachev wanted to cut military spending. Reagan wanted to end the nuclear threat and believed the shield would help.
events.then: The INF Treaty of December 1987 eliminated both sides' intermediate-range missiles. The START treaty of July 1991 cut long-range weapons.
events.sig: The INF Treaty of December 1987 eliminated both sides' intermediate-range missiles. The START treaty of July 1991 cut long-range weapons.
events.now: US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev both later called it a turning point in the Cold War, and missile defence remains the main obstacle in arms talks with Russia.

causes.why: Gorbachev sought arms cuts to save money for reform.

q.before: A costly nuclear arms race.
q.how: A summit between the two leaders.
q.winners: Neither, at the time; both, later.
q.lasted: It led to real arms cuts.

events.bluf: Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev wanted deep cuts in nuclear arms to relieve his economy; US President Ronald Reagan wanted the nuclear threat ended and his missile shield kept. For two days they came close to agreeing to abolish all nuclear weapons, and the talks broke over the shield. The trust built in the failure produced the INF Treaty a year later and the START treaty in 1991.
events.lens: Failed summits can still lay the groundwork for later agreements.
events.fact: Reagan's offer to eliminate all ballistic missiles alarmed his own allies, whose defence rested on them.
