events.hook: An army officer overthrew Fiji's newly elected government, beginning a cycle of coups.
events.what: An army officer overthrew Fiji's newly elected government, beginning a cycle of coups.
events.story: Britain brought about 60,000 indentured Indian labourers to Fiji's sugar plantations between 1879 and 1916, and by 1987 their descendants were nearly half the population. In April 1987 a coalition led by Fijian Prime Minister Timoci Bavadra, an Indigenous Fijian backed mainly by Indo-Fijian voters, won the election. On 14 May Lieutenant Colonel Sitiveni Rabuka led soldiers into Parliament and arrested the government. He staged a second coup on 25 September and declared a republic in October.
events.why: Indigenous Fijian nationalists feared losing land and political power to a population their own size. The army was almost entirely Indigenous Fijian.
events.then: A 1990 constitution reserved power for Indigenous Fijians, and tens of thousands of Indo-Fijians emigrated. Businessman George Speight held Parliament hostage in 2000, and Commodore Frank Bainimarama seized power in 2006 and ruled until 2022. Rabuka returned as elected prime minister in 1992 and in 2022.
events.sig: A 1990 constitution reserved power for Indigenous Fijians, and tens of thousands of Indo-Fijians emigrated. Businessman George Speight held Parliament hostage in 2000, and Commodore Frank Bainimarama seized power in 2006 and ruled until 2022. Rabuka returned as elected prime minister in 1992 and in 2022.
events.now: The coups fixed ethnicity as the organising fact of Fijian politics and shrank the Indo-Fijian population from nearly half to about a third; the coup leader of 1987 was elected prime minister in 1992 and again in 2022.

q.before: An elected government backed by Indo-Fijians.
q.how: Military coups.
q.lasted: Further coups followed.

events.bluf: Fijian Lieutenant Colonel Sitiveni Rabuka set out to keep political power with Indigenous Fijians after an election had produced a government backed mainly by Indo-Fijians. His coup of 14 May 1987 removed Prime Minister Timoci Bavadra's government; a second coup in September made Fiji a republic outside the Commonwealth. Tens of thousands of Indo-Fijians emigrated, and the country entered a cycle of coups in 2000 and 2006 rooted in the colonial labour migration that had made it two peoples.
events.lens: Colonial labor migration can create ethnic divisions that dominate post-colonial politics.
events.fact: Rabuka's coup was the first military coup in the Pacific islands.

events.what: Eliminated a whole class of nuclear missiles.
events.why: Gorbachev needed to cut military spending and his reforms had opened room for agreement. Both sides wanted rid of weapons whose short flight times left no room for decision.
events.sig: By 1991 the two countries had destroyed 2,692 missiles, checked by each other's inspectors. The treaty opened the way to the START agreement of 1991. The United States withdrew in August 2019, citing Russia's 9M729 missile, and Russia declared the treaty void.
events.hook: For the first time, the superpowers destroyed a whole class of nuclear weapons.
events.story: The Soviet SS-20 and the American Pershing II and cruise missiles deployed in reply in 1983 could strike within minutes. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, after summits in Geneva in 1985 and Reykjavik in 1986, signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in Washington on 8 December 1987. It eliminated every ground-launched missile with a range of 500 to 5,500 kilometres and allowed on-site inspection. By 1991 the two countries had destroyed 2,692 missiles.
events.then: By 1991 the two countries had destroyed 2,692 missiles, checked by each other's inspectors. The treaty opened the way to the START agreement of 1991. The United States withdrew in August 2019, citing Russia's 9M729 missile, and Russia declared the treaty void.
events.now: The US left the treaty in 2019, accusing Russia of deploying a banned missile, and Russia has since fired an intermediate-range missile at Ukraine.

causes.why: Gorbachev and Reagan agreed to scrap a whole class of nuclear missiles, the first treaty to reduce nuclear arsenals.
Reagan combined a military build-up with a willingness to negotiate once Gorbachev was in power.
The talks at Reykjavík laid the groundwork for the INF Treaty.

q.before: Both sides had hundreds of medium-range nuclear missiles in Europe.
q.how: A treaty with inspections.
q.lasted: Until the US left in 2019.

events.bluf: President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev set out to remove the missiles that could reach each other's forces in Europe within minutes. The treaty signed in Washington on 8 December 1987 banned all ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometres and let each side inspect the other. By 1991 the two countries had destroyed 2,692 missiles; the treaty was the high point of Cold War arms control, and its collapse in 2019 marked the unravelling of that system.
events.lens: Arms control depends on verification and mutual interest; when either fails, treaties collapse.
events.fact: Reagan's rule for the treaty, 'trust, but verify', was a Russian proverb his advisers had taught him, and Gorbachev complained that he said it at every meeting.

events.who: Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza; Israeli forces
events.hook: Palestinians in the occupied territories rose up with strikes, boycotts and stone-throwing.
events.what: Palestinians in the occupied territories rose up with strikes, boycotts and stone-throwing.
events.story: On 8 December 1987 an Israeli truck killed four Palestinians in Gaza. Protests spread across the West Bank and Gaza and ran until 1993. Over 1,000 Palestinians and over 150 Israelis were killed by Israeli rights-group counts.
events.why: Twenty years of occupation, settlement and economic hardship came first. Palestinians also felt the PLO abroad and the Arab states had failed them.
events.then: Hamas was founded in Gaza at the start of the uprising. In 1988 the PLO moved toward accepting a two-state framework.
events.sig: Hamas was founded in Gaza at the start of the uprising. In 1988 the PLO moved toward accepting a two-state framework.
events.now: The intifada pushed both sides toward the Oslo talks. Its largely unarmed mass protest contrasts with the far deadlier armed Second Intifada of 2000-05.

causes.why: Twenty years of occupation of the West Bank and Gaza after 1967 led to the uprising.

q.how: Mass protest, strikes and stone-throwing.
q.winners: It put Palestinians on the world agenda.
q.lasted: It ended with the Oslo Accords.

events.bluf: Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza rose against 20 years of occupation with strikes, stones and boycotts, organised locally rather than by the PLO abroad. The uprising ran for six years and killed over 1,000 Palestinians and over 150 Israelis. It won Palestinians international attention, produced Hamas, and pushed Israel and the PLO toward the Oslo talks.
events.lens: Grassroots uprisings can change a conflict's dynamics and force leaders to negotiate.
events.fact: 'Intifada' means 'shaking off' in Arabic.

events.who: General Boris Gromov and the Soviet 40th Army
events.hook: The last Soviet soldiers crossed the Friendship Bridge home, ending a nine-year war.
events.what: The last Soviet soldiers crossed the Friendship Bridge home, ending a nine-year war.
events.story: Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev had sought a way out since 1985. The Geneva Accords signed on 14 April 1988 set a withdrawal, and Soviet forces left in two stages from May 1988. On 15 February 1989 their commander General Boris Gromov was the last to walk across the Friendship Bridge over the Amu Darya at Termez. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers had died in nine years.
events.why: Gorbachev called the war a 'bleeding wound' in 1986 and wanted to end its costs in money, men and standing abroad.
events.then: Afghan President Mohammad Najibullah's government held on with Soviet aid until the aid stopped in 1992 and fell that April. Civil war among the mujahideen destroyed much of Kabul, and the Taliban took the city in 1996 and hanged Najibullah.
events.sig: Afghan President Mohammad Najibullah's government held on with Soviet aid until the aid stopped in 1992 and fell that April. Civil war among the mujahideen destroyed much of Kabul, and the Taliban took the city in 1996 and hanged Najibullah.
events.now: The defeat weakened the Soviet Union in its final years, and the bitterness of its veterans echoed in Russia's later wars.

causes.why: Mounting losses convinced Gorbachev to withdraw.

q.before: A Soviet-backed government under Mohammad Najibullah.
q.how: A negotiated withdrawal.
q.winners: The mujahideen, who soon turned on each other.
q.lasted: The Soviet-backed regime survived three more years.

events.bluf: Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev set out to end a war he called a 'bleeding wound' and to free resources for reform at home. Under the Geneva Accords of April 1988 the 40th Army left in stages, and its commander General Boris Gromov walked across the Amu Darya bridge on 15 February 1989 as the last man out. The retreat weakened the Soviet state in its last years, and Afghanistan's communist government fell three years later to a civil war that ended in Taliban rule.
events.lens: Withdrawing from a failed war does not end the conflict; it changes who fights it.
events.fact: Gromov's teenage son met him in the middle of the bridge with a bunch of carnations.

events.what: Pro-democracy protests crushed.
events.why: Students demanded political reform and an end to corruption amid the highest inflation since 1949. The leadership was split between Zhao Ziyang's conciliation and Li Peng's hard line, and Deng Xiaoping sided with force.
events.sig: The party purged reformers, tightened control of the press and universities and, after a pause, pushed economic growth harder.
events.hook: China's army crushed pro-democracy protests in Beijing.
events.story: Reformist former party leader Hu Yaobang died on 15 April 1989, and students occupied Tiananmen Square calling for reform and an end to corruption; workers joined them and protests spread to other cities. Party General Secretary Zhao Ziyang urged conciliation and was removed; Premier Li Peng declared martial law on 20 May. On the night of 3-4 June the army cleared the square and surrounding streets. Chinese government statements of June 1989 put the dead at about 200 to 300, soldiers included; estimates by foreign governments and rights groups since then run from several hundred to several thousand.
events.then: The party purged reformers, tightened control of the press and universities and, after a pause, pushed economic growth harder.
events.now: The party's choice of force over reform in 1989 set its course: economic opening without political liberalisation. The event is censored inside China; the party holds that the suppression secured the stability on which growth rested, and the protesters' supporters hold that it closed the path to political reform.
events.fact: The identity of 'Tank Man', who stood in front of the column of tanks, has never been confirmed.

causes.why: Reform brought inflation, corruption and hopes for political change that students voiced in 1989.

q.before: The Communist Party, divided between reformers and hard-liners.
q.how: A military crackdown.
q.lasted: The party still rules.

events.bluf: Students occupied Tiananmen Square in spring 1989 to demand political reform and an end to corruption; the Communist Party leadership under Deng Xiaoping decided to clear them by force. Troops entered Beijing on the night of 3-4 June and killed hundreds by the Chinese government's count of 1989, and more by foreign estimates. The party purged its reformers, chose economic growth without political liberalisation, and has followed that course since.
events.lens: Regimes that survive a crisis by force often double down on economic performance as their source of legitimacy.

events.what: Border opened; wall torn down.
events.why: Economic stagnation and mass emigration came first. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev refused to send Soviet troops to prop up the regime, and East German leader Erich Honecker had been removed three weeks earlier.
events.sig: Communist governments fell across Eastern Europe within weeks; Germany reunified on 3 October 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
events.hook: Crowds poured through the Berlin Wall, and the Cold War started to end.
events.story: Through 1989 East Germans fled west via Hungary, which had opened its Austrian border, and marched every Monday in Leipzig. On 9 November the government loosened travel rules, and at a press conference Politburo spokesman Günter Schabowski, misreading his note, said they applied 'immediately'. Crowds gathered at the checkpoints, and at Bornholmer Strasse overwhelmed border guards opened the gates.
events.then: Communist governments fell across Eastern Europe within weeks; Germany reunified on 3 October 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
events.now: Germany's reunification and NATO's later enlargement follow from that night; Russia holds that the West promised in 1990 that NATO would stay put, and Western governments hold that no such pledge was written down, an argument that runs to the war in Ukraine.
events.fact: The first checkpoint, at Bornholmer Strasse, was opened around 11.30 pm by border officer Harald Jäger, who had been given no orders.

causes.why: The Wall stood for 28 years as the Cold War's symbol, until East Germans broke through it.
Poland's partly free election in June 1989, won by Solidarity, set off the revolutions that toppled communist regimes across Eastern Europe.
Gorbachev made clear that the USSR would not send tanks to save Eastern Europe's regimes.

q.before: The Wall divided Berlin since 1961.
q.how: Crowds forced open the border.
q.lasted: Germany reunited within a year.

events.bluf: East Germany's government, losing its citizens through Hungary and facing weekly marches in Leipzig, tried to ease the pressure with new travel rules. A botched announcement sent crowds to the checkpoints, and the guards opened the gates. The division of Germany ended in practice that night, communist governments fell across Eastern Europe within weeks, and Germany was reunified within a year.
events.trig: The botched announcement of new travel rules on the evening of 9 November 1989.
events.lens: Regimes that rely on force collapse fast when their protector will not use it.

events.what: Noriega removed.

events.sig: Civilian deaths are disputed: the US military counted about 200, and Panamanian and human rights groups estimated hundreds to several thousand. Noriega was convicted in Miami in 1992. Panama abolished its army.
events.hook: The US invaded Panama to arrest its leader, a former CIA ally.
events.story: Panamanian military ruler Manuel Noriega had worked with the CIA for years and was indicted in Florida in 1988 for drug trafficking. He annulled the May 1989 election his opponents had won. After Panamanian forces killed a US Marine officer at a checkpoint on 16 December, 26,000 US troops invaded on 20 December. Noriega took refuge in the Vatican embassy and surrendered on 3 January 1990.
events.then: Civilian deaths are disputed: the US military counted about 200, and Panamanian and human rights groups estimated hundreds to several thousand. Noriega was convicted in Miami in 1992. Panama abolished its army.
events.now: The invasion is the precedent for US military action to seize a foreign leader indicted on US drug charges, and it was cited in debates over US action against the government of Venezuela from 2020.

causes.why: The canal kept Panama strategic. In 1989 the US invaded to remove Manuel Noriega, a former US intelligence asset indicted for drug trafficking.

q.why: The US wanted to remove Noriega.
q.decided: Overwhelming US force.
q.cost: Hundreds of Panamanians killed.
q.changed: Noriega was captured.

events.bluf: US President George H. W. Bush set out to remove Panamanian military ruler Manuel Noriega, a former CIA asset indicted in the United States for drug trafficking. About 26,000 US troops invaded on 20 December 1989, and Noriega surrendered on 3 January 1990. It was the last large-scale US invasion in Latin America and showed that, with the Cold War ending, Washington faced no Soviet check on force in its own hemisphere.
events.lens: Former allies can become targets when their usefulness ends.
events.fact: US troops played loud rock music outside the Vatican embassy to pressure Noriega to surrender.

events.who: Václav Havel; Czechoslovak students and citizens
events.hook: Peaceful mass protests ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia in six weeks.
events.what: Peaceful mass protests ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia in six weeks.
events.story: Police beat student marchers in Prague on 17 November 1989. Protests grew to hundreds of thousands in Wenceslas Square, and a two-hour general strike followed on 27 November. The communist government gave up its monopoly on power, and playwright Václav Havel, leader of Civic Forum, became president on 29 December.
events.why: The Berlin Wall had opened eight days before. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev had ruled out intervention, and the police violence of 17 November turned a student march into a national movement.
events.then: Free elections in June 1990 gave Civic Forum a majority. Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993.
events.sig: Free elections in June 1990 gave Civic Forum a majority. Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993.
events.now: The revolution showed that once Moscow withdrew its guarantee, a communist government with no will to shoot fell in weeks; Czechoslovakia's peaceful split in 1993 kept the same pattern.

causes.why: The fall of the Wall emboldened Czechoslovaks.

q.before: A hard-line communist government.
q.how: Peaceful protest and a general strike.
q.lasted: Yes: free elections followed in 1990.

events.bluf: Czechoslovak students and citizens, with playwright Václav Havel's Civic Forum speaking for them, set out to end communist rule once Soviet backing was gone. Mass protest and a general strike brought the government down in six weeks without a death. Havel was president by the end of the year, and the country became the model of a nonviolent transition.
events.lens: When a regime's outside guarantor withdraws, peaceful protest can bring it down quickly.
events.fact: Crowds in Wenceslas Square jingled their keys to tell the regime it was time to go.

events.who: Nicolae Ceaușescu; Romanian protesters and soldiers
events.hook: Romania's dictator was booed at his own rally, fled, and was executed on Christmas Day.
events.what: Romania's dictator was booed at his own rally, fled, and was executed on Christmas Day.
events.story: Protests began in Timișoara on 16 December 1989 over the eviction of a Hungarian pastor, László Tőkés. On 21 December crowds jeered Romanian dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu during a speech in Bucharest; the next day he and his wife Elena fled by helicopter as the army joined the revolt. They were tried by a hasty military court and shot on 25 December. About 1,100 people died in the fighting.
events.why: Years of hunger and repression under a cult of personality came first. Communist regimes had fallen next door within weeks, and the army chose the crowd.
events.then: Former communists led by Ion Iliescu took power as the National Salvation Front and held it until 1996. In June 1990 Iliescu brought miners to Bucharest to beat opposition protesters. Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007.
events.sig: Former communists led by Ion Iliescu took power as the National Salvation Front and held it until 1996. In June 1990 Iliescu brought miners to Bucharest to beat opposition protesters. Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007.
events.now: Because former communists captured the transition, Romania reformed later and slower than its neighbours and joined the EU only in 2007; the hasty trial remains the core of the argument over whether the revolution was also a coup.

causes.why: Romania was the last Eastern Bloc regime to fall in 1989.

q.before: Ceaușescu's personal dictatorship.
q.how: Uprising, army defection and execution.
q.lasted: Romania held free elections and joined the EU in 2007.

events.bluf: Romanians rose against dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu after years of hunger and repression, and the army joined them. Ceaușescu fled, was tried by a hasty military court and shot with his wife on Christmas Day; about 1,100 people died, the only violent overthrow of a communist regime in 1989. Former communists under Ion Iliescu seized the transition and held power until 1996, which slowed Romania's reforms.
events.lens: Revolutions that end in hasty executions often leave the old elite in power.
events.fact: Most of the dead were killed after Ceaușescu fled, in confused fighting with 'terrorists' who were never identified.

events.what: Released after 27 years in prison.

events.sig: Four years of negotiations, with political violence that killed thousands, led to the election of 27 April 1994.
events.hook: Nelson Mandela walked free after 27 years in prison.
events.story: On 2 February 1990 South African President F. W. de Klerk told parliament he was legalising the ANC, the PAC and the Communist Party. On 11 February ANC leader Nelson Mandela walked out of Victor Verster prison near Paarl after 27 years. He addressed a crowd in Cape Town that evening.
events.then: Four years of negotiations, with political violence that killed thousands, led to the election of 27 April 1994.
events.now: Mandela's release opened four years of negotiations that ended apartheid by agreement rather than war, which made South Africa the model for negotiated transitions from Northern Ireland to Colombia.
events.fact: Mandela was prisoner 46664 on Robben Island, and he stayed on a US terrorism watch list until 2008.

causes.why: Decades of protest, the armed struggle, township uprisings and international sanctions forced the government to negotiate.
Years of unrest and sanctions pushed the government to negotiate.

q.before: Apartheid, under pressure.
q.how: Release and negotiations.
q.lasted: Democratic elections followed in 1994.

events.bluf: South African President F. W. de Klerk decided that sanctions, internal resistance and a failing economy left white minority rule no future, and chose to negotiate while his government still held power. He legalised the ANC on 2 February 1990 and released ANC leader Nelson Mandela nine days later after 27 years in prison. Negotiations to end apartheid followed and produced the democratic election of 1994.
events.lens: Regimes negotiate when the cost of repression exceeds the cost of change.

events.who: Chancellor Helmut Kohl; the four wartime Allies; East Germany's last government
events.what: East and West Germany united.
events.why: East Germany's government collapsed after the Wall opened, and East Germans voted for rapid unity. Kohl moved fast because Gorbachev's position in Moscow was weak.
events.sig: Germany became Europe's largest economy and leading power. Rebuilding the east cost well over a trillion euros, and unemployment there soared as its industry closed.
events.hook: East and West Germany became one country again after 41 years.
events.story: After the Berlin Wall opened, East Germans voted in March 1990 for parties promising quick unity, and a monetary union on 1 July brought them the West German mark. West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl negotiated the 'Two Plus Four' treaty with the four wartime victors: united Germany would stay in NATO, accept its border with Poland and cap its army, and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev agreed in return for German money. East Germany joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990.
events.then: Germany became Europe's largest economy and leading power. Rebuilding the east cost well over a trillion euros, and unemployment there soared as its industry closed.
events.now: Gaps in wages and politics between east and west persist; the far-right AfD's strength in the east reflects those divides.

causes.why: Within a year of the Wall's fall, East Germany joined the Federal Republic.

q.before: Two German states.
q.how: A treaty with the four Allied powers.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl set out to absorb a collapsing East Germany into the Federal Republic before Moscow changed its mind, and to keep the whole inside NATO. He got both, with the consent of the four wartime Allies and a payment to the Soviet Union. Europe's largest economy and state took shape at a cost of well over a trillion euros for the east, with gaps in wages and politics that persist.
events.lens: Rapid unification can solve a political problem and create long-term economic ones.
events.fact: The Two Plus Four treaty capped the German armed forces at 370,000.

events.what: Internet companies boomed (bust in 2000).
events.why: The commercial internet was real. Cheap capital, a long bull market and the belief that the web had rewritten the rules did the rest.
events.sig: Trillions of dollars in paper wealth vanished and hundreds of start-ups closed. The fibre-optic networks laid during the boom made bandwidth cheap, and survivors such as Amazon and Google became the largest companies in the world.
events.hook: The internet economy was born in a bubble.
events.story: The web opened to public and commercial use in the early 1990s, and Netscape's flotation in 1995 showed what investors would pay. Money flowed into internet start-ups, many with no revenue, on the belief that market share mattered more than profit. The Nasdaq index rose fivefold between 1995 and its peak of 5,048 in March 2000. It lost about three-quarters of its value by October 2002.
events.then: Trillions of dollars in paper wealth vanished and hundreds of start-ups closed. The fibre-optic networks laid during the boom made bandwidth cheap, and survivors such as Amazon and Google became the largest companies in the world.
events.now: Today's tech platforms grew out of this era, and investors still measure new booms, such as AI, against the dot-com bubble.
events.fact: Pets.com went from IPO to shutdown in about nine months.

causes.why: Sputnik led the Pentagon to create ARPA, whose ARPANET became the core of the internet.

q.what: Shares in internet companies.
q.who: Early investors and survivors like Amazon won; many lost fortunes.
q.scale: Trillions of dollars in paper wealth vanished.
q.daily: Email and the web became part of everyday life.
q.system: The platform economy.

events.bluf: Investors and founders set out to capture the commercial internet after the web opened to the public in the early 1990s, and poured capital into companies with no profits. The Nasdaq rose fivefold between 1995 and March 2000 and lost about three-quarters of its value by 2002. The survivors and the fibre laid in the boom built the digital economy, which made the bubble the case for the claim that manias can fund lasting technology.
events.lens: Speculative bubbles often finance the infrastructure of the next economy.

events.who: Slobodan Milošević; Slovenian, Croatian and Bosnian leaders
events.hook: Yugoslavia broke apart in a decade of wars, the worst in Europe since 1945.
events.what: Yugoslavia broke apart in a decade of wars, the worst in Europe since 1945.
events.story: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991. The Yugoslav army fought a ten-day war in Slovenia and withdrew. In Croatia, Serb-dominated Yugoslav forces and local Serb militias fought a long war; Vukovar fell in November 1991. Bosnia's war from April 1992 brought the siege of Sarajevo, 'ethnic cleansing' and genocide.
events.why: Communism's collapse removed the party that had held the federation together. Serbian President Slobodan Milošević and Croatian President Franjo Tuđman mobilised ethnic fears, and the Yugoslav army sided with Serbia.
events.then: About 130,000-140,000 people died and millions were displaced. NATO bombing helped end the wars in Bosnia in 1995 and Kosovo in 1999. Milošević died in 2006 while on trial at The Hague.
events.sig: About 130,000-140,000 people died and millions were displaced. NATO bombing helped end the wars in Bosnia in 1995 and Kosovo in 1999. Milošević died in 2006 while on trial at The Hague.
events.now: The UN tribunal at The Hague convicted leaders of war crimes and genocide; the settlements in Bosnia and Kosovo remain contested and keep both outside the EU.

causes.why: The collapse of communism across Eastern Europe let nationalists in Yugoslavia's republics break away.

q.why: Nationalist leaders broke up Yugoslavia.
q.stakes: Borders and who would rule which territory.
q.decided: Force, and finally NATO intervention.
q.cost: About 130,000 to 140,000 dead.
q.changed: Yugoslavia broke into seven states.

events.bluf: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence to leave a Yugoslavia that Serbian President Slobodan Milošević was bending to Serbian ends; Milošević and the Yugoslav army fought to keep Serb-populated territory in one state. The wars that followed over the decade killed about 130,000-140,000 people and brought the Srebrenica genocide. Europe's worst fighting since 1945 ended only through NATO's first combat operations, and the disputes over Bosnia and Kosovo remain open.
events.lens: When a multi-ethnic state collapses, nationalist leaders can turn fear into war.
events.fact: The siege of Sarajevo lasted 1,425 days, the longest siege of a capital in modern warfare.

events.what: Iraq expelled from Kuwait.
events.why: Saddam wanted Kuwait's oil and an end to the debts of the Iran-Iraq war. The coalition feared he would move on Saudi Arabia next.
events.sig: US troops stayed in Saudi Arabia, which angered Osama bin Laden. Saddam survived, crushed Shi'a and Kurdish uprisings and faced sanctions and no-fly zones.
events.hook: A US-led coalition drove Iraq out of Kuwait.
events.story: Iraqi President Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990. US President George H. W. Bush built a 35-nation coalition under a UN mandate. After five weeks of air attack, the coalition drove Iraq out of Kuwait in 100 hours of ground fighting in February 1991.
events.then: US troops stayed in Saudi Arabia, which angered Osama bin Laden. Saddam survived, crushed Shi'a and Kurdish uprisings and faced sanctions and no-fly zones.
events.now: The war opened an era of US military dominance in the Gulf, and the unfinished business with Saddam led to the invasion of 2003.

sites.d: Invaded August 1990.
Retreating Iraqi convoy destroyed.
Coalition HQ; Scud missile target.

causes.why: Iraq emerged from eight years of war with huge debts, including to Kuwait. In 1990 Saddam invaded Kuwait.

events.fact: Retreating Iraqi troops set about 600 Kuwaiti oil wells on fire.

q.why: Iraq invaded Kuwait.
q.decided: Coalition air power and a quick ground war.
q.cost: Thousands of Iraqi soldiers killed.
q.changed: Kuwait was freed; Saddam stayed in power.

events.bluf: Iraqi President Saddam Hussein took Kuwait for its oil and to cancel his debts; US President George H. W. Bush built a 35-nation coalition to reverse the conquest and protect Saudi Arabia. The coalition drove Iraq out in 100 hours of ground fighting in February 1991. American military dominance after the Cold War was on display, and the US troops left in Saudi Arabia became one of Osama bin Laden's stated grievances.
events.lens: Decisive victories create new commitments, and those commitments create new enemies.

toll.n: Estimates. Thousands of Iraqi civilians also died.

events.who: Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao; Finance Minister Manmohan Singh
events.hook: Facing bankruptcy, India dismantled its 'licence raj' and opened to the world economy.
events.what: Facing bankruptcy, India dismantled its 'licence raj' and opened to the world economy.
events.story: In mid-1991 India's foreign reserves covered about two weeks of imports after the Gulf War oil shock and the loss of Soviet trade. The government flew gold to London as collateral and turned to the IMF. Indian Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao took office in June 1991; Finance Minister Manmohan Singh's budget of 24 July 1991 devalued the rupee, cut tariffs, scrapped most industrial licensing and opened sectors to foreign investment.
events.why: A balance-of-payments crisis, worsened by the Gulf War oil shock and the collapse of trade with the Soviet Union, came first. Four decades of licensing had held growth to about 3.5 per cent a year.
events.then: Growth rose above 6 per cent a year from the mid-1990s. India's IT and services industries grew into exporters, and hundreds of millions rose out of extreme poverty. Singh became prime minister in 2004.
events.sig: Growth rose above 6 per cent a year from the mid-1990s. India's IT and services industries grew into exporters, and hundreds of millions rose out of extreme poverty. Singh became prime minister in 2004.
events.now: India is now one of the world's largest economies, and its rise makes it a key swing power between the United States and China.

causes.why: The collapse of Soviet-bloc trade, India's main export market, deepened its 1991 crisis and discredited Soviet-style planning.
The Gulf crisis spiked oil prices and cut remittances from Indian workers in the Gulf, draining India's reserves.

q.what: Trade, investment and industry.
q.who: Businesses and the middle class gained.
q.scale: Growth roughly doubled.
q.daily: More goods, jobs and choice.
q.system: A market economy.

events.bluf: Indian Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh set out to avert default on India's foreign debt and used the crisis to dismantle the 'licence raj'. The budget of July 1991 devalued the rupee, cut tariffs and scrapped most industrial licensing, with an IMF loan secured against pledged gold. Growth accelerated from the 1990s, hundreds of millions left extreme poverty and India became a power the United States and China both court.
events.lens: Economic crises often force reforms that politics alone could not.
events.fact: Singh closed the budget speech with Victor Hugo's line that no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come.

events.who: Soviet hardliners; Boris Yeltsin; Mikhail Gorbachev
events.hook: Hardliners put Gorbachev under house arrest; Yeltsin stood on a tank, and the coup collapsed in three days.
events.what: Hardliners put Gorbachev under house arrest; Yeltsin stood on a tank, and the coup collapsed in three days.
events.story: On 19 August 1991 a committee of communist hardliners, including the KGB chief and the defence minister, declared a state of emergency and held Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev at his Crimean dacha, a day before the Union Treaty was to be signed. Crowds defended Russia's parliament, the White House; Russian President Boris Yeltsin denounced the coup from atop a tank. Troops refused to attack, and the plotters gave up on 21 August.
events.why: The planned Union Treaty would have handed the republics far more power. The plotters wanted the party, the KGB and the army back in control.
events.then: Yeltsin suspended the Communist Party in Russia. Republics declared independence one after another, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
events.sig: Yeltsin suspended the Communist Party in Russia. Republics declared independence one after another, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
events.now: The coup's failure showed the Soviet state could no longer command obedience, and Yeltsin's victory began a decade of chaotic reform in Russia that shaped the rise of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

q.before: Gorbachev led a weakening Soviet Union.
q.how: An attempted coup, defeated by popular resistance.
q.lasted: No: it collapsed in three days.

events.bluf: Soviet hardliners seized power to stop a Union Treaty that would have handed the republics far more power and to restore central control. The coup collapsed in three days when crowds defended Russia's parliament, Russian President Boris Yeltsin defied the plotters and troops refused to attack. The plotters destroyed the centre they had tried to save, Yeltsin became the dominant figure and the Soviet Union dissolved within four months.
events.lens: A failed coup can hasten the very collapse it aimed to prevent.
events.fact: Three young men killed under armoured vehicles on the Garden Ring on the night of 20-21 August were the coup's only deaths in Moscow.

events.who: Gorbachev; Boris Yeltsin; leaders of the republics
events.hook: The Soviet Union broke apart into 15 independent countries.
events.what: The Soviet Union broke apart into 15 independent countries.
events.story: A failed hard-line coup in August 1991 destroyed Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev's authority. Ukraine voted for independence by more than 90 per cent on 1 December. On 8 December the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, meeting at Belavezha, declared that the Union had ceased to exist, and eleven republics formed a Commonwealth of Independent States at Alma-Ata on 21 December. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December.
events.why: Gorbachev's reforms had loosened the controls that held the system together. Nationalism in the republics, a failing economy and the loss of Eastern Europe in 1989 did the rest.
events.then: Russia's economy collapsed in the 1990s amid 'shock therapy', hyperinflation and the rise of oligarchs. Vladimir Putin rose to power in 1999-2000.
events.sig: Russia's economy collapsed in the 1990s amid 'shock therapy', hyperinflation and the rise of oligarchs. Vladimir Putin rose to power in 1999-2000.
events.now: Ukraine, the Baltic states and the Central Asian states became independent. Russian President Vladimir Putin has called the collapse 'the greatest geopolitical catastrophe' of the century, and the war in Ukraine is partly a struggle over its legacy.

causes.why: Gorbachev later wrote that Chernobyl, even more than perestroika, was 'perhaps the real cause' of the Soviet collapse; the cover-up drove his push for openness.
The loss of Eastern Europe emboldened nationalists in the Soviet republics; after a failed coup in 1991, the Union dissolved.
Defeat in Afghanistan weakened the Soviet state.
The failed coup destroyed the old system's authority.

q.before: The Soviet Union.
q.how: Republics declared independence; leaders dissolved the Union.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev tried to hold the Union together in a looser form; the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, led by Russian President Boris Yeltsin, chose to end it. Fifteen states became independent and Russia lost an empire. The Cold War ended with the United States the sole superpower, and Russia's sense of loss became the material of its politics, which Russian President Vladimir Putin draws on in the war in Ukraine.
events.trig: The failed hardliners' coup of August 1991.
events.lens: Empires that dissolve leave the former imperial centre with grievances and an urge to reclaim influence.
events.fact: The Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin on the evening of 25 December 1991 and the Russian tricolour went up in its place.

events.hook: Retired but still powerful, Deng toured the south to restart market reforms after Tiananmen.
events.what: Retired but still powerful, Deng toured the south to restart market reforms after Tiananmen.
events.story: In January and February 1992, 87-year-old Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping visited Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Shanghai, urging officials to be bolder and saying that markets served socialism as well as capitalism. His remarks spread through the press and pushed conservatives aside.
events.why: After Tiananmen, hardliners had slowed reform, and Deng feared stagnation would threaten the party's hold on power.
events.then: Growth surged, and in October 1992 the party adopted the goal of a 'socialist market economy'.
events.sig: Growth surged, and in October 1992 the party adopted the goal of a 'socialist market economy'.
events.now: It fixed China's path of market economics under one-party rule, which made it the world's second-largest economy.

causes.why: After Tiananmen, Deng toured the south to revive reform.

q.before: Conservatives were pushing back against reform after 1989.
q.how: A tour and speeches by a retired leader.
q.lasted: Yes: market reform continued.

events.bluf: Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, aged 87 and holding no formal post, toured Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Shanghai in January and February 1992 to restart market reforms stalled since Tiananmen. His remarks spread through the press and the party's conservatives gave way. The 14th Party Congress in October 1992 adopted the 'socialist market economy', and two decades of growth near 10 per cent a year followed under one-party rule.
events.lens: In personalist systems, a single leader's push can redirect a whole country.
events.fact: Deng held no official post at the time; he had given up his last, chairman of the Central Military Commission, in 1989.

events.what: European Union founded.
events.why: European leaders wanted to deepen integration after the Cold War. French President François Mitterrand wanted a reunified Germany anchored in Europe, and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl accepted a shared currency as the price.
events.sig: The euro launched in 1999 and entered circulation in 2002. The EU expanded east in 2004.
events.hook: The European Union was born, with a plan for one currency.
events.story: Signed in Maastricht on 7 February 1992 and in force from 1 November 1993, the treaty turned the European Community into the European Union. It created EU citizenship, cooperation on foreign policy and justice, and a timetable and rules for a single currency. Danish voters rejected it in June 1992 and approved it with opt-outs in 1993; French voters approved it in September 1992 by 51 per cent.
events.then: The euro launched in 1999 and entered circulation in 2002. The EU expanded east in 2004.
events.now: The treaty made the EU a political union with its own currency, which bound members tighter than a market and gave the euro crisis of 2010 and Brexit in 2016 their stakes.

causes.why: Thirty-five years of a common market grew into political union and plans for a single currency.
France wanted a reunited Germany locked firmly into Europe; the bargain included a common currency to replace the Deutschmark.

q.before: The European Community, mainly a common market.
q.how: A treaty ratified by all members, narrowly in France and after a second vote in Denmark.
q.claim: An 'ever closer union' of Europe's peoples.
q.lasted: Yes: the EU has grown to 27 members.

events.bluf: The European Community's leaders, with French President François Mitterrand and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl at the front, wanted a reunified Germany bound into Europe and integration deepened after the Cold War. The treaty created the European Union, EU citizenship, cooperation on foreign policy and a timetable for a single currency. It delivered the euro in 1999 and set off lasting arguments over sovereignty, from close referendums in Denmark and France to Brexit.
events.lens: Deep integration needs popular consent; when publics feel it is imposed, backlash follows.
events.fact: Britain negotiated opt-outs from the single currency and the social chapter.

events.who: Eddie Koiki Mabo and other Meriam people; the High Court of Australia
events.hook: Australia's High Court rejected the idea that the continent had belonged to no one when Britain arrived.
events.what: Australia's High Court rejected the idea that the continent had belonged to no one when Britain arrived.
events.story: Eddie Koiki Mabo, a Meriam man working as a gardener at a Townsville university, learned in conversation with staff there that the law regarded his family's land on Mer as Crown land. With four other Meriam plaintiffs he brought a case in the High Court in 1982. Mabo died of cancer in January 1992. On 3 June 1992 the High Court ruled six to one that native title existed under Australian common law and that the Meriam people held it over Mer.
events.why: Indigenous campaigners challenged the legal basis of British possession, and the Meriam people's gardens and inherited plots gave the court a clear case of continuous ownership.
events.then: Parliament passed the Native Title Act in 1993 under Prime Minister Paul Keating. The Wik decision of 1996 held that native title could coexist with pastoral leases, and the Howard government's 1998 amendments narrowed it. Indigenous groups have since won recognition of native title over a large share of Australia's land, much of it remote.
events.sig: Parliament passed the Native Title Act in 1993 under Prime Minister Paul Keating. The Wik decision of 1996 held that native title could coexist with pastoral leases, and the Howard government's 1998 amendments narrowed it. Indigenous groups have since won recognition of native title over a large share of Australia's land, much of it remote.
events.now: Native title has since been recognised over more than a third of Australia's land, most of it remote; the decision moved land and reconciliation politics onto a legal footing.

causes.why: The referendum was part of a movement that culminated in land-rights cases like Mabo.

q.before: Australian law treated the land as 'terra nullius', belonging to no one before 1788.
q.how: A High Court ruling.
q.claim: Native title had survived British settlement.
q.lasted: Yes: native title is now law.

events.bluf: Meriam man Eddie Koiki Mabo and four others went to court in 1982 to prove that their people owned their land on Mer under their own law before and after the Crown arrived. On 3 June 1992 the High Court ruled six to one that 'terra nullius' was wrong as a description of Australia and that native title survived British sovereignty wherever it had not been extinguished. The ruling rewrote Australian land law, produced the Native Title Act of 1993 and gave the reconciliation debate its legal footing.
events.lens: Courts can overturn foundational legal myths and force political change.
events.fact: Mabo's grave in Townsville was vandalised in 1995, the night after its unveiling, and his family reburied him on Mer.

events.who: Yitzhak Rabin; Yasser Arafat; Bill Clinton
events.hook: Israel and the PLO recognised each other and agreed on Palestinian self-rule.
events.what: Israel and the PLO recognised each other and agreed on Palestinian self-rule.
events.story: After secret talks in Norway, Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat shook hands on the White House lawn before US President Bill Clinton in September 1993. Israel recognised the PLO and the PLO recognised Israel. A Palestinian Authority was to govern parts of the West Bank and Gaza while Jerusalem, borders, refugees and settlements were negotiated.
events.why: The intifada, the end of the Cold War and the Gulf War pushed both sides to talk. Each read the other as weakened enough to deal.
events.then: Rabin was assassinated by an Israeli extremist in 1995. Final-status talks failed in 2000 and the second intifada followed. Israelis blame Palestinian violence for the collapse; Palestinians blame continued settlement growth.
events.sig: Rabin was assassinated by an Israeli extremist in 1995. Final-status talks failed in 2000 and the second intifada followed. Israelis blame Palestinian violence for the collapse; Palestinians blame continued settlement growth.
events.now: The Palestinian Authority the accords created still governs parts of the West Bank, and a final peace was never reached.

causes.why: The uprising convinced Israeli leaders that the occupation could not continue unchanged, and weakened the PLO's exile leadership.
After the Gulf War, the US convened the 1991 Madrid peace conference, which led to secret Israeli-PLO talks in Oslo.

q.before: Israel and the PLO did not recognise each other.
q.how: Secret talks, then a public agreement.
q.winners: At first both sides; the peace process later collapsed.
q.lasted: The Palestinian Authority still exists; final peace never came.

events.bluf: Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat set out to trade recognition for self-rule and to defer the hardest questions to later talks. The accords of 1993 brought mutual recognition and a Palestinian Authority in parts of the West Bank and Gaza. The hardest issues stayed open, attacks and settlement growth continued, and the process collapsed in 2000.
events.lens: Deferring the hardest issues lets talks begin, but leaves them vulnerable to spoilers.
events.fact: Rabin, Arafat and Israeli Foreign Minister Shimon Peres shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize.
