events.fact: Radio Mille Collines read out the names and hiding places of people to be killed; its founders were convicted of genocide in 2003.

sites.d: President's plane shot down April 6, 1994; killings began that night.
Church massacre site, now a memorial.
Over a million refugees fled here; led to the Congo wars.

events.who: Hutu extremists; the interim government; Tutsi and moderate Hutu victims
events.hook: In 100 days, Hutu extremists killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi.
events.what: In 100 days, Hutu extremists killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi.
events.story: Rwanda had been at civil war since 1990 between the Hutu-led government and the Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front, and a 1993 peace deal provided for power sharing. After Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana's plane was shot down on 6 April 1994, soldiers, the Interahamwe militia and radio broadcasts directed the killing of Tutsi and moderate Hutu across the country. The UN Security Council cut its peacekeeping force. The RPF under Paul Kagame took Kigali on 4 July 1994.
events.why: Ethnic categories hardened under Belgian rule and the civil war since 1990 came first. Extremists feared losing power under the 1993 peace deal, and the state had the radio, the militias and the lists.
events.then: Perpetrators and some two million Hutu refugees fled into Zaire, and Rwanda's pursuit of them began the Congo wars in 1996. The UN tribunal convicted 61 people. RPF leader Paul Kagame has governed Rwanda since; his supporters cite growth and order, his critics cite suppressed opposition and reprisal killings in 1994 and in Congo that the RPF denies.
events.sig: Perpetrators and some two million Hutu refugees fled into Zaire, and Rwanda's pursuit of them began the Congo wars in 1996. The UN tribunal convicted 61 people. RPF leader Paul Kagame has governed Rwanda since; his supporters cite growth and order, his critics cite suppressed opposition and reprisal killings in 1994 and in Congo that the RPF denies.
events.now: The world's failure to act led to the 'Responsibility to Protect' principle adopted by the UN in 2005; the flight of perpetrators into Congo set off wars there that continue, and Rwanda rebuilt under RPF leader Paul Kagame with rapid development and tight control.

q.why: Extremists sought to exterminate the Tutsi.
q.decided: The Rwandan Patriotic Front's victory.
q.cost: About 500,000 to 800,000 killed in 100 days.
q.changed: The RPF took power; the conflict spread to Congo.

events.bluf: Hutu extremists in Rwanda's interim government set out to kill the Tutsi minority and Hutu opponents after President Juvénal Habyarimana's plane was shot down on 6 April 1994. In about 100 days militias and soldiers killed about 800,000 people by the UN's count, above a million by a Rwandan government census, while UN peacekeepers stood aside. The Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front took Kigali in July, perpetrators fled into Congo and set off the Congo wars, and the world's failure produced the 'Responsibility to Protect' doctrine.
events.trig: The shooting down of President Habyarimana's plane on 6 April 1994; who fired the missile is still disputed, with one inquiry blaming Hutu extremists and another the RPF.
events.lens: Genocide is planned: hate propaganda, militias and lists of targets come before the killing.
events.myth: The genocide was a spontaneous outburst of ancient tribal hatred. The killing was organised by the state, with militias trained, weapons distributed and lists prepared in advance.

events.hook: South Africa held its first election open to all races, and Nelson Mandela became president.
events.what: South Africa held its first election open to all races, and Nelson Mandela became president.
events.story: Millions queued for hours on 27 April 1994, many voting for the first time. The ANC won 62 per cent, the National Party 20 per cent and the Inkatha Freedom Party 10 per cent. ANC leader Nelson Mandela, imprisoned for 27 years, was inaugurated president in Pretoria on 10 May 1994.
events.why: Four years of talks between the ANC and the National Party came first, pushed by sanctions, resistance and township violence that threatened civil war.
events.then: A Truth and Reconciliation Commission heard testimony on apartheid-era crimes from 1996, and the 1996 constitution became one of the most liberal in the world.
events.sig: A Truth and Reconciliation Commission heard testimony on apartheid-era crimes from 1996, and the 1996 constitution became one of the most liberal in the world.
events.now: The negotiated transition became the model for ending conflict by settlement, and the inequality and corruption that followed remain South Africa's standing political questions into the 2020s.

causes.why: Four years of negotiations led to South Africa's first election open to all races in April 1994.

q.before: White-minority rule under apartheid.
q.how: South Africa's first democratic election.
q.lasted: Yes: democracy has endured.

events.bluf: The ANC and South African President F. W. de Klerk's National Party negotiated for four years to replace apartheid with majority rule without civil war. On 27 April 1994 South Africans of every race voted in the first democratic election; the ANC won 62 per cent and ANC leader Nelson Mandela was inaugurated president in May. Apartheid ended by agreement, and the economic inequality it built remained.
events.lens: A political transition can end legal discrimination without ending economic inequality.
events.fact: 27 April is Freedom Day; the ballot listed 19 parties with photographs of their leaders for voters who could not read.

events.what: Trade deal took effect; Indigenous rebellion.
events.why: Indigenous poverty and land loss came first. A 1992 constitutional change ended land redistribution, and the rebels feared NAFTA's cheap US maize would ruin small farmers.
events.sig: The San Andrés Accords on Indigenous rights were signed in 1996. Paramilitaries killed 45 people at Acteal in December 1997. Congress passed a narrower Indigenous-rights reform in 2001, which the Zapatistas rejected.
events.hook: On the day NAFTA began, Indigenous rebels rose up in southern Mexico.
events.story: On 1 January 1994, the day NAFTA took effect, the masked Zapatista Army of National Liberation seized towns in Chiapas, Mexico's poorest state. Its spokesman, Subcomandante Marcos, issued communiqués to the national and foreign press. After 12 days of fighting the government declared a ceasefire, and talks followed.
events.then: The San Andrés Accords on Indigenous rights were signed in 1996. Paramilitaries killed 45 people at Acteal in December 1997. Congress passed a narrower Indigenous-rights reform in 2001, which the Zapatistas rejected.
events.now: The uprising put Indigenous rights on Mexico's national agenda and produced the constitutional reform of 2001. Zapatista communities in Chiapas have governed themselves outside state institutions since 2003.

causes.why: The Zapatistas took their name from the revolutionary Emiliano Zapata, and rose against reforms that ended the revolution's promise of land redistribution.
The Zapatistas rose on the day NAFTA took effect, saying free trade would ruin Indigenous farmers.

q.before: Mexico's long-ruling PRI government.
q.how: An armed uprising, then a ceasefire.
q.winners: Zapatista communities gained autonomy in practice.
q.lasted: They still run self-governing communities.

events.bluf: The Zapatista Army of National Liberation, a movement of Indigenous Maya peasants in Chiapas, rose on 1 January 1994, the day NAFTA took effect, to demand land, autonomy and an end to their exclusion. Twelve days of fighting ended in a ceasefire and talks. The rebels won national attention and self-governing communities, and their use of media made them a model for the global anti-globalisation movement.
events.lens: Movements can win attention through media strategy even without military power.
events.fact: The government identified Subcomandante Marcos in 1995 as Rafael Guillén, a former university lecturer in design.

events.what: Free trade zone launched.
events.why: Leaders in all three countries expected freer trade to raise growth. Mexican President Carlos Salinas wanted to lock in market reforms against a future government.
events.sig: Trade among the three roughly tripled, and supply chains for cars and food crossed borders many times. Small Mexican farmers were undercut by US grain. One reading counts hundreds of thousands of US factory jobs lost to Mexico; the other finds the net effect on US employment small and the losses concentrated in particular towns. President Donald Trump renegotiated it as the USMCA, in force from July 2020.
events.hook: North America became one big free-trade zone.
events.story: US President George H. W. Bush, Mexican President Carlos Salinas and Canadian Prime Minister Brian Mulroney signed the agreement in December 1992. President Bill Clinton won ratification in Congress in November 1993 with side agreements on labour and the environment, over opposition from unions and from businessman Ross Perot. In force from 1 January 1994, the North American Free Trade Agreement phased out most tariffs between the three countries over 15 years. Car-making and farming supply chains spread across all three.
events.then: Trade among the three roughly tripled, and supply chains for cars and food crossed borders many times. Small Mexican farmers were undercut by US grain. One reading counts hundreds of thousands of US factory jobs lost to Mexico; the other finds the net effect on US employment small and the losses concentrated in particular towns. President Donald Trump renegotiated it as the USMCA, in force from July 2020.
events.now: It was renegotiated in 2020 as the USMCA, and US tariffs on Canada and Mexico in 2025 strained the integrated North American economy it built.

causes.why: Mexico's 1982 debt crisis pushed it away from protectionism toward market reforms and, finally, free trade with the US and Canada.

q.what: Cars, farm goods and manufactured parts.
q.who: Exporters and consumers gained; some factory workers and small farmers lost.
q.scale: Trade among the three countries more than tripled.
q.daily: Cheaper goods and cross-border supply chains.
q.system: An integrated North American economy.

events.bluf: The governments of the United States, Canada and Mexico set out to create one market; Mexico wanted its reforms locked in and the other two wanted growth. The agreement in force from 1 January 1994 phased out most tariffs, and trade among the three roughly tripled. Supply chains for cars and food crossed the borders many times, and the agreement became the symbol of lost factory jobs that fed the backlash against globalisation.
events.lens: Free trade raises overall wealth but concentrates losses on particular workers and regions.
events.fact: The Zapatista uprising in Chiapas began on 1 January 1994, the day NAFTA took effect, in declared opposition to it.

events.what: ~8,000 Bosniak men and boys killed.
events.why: Mladić's forces aimed to remove Bosniaks from eastern Bosnia to create an ethnically Serb territory. The UN peacekeepers were too few and too lightly armed to stop them, and air support was refused.
events.sig: NATO bombing in August and September and the Dayton Accords of November 1995 ended the war, dividing Bosnia into two largely self-governing entities. The International Court of Justice ruled the massacre genocide in 2007.
events.hook: Bosnian Serb forces murdered about 8,000 Muslim men and boys in a UN 'safe area'.
events.story: In July 1995 Bosnian Serb forces under General Ratko Mladić overran the UN 'safe area' of Srebrenica, defended by lightly armed Dutch peacekeepers. Over the following days they separated Bosniak men and boys from the women and killed more than 8,000 of them. The bodies were buried in mass graves and later moved to hide them.
events.then: NATO bombing in August and September and the Dayton Accords of November 1995 ended the war, dividing Bosnia into two largely self-governing entities. The International Court of Justice ruled the massacre genocide in 2007.
events.now: International courts ruled it genocide, and Mladić and Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadžić were jailed for life; denial remains common in Serb nationalist politics.

causes.why: As Yugoslavia broke apart, Bosnia's war produced the worst massacre in Europe since World War II.

q.why: Bosnian Serb forces sought to 'ethnically cleanse' eastern Bosnia.
q.stakes: The lives of the town's Bosniak population.
q.decided: UN peacekeepers were outnumbered and air support never came.
q.cost: More than 8,000 men and boys murdered.
q.changed: NATO bombing and the Dayton peace followed.

events.bluf: Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić set out to remove Bosniaks from eastern Bosnia and take the UN 'safe area' of Srebrenica. His forces overran it and killed more than 8,000 men and boys, Europe's worst atrocity since 1945. The failure of UN peacekeeping pushed NATO to intervene and the United States to broker the Dayton Accords, and international courts ruled the killings genocide.
events.lens: 'Safe areas' without the force to protect them can lure civilians into danger.
events.fact: The Dutch government resigned in 2002 after a report on its peacekeepers' failure at Srebrenica.

kv: the World Court ruled it genocide

events.who: Archbishop Desmond Tutu; victims and perpetrators of apartheid-era violence
events.hook: South Africa offered amnesty for full confessions of political crimes, and heard the victims in public.
events.what: South Africa offered amnesty for full confessions of political crimes, and heard the victims in public.
events.story: Chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, the commission held public hearings from April 1996 at which thousands of victims told their stories. Perpetrators could apply for amnesty if they fully disclosed politically motivated crimes; fewer than a thousand of about 7,000 applicants received it. The final report of October 1998 blamed the apartheid state most and also criticised the ANC.
events.why: The negotiated transition left the old security forces intact, and the new government needed the record without prosecutions that could destabilise the country.
events.then: Few of those refused amnesty were ever prosecuted. Reparations paid to victims fell short of what the commission recommended.
events.sig: Few of those refused amnesty were ever prosecuted. Reparations paid to victims fell short of what the commission recommended.
events.now: It became a model for truth commissions from Latin America to Africa, and debate over whether it traded justice for peace continues.

causes.why: The new democracy chose truth-telling over mass trials.

q.before: Apartheid-era crimes were hidden or denied.
q.how: Public hearings and conditional amnesty.
q.claim: Healing a nation through the truth.
q.winners: Victims won a public hearing; many also wanted justice.
q.lasted: Its findings stand; few prosecutions followed.

events.bluf: South Africa's new government wanted the truth about apartheid-era crimes without trials that could break the negotiated transition. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission under Archbishop Desmond Tutu held public hearings from April 1996 and offered amnesty for full disclosure of political crimes; fewer than a thousand of about 7,000 applicants received it. Truth commissions from Latin America to Africa copied the model, and the trade of justice for peace is still argued over.
events.lens: Truth commissions can help societies move on but may leave victims without justice.
events.fact: Tutu wept openly at the first hearing and was criticised for it; he said the stories left him no choice.

events.who: Rwanda, Uganda, Laurent Kabila; later 9 countries
events.what: Wars toppled Mobutu and drew in neighbors.
events.why: The genocide's perpetrators and refugees in Zaire came first. Mobutu's state had collapsed, and eastern Congo's minerals paid every army.
events.sig: One estimate, by the International Rescue Committee in 2008, put excess deaths at 5.4 million from 1998; other counts put the figure far lower, and all agree most died of disease and hunger. Eastern Congo is still fought over by dozens of armed groups, among them the M23 rebels, who seized Goma in January 2025; UN experts' reports of 2024 say Rwanda directs M23, which Rwanda denies.
events.hook: Congo's wars drew in nine countries and became the deadliest conflict since WWII.
events.story: Rwanda and Uganda invaded Zaire in October 1996 to break the Hutu militias in its refugee camps, and their ally Laurent Kabila took Kinshasa in May 1997 as Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko fled. In August 1998 Rwanda and Uganda turned against Congolese President Laurent Kabila, and Angola, Zimbabwe and Namibia came to his defence. Armies and militias mined coltan, gold and diamonds to pay for the war.
events.then: One estimate, by the International Rescue Committee in 2008, put excess deaths at 5.4 million from 1998; other counts put the figure far lower, and all agree most died of disease and hunger. Eastern Congo is still fought over by dozens of armed groups, among them the M23 rebels, who seized Goma in January 2025; UN experts' reports of 2024 say Rwanda directs M23, which Rwanda denies.
events.now: Fighting continues in eastern Congo, tied to minerals used in phones and electric cars.

causes.why: Mobutu, who rose in the crisis after Lumumba's murder, ruled Congo (Zaire) for 32 years until rebels backed by Rwanda and Uganda overthrew him in 1997.
The génocidaires fled into Congo; Rwanda invaded to pursue them and helped topple Mobutu.

q.why: Rwanda pursued genocide perpetrators; then many states fought over power and minerals.
q.stakes: Control of Congo and its minerals.
q.decided: Foreign armies and shifting alliances.
q.cost: Millions dead, mostly from disease and hunger.
q.changed: Mobutu fell, but eastern Congo remained at war.

events.bluf: Rwanda and Uganda invaded Zaire in 1996 to destroy the Hutu forces that had fled there after the genocide and to replace Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko with Laurent Kabila. They succeeded in 1997, then turned on Kabila in 1998 and drew nine countries into a war over territory and minerals. Estimates of the dead run into the millions, most from disease and hunger, and fighting over eastern Congo's minerals continues.
events.lens: Where states are weak and resources rich, wars become businesses.
events.fact: The second war drew in nine African armies, more than any conflict on the continent before or since.

kv: deaths, most from disease and hunger (estimates vary widely)

events.fact: The handover ceremony took place in heavy rain, and Britannia's voyage home was the royal yacht's last before decommissioning.
events.hook: Britain handed Hong Kong back to China after 155 years.
events.what: Britain handed Hong Kong back to China after 155 years.
events.story: At midnight on 30 June 1997, in a ceremony attended by Chinese President Jiang Zemin, British Prime Minister Tony Blair and Prince Charles, Hong Kong became a Special Administrative Region of China under 'one country, two systems', with promises of a high degree of autonomy for 50 years. British Governor Chris Patten left with the prince aboard the royal yacht Britannia.
events.why: Most of Hong Kong's land, the New Territories, was held on a 99-year lease signed in 1898, which made 1997 the deadline. The Joint Declaration of 1984 set the terms of the transfer.
events.then: Hong Kong kept its own laws, currency and freedoms at first. Beijing resisted full democracy, which produced mass protests in 2003, 2014 and 2019, and imposed a national security law in June 2020.
events.sig: Hong Kong kept its own laws, currency and freedoms at first. Beijing resisted full democracy, which produced mass protests in 2003, 2014 and 2019, and imposed a national security law in June 2020.
events.now: The national security law of June 2020 ended much of Hong Kong's political autonomy as Britain, the United States and Hong Kong's democrats read the Joint Declaration of 1984; Beijing holds that the law restored order after months of violent protest and that 'one country, two systems' continues.

causes.why: The island ceded in 1842 returned to China after 155 years.

q.before: British colonial rule.
q.how: A handover agreed in 1984.
q.lasted: Autonomy was sharply curtailed after 2020.

events.bluf: Britain returned Hong Kong to China at midnight on 30 June 1997 because the lease on most of its territory expired, and China accepted 'one country, two systems' to keep the colony's economy intact. Hong Kong kept its own laws, currency and freedoms for a promised 50 years. Beijing's resistance to full democracy produced mass protests in 2003, 2014 and 2019, and the national security law of 2020 ended much of the autonomy as its critics read it, while Beijing holds that the framework stands.
events.lens: Autonomy promised by a stronger power lasts only as long as that power finds it useful.

events.who: Thailand, Indonesia, South Korea; the IMF
events.hook: Currencies collapsed across East and Southeast Asia, and Indonesia's dictator fell.
events.what: Currencies collapsed across East and Southeast Asia, and Indonesia's dictator fell.
events.story: Thailand floated the baht on 2 July 1997 after failing to defend its dollar peg. Foreign money fled. Currencies and stock markets crashed in Indonesia, South Korea and Malaysia. IMF bailouts for Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea came with harsh conditions.
events.why: Fixed exchange rates came first. Short-term foreign borrowing and property bubbles left banks and companies exposed when the pegs broke.
events.then: Indonesian President Suharto resigned in May 1998 amid riots. South Korea restructured its giant conglomerates, and Malaysia imposed capital controls in September 1998.
events.sig: Indonesian President Suharto resigned in May 1998 amid riots. South Korea restructured its giant conglomerates, and Malaysia imposed capital controls in September 1998.
events.now: East Asian states built foreign reserves after 1997 to avoid ever again needing the IMF; the Chiang Mai currency-swap network of 2000 and China's reserve accumulation grew from the same lesson.

causes.why: Suharto, who rose to power through the killings, ruled for 31 years until the 1997-98 crisis brought him down.

q.what: Currencies, shares and short-term loans.
q.who: Speculators who sold early; ordinary workers lost jobs.
q.scale: Several Asian economies shrank sharply in 1998.
q.daily: Layoffs, bankruptcies and riots in Indonesia.
q.system: Asian countries built big reserves to avoid relying on the IMF.

events.bluf: Thailand set out to defend a baht pegged to the dollar against speculators and gave up on 2 July 1997. Foreign money fled, currencies and stock markets crashed in Indonesia, South Korea and Malaysia, and IMF bailouts came with harsh conditions. Indonesian President Suharto fell in 1998, South Korea restructured its conglomerates, Malaysia imposed capital controls, and Asian states built foreign reserves so as never to depend on the IMF again.
events.lens: Short-term foreign borrowing leaves a country exposed to sudden stops in capital.
events.fact: The Indonesian rupiah lost more than three-quarters of its value against the dollar within a year.

kv: the rupiah's fall against the dollar
IMF-led rescues for Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea

events.h: India and Pakistan test nuclear weapons
events.hook: Within three weeks, India and Pakistan each declared themselves nuclear powers.
events.what: Within three weeks, India and Pakistan each declared themselves nuclear powers.
events.story: On 11 and 13 May 1998 India set off five nuclear devices at Pokhran in the Rajasthan desert, its first tests since 1974, two months after a BJP-led government took office under Indian Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee. Pakistan under Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif answered on 28 and 30 May with six tests in the Chagai Hills of Balochistan. Both declared themselves nuclear-weapon states; neither had signed the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
events.why: Rivalry with Pakistan over Kashmir came first, with India's concern about China's arsenal. The BJP had promised to exercise the nuclear option and saw nuclear status as a mark of great-power standing. Pakistan's government judged that it could not leave India's tests unanswered.
events.then: The United States and Japan imposed sanctions, lifted by 2001. In May to July 1999 the two fought a limited war at Kargil in Kashmir. India and the United States signed a civil nuclear agreement in 2008.
events.sig: The United States and Japan imposed sanctions, lifted by 2001. In May to July 1999 the two fought a limited war at Kargil in Kashmir. India and the United States signed a civil nuclear agreement in 2008.
events.now: Two nuclear-armed states have fought a limited war and exchanged air strikes since 1998, which makes Kashmir the dispute most likely to involve nuclear weapons.

causes.why: India's 1974 test set off Pakistan's nuclear programme; in 1998 both tested openly.

q.problem: Proving a working nuclear arsenal.
q.how: Underground test explosions.
q.replaced: Ambiguity about both countries' weapons.
q.spread: Pakistan replied within weeks.
q.next: Sanctions, and a nuclear-armed standoff.

events.bluf: India's new BJP-led government under Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee set out to declare India a nuclear-weapon state, and Pakistan's government under Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif to match it. India fired five devices at Pokhran on 11 and 13 May 1998 and Pakistan six in the Chagai Hills within three weeks. South Asia was openly nuclear-armed, and deterrence has coexisted since with a limited war at Kargil in 1999 and strikes between the two in 2019 and 2025.
events.lens: Nuclear weapons deter all-out war but can embolden limited conflicts below that threshold.
events.fact: US satellites missed the preparations at Pokhran, and the CIA director ordered a review of the intelligence failure.

events.who: Hugo Chávez, a former army officer
events.what: Took office as president.
events.why: Venezuelan incomes had fallen since the oil price collapse of the 1980s, and the two traditional parties were discredited by corruption. Chávez's 1992 coup attempt had made him the best-known opponent of the system.
events.sig: A coup removed Chávez for two days in April 2002 before loyal troops restored him. Leftist leaders won across the region in the 2000s, from Bolivia and Ecuador to Brazil and Argentina, financed partly by the commodity boom. Chávez died in March 2013 and had named Nicolás Maduro his successor.
events.hook: Hugo Chávez took power and launched Latin America's 'pink tide' to the left.
events.story: Hugo Chávez, a former army officer who had led a failed coup in 1992, won Venezuela's presidential election in December 1998, promising to sweep away a corrupt two-party system. In office from 1999 he wrote a new constitution and, as oil prices rose, spent heavily on programmes for the poor, while taking control of the courts, the state oil company and much of the media. He won repeated elections until his death in 2013.
events.then: A coup removed Chávez for two days in April 2002 before loyal troops restored him. Leftist leaders won across the region in the 2000s, from Bolivia and Ecuador to Brazil and Argentina, financed partly by the commodity boom. Chávez died in March 2013 and had named Nicolás Maduro his successor.
events.now: The constitution and movement Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez built from 1999 have kept his party in power since. His supporters hold that he gave the poor a share of oil wealth and a political voice; his opponents hold that he dismantled checks on power and left an economy that collapsed under his successor.

causes.why: Debt, austerity and corruption in the 'lost decade' discredited Venezuela's old parties; Chávez won promising to share oil wealth with the poor.

q.before: Two traditional parties had dominated since 1958.
q.how: Election, then a new constitution.
q.lasted: He ruled until his death in 2013.

events.bluf: Former paratrooper Hugo Chávez won Venezuela's presidency in December 1998 promising to sweep away the two parties that had shared power for 40 years. He rewrote the constitution, spent oil revenue on programmes for the poor and brought the courts, the state oil company and much of the media under his control. His government led Latin America's turn to the left in the 2000s, and the oil dependence and weakened institutions he left preceded Venezuela's collapse after 2014.
events.lens: Petro-states that spend oil windfalls without building institutions are exposed when prices fall.
events.fact: Chávez hosted a live Sunday television programme, 'Aló Presidente', that sometimes ran for more than six hours.

events.who: President Fernando de la Rúa; the IMF; Argentine savers
events.what: Largest sovereign default then.
events.why: The peg made exports uncompetitive once Brazil devalued in 1999 and the dollar rose. Federal and provincial deficits were financed by foreign borrowing. The IMF withheld a loan payment in December 2001.
events.sig: The peso lost about three-quarters of its value against the dollar in 2002, and poverty passed 50 per cent. Argentine President Néstor Kirchner restructured the debt at a deep discount in 2005 and paid off the IMF in 2006. Holdout creditors litigated in New York until 2016.
events.hook: Argentina defaulted on about $100 billion of debt.
events.story: Argentina pegged its peso to the US dollar in 1991. A recession began in 1998, and foreign debt grew. In December 2001 the government froze bank deposits, the 'corralito', and riots broke out. Argentine President Fernando de la Rúa resigned on 20 December, the country declared default days later, and five presidents held office in about two weeks. The peg was abandoned in January 2002.
events.then: The peso lost about three-quarters of its value against the dollar in 2002, and poverty passed 50 per cent. Argentine President Néstor Kirchner restructured the debt at a deep discount in 2005 and paid off the IMF in 2006. Holdout creditors litigated in New York until 2016.
events.now: Argentina has defaulted nine times, and the 2001 crisis framed its politics from the Kirchner governments, which ran against IMF austerity, to Argentine President Javier Milei, who ran on dollarisation.

causes.why: After the Asian and Russian crises of 1997-98, investors fled emerging markets, and Argentina's peg of its peso to the dollar became unsustainable.

q.what: Government bonds, pesos and bank deposits.
q.who: Savers and the poor lost most.
q.scale: About $100 billion in defaulted debt, then the largest sovereign default.
q.daily: Frozen bank accounts and street protests.
q.system: A devalued peso and years of debt disputes.

events.bluf: Argentina had pegged the peso one-to-one to the dollar since 1991 to end hyperinflation, and borrowed abroad to sustain it. By late 2001 recession and debt broke the peg; banks froze deposits, riots forced Argentine President Fernando de la Rúa out, and the country defaulted on close to $100 billion, then the largest sovereign default on record. Poverty passed 50 per cent, and distrust of the peso and of the IMF became fixed features of Argentine politics.
events.lens: A currency peg buys credibility until the economy can no longer bear it, and then breaks all at once.
events.fact: Middle-class protesters banging pots and pans, the 'cacerolazo', became the sound of the crisis.

figs.rec: Then the largest sovereign default in history
kv: of Argentines below the poverty line in 2002

events.what: Hijacked planes killed ~3,000.
events.why: Al-Qaeda opposed the US military presence in Saudi Arabia, US support for Israel and US backing for Arab governments it called apostate. Bin Laden hoped a war would draw Muslims to his cause and bleed the United States.
events.sig: The United States invaded Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003, created the Department of Homeland Security, passed the Patriot Act and held detainees at Guantánamo Bay. The wars cost trillions of dollars and hundreds of thousands of lives. Bin Laden was killed by US forces in Pakistan in May 2011.
events.hook: Nineteen hijackers killed nearly 3,000 people and changed the world's security.
events.story: On the morning of 11 September 2001 nineteen al-Qaeda hijackers seized four airliners. Two struck the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, which collapsed within two hours; one struck the Pentagon; the fourth crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought the hijackers. About 2,977 people died. Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden claimed the attacks on video in 2004.
events.then: The United States invaded Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003, created the Department of Homeland Security, passed the Patriot Act and held detainees at Guantánamo Bay. The wars cost trillions of dollars and hundreds of thousands of lives. Bin Laden was killed by US forces in Pakistan in May 2011.
events.now: The attacks produced the security and surveillance apparatus Americans still pass through, two wars that ran to 2011 and 2021, and the 2001 authorisation for the use of military force that presidents of both parties have cited since.
events.fact: It was the deadliest day for US firefighters in history: 343 died.

causes.why: US troops based in Saudi Arabia after 1991 were the central grievance in bin Laden's 1996 declaration of war on America.
Bin Laden's network formed among the foreign fighters of the Afghan war against the Soviets.

q.why: Al-Qaeda wanted to strike the US for its presence in the Muslim world.
q.decided: Hijacked airliners used as weapons.
q.cost: Nearly 3,000 killed.
q.changed: The US launched the 'War on Terror'.

events.bluf: Al-Qaeda, led by Osama bin Laden, set out to strike the United States at home and provoke a war that would rally Muslims to its cause. Nineteen hijackers flew airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on 11 September 2001, killing nearly 3,000 people, the deadliest terrorist attack on record. The United States answered with wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, a surveillance apparatus and a global campaign against jihadist groups that defined two decades of world politics.
events.trig: Nineteen hijackers seized four airliners on the morning of 11 September 2001.
events.lens: Terrorism aims to provoke overreaction: how a state responds can matter more than the attack itself.

kv: from the first impact to the North Tower's collapse

events.who: US and allies; the Afghan Northern Alliance; the Taliban
events.hook: After 9/11, the US and its allies toppled the Taliban in weeks.
events.what: After 9/11, the US and its allies toppled the Taliban in weeks.
events.story: After the Taliban refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, US and British air strikes began on 7 October 2001. US special forces and CIA teams backing the Northern Alliance took Mazar-i-Sharif on 9 November and Kabul on 13 November. Kandahar fell in December, and bin Laden escaped from the Tora Bora mountains into Pakistan that month. The Bonn conference in December installed Hamid Karzai at the head of an interim government.
events.why: The Taliban refused to hand over bin Laden after the 9/11 attacks, and the United States wanted to destroy al-Qaeda's bases.
events.then: The war lasted 20 years as a Taliban insurgency regrouped from Pakistan after 2005. US troops peaked at about 100,000 in 2010-11. The Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021.
events.sig: The war lasted 20 years as a Taliban insurgency regrouped from Pakistan after 2005. US troops peaked at about 100,000 in 2010-11. The Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021.
events.now: The Taliban returned to power in 2021 and have barred girls from secondary school and women from most work, while the chaotic US exit damaged American credibility.

causes.why: When the Taliban refused to hand over bin Laden, the US and its allies invaded Afghanistan in October 2001.

q.why: The Taliban sheltered bin Laden after 9/11.
q.decided: US air power and the Northern Alliance.
q.cost: The 20-year war killed over 170,000 people.
q.changed: The Taliban fell, but returned in 2021.

events.bluf: The United States set out to destroy al-Qaeda's bases and remove the Taliban government that sheltered Osama bin Laden after the 11 September attacks. Air power and special forces backing the Northern Alliance drove the Taliban from Kabul by November 2001; bin Laden escaped into Pakistan. The war ran 20 years, NATO's longest, and the Taliban's return in 2021 made it the case cited for the limits of state-building by outside powers.
events.lens: Defeating a regime is quick; building a legitimate state in its place is slow, and may be impossible from outside.
events.fact: The Taliban offered in October 2001 to hand bin Laden to a third country if the United States stopped bombing and produced evidence; Washington refused.

toll.n: Brown University Costs of War estimates. Direct deaths only.

events.hook: China joined the global trading system and became the world's workshop.
events.what: China joined the global trading system and became the world's workshop.
events.story: After 15 years of negotiation, led on the Chinese side by Premier Zhu Rongji, China joined the World Trade Organization on 11 December 2001. It cut tariffs and opened to foreign investment in return for access to world markets.
events.why: Deng Xiaoping's heirs saw global markets as the path to growth, and Western governments hoped trade would encourage political liberalisation in China.
events.then: Chinese exports grew roughly sevenfold in a decade. The term 'China shock' names the job losses in Western factory towns whose products competed with them.
events.sig: Chinese exports grew roughly sevenfold in a decade. The term 'China shock' names the job losses in Western factory towns whose products competed with them.
events.now: Trade tensions grew into US-China tariff wars from 2018. The political bet behind accession, that trade would liberalise China, produced a richer one-party state instead.
events.wk: China and the World Trade Organization

causes.why: Two decades of export-led growth culminated in China's entry into the World Trade Organization.
Renewed reform prepared China to join the world trading system.

q.what: Manufactured exports.
q.who: Chinese industry and global consumers gained; some Western factory workers lost.
q.scale: Chinese exports grew roughly sevenfold in a decade.
q.daily: Cheaper goods in shops worldwide.
q.system: China as the 'workshop of the world'.

events.bluf: China's leaders sought WTO membership to lock in access to world markets; Western governments backed it in the hope that trade would liberalise China's politics. After 15 years of talks China joined in December 2001, cut tariffs and opened to foreign investment. Chinese exports grew about sevenfold in a decade, living standards rose, prices fell worldwide and factory towns in the West lost jobs; that 'China shock' feeds the tariff wars that began in 2018.
events.lens: Economic integration with a rival creates mutual dependence, and mutual vulnerability.
events.fact: China's application began in 1986 under the WTO's predecessor, the GATT.

kv: China's share of world exports, 2001 → today

events.who: Xanana Gusmão; José Ramos-Horta; the UN
events.hook: After 24 years of Indonesian occupation, East Timor became the 21st century's first new country.
events.what: After 24 years of Indonesian occupation, East Timor became the 21st century's first new country.
events.story: Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony in December 1975. Perhaps 100,000 to 180,000 Timorese died during the occupation, the range of Timor-Leste's truth commission in 2005. After Indonesian President Suharto fell in 1998, a UN-run vote in August 1999 chose independence by 78.5 per cent, and pro-Indonesian militias destroyed much of the territory in revenge. A UN administration led to independence on 20 May 2002 with resistance leader Xanana Gusmão as president.
events.why: Indonesia's democratisation after Suharto's fall in 1998 came first. Indonesian President B.J. Habibie's surprise offer of a vote in January 1999 opened the way.
events.then: UN peacekeepers stayed until 2012. Timor-Leste remains one of Asia's poorest and most democratic states.
events.sig: UN peacekeepers stayed until 2012. Timor-Leste remains one of Asia's poorest and most democratic states.
events.now: Independence ended 24 years of Indonesian occupation that had killed up to a quarter of the population, and it was the first new state the United Nations itself administered into existence.

causes.why: Suharto's regime invaded East Timor in 1975; only his fall in 1998 opened the way to a vote on independence.
The crisis brought down Suharto, and his successor allowed East Timor's 1999 independence vote.

q.before: Indonesian occupation since 1975.
q.how: A UN-run referendum, then UN administration.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: East Timor's independence movement under Xanana Gusmão and José Ramos-Horta set out to end an Indonesian occupation begun in 1975, in which an estimated 100,000 to 180,000 people died. A UN-run vote in 1999 chose independence, pro-Indonesian militias destroyed much of the territory, and a UN administration brought independence on 20 May 2002. The first new state of the century was also the first the United Nations itself administered into existence.
events.lens: Democratization in an occupying power can open the door to independence for the territories it holds.
events.fact: Timor-Leste joined ASEAN in 2025. Ramos-Horta shared the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize with Bishop Carlos Belo.

events.what: Replaced the OAU.
events.why: The OAU had failed to prevent atrocities such as Rwanda's, and leaders wanted stronger cooperation and peacekeeping. Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi pushed for a union and paid much of the bill.
events.sig: It has sent peacekeepers to Somalia, Sudan and elsewhere and suspended members after coups. The Sahel juntas of 2020-23 defied its suspensions.
events.hook: Africa replaced the OAU with a stronger union.
events.story: The African Union launched in Durban on 9 July 2002 to replace the Organisation of African Unity. Its Constitutive Act gave it the right to intervene in a member state in cases of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, a break with the OAU's non-interference rule.
events.then: It has sent peacekeepers to Somalia, Sudan and elsewhere and suspended members after coups. The Sahel juntas of 2020-23 defied its suspensions.
events.now: The Union replaced an organisation that could not intervene with one that can in principle, and it has since mandated peacekeeping in Somalia and suspended members after coups, while lacking the money to enforce its decisions.

causes.why: The AU replaced the OAU, criticised for shielding dictators under its rule of non-interference; the AU claimed a right to intervene against genocide and war crimes.

q.before: The Organisation of African Unity.
q.how: A new charter adopted by member states.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: African leaders wanted a body that could act where the OAU had stood aside, after Rwanda in 1994 had shown the cost of strict non-interference. The African Union launched in Durban in July 2002 with a charter right to intervene in member states against genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. It has mandated peacekeeping in Somalia and suspended members after coups, while lacking the money to enforce its decisions.
events.lens: Institutions rewrite their rules after failures: Rwanda pushed Africa from non-interference toward 'non-indifference'.
events.fact: The AU became a permanent member of the G20 in September 2023.

events.what: Single currency in daily use.
events.why: Europe's leaders wanted a single market with one money and a symbol of political unity. German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had accepted the currency at Maastricht as the price of a reunified Germany inside Europe.
events.sig: Trade across the zone became easier. Cheap credit flowed to Greece, Ireland, Spain and Portugal; when it stopped in 2010 they could neither devalue nor borrow, and the eurozone improvised rescue mechanisms.
events.hook: Twelve countries swapped their old currencies for the euro.
events.story: On 1 January 2002 euro notes and coins entered circulation in 12 countries, replacing the mark, franc, lira and nine other currencies; the euro had existed for banks and markets since 1999. The European Central Bank in Frankfurt set one interest rate for all of them. The old currencies ceased to be legal tender within two months.
events.then: Trade across the zone became easier. Cheap credit flowed to Greece, Ireland, Spain and Portugal; when it stopped in 2010 they could neither devalue nor borrow, and the eurozone improvised rescue mechanisms.
events.now: One interest rate for economies as different as Germany's and Greece's, with no shared budget, is the mechanism behind the 2010 debt crisis and the reason the eurozone built a rescue fund and a banking union after it; 21 countries use the euro since Bulgaria joined in 2026.
events.fact: The bridges and windows on euro notes are imaginary, so no country is favoured.

causes.why: Maastricht set the timetable and rules for the single currency.

q.what: A single currency.
q.who: Exporters and travellers gained; weaker economies lost the ability to devalue.
q.scale: About 350 million people use it.
q.daily: One currency across borders.
q.system: Monetary policy set by the European Central Bank.

events.bluf: Twelve EU governments replaced their national currencies with one money run by the European Central Bank, to complete the single market and to bind their states together. The changeover went smoothly, and about 350 million people now use the euro in 21 countries. The currency eased trade and locked very different economies into one monetary policy without a shared budget, the flaw the debt crisis of 2010 exposed.
events.lens: A monetary union without a fiscal union pushes the stress onto its weakest members.

events.what: Mass killing of non-Arab civilians.
events.why: Darfur's non-Arab groups rebelled against marginalisation by Khartoum. The government, with its army tied up in the south, chose militias to crush them.
events.sig: The ICC issued a warrant for al-Bashir in 2009 and added genocide in 2010, the first charges against a sitting head of state. Janjaweed units became the Rapid Support Forces in 2013 under Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo.
events.hook: Sudan's government and Janjaweed militias killed hundreds of thousands in Darfur.
events.story: In 2003 rebels from Darfur's Fur, Zaghawa and Masalit communities attacked government posts. Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir's government armed Arab militias, the Janjaweed, which with air and army support burned villages, killed and raped across Darfur. A UN estimate of 2008 put the dead at around 300,000 and the displaced at more than 2 million; the Sudanese government put deaths at about 10,000.
events.then: The ICC issued a warrant for al-Bashir in 2009 and added genocide in 2010, the first charges against a sitting head of state. Janjaweed units became the Rapid Support Forces in 2013 under Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo.
events.now: Janjaweed leaders formed the RSF, now fighting Sudan's army in a war marked by fresh mass killings in Darfur, including after the fall of El Fasher in 2025.

q.why: The government crushed a rebellion using militias.
q.decided: Government-backed militias.
q.cost: About 300,000 dead.
q.changed: President al-Bashir was charged by the International Criminal Court.

events.bluf: Rebels from Darfur's non-Arab groups attacked government posts in 2003 to end their region's marginalisation, and Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir's government chose to crush them with Arab militias, the Janjaweed. The militias and the army burned villages, killed and raped; about 300,000 died by a UN estimate of 2008 and more than 2 million were displaced. The International Criminal Court charged a sitting head of state for the first time, and the Janjaweed became the Rapid Support Forces now fighting Sudan's army.
events.lens: Militias armed by a state to fight its wars can become rivals to that state.
events.fact: Al-Bashir travelled to several ICC member states after the warrant, and none arrested him.

events.what: Former union leader became president.
events.why: Disappointment with the market reforms of the 1990s came first. Deep inequality and the appeal of a former metalworker who had led strikes against the military regime did the rest.
events.sig: The 'mensalão' vote-buying scandal of 2005 and the Lava Jato investigation from 2014 reached his party. Lula was convicted of corruption in 2017 and jailed in 2018; the Supreme Federal Court annulled the convictions in 2021. He defeated Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro in 2022.
events.hook: A former shoeshine boy and union leader became Brazil's president.
events.story: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who had lost three presidential elections, won in October 2002 and took office on 1 January 2003. His government launched Bolsa Família in 2003, paying poor families monthly cash on condition that their children attended school and were vaccinated. High prices for soy, iron ore and oil financed rising wages and spending. He left office at the end of 2010 with approval above 80 per cent.
events.then: The 'mensalão' vote-buying scandal of 2005 and the Lava Jato investigation from 2014 reached his party. Lula was convicted of corruption in 2017 and jailed in 2018; the Supreme Federal Court annulled the convictions in 2021. He defeated Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro in 2022.
events.now: Lula won the presidency again in 2022 after a corruption conviction that was later annulled; the contest between his camp and Bolsonaro's has organised Brazilian politics since 2018.

causes.why: Lula rose as a metalworkers' union leader in the strikes of 1978-80 that challenged the dictatorship, and co-founded the Workers' Party in 1980.

q.before: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.
q.how: Election.

events.bluf: Former metalworker and union leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil's presidency in 2002 promising to cut poverty without breaking the markets that feared him. He kept orthodox fiscal policy, expanded cash transfers through Bolsa Família and rode a commodity boom, and millions left poverty. Corruption scandals later engulfed his Workers' Party, and the fight over his record defined Brazil's left-right polarisation.
events.lens: Pairing redistribution with economic stability can broaden a centre-left coalition.
events.fact: Bolsa Família cost about 0.5 per cent of GDP.

events.what: Saddam toppled.

events.hook: The US toppled Saddam Hussein, unleashing years of war.
events.story: The US and its allies invaded Iraq in March 2003, saying Iraqi President Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction and links to terrorists. Baghdad fell within weeks. No such weapons were found. An insurgency and a sectarian civil war followed.
events.then: Well over 100,000 Iraqi civilians died in the years of violence that followed, by documented counts. ISIS later grew out of the chaos.
events.now: The invasion damaged trust in US intelligence and leadership, and greatly increased Iran's influence in Iraq.

events.bluf: US President George W. Bush's administration invaded Iraq to remove Saddam Hussein, saying he held weapons of mass destruction and had ties to terrorists. Baghdad fell in three weeks and no such weapons were found. The occupation's failures produced an insurgency, a sectarian war and ISIS, enlarged Iran's influence in Iraq and damaged US credibility worldwide.
events.lens: Removing a regime without a plan for what follows can unleash forces worse than the regime itself.
events.fact: Saddam was found in December 2003 hiding in a hole near Tikrit and was hanged in 2006.

events.what: Largest enlargement in EU history.
events.why: The EU wanted former Soviet-bloc states anchored in the West before Russia recovered. The candidates wanted the market, the money and the security that membership carried.
events.sig: Millions moved west for work, especially to Britain, Ireland and Germany, which later fed the Brexit debate. Romania and Bulgaria joined in 2007 and Croatia in 2013. Russia treated the expansion as encroachment.
events.hook: Ten countries, mostly former communist states, joined the EU in one day.
events.story: On 1 May 2004 ten countries joined the European Union: Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Cyprus and Malta. Eight had been in the Soviet bloc 15 years earlier. Britain, Ireland and Sweden opened their labour markets to the new members at once; most other states kept transition periods of up to seven years.
events.then: Millions moved west for work, especially to Britain, Ireland and Germany, which later fed the Brexit debate. Romania and Bulgaria joined in 2007 and Croatia in 2013. Russia treated the expansion as encroachment.
events.now: The new members' fear of Russia, carried into Brussels from 2004, shapes EU policy on Ukraine and sanctions; the migration the enlargement set off fed the Brexit vote of 2016.

causes.why: Freed from Soviet control, Eastern European countries rebuilt their economies and laws to qualify for membership.
Independent at last, former Soviet-bloc states sought security and prosperity by joining NATO and the EU.

q.before: The EU had 15 Western European members.
q.how: Accession treaties after years of reform.
q.lasted: Yes.

events.bluf: The EU admitted ten states, eight of them from the former Soviet bloc, to anchor them in the West's political and economic system and to close the division of the Cold War. The enlargement, the largest in its history, raised the new members' growth and sent millions of their workers west. It also hardened the line between the EU and Russia, which treated the expansion as encroachment, and made the new members' fear of Russia a force in EU policy.
events.lens: Membership in a rules-based club can lock in democratic and market reforms.
events.fact: Poland alone brought 38 million people, more than the other nine together.

events.hook: An undersea earthquake sent a tsunami across the Indian Ocean that killed about 230,000 people.
events.what: An undersea earthquake sent a tsunami across the Indian Ocean that killed about 230,000 people.
events.story: On 26 December 2004 a magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra sent waves up to 30 metres high onto coasts from Indonesia to Thailand, Sri Lanka, India and East Africa. About 230,000 people died in 14 countries. Aceh, nearest the epicentre, was the worst hit, and more than half the dead were Indonesian.
events.why: An undersea earthquake of magnitude 9.1 off Sumatra. The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning system, so coastal populations had no warning.
events.then: Aceh's rebels and Indonesia's government signed a peace deal at Helsinki in August 2005. An Indian Ocean warning system was built.
events.sig: Aceh's rebels and Indonesia's government signed a peace deal at Helsinki in August 2005. An Indian Ocean warning system was built.
events.now: The Helsinki agreement of 2005 that ended Aceh's three-decade insurgency grew directly from the disaster, the model case of a catastrophe opening space for peace; the Indian Ocean warning system built from 2005 covers coasts that had none.

q.problem: A huge earthquake under the sea with no warning system.
q.how: The sea floor shifted, sending waves across the ocean.
q.replaced: Complacency about tsunami risk in the Indian Ocean.
q.spread: Waves hit 14 countries within hours.
q.next: An Indian Ocean warning system.

events.bluf: A magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra on 26 December 2004 sent waves up to 30 metres high onto coasts from Indonesia to East Africa, and the Indian Ocean had no warning system to alert anyone. About 230,000 people died in 14 countries, Aceh worst of all. The disaster pushed Aceh's rebels and Indonesia's government into a peace deal in 2005 and produced an Indian Ocean tsunami warning system.
events.lens: Disasters can open the way to peace by changing the calculations of warring parties.
events.fact: The fault rupture lasted some eight to ten minutes, the longest ever recorded by instruments.

events.h: Australia apologises to the Stolen Generations
events.hook: Australia's government formally apologised to Aboriginal children taken from their families.
events.what: Australia's government formally apologised to Aboriginal children taken from their families.
events.story: Between about 1910 and the 1970s state governments and missions removed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, many of mixed descent, from their families under protection and welfare laws. The 1997 'Bringing Them Home' inquiry report estimated that between one in ten and one in three Indigenous children were removed in that period and called for an apology. Prime Minister John Howard declined to give one. Prime Minister Kevin Rudd, elected in November 2007, apologised in the House of Representatives on 13 February 2008 with members of the Stolen Generations in the gallery.
events.why: Years of campaigning after the 1997 report, and a change of government in 2007, made the apology possible.
events.then: The government set 'Closing the Gap' targets in 2008. One reading holds the removals were a deliberate policy to absorb Aboriginal people into the white population and met the definition of genocide, as the 1997 report concluded; the other holds that most removals were welfare cases under laws applied to neglected children of every background and that the report's estimate overstates the number. Compensation schemes followed in several states, Tasmania first in 2006.
events.sig: The government set 'Closing the Gap' targets in 2008. One reading holds the removals were a deliberate policy to absorb Aboriginal people into the white population and met the definition of genocide, as the 1997 report concluded; the other holds that most removals were welfare cases under laws applied to neglected children of every background and that the report's estimate overstates the number. Compensation schemes followed in several states, Tasmania first in 2006.
events.now: The apology made the removals an acknowledged fact of national history and set 'Closing the Gap' targets for Indigenous health and education; the 2023 referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament failed, so the question of a structural settlement remains open.

causes.why: Mabo opened a decade of reckoning, including the 1997 'Bringing Them Home' report on the Stolen Generations.

q.before: Governments had refused to apologise.
q.how: A formal apology in Parliament.
q.winners: Survivors of the Stolen Generations, symbolically.
q.lasted: Yes, though gaps in health and education persist.

events.bluf: Prime Minister Kevin Rudd set out to acknowledge in Parliament the removal of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families between about 1910 and the 1970s, which his predecessor had declined to do. On 13 February 2008 the House passed the apology as the first business of the new Parliament. The apology settled the symbolic question and left the material ones open; gaps in health, schooling and imprisonment remain wide, and the scale and purpose of the removals are still argued.
events.lens: Apologies matter symbolically; outcomes depend on what follows.
events.fact: The apology was the first item of business of the 42nd Parliament, and its text says 'we say sorry' three times.

events.what: Five-day war; Russia occupied breakaway regions.
events.why: Georgia's push to join NATO came first; the Bucharest summit of April 2008 had promised it membership without a date. Russia was determined to stop it, and the breakaway regions gave both sides the ground to fight on.
events.sig: The West's response was limited to suspended talks and a ceasefire. Russian troops have stayed in both regions since, and Georgia's NATO bid stalled.
events.hook: Russia fought a five-day war with Georgia, a preview of Ukraine.
events.story: After weeks of skirmishes, Georgian forces shelled Tskhinvali, capital of the breakaway region of South Ossetia, on the night of 7-8 August 2008. Russian forces entered through the Roki tunnel, pushed deep into Georgia within five days and bombed Gori and Poti. French President Nicolas Sarkozy brokered a ceasefire on 12 August. Russia recognised South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent on 26 August.
events.then: The West's response was limited to suspended talks and a ceasefire. Russian troops have stayed in both regions since, and Georgia's NATO bid stalled.
events.now: The war fixed the pattern of breakaway regions held by Russian troops that Moscow applied in Ukraine from 2014; one reading holds that the mild Western response encouraged those moves, the other that Russia acted on its own calculation of Ukraine's turn west.

causes.why: After eastern expansion, NATO promised in April 2008 that Georgia and Ukraine 'will become members'. Russia fought Georgia four months later.

q.why: South Ossetia, and Georgia's westward turn.
q.decided: Russia's overwhelming force.
q.cost: Hundreds killed and thousands displaced.
q.changed: Russia occupied two breakaway regions.

events.bluf: Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili moved to retake the breakaway region of South Ossetia; Russia under Prime Minister Vladimir Putin and President Dmitry Medvedev went to war to stop him and to block Georgia's path into NATO. Russian forces won in five days and recognised South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent. Georgia's NATO bid stalled, and Russian troops have garrisoned both regions since.
events.lens: Mild responses to a first use of force can encourage the next.
events.fact: An EU inquiry in 2009 found that Georgia fired first and that Russia's response went far beyond defence.

events.hook: Wall Street nearly collapsed, and the world fell into the deepest recession since the 1930s.
events.what: Wall Street nearly collapsed, and the world fell into the deepest recession since the 1930s.
events.story: US house prices peaked in 2006 after years of lending to borrowers with weak credit, packaged into securities rated as safe. Bear Stearns was rescued in March 2008, the mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac were taken over in September, and Lehman Brothers failed on 15 September. Interbank lending stopped. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson and Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke won a $700 billion bailout from Congress in October, and governments in Europe rescued their own banks.
events.why: Subprime lending and the securities built on it came first. Heavy borrowing by banks and thin regulation let the losses spread. Global savings flows and low interest rates had fed the bubble.
events.then: US unemployment reached 10 per cent in October 2009 and millions of homes went into foreclosure. Central banks cut rates to zero and bought bonds. The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 forced banks to hold more capital, and the eurozone debt crisis followed from 2010.
events.sig: US unemployment reached 10 per cent in October 2009 and millions of homes went into foreclosure. Central banks cut rates to zero and bought bonds. The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 forced banks to hold more capital, and the eurozone debt crisis followed from 2010.
events.now: The bailouts of banks while households lost homes fed the Tea Party and Occupy movements within three years and the populist politics of the 2010s; the zero rates and bond-buying used to fight the slump ran for a decade.

causes.why: After the dot-com bust, low interest rates and loose lending fed a housing bubble that burst in 2007-08.
Lehman's failure froze credit markets worldwide.

q.what: Mortgages and the securities built on them.
q.who: Bankers were bailed out; homeowners and workers paid.
q.scale: The worst downturn since the 1930s.
q.daily: Lost jobs, homes and savings.
q.system: Stricter bank rules and years of low interest rates.

events.bluf: Banks, mortgage lenders and investors had bet on ever-rising US house prices through securities built on subprime loans. When prices fell from 2006 the losses spread through a system that had borrowed heavily and was lightly regulated; Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008 and credit froze worldwide. Governments bailed out banks while millions lost homes and jobs in the worst recession since the 1930s, and the anger fed populist movements on left and right.
events.trig: The bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers on 15 September 2008.
events.lens: Financial crises that seem to reward insiders and punish ordinary people produce political backlash for a decade or more.
events.fact: No chief executive of a major US bank was prosecuted over the crisis, a fact populists of left and right both cited.

events.who: Lehman Brothers; the US Treasury and Federal Reserve
events.hook: America's fourth-largest investment bank went bankrupt, and panic spread through world markets.
events.what: America's fourth-largest investment bank went bankrupt, and panic spread through world markets.
events.story: Lehman Brothers, the fourth-largest US investment bank, held tens of billions of dollars in mortgage-linked assets as house prices fell through 2007 and 2008. The government had arranged the rescue of Bear Stearns in March 2008 and taken over Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac on 7 September. Over the weekend of 13-14 September Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson and New York Fed President Timothy Geithner failed to find a buyer; Barclays was blocked by British regulators and Bank of America bought Merrill Lynch instead. Lehman filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008 with more than $600 billion in assets. Credit markets froze worldwide.
events.why: Lehman had borrowed about 30 dollars for every dollar of capital to bet on mortgages, many made to borrowers who could not repay. One reading holds the authorities chose to let it fail to deter others; the other holds they lacked the legal power to lend against its collateral.
events.then: The insurer AIG was rescued with $85 billion the next day. Congress passed the $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program on 3 October after first rejecting it. The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 raised capital requirements and created a process for winding down large banks.
events.sig: The insurer AIG was rescued with $85 billion the next day. Congress passed the $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program on 3 October after first rejecting it. The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 raised capital requirements and created a process for winding down large banks.
events.now: Banks now face much stricter capital rules, and anger at the bailouts fed populist movements on both left and right.

causes.why: After the dot-com crash, low interest rates fed a housing bubble.

q.what: Securities backed by mortgages, and the debts used to buy them.
q.who: Executives earned fortunes; taxpayers and workers paid.
q.scale: The biggest bankruptcy in US history.
q.daily: Lost jobs, homes and savings around the world.
q.system: Tighter banking rules, and a decade of very low interest rates.

events.bluf: Lehman Brothers had borrowed heavily to hold mortgage-linked assets and had little capital when house prices fell; Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson and Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke declined to rescue it. The bank filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, the largest in US history, with more than $600 billion in assets, and credit markets froze worldwide. Governments rescued the banks that remained, and the rule that some institutions are too interconnected to fail was written into law.
events.lens: Letting one big institution fail can trigger a chain reaction; the dilemma is moral hazard versus systemic risk.
events.fact: Lehman had survived the Civil War, the 1929 crash and two world wars in its 158 years.

events.hook: America elected its first Black president.
events.what: America elected its first Black president.
events.story: Illinois Senator Barack Obama won the Democratic nomination over New York Senator Hillary Clinton in June 2008. The collapse of Lehman Brothers in September turned the campaign to the economy. On 4 November 2008 he defeated Arizona Senator John McCain with about 53 per cent of the popular vote and 365 electoral votes, and spoke to a crowd in Chicago's Grant Park that night.
events.why: The financial crisis and the unpopular Iraq War sank the Republican brand. Obama's campaign raised record sums online and mobilised young and minority voters.
events.then: Congress passed a $787 billion stimulus in February 2009, the Affordable Care Act in March 2010 and the Dodd-Frank financial law in July 2010. The Tea Party movement formed in 2009 and Republicans gained 63 House seats in 2010.
events.sig: Congress passed a $787 billion stimulus in February 2009, the Affordable Care Act in March 2010 and the Dodd-Frank financial law in July 2010. The Tea Party movement formed in 2009 and Republicans gained 63 House seats in 2010.
events.now: Obama's victory assembled a coalition of young, Black, Hispanic and college-educated voters that Democrats have relied on since, and the reaction to his presidency, from the Tea Party onward, remade the Republican Party.

causes.why: The crash, weeks before the election, shifted voters toward Obama.

q.before: President George W. Bush.
q.how: Election.
q.lasted: He served two terms.

events.bluf: Illinois Senator Barack Obama set out to win the presidency on opposition to the Iraq War and a promise of change, and the financial crisis of September 2008 carried him. He defeated Arizona Senator John McCain on 4 November 2008 with about 53 per cent of the vote and became the first Black president. His administration passed a stimulus, a health law and financial reform, and the polarisation of the two parties deepened through his two terms.
events.lens: Historic firsts can coincide with, and provoke, intensified backlash.
events.fact: Obama was the first sitting senator elected president since John F. Kennedy in 1960.

events.what: Bailouts and harsh austerity.
events.why: A shared currency without a shared budget left weak economies unable to devalue. Greece had hidden the true size of its deficits, and cheap credit in the 2000s had built up debts across the south.
events.sig: Greek unemployment passed 25 per cent and the economy shrank by about a quarter. Draghi's 2012 pledge calmed markets. The eurozone created a permanent rescue fund, the European Stability Mechanism, in 2012 and a banking union from 2014.
events.hook: Greece nearly went bankrupt and the euro almost broke apart.
events.story: In late 2009 Greece's new government revealed that its deficits had been hidden and were far larger than reported. Bond markets panicked about Portugal, Ireland, Spain and Italy too. The EU and the IMF offered bailouts from May 2010 in exchange for austerity; Ireland followed in November 2010, Portugal in 2011 and Cyprus in 2013. European Central Bank President Mario Draghi pledged in July 2012 to do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro.
events.then: Greek unemployment passed 25 per cent and the economy shrank by about a quarter. Draghi's 2012 pledge calmed markets. The eurozone created a permanent rescue fund, the European Stability Mechanism, in 2012 and a banking union from 2014.
events.now: Anti-EU populism surged across Europe, and the eurozone built new tools, such as a permanent rescue fund and banking union, to prevent a repeat.

causes.why: A shared currency without a shared budget left countries like Greece unable to devalue or borrow cheaply when crisis hit.
The global crash exposed hidden deficits in Greece and banking bubbles in Ireland and Spain.

q.what: Government bonds.
q.who: Banks were protected; Greeks and others paid through austerity.
q.scale: Bailouts for Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus.
q.daily: Unemployment and cuts in Southern Europe.
q.system: New EU rescue funds and closer budget oversight.

events.bluf: Greece and then Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus faced bankruptcy inside a currency they could not devalue; the EU, the European Central Bank and the IMF lent to them to keep the euro whole and demanded austerity in return. The euro survived, at a cost of a quarter of Greek output and unemployment above 25 per cent. The crisis exposed the flaw of a single currency without shared budgets and fed anti-EU parties across the continent.
events.lens: In a currency union, the weakest members bear the adjustment, politically as well as economically.
events.fact: Greece needed three bailouts, in 2010, 2012 and 2015, and left the last programme in 2018.

events.who: Haitians; the UN and international aid agencies
events.why: Haiti lies on a major fault, and poverty meant few buildings were built to resist earthquakes.
events.sig: Donors pledged about $10 billion, much of it spent through foreign contractors and agencies. Cholera brought by UN peacekeepers from October 2010 killed about 10,000 Haitians; the UN acknowledged its role in 2016.
events.hook: An earthquake destroyed much of Haiti's capital and killed over 200,000 people.
events.story: On 12 January 2010 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck near Port-au-Prince. Poorly built concrete buildings collapsed, including the National Palace and the headquarters of the UN mission. Estimates of the dead range from about 100,000 to over 200,000.
events.then: Donors pledged about $10 billion, much of it spent through foreign contractors and agencies. Cholera brought by UN peacekeepers from October 2010 killed about 10,000 Haitians; the UN acknowledged its role in 2016.
events.now: Haiti never recovered, and the collapse of its state after 2021, with gangs controlling most of the capital, has roots in the failures of reconstruction.

q.problem: A strong earthquake beneath a crowded, poorly built city.
q.how: A shallow quake on a fault near the capital.
q.replaced: Much of Port-au-Prince.
q.spread: Aid poured in from around the world.
q.next: A cholera epidemic and slow, troubled reconstruction.

events.bluf: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck near Port-au-Prince on 12 January 2010, in the poorest country in the Americas. Estimates of the dead run from about 100,000 to more than 200,000. Billions of dollars in pledged aid produced little lasting reconstruction, UN peacekeepers introduced cholera, and the weakening of the Haitian state set up the collapse that followed after 2021.
events.lens: Disasters kill more where states are weak, and aid without strong local institutions often fails.
events.fact: The head of the UN mission in Haiti, Tunisian diplomat Hédi Annabi, died when the mission's headquarters collapsed.

events.what: Health insurance overhaul.
events.why: Tens of millions had no insurance and costs were rising faster than wages. Democrats held both chambers for the first time since 1994, and Obama judged the window short.
events.sig: About 20 million more people gained coverage and the uninsured rate fell to record lows. Republicans voted to repeal it dozens of times and failed by one vote in the Senate in July 2017. The Supreme Court upheld it in 2012, 2015 and 2021.
events.hook: The biggest expansion of US health coverage since the 1960s.
events.story: Tens of millions of Americans had no health insurance and President Barack Obama made coverage his first domestic priority. The Senate passed its bill on 24 December 2009 with 60 votes; after Massachusetts elected a Republican senator in January 2010, Speaker Nancy Pelosi carried the Senate version through the House on 21 March 2010 without a Republican vote. Obama signed it on 23 March. It required most Americans to have insurance, barred insurers from refusing people with pre-existing conditions, offered subsidies and expanded Medicaid.
events.then: About 20 million more people gained coverage and the uninsured rate fell to record lows. Republicans voted to repeal it dozens of times and failed by one vote in the Senate in July 2017. The Supreme Court upheld it in 2012, 2015 and 2021.
events.now: It survived repeated repeal attempts, and a dispute over extending its expanded subsidies was at the centre of the 2025 federal government shutdown.

causes.why: Large Democratic majorities elected with Obama in 2008 passed his health-care law in 2010 without Republican votes.

q.before: Insurers could refuse people with pre-existing conditions.
q.how: An act of Congress passed on party lines.
q.winners: About 20 million people who gained coverage.
q.lasted: Yes, despite repeated repeal attempts.

events.bluf: President Barack Obama and Democratic majorities in Congress set out to cover the tens of millions of Americans without health insurance. The act signed on 23 March 2010 required most people to carry insurance, barred insurers from refusing the sick, subsidised premiums and expanded Medicaid; about 20 million more people gained coverage. It became the defining partisan battle of the decade and survived repeal votes and three Supreme Court challenges.
events.lens: Social programmes become harder to repeal once millions depend on them.
events.fact: 'Obamacare' began as an insult from opponents; Obama adopted the name in 2012.
events.btt: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act

events.where: Tunisia, Egypt, Libya, Syria, Yemen and Bahrain
events.hook: Protests toppled dictators in Tunisia, Egypt and Libya.
events.what: Protests toppled dictators in Tunisia, Egypt and Libya.
events.story: After Tunisian street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire in December 2010, protests forced Tunisian President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali out in January 2011. Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak fell in February. Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown with NATO air support and killed in October.
events.why: Corruption, repression, youth unemployment and food prices came first. Satellite television and social media spread the protests.
events.then: Only Tunisia became a democracy. Egypt returned to military rule, and Libya, Syria and Yemen fell into civil wars that drew in outside powers, produced refugee flows to Europe and let ISIS rise.
events.sig: Only Tunisia became a democracy. Egypt returned to military rule, and Libya, Syria and Yemen fell into civil wars that drew in outside powers, produced refugee flows to Europe and let ISIS rise.
events.now: Tunisia's democracy backslid after 2021; the grievances behind the protests remain across the region.

q.before: Long-ruling dictators across the Arab world.
q.how: Mass protests, and in some places civil war.
q.winners: Few: only Tunisia built a democracy, for a decade.
q.lasted: Most gains were reversed.

events.bluf: Protesters across the Arab world set out to end regimes they held responsible for corruption, repression and unemployment. They toppled rulers in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen within a year. Apart from Tunisia, for a decade, the uprisings ended in restored authoritarianism or civil war, and the grievances behind them remain.
events.trig: The self-immolation of Tunisian street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi in December 2010.
events.lens: Toppling a dictator is easier than building what replaces him; the most organized forces, often the army or Islamists, win the aftermath.
events.fact: Tunisia's National Dialogue Quartet won the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize.
