stayed democratic for a decade: Tunisia

events.who: Hosni Mubarak; protesters in Tahrir Square; the Egyptian army
events.hook: After 18 days of protest centred on Tahrir Square, Egypt's president of 30 years stepped down.
events.what: After 18 days of protest centred on Tahrir Square, Egypt's president of 30 years stepped down.
events.story: Protests began in Cairo's Tahrir Square on 25 January 2011. Attacks by police and hired thugs failed to disperse the crowds, which grew. On 11 February the army pushed Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak out.
events.why: Repression, corruption and youth unemployment came first. Tunisia supplied the spark.
events.then: The Muslim Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi was elected president in 2012 and overthrown by the army in 2013.
events.sig: The Muslim Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi was elected president in 2012 and overthrown by the army in 2013.
events.now: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has ruled since 2014 with tighter repression than Mubarak's, a common end for the Arab Spring revolts.

causes.why: Inspired by Tunisia, Egyptians filled Tahrir Square.

q.before: Hosni Mubarak, in power since 1981.
q.how: Mass protest and pressure from the army.
q.claim: 'The people want the fall of the regime.'
q.lasted: No: military rule returned in 2013.

events.bluf: Egyptian protesters set out to end Hosni Mubarak's 30-year rule, and the army set out to survive his fall. Eighteen days of mass protest from 25 January 2011 ended when the army pushed Mubarak out. The uprising showed the power of a crowd and the army's role as kingmaker, and Egypt's democratic experiment ended in a military coup in 2013.
events.lens: When the army decides a leader must go, he goes, and the army often stays.
events.fact: Mubarak was tried in a cage in a Cairo courtroom, sentenced to life in 2012 and cleared on retrial in 2017.

events.who: Japan; the Tokyo Electric Power Company
events.hook: An earthquake and tsunami caused nuclear meltdowns at Fukushima.
events.what: An earthquake and tsunami caused nuclear meltdowns at Fukushima.
events.story: On 11 March 2011 a magnitude 9.0 earthquake triggered a tsunami that killed about 18,000 people and flooded the Fukushima Daiichi plant, operated by the Tokyo Electric Power Company. Three reactors melted down. Japanese Prime Minister Naoto Kan's government ordered more than 100,000 residents evacuated from the surrounding area.
events.why: The plant's sea wall and backup power were not designed for a tsunami that large; the wave of about 14 metres overtopped a wall built for under 6, and the backup generators sat in basements that flooded.
events.then: Germany decided to phase out nuclear power, and Japan shut down its reactors for years.
events.sig: Germany decided to phase out nuclear power, and Japan shut down its reactors for years.
events.now: Debates over nuclear power's safety against its role in cutting emissions still turn on Fukushima; Germany closed its last reactors in April 2023 and Japan has restarted a minority of its fleet.

causes.why: Fukushima was the second accident, after Chernobyl, rated at the maximum level 7 on the international nuclear event scale.

q.problem: Keeping reactors cool after a huge tsunami.
q.how: Flooded backup generators failed, and three reactors melted down.
q.replaced: Japan's reliance on nuclear power, for years.
q.spread: Radiation forced over 100,000 people to evacuate.
q.next: Germany's nuclear phase-out and new safety rules.

events.bluf: A magnitude 9.0 earthquake off Japan's north-east coast on 11 March 2011 sent a tsunami that killed about 18,000 people and flooded the Fukushima Daiichi plant, run by the Tokyo Electric Power Company. Backup power failed and three reactors melted down, the worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl. Japan shut its reactors for years, Germany decided to leave nuclear power, and the accident set the terms of the argument between nuclear safety and climate policy.
events.lens: Rare disasters can reshape energy policy far beyond the country where they happen.
events.fact: Germany closed its last three reactors in April 2023, twelve years after deciding to leave nuclear power over Fukushima.

events.who: Bashar al-Assad; protesters and rebel groups
events.hook: Syria's crackdown on protests became a civil war that killed about half a million people.
events.what: Syria's crackdown on protests became a civil war that killed about half a million people.
events.story: Peaceful protests in March 2011 were met with gunfire. Armed rebellion followed, and the war drew in Iran, Russia, Turkey, the United States and jihadist groups including ISIS. About half of Syria's population was displaced.
events.why: Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's regime chose force over reform. Sectarian divisions and foreign backers turned the conflict into a long war.
events.then: Millions of refugees fled to Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Europe. Russia, Iran, Hezbollah, Turkey and the United States all sent forces.
events.sig: Millions of refugees fled to Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Europe. Russia, Iran, Hezbollah, Turkey and the United States all sent forces.
events.now: Assad's regime fell to a rebel offensive led by the Islamist group HTS in December 2024, and its leader Ahmed al-Sharaa now heads Syria's government.

causes.why: Inspired by Tunisia and Egypt, Syrians began protesting in March 2011.

q.why: Assad crushed protests, and rebellion followed.
q.decided: For years, Russian and Iranian support for Assad; finally a rebel offensive in 2024.
q.cost: Hundreds of thousands killed and millions displaced.
q.changed: Syria was shattered.

events.bluf: Syrian President Bashar al-Assad chose force over reform when protests spread in March 2011, and the opposition took up arms. The war killed about half a million people, displaced half the population and drew in Russia, Iran, Turkey, the United States and jihadist groups including ISIS. Assad fell to a rebel offensive in December 2024.
events.lens: Regimes that choose force over reform can survive for years but destroy their country in the process.
events.trig: The arrest and torture of boys in Deraa for anti-regime graffiti in March 2011.
events.fact: Assad fled to Moscow as the rebels entered Damascus in December 2024.

events.what: Al-Qaeda leader killed in a raid.
events.why: The courier lead came first. US President Barack Obama chose a raid over an air strike to confirm the death and limit civilian casualties.
events.sig: Al-Qaeda's central leadership weakened under Ayman al-Zawahiri, though its regional branches and its rival ISIS survived. Pakistan's parliament condemned the violation of its sovereignty, and the United States asked how bin Laden had lived there for five years.
events.hook: US commandos killed Osama bin Laden in a night raid in Pakistan.
events.story: CIA analysts tracked one of bin Laden's couriers to a walled compound in Abbottabad, near Pakistan's main military academy. On 2 May 2011 about two dozen US Navy SEALs flew in two helicopters from Jalalabad in Afghanistan, one of which crash-landed inside the compound. They killed bin Laden and four others and took his body, which was buried at sea from the USS Carl Vinson. Pakistan learned of the raid after the helicopters had left.
events.then: Al-Qaeda's central leadership weakened under Ayman al-Zawahiri, though its regional branches and its rival ISIS survived. Pakistan's parliament condemned the violation of its sovereignty, and the United States asked how bin Laden had lived there for five years.
events.now: It closed a chapter of the post-9/11 era, and US attention shifted from counterterrorism toward rivalry with China and Russia.

causes.why: After a ten-year hunt, US special forces killed bin Laden in Pakistan.

q.why: To kill the leader of al-Qaeda.
q.decided: Intelligence and a special-forces raid.
q.cost: Bin Laden and four others killed.
q.changed: Al-Qaeda lost its founder.

events.bluf: US President Barack Obama ordered a raid to kill or capture Osama bin Laden at a compound the CIA had traced through a courier, choosing a raid over an air strike so that the death could be confirmed. Navy SEALs flew from Afghanistan into Abbottabad on 2 May 2011 and killed him. Al-Qaeda lost its founder ten years after 9/11, and the raid on Pakistani soil, carried out without Pakistan's knowledge, deepened mistrust between Washington and Islamabad.
events.lens: Killing a terrorist leader can weaken a group but rarely ends the movement.
events.fact: A Pakistani IT consultant live-tweeted the raid without knowing what it was, complaining about a helicopter over Abbottabad at 1 am.

events.hook: South Sudan became the world's newest country after decades of war.
events.what: South Sudan became the world's newest country after decades of war.
events.story: Two civil wars between Sudan's government and southern rebels, from 1955 to 1972 and 1983 to 2005, ended in a peace deal that promised a referendum. In January 2011 nearly 99 per cent of southern voters chose secession. South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 with former rebel commander Salva Kiir as president.
events.why: Decades of war and discrimination by Khartoum against the mostly non-Arab, non-Muslim south came first. Oil in the south gave both sides something to fight for.
events.then: A power struggle between President Salva Kiir and Vice President Riek Machar became civil war in December 2013, killing an estimated 400,000 people before a 2018 peace deal.
events.sig: A power struggle between President Salva Kiir and Vice President Riek Machar became civil war in December 2013, killing an estimated 400,000 people before a 2018 peace deal.
events.now: South Sudan remains one of the world's most fragile states, and renewed fighting and the arrest of Vice President Machar in 2025 threatened its peace deal.

causes.why: Sudan's wars against its peripheries, in the south and in Darfur, ended with South Sudan's independence in 2011.

q.before: Rule from Khartoum.
q.how: A referendum after a peace deal.
q.lasted: Independence held, but civil war followed.

events.bluf: Southern Sudanese leaders wanted a state of their own after two civil wars with Khartoum, and the 2005 peace deal gave them a referendum. Nearly 99 per cent voted to secede, and South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 under President Salva Kiir. Within two years a power struggle between Kiir and Vice President Riek Machar became a civil war, and the state built by armed struggle had few institutions to hold it.
events.lens: Liberation movements often struggle to become governments, especially when their leaders were held together only by a common enemy.
events.fact: South Sudan is the world's newest widely recognised state and the UN's 193rd member.

events.hook: A NATO-backed rebellion overthrew Muammar Gaddafi, who was killed after 42 years in power.
events.what: A NATO-backed rebellion overthrew Muammar Gaddafi, who was killed after 42 years in power.
events.story: Protests in February 2011 became an armed revolt. The UN authorised a no-fly zone to protect civilians in March, and NATO air strikes helped the rebels take Tripoli in August. Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi was captured and killed near Sirte on 20 October.
events.why: Gaddafi's violent crackdown on protesters led the UN to authorise a no-fly zone to protect civilians.
events.then: Libya split between rival governments in Tripoli and the east and dozens of militias, and became a hub for arms and for migration to Europe.
events.sig: Libya split between rival governments in Tripoli and the east and dozens of militias, and became a hub for arms and for migration to Europe.
events.now: Libya remains divided between rival governments, and the intervention's outcome made Russia and China wary of approving UN action to protect civilians.

causes.why: Protest spread from Tunisia and Egypt to Libya.

q.why: Rebels rose against Gaddafi's crackdown.
q.decided: NATO air power and rebel advances.
q.cost: Thousands killed.
q.changed: Libya fell into long-term division.

events.bluf: Libyan rebels set out to end Muammar Gaddafi's 42-year rule, and NATO intervened under a UN mandate to protect civilians from his crackdown. Air strikes helped the rebels take Tripoli in August 2011, and Gaddafi was captured and killed in October. Libya fragmented into rival governments and militias, and Russia and China turned against UN-authorised interventions.
events.lens: An intervention to protect civilians can become regime change, and regime change without a plan leaves chaos.
events.fact: Russia and China abstained on the UN resolution of March 2011 and later cited its use to block action on Syria.

events.who: Xi Jinping; the Chinese Communist Party
events.what: Became Communist Party leader.
events.why: He was chosen by the party leadership in a planned succession from Hu Jintao. Xi and his allies judged that corruption and factional bargaining under Hu had weakened the party's grip.
events.sig: In Xinjiang from 2017 the state detained large numbers of Uyghurs in what it calls vocational training centres against extremism and says closed in 2019; the UN human rights office said in 2022 that the detentions may amount to crimes against humanity, which Beijing rejects. Hong Kong received a national security law in 2020 after the protests of 2019. The presidential term limit was scrapped in 2018.
events.hook: Xi Jinping became China's leader and its most powerful since Mao.
events.story: In November 2012 Xi Jinping became General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, and president in March 2013. His anti-corruption campaign punished more than a million officials and removed rivals including former Politburo member Bo Xilai and former security chief Zhou Yongkang. In 2018 the constitution's two-term limit on the presidency was scrapped, and in 2022 Xi took a third term as general secretary.
events.then: In Xinjiang from 2017 the state detained large numbers of Uyghurs in what it calls vocational training centres against extremism and says closed in 2019; the UN human rights office said in 2022 that the detentions may amount to crimes against humanity, which Beijing rejects. Hong Kong received a national security law in 2020 after the protests of 2019. The presidential term limit was scrapped in 2018.
events.now: China grew more assertive abroad and tighter at home, and Xi began a third term in 2022-23 with no clear successor.

causes.why: By 2010 China was the world's second-largest economy, and its new leader promised a 'great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation'.

q.before: Collective leadership under Hu Jintao.
q.how: Party succession, then centralisation of power.
q.lasted: He began a third term in 2022.

events.bluf: Xi Jinping took the Communist Party leadership in November 2012 in a planned succession and set out to end the collective leadership and corruption he saw weakening the party. His anti-corruption campaign punished more than a million officials and removed rivals, and in 2018 the presidential term limit was scrapped. Xi became China's most powerful leader since Mao, tightened control at home and asserted China abroad, and the US-China rivalry took the shape it has today.
events.lens: Concentrating power can make a state more decisive, and also more prone to costly mistakes.
events.fact: Xi was sent to a village in Shaanxi for seven years at the age of 15 after his father, a revolutionary veteran, was purged under Mao.

events.hook: Months of protest in Kyiv drove out Ukraine's pro-Russian president.
events.what: Months of protest in Kyiv drove out Ukraine's pro-Russian president.
events.story: Protests began on Maidan Nezalezhnosti in Kyiv in November 2013 after President Viktor Yanukovych dropped an association agreement with the European Union under Russian pressure. They grew after police beat students on 30 November. On 18-20 February 2014 security forces and snipers killed more than 100 protesters. Yanukovych fled to Russia on 22 February, and parliament voted to remove him.
events.why: Anger at corruption came first. Yanukovych's sudden decision, under Russian pressure, to drop the EU agreement turned it into a movement, and the killings of February turned the movement against him.
events.then: Ukraine's new government signed the EU agreement in 2014. Russia seized Crimea in March and backed separatists in the Donbas from April; the fighting there killed about 14,000 people by 2021 (UN count, 2021). Petro Poroshenko was elected president in May 2014.
events.sig: Ukraine's new government signed the EU agreement in 2014. Russia seized Crimea in March and backed separatists in the Donbas from April; the fighting there killed about 14,000 people by 2021 (UN count, 2021). Petro Poroshenko was elected president in May 2014.
events.now: Ukrainians call it the Revolution of Dignity, the moment the country chose Europe over Moscow; Russia calls it a coup backed by the West against an elected president. Russia's seizure of Crimea and its backing of separatists in the Donbas followed within weeks, and the war that escalated in 2022 began there.

q.before: President Yanukovych, close to Moscow.
q.how: Mass protest; the president fled.
q.claim: Ukraine's European future and an end to corruption.
q.lasted: Yes, but Russia answered with war.

events.bluf: Ukrainians protested for three months to reverse President Viktor Yanukovych's turn away from an EU agreement and to end corruption; Yanukovych, with Moscow's backing, tried to hold on by force. More than 100 protesters were killed in February 2014 and Yanukovych fled to Russia. Ukraine's new government signed the EU agreement, Russia seized Crimea and backed separatists in the Donbas, and the war that escalated in 2022 began.
events.lens: A neighbour's revolution can look like an existential threat to a regime that fears the same at home.
events.fact: The movement took its name from a hashtag, #euromaidan, used on its first night.

events.what: Epidemic killed ~11,000.
events.why: Health systems broken by civil war in Liberia and Sierra Leone came first. The virus reached cities for the first time, and burial customs spread it.
events.sig: A vaccine trial in Guinea in 2015 proved effective, and the rVSV vaccine was licensed in 2019. WHO created an emergency programme and a contingency fund.
events.hook: Ebola killed about 11,000 people in West Africa.
events.story: The outbreak began with a child in Meliandou in Guinea in December 2013 and spread to Liberia and Sierra Leone in 2014, the first Ebola epidemic in crowded cities. The World Health Organization declared an international emergency in August 2014. By 2016 there had been about 28,600 cases and over 11,300 deaths.
events.then: A vaccine trial in Guinea in 2015 proved effective, and the rVSV vaccine was licensed in 2019. WHO created an emergency programme and a contingency fund.
events.now: An Ebola vaccine was approved in 2019, and the epidemic offered lessons, often unheeded, for COVID-19.

q.problem: A deadly virus spreading in cities for the first time.
q.how: Spread through contact with bodily fluids, including at funerals.
q.replaced: Slow, under-funded epidemic responses.
q.spread: Three countries, with a few cases abroad.
q.next: An Ebola vaccine, approved in 2019.

events.bluf: The Ebola virus spread from a Guinean village in December 2013 into Liberia and Sierra Leone, where health systems weakened by years of war could neither trace nor isolate it. By 2016 there had been about 28,600 cases and over 11,300 deaths, with the World Health Organization slow to declare an emergency. The epidemic produced faster international outbreak responses, a WHO emergency fund and the first licensed Ebola vaccine.
events.lens: Epidemics expose state weakness: public health is national security.
events.fact: Health workers made up about 10 per cent of the dead in Liberia and Sierra Leone, countries that had fewer than 300 doctors between them.

events.what: Crimea seized; war in the Donbas.
events.why: Putin feared Ukraine's turn to the West after the Euromaidan revolution, and the loss of Russia's naval base at Sevastopol. Russia holds that Crimea's Russian-speaking majority wanted to rejoin it; Ukraine holds that the vote was staged under occupation.
events.sig: The West imposed sanctions and Russia was suspended from the G8. Russia backed separatists in eastern Ukraine, and the fighting there killed about 14,000 people by 2021 (UN count, 2021).
events.hook: Russia seized Crimea from Ukraine, the first annexation in Europe since WWII.
events.story: After Ukraine's pro-EU protests ousted President Viktor Yanukovych on 22 February 2014, unmarked Russian troops took control of Crimea's airports and parliament from 27 February. A referendum on 16 March, held under occupation and recognised by few governments, reported 97 per cent for joining Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin signed the annexation on 18 March. War broke out in the Donbas in April.
events.then: The West imposed sanctions and Russia was suspended from the G8. Russia backed separatists in eastern Ukraine, and the fighting there killed about 14,000 people by 2021 (UN count, 2021).
events.now: The annexation was the prelude to the full-scale invasion of 2022; Crimea's status is central to any peace settlement, with Russia treating it as closed and Ukraine treating it as occupied territory.

causes.why: In both cases Russia used troops and backed separatists in a former Soviet republic that was leaning toward the West.
Days after Yanukovych fled, Russian troops seized Crimea.

events.wk: Annexation of Crimea by the Russian Federation

q.why: Russia opposed Ukraine's westward turn.
q.decided: Russian troops seized the peninsula.
q.cost: War in the Donbas killed about 14,000 by 2021.
q.changed: Russia annexed Crimea.

events.bluf: Russian President Vladimir Putin moved troops into Crimea to keep the naval base at Sevastopol and to answer Ukraine's turn west after the Euromaidan revolution. Russia held a referendum under occupation and annexed the peninsula within a month, the first forcible annexation in Europe since 1945. Russia calls it a reunification endorsed by Crimea's people; Ukraine and most governments call it an illegal seizure, and Crimea's status sits at the centre of any settlement of the war.
events.lens: Faits accomplis that go unreversed encourage more of them: the limited response in 2014 shaped Moscow's calculation in 2022.
events.fact: The UN General Assembly declared the referendum invalid by 100 votes to 11, with 58 abstentions.

kv: UN General Assembly vote calling the referendum invalid

events.what: Oil crash, hyperinflation.
events.why: Oil provided almost all export earnings, and price controls, expropriations and corruption had already cut output at the state oil company. US financial sanctions from 2017 and oil sanctions from 2019 cut access to credit and markets.
events.sig: Nearly 8 million Venezuelans left. Maduro claimed victory in disputed elections in 2018 and 2024; in 2024 the electoral council declared him the winner without publishing a breakdown, and the opposition published tally sheets it said showed its candidate, Edmundo González, had won. The United States imposed sweeping sanctions.
events.hook: Venezuela's economy collapsed, and millions fled.
events.story: Oil supplied about 95 per cent of Venezuela's export earnings. When prices fell from over $100 a barrel in mid-2014 to under $30 in early 2016, the government kept spending, printed money and tightened price controls. The economy shrank by roughly three-quarters over the following years, hyperinflation wiped out wages and savings, and food and medicine ran short.
events.then: Nearly 8 million Venezuelans left. Maduro claimed victory in disputed elections in 2018 and 2024; in 2024 the electoral council declared him the winner without publishing a breakdown, and the opposition published tally sheets it said showed its candidate, Edmundo González, had won. The United States imposed sweeping sanctions.
events.now: UN figures for 2024 put Venezuelans abroad at nearly 8 million, one of the world's largest displacement crises, and in 2025 the United States built up naval forces in the Caribbean against Maduro's government. The government blames the collapse on US sanctions and economic war; its opponents blame mismanagement, expropriation and corruption that began before the sanctions.

causes.why: When oil prices fell in 2014, an economy dependent on oil and weakened by price controls and mismanagement collapsed.

q.what: Oil, and imported food and medicine.
q.who: Ordinary Venezuelans suffered; insiders profited from currency controls.
q.scale: The economy shrank by about three-quarters.
q.daily: Shortages and hyperinflation.
q.system: Mass emigration.

events.bluf: Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro set out to keep his government's programmes and control after oil fell from over $100 a barrel in mid-2014, and kept spending, printing money and controlling prices. The economy shrank by about three-quarters, hyperinflation wiped out wages, and nearly 8 million people, about a quarter of the population, left. The exodus reshaped migration across the region, and Venezuela became a target of US sanctions and military pressure.
events.lens: Petro-states without diversified economies collapse when oil revenue falls.
events.fact: Venezuela's central bank put inflation in 2018 at about 130,000 per cent.

events.what: Declared a caliphate.
events.why: Syria's war left ungoverned space. Iraq's exclusion of Sunnis gave ISIS recruits.
events.sig: A US-led coalition with Iraqi and Kurdish forces destroyed the caliphate by 2019, after battles that ruined Mosul and Raqqa.
events.hook: ISIS declared a caliphate across Iraq and Syria.
events.story: Syria's civil war and Iraq's sectarian exclusion of Sunnis gave ISIS space and recruits. In June 2014 ISIS fighters captured Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city. ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi declared a 'caliphate' across eastern Syria and western Iraq. ISIS massacred and enslaved Yazidis and staged killings for propaganda.
events.then: A US-led coalition with Iraqi and Kurdish forces destroyed the caliphate by 2019, after battles that ruined Mosul and Raqqa.
events.now: ISIS offshoots remain active, especially in Africa's Sahel and in Afghanistan, and thousands of its fighters and their families are still held in camps in Syria.

causes.why: Disbanding Iraq's army and the sectarian conflict that followed the 2003 invasion created the insurgency from which ISIS grew.
Syria's civil war gave ISIS territory and recruits; in 2014 it declared a 'caliphate' across Syria and Iraq.

q.why: ISIS sought a caliphate by force.
q.decided: A US-led coalition and local forces.
q.cost: Tens of thousands killed, including a genocide of Yazidis.
q.changed: The caliphate was destroyed by 2019.

events.bluf: ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi set out to hold territory and rule it as a caliphate. In 2014 his fighters took Mosul and declared one across eastern Syria and western Iraq, enslaved and massacred Yazidis and inspired attacks worldwide. A US-led coalition and local forces destroyed the territorial caliphate by 2019, and its offshoots remain active in Africa and Asia.
events.lens: Jihadist movements thrive in the vacuum left by state collapse and sectarian exclusion.
events.fact: Al-Baghdadi died in a US raid in northwest Syria in October 2019.
events.btt: Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant

events.who: Russian-backed forces in eastern Ukraine; Malaysia Airlines Flight 17
events.hook: A Russian-made missile destroyed a passenger jet over eastern Ukraine, killing all 298 aboard.
events.what: A Russian-made missile destroyed a passenger jet over eastern Ukraine, killing all 298 aboard.
events.story: On 17 July 2014 a Buk missile hit the Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur flight over territory held by Russian-backed separatists near Hrabove, killing all 298 aboard. A Dutch-led joint investigation team found that the launcher came from Russia's 53rd anti-aircraft brigade and returned to Russia after the shooting. Russia's government rejected the finding and said the missile was Ukrainian or the evidence fabricated.
events.why: War in the Donbas came first, where Russian-backed separatists had received heavy anti-aircraft weapons from Russia and had been shooting down Ukrainian military planes. The flight was routed over the war zone at an altitude the airlines treated as safe.
events.then: The EU widened sanctions on Russia within two weeks. In November 2022 a Dutch court convicted two Russians and one Ukrainian of murder in their absence, and in 2025 the UN's aviation agency held Russia responsible. Russia rejects the verdicts.
events.sig: The EU widened sanctions on Russia within two weeks. In November 2022 a Dutch court convicted two Russians and one Ukrainian of murder in their absence, and in 2025 the UN's aviation agency held Russia responsible. Russia rejects the verdicts.
events.now: Most of the victims were Dutch, and the case made the Netherlands one of Europe's firmest supporters of Ukraine; the dispute over blame, with Western courts and investigators assigning it to Russia and Russia rejecting their findings, is the pattern of the wider war.

causes.why: Russia's backing of separatists brought heavy weapons into the Donbas.

q.why: Russian-backed separatists were fighting Ukrainian forces in the Donbas.
q.decided: A missile fired from separatist-held ground.
q.cost: 298 people killed, 196 of them Dutch.
q.changed: Western sanctions on Russia were tightened.

events.bluf: Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur was shot down over the Donbas by a Buk missile fired from territory held by Russian-backed separatists, killing all 298 aboard, 196 of them Dutch. Dutch-led investigators traced the launcher to a Russian army brigade; Russia denies responsibility and has offered alternative accounts. The deaths hardened EU sanctions on Russia and made the Netherlands one of Ukraine's firmest supporters.
events.lens: Proxy wars draw in third countries when weapons are used carelessly.
events.fact: A memorial near Schiphol airport has 298 trees, one for each victim.

kv: a Dutch court convicted three men in absentia

events.who: Refugees from Syria and elsewhere; EU
events.what: Over 1M arrived in a year.
events.why: The Syrian civil war came first. Cuts in aid to refugee camps in Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan in 2015 pushed people on, and the open Balkan route showed that the journey could be made.
events.sig: Border fences went up along the Balkan route. The EU paid Turkey 6 billion euros under a March 2016 deal to stop crossings. Germany's welcome gave way to tighter asylum rules, and the Alternative für Deutschland rose on the issue.
events.hook: Over a million refugees reached Europe in one year.
events.story: In 2015 more than a million refugees and migrants reached Europe, most crossing from Turkey to Greek islands and walking north through the Balkans. Most were fleeing wars in Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq. German Chancellor Angela Merkel said on 31 August 'we can do this' and kept Germany's borders open; Germany took in about 890,000 asylum seekers that year. Hungary closed its Serbian border with a fence in September.
events.then: Border fences went up along the Balkan route. The EU paid Turkey 6 billion euros under a March 2016 deal to stop crossings. Germany's welcome gave way to tighter asylum rules, and the Alternative für Deutschland rose on the issue.
events.now: Migration became the most divisive issue in European politics, and the EU adopted a new pact on migration and asylum in 2024.

causes.why: Syrian refugees were the largest group in Europe's 2015 refugee crisis.

q.before: EU rules required asylum claims in the first country of arrival.
q.how: Mass arrivals overwhelmed the system.
q.claim: Germany's Merkel said 'We can do this'.
q.winners: Refugees who found safety; populist parties gained votes.
q.lasted: Borders tightened afterwards.

events.bluf: More than a million refugees and migrants, most fleeing wars in Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq, crossed to Europe in one year, and EU governments split over whether to take them in or keep them out. German Chancellor Angela Merkel's government took about 890,000 asylum seekers; others built fences. The EU's asylum rules broke down, the EU paid Turkey to stop crossings, and migration became the most divisive issue in European politics.
events.lens: Large, sudden migrations reshape the politics of receiving countries far more than gradual ones.
events.fact: The photograph of Alan Kurdi, a three-year-old Syrian found drowned on a Turkish beach on 2 September 2015, became the image of the crisis.

kv: asylum claims in the EU in 2015

events.who: Iran; the US, Britain, France, Germany, Russia and China
events.hook: Iran agreed to limit its nuclear programme in return for lifting sanctions.
events.what: Iran agreed to limit its nuclear programme in return for lifting sanctions.
events.story: After two years of talks, Iran and the United States, Britain, France, Germany, Russia and China signed the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action in Vienna in July 2015. It capped Iran's uranium enrichment and stockpile under international inspection in exchange for relief from nuclear-related sanctions.
events.why: Western governments feared Iran was moving toward a nuclear weapon. Iran needed sanctions relief.
events.then: US President Donald Trump withdrew in 2018 and reimposed sanctions. Iran then expanded enrichment. In June 2025 Israel and then the United States struck Iran's nuclear sites.
events.sig: US President Donald Trump withdrew in 2018 and reimposed sanctions. Iran then expanded enrichment. In June 2025 Israel and then the United States struck Iran's nuclear sites.
events.now: Iran's nuclear programme remains one of the region's most dangerous disputes, and the strikes of 2025 left its future unclear.

causes.why: The Islamic Republic's nuclear programme, and Western suspicion of it, made Iran the target of sanctions.

q.before: Iran was expanding enrichment under sanctions.
q.how: A multilateral agreement.
q.claim: Limits on enrichment in return for sanctions relief.

The US withdrawal in 2018 unravelled it, Iran expanded enrichment, and in 2025 Israel and the United States struck Iran's nuclear sites.
events.lens: Agreements that depend on one government's continued support can collapse with a change of leader.
events.fact: The deal cut Iran's enriched uranium stockpile by about 98 per cent, by the White House's account of 2015.

events.who: UK voters; Prime Minister David Cameron; Leave campaigners such as Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage
events.what: Voted 52-48 to leave the EU.
events.why: Concerns over sovereignty and immigration came first, sharpened by the arrival of workers from the 2004 member states and the 2015 refugee crisis. Long-standing British ambivalence about Europe and discontent in regions that felt left behind did the rest.
events.sig: Four years of political turmoil followed; Theresa May's government fell over the withdrawal terms and Boris Johnson won a majority in 2019. Britain left the EU on 31 January 2020. The pound fell about 10 per cent against the dollar in the days after the vote.
events.hook: Britain voted to leave the European Union.
events.story: In a referendum on 23 June 2016, called by Prime Minister David Cameron, 52 per cent of voters chose to leave the European Union on a turnout of 72 per cent. England and Wales voted Leave; Scotland, Northern Ireland and London voted Remain. Cameron resigned the next day.
events.then: Four years of political turmoil followed; Theresa May's government fell over the withdrawal terms and Boris Johnson won a majority in 2019. Britain left the EU on 31 January 2020. The pound fell about 10 per cent against the dollar in the days after the vote.
events.now: Leavers hold that Britain recovered control of its laws, borders and trade policy; Remainers hold that it lost market access and influence for little gain, and polls since 2022 have shown more voters regretting the result than endorsing it. Relations with the EU are being rebuilt piece by piece.
events.fact: The ballot question was changed before the vote from a Yes/No form to Remain/Leave on the Electoral Commission's advice.

causes.why: Free movement from the new member states made immigration a central issue in Britain's referendum.

events.bluf: Prime Minister David Cameron called a referendum to settle his party's argument over Europe and expected to win it; Leave campaigners, among them Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage, set out to take Britain out. Leave won by 52 to 48 per cent and Cameron resigned the next day. Britain became the first member to leave the EU, the union with Scotland and Northern Ireland came under strain, and the vote became the emblem of the revolt against globalisation.
events.lens: Referendums on complex questions can expose social divides that elections had hidden.

events.hook: Colombia made peace with the FARC guerrillas after 52 years of war.
events.story: After four years of talks in Havana, Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and the FARC signed a peace deal in September 2016 to end a war that had lasted since 1964. Voters narrowly rejected it in a referendum on 2 October. A revised deal was approved by Congress in November.
events.then: Santos won the Nobel Peace Prize in October 2016. About 13,000 FARC members disarmed and the group became a political party. Hundreds of former fighters and social leaders were later killed, and dissident factions rearmed.
events.now: The deal turned the FARC into a political party in 2017 and created a transitional court for war crimes; dissident factions and other armed groups have expanded into former FARC areas since.

causes.why: The FARC, founded in 1964 and inspired by Cuba's revolution, fought Latin America's longest insurgency; the peace talks were held in Havana.

events.bluf: Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and the FARC guerrillas negotiated for four years to end a war that had run since 1964. Voters narrowly rejected the first deal in October 2016; a revised version passed Congress in November, and about 13,000 FARC members disarmed. Latin America's longest insurgency ended as an armed force, while other armed groups expanded into the territory the FARC left.
events.lens: Peace agreements end wars between the signatories, not violence by those left out.
events.fact: Colombia's truth commission estimated in 2022 that about 450,000 people were killed in the conflict between 1985 and 2018.

events.what: Political outsider won the presidency.

events.sig: US policy shifted toward tariffs, especially on China, tighter immigration and scepticism of alliances. Trump appointed three Supreme Court justices. He lost to Joe Biden in 2020 and won again in 2024.
events.hook: An outsider with no political experience won the presidency.

events.then: US policy shifted toward tariffs, especially on China, tighter immigration and scepticism of alliances. Trump appointed three Supreme Court justices. He lost to Joe Biden in 2020 and won again in 2024.

events.bluf: Businessman Donald Trump set out to win the presidency as an outsider against free trade, immigration and the political establishment of both parties. His victory moved US policy toward tariffs and scepticism of alliances and remade the Republican Party in his image.

events.story: On 31 December 2019 Wuhan officials reported unexplained pneumonia cases; Wuhan doctor Li Wenliang had warned colleagues the day before and was reprimanded by police. Chinese scientists identified a new coronavirus within days and published its genome on 11 January 2020. On 23 January Wuhan, a city of 11 million, was locked down.

A WHO-convened mission to Wuhan in 2021 called a laboratory origin 'extremely unlikely', and the WHO's own director-general said the inquiry had been limited. About 7 million deaths were officially reported by 2023, and estimates of excess deaths are several times higher.
events.now: The virus's origin is unresolved. One reading holds that it passed from animals at Wuhan's Huanan market, citing the early cluster of cases there; the other holds that it escaped from a Wuhan laboratory, citing the city's coronavirus research and China's limits on an inquiry. The question keeps the pandemic a live issue between Washington and Beijing.

About 7 million deaths were reported by 2023 and excess deaths ran several times higher; early delays in disclosure and the unresolved origin of the virus became flashpoints between Washington and Beijing.
events.lens: Transparency in the first weeks of an outbreak can decide whether it stays local or goes global.

events.hook: Ethiopia's war in Tigray killed hundreds of thousands.
events.story: The Tigray People's Liberation Front had led Ethiopia's ruling coalition until Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018, and it held a regional election in 2020 that Addis Ababa called illegal. On 4 November 2020 Abiy, the 2019 Nobel Peace laureate, sent federal troops into Tigray; the government said the TPLF had attacked a federal army base, and the TPLF said the attack pre-empted a planned federal assault. Eritrean forces joined the government side, and aid access to Tigray was cut for most of 2021-22.
events.then: The Pretoria peace agreement of 2 November 2022 ended the fighting. Estimates of the dead published since 2022 run to hundreds of thousands, most from hunger and lack of medical care; the government disputes the higher figures. Tensions with Eritrea and fighting in Amhara and Oromia continued.
events.now: It stalled Ethiopia's economic rise, and tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, including over Ethiopia's demand for access to the sea, raise fears of a new war.

Two years of war with Eritrean troops on the government side killed hundreds of thousands by estimates published since 2022, many from famine, and ended in a peace deal in November 2022. Ethiopia's standing as a rising power fell, and the strain on its ethnic federal system spread to Amhara and Oromia.
events.lens: Ethnic federations can break into war when the centre and a powerful region fight over control.
events.trig: The TPLF's regional election of September 2020 and the fighting at the army's Northern Command bases on 3-4 November 2020.

events.who: Prime Minister Boris Johnson's government; the European Union

events.hook: Britain formally left the European Union.
events.story: After years of deadlock in Parliament, Prime Minister Boris Johnson won a large majority in December 2019 promising to 'get Brexit done'. The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020. A transition period ended on 31 December 2020 with a trade deal agreed on 24 December. The deal kept goods trade free of tariffs and brought customs checks, rules-of-origin paperwork and an end to free movement.
events.then: New customs checks hit trade with Europe. A special arrangement kept Northern Ireland inside EU goods rules, creating a trade border in the Irish Sea, which the Windsor Framework of 2023 eased.
events.now: Leavers hold that Britain recovered control of its laws and trade policy; Remainers hold that the barriers cost trade and growth, and the government's budget forecaster put the long-run loss at about 4 per cent of output (2021 estimate). In 2025 the two sides agreed a new partnership on defence and trade.

causes.why: After three and a half years of negotiation and political turmoil, Britain formally left on January 31, 2020.

events.bluf: Prime Minister Boris Johnson's government set out to take Britain out of the EU's single market and customs union on the terms of the 2016 vote, and the EU set out to protect its market and the open Irish border. Both got most of what they wanted: Britain left on 31 January 2020 with a trade deal at the end of the year, and Northern Ireland stayed inside EU goods rules. New barriers cut trade with Europe, and the two sides are still settling their relationship.
events.lens: Leaving a deep economic union is slower and costlier than joining it.

events.what: Over 1 million US deaths by 2022; lockdowns.
events.why: A respiratory virus that spread before symptoms moved through global air travel faster than surveillance. Most countries had no stock of tests or protective equipment and reacted after community spread had begun.
events.sig: Vaccines were authorised in December 2020, under a year after the virus was sequenced. Governments spent trillions on relief, and inflation followed in 2021-23. One reading holds that lockdowns and school closures saved lives at an acceptable cost; the other holds that the costs to children, businesses and liberty outweighed benefits that targeted measures could have delivered. The virus's origin, a market or a laboratory in Wuhan, remains unresolved.
events.hook: A new virus shut down the world.
events.story: The virus was identified in Wuhan in December 2019 and the World Health Organization declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Governments closed schools and businesses; US President Donald Trump declared a national emergency on 13 March and Congress passed a $2.2 trillion relief act on 27 March. More than 1 million Americans died over the following three years (CDC count).
events.then: Vaccines were authorised in December 2020, under a year after the virus was sequenced. Governments spent trillions on relief, and inflation followed in 2021-23. One reading holds that lockdowns and school closures saved lives at an acceptable cost; the other holds that the costs to children, businesses and liberty outweighed benefits that targeted measures could have delivered. The virus's origin, a market or a laboratory in Wuhan, remains unresolved.
events.now: The pandemic fixed remote work in white-collar life, produced the largest peacetime government spending in US history and the inflation of 2021-23, and left public trust in health authorities divided along party lines.

events.bluf: A new coronavirus identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019 spread worldwide in early 2020 before most governments reacted. It killed millions, including more than 1 million Americans, shut down economies and moved work, schooling and commerce online. Vaccines built on mRNA technology arrived within a year and saved millions of lives; lockdowns, mandates and disputes over the virus's origin and the response deepened political divisions.
events.lens: Pandemics test state capacity and public trust; countries with more of both fared better.
events.fact: The Moderna vaccine was designed within days of the virus's genome being published in January 2020; the rest of the year went on testing.

events.who: Israel; the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain (later Morocco and Sudan); the Trump administration

events.story: US President Donald Trump's administration brokered the accords, signed at the White House in September 2020 by Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. They were the first Arab normalisations with Israel since Jordan in 1994 and did not depend on a Palestinian settlement. Morocco and Sudan joined later in 2020.
events.why: Shared concern about Iran came first. Trade and technology ties, and US inducements to each signatory, followed.

events.bluf: Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, with the Trump administration brokering, set out to normalise relations over shared concern about Iran and the appeal of trade, without waiting for a Palestinian state. The accords of 2020 were the first Arab normalisations with Israel since Jordan in 1994, and Morocco and Sudan followed. They survived the Gaza war, and Saudi Arabia says its own normalisation depends on a path to a Palestinian state.
events.lens: Shared threats can bring former enemies together faster than resolving their core disputes.

events.who: BioNTech and Pfizer; Moderna; Britain's medicines regulator
events.hook: Less than a year after the virus was identified, the first vaccines were approved.
events.what: Less than a year after the virus was identified, the first vaccines were approved.
events.story: On 2 December 2020 Britain's medicines regulator, the MHRA, became the first in the world to approve the Pfizer-BioNTech mRNA vaccine, eleven months after the virus's genome was published. Margaret Keenan, aged 90, received the first shot in Coventry on 8 December. The United States approved it on 11 December and Moderna's vaccine a week later. Billions of doses followed worldwide.
events.why: Decades of mRNA research came first. Public funding and advance purchases removed the commercial risk, and regulators ran trials and reviews in parallel instead of in sequence.
events.then: Vaccines cut deaths sharply in 2021. Rich countries had vaccinated most adults by mid-2021 while much of Africa waited into 2022. Karikó and Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize in medicine.
events.sig: Vaccines cut deaths sharply in 2021. Rich countries had vaccinated most adults by mid-2021 while much of Africa waited into 2022. Karikó and Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize in medicine.
events.now: mRNA technology now promises vaccines and treatments for other diseases, and its pioneers Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize in medicine.

causes.why: Researchers raced to develop vaccines.

q.problem: How to stop a new virus that was killing millions.
q.how: mRNA vaccines tell cells to make a harmless piece of the virus, training the immune system.
q.replaced: Vaccine development that usually took a decade.
q.spread: Over 13 billion doses were given worldwide by 2023.
q.next: mRNA vaccines under development for other diseases.

events.bluf: Drug companies BioNTech and Pfizer, and Moderna, set out to make a vaccine against a new virus in under a year using mRNA technology that had never produced a licensed product, and governments paid in advance. Britain's regulator approved the first on 2 December 2020 and billions of doses followed. Deaths fell sharply where the vaccines were given, rich countries got them a year before poor ones, and mRNA became a platform for other diseases.
events.lens: Long-term public investment in basic science pays off in emergencies.
events.fact: The second person vaccinated in Britain was an 81-year-old named William Shakespeare.

events.who: Senior General Min Aung Hlaing; Aung San Suu Kyi's government
events.hook: Myanmar's army overthrew the elected government, setting off a civil war.
events.what: Myanmar's army overthrew the elected government, setting off a civil war.
events.story: Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy won the November 2020 election by a landslide. The army claimed fraud; the election commission and foreign observers rejected the claim. On 1 February 2021 the army under Senior General Min Aung Hlaing arrested Suu Kyi, President Win Myint and other leaders and declared a state of emergency. Security forces shot protesters in the streets, and armed resistance spread across the country.
events.why: The army refused to accept further loss of power to the civilian government. Its case rests on alleged fraud in the 2020 vote; the opposition's case rests on the election commission's and foreign observers' finding that the vote was credible.
events.then: Resistance forces under a National Unity Government and ethnic armies took large parts of the country from 2023. The army, backed by China and Russia, answered with air strikes on villages. Civilians killed by security forces passed 6,000 by 2025 in the count of a Burmese rights group.
events.sig: Resistance forces under a National Unity Government and ethnic armies took large parts of the country from 2023. The army, backed by China and Russia, answered with air strikes on villages. Civilians killed by security forces passed 6,000 by 2025 in the count of a Burmese rights group.
events.now: The war has displaced more than 3 million people (UN count, 2024); the junta's phased elections that began in December 2025 are, in the army's account, a return to constitutional rule and, in the account of the opposition and most Western governments, a device to legitimise the coup.

causes.why: The army, which seized power in 1962, has dominated Myanmar's politics ever since.

q.before: A civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, sharing power with the army.
q.how: A military coup.
q.winners: The army, though it has since lost ground.
q.lasted: Civil war continues.

events.bluf: Myanmar's army under Senior General Min Aung Hlaing set out to reverse the November 2020 election, which Aung San Suu Kyi's party had won by a landslide and which the army said was fraudulent. On 1 February 2021 it arrested her and her government and crushed mass protests. Armed resistance spread into a nationwide civil war in which resistance forces and ethnic armies hold large parts of the country, the most serious challenge the army has faced since 1948.
events.lens: Coups against popular elected governments can provoke resistance that unites former rivals.
events.fact: Aung San Suu Kyi, 75 at the time of the coup, was sentenced in closed trials to a total of 33 years, later reduced to 27.

events.who: Militaries in Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger

events.hook: Military coups swept the Sahel, pushing out France and bringing in Russia.
events.story: Soldiers took power in Mali in August 2020 and again in May 2021, in Burkina Faso in January and September 2022 and in Niger in July 2023. Each junta blamed the civilian government and French troops for failing to stop jihadist insurgents who had killed thousands and displaced millions. France withdrew its forces from Mali in 2022, Burkina Faso in 2023 and Niger by December 2023.
events.then: Russian contractors of the Wagner Group, later the Africa Corps, deployed in Mali from 2021. The three juntas formed the Alliance of Sahel States in 2023 and left ECOWAS in January 2025. The juntas say they have restored sovereignty; their critics cite rising deaths and postponed elections.

Gaddafi's fall in 2011 sent fighters and weapons into the Sahel, fuelling jihadist insurgencies that soldiers later cited to justify coups.

events.bluf: Soldiers in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger seized power between 2020 and 2023 to end civilian governments they blamed, with French troops, for failing to stop jihadist insurgencies. The juntas expelled French forces, brought in Russian military contractors and left the regional bloc ECOWAS in 2025. The Sahel's alliances were reshaped, and jihadist violence kept rising, with the region recording the most terrorism deaths in the world by 2024.
events.lens: Military regimes that blame foreign partners for security failures often fail to do better.

events.what: Killed at home.
events.why: Haiti was in deep political crisis: Haitian President Jovenel Moïse had been ruling by decree, and the end of his term was disputed. Who ordered the killing remains unclear.

events.hook: Mercenaries killed Haiti's president in his bedroom.
events.story: On 7 July 2021 a commando unit that included more than 20 former Colombian soldiers stormed Haitian President Jovenel Moïse's home in Port-au-Prince and shot him dead.
events.then: Haiti was left without a single elected national official. Gangs took over most of Port-au-Prince. A Kenyan-led international mission arrived in 2024, and in 2025 the UN authorised a larger force to fight the gangs.

events.bluf: Haitian President Jovenel Moïse was ruling by decree, with no sitting parliament and the end of his term disputed, when a commando that included more than 20 former Colombian soldiers killed him at home on 7 July 2021. Who ordered the killing remains unresolved. Haiti was left without a single elected national official, and armed gangs took control of most of Port-au-Prince.
events.lens: When a weak state loses its leader, armed groups fill the vacuum.
events.fact: Several suspects were tried in a US federal court in Miami, where some pleaded guilty.

events.what: Mob stormed the Capitol during vote certification.
events.why: Trump and his allies claimed the 2020 election had been stolen through fraud; courts rejected more than 60 suits and his own Justice Department found no fraud on a scale to change the result. His supporters believed the claim and came to Washington to act on it.
events.sig: More than 1,500 people were charged. The House impeached Trump a second time on 13 January 2021 and the Senate acquitted him 57-43, short of the two-thirds needed. On returning to office in January 2025 he pardoned or commuted the sentences of nearly all of those charged. Democrats call the day an insurrection incited by the president; Trump and most Republicans call it a protest that got out of hand, the prosecutions political and the pardons a correction.
events.hook: A mob stormed the Capitol to stop the count of an election.
events.story: On 6 January 2021, as Congress met to certify Joe Biden's victory, President Donald Trump told a rally near the White House that the election had been stolen and urged the crowd to march to the Capitol, to make their voices heard 'peacefully and patriotically' and to 'fight like hell'. Thousands broke through police lines and into the building, forcing Vice President Mike Pence and lawmakers to flee; about 140 police officers were injured and one rioter was shot dead by police. Congress completed the certification that night.
events.then: More than 1,500 people were charged. The House impeached Trump a second time on 13 January 2021 and the Senate acquitted him 57-43, short of the two-thirds needed. On returning to office in January 2025 he pardoned or commuted the sentences of nearly all of those charged. Democrats call the day an insurrection incited by the president; Trump and most Republicans call it a protest that got out of hand, the prosecutions political and the pardons a correction.
events.now: It remains a defining event in debates over the peaceful transfer of power, and Americans are deeply divided over how to remember it.

causes.why: After losing the 2020 election, Trump disputed the result; on January 6, 2021, a crowd of his supporters stormed the Capitol as Congress certified the vote.

q.before: President Trump, whose term was ending after he lost the 2020 election.

events.bluf: Supporters of President Donald Trump set out to stop Congress certifying Joe Biden's election victory on 6 January 2021, after Trump had told a rally that the election was stolen. Thousands broke into the Capitol, lawmakers fled and about 140 police officers were injured; Congress completed the certification that night. The attack failed in its aim and became the defining event in American arguments over the transfer of power, with the two parties disagreeing over what it was.
