arcs.title: Japan: From Closed Country to Empire
arcs.summary: For two centuries Japan shut itself off from the West. Then, in a single lifetime, it went from samurai with swords to an empire that beat Russia and swallowed Korea. The story is a chain: China's humiliation in the Opium War warned Japan what was coming; American warships forced the door open; unequal treaties and foreign bombardments convinced young samurai that the shogun had failed; they overthrew him in the name of the emperor and copied the West at astonishing speed. Victory over China in 1895 should have been Japan's arrival as a power, but Russia, France and Germany forced it to hand back its prize. That humiliation, and Russia grabbing the same land three years later, set Japan on the road to war with Russia, alliance with Britain, and the annexation of Korea.

chapters.d: Japan limits contact with the outside world, but Dutch books and foreign ships keep leaking in.
American warships, unequal treaties and foreign bombardments discredit the shogun.
Samurai overthrow the shogun and remake Japan on Western lines.
Japan beats China, is humiliated by the Triple Intervention, beats Russia and takes Korea.

arcs.title: World War II in Europe
arcs.summary: World War II in Europe grew out of the last war's unfinished business. A punishing peace and the Great Depression gave Hitler his opening; once in power he destroyed German democracy in months, persecuted Jews by law, and tested the democracies with a string of gambles they let him win. The deal with Stalin in August 1939 cleared the way to invade Poland. Germany won stunning victories in 1939–41, but two decisions sealed its fate: invading the Soviet Union and declaring war on the United States. From Stalingrad on, the Soviets ground down the German army in the east while Britain and America attacked from the west and the air. Germany surrendered in May 1945, leaving 6 million Jews murdered, Europe in ruins and the continent split between the two new superpowers.

chapters.d: A harsh peace and an economic collapse.
Dictatorship, persecution and a string of unanswered gambles.
Germany conquers most of Europe; Britain holds on.
The USSR and the US enter; Germany's defeats begin.
Invasion from east and west, surrender, and justice.

arcs.title: The Scramble for Africa & East Africa
arcs.summary: In 1870 Europeans controlled about a tenth of Africa, mostly coastal footholds. By 1914 they controlled about 90%. The Suez Canal made East Africa strategic; explorers like Stanley mapped the interior for European audiences and kings; Britain's occupation of Egypt set off a rush. At Berlin in 1884–85 the powers agreed rules for carving up the continent, and companies like Carl Peters' German East Africa Company moved in with dubious treaties. East Africans fought back: the Swahili coast under Abushiri, the Hehe under Mkwawa, the Nandi, and the vast Maji Maji uprising. Each was crushed with machine guns, famine and scorched earth. Railways and cash crops tied the region to Europe's economy. World War I turned East Africa into a battlefield, and in 1919 Germany's colony passed to Britain as Tanganyika, the territory that would become Tanzania.

chapters.d: A canal, explorers and anti-slavery campaigns draw Europe toward East Africa.
Berlin rules, company treaties and coastal revolt.
Hehe, Nandi and Maji Maji resistance; railways and brutal 'pacification'.
Reforms, settler rule, WWI in East Africa and German East Africa becomes Tanganyika.

arcs.title: The Renaissance and the Printing Revolution
arcs.summary: Between 1440 and 1550, Europe's elites rediscovered classical learning, and Gutenberg's printing press let ideas spread faster than any ruler or church could control. Wealth from trade made Italy's city-states patrons of a new art, and Greek scholars, some fleeing the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople, brought ancient texts west. Then the Italian Wars (1494-1559) dragged France and Spain into Italy. They spread Renaissance styles north, and they taught Machiavelli his hard lessons about power. Printing turned a German monk's protest into the Reformation, and a Polish astronomer's book into the start of a scientific revolution.

chapters.d: Printing arrives just as Byzantium falls.

chapters.t: Italy's golden age, and its wars
chapters.d: Art flourishes while French and Spanish armies fight over Italy.

chapters.t: Ideas that broke the old order
chapters.d: Printed ideas transform religion and science.

reading: Elizabeth Eisenstein, The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979)
Peter Burke, The Italian Renaissance: Culture and Society in Italy (3rd ed., 2014)
Michael Mallett & Christine Shaw, The Italian Wars, 1494-1559 (2nd ed., 2019)
Quentin Skinner, Machiavelli: A Very Short Introduction (2000)

arcs.title: The Reformation and the Wars of Religion
arcs.summary: Martin Luther's protest of 1517 split Western Christianity. Within decades, German princes, Swiss cities, Scandinavian kings, the English crown and Dutch rebels had broken with Rome, often as much for power and church wealth as for faith. The Catholic Church answered with its own reform at the Council of Trent and new orders like the Jesuits. For over a century Europe fought over religion: civil wars in France, the Dutch Revolt against Spain and finally the Thirty Years' War, which killed perhaps a fifth of Germany's population. The 1648 Peace of Westphalia ended the era. It confirmed that each ruler would decide religion within his own lands, a step toward the modern system of sovereign states.

chapters.d: Luther's challenge spreads, and princes take sides.
France and the Netherlands fight over faith and power.
The Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia.

reading: Diarmaid MacCulloch, The Reformation: A History (2003)
Peter H. Wilson, Europe's Tragedy: A History of the Thirty Years War (2009)
Mack P. Holt, The French Wars of Religion, 1562-1629 (2nd ed., 2005)
Andrew Pettegree, Brand Luther (2015)

arcs.title: Spain's Golden Age and Decline
arcs.summary: The marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile in 1469 created a new power. In 1492 they conquered Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Iberia, expelled Spain's Jews and funded Columbus. Their grandson Charles V ruled Spain, the Low Countries, much of Italy, the Habsburg lands and a growing American empire. American silver paid for a century of wars against France, the Ottomans and the Protestants. Even so, the crown went bankrupt four times under Philip II. By 1700 Spain was in decline, and the War of the Spanish Succession put a French Bourbon prince on its throne.

chapters.d: Ferdinand and Isabella build a new monarchy.

chapters.t: The empire on which the sun never set
chapters.d: Charles V and Philip II, funded by American silver.
Wars, revolt and a disputed succession.

reading: J. H. Elliott, Imperial Spain, 1469-1716 (1963)
Henry Kamen, Spain's Road to Empire (2002)
Geoffrey Parker, The Grand Strategy of Philip II (1998)

arcs.title: The Ottoman Empire: Rise, Peak and Fall
arcs.summary: For nearly five centuries the Ottomans ruled where Europe, Asia and Africa meet. Taking Constantinople in 1453 made them heirs to Rome. Conquering Egypt in 1517 made them guardians of Islam's holy cities. Under Suleiman they besieged Vienna. After the failed siege of 1683 the tide turned. Austria and Russia advanced, nationalist revolts tore away the Balkans, and reforms could not keep pace with Europe's industrial powers. Joining Germany in World War I proved fatal. Britain and France divided the Arab provinces, and Mustafa Kemal (Atatürk) built a Turkish republic from the ruins. Those settlements still shape the Middle East.

chapters.d: Constantinople and the conquest of the Arab heartlands.
Suleiman's peak and the long struggle with the Habsburgs.
Reform, retreat and nationalist revolts.
World War I ends the empire.

reading: Caroline Finkel, Osman's Dream: The History of the Ottoman Empire (2005)
Eugene Rogan, The Fall of the Ottomans (2015)
Şükrü Hanioğlu, A Brief History of the Late Ottoman Empire (2008)

arcs.title: The Islamic Gunpowder Empires: Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals
arcs.summary: Three Muslim dynasties used cannon and musket armies to build vast states stretching from the Balkans to Bengal. Historians Marshall Hodgson and William McNeill called them the 'gunpowder empires'. The Ottomans were Sunni. The Safavids made Shi'ism the religion of Iran, which it still is. The Mughals, Sunni rulers of a mostly Hindu land, reached their height under Akbar's policy of tolerance. All three peaked around 1600 and weakened in the 1700s, opening the way for European empires.

chapters.d: Ismail in Iran, Babur in India, Suleiman in Istanbul.
Akbar's tolerance and Shah Jahan's monuments.
Mughal collapse invites invaders and the East India Company.

reading: Douglas Streusand, Islamic Gunpowder Empires: Ottomans, Safavids, and Mughals (2011)
Stephen Dale, The Muslim Empires of the Ottomans, Safavids, and Mughals (2010)
John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire (1993)

arcs.title: East Asia: Ming to Qing, Warring States to Tokugawa
arcs.summary: In 1449 Mongols captured a Ming emperor at Tumu, and China turned defensive. Over the next century it rebuilt the Great Wall in the brick-and-stone form seen today. Japan collapsed into a century of civil war after the Ōnin War. Then three warlords, Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu, reunified it, using Portuguese-style guns. Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea (1592-98) drained Ming China. Weakened by fiscal crisis, famine and rebellion, the Ming fell in 1644 to rebels and then to the Manchus, who founded the Qing. Under the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors, the Qing became the largest and richest state in the world. In 1793 it was confident enough to tell Britain that it needed nothing from it.

chapters.d: Hangul in Korea; disaster at Tumu.
A century of civil war ends in unification.
The Tokugawa shogunate and the Qing conquest.
China at its largest and most confident.

reading: Timothy Brook, The Troubled Empire: China in the Yuan and Ming Dynasties (2010)
William T. Rowe, China's Last Empire: The Great Qing (2009)
Mary Elizabeth Berry, Hideyoshi (1982)
Kenneth Swope, A Dragon's Head and a Serpent's Tail: Ming China and the First Great East Asian War (2009)

arcs.title: The Iberian Conquest of the Americas
arcs.summary: In little more than a lifetime, Spain and Portugal claimed two continents. Columbus's voyage of 1492 opened the way, and a 1494 treaty divided the newly found lands between the two Iberian crowns. Small bands of conquistadors toppled the Aztec and Inca empires with the help of thousands of Indigenous allies and, above all, smallpox and other European diseases. Within a century, the Indigenous population of the Americas fell by perhaps 80-90%, mostly from disease. American silver from Potosí and Mexico then flowed across the Atlantic and the Pacific, funding Spain's wars and much of China's money supply. It was the first truly global economy.

chapters.d: Columbus, Tordesillas and Brazil.
Mexico and Peru conquered.
Mines, galleons and the first global economy.

reading: Matthew Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003)
Camilla Townsend, Fifth Sun: A New History of the Aztecs (2019)
Alfred Crosby, The Columbian Exchange (1972)
Dennis Flynn & Arturo Giráldez, 'Born with a Silver Spoon' (Journal of World History, 1995)

arcs.title: Sea Routes to Asia and the First Global Trade
arcs.summary: Portuguese sailors rounded Africa in 1488 and reached India ten years later. They aimed to cut out the Venetian and Muslim middlemen who had long controlled the spice trade. Armed trading posts at Goa and Malacca gave Portugal control of key sea lanes. Then the Dutch and English arrived with joint-stock companies, the ancestors of the modern corporation. Europeans brought guns, Christianity and American silver to Asia. Japan adopted the guns, then expelled the missionaries. By 1757 one company, the English East India Company, had its own army and was conquering Bengal.

chapters.d: Portugal opens the sea route.
Europeans reach East Asia.
English and Dutch companies take over.

reading: Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Portuguese Empire in Asia, 1500-1700 (2nd ed., 2012)
Om Prakash, European Commercial Enterprise in Pre-Colonial India (1998)
K. N. Chaudhuri, Trade and Civilisation in the Indian Ocean (1985)

arcs.title: The Swahili Coast and the Indian Ocean
arcs.summary: For centuries, the Swahili city-states of East Africa, such as Kilwa, Mombasa and Malindi, traded gold, ivory and enslaved people across the Indian Ocean to Arabia, India and beyond. The Portuguese arrived with cannon after 1498, sacking Kilwa and later seizing Mombasa. Ethiopia, Africa's ancient Christian kingdom, nearly fell to the Adal Sultanate until Portuguese musketeers helped save it. In 1698 Omani Arabs drove the Portuguese out of Mombasa. By 1840 Oman's sultan ruled from Zanzibar, whose clove plantations and caravan routes, worked by enslaved people, reached deep into the continent. That set the stage for the Scramble for Africa.

chapters.d: Portugal and Adal upend the region.
Oman replaces Portugal; Zanzibar's plantation and caravan economy grows.
Britain forces the slave market closed.

reading: Abdul Sheriff, Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar (1987)
Mark Horton & John Middleton, The Swahili (2000)
Richard Pankhurst, The Ethiopians: A History (1998)

arcs.title: Empires and Kingdoms of West and Central Africa
arcs.summary: Songhai, centred on the Niger bend and the scholarly city of Timbuktu, was one of the largest states in African history until a Moroccan army with firearms shattered it in 1591. As trade shifted from the Sahara to the Atlantic coast, the forest kingdoms grew rich on gold and on selling captives to European ships. Kongo's Christian king protested the trade; Asante built an empire partly on it. Around 1800, Islamic reform movements created the Sokoto Caliphate, which became the largest state in West Africa by the eve of colonial conquest.

chapters.d: An empire of the Sahel and its fall.
Gold, captives and new states.

reading: John Thornton, Africa and Africans in the Making of the Atlantic World, 1400-1800 (2nd ed., 1998)
John Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire (1999)
Paul Lovejoy, Transformations in Slavery (3rd ed., 2011)
Toby Green, A Fistful of Shells (2019)

arcs.title: The Atlantic Slave Trade and Its Abolition
arcs.summary: Over four centuries, about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships bound for the Americas; about 1.8 million died during the crossing. The trade began with Portuguese raids and purchases on Africa's coast. It grew with sugar in Brazil and the Caribbean, then tobacco, rice and cotton, and made possible the plantation economies of the Americas and much of Europe's commercial wealth. Enslaved people never stopped resisting. The revolution in Haiti created the first state founded by formerly enslaved people. Abolitionists, revolts and changing economics ended Britain's slave trade in 1807, but slavery itself lasted in the United States until 1865 and in Brazil until 1888.

chapters.d: Portugal opens the trade.
Sugar, tobacco and gold drive the trade to its peak.
Revolt, abolition and the long end of slavery.

reading: David Eltis & David Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010); data at slavevoyages.org
Herbert Klein, The Atlantic Slave Trade (2nd ed., 2010)
Laurent Dubois, Avengers of the New World: The Story of the Haitian Revolution (2004)
Christopher Leslie Brown, Moral Capital: Foundations of British Abolitionism (2006)

arcs.title: Colonial North America and the American Revolution
arcs.summary: England's American colonies began as struggling ventures in Virginia and New England. Tobacco, and then the forced labour of enslaved Africans, made the Chesapeake rich; Puritan migrants shaped New England. Britain's victory over France in the Seven Years' War in 1763 removed the French threat but left Britain deep in debt. When Parliament taxed the colonies, colonists who had governed themselves for generations rebelled. With French help they won independence, and in 1787 wrote a constitution that still governs the United States.

chapters.d: Explorers, settlers and wars with Native nations.
War with France, then taxes and protest.
Independence and a new constitution.

reading: Alan Taylor, American Colonies (2001) and American Revolutions (2016)
Gordon S. Wood, The Radicalism of the American Revolution (1991)
Bernard Bailyn, The Ideological Origins of the American Revolution (1967)
Fred Anderson, Crucible of War (2000)

arcs.title: The Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment
arcs.summary: In two and a half centuries, European thinkers moved from questioning whether the Earth was the centre of the universe to questioning whether kings ruled by divine right. Copernicus, Galileo and Newton showed that nature followed mathematical laws that anyone could test. Hobbes and Locke asked why people should obey governments at all. Voltaire, Rousseau and Adam Smith applied reason to religion, politics and trade. Printed and debated in coffeehouses and salons, these ideas helped inspire the American and French revolutions and the modern idea of progress.

chapters.d: The Earth moves; observation challenges authority.

chapters.t: Laws of nature and of government
chapters.d: Newton, Hobbes and Locke.
Ideas that inspired revolutions.

reading: Steven Shapin, The Scientific Revolution (1996)
Anthony Pagden, The Enlightenment: And Why It Still Matters (2013)
Ritchie Robertson, The Enlightenment: The Pursuit of Happiness, 1680-1790 (2020)

arcs.title: England's Centuries of Revolution
arcs.summary: Defeat in the Hundred Years' War was followed by thirty years of civil war in England, the Wars of the Roses, until Henry Tudor took the crown in 1485. His son Henry VIII broke with Rome. The following century brought civil war, the execution of a king, a republic, a military dictatorship, a restoration and finally a second, bloodless revolution. The result was unusual in Europe: a monarch bound by Parliament and law, and a state that could borrow cheaply through the new Bank of England. That combination helped Britain outspend and outfight larger rivals for the next two centuries.

chapters.t: From French war to Tudor peace
chapters.d: Defeat abroad, civil war at home.
Henry VIII and Elizabeth I.
Civil war and the republic.
Glorious Revolution, bank and union.

reading: Steve Pincus, 1688: The First Modern Revolution (2009)
Michael Braddick, God's Fury, England's Fire (2008)
Susan Brigden, New Worlds, Lost Worlds: The Rule of the Tudors (2000)
John Brewer, The Sinews of Power (1989)

arcs.title: The Wars for Europe and Empire, 1701-1772
arcs.summary: In the 1700s Europe's wars became world wars. Britain, France, Austria, Prussia and Russia fought over successions and the balance of power, and also over colonies and trade from India to the Ohio Valley. The Seven Years' War (1756-63), sometimes called the first true world war, left Britain dominant at sea, in North America and in India, but deep in debt. That debt would help spark the American Revolution. Prussia and Russia emerged as great powers, and together with Austria they carved up Poland.

chapters.d: Spain, Sweden and the rise of Russia.
Prussia rises; Britain wins a global war.
The great powers divide Poland.

reading: Brendan Simms, Three Victories and a Defeat: The Rise and Fall of the First British Empire (2007)
Tim Blanning, Frederick the Great (2015)
Fred Anderson, Crucible of War (2000)
Daniel Baugh, The Global Seven Years War (2011)

arcs.title: The French Revolution and Napoleon
arcs.summary: France's monarchy was nearly bankrupt, partly from paying for wars including its support of the American Revolution. In 1789 Louis XVI called the Estates-General to raise taxes and lost control. Revolutionaries abolished noble privileges, declared the Rights of Man, executed the king and, under threat of foreign invasion, launched the Terror. Napoleon Bonaparte, a general who rose in the revolutionary wars, seized power in 1799 and crowned himself emperor in 1804. His armies spread the Revolution's legal reforms across Europe and ended the Holy Roman Empire. His seizure of Spain set off independence movements across Latin America. After defeat in Russia and finally at Waterloo, the Congress of Vienna redrew Europe's map to keep the peace.

chapters.d: From the Estates-General to the Terror.
Consul, emperor and master of Europe.
Russia, Leipzig and Waterloo.

reading: William Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (3rd ed., 2018)
Peter McPhee, Liberty or Death: The French Revolution (2016)
Andrew Roberts, Napoleon: A Life (2014)
David Bell, The First Total War (2007)

arcs.title: Nationalism and the Making of New Nations, 1815-1878
arcs.summary: The Congress of Vienna tried to restore the old monarchies after Napoleon. But the Revolution had spread two explosive ideas: that sovereignty belongs to the people, and that each nation should have its own state. Greeks and Belgians won independence. In 1848 revolutions swept across much of Europe and mostly failed, but within a generation conservative statesmen harnessed nationalism instead of fighting it. Cavour and Garibaldi unified Italy; Bismarck unified Germany through three short wars. Multinational empires such as Austria, Russia and the Ottomans struggled to adapt.

chapters.d: Vienna's order is challenged.
Revolution, failure and the Crimean War.
Italy and Germany are made.

reading: Eric Hobsbawm, The Age of Revolution, 1789-1848 (1962) and The Age of Capital, 1848-1875 (1975)
Christopher Clark, Revolutionary Spring: Europe Aflame, 1848-1849 (2023)
Jonathan Sperber, The European Revolutions, 1848-1851 (2nd ed., 2005)
Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983)

arcs.title: Latin American Independence
arcs.summary: Spain's American empire broke apart in less than twenty years. Creole elites, the American-born descendants of Spaniards, resented rule by officials from Spain. But they also feared revolts from below, like Túpac Amaru II's Andean uprising of 1780 and the slave revolution in Haiti. When Napoleon seized Spain's throne in 1808, the empire was left without a legitimate king, and juntas from Buenos Aires to Caracas began governing themselves. Armies led by Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín won the wars. Brazil took a different path and became an independent empire under a Portuguese prince. Independence left the new nations with powerful armies, weak institutions and the old social hierarchy largely intact.

chapters.d: Andean revolt and Haitian revolution.
Napoleon's invasion of Iberia sets off self-rule.
Bolívar, San Martín and new nations.

reading: John Lynch, The Spanish American Revolutions, 1808-1826 (2nd ed., 1986)
Jaime Rodríguez O., The Independence of Spanish America (1998)
Marie Arana, Bolívar: American Liberator (2013)

arcs.title: Manifest Destiny: The United States Expands West
arcs.summary: In less than a century the United States grew from the Atlantic seaboard to the Pacific, and then beyond. It bought Louisiana from Napoleon, pushed Spain out of Florida, annexed Texas and took California and the Southwest in a war with Mexico. Canals and railroads pulled settlers west. For Native nations it was a catastrophe. Forced removals like the Trail of Tears, wars on the Plains and the reservation system reduced their lands from most of the continent to scattered fragments. By 1898, with the frontier declared closed, the US was taking overseas colonies too.

chapters.d: Louisiana, Florida and the War of 1812.
The Trail of Tears and the war with Mexico.
Railroads, Plains wars and empire overseas.

reading: Daniel Walker Howe, What Hath God Wrought: The Transformation of America, 1815-1848 (2007)
Richard White, 'It's Your Misfortune and None of My Own' (1991)
Pekka Hämäläinen, Lakota America (2019)
Claudio Saunt, Unworthy Republic: The Dispossession of Native Americans (2020)

arcs.title: Slavery, Civil War and Reconstruction
arcs.summary: The cotton gin made slavery more profitable than ever. By 1860 nearly four million people were enslaved in the United States. Each new western territory reopened the question of whether slavery could spread, and the compromises of 1820 and 1850 only postponed the conflict. When Abraham Lincoln, whose party opposed slavery's expansion, won the 1860 election, eleven Southern states seceded. The war that followed killed an estimated 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers and ended slavery. During Reconstruction, Black men voted and held office. Then white Southern governments imposed Jim Crow segregation, which lasted into the 1960s.

chapters.d: Slavery expands west.
Compromise fails.
Civil War and emancipation.
Rights won, then taken away.

reading: James McPherson, Battle Cry of Freedom (1988)
Eric Foner, Reconstruction: America's Unfinished Revolution (1988) and The Second Founding (2019)
David Potter, The Impending Crisis, 1848-1861 (1976)
Walter Johnson, River of Dark Dreams (2013)

arcs.title: Money, Machines and the Industrial Revolution
arcs.summary: Britain industrialised first. Historians still debate why, but cheap coal, high wages that made labour-saving machines pay off (Robert Allen's argument), a culture of practical experiment (Joel Mokyr's), a large empire and trade network, and a financial system able to fund big projects all played a part. Steam engines and railways transformed production and travel. By 1900 Germany and the US had overtaken Britain in steel. Industry made the West vastly richer than the rest of the world, which historians call the 'Great Divergence'. Early factory life was brutal, however, and inspired Marx's Communist Manifesto and the labour movements that won shorter hours, unions and eventually the welfare state.

chapters.d: Banks, bubbles and public debt.
Engines, railways and canals.
Global markets, socialism and reform.

reading: Robert C. Allen, The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective (2009)
Joel Mokyr, The Enlightened Economy (2009)
Kenneth Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000)
Jürgen Osterhammel, The Transformation of the World (2014)

arcs.title: China's 'Century of Humiliation'
arcs.summary: In 1793 the Qing emperor told Britain that China needed nothing from it. Fifty years later, British gunboats forced China to accept the opium trade and hand over Hong Kong. What followed is remembered in China as the 'century of humiliation'. The Taiping Rebellion became the deadliest civil war of the 19th century, with perhaps 20-30 million dead. More unequal treaties followed, then defeat by Japan in 1895 and a scramble by foreign powers for ports and railways. The anti-foreign Boxer uprising of 1900 ended with eight foreign armies in Beijing. The Qing dynasty fell in 1911, and after 1916 China split among rival warlords. Nationalists and Communists fought each other and Japan, which seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded China in 1937. The Communists won in 1949. Hong Kong's return in 1997 closed the circle.

chapters.d: The Opium Wars and the Taiping.
Defeat by Japan, foreign concessions and the Boxers.
The Qing falls; Japan invades; the Communists win.
Hong Kong returns.

reading: Jonathan Spence, The Search for Modern China (3rd ed., 2013)
Stephen Platt, Imperial Twilight (2018) and Autumn in the Heavenly Kingdom (2012)
Julia Lovell, The Opium War (2011)
Rana Mitter, Forgotten Ally: China's World War II, 1937-1945 (2013)

arcs.title: Russia: From Tsars to Soviets
arcs.summary: Peter the Great pushed Russia toward Europe, building St Petersburg and a modern army that defeated Sweden. Catherine the Great extended the empire to the Black Sea and swallowed much of Poland. Russia helped defeat Napoleon, but its economy, built on serfdom, fell behind. Defeat in the Crimean War forced the emancipation of the serfs in 1861. Defeat by Japan in 1905 sparked a revolution that the tsar survived. World War I, with its millions of Russian casualties, brought the one he did not. Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917 and won a brutal civil war. Stalin then built a totalitarian state that industrialised at an enormous human cost.

chapters.d: Peter and Catherine.
Napoleon, Crimea and the serfs.
1905, 1917 and the Soviet Union.
Terror and industrialisation.

reading: Orlando Figes, A People's Tragedy: The Russian Revolution, 1891-1924 (1996)
Geoffrey Hosking, Russia: People and Empire, 1552-1917 (1997)
Stephen Kotkin, Stalin, vol. 1: Paradoxes of Power (2014)
Lindsey Hughes, Russia in the Age of Peter the Great (1998)

arcs.title: India: From the East India Company to Independence
arcs.summary: The English East India Company began as a trading venture in 1600. As the Mughal Empire broke up after 1707, the Company used its private army to win Bengal at Plassey in 1757, and by the 1850s it ruled most of India. After the great rebellion of 1857, the British crown took over directly. Western-educated Indians founded the Indian National Congress in 1885; under Gandhi it became a mass movement of nonviolent civil disobedience. Weakened by World War II, Britain left in 1947 and partitioned the subcontinent into India and Pakistan. The violence killed somewhere between a few hundred thousand and two million people and uprooted some 15 million.

chapters.d: From trading post to territorial power.
Rebellion, crown rule and the first nationalists.
Gandhi, the Salt March and partition.

reading: William Dalrymple, The Anarchy: The Relentless Rise of the East India Company (2019)
Barbara & Thomas Metcalf, A Concise History of Modern India (3rd ed., 2012)
Yasmin Khan, The Great Partition (2007)
Ramachandra Guha, Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World (2018)

arcs.title: South Africa: From the Cape to the End of Apartheid
arcs.summary: The Dutch East India Company founded Cape Town in 1652 as a supply station. Its settlers, the Boers or Afrikaners, pushed inland against the Khoikhoi and Xhosa. Britain took the Cape in 1795 and kept it from 1806. When it abolished slavery, thousands of Boers trekked north to found their own republics, clashing with African kingdoms like the Zulu state built by Shaka. The discovery of diamonds (1867) and gold (1886) drew Britain inland. It conquered the Zulu in 1879 and the Boer republics in 1899-1902. The Union of South Africa (1910) gave political power to whites only. From 1948 the National Party built apartheid. Decades of resistance, international sanctions and negotiation ended it with Nelson Mandela's election in 1994.

chapters.d: Company settlement, then British rule.
Boer republics, the Zulu and the gold wars.
Segregation, resistance and democracy.

reading: Leonard Thompson, A History of South Africa (4th ed., 2014)
Hermann Giliomee, The Afrikaners: Biography of a People (2003)
Thomas Pakenham, The Boer War (1979)
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (1994)

arcs.title: Mexico from Independence to NAFTA
arcs.summary: Independent Mexico spent its first half-century fighting itself and foreign invaders. It lost Texas, then half its territory to the United States in 1848. Then France invaded and installed the Austrian archduke Maximilian as emperor. Benito Juárez's liberals won and executed him. Porfirio Díaz then imposed order and built railways with foreign investment for 35 years, while land became concentrated in a few hands. The Revolution of 1910-20 killed perhaps a million people and produced a constitution promising land reform. In 1938 President Cárdenas nationalised the foreign oil companies. One party ruled until 2000. NAFTA tied Mexico's economy to the US in 1994, and on the day it took effect the Zapatistas rose in Chiapas.

chapters.d: Texas and the war with the US.
Juárez against the French.
Order, upheaval and oil.
Stability and its limits.

reading: Enrique Krauze, Mexico: Biography of Power (1997)
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution (2 vols., 1986)
Brian Hamnett, A Concise History of Mexico (3rd ed., 2019)

arcs.title: The Road to World War I and the Peace That Failed
arcs.summary: Germany's unification in 1871 created a powerful new state in the heart of Europe and left France bitter over losing Alsace-Lorraine. Bismarck's alliances kept the peace. After he left office, however, Germany let its treaty with Russia lapse, Russia allied with France, and Germany's naval build-up pushed Britain toward France and Russia. In June 1914 a Bosnian Serb assassinated the heir to Austria-Hungary's throne in Sarajevo, and the alliance system turned a Balkan crisis into a world war. About nine million soldiers died, along with millions of civilians. The war destroyed four empires: German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman. The peace treaties redrew the maps of Europe and the Middle East and left grievances that fed the next war.

chapters.d: A new empire and a web of alliances.
Alliances harden and the Balkans burn.
Total war and revolution.
Versailles and the new map.

reading: Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914 (2012)
Margaret MacMillan, The War That Ended Peace (2013) and Paris 1919 (2001)
Hew Strachan, The First World War (2003)
Robert Gerwarth, The Vanquished (2016)

arcs.title: Between the Wars: Depression and Dictators
arcs.summary: The post-war world was unstable from the start. New democracies were fragile, Italy and Germany felt cheated by the peace, and the United States stayed out of the League of Nations. Mussolini's Fascists took power in 1922. The Wall Street crash of 1929 became a worldwide depression as banks failed and trade collapsed. Unemployment reached about a quarter of workers in the US and around 30% in Germany. Desperate voters turned to radical answers: Hitler in Germany, militarists in Japan and strongmen like Vargas in Brazil. In the US, the answer was Roosevelt's New Deal, which greatly expanded the role of democratic government. Aggression by Japan, Italy and Germany went largely unpunished by a weak League of Nations.

chapters.d: Mussolini and Stalin take power.
Crash, collapse and radical answers.
Ethiopia, Spain and the road to war.

reading: Zara Steiner, The Lights That Failed: European International History, 1919-1933 (2005)
Barry Eichengreen, Golden Fetters: The Gold Standard and the Great Depression (1992)
David Kennedy, Freedom from Fear (1999)
Charles Kindleberger, The World in Depression, 1929-1939 (1973)

arcs.title: Japan's Empire and the Pacific War
arcs.summary: After annexing Korea in 1910 and taking Germany's Pacific islands and its rights in China's Shandong province in World War I, Japan was Asia's leading power. Its army increasingly acted on its own. In 1931 officers staged an explosion as a pretext for seizing Manchuria. In 1937 a clash near Beijing became full-scale war with China, including the Nanjing Massacre. In 1941 the US cut off oil exports to stop Japan's advance into Southeast Asia. Japan responded by attacking Pearl Harbor and European colonies across Asia at once. The war ended in August 1945 with Japan's cities burned, Hiroshima and Nagasaki destroyed by atomic bombs, and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria.

chapters.d: Korea, Shandong and Manchuria.
Full-scale war and atrocity.
Pearl Harbor to Hiroshima.

reading: S. C. M. Paine, The Wars for Asia, 1911-1949 (2012)
Rana Mitter, Forgotten Ally (2013)
John Dower, Embracing Defeat (1999)
Richard B. Frank, Downfall (1999)

arcs.title: The Cold War
arcs.summary: The wartime alliance between the US and the USSR collapsed within two years of victory. Europe split along an 'Iron Curtain', and the US committed itself to 'containing' communism with aid (the Marshall Plan) and alliances (NATO). Nuclear weapons made direct war between the superpowers suicidal. Instead the Cold War was fought through arms and space races, propaganda and 'hot' proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Africa and Latin America. The closest call came over Cuba in 1962. In the 1980s a stagnant Soviet economy, the costly war in Afghanistan and Gorbachev's reforms unravelled the Soviet bloc. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989, and the USSR dissolved in 1991.

chapters.d: From allies to enemies.
Revolts, rockets and Cuba.
Arms control, Helsinki and a second Cold War.
Gorbachev, 1989 and the Soviet collapse.

reading: John Lewis Gaddis, The Cold War: A New History (2005)
Odd Arne Westad, The Global Cold War (2005) and The Cold War: A World History (2017)
Vladislav Zubok, A Failed Empire (2007)
Mary Elise Sarotte, 1989: The Struggle to Create Post-Cold War Europe (2009)

arcs.title: Colonial Asia and Its Liberation
arcs.summary: By 1900 almost all of South and Southeast Asia was ruled by Britain, France, the Netherlands or the United States. Japan's conquests in 1941-42 shattered the myth of European invincibility. Afterwards nationalists from India to Indonesia demanded independence. Some empires left by negotiation, like the US in the Philippines (1946) and Britain in India (1947); others fought. France's war in Vietnam ended at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, but the country was split between a communist North and a Western-backed South. That drew the US into a war that killed between one and three million Vietnamese, by differing estimates, and spread into Cambodia and Laos. It ended with communist victory in 1975, followed by the Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia.

chapters.d: Britain, France and the US divide the region.
Japan's conquest and the end of European rule.
From Dien Bien Phu to the fall of Saigon.
Hong Kong returns.

reading: Christopher Bayly & Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004) and Forgotten Wars (2007)
Fredrik Logevall, Embers of War (2012)
Christopher Goscha, Vietnam: A New History (2016)
Ben Kiernan, The Pol Pot Regime (3rd ed., 2008)

arcs.title: African Independence
arcs.summary: World War II weakened Europe's empires and strengthened Africans' case for freedom: more than a million African soldiers had served in the Allied armies. Ghana led the way in 1957, and in 1960 seventeen African countries became independent. Where white settlers were numerous, as in Kenya, Algeria, Rhodesia and the Portuguese colonies, independence came only after bitter wars. The new states inherited borders drawn in Europe and economies built to export raw materials. They also faced superpowers eager to intervene, as the murder of Congo's first prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, showed.

chapters.d: Conquest, then the first cracks in empire.
Mau Mau, Algeria, Suez and Ghana.
Congo, settler wars and the last colonies.

reading: Frederick Cooper, Africa Since 1940: The Past of the Present (2nd ed., 2019)
Martin Meredith, The Fate of Africa (2005)
Caroline Elkins, Imperial Reckoning (2005)
Alistair Horne, A Savage War of Peace: Algeria 1954-1962 (1977)

arcs.title: The Modern Middle East
arcs.summary: In the 1700s and 1800s a Wahhabi revival in Arabia and Muhammad Ali's reforms in Egypt began to reshape the region, and in 1908 oil was found in Persia. When the Ottoman Empire collapsed, Britain and France divided its Arab provinces into mandates, drawing borders that often ignored local identities. Britain's 1917 Balfour Declaration also promised a Jewish 'national home' in Palestine. Oil, found in Iran in 1908 and Saudi Arabia in 1938, made the region strategically vital. Israel's founding in 1948 and the flight or expulsion of some 700,000 Palestinians began a conflict that produced wars in 1956, 1967 and 1973 and continues today. Iran's 1979 revolution created an Islamic republic hostile to the US. Iraq's Saddam Hussein fought Iran and then invaded Kuwait. After 2001, US wars and the Arab Spring of 2011 toppled regimes, but also opened the way to civil wars and the rise of ISIS.

chapters.d: Saudi-Wahhabi pact, Muhammad Ali, and the first oil strike.
Ottoman collapse and Israel's founding.
Suez, 1967 and 1973.

chapters.t: Revolution and war in the Gulf
chapters.d: Iran, Iraq and Kuwait.
Iraq, the Arab Spring, ISIS and Gaza.

reading: Eugene Rogan, The Arabs: A History (3rd ed., 2018)
James Gelvin, The Modern Middle East: A History (5th ed., 2020)
Charles D. Smith, Palestine and the Arab-Israeli Conflict (10th ed., 2020)
Ervand Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2nd ed., 2018)

arcs.title: China Since 1949
arcs.summary: Mao Zedong's Communists unified China in 1949 and launched campaigns to remake it: land reform, collectivisation and the Great Leap Forward, whose famine killed tens of millions (estimates range from about 15 to 45 million). The Cultural Revolution followed. After Mao's death in 1976, Deng Xiaoping opened the economy to markets and foreign investment while keeping the party's monopoly on power, as the 1989 crackdown in Tiananmen Square made clear. Growth averaged about 10% a year for three decades and lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Joining the WTO in 2001 made China the world's workshop. Under Xi Jinping, from 2012, the party tightened control at home and asserted China's power abroad.

chapters.d: Campaigns, famine and the Cultural Revolution.
Deng's markets and Tiananmen.
The WTO and Xi Jinping.

reading: Frank Dikötter, Mao's Great Famine (2010)
Roderick MacFarquhar & Michael Schoenhals, Mao's Last Revolution (2006)
Ezra Vogel, Deng Xiaoping and the Transformation of China (2011)
Elizabeth Economy, The Third Revolution: Xi Jinping and the New Chinese State (2018)

arcs.title: Civil Rights and Democracy in America
arcs.summary: The Declaration of Independence promised that 'all men are created equal'. Much of American history is a struggle over who that includes. Women organised at Seneca Falls in 1848 and won the national vote in 1920. The Civil War amendments promised Black Americans freedom, citizenship and the vote. After Reconstruction, however, Jim Crow laws, approved by the Supreme Court in Plessy v. Ferguson, imposed segregation and stripped most Black Southerners of the vote. The NAACP's legal campaign won Brown v. Board of Education in 1954. Boycotts, sit-ins and marches led by Martin Luther King Jr. and thousands of others won the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

chapters.d: Seneca Falls and the Civil War amendments.

chapters.t: Jim Crow and the vote for women
chapters.d: Segregation upheld; suffrage won.
From Brown to the Voting Rights Act.

reading: Eric Foner, The Story of American Freedom (1998)
Taylor Branch, Parting the Waters: America in the King Years, 1954-63 (1988)
Michael Klarman, From Jim Crow to Civil Rights (2004)
Ellen Carol DuBois, Suffrage: Women's Long Battle for the Vote (2020)

arcs.title: The United States and Latin America
arcs.summary: In 1823 the Monroe Doctrine warned Europe away from the Americas. By 1900 the United States was the hemisphere's dominant power. It took Puerto Rico and controlled Cuba after 1898, backed Panama's split from Colombia so it could build a canal, and under the Roosevelt Corollary sent troops into Caribbean and Central American countries many times. In the Cold War, Washington backed coups against governments it saw as communist or hostile, such as Guatemala's in 1954 and Chile's in 1973, and tried to overthrow Castro's Cuba. Many Latin Americans see this history as imperialism; US leaders presented it as defending the hemisphere's security.

chapters.d: From Monroe to the war with Spain.
Canals, Marines and dollar diplomacy.
Coups, Cuba and the Contras.

reading: Lars Schoultz, Beneath the United States: A History of U.S. Policy toward Latin America (1998)
Greg Grandin, Empire's Workshop (2006)
Hal Brands, Latin America's Cold War (2010)
Tanya Harmer, Allende's Chile and the Inter-American Cold War (2011)

arcs.title: Latin America: Booms, Strongmen and Democracy
arcs.summary: Independent Latin America grew by exporting coffee, beef, copper and oil, and booms and busts in commodity prices repeatedly shaped its politics. Populist leaders like Getúlio Vargas in Brazil and Juan Perón in Argentina built mass followings among urban workers in the 1930s-50s. In the Cold War, fear of revolution brought military dictatorships to Brazil, Chile, Argentina and other countries. They killed or 'disappeared' tens of thousands of people. Democracy returned in the 1980s, but debt crises and deep inequality fuelled swings between market reformers and left-wing leaders, from Chávez to Lula, and more recently to outsiders like Argentina's Javier Milei.

chapters.d: War, abolition and the coffee republics.
Vargas and Perón.
Generals in power.
Booms, defaults and outsiders.

reading: Thomas Skidmore, Peter Smith & James Green, Modern Latin America (9th ed., 2018)
Edwin Williamson, The Penguin History of Latin America (2nd ed., 2009)
Michael Reid, Forgotten Continent (2nd ed., 2017)

arcs.title: The American Century at Home
arcs.summary: By 1900 the United States was the world's largest industrial economy. Progressive reformers, the New Deal and the post-war boom built a strong federal government and a vast middle class. Vietnam, Watergate and the inflation of the 1970s eroded trust in Washington and helped elect Ronald Reagan, who promised to shrink government. Globalisation and technology made the economy more productive but more unequal. Since the 2008 financial crisis, by most political-science measures, the two parties have been further apart than at any time since the late 19th century. Disputes over the 2020 election culminated in the January 6 attack on the Capitol, and Donald Trump won a second, non-consecutive term in 2024.

chapters.d: Reform, cars and planes.
Kennedy, Nixon and the 1970s.

chapters.t: The Reagan era and the new economy
chapters.d: Markets, tech and terror.
Crisis, pandemic and polarisation.

reading: James Patterson, Grand Expectations (1996) and Restless Giant (2005)
Robert Gordon, The Rise and Fall of American Growth (2016)
Gary Gerstle, The Rise and Fall of the Neoliberal Order (2022)
Jill Lepore, These Truths: A History of the United States (2018)

arcs.title: Europe United, and Divided
arcs.summary: After two world wars, Western European leaders bound their economies together so that war between them would become, in Robert Schuman's words, 'not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible'. The Coal and Steel Community of 1951 grew into the European Economic Community in 1957 and the European Union in 1992, with a single currency from 1999 (notes and coins from 2002). After the Cold War the EU expanded into Eastern Europe. But the euro's design left weaker economies exposed in the debt crisis of 2010, the refugee crisis of 2015 divided members, and in 2016 British voters chose to leave.

chapters.d: Marshall aid and the Common Market.
Maastricht, the euro and the East.
Debt, migration and Brexit.

reading: Tony Judt, Postwar: A History of Europe Since 1945 (2005)
Desmond Dinan, Europe Recast: A History of European Union (2nd ed., 2014)
Luuk van Middelaar, The Passage to Europe (2013)

arcs.title: Russia and Its Neighbours after the Soviet Union
arcs.summary: The Soviet Union's collapse in 1991 created fifteen independent states and left Russia in economic free fall through the 1990s. In Yugoslavia, the end of communism unleashed nationalist wars and the genocide at Srebrenica. NATO and the EU expanded east. Countries that had lived under Soviet domination welcomed it; Moscow saw it as encroachment. Under Vladimir Putin, Russia rebuilt central power, fought Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and in 2022 launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the largest war in Europe since 1945.

chapters.d: Gorbachev, the end of the USSR and Yugoslavia's wars.
Expansion of the West, and Russia's wars.

reading: Serhii Plokhy, The Last Empire (2014) and The Russo-Ukrainian War (2023)
Mary Elise Sarotte, Not One Inch (2021)
Misha Glenny, The Fall of Yugoslavia (3rd ed., 1996)

arcs.title: Globalisation and Its Crises
arcs.summary: When Nixon ended the dollar's link to gold in 1971, the post-war system of fixed exchange rates collapsed, and money began to move freely around the world. Oil shocks and inflation in the 1970s led to a turn toward markets, deregulation and free trade. China's opening, NAFTA, the WTO and the internet created a global economy of long supply chains. It lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty but cost jobs in old industrial regions. Free-flowing capital also brought crises: Latin American debt in 1982, Asia in 1997, Argentina in 2001 and the global financial crisis of 2008. The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 exposed how fragile global supply chains had become.

chapters.d: Gold, oil and debt.
NAFTA, the WTO and the internet.
2008, the euro crisis and COVID.

reading: Barry Eichengreen, Globalizing Capital (3rd ed., 2019)
Adam Tooze, Crashed (2018) and Shutdown (2021)
Dani Rodrik, The Globalization Paradox (2011)

arcs.title: Afghanistan, 9/11 and the War on Terror
arcs.summary: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 drew in thousands of foreign Muslim volunteers, while the US, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan armed the Afghan resistance. One of the volunteers was a Saudi, Osama bin Laden. His al-Qaeda turned against the US after American troops were stationed in Saudi Arabia during the 1991 Gulf War. On September 11, 2001, al-Qaeda attacks killed nearly 3,000 people in the US. The US overthrew the Taliban in Afghanistan, then invaded Iraq in 2003 on claims about weapons of mass destruction that proved false. The wars cost hundreds of thousands of lives. ISIS grew out of Iraq's insurgency, and after twenty years the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

chapters.d: The Afghan jihad and the Gulf War.
Afghanistan and Iraq.
Bin Laden, ISIS and the Taliban's return.

reading: Steve Coll, Ghost Wars (2004) and Directorate S (2018)
Lawrence Wright, The Looming Tower (2006)
Carter Malkasian, The American War in Afghanistan (2021)

arcs.title: Africa Since Independence
arcs.summary: Independence brought high hopes and real gains in schooling and health. But many new states struggled with borders that grouped rival communities, economies dependent on a few exports, and Cold War meddling. Military coups became common: Africa saw more than 200 coup attempts after 1950, about half of them successful. Ethnic politics and state collapse produced catastrophes such as the Biafran war, the Rwandan genocide of 1994 and the Congo wars, among the deadliest conflicts since World War II. Since 2000 many African economies have grown fast and democracy has spread. Coups in the Sahel and wars in Sudan and Ethiopia show how fragile those gains can be.

chapters.d: Biafra, Amin and famine.
Rwanda, Congo and the African Union.
Arab Spring, Ebola, Tigray and the Sahel.

reading: Frederick Cooper, Africa Since 1940 (2nd ed., 2019)
Martin Meredith, The Fate of Africa (2005)
Jason Stearns, Dancing in the Glory of Monsters (2011)
Alison Des Forges, Leave None to Tell the Story: Genocide in Rwanda (1999)

arcs.title: Science and Technology That Remade the World
arcs.summary: Some of history's biggest turning points came from workshops and laboratories. The printing press spread knowledge, and the Scientific Revolution established that nature follows laws that can be tested. Steam power and railways created the industrial world, and Darwin explained the diversity of life through natural selection. In the 20th century science became a matter of state power. The discovery of nuclear fission led to the atomic bomb, rockets built to carry nuclear warheads took humans to the Moon, and a US military network grew into the internet. Every breakthrough also brought new risks, as Chernobyl and the COVID-19 pandemic showed.

chapters.d: Gutenberg to Newton.
Engines, railways and Darwin.
Flight, the bomb, space and the internet.

reading: David Wootton, The Invention of Science (2015)
Janet Browne, Darwin's Origin of Species: A Biography (2006)
Richard Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)
Walter Isaacson, The Innovators (2014)

arcs.title: Oceania: Voyagers, Convicts and New Nations
arcs.summary: Polynesian, Melanesian and Micronesian peoples had settled the Pacific's islands, and Aboriginal Australians the continent, long before Europeans arrived. Dutch ships charted Australia's coasts in the 1600s, but it was James Cook's voyages and American independence, which closed America to British convicts, that led to the First Fleet in 1788. British colonisation brought frontier wars, epidemics and dispossession; in New Zealand, the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840 was followed by wars over land. Gold rushes, federation and the ANZAC landing at Gallipoli shaped new national identities, often defined by the White Australia policy. The Pacific War brought fighting to New Guinea and the Solomons, and nuclear testing followed. Since the 1960s, Pacific island nations have won independence, and Australia and New Zealand have begun to reckon with their colonial past.

chapters.d: Dutch and British navigators reach Australia and New Zealand.
Convicts, gold, treaties and wars over land.

chapters.t: New nations in a world at war
chapters.d: Federation, Gallipoli and the Pacific War.
Nuclear tests, independence and reckoning.

reading: Stuart Macintyre, A Concise History of Australia (5th ed., 2020)
James Belich, Making Peoples: A History of the New Zealanders (1996)
Nicholas Thomas, Islanders: The Pacific in the Age of Empire (2010)
Henry Reynolds, The Other Side of the Frontier (1981)

arcs.title: Southeast Asia: Trade, Empire and Independence
arcs.summary: Southeast Asia sat on the sea lanes between India and China, and its ports grew rich on spices and trade. Europeans arrived with cannon: the Portuguese took Malacca in 1511, Spain the Philippines and the Dutch Java. By 1900 only Siam, which modernised and played Britain off against France, remained independent. Colonial rule brought plantations, forced cultivation and new nationalist movements. Japan's conquest in 1941-42 broke European authority, and after 1945 the region won independence through negotiation or war, from Indonesia to Vietnam. The Cold War brought mass killings in Indonesia, genocide in Cambodia and America's war in Vietnam. Since the 1970s, much of the region has become an economic powerhouse, though authoritarian rule and conflict persist in places like Myanmar.

chapters.d: European traders seize the sea lanes.
Plantations, wars and the one kingdom that stayed free.
Japan's conquest and the end of European rule.
War's end, growth and new crises.

reading: Anthony Reid, A History of Southeast Asia: Critical Crossroads (2015)
Milton Osborne, Southeast Asia: An Introductory History (13th ed., 2021)
Norman Owen (ed.), The Emergence of Modern Southeast Asia (2005)
Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983)

arcs.title: India, Pakistan and Bangladesh since 1947
arcs.summary: Independence in 1947 came with partition. In its first year, India and Pakistan fought over Kashmir, and Gandhi was assassinated by a Hindu nationalist. India adopted a democratic constitution in 1950 and held the world's largest elections; Pakistan swung between civilian and military rule. Pakistan's eastern wing broke away as Bangladesh in 1971 after a brutal war. Wars with China and Pakistan led to nuclear tests, and India's 1991 reforms opened a long economic boom. Afghanistan, on the region's western edge, became a battleground for the superpowers and then for America's war on terror.

chapters.d: Kashmir, Gandhi's death and a new republic.
China, Bangladesh and the bomb.
Bhopal, reform, nuclear tests and Afghanistan.

reading: Ramachandra Guha, India After Gandhi (2007)
Ian Talbot, Pakistan: A New History (2012)
Srinath Raghavan, 1971: A Global History of the Creation of Bangladesh (2013)
